Resolution depth improves held-out prediction beyond final-layer surprisal, entropy and the best single layer by 0.26 millinats per word (pooled p = 0.001), about a third of entropy's gain, and each model family gains, GPT-2 and Pythia through one corpus each. The net gain varies between corpora (random-effects mean 0.07, p = 0.37); against layer-shuffled depth, which adds as many coefficients, it is positive in seven of eight corpora (random-effects mean 0.23, p = 0.016), and untrained networks show no gain under the logit lens. Pooled over corpora, the effect holds with corrected word probabilities and beyond first-to-last-layer divergences, and a whole-trajectory functional regression adds no significant information beyond resolution depth.

Machine Learning.title: Power Setpoint Tracking for Large-Scale EV Charging: Transformer-Constrained Charging Policy Learning with Self-Tuning Constraint Prices
Machine Learning.summary: In power setpoint tracking (PST), an operator follows a purchased charging profile without overloading shared transformers or undercharging vehicles. PST is cast as a constrained Markov decision process that minimizes tracking error subject to overload and mean user-satisfaction constraints. Transformer-Constrained Charging Policy Learning (TC-CPL) extends soft actor-critic with proportional-integral Lagrange-multiplier updates from measured violations, a residual on the incumbent dispatcher that is warm-started from its demonstrations, and a transformer-aware encoder shared by all ports. It observes no departure times or states of charge. Simulations (five seeds, 100 paired days) compare it with the incumbent, Round-Robin. On a 600-port, 122-substation district, raw overload falls from 3.59 to 0.0017 kWh/day (overloaded seed-days from 77% to 0.4%), and absolute tracking error falls by 27%. Delivered energy rises by 16%, and satisfaction rises from 0.959 to 0.989. On a 42-kW transformer with household load, overload falls from 1.86 to 0.0014 kWh/day and satisfaction rises from 0.974 to 0.985, but absolute tracking error is 22% higher. Against hand-set fixed multipliers, self-tuning is statistically indistinguishable on the district. On the single transformer, it raises satisfaction by 0.011 at similar overload, but a short sweep found a better-serving fixed pair. The overload multipliers stay below their cap.
Machine Learning.comment: 13 pages, 7 figures, 6 tables. Submitted to IEEE Transactions on Transportation Electrification

Machine Learning.title: Survival of the fittest Cox model: Pivotal variable selection for time-to-event data
Machine Learning.summary: We revisit Cox's proportional hazards model to improve variable selection in survival analysis. A square-root transformation of the partial likelihood renders the selection of the regularization parameter asymptotically pivotal: the baseline hazard and the censoring rate cancel exactly, and the way censoring is spread over time only enters through a bounded correction of order $1/\log n$. Using martingale residuals, we compute this penalty level by Monte Carlo without reordering the design matrix. The resulting criterion borrows from information criteria such as BIC and from penalized regression methods such as the lasso, taking the best of both. On simulated and real data, our method substantially improves upon state-of-the-art approaches used daily.

Machine Learning.title: Agnostic Smoothed Online Regression with Adversarial Responses
Machine Learning.summary: We study smoothed online prediction with bounded adversarial responses. This widely studied framework bridges i.i.d. sampling and adversarial covariate selection through a smoothness parameter $\textsf{C}_{\textsf{cov}}$, which bounds conditional covariate densities relative to a fixed, unknown base measure. We propose Hedge-Cover, an information-theoretic algorithm that achieves sublinear regret $\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{\text{Pdim}(\mathcal{F}) \textsf{C}_{\textsf{cov}} T})$ for function classes with bounded pseudo-dimension. The algorithm aggregates a carefully constructed family of experts using Hedge, with a prior that links regret to the number of disagreements between a consistent selector and a target function. We bound this number by exploiting covariate smoothness. This answers an open problem posed in \cite{blanchard2025agnostic} on the minimax optimal adaptive regret of the smoothed online regression problem. We establish a matching lower bound for the class of linear predictors. The main intricacy of the lower bound lies in explicitly constructing a challenging sequential covariate distribution supported on mutually orthogonal hyperplanes. This construction may be of independent technical interest. Finally, we revisit the well-specified setting and quantify the effect of response noise. For conditionally $ν^2$-subGaussian responses, we extend the existing lower bound under realizable responses by showing that the minimax expected regret is $Ω((1\vee ν)\sqrt{(\textsf{C}_{\textsf{cov}}-1)dT})$ for a function class of VC dimension $d$. A corresponding upper bound for ERM matches this dependence on $ν$.

Machine Learning.title: Security of Deep Reinforcement Learning for Autonomous Driving: A Survey
Machine Learning.summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) enables agents to learn optimal behaviors through interaction with their environment and has been increasingly deployed in safety-critical applications, including autonomous driving. Despite its promise, RL is susceptible to attacks designed either to compromise policy learning or to induce erroneous decisions by trained agents. Although the literature on RL security has grown rapidly and several surveys exist, existing categorizations often fall short in guiding the selection of appropriate defenses for specific systems. In this work, we present a comprehensive survey of 86 recent studies on RL security, addressing these limitations by systematically categorizing attacks and defenses according to defined threat models and single- versus multi-agent settings. Furthermore, we examine the relevance and applicability of state-of-the-art attacks and defense mechanisms within the context of autonomous driving, providing insights to inform the design of robust RL systems.
Machine Learning.comment: IEEE Transactions on Intelligent Transportation Systems (T-ITS)

Machine Learning.title: Can Computation from Earlier Problems Help LLMs Solve New Ones?
Machine Learning.summary: Large language models often solve independent problems in the same conversation. Can computation from earlier problems help them solve new ones? Preliminary experiments show that retained history can raise or lower later-turn accuracy, even within the same domain. To trace this effect, we hold each problem fixed and vary its preceding history. The resulting changes in the model's internal states contain a recurring, problem-dependent component. To improve reasoning with retained history, we introduce STAIR (Stale-Token Attention for Inter-query Reuse). It captures attention keys and values from earlier response generation in a read-only bank. STAIR learns to reflect current query vectors to redirect attention over this bank during prompt processing. The backbone and stored entries remain fixed; only 12,288 parameters are trained. Across three Qwen models and four reasoning benchmarks, STAIR improves average later-turn accuracy by up to 11.67 percentage points over the unmodified model with history. The math-trained Qwen3.5-9B controller also improves code generation on HumanEval+ without further training.
Machine Learning.comment: 42 pages, 8 figures. v2: Expanded experiments and analyses; revised presentation

Machine Learning.title: Gradient Boosting with Kolmogorov-Arnold Units for Interpretable Regression beyond Pairwise Interactions
Machine Learning.summary: Interpretable models for tabular regression, such as the explainable boosting machine (EBM), restrict a prediction to main effects and pairwise interactions so that every part of it can be plotted. When the target depends on three or more inputs jointly, this restriction costs accuracy, and a black-box model with post hoc explanations becomes the usual fallback. Here we present MJBoost, a gradient boosting method whose weak learner is a single Kolmogorov-Arnold unit $g(\sum_p φ_p(x_p))$ with penalized spline inner and outer functions. Each unit is fitted in closed form by alternating penalized least squares, starting from principal Hessian directions of the residual, and categorical and missing inputs enter the units directly. Because a unit depends on each input only through one inner function, the fitted model has an exact functional ANOVA decomposition into main effects, pair effects and a higher-order remainder, which one-dimensional convolutions compute. On synthetic targets of interaction order three to six, the test error of MJBoost is up to 13 times lower than that of EBM, and its decomposition recovers the true variance share of every order to within 0.04. On the 35 regression tasks of the OpenML-CTR23 benchmark, it has a lower test RMSE than EBM on 21 tasks and a higher one on 2 (geometric-mean RMSE -29.1%). On these tasks the main and pair effects of the fitted model explain a median 0.992 of its variance, so the model reads as plots where the data allow, and the decomposition measures the higher-order part where they do not. With Newton steps the same algorithm classifies: on 32 binary tasks of OpenML-CC18 its test log-loss is on par with that of EBM, and on 11 multiclass tasks its mean log-loss is lower than that of EBM on 8 and than that of tuned LightGBM on 7.

Machine Learning.title: DTS: Delta-Based Tile Scoring for Efficient Long-Context Sparse Attention
Machine Learning.summary: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly need to process long documents and codebases, making long-context attention a major prefill bottleneck. Block sparse attention reduces computation by skipping unimportant blocks of the attention matrix, but scoring blocks accurately can itself be expensive. We propose Delta-Based Tile Scoring (DTS), a training-free, content-adaptive tile scoring method for sparse block attention. DTS selects query and key anchors according to local vector changes, using fewer representatives in redundant regions while retaining more detail in heterogeneous regions. To accelerate anchor selection, parallel delta packing partitions the query and key sequences into tile-aligned chunks and performs bounded local scans over these chunks concurrently. The selected tiles are then computed using the original query, key, and value vectors. On LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct, DTS keeps average RULER and LongBench scores within 0.10 percentage points of full attention, with RULER evaluated up to 128K tokens. At 128K tokens, DTS reduces measured scoring-pipeline latency by 38% compared with XAttention. On four NVIDIA H100 GPUs, it achieves a 3.3$\times$ prefill speedup over a PyTorch full-attention baseline using FlashAttention-2 at 512K tokens.
Machine Learning.comment: 7 pages, 4 figures. Accepted at DATE 2027. Emre Uğur and Jiawen Qi contributed equally

Machine Learning.title: Hellinger Decision Trees for Density Ratio Estimation: Finite-Sample Guarantees
Machine Learning.summary: Density ratios play a central role in two-sample comparison, distribution-shift adaptation, and generative-model evaluation. However, estimating a density ratio through separate estimation of the underlying densities can be unnecessarily challenging. In this paper, we develop a direct approach to the log density ratio estimation by minimizing a balanced Hellinger risk over additive ensembles of axis-aligned decision trees, trained using Newton boosting. We establish finite-sample guarantees for the estimator produced by the algorithm and derive an explicit convergence rate. Under suitable tail and Hölder smoothness conditions, together with an additional assumption on the progress made at each boosting iteration, our rate matches, up to logarithmic factors, the classical minimax-optimal $ \mathscr{L}^{2} $ rate for function estimation. A key technical contribution is an optimization analysis that exploits the special exponential structure of the Hellinger risk. In particular, we show that the decrease in the second-order Taylor approximation (which is computable) of the empirical risk controls the actual decrease in that risk, yielding a direct optimization guarantee for the boosting algorithm. This allows us to establish statistical convergence guarantees for the algorithm's output without relying on an idealized empirical-risk minimizer. Experiments on synthetic data corroborate the predicted convergence behavior, while experiments on public datasets demonstrate the practical effectiveness of the proposed estimator.

Machine Learning.title: ArrivalBench: Agent-Generated Data Pipelines Are Correct Once and Wrong Under Time
Machine Learning.summary: Benchmarks for agent-generated data work grade a pipeline by running it once against a fixed snapshot. ArrivalBench instead re-executes the pipeline an agent leaves behind under adversarial but replayable delivery schedules (late, duplicated, out-of-order and retried records) and requires its final state to equal a batch recomputation of the complete log. Because the oracle recomputes rather than classifies, a wrong table and a crash are distinct verdicts: a crash is visible to monitoring a team already runs, and a wrong table is not. On 40 tasks we built, our reimplementation of single-execution grading certifies 86-100% of the pipelines eleven models produce; re-executing the same artifacts finds 7.0-79.2% of the certified ones silently wrong. The gap is not produced by the repair loop: within the same model and task, pipelines repaired against the snapshot test fail replay about as often as those that passed it first time. In every model, idempotency hazards fail more often than ordering hazards. Separating a wrong answer from a crash also changes how interventions read: a hazard warning cuts one model's silent failure from 48.2% to 10.5% while raising its crash rate from 9.0% to 37.0%, so all-in failure moves only from 51.0% to 44.0%. All eleven arms were independently re-run, and rates moved by at most 5.9 points.
Machine Learning.comment: Accepted as a poster at the NeurIPS 2026 Workshop "Who Verifies the Agents?". 20 pages

Machine Learning.title: TabPFN: One Model to Rule Them All?
Machine Learning.summary: Hollmann et al. (Nature 637 (2025) 319-326) recently introduced TabPFN, a transformer-based deep learning model for regression and classification on tabular data, which they claim "outperforms all previous methods on datasets with up to 10,000 samples by a wide margin, using substantially less training time." Furthermore, they have called TabPFN a "foundation model" for tabular data, as it can support "data generation, density estimation, learning reusable embeddings and fine-tuning". In this paper, we provide a tailored explanation of how TabPFN works for a statistics audience, by emphasizing its interpretation as approximate Bayesian inference. We then explore the significance of TabPFN to the field of statistics: We show that an out-of-the-box application of TabPFN can sometimes outperform specialized state-of-the-art methods for semi-supervised parameter estimation, prediction under covariate shift, and heterogeneous treatment effect estimation. As a partial explanation for the predictive effectiveness of TabPFN, we show that it can simultaneously adapt to both nonparametric structure and parametric structure, for instance, sometimes outperforming LASSO even when assumptions are correctly specified. All experiments can be reproduced using the code provided at https://github.com/qinglong-tian/tabpfn_study (https://github.com/qinglong-tian/tabpfn_study).

Machine Learning.title: Optimizer-dependent training dynamics converge to the same one-third optimal data scaling
Machine Learning.summary: Neural scaling, in which loss falls as a power law with training, is central to large language models, and one recent proposal is that a $1/3$ exponent emerges from learning peaked distributions. That account describes SGD, but models in practice are trained with adaptive optimizers. Here we separate two exponents the $1/3$ account does not distinguish: how fast the loss falls with training steps along a single run, and how fast the optimally tuned loss falls with dataset size $D$. We show that the first, a dynamic exponent, is optimizer-specific while the second, an optimal data exponent, converges to $1/3$ across optimizers. In an online teacher-student model we decompose the loss into norm growth (radial) and alignment toward the teacher direction (tangential), each decaying as a power law with dynamic exponents $α_{r}$ and $α_{t}$. Under SGD, both are close to $1/3$, so the data exponent is also $1/3$ across different learning rates. Under Adam the two separate: $α_{r} \simeq 0.48$ but $α_{t} \simeq 0.08$. Since the total loss is minimized when these two parts are balanced, the optimal learning rate is optimizer-dependent: $D$-independent for SGD but falls with $D$ for Adam. Yet tuned to that optimum, the loss returns to $D^{-1/3}$ for both. A stochastic-dynamics analysis explains why: the optimizers can trade decay speed between the two channels, but they all fall on a single dynamic exponent relation, $2α_{r}+ α_{t} = 1$, which fixes the optimal data exponent at $1/3$. Across seven optimizers, including Muon, the measured exponents are consistent with this relation, and the optimal-loss envelopes agree with $D^{-1/3}$ across them. The optimizer sets how fast a model learns per step; tuned optimally, it changes the prefactor but not the rate at which loss falls per sample.

Machine Learning.title: Best-of-Depth: Learning Exploratory Dynamics in Looped Transformers
Machine Learning.summary: Looped Transformers extend inference-time computation through repeated latent-state updates, but final-depth training does not directly encourage useful intermediate alternatives. We introduce Best-of-Depth (BoD), which trains a recurrent trajectory as a candidate set by minimizing prediction loss across depths. Different valid targets can be matched at different depths without architectural changes or depth-specific labels. An exact-match analysis connects this objective to solution coverage. On N-Queens completion and graph coloring, BoD improves coverage over final-depth and intermediate-supervision objectives. N-Queens coverage reaches 91.03%, versus 45.75% for final-depth training. Further experiments show discovery beyond the training depth and recovery of solutions withheld from teacher pools on familiar inputs. Fine-tuning a pretrained looped language model with BoD yields higher pooled code-generation success than final-depth training when programs are generated separately at evaluated fixed depths. These results support training recurrent computation for solution discovery along its trajectory.

Machine Learning.title: A Lightweight Hybrid Approach for Milling Force Reconstruction from Internal Machine Signals
Machine Learning.summary: Data-driven monitoring based on milling force can enable advanced manufacturing services including process optimization and condition monitoring. However, industrial implementation is often hindered by costly and intrusive hardware and large training data requirements. This paper therefore presents a hybrid approach using machine-internal signals and machining metadata to enable force-based monitoring on brownfield machines without additional sensors. Commonly available machine signals have relatively low sampling rates and cannot directly represent high-frequency milling-force variations, especially at higher spindle speeds. Instead of learning the complete force signal, which would increase model complexity, data requirements, and overfitting risk, a supervised machine-learning model predicts only the average milling force from selected machine-signal features and machining parameters. This low-frequency estimation parameterizes a static milling force model that reconstructs the force behavior over one spindle revolution. Although the static model does not reproduce all dynamic effects, it captures the force distribution, load levels, and angular regions of highest tool engagement. The approach is evaluated on one milling machine across varying process parameters, engagement conditions, cutting tools, and two workpiece materials. Dynamometer measurements are required only for development and validation. Ridge regression achieves an $R^2$ of $0.984$ and $0.991$ for average-force prediction on the test data ($\bar{F}_x$ and $\bar{F}_y$). The reconstructed force behavior over one spindle revolution achieves an $R^2$ of $0.962$ and $0.982$ ($F_x$ and $F_y$) compared with the reconstruction based on measured force features. The method provides a cost and computationally efficient basis for process monitoring, tool condition assessment, and process optimization on existing machines.

Cryptography and Security.title: SoK: Assessing the Evolution of LLM Capability in Software Vulnerability Research
Cryptography and Security.summary: LLM-based agents are becoming increasingly capable at discovering, validating and patching vulnerabilities in real software, and vendors and researchers report that this is already changing how vulnerabilities are found and fixed. These claims, however, are scattered across papers, vendor reports and disclosures and are rarely comparable. We introduce a framework that rates these capabilities on an autonomy scale modeled on the levels of driving automation, and qualifies each claim by its correctness, its availability and the strength of its evidence. We use this framework to systematize the published evidence on LLM capability in vulnerability research. We find that agents discovered, validated, and patched vulnerabilities in real-world software without human intervention before the restricted frontier models of 2026, and that open-weight models subsequently attained comparable autonomy for discovery and validation. We then measure the consequences of evolving LLM security capabilities in a decade of public vulnerability records, advisories and exploitation data. In 2026 the number of disclosed vulnerabilities more than doubled, with an increasing share rated critical or high, and severe bugs that had survived a decade or more in widely used code were reported several times more often than before. Yet the time between the stages of a vulnerability's life, from report to fix and from disclosure to attack, has not shifted noticeably so far. We grade the mitigations proposed in the literature with an explicit rubric and draw guidance for each group of stakeholders from the best-supported ones.

Cryptography and Security.title: Classical Oracle Separation of QMA from the QCMA Hierarchy and Quantum Cryptography Even When P = QCMA
Cryptography and Security.summary:
Remark: This work is in submission at STOC'27 and thus the full manuscript has been publicly posted on the conference website since November 3rd, 2026.
  Inspired by the Codeword-Hash Structure problem recently introduced by Cakan (arXiV, 2026) to separate $\mathsf{QMA}$ from $\mathsf{QCIP}$, we introduce a new problem called Codeword-Hash pairs in Noise ($\mathsf{CHN}$) and prove that, in the query complexity model, it is in $\mathsf{QMA}$ but hard for the $\mathsf{QCMA}$ hierarchy $\mathsf{QCMAH} = \bigcup_{d\geq1}\mathsf{QCMA}^{\mathsf{QCMA}^{\cdots^{\mathsf{QCMA}}}}$, the classical-witness quantum-verifier analogue of $\mathsf{PH}=\bigcup_{d\ge1}\mathsf{NP}^{\mathsf{NP}^{\cdots^{\mathsf{NP}}}}$.
  Using this problem, we show that there exists a classical oracle ${O}$ such that $\mathsf{P}^{O}=\mathsf{BQP}^{O}=\mathsf{QCMA}^{O} =\mathsf{QCMAH}^{O} \subset \mathsf{QMA}^{O} \text{ but } \mathsf{QMA}^{O}\not\subseteq\mathsf{QCMAH}^{O},$ thus showing that quantum state or quantum proof advantage could exist even if classical computers can efficiently solve any problem that can be quantumly verified with a classical proof.
  Further, using our problem, we show that various quantum cryptographic primitives can exist even when $\mathsf{P} = \mathsf{QCMA}$ and thus neither quantum-computable one-way functions nor (verifiable) quantum computational advantage exist. In particular, relative to a classical oracle ${O}$ with $\mathsf{P}^{O}=\mathsf{BQP}^{O}=\mathsf{QCMA}^{O}=\mathsf{QCMAH}^{O}$, there exist pseudorandom states with classical keys and public-key encryption with copy-protected quantum decryption keys and classical public keys and ciphertexts, among other primitives, answering an open question of Kretschmer, Qian, and Tal (STOC 2025).

Cryptography and Security.title: Text-Aware, Vision-Blind: How Multimodal Image Editing Systems Handle Unsafe Inputs
Cryptography and Security.summary: Multimodal image generation systems have made rapid progress and increasingly emphasize content safety. However, their safety mechanisms tend to rely on a single modality and lack joint consideration of both visual content and text prompts, particularly in instruction-guided image editing, where the uploaded image may itself carry risk. We thus introduce EditSafetyBench, a benchmark that measures system-level safety awareness of advanced image editing systems, containing 5,940 image-instruction pairs, covering safe and unsafe images across 11 risk categories and three edit intents. We then probe the benchmark dataset on four systems, including Gemini, GPT, Qwen API, and Qwen Local. Based on our evaluation, we observe a systematic text-vision safety mismatch: Gemini and GPT refuse 87.1\% and 81.6\% cases containing unsafe-intent editing prompts, while only refusing 24.2\% and 22.4\% cases with both unsafe images and neutral instructions. At the category level, most risks are considered inconsistently by different systems, e.g., GPT allows 70.4\% editing attempts of unsafe political content while Gemini only allows 34.8\%. Notably, sexual content shows the strongest visual sensitivity, likely benefiting from mature NSFW identification works. Our findings highlight the need for safety guardrails that jointly reason over both visual and textual modalities in image editing systems.

Cryptography and Security.title: GEOHunter: Mapping a Generative Engine Optimization Network in the Wild
Cryptography and Security.summary: Generative engines synthesize retrieved web pages into answers, recommendations, and rankings. Generative engine optimization (GEO) services sell visibility in these answers by publishing promotional articles on user-generated-content (UGC) platforms for paying clients. Such promotion raises concerns in medical and financial domains, where misleading advice can cause harm. To study the severity of this problem, we measure one such paid-content operation across three major Chinese UGC platforms, uncovering 1,985 accounts associated with the network comprising 466,357 inferred promotional placements. We find that the network promotes products across diverse categories through a growing pool of accounts, conducting coordinated campaigns spanning months across multiple platforms while evolving its listicle content over time. Across nine generative engines from both the US and China, we find that 4.5% to 20% of retrievable cited pages are attributable to the network, depending on how strictly attribution is drawn. On eight of these engines, its clients are named in 52% of answers, against 68% for category leaders. Our work demonstrates the effectiveness of UGC GEO placement at influencing generative engine outcomes, and reveals content-level defenses as insufficient against coordinated UGC placements, where account-level and platform-level signals are necessary for proper defense.

Cryptography and Security.title: Replication of Agentic Security Events: Audit and Investigation (ROGUE-AI)
Cryptography and Security.summary: Agents based on large language models (LLMs) can now delete files and send payments on behalf of their users. News media reports routinely describe failures of these agents (e.g., Replit's coding agent deleting a production database), but a report often only says what went wrong and rarely (in)validates the incident or finds its root cause. Incident catalogs collect these reports, and benchmarks record whether agents fail, but neither replicates an incident nor tests the cause its report might identify. In this paper, we present ROGUE-AI (Replication of Agentic Security Events: Audit and Investigation), a multi-agent framework that closes the above gap and rebuilds each reported incident offline together with a matched control that lacks only the blamed cause, and runs agents on both. Our results suggest that ROGUE-AI is able to reproduce the reported harm in 89% of its 108 attempted replications. Agents built on five current GPT, Claude, Gemini and DeepSeek models made the reported mistake in 18% to 33% of runs, against at most 1% without the blamed cause. Of the 72 incidents with real-world harm, 62 had no underlying attacker, and in these, agents did what their task asked for but missed an ordinary hazard, such as a database shared with the live site. Replications without an attacker caused more harm than replications of prompt injection for all five models. Defenses against prompt injection look for injected instructions, but these replications contain none. Further, a warning after each tool output that names the hazard and its consequence lowered harm for all five models, whereas a note of the same length that does not mention the hazard left most of the harm in place. Built from real incidents, the ROGUE-AI replications form a reusable audit framework that vendors can rerun before each new release.
Cryptography and Security.comment: 21 pages, 5 figures, 13 tables. Project page: https://rogue-ai.surge.sh

Cryptography and Security.title: No Country for Old Privacy: The Evolving Challenges of Anonymity in Bitcoin
Cryptography and Security.summary: We present a longitudinal measurement study on the adoption of detectable, second-generation anonymisation protocols in the Bitcoin network, including CoinJoin, CoinSwap, CoinShuffle and Stealth Addresses. By implementing and refining a suite of heuristic filters, we identify over 5 million candidate CoinJoin and 23.3 million candidate CoinSwap transactions. Notably, the use of CoinShuffle was unexpectedly found to be closely aligned with the operation of coordinator-based CoinJoin services such as Wasabi and Whirlpool. Our analysis reveals consistently low adoption rates, with these protocols typically constituting less than 1% of network transactions, and a sharp decline in detectable usage following key regulatory events. Furthermore, we find no evidence of standardised Stealth Address adoption, indicating a failure to converge on a common privacy standard. This study provides a comprehensive picture of a niche ecosystem whose on-chain visibility has been largely suppressed, strongly suggesting the migration of privacy-seeking users to less transparent and less detectable methods.
Cryptography and Security.comment: 9 pages, 7 figures, Accepted to the 2nd IEEE International Conference on Distributed Ledger Technologies (ICDLT 2026)

Cryptography and Security.title: Backtracking Agent Applications Security Incidents
Cryptography and Security.summary: Agent applications are increasingly deployed, yet agent-specific attacks pose real threats to them. Upon a security incident, organizations backtrack to identify the CEP (compromise entry point), remediate the damage, and prevent its recurrence. The main artifacts available for backtracking are trajectory logs, which record agent functionalities, and source code; app(lication)-specific function call logs are often fairly limited. However, trajectory logs are at the agent functionality abstraction layer, while the CEP candidates are function calls at the app code execution layer. Due to this semantic gap, the analyst needs to manually inspect the relevant code for each CEP candidate to infer its corresponding agent functionality. In this work, we present Origin, a backtracking tool for the analyst to submit a small number of queries to identify CEPs that existing tools cannot provide. Our approach poses two challenges: (1) define the intermediate abstraction that captures the mapping relationships between the two semantic layers; (2) determine the region-to-variable mapping for constructing the cross-layer graph defined in the intermediate abstraction. Each region is a specific group of agent functionalities. Origin addresses the challenges by (1) the cross-layer dependency graph (CLDG) that connects region-inferred functions at the semantic level to the variables in the low-level taint propagation subgraph, plus the associated query language, and (2) the region inference algorithm. Case studies on five popular agent applications across eight attack incidents show that an analyst using Origin correctly identifies all the CEPs.
Cryptography and Security.comment: 33 pages (12 pages of main text, 3 pages of references, 18 pages of appendices), 9 figures, 12 tables

Cryptography and Security.title: Visual Attribution Limits and Graded Provenance Auditing in Commercial Video-Generation APIs
Cryptography and Security.summary: Commercial video-generation APIs bill by model and tier, while intermediaries could substitute cheaper models, lower tiers, or cached clips. What can a delivered file establish about its origin? We combine measurements of passive attribution and cryptographic provenance into a graded audit. We test attribution probes and zero-shot detectors under re-encoding, downscaling, and frame-rate changes, and survey C2PA and GB 45438 metadata across 19 commercial endpoints. Only authenticated provenance supports accusations: tier contradictions or duplicate signed instances under fresh-generation contracts, excluding retries and idempotent returns. Unverifiable signed-endpoint deliveries trigger original-file demands under pass-through clauses; archive-reuse and delivery-parameter screens support review only. Six-model container and bitstream accuracy falls from 83.9% on raw files to 45.3% after uniform re-encoding, using different feature sets. Subsampling real references from 24 to 3 fps raises pooled D3 AUROC from 0.845 to 0.988. Only BytePlus authenticates tier claims under our pinned policy, including 187/187 audited deliveries across three Seedance tiers; tested remuxing and re-encoding leave processed Seedance files unverifiable. The audit identifies authenticated contradictions in 100/100 raw 720p signed tier-swap cases, with zero observed false flags on the tested honest pools.

Cryptography and Security.title: ROPE: Routed Origin Policy Enforcement against Indirect Prompt Injection
Cryptography and Security.summary: Tool-using LLM agents execute consequential operations on behalf of users. Because the LLM driving an agent processes trusted user instructions and untrusted content in the same context, agents are vulnerable to indirect prompt injection attacks that induce unintended actions by mixing malicious instructions into benign data. Defenses based on prompting or content detection are easily evaded by paraphrasing attacks, while system-level defenses that constrain tool calls using inferred user intent, or restrict which sources can supply values to sensitive tools, greatly compromise utility. We present ROPE (Routed Origin Policy Enforcement), a defense that greatly improves the utility-security tradeoff by leveraging system roots of trust to create and enforce per-task policies on sensitive tool parameters. Our key insight is that authentication and integrity protection provide a basis for identifying the source of content independently of instructions embedded in it. Before a task unfolds, an LLM router reads only trusted task input to set a provenance rule for each sensitive tool parameter, accounting for the nature of the task and the values and sources the user specified. As the agent works, an origin labeler records where each piece of content came from, using the user's request, platform metadata, and protected record fields as trust anchors. Before any sensitive tool executes, a deterministic verifier requires each of its origin-guarded values to match a value in a source its rule accepts. We show that ROPE provably guarantees parameter value provenance to sensitive tool calls and is immune to paraphrasing attacks. Against eleven defenses on AgentDojo and AgentDyn under static, adaptive, and long-horizon attacks, ROPE exhibits near-perfect security while compromising far less utility than the best baseline defenses. Code and data are available at https://github.com/xhOwenMa/ROPE.

Cryptography and Security.title: SST-Guard: Detecting and Characterizing Server-Side Google Analytics in the Wild
Cryptography and Security.summary: As web browsers increasingly implement anti-tracking features, the web tracking ecosystem has been shifting from the client-side to the server-side. Instead of sending requests directly to the tracker's endpoint, server-side tracking (SST) sends tracking requests to publisher-controlled or intermediary endpoints that then forward the information to trackers from the server-side. As a result, client-side tracking protections are becoming fragile because direct client-to-tracker requests may no longer be observed. In this paper, we investigate the server-side Google Analytics (sGA), the most widely deployed third-party tracking service on the web today. We present SST-GUARD, a multi-modal browser-based approach for detecting sGA. The key insight behind SST-GUARD is that common sGA deployments change the standard Google Analytics endpoints, but still leave semantic artifacts of data collection by Google Analytics in the browser, including identifiers, event metadata, cookies, and JavaScript state. SST-GUARD detects these artifacts using value-templates, which use regular expressions to match semantic value patterns across multiple modalities: network requests, cookies, and the window object, providing robustness against obfuscation of one modality. We validate SST-GUARD on Tranco top-10k websites, detecting 4.0% (401) sGA domains with over 93.0% accuracy across three modalities, with network request classifier demonstrating the highest accuracy (99.8%). Additionally, SST-GUARD identifies atleast 43.2% more websites that integrate sGA as compared to prior approaches. Deploying SST-GUARD at scale, we detect sGA on 6,314 of Tranco top-150K websites. Our analysis shows that many sGA deployments use first-party subdomains, direct A/AAAA records, custom paths, or encoded payloads that circumvent existing defenses. We reported our findings to the authors of EasyPrivacy, who have integrated them.

Cryptography and Security.title: ScenarioForge: Resource-Grounded Generation and Execution Validation of Cyber Exercises
Cryptography and Security.summary: Cyber-range and capture-the-flag scenario construction remains labor-intensive because authors must coordinate infrastructure, vulnerable services, attack paths, artifacts, and success conditions. LLMs can propose detailed exercises, but plausible descriptions do not guarantee deployable software or verifiable objectives. We present ScenarioForge, which turns high-level requirements into resource-grounded topologies, services, traffic, segmentation, and challenge chains, then instantiates and validates them in the Common Open Research Emulator (CORE). The ScenarioForge Execution Dataset contains 226 materialized scenarios covering 294 Vulhub images and all 85 custom-built challenge-resource generators developed with our AI-assisted scaffolding. All 226 passed construction, preview, sequencing, deployment, strict runtime validation, and live artifact checks; their 867 steps, each an individually verifiable challenge objective, comprise 457 vulnerability-backed and 410 generated-resource-backed instances. In a separate 50-prompt matched benchmark, ScenarioForge+Qwen3.8 and ScenarioForge+GPT5.6 each achieved 50/50 (100%) topology/build success and 160/160 intent fields; direct frontier generation reached 41/50 builds and 147/160 fields only with the full cumulative scaffold: structure, vocabulary, policy, and container-image guidance. The test still omitted ScenarioForge's downstream challenge-resource generation, dependency/flag sequencing, deployment, and live validation. The artifacts support operationally rich, reproducible exercises for training and evaluation.

Cryptography and Security.title: Privacy-Utility Tradeoffs with Quantum Local Differential Privacy
Cryptography and Security.summary: When sensitive information is encoded in data, it is important to ensure the privacy of information when attempting to learn useful information from the data. There is a natural tradeoff whereby increasing privacy requirements may decrease the utility of a learning protocol. In the quantum setting of differential privacy, such tradeoffs between privacy and utility have so far remained largely unexplored. In this work, we study optimal privacy-utility tradeoffs for both generic and application-specific utility metrics when privacy is quantified by $(\varepsilon,δ)$-quantum local differential privacy. In the generic setting, we focus on optimizing fidelity and trace distance between the original state and the privatized state. We show that the depolarizing mechanism achieves the optimal utility for given privacy requirements. We then study the specific application of learning the expectation of an observable with respect to an input state when only given access to privatized states. We derive a lower bound on the number of samples of privatized data required to achieve a fixed accuracy guarantee with high probability. To prove this result, we employ existing lower bounds on private quantum hypothesis testing, thus showcasing the first operational use of them. We also devise private mechanisms that achieve optimal sample complexity with respect to the privacy parameters and accuracy parameters, demonstrating that utility can be significantly improved for specific tasks in contrast to the generic setting. In addition, we show that the number of samples required to privately learn observable expectation values scales as $Θ((\varepsilon β)^{-2})$, where $\varepsilon \in (0,1)$ is the privacy parameter and $β$ is the accuracy tolerance. We conclude by initiating the study of private classical shadows, which promise useful applications for private learning tasks.
Cryptography and Security.comment: v2:accepted to Quantum Science and Technology, November 2026, 25pages; v1:23 pages, 2 figures

Cryptography and Security.title: When Suspicion Adds Up: A Stochastic Framework for Optimizing Honeypot-Based Insider-Threat Detection
Cryptography and Security.summary: Insider threats pose security risks when employees or other trusted users misuse their access to organizational systems. Detecting these threats is difficult because harmful activity can resemble routine behavior. Honeypots, or decoy resources monitored for suspicious interactions, can provide evidence of potentially malicious activity. We develop a decision framework that models evidence accumulation through honeypot interactions using a continuous-time Markov chain and jointly selects honeypot counts and monitoring horizons to minimize expected losses from malicious activity and false detections. For thresholds of two and three interactions, we derive closed-form true- and false-detection probabilities and expected detection times conditional on detection within the monitoring horizon. We characterize boundary cases and establish stochastic-ordering results. Our numerical results highlight the value of the proposed framework across different settings.

Cryptography and Security.title: DailySafe: Benchmarking Dynamic Safety Awareness in Everyday Multi-Turn Multimodal Interactions
Cryptography and Security.summary: As multimodal large language models (MLLMs) become increasingly integrated into everyday life, their ability to provide safe and reliable assistance in realistic daily activities remains insufficiently explored. Existing safety benchmarks primarily focus on isolated harmful requests or adversarial scenarios, overlooking the safety risks that may arise as ordinary tasks unfold. In practice, users pursue legitimate goals through multi-turn, multimodal interactions, where seemingly benign requests may become safety-critical when considered alongside earlier actions and visual observations. This calls for Dynamic Safety Awareness, the ability to track evolving task conditions, recognize implicit contextual risks, and provide safe and helpful assistance. To systematically evaluate this capability, we introduce DailySafe, a benchmark comprising 195 naturalistic multi-turn, multi-image interactions across 10 everyday domains and 42 task categories. Grounded in authentic user dialogue topics and documented safety knowledge, DailySafe captures realistic scenarios where safety-critical evidence is progressively revealed across conversational turns and visual observations. Using case-specific safety annotations, DailySafe assesses whether MLLMs can recognize and appropriately address evolving risks while supporting users' legitimate goals, bringing multimodal safety evaluation closer to real-world everyday AI assistance. DailySafe is publicly available at: https://github.com/XuankunRong/DailySafe.

Cryptography and Security.title: Evaluating LIM Trading Agents: A Critical Review of Backtesting Validity and Reporting Practices
Cryptography and Security.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in investment research, and many studies report promising historical returns. However, such results are only credible if researchers can demonstrate that the model used only information available at the time, account for how strategies and configurations were selected, and explain how reported returns were generated. We identify six common threats to validity in LLM investment evaluations and apply them to 18 published studies. Across 108 assessments, we find substantial gaps in reporting. No paper fully addresses information timing, model-memory exposure, universe selection, trading costs, or configuration-selection bias. Only four studies provide minimum evidence that results hold across multiple market periods. Our analysis reveals that commonly used safeguards often address different problems than researchers assume. For example, using dated inputs does not guarantee that a pretrained model lacked knowledge of future events, and repeated experimental runs do not correct for strategy-selection bias. We therefore propose an evaluation protocol for future LLM investment research. Rather than judging whether LLMs can generate profits, our study examines whether existing evidence is sufficient to support such claims. We conclude that current reporting practices are generally insufficient for that purpose.
Cryptography and Security.comment: Withdrawn by the submitter because not all co-authors agreed to the posting of this preprint

Cryptography and Security.title: Why Trust Your Agent? Empirical Security Gains from TRiSM-Guided Agentic Workflows in Healthcare
Cryptography and Security.summary: Agent-based AI has enabled the automation of tasks by exposing application tools and resources to large language models (LLMs). However, to improve scope and accuracy, agents are often given access rights that exceed those of ordinary users, introducing significant security risks and potential regulatory breaches. This paper applies the AI Trust, Risk, and Security Management (TRiSM) framework to a medical report-generation application to demonstrate how an insecure baseline workflow can be transformed into a security-conscious agentic workflow. Both designs were evaluated with five LLMs (Claude Haiku 4.5, GPT-4.1-nano, GPT-4.1-mini, GPT-5.4-mini and Gemini 2.5 Flash) across 800 report generations and 500 attack trials covering RAG poisoning, data-field injection and client-side network injection. The redesign reduced attack success from 31% to 10% for RAG poisoning and from 42% to 25% for data-field injection (McNemar p < 0.001 for both), removed network injection by construction, and raised report accuracy from 72.5% to 86.5%. In an exploratory post-hoc grouping by attack goal, success against attacks aimed outside the report task, such as data disclosure and tool abuse, fell from 21.7% to 2.5% and no patient record was disclosed under the redesign. Attacks altering the reported Covid-19 diagnosis remained effective, accounting for 32 of the 35 successful attacks against the redesign. Least-privilege architecture limits what an injection can reach, but not whether a model follows injected content within its task, so clinical outputs need verification independent of the LLM. No model resisted all three attack vectors, so model selection cannot substitute for secure workflow design.
Cryptography and Security.comment: 19 pages, 6 figures, 8 tables. v2: Substantially revised. Adds threat model and attack-goal analysis; corrects Gemini 2.5 Flash cost figures (output-token price); revises statistical analysis and limitations

Cryptography and Security.title: Products of Distinguisher Hulls
Cryptography and Security.summary: The distinguisher hull of two distributions is the convex hull of the pairs of acceptance probabilities of tests in a specified class. We study its behavior under independent products for size-bounded Boolean circuits. We derive a geometric consequence of Dwork and Tankala's supersimulator theorem (FOCS 2026), giving a substantially different proof of approximate product containment for distinguisher hulls. In particular, our construction uses nonadaptive sampling in place of adaptive score corrections.

Cryptography and Security.title: Multidimensional Reconciliation in Continuous-Variable QKD: Review, Coding Schemes, and Open-Source Simulation
Cryptography and Security.summary: Continuous-variable quantum key distribution (CV-QKD) requires highly efficient reconciliation techniques to operate at low signal-to-noise ratios and long distances. Multidimensional reconciliation addresses this challenge by transforming the physical Gaussian quantum channel into a virtual binary-input additive white Gaussian noise (BIAWGN) channel, enabling the use of modern errorcorrecting codes. In this work, we review the principles of multidimensional reconciliation, with a particular focus on high-dimensional constructions beyond the algebraic dimensions 1, 2, 4, 8. We describe the construction of the virtual channel, discuss practical coding schemes for reverse reconciliation, and analyse their integration with linear error-correcting codes. We also present an opensource simulation framework, HDirac, implementing multidimensional reconciliation for arbitrary dimensions, and use it to evaluate state-of-the-art LDPC codes. The results highlight key trade-offs between dimension, reconciliation efficiency, and frame error rate, providing practical guidance for CV-QKD system design.
Cryptography and Security.comment: 15 pages, 8 figures. Link to the open-source project: https://github.com/aff3ct/HDirac

Cryptography and Security.title: SCARVA: Interpretable Agentic Reasoning in Software Supply-Chain Analysis
Cryptography and Security.summary:
Complex applications may inherit security vulnerabilities from their dependencies, though a vulnerable dependency does not necessarily endanger the application. Existing tools flag dependencies associated with public vulnerabilities, and more advanced ones analyze the call graph to assess whether the vulnerable code is reachable. However, these approaches are limited to specific programming languages and ecosystems. LLM agents are promising candidates for this task, yet they hallucinate, take shortcuts, and reward hack. As these behaviors are opaque, the agents' conclusions may not be trusted.
  We present SCARVA a framework designed to produce interpretable reports. SCARVA combines advanced agent reasoning with an evidence-collection methodology that assesses the agent's analysis and improves its trustworthiness. Specifically, the ANALYST performs a software security assessment while SCARVA records every tool call, file access, and web request. Then, one or more independent JUDGE agents inspect the ANALYST's result and produce an evidence-backed report. We evaluate SCARVA on 54 manually curated cases, balanced across exploitable, non-exploitable, and vulnerability-free projects, using both open-weight and frontier models. The best ANALYST model, Qwen 3.8, reaches 82% balanced accuracy and surpasses the evaluated proprietary models. Human annotation validates the JUDGE findings: Claude Opus 5.5 performs best, agreeing with annotators in 94% of claim checks. Finally, we discuss the most common failure modes of agents on supply-chain vulnerability assessment.

Cryptography and Security.title: ChronoPatch: Black-Box Energy-Latency Attacks on Vision-Language Models
Cryptography and Security.summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) are increasingly deployed as generative inference services, where autoregressive decoding makes response length a key determinant of latency and computational cost. This creates an availability risk: adversarial visual inputs can prolong generation and increase serving overhead. Existing energy-latency attacks typically rely on gradients, logits, or token-level feedback, leaving open whether such risks persist when an attacker observes only the final response. We present ChronoPatch, a black-box attack that induces prolonged VLM generation requiring only the final response. It discovers visual delay anchors through response-length-guided evolutionary search, then minimizes perturbation magnitude through subspace-calibrated decision-based optimization. Across four open-source VLMs, ChronoPatch increases inference latency by 47.86%--293.34% and GPU energy consumption by 41.44%--249.70% under a 5% spatial budget. It also induces more repetitive outputs, as reflected by increased n-gram repetition ratios. On three commercial VLM APIs, ChronoPatch increases response length by 37.6%--81.5% and client-observed latency by 1.82x--2.29x under query budgets of 500 per API. These results reveal a generation-based availability risk that persists under final-response-only access and motivate generation-aware safeguards for deployed generative AI services.

Cryptography and Security.title: Causal Overtaking in Fair Transaction Ordering
Cryptography and Security.summary: Fair transaction ordering protocols aim to mitigate front-running using replica-local arrival orders, but prior work often assumes a single submission origin for each responsive transaction. We identify causal overtaking, in which corrupted replicas observe a target and submit identical signed copies of a responsive transaction through multiple client entries. The copies' first arrivals at different replicas can collectively provide ordering support that no individual path achieves, allowing the response to execute before its target. We formalize a class of receipt-order protocols, including Themis, characterize the timing and network conditions under which the attack is feasible, and show that delayed gossip does not rule it out. We further prove that, under our network model, histories requiring opposite transaction orders can produce identical receipt evidence. Thus, receipt-only mechanisms cannot always preserve earlier-submission priority while preventing responsive overtaking. We propose a mitigation and analyze its assumptions and limitations. Finally, we evaluate the attack and mitigation on Themis through simulations driven by AWS and WonderProxy latency measurements.

Cryptography and Security.title: Phantom of the Masquerade: Graph Neural Network-Based Detection of Masquerade Attacks in Controller Area Networks
Cryptography and Security.summary: The lack of built-in security in controller area networks (CANs) exposes modern vehicles and industrial systems to masquerade attacks that can compromise safety and reliability. These attacks inject malicious messages that mimic legitimate communication patterns, making them difficult to detect using existing intrusion detection systems (IDS). Prior graph-based IDS approaches often rely on shallow embeddings that decouple representation learning from classification, which may limit their ability to fully exploit structural and signal-level information. In this paper, we propose PhantoMasq, a graph neural network (GNN)-based framework for detecting masquerade attacks in CAN systems. PhantoMasq models CAN traffic as message sequence graphs enriched with lightweight statistical features derived from signal behavior, enabling joint learning of structural dependencies and temporal characteristics. The detection task is formulated as a graph-level classification problem and solved using graph convolutional networks (GCNs). We evaluate PhantoMasq on the ROAD dataset under a protocol that prevents overlapping windows from spanning training and test data. Across five masquerade attack types, PhantoMasq achieves mean AUC-ROC between 0.831 and 0.999, with performance depending on the transmission rate of the targeted identifier and the magnitude of the induced signal deviation. Against a state-of-the-art graph-embedding baseline evaluated on the same sliding-window configurations, PhantoMasq achieves higher AUC-ROC on all five attack types, by 0.13 to 0.36, and is less sensitive to window configuration. Window-processing latency ranges from 2.33 to 5.94 ms per window on CPU, corresponding to a throughput of 168 to 429 windows per second. We make our implementation and experimental artifacts available to support reproducibility.

Cryptography and Security.title: Triosecuris: Formally Verified Protection Against Speculative Control-Flow Hijacking
Cryptography and Security.summary: This paper introduces Triosecuris, a formally verified defense against Spectre BTB, RSB, and PHT that combines CET-style hardware-assisted control-flow integrity with compiler-inserted speculative load hardening (SLH). Triosecuris is based on the novel observation that in the presence of CET-style protection, we can precisely detect BTB misspeculation for indirect calls and RSB misspeculation for returns and set the SLH misspeculation flag. We formalize Triosecuris as a transformation in Rocq and provide a machine-checked proof that it achieves relative security: any transformed program running with speculation leaks no more than what the source program leaks without speculation. This strong security guarantee applies to arbitrary programs, even those not following the cryptographic constant-time programming discipline.
Cryptography and Security.comment: Appeared at CSF'26; extended version with appendices and a bit more related work. W.r.t. first arXiv version: extended with concrete protection against Spectre RSB and renamed to Triosecuris

Cryptography and Security.title: Detecting Formation-Preserving GNSS Spoofing of UAV Swarms through Transmitter Parallax in Pseudorange and Doppler
Cryptography and Security.summary: Swarms of unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) detect Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS) spoofing by checking the drones' reported positions against their known formation. Formation-preserving spoofing evades this check: in GNSS-WASP, one transmitter per satellite, a few kilometres away, shifts the whole swarm while keeping its formation. We show that such an attack still leaves a trace below the position level. Because the transmitters are close, each drone sees them under a slightly different angle, and this parallax bends the signal arrival times across a 90 m swarm by 20-40 cm for a transmitter at 5 km, whatever delays the attacker applies. We propose a likelihood ratio test that reads this trace from the pseudoranges and Doppler every drone already measures, with all clocks and attacker delays unknown and no extra antennas. In simulations with real GPS and Galileo orbits and white receiver noise, 16 drones detect GNSS-WASP at 5 km in 13-60% of 10 s windows in straight flight and in every window during a formation turn with a precise Doppler receiver, where the countermeasure proposed with GNSS-WASP detects at most 5%. The same test also catches single-transmitter and ground-array spoofing.
Cryptography and Security.comment: 16 pages, 7 main figures, 7 main tables. Includes supplementary appendices

Cryptography and Security.title: BlockJack: Cross-Tenant Redirection Fault Attacks on Paged KV Cache Address Translation in LLM Serving
Cryptography and Security.summary:
Large language model (LLM) serving frameworks accelerate inference by retaining previously computed states in a key-value (KV) cache. Paged serving frameworks such as vLLM organize this cache through block tables analogous to OS page tables, which map each request's logical KV blocks to physical KV blocks, forming a software-managed address translation layer. Although fault attacks such as Rowhammer have exploited OS page tables to redirect memory accesses, prior fault attacks on LLMs have largely targeted the data plane, i.e., model weights or KV-cache contents, leaving KV-cache mapping unexplored.
  We present BlockJack (i.e., Block Hijack), the first KV cache address-translation fault attack in LLM inference. By corrupting block-table entries, BlockJack redirects a request's KV cache reads to blocks assigned to another tenant's request without modifying model parameters, prompts, or cached KV states. It achieves both confidentiality violation (victim information appears in attacker responses) and integrity violation (attacker-supplied context steers victim answers). We study paged KV cache mappings in vLLM and formally characterize when redirect targets are predictable. Across seven models spanning the Qwen, Llama, Gemma, and Phi families, a faulted mapping exposes victim context. For the integrity attack, we examine how topic proximity, intra-topic divergence, and model behavior shape redirected responses. On a 248-scene medical benchmark, the integrity attack causes up to 41.1% of responses to recommend less urgent care, while still appearing consistent with the victim's question. We demonstrate physical feasibility of BlockJack with Rowhammer and subsequently evaluate assignment validation as a defense. Following responsible disclosure, vLLM and Sonar confirmed the vulnerability and proposed patches that we reviewed and validated.

Cryptography and Security.title: Question, Then Affirm: Restoring Commitment Does Not Restore Refusal
Cryptography and Security.summary: We find that safeguards for image generation can be bypassed without changing what a message says. A sign stating a harmful proposition is blocked, but the same proposition phrased as a question and followed by a check mark is generated, even though the resulting image endorses the original claim. On a 300-case challenge set, gpt-image-2 returns images for 43.3% of question-affirmation requests versus 16.3% of direct statements, with 41.3% versus 15.3% of cases yielding images that endorse the original proposition. We define this as Deferred Semantic Commitment (DSC): commitment is withdrawn by the question and restored by a separate element, while safety behavior follows only the withdrawal. To investigate why, we study an open-weight language model and find that re-endorsement only partially reverses the refusal-related change introduced by questioning. These findings reveal a mismatch between recovered meaning and refusal behavior, motivating safeguards that assess the completed message rather than its individual elements.

Cryptography and Security.title: RAVEN: A Self-RAG Based Agent for Threat Classification and Response
Cryptography and Security.summary: Security event analysis in large enterprises can be overwhelming, as each alert typically requires manual in- spection by human operators. This process is time-consuming and prone to inconsistencies, especially in high-volume Secu- rity Operations Center (SOC) environments. In this work- in-progress paper, we present RAVEN: Retrieval-Augmented Vulnerability & Event aNalysis, an agentic framework designed to support SOC analysts by automating the initial stages of alert investigation. The proposed system leverages a Self- Reflective Retrieval-Augmented Generation-based approach to provide an initial classification of security events and enables interactive refinement through analyst-in-the-loop queries. Un- like traditional approaches that rely on generic mitigation strategies, RAVEN generates context-aware remediation sug- gestions by incorporating knowledge of the target enterprise infrastructure. We implement an early-stage prototype and report preliminary results on three balanced test sets of 400 curated web payloads each (SQLi, XSS, SSTI) and a qualitative case study of mitigation generation; an evaluation on IDS- generated alerts and a user study are ongoing and outlined as remaining work.

Cryptography and Security.title: GPUThor: Amplifying Rowhammer Attacks via Non-Uniform Patterns to Exploit ECC-Protected GPUs
Cryptography and Security.summary:
GDDR memory in GPUs is vulnerable to Rowhammer attacks, where rapid memory accesses induce bit flips in adjacent cells, enabling data tampering and privilege escalation. However, prior GPU Rowhammer attacks trigger only tens to hundreds of bit flips, orders of magnitude fewer than CPU attacks, severely limiting their practical impact. This gap stems from the reliance of existing GPU Rowhammer attacks on uniform hammering patterns that activate aggressor and decoy rows equally, which results in low hammering intensity for aggressor rows.
  We present GPUThor, a high-intensity Rowhammer attack on NVIDIA GPUs leveraging non-uniform hammering. GPUThor reverse engineers GPU memory-access coalescing behavior to enable non-uniform hammering patterns on GPUs, that activate aggressor rows more intensely than decoy rows. Additionally, by identifying refresh instances when in-DRAM mitigations are applied, it constructs longer attack patterns that escape mitigation across refresh intervals, further increasing hammering intensity. Together, these techniques yield 500X to 23,500X more bit flips than prior GPU Rowhammer attacks, across several NVIDIA GPUs (A4000, A4500, A5000, A6000), reaching bit flip rates close to state-of-the-art CPU Rowhammer attacks. GPUThor also enables the first Rowhammer exploits on ECC-protected GPUs, inducing uncorrectable double and triple bit flips, making denial-of-service and privilege-escalation attacks practical even on GPUs with ECC enabled.
Cryptography and Security.comment: 17 pages, including appendices. The paper was presented at CCS'26 (https://www.sigsac.org/ccs/CCS2026/)

Cryptography and Security.title: Signed but Unbound: The Authority Gap Between Agent Commerce Mandates and Crypto Wallet Signatures
Cryptography and Security.summary: When an artificial intelligence agent pays with a stablecoin, the commerce protocol can specify the merchant, order, amount, and facilitator. The token contract enforces the fields the wallet signs. We call the difference the authority gap, define nine constraint classes, and derive them for 12 authorization configurations, including Coinbase's deployed Commerce Payments Protocol. All 31,800 trials on local copies of deployed contract code match the derivation. A controlled comparison shows that committing the terms in the signed nonce binds the order. When the facilitator submits a payment to a merchant account without code, binding the facilitator requires a separate recipient contract. Of 26,653 sampled USD Coin authorizations redeemed on Base, 98.7% followed a path that any holder of the signature could redeem. We prove sufficient conditions for a recipient contract to enforce the signed mandate under a trusted signer and show which recipient a wallet displays. MandateLock, a minimal implementation for immediate payments, rejects all 10,800 modified mandates on deployed token code and accepts signatures from two independent signers. It uses 25% more gas than a transfer that only the recipient can submit.
Cryptography and Security.comment: 10 pages, 3 figures. Reproducibility artifact linked in the manuscript

Cryptography and Security.title: ALIoTh: Orchestrating Multi-Agent LLMs for Autonomous IoT Penetration Testing
Cryptography and Security.summary: Penetration testing in Internet of Things (IoT) environments, especially those composed of various different devices, e.g., smart plugs, smart cameras, and smart doors, presents great challenges across the phases of information gathering, attack surface enumeration, privilege escalation, and lateral movement. This paper introduces ALIoTh, a multi-agent, workflow-driven penetration testing framework that integrates Large Language Models agents within a Self-Retrieval-Augmented Generation (Self-RAG) architecture to autonomously identify and exploit vulnerabilities in IoT and Industrial-IoT (IIoT) environments. By leveraging state-of-the-art language models and orchestrating specialized agents via the LangGraph framework, ALIoTh dynamically plans and executes a full-spectrum offensive pipeline. This includes network, devices, and service enumeration, vulnerability assessment, payload generation, reverse shell deployment, and privilege escalation on each device. The Self-RAG mechanism equips expert agents with contextual access to IoT security knowledge, e.g., related documentation, tool manuals, and known attack techniques, enhancing their reasoning capabilities in scenarios involving multiple device exploitation and group policy manipulation.

Cryptography and Security.title: On the Reliability of CyberGym Evaluation: Task Material Consistency and Reference-Target Identity
Cryptography and Security.summary: CyberGym evaluates vulnerability reproduction by checking whether a proof-of-concept input (PoC) crashes a vulnerable program version but not a fixed version. Interpreting this differential pass as successful reproduction requires consistent task materials and evidence that the PoC triggers the intended defect. We examine these requirements through a material audit of all 1,507 CyberGym tasks and an identity assessment of the final PoCs from one complete Level-1 GLM-5.3 run. Taking the defect associated with each reference crash report as the target, the audit assigns inconsistency labels to 338 tasks (22.4%) after correcting two labels identified by stratified blind review. The largest categories are coverage inconsistency (205 tasks) and descriptions and patches that jointly point to another defect (110 tasks). We assess PoC identity using an execution check, crash-signature matching, and LLM-assisted root-cause review. Of the 1,286 differential passes, the procedure assigns 89 non-target and 10 insufficient-evidence verdicts; requiring a target hit lowers the pass rate from 85.3% to 78.8%. Non-target verdicts also occur in tasks with no material inconsistency found: 39 of 1,052 differential passes (3.7%). Although the identity verdicts require independent validation, these findings motivate separate checks of task-material consistency and submission identity when interpreting vulnerability-reproduction scores.

Cryptography and Security.title: Cross-Modal Backdoor Attack on Connector-based Multimodal Large Language Models
Cryptography and Security.summary: Assembling multimodal large language models (MLLMs) from pretrained components has become a widely adopted practice in the open-source ecosystem, yet the supply-chain risks of lightweight connectors remain largely unexplored. We propose a cross-modal backdoor attack that exploits this gap. By poisoning only the connector with a single seed sample and a small set of augmented variants from one modality, the adversary establishes a compact malicious region in the shared latent space associated with a target output. A centroid extracted from this region then serves as a latent anchor for cross-modal activation: adversarial inputs from any other modality can be optimized offline to reach this anchor, triggering the target response without access to the deployed model. Evaluations on PandaGPT and NExT-GPT show same-modality attack success rates (ASR) up to 99.9%, with most cross-modal settings exceeding 95.0% ASR under bounded perturbations. Experiments on ChatBridge further demonstrate the attack's effectiveness across different connector architectures. The attack produces 0.0% backdoor leakage on clean inputs and maintains weight-cosine similarity above 0.97 relative to benign connectors. Existing defenses fail to neutralize the threat without substantial utility degradation, revealing that a single poisoned connector can establish a reusable backdoor pathway across modalities.

Cryptography and Security.title: Hardening JavaScript Programs against LLM-Based Vulnerability Detection
Cryptography and Security.summary:
JavaScript programs are often distributed as source code, so attackers can analyze them for vulnerabilities. LLM-based vulnerability detection agents now make this analysis much easier. To mitigate this emerging threat, we present AntiAgent, a defense that lets developers harden their programs against such detection agents. AntiAgent transforms a program before release to impede an agent's analysis. To find effective transformations, AntiAgent evolves a corpus of programs with known vulnerabilities and traces how a detection agent analyzes each evolved version. It keeps the versions on which the agent misses or misreports the vulnerability and extracts their transformations into reusable rules. To protect a new program, AntiAgent carefully divides the task between an LLM and the rules, so that the transformations adapt to the program while preserving its semantics.
  We evaluate AntiAgent on real-world JavaScript applications against four detection agents, including Claude Code and Codex. AntiAgent reduces the number of vulnerabilities that each agent detects by 52.0-60.7%, outperforming the conventional obfuscator JS-Obfuscator and the LLM-based transformation method FPA on every agent. The transformed programs pass all project tests, indicating that AntiAgent preserves the original program semantics. The transformation rules also remain effective on vulnerability types absent from the corpus and on programs written in another language like Python.

Cryptography and Security.title: Ask in the Crowd: Differentially Private LLM Inference via Dummy-Augmented Shuffling
Cryptography and Security.summary:
Large language models are increasingly deployed as LLM-as-a-Service (LLMaaS), where user queries are sent to remote LLMs for inference, raising severe privacy concerns about the exposure of sensitive user inputs. Differentially private inference mitigates these risks by injecting noise into input embeddings. However, existing methods struggle to balance privacy and utility, as stronger privacy protection often leads to substantial accuracy degradation in LLM inference.
  In this work, we propose DP-SPD, a differentially private LLM inference framework that protects user queries by hiding the real query among client-generated dummy queries. All queries are randomly shuffled before being sent to the server, preventing direct identification of the user's true intent. To improve inference efficiency, we exploit the shared-prefix structure among queries and reuse transformer key--value (KV) caches during decoding. We analyze the privacy guarantee of DP-SPD and evaluate its utility on classification and generation tasks, as well as its privacy protection under QIA, EIA, and GPT-based attacks. Experimental results show that our method achieves strong inference-time privacy protection and near-plaintext utility while improving inference efficiency through shared-prefix KV-cache reuse.

Cryptography and Security.title: GPU-Accelerated Secure Inference for Drug--Target Interaction Prediction
Cryptography and Security.summary: Deep learning models that predict drug--target interactions (DTI) can speed up drug discovery, but the candidate drugs they score are valuable intellectual property that their owners cannot reveal. Secure multiparty computation (MPC) lets two servers compute a prediction on a secret-shared drug, without either server learning the drug. However, secure inference of deep models is slow. Non-linear operations require communication between the servers, and MPC arithmetic does not map naturally to GPUs. In this paper, we present our solution to Track~III of the iDASH 2026 privacy and security competition, which asked for fast two-party secure DTI inference on GPUs. Our solution is built on the co-design of MPC-friendly models and MPC protocols. On the model side, we design SlimDTA, a DTI model that reduces the operations on the secret drug, and in particular the non-linear operations that require communication. On the protocol side, we build a GPU framework that evaluates the linear layers with additive secret sharing and the non-linear layers with function secret sharing, including a custom CUDA kernel for the comparisons. Our solution won first place in the competition, at under 10,ms per prediction on average, and its secure predictions match the plaintext model to within 0.02%.

Cryptography and Security.title: Correctable Enrollment and One-Transaction Seed Proofs for Ethereum's Post-Quantum Transition
Cryptography and Security.summary: A quantum computer running Shor's algorithm can extract the private key of every Ethereum account whose public key is published, and accounts exposed by their own transactions hold 54.6% of execution-layer ETH. As the first such machine may stay secret, a migration cannot wait for visible thefts, and once keys are extractable, legacy signatures no longer tell owners from attackers. We design a migration in which owners enroll post-quantum keys cheaply with their existing signatures before ECDSA is retired at a scheduled time, while a zero-knowledge proof of the wallet's BIP-39 seed can correct any such enrollment until a common deadline afterward; an account nobody enrolled stays frozen and recoverable by seed proof without a deadline. Each proof binds the new key, a nonce and a fee cap, so neither a paying sponsor nor a reordering block builder can redirect or replay it. Validators switch to hash-based keys first, at a finalized checkpoint and under a stated bound on the attacker's voting power. We prove the account guarantees under explicit assumptions, model-check the rules, and implement the design in go-ethereum and a Lean consensus client. A three-layer recursive hash-based STARK yields a seed proof of about 190 KB that fits one transaction, verifies in 38 ms and takes a median of 111 s to generate on a laptop; four proofs aggregate into one. In a ten-node simulation with mainnet-derived accounts and fee demand, block space rather than proving sets the duration: the 4.45 million accounts with at least 0.1 ETH would migrate in 29.4 days if all enroll before ECDSA is retired and in 235 days if all recover after it in batches of four. In a mass enrollment, an enrollment waits a median of 19.1 minutes in the public mempool, longer than published estimates for a fast quantum computer to extract its key, so owners with a seed and an unexposed key should migrate by seed proof.
