Experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of World-delta in incremental 3D scene generation, observation-driven correction, scene consistency, and update efficiency over successive scene updates.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: Fast and Accurate Body Estimation in Pixels, World Space and Scenes
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: We present FAB (Fast and Accurate Body estimation), a human body estimator that jointly improves inference efficiency and body-recovery fidelity. Rather than predicting only parametric mesh-model parameters, FAB directly predicts human skeleton joints and dense surface points. In images, it predicts dense 2D and 3D body points alongside a parametric Momentum Human Rig (MHR) head, then fits SMPL in one learned pass followed by two Gauss-Newton steps. Its ViT-L student, FAB-L, distilled from a fine-tuned SAM 3D Body, runs in real time for one person on an RTX 4070 Ti SUPER, from detection to a fitted body, at 4.6x the speed of SAM 3D Body's eager-PyTorch body-only path, while improving accuracy on most camera-space benchmarks. The same network predicts heel, toe, hand, and knee contacts, which connect the body to the scene. FAB also estimates world-space motion, fuses static-scene depth around the visible person, and aligns body and scene using predicted contacts. For human-to-humanoid real-to-sim transfer, an in-model G1 head and FAB-Retarget, a motion-level retargeter that reads dense points or the fitted mesh, map motion to a Unitree G1. FAB-Retarget produces references that follow the person more closely than specialized retargeters including SOMA, GMR, UMR, and OmniRetarget, and substantially more closely than Fast SAM 3D Body retargeted with our sequence IK. Project page: https://www.jinkuncao.com/FAB.
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.comment: 28 pages, 9 pages of main text. 16 figures

Information Retrieval.title: Variants of Beam Search for DiskANN
Information Retrieval.summary: Graph-based data structures such as DiskANN, HNSW, and NSG constitute the state of the art for large-scale approximate nearest-neighbor (ANN) search. Indyk and Xu introduced the notion of $α$-reachable graphs, which include graphs built by DiskANN's slow-preprocessing construction, and proved that greedy search achieves an approximation factor of $\tfrac{α+1}{α-1}$. Independently, Al-Jazzazi et al. proposed adaptive beam search (ABS) with a relaxation parameter $γ> 0$, showing a $\tfrac{2}γ$ approximation on navigable graphs ($α\approx 1$), where greedy search admits no guarantees. In this work, we unify and generalize these results by proving that ABS with parameter $γ$ on $α$-reachable graphs achieves an approximation of $\tfrac{α+1}{α(γ+1)-1}$ for any metric. Moreover, on sorted $α$-reachable graphs (introduced by Gollapudi et al.) under the $\ell_2$ metric, we obtain the tighter bound $\max\bigl(\tfracα{α(γ+1)-1}, \tfrac{α^{2}+1}{α^{2}(γ+1)-1}\bigr)$. Beyond these theoretical results, we design a beam predictor using features inspired by fine-grained analysis of ABS, trained via a constrained objective that minimizes mean distance computations subject to a target recall. On three 100-million-point benchmarks, using graphs built by DiskANN's practical construction, beam predictor lowers mean query latency on SSD-resident indices at matched recall by up to $29.6\%$ relative to classical beam search (CBS). Relative to ABS, it is faster in $11$ of $15$ settings, by up to $6.5\%$, and at most $1.4\%$ slower in the other $4$; at $95\%$ recall, its advantage over ABS grows from $0.8$--$4.2\%$ for $100$ neighbors to $4.6$--$5.6\%$ for $500$ neighbors. In memory, it needs $1.3$--$23.7\%$ fewer distance computations than CBS and $0.0$--$3.9\%$ fewer than ABS.

Information Retrieval.title: Cost-Aware Agentic Feature Optimization System for Fleet-Scale Ranking Models
Information Retrieval.summary: Large Web platforms operate large fleets of ranking models, each selecting features from a shared pool of tens of thousands. We present an end-to-end agentic system that optimizes features across the fleet under resource constraints shared across models and those set per model, such as feature pipeline cost and serving throughput (QPS), respectively. In this system, LLM agents propose hypotheses, and deterministic tools execute experiments and verify them. For each model, an LLM generates and shortlists cross features from a combinatorial candidate space, and all features are then ranked by several importance methods. Feature blending mixes these rankings into a single selection, using Pareto fronts across tasks for multi-task models. An LLM Researcher agent then tunes the feature selection in 10--25 asynchronous trials under resource caps, and a trimming step keeps the pipeline cost within budget. Across production models, the system improves normalized entropy by 0.31% on average within each model's budget, and the trimming step cuts pipeline cost by 2.3% with no regression beyond measurement noise. The optimized models were launched, and in online A/B tests they improved a primary online metric by 0.20%.

Information Retrieval.title: The Window Lever: Longer Observation Windows Outweigh the Observed Effects of Data, Capacity, and Architecture in Customer Behavior Forecasting
Information Retrieval.summary: In our experiments on long-horizon customer-behavior forecasting, a longer observation window outweighed the observed effects of more data, more capacity and newer architectures. The window is the weeks of history a model sees before the week it forecasts from. Going from an 8- to a 16-week window adds a raw +0.070 to 0.107 log-space $R^2$ in every family at 1M. Matched test cohorts, which score the same customer-weeks at every window, show this raw comparison understates the gain in every family they cover. The direction holds on five public datasets, four spanning over a year (ridge and our transformer on all five). On our internal data, longer windows admit up to 10% more and colder training customers, which matching does not fix. Our design does not separate window length from calendar coverage, because every test anchor (the week a forecast is made from) falls in one eight-week band. On training-period anchors, the weekly ridge probe's gain persists outside the holiday season, keeping about 72% of it. We therefore report a robust positive association with longer windows and do not identify the magnitude of a calendar-independent history effect. Of four internally registered predictions, the only fully blind one failed. An activity-mixture model predicted +0.014 from 24 to 32 weeks; the weekly-aggregate probe returned -0.0004. For the sequence families, the other three levers are about an order of magnitude smaller, bounded and unresolved. Their observed effects are at most 0.006 between the nominal 1M and 10M tiers and 0.0052 among five sequence families at 16 weeks with clocks as built, both single-seed on the full test split, and 0.006 for capacity on three-seed means. These are observed intervals, not equivalence bounds. Our claim is the order-of-magnitude contrast between the window and those bounds. A team building on this class of data should start by lengthening the window.

Information Retrieval.title: Stop Removing Stopwords: How an Inherited Preprocessing Default Distorts Legal Text-as-Data
Information Retrieval.summary: Empirical legal scholarship increasingly treats judicial text as data, and much of it still runs on sparse, interpretable pipelines -- TF-IDF features and linear classifiers -- because the textual feature is often the object of study rather than a means to prediction. Yet these pipelines inherit preprocessing defaults from mid-century information retrieval that were never validated against classification accuracy. The most entrenched of these is stopword removal. This study introduces an exhaustive single word ablation that measures the effect of a preprocessing step directly against the downstream objective, and applies it to stopword removal as the hardest case to dislodge. Matching Supreme Court Database labels to Caselaw Access Project opinion texts, the study examines two binary tasks that bracket F1 headroom, ideological direction (no-removal baseline F1 ~0.68) and constitutional versus non-constitutional law type (~0.92), across 7,668 and 7,001 opinions. For each task, the ablation removes each of about 18,500 candidate words in turn, and a task-specific stoplist is built from the measurements. Common generic stoplists fall below the no-removal baseline in all twelve held-out tests. The task-specific stoplists move held-out F1 by +0.0023 (95% CI [-0.0124, +0.0170]) on ideology and by +0.0001 ([-0.0082, +0.0085]) on law type. Neither task shows a detectable benefit from removal, and supplemental analysis finds that word-level statistics predict removal effects poorly, because true removal effects differ by less than the measurement can register, leaving little to predict. The method generalizes to any inherited preprocessing default; the result is a caution specific to interpretable legal text-as-data, where a step that reshapes which features a model sees can distort the doctrinal and ideological signal the research is meant to recover. The burden of proof sits with removal.

Information Retrieval.title: Democratizing Cross-Project Knowledge for Transforming Water Governance and Climate Resilience: an Agentic AI Ecosystem
Information Retrieval.summary: EU-funded projects produce extensive evidence in the form of deliverables, reports, and case studies. However, this knowledge is typically scattered across projects and document structures, making it difficult to locate relevant, contextual information when making decisions. This paper introduces an Agentic AI Ecosystem that consolidates heterogeneous project documentation into a domain-aware knowledge base and provides adaptive access through an agentic Retrieval-Augmented Generation pipeline. Documents from three EU-funded projects (IMPETUS, NATALIE, and InnWater) are reconstructed into hierarchical section trees and indexed with structured metadata. Retrieval is supported by two domain-specific embedding models fine-tuned on domain data (water and climate). On top of this knowledge base, a ReAct-style controller iteratively orchestrates retrieval actions by allocating retrieval budget across domain collections and accumulating evidence until a stopping criterion is met. In a retrieval benchmark over the corpus, the proposed approach improves Mean Reciprocal Rank by 26.7% (relative) compared to a single-domain embedding baseline, indicating more consistent retrieval of relevant evidence to support cross-project knowledge synthesis and climate-resilient decision-making.
Information Retrieval.comment: 8 pages, 2 figures. Accepted at WDSA/CCWI 2026. Proceedings publication pending

Information Retrieval.title: Beyond Dimensionality: Domain Shift and Catastrophic Forgetting in Single- vs. Multi-Vector Retrieval
Information Retrieval.summary: Recent work by Weller et al. introduced the naturalistic benchmark LIMIT and showed that widely used single-vector embedding models suffer substantial degradation in retrieval quality, attributing this primarily to limited embedding dimensionality. In our work, we revisit this explanation and argue that dimensionality alone is unlikely to account for the observed failures; in fact, results of Alon et al. imply that $2k+1$ dimensions suffice for top-$k$ retrieval over a fixed set of queries and documents. Motivated by this, we investigate alternative drivers of poor performance, including tokenization, linguistic structure, and domain shift. Our empirical analysis shows that tokenization artifacts and linguistic similarity yield only modest improvements, whereas domain shift and misalignment between embedding similarity and task-specific relevance are the dominant factors. While finetuning partially mitigates these issues and improves recall, it introduces catastrophic forgetting: finetuning single-vector models on LIMIT-like datasets reduces their MS MARCO Recall@10 by more than half, whereas multi-vector models forget much less. We observe the same pattern when finetuning on the real-world HotpotQA dataset, and between the single-vector and multi-vector heads of Jina-v4, which share one backbone.

Information Retrieval.title: Keep it Simple! A Multiple-Choice Task can Benefit Generative Recommendation
Information Retrieval.summary:
Sequential recommendation has recently witnessed growing interest in generative retrieval. One of the most popular approaches is to autoregressively generate the semantic identifiers (SIDs) of items as recommendations. Existing efforts mainly rely on semantic alignment, sophisticated architectural designs, and extensive hyperparameter tuning. However, the conventional learning framework for generative models could have foundational limitations. Specifically, most generative models directly predict target items without explicitly learning negative compositions and relative ranking signals. This is not well aligned with the philosophy of Bayesian personalized ranking (BPR), which emphasizes the importance of relative rankings between positive and negative samples.
  In this paper, we show that adding a simple multiple-choice auxiliary task into the learning objective can effectively address this issue. With minimal adaptation, we introduce Task Identifiers and Candidate Constructions to synthesize training data for the multiple-choice auxiliary task. In addition, we provide theoretical analysis of the fundamental benefits of the multiple-choice auxiliary task from the perspectives of information theory and compositional generalization. Extensive experiments on four publicly available benchmark datasets show that our approach can improve TIGER, a conventional generative recommendation model, by 4.9% to 79% in NDCG@10.

Information Retrieval.title: When Is Additional Retrieval Worthwhile? A Cost-Aware Study of Evidence Gain and Answer Reliability in RAG
Information Retrieval.summary: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) can benefit from more sophisticated retrieval, but extra retrieval may be unnecessary for many questions and gains in evidence retrieval may not translate into faithful or correct answers. We study a cost-aware, two-action retrieval policy that chooses between a dense-retrieval-plus-reranking baseline and a hybrid lexical--dense retriever. Rather than classifying baseline retrieval as simply successful or unsuccessful, we estimate the question-specific incremental evidence-retrieval benefit of hybrid retrieval using features available before the routing decision. A regularized linear model and decision threshold are selected using document-grouped cross-validation and frozen prior to held-out evaluation. On 60 previously unseen QASPER training-split articles (188 questions, 169 evidence-evaluable), the policy triggers hybrid retrieval on 46 questions (24.5\%) and obtains the same evidence Hit@10 as always-hybrid retrieval (78.70\%, versus 76.92\% for always-keep). Paired, paper-cluster bootstrap intervals do not establish a reliable utility advantage. We further compare generated answers from a 4-bit Qwen3-4B model under the three retrieval policies. Provisional answer-level assessments show no clear correctness or faithfulness improvement after partial review, despite the evidence-retrieval result. The generation assessments remain model-assisted and lack independent human validation. These results expose an important distinction between retrieving relevant evidence efficiently and improving the reliability of the generated answer. The work is presented as a reproducible empirical study, not a claim of statistically established answer-quality superiority.

Information Retrieval.title: Ontology Interoperability: A Comprehensive Framework for Industry-Scale Applications
Information Retrieval.summary: Different ontologies with conflicting and overlapping concepts cause havoc in the design, develop, and deploy of ontology-driven applications. In this work, we propose a comprehensive ontology interoperability framework for industry-scale ontology-driven applications. The framework employs three state-of-the-art semantic techniques in different phases of the ontology engineering (OE) life cycle: ontology design patterns (ODPs) in the design phase, ontology matching and versioning (OM&OV) in the develop phase, and ontology validation (OVA) in the deploy phase, to achieve better ontology interoperability.

Information Retrieval.title: From Sessions to Serving: Integrating LLM-Based Embeddings into Retrieval for Production Content Recommendation
Information Retrieval.summary: Personalized content recommendation on large marketplace websites must reconcile heterogeneous candidate content (e.g., customer stories, product pages, industry pages, and learning content) with sparse, fast-changing user behavior, placing increasing demands on the retrieval stage to represent user interest well, not just the downstream ranking stage. We present LSER (LLM Session Embedding Retrieval), a production content recommendation system for autodesk.com that derives session- and history-level embeddings from a pretrained large language model (LLM) and adds them as auxiliary user-side features in the retrieval-stage user tower alongside existing learned sequence encoders. To keep user-side embeddings fresh under real-time behavior, we build a nearline serving path that asynchronously refreshes sequential and LLM-derived user vectors for our main content recommendation server. We validate the incremental value of the LLM features through an ablation study across our full multi-content-type catalog. Our results indicate that integrating LLM-derived embeddings as additional retrieval signals, together with production-grade nearline serving, is technically feasible and can improve model performances.

Information Retrieval.title: From transcription to semantic corpus analysis: unsupervised learning of sentence representations for ancient languages
Information Retrieval.summary: Automatic Text Recognition (ATR) now supplies digital humanities with large volumes of unstruc- tured, heterogeneous, and often noisy text in ancient languages. Downstream semantic analyses- text reuse identification, alignment, and semantic search-rely on sentence embeddings, yet ex- isting methods transfer poorly to ancient languages: generic multilingual encoders underperform, specialized language models yield anisotropic representation spaces, and labeled similarity data is scarce. We study two fully unsupervised strategies-TSDAE and unsupervised SimCSE (hence- forth CSE)-that adapt a specialized token-level language model into a corpus-specific sentence encoder using only raw sentences. We validate them on biblical reuse in patristic literature in Latin and Ancient Greek: 2,936 sentences carrying expert-verified reuses in works of Augustine, Jerome, and Athanasius, matched against the Vulgate, the Septuagint, and the Nestle--Aland New Testament. We decompose reuse identification into binary detection and correspondence retrieval, evaluate both tasks separately, and benchmark the adapted encoders against multilingual, specialized, distilled, and supervised fine-tuned baselines, on clean text and on text perturbed by simulated HTR errors and scribal abbreviations. On these test sets, the adapted encoders lead all baselines on both tasks, with complementary profiles: TSDAE leads detection given a large in-domain corpus, while CSE leads retrieval, reaches its optimum with as few as 4--8k raw in-domain sentences-a few tens of sec- onds of training on a laptop GPU-and transfers across works and authors. Under simulated noise, retraining CSE on the perturbed text itself outperforms a clean-trained encoder. Measurements of alignment, uniformity, and anisotropy relate the geometric effect of each strategy to the measured gains. The full pipeline-segmentation, fine-tuning, cross-corpus semantic search-is available to non-specialists through the online tool Paraphrasis.

Information Retrieval.title: The Missing Complement: State-Conditioned Minimal Sufficient Evidence for Coding Agents
Information Retrieval.summary: Retrieval assembles repository context by ranking passages for relevance to the current query. A coding agent halfway through an issue has already read much of what such a ranker returns. Relevance is scored per passage, but sufficiency belongs to the set: independently scored passages can fill the budget with support for one requirement while another goes unmet. We formulate state-conditioned minimal sufficient evidence recovery: given a captured agent state, recover a compact evidence combination supplying what its next decision still lacks. SERBench measures this on 500 held-out states from 45 repositories, recording what the agent has seen, crediting only sets that satisfy every annotated evidence requirement of the current decision, and separating set recovery from candidate discovery. MSS-Complement treats acquisition as set construction, not ranking. Three semantic calls propose a jointly sufficient set, search for what it lacks, and return 4-8 intact source units within 6,144 tokens. One configuration, fixed on calibration data, recovers a complete set for 73.0% of those states at five items and 80.6% at eight, against 61.4% and 72.4% for Qwen3 embedding with reranking. A matched control ranking by similarity alone recovers fewer complete sets, placing the margin over it in the set-level policy, not the computation. The lead persists from frozen repository source with no gold-derived pool. On AMA-Bench it answers from a 76.2% smaller answer prompt, with accuracy 2.08 points above that benchmark's own memory agent. Removing one required group from a complete set costs repair-localization precision under two executors. Retrieval for agents is better posed as recovering what a decision lacks than re-ranking what an issue resembles.
Information Retrieval.comment: 32 pages, 3 figures. Benchmark and evaluation resources: https://github.com/LordTARN1SHED/SERBench

Information Retrieval.title: A Task-Level Bias Taxonomy for Historical Image Retrieval
Information Retrieval.summary: In recent decades, galleries, libraries, archives, and museums (GLAM institutions) have digitised vast amounts of cultural heritage material, including historical imagery. A major challenge in making these collections publicly accessible is enabling effective search and discovery. Many historical images contain incomplete, sparse, or no descriptive metadata. Consequently, machine learning (ML) methods are increasingly being used to generate or enrich metadata to improve the searchability of such collections. However, artificial intelligence (AI)-based systems can reproduce or amplify existing biases, particularly when applied to historical imagery. Factors such as differences between the data used to train the models and the historical images on which they are applied, degraded image quality, monochrome photographs, and historically biased or incomplete descriptions can reduce model performance and introduce bias into search and retrieval results. In this paper, we examine different forms of bias in historical image collections and review current methods to mitigate them. We investigate how these biases arise and how they influence AI-supported search and retrieval systems.
Information Retrieval.comment: Presented at Bias In GLAM workshop at TPDL 2026

Information Retrieval.title: LINEAGE: A Benchmark for Empirical Lineage Retrieval in AI Scientific Literature
Information Retrieval.summary: Current research agents are moving beyond academic search toward literature synthesis and experiment planning. These workflows increasingly rely on literature retrieval systems, which serve as standalone systems or as components of research agents. However, existing scientific literature retrieval benchmarks mainly evaluate these methods using topical relevance or citation links as supervision, which cannot capture which prior methods are used for empirical comparison. To address this gap, we introduce Lineage, a benchmark for empirical lineage retrieval in AI scientific literature. An empirical lineage relation links a prior paper to a source paper that explicitly uses its method as an empirical comparison baseline. These relations form lineage graphs whose multi-hop neighborhoods provide retrieval ground truth for structural evaluation. To construct these graphs at scale, we develop Lineage-Constructor, which converts heterogeneous paper records and full-paper empirical baseline evidence into calibrated lineage graphs. Built from 121,048 papers across 17 top AI venues from 2018 to 2025, Lineage contains 3,950 graph components, 67,502 paper nodes, 164,948 lineage edges, and 80,000 multi-facet retrieval queries. Experiments with 19 representative retrieval systems show that empirical lineage retrieval remains challenging. Performance drops sharply with lineage distance, while structural metrics reveal that isolated retrieval hits often fail to recover closely connected empirical comparison neighborhoods.

Information Retrieval.title: CACO: Coverage-Aware Coordinated Optimization for Continuous Generative Retrieval
Information Retrieval.summary: Continuous generative retrievers powered by flow matching and diffusion sample multiple queries in item embedding space for parallel approximate nearest-neighbor (ANN) search under fixed retrieval budgets. However, optimizing distribution diversity or target-level interest separation ignores set-level retrieval geometry: sampled queries collapse onto overlapping ANN neighborhoods, while discrete top-K lookup and single-target supervision block end-to-end coverage optimization. We introduce CACO (Coverage-Aware Coordinated Optimization), a lightweight self-supervised post-training framework that coordinates queries from frozen flow-matching and diffusion retrievers toward complementary item coverage with negligible additional inference latency. CACO uses empirical retrieval frequencies across sampled reference queries as a relevance proxy, formulating a label-free coverage objective that improves recall across all 30 backbone-dataset settings in offline greedy selection experiments. To avoid the inference overhead of generating a large query pool, CACO employs a coordinated query adjustment network that combines inter-query bidirectional attention with gated relative directions, finally updating queries by bounded tangent-space projection and spherical retraction. During training, CACO applies tangential antithetic perturbations and measures each query's marginal gain via counterfactual single-query replacement, yielding an unbiased gradient estimator of smoothed set coverage across non-differentiable ANN search. On eight public benchmarks and an in-house 24-partition streaming industrial dataset, CACO improves Recall@100 by up to 23.7% and Recall@400 by up to 23.9% over the strongest baseline, cuts inter-query overlap by 53.3%-64.9%, and adds only 0.5%-3.0% inference latency.

Information Retrieval.title: Can LLMs Resolve Entity Conflicts in Domain Specific NLU Pipelines?
Information Retrieval.summary: Resolving entity conflicts is a critical step in Pipeline-based NLU architectures, especially when multiple extractors provide overlapping or conflicting outputs. Traditional rule-based entity conflict resolution methods often lack flexibility and are unscalable. In this work, we aim to study if the broad knowledge of LLMs can be leveraged to resolve entity conflicts in domain specific NLU pipelines. We present an experimental comparison between a traditional rule-based conflict resolution method, and two LLM-based approaches: a multi-shot prompting method using the Llama3.1-8B-Instruct model and a LoRA fine-tuned Llama3.1-8B-Instruct model. The evaluation was conducted under two setups: (1) a broad assessment of LLM's capability to match existing NLU pipeline output, and (2) a more controlled scenario assessing the LLM accuracy on human-labeled data. Results show that while multi-shot prompting offers ease of adaptation and rapid behavioral changes, the fine-tuned model delivers superior performance on complex, ambiguous cases. Ultimately, the best approach appears to be a combination of both strategies, leveraging multi-shot prompting's flexibility alongside the broad accuracy gains of LoRA fine-tuning for a more comprehensive performance.
Information Retrieval.comment: This work was completed in February, 2025

Information Retrieval.title: STARK: Moving towards Personalized Agents That Truly Learn and Remember
Information Retrieval.summary: Long-term memory is essential for personalized agentic systems that interact with users over long time periods, yet current architectures only capture what happened while leaving the reasoning of why it happened to be derived later by underlying LLMs.%, and silo knowledge within individual users. These events can, however, convey not only what a user experienced but also how that experience shaped their behavioral patterns. We introduce STARK, a dual-graph memory architecture which treats these events not just as nodes but also as edges between behavioral insights. STARK maintains an Episodic Graph which records interactions as temporally, causally, and semantically linked episodes; and an Insight Graph which represents LLM-extracted behavioral signals scored by how many events support them, connected by the very events that led to them. At inference, behavioral knowledge is retrieved directly from insight nodes grounded by event-as-edges, eliminating repeated episodic traversal. The event-as-edge structure also naturally enables projecting the knowledge graph into a relational embedding space where cross-user transfer becomes possible under shared contextual circumstances, allowing the system to infer missing insights for cold-start users. Evaluations show that STARK improves by 1.48 judge score on LongMemEval information extraction and 0.93 on LoCoMo open domain questions over state of the art. On the public LongLaMP abstract-generation benchmark, cross-user transfer improves open-ended judge scores by 0.7 points and ROUGE-L by 3 at 5% graph sparsity.

Information Retrieval.title: Exploring Semantic Table Search in Data Lakes
Information Retrieval.summary: Discovery of relevant datasets within data lakes remains a key challenge. Union and join search are effective techniques for discovering data when augmenting an existing table. In exploratory search, instead, keyword search is commonly adopted to find a relatively small set of highly relevant tables matching some search terms. In this context, semantic search is a new technique that exploits the presence of named entities in exemplar tuples used as queries and in target tables. Hence, keyword search and entity search are able to find a diverse set of tables. In this work, we propose \texttt{Thetis++}, which combines keyword and semantic table search to discover relevant tables that combine the semantic signal with the presence of exact keyword matches. Incorporating multiple paradigms and sources of information allow us to combine the best of multiple worlds. Therefore, we study many alternative techniques for combining rankings and evaluate these for the table search task in data lakes. We explore both unsupervised and supervised techniques, including TOPSIS. Finally, alternative to Thetis++ combining keyword and semantic relevance signals, we study a variant of learning-to-rank for the table search task in data lakes. Our evaluation highlights both the limitations of many standard approaches along with some promising directions offered by learned approaches. Furthermore, while indexes for keyword search are quite efficient, here we provide insights into how to improve the scalability of prefiltering techniques for semantic search, comparing LSH indexes with Hierarchical Navigable Small Worlds. Our experiments show that HNSW drastically improves the runtime of semantic table search by 4.7X on average whilst retaining the high-quality tables. Together, our findings plot the line for effective and efficient data discovery techniques for semantic data lakes.

Information Retrieval.title: DNA: Unlocking Depth Scaling in CTR Models
Information Retrieval.summary: Long user behavior sequences are among the strongest signals for click-through rate (CTR) prediction. Cross-attention makes these sequences practical for industrial ranking by keeping compute linear in sequence length. Yet the gains from stacking cross-attention layers taper off: on Taobao search, growing a cross-attention stack from 16 to 28 layers adds only 0.02 percentage points (pt) of AUC. We argue that the key-value side is the bottleneck. Each layer projects the same behavior sequence into keys and values, so adding depth gives the model more reads of a fixed sequence. We propose DNA (Dual-stream Nexus Attention), which lets the sequence itself evolve with depth. At each layer, the request representation (the search query, user features and scene) first reads the sequence. Each behavior token then attends to the updated request representation and uses what it reads to update itself, so the next layer reads a sequence shaped by the current request. The update runs once per request, all candidates share the resulting sequence, and both the reads and the update keep linear complexity in sequence length. At comparable forward FLOPs, DNA improves AUC over cross-attention stacks by 0.08 to 0.26 pt and keeps improving in the depth range where those stacks level off. DNA-4 is deployed in Taobao search. In an online A/B test against the production model, it improves CTR by 0.8% and GMV by 0.5%.

Information Retrieval.title: Uncontrolled source titles: When Nature, Science, and PNAS meet Scopus
Information Retrieval.summary: Bibliographic databases such as Scopus and Web of Science play a critical role in literature discovery, systematic reviews, bibliometric analyses, and research evaluation, yet their reliability depends on effective control of the quality of the bibliographic data. This study examines the problem of uncontrolled source titles in Scopus by comparing five possibly adopted journal-level retrieval strategies across three flagship journals-Nature, Science, and PNAS. Substantial discrepancies across retrieval results indicate persistent fragmentation in the source title field. A comparative analysis using the Web of Science Core Collection shows that no comparable degree of uncontrolled source-title variation is observed for the same journals. The study further explores possible mechanisms, including inheritance of different title forms from (different) upstream providers, automated parsing and OCR-related artifacts, and insufficient cross-validation. Based on these findings, the study proposes recommendations at both the user and database-provider levels to improve source-title normalization and strengthen source-level metadata governance, with implications for the accuracy and reproducibility of journal-level retrieval and evaluative uses.
Information Retrieval.comment: Forthcoming in Journal of Information Science

Information Retrieval.title: Generative News Recommendation Reproduces Popularity: A Memorization-Based Analysis
Information Retrieval.summary: Text-based generative recommenders can go beyond ranking existing items by directly generating item titles or other textual representations. In the news domain, this raises a societal concern that models may repeatedly surface already popular articles and thereby narrow the diversity of information to which users are exposed. We investigate training-data memorization as one mechanism behind this concentration. Using approximately 20 million browsing sessions from a Japanese news service, we continually trained an instruction-tuned Llama 3 8B model to generate the next article title in a session. The generated-title distribution was more concentrated and less diverse than the distribution of titles observed in the browsing logs. Frequently repeated target titles exhibited greater verbatim and approximate memorization, and more strongly memorized titles were generated in response to a wider range of prompts. These findings support a pathway in which popularity in behavioral logs becomes repeated training text, is preferentially memorized, and is subsequently reproduced by a generative recommender. An exploratory target-level deduplication condition reduced both memorization and output concentration, while substantially reducing the training-set size and recommendation accuracy. Our results suggest that popularity bias in generative recommendation may arise not only from user preferences or ranking objectives, but also from the model's tendency to reproduce frequently encountered strings, with important implications for information diversity on news platforms.
Information Retrieval.comment: The 11th International Workshop on Application of Big Data for Computational Social Science (ABCSS2026 @ IEEE BigData 2026)

Information Retrieval.title: Variance-Optimal Counterfactual Policy Design for Sample-Efficient Online A/B Testing
Information Retrieval.summary:
Online A/B testing is the standard approach for evaluating changes to user-facing systems, such as a new recommendation or ranking policy, before deployment. While the difference-in-means estimator of a standard A/B test is unbiased, it often suffers from high variance. When the treatment and production policies choose the same actions with similar probabilities, the resulting observations can add noise while providing little information about the difference between the policies. Consequently, A/B tests can require large amounts of traffic and long durations to detect small treatment effects. Existing variance-reduction methods mainly improve the estimator after the data-collection scheme has been fixed, and recent overlap-aware designs only optimize a single traffic split between the two policies; thereby, they cannot direct traffic to the actions on which the policies disagree.
  In this paper, we jointly optimize how actions are sampled and how the resulting observations are used to estimate the treatment effect. Our contributions are two-fold. First, building on pairwise off-policy evaluation, we derive the variance-optimal action-level logging policy for estimating the average treatment effect between two policies, which has a closed-form solution for any fixed control variate. Second, we use historical logs to jointly optimize the logging policy and a control variate to further reduce variance. Our experimental results in simulated policy A/B tests show that our designs estimate the average treatment effect more accurately than existing variance reduction methods on every evaluated setting, while generally improving statistical power and reducing how often the worse policy is selected. As a result, our designs enable practitioners to reach reliable deployment decisions with considerably less online traffic.

Information Retrieval.title: AutoRAGBench: A Benchmark for LLM Agents Automating RAG System Development
Information Retrieval.summary: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is a well-established paradigm for augmenting large language models (LLMs) with information retrieved from external corpora. However, developing effective RAG systems requires substantial engineering effort and iterative experimentation, as effective design choices vary across tasks and domains. With rapid advances in LLM agent capabilities, we ask how well these agents can autonomously build RAG systems and how effectively they can improve them through iteration. In this paper, we propose AutoRAGBench, the first benchmark to evaluate how well LLM agents develop RAG systems from scratch in an open code space. It comprises nine RAG system development tasks. For each task, agents build RAG systems from scratch without starter code or prescribed strategies, under a six-hour budget on a single H800 GPU. They analyze task data, implement RAG pipelines, and iteratively refine their designs based on experimental feedback. We evaluate nine agent configurations and analyze both the effectiveness of the resulting RAG systems and their development trajectories. GPT-6.1 Sol with Codex CLI achieves the highest average score of 56.1. The composite Human-SOTA baseline averages 44.4. These results show that LLM agents can automate effective RAG system development. When starting from a human-designed system on each of seven tasks, GPT-6.1 Sol with Codex CLI improves the score by 16.6 points on average.

Information Retrieval.title: MMIntentFlow: An Intent-Driven Real-Time Multimodal Search System with Image-Text Queries at Xiaohongshu
Information Retrieval.summary: Multimodal search with image-text queries helps users find notes in user-generated content (UGC) communities and serves as a key search tool for multimodal search agents. For such queries, query-note relevance depends on the user's retrieval intent and cannot be determined by visual or topical similarity alone. Simply reranking visual search results cannot fully address this challenge, as notes relevant to the user's intent may be missing from the initial candidate set. This motivates explicit intent modeling to align candidate retrieval and reranking under consistent relevance criteria. We present MMIntentFlow, an intent-driven real-time multimodal search system deployed at Xiaohongshu over an index on the order of ten billion entries. MMIntentFlow represents retrieval objectives with a hierarchical intent taxonomy and uses intent-specific relevance criteria to guide data construction, representation learning, and reranking. An offline agentic data workflow acquires candidates and verifies their relevance under these criteria to produce training supervision. The embedding model combines intent-aware contrastive learning, graded ranking, and distribution distillation, while a compact reranker assesses query-candidate evidence conditioned on predicted hierarchical intents. Evaluations demonstrate that MMIntentFlow delivers substantial gains in search engagement while supporting real-time search at industrial scale. In a user-level A/B test on the Xiaohongshu platform, MMIntentFlow outperforms the existing production system based on visual search followed by reranking, achieving relative gains of 28.17% in Top-4 query click-through rate, 18.96% in query click-through rate, and 12.56% in average time spent on search results pages per user. Production monitoring records an end-to-end P50 latency of 1.07 s.
Information Retrieval.comment: 29 pages, 7 figures. Technical report. v2: Renamed IntentFlow to MMIntentFlow; technical content unchanged

Information Retrieval.title: Can Explanations Improve Recommendations? Evidence from Prediction-Informed Explanations
Information Retrieval.summary: Recommender systems are central to digital platforms, yet they face a fundamental trade-off between accuracy and explainability: Black-box models achieve strong performance but lack interpretability needed for trust and adoption, while existing explainable AI approaches often generate explanations post hoc or sacrifice accuracy. We challenge this view, proposing that explanations, when designed as an integral component of the system and aligned with predictions, can improve \emph{both} interpretability and accuracy. We introduce RecPIE (Recommendation with Prediction-Informed Explanations), a framework that jointly optimizes recommendation predictions and natural-language explanations. RecPIE embeds explanation generation into the learning loop: predictions guide explanation generation (prediction-informed explanations), which are fed back to refine subsequent predictions (explanation-informed predictions) via alternating training. The LLM is fine-tuned using LoRA and reinforcement learning with a usefulness reward derived from recommendation accuracy. We evaluate RecPIE on large-scale point-of-interest recommendation data from Google Maps, where consumer preferences span diverse place categories. RecPIE improves predictive accuracy by 1.7-3.6\% over state-of-the-art baselines and outperforms the strongest full-data baselines using only 25\% of the training data. In human evaluations with 566 participants, RecPIE explanations are preferred 61.5% of the time (versus 16.6% for the best baseline) and rated closer to human-generated explanations. Together, these results suggest that insights about consumer behavior and AI decisions need not be imposed externally or generated post hoc; they can be learned as an integral component \emph{within} the AI systems, allowing systems themselves to discover which insights are useful for improving predictive performance.

Information Retrieval.title: Learning Generative Ranking Policies for Whole-Page Optimization
Information Retrieval.summary: A recommendation page is consumed as a whole: the items on it compete for attention and complement one another, so the best page is not simply the individually best items placed side by side. We study whole-page optimization, which selects and orders the items on a page jointly to maximize the score of the page. The number of possible pages grows combinatorially, so good pages must be generated rather than enumerated. Some generative re-ranking methods use the same page-level training signal for every choice in a sampled page. Others imitate target pages built before training, which remain largely fixed as the generator improves. We address both limitations with one local page-level objective, which repeatedly moves the current generator toward pages with higher score. This objective splits exactly into one training target per position, and each target compares candidates at the same partial page by the scores of the complete pages they lead to. Every position therefore learns to choose the item that is better for the whole page, rather than the item that looks best on its own. We call this procedure whole-page policy improvement. On two public datasets, KuaiRand-1K and RL4RS-SeqSlate, which cover multi-objective item selection and constrained ordering, and on an industrial dataset of logged pages, our method outperforms the evaluated generative re-ranking baselines. On a synthetic benchmark with a known optimal page, it also comes closest to the optimum, showing that its improvements come from better whole-page decisions.

Information Retrieval.title: VideoTrail: Interactive Video Foraging Through Hierarchical Visualization
Information Retrieval.summary: People often watch videos to find information, but locating relevant moments can be difficult and time-consuming. Existing strategies like scrubbing rely primarily on visual scanning and linear search, providing limited support for goal-directed navigation. We present VideoTrail, an AI-powered browser extension that supports information seeking in videos through a hierarchical visualization. Inspired by information foraging theory, VideoTrail surfaces semantic and structural cues as information scent, creating an explorable roadmap of segments. The system is multimodal and adaptive, prioritizing visual or textual scent based on the video's content. In a user study (N=16), VideoTrail helped participants efficiently locate key moments and enabled new navigation strategies compared to traditional timelines, highlighting how exposing an adaptive video structure can enhance goal-directed viewing.

Information Retrieval.title: Close the Loop on the Retrievability Gap
Information Retrieval.summary: A frozen vision-language encoder now guides image restoration and later indexes what it produced. Over a fixed set of eighteen pansharpening systems on one WorldView-III test set, the fidelity index that ranks them, $Q2^n$ with a reference and HQNR without one, picks the less retrievable of two systems one time in three and one in two; the disagreement lies between the pixel-supervised and the language-conditioned family, and even the best system falls short of the reference, small objects first. We call this the retrievability gap and trace it to the area weighting of position-averaged losses. LEDGER closes the loop around the encoder: it indexes the input into a set of named concepts, generates, re-encodes the output alone with the same frozen encoder, and minimises a set-level soft-Jaccard loss on the coverage of that set, a label-free target available at test time, so that every present concept of a scale receives a gradient share independent of its area. Measured outside the loop by label-grounded probes, held-out retrievers, language-free evaluators, detectors and human raters, LEDGER matches or exceeds the strongest baselines in fidelity on four sensors, raises retrieval by seven to nine points within its vocabulary and two to five outside it, closes two thirds of the reduced-resolution gap to the reference, lifts extraction on raw SpaceNet imagery above the vendor product in each of four cities, and transfers to existing generators as a training-only loss at no inference cost.

Mathematical Software.title: Fast Mixed-Precision Real Evaluation
Mathematical Software.summary: Evaluating real numbers to high precision is important in computational science, numerical computing, and in hardware and software design. Efficient algorithms exist for computing arithmetic operations and common elementary functions, but composing these primitives into larger expressions remains a challenge. The typical expression-evaluation algorithm computes all primitives in the expression to a uniform precision, doubling that precision until a sufficiently-accurate result is achieved. This is wasteful: usually only a few operations really need to be performed at high precision, and the bulk of the expression could be computed at a much lower, faster precision. However, no rigorous algorithm currently exists to compute these non-uniform precision assignments, nor to leverage non-uniform precision to reduce the number of primitive computations needed to evaluate an expression. We propose a new algorithm for deriving such rigorous precision assignments and reducing the number of primitive computations needed. This algorithm can leverage results computed at lower precisions to analytically determine a precision for each primitive that will result in a sufficiently-accurate evaluation. It can also use information from constant subexpressions, movability flags, and repeat flags to skip the computation of certain primitives, further reducing the time to evaluate real expressions. Our implementation, Reval, achieves an average speed-up of 3.97x compared to the widely-used Sollya tool, with the speed-up increasing to 9.26x on the most difficult inputs. A detailed evaluation shows that this speed-up results from both assigning lower precisions to the majority of primitives and from computing fewer primitives overall.

Mathematical Software.title: Certified pandigital approximations of $π$, $γ$, $δ$ and $e$
Mathematical Software.summary: In 2004 Erich Friedman asked for the best approximations of $π$, $e$, the Euler-Mascheroni constant $γ$ and Feigenbaum's constant $δ$ that use each of the digits $1,\dots,n$ exactly once, with addition, subtraction, multiplication, division, exponentiation, parentheses and the decimal point. We determine the optimal expressions for $π$, $γ$ and $δ$ for every $n \le 9$, with the digits in any order and in increasing order, and for $e$ when $n \le 6$. The optima are found by exhaustive search and certified by an independent algorithm that encloses every expression rigorously and decides each candidate with Arb and exact arithmetic; a second certified computation covers intermediate values of any size. Twenty-one entries improve the published records; for $π$ with the digits 1-9 the optimal error is $2.81\cdot 10^{-14}$. For $e$, whose records come from identities between power towers, we prove that Bamberger's formula is optimal within the natural family of such identities. All code and certificates are public.
Mathematical Software.comment: 50 pages, 1 figure. Code, data and certificates: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24356239

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Variants of Beam Search for DiskANN
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: Graph-based data structures such as DiskANN, HNSW, and NSG constitute the state of the art for large-scale approximate nearest-neighbor (ANN) search. Indyk and Xu introduced the notion of $α$-reachable graphs, which include graphs built by DiskANN's slow-preprocessing construction, and proved that greedy search achieves an approximation factor of $\tfrac{α+1}{α-1}$. Independently, Al-Jazzazi et al. proposed adaptive beam search (ABS) with a relaxation parameter $γ> 0$, showing a $\tfrac{2}γ$ approximation on navigable graphs ($α\approx 1$), where greedy search admits no guarantees. In this work, we unify and generalize these results by proving that ABS with parameter $γ$ on $α$-reachable graphs achieves an approximation of $\tfrac{α+1}{α(γ+1)-1}$ for any metric. Moreover, on sorted $α$-reachable graphs (introduced by Gollapudi et al.) under the $\ell_2$ metric, we obtain the tighter bound $\max\bigl(\tfracα{α(γ+1)-1}, \tfrac{α^{2}+1}{α^{2}(γ+1)-1}\bigr)$. Beyond these theoretical results, we design a beam predictor using features inspired by fine-grained analysis of ABS, trained via a constrained objective that minimizes mean distance computations subject to a target recall. On three 100-million-point benchmarks, using graphs built by DiskANN's practical construction, beam predictor lowers mean query latency on SSD-resident indices at matched recall by up to $29.6\%$ relative to classical beam search (CBS). Relative to ABS, it is faster in $11$ of $15$ settings, by up to $6.5\%$, and at most $1.4\%$ slower in the other $4$; at $95\%$ recall, its advantage over ABS grows from $0.8$--$4.2\%$ for $100$ neighbors to $4.6$--$5.6\%$ for $500$ neighbors. In memory, it needs $1.3$--$23.7\%$ fewer distance computations than CBS and $0.0$--$3.9\%$ fewer than ABS.
Data Structures and Algorithms.comment: 22 pages, 1 figure, 9 tables

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: An Efficient Algorithm for Matroid Cups
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: We design a polynomial-time algorithm for matroid cups with $O(1)$ discrepancy. Our matroid cups algorithm design consists of a sequence of reductions to simpler instances, culminating in $O(n)$ instances of matroid cups where the matroid has rank 1.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: End-to-End Quantum Algorithm for Differential Equations: Application to Simulating a Biomolecular System
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: Quantum algorithms for differential equations have the potential for substantial algorithmic speedups over classical methods. However, they rely on certain assumptions and abstract oracle specifications that leave their practical feasibility and computational advantages for realistic applications unclear. Here we formalize the concept of an end-to-end quantum algorithm for differential equations as one that accepts classical inputs and returns classical outputs, and provide implementations for algorithmic primitives in constructing such algorithms. We present a tailored end-to-end quantum algorithm for the linearized Poisson-Boltzmann (LPB) equation, a partial differential equation (PDE) with variable coefficients widely used in simulating a biomolecular system. We explicitly implement all aspects of the algorithm, from preparing an initial state to generating a quantum solution and estimating properties of the system. In particular, we develop a new discrete representation for variable-coefficient PDEs on a grid that enables efficient implementation of the operator oracle, and build on a recent technique based on optimal wavelet preconditioning to generate a quantum solution with a cost independent of the condition number of the discretized operator. We show the algorithm can be implemented by quantum circuits of size polylogarithmic in both the number of grid points $N_g$ and the inverse of the desired accuracy $\varepsilon$, with an overall gate cost polylogarithmic in $N_g$ and quasilinear in $1/\varepsilon$. We also show the classical preprocessing to construct the circuits has polylogarithmic cost in $N_g$ and $1/\varepsilon$. Our work provides a concrete end-to-end quantum algorithm for a PDE of practical value, demonstrates an exponential improvement in scaling with $N_g$ over classical methods, and provides a foundation for assessing its potential quantum advantage in practice.
Data Structures and Algorithms.comment: 61 pages, 11 figures, 3 tables

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Improved Bounds for Directed SSSP in Sparse and Intermediate-Density Graphs
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: We give a deterministic algorithm for exact single-source shortest paths (SSSP) in directed graphs with $n$ vertices, $m$ edges and nonnegative real edge weights. In the comparison-addition model, with unit-cost elementary operations on $O(\log(n+m+2))$-bit integer words, its running time for $m=O(n)$ is $O(n\sqrt{\log n}(\log\log n)^{1/4})$. For $m=Θ(n)$, this reduces the exponent of $\log\log n$ in the bound of Duan, Mao, Shu and Yin from $1/2$ to $1/4$ and removes the factor $(\log\log\log n)^{1/4}$ from the sparse bound stated in a public draft. The same algorithm improves on the bound of Duan et al. over a range of intermediate densities. At $m=Θ(n\sqrt{\log\log n})$, the running time is $O(n\sqrt{\log n}(\log\log n)^{5/8})$, reducing their exponent from $3/4$ to $5/8$. This is a consequence of a uniform bound for intermediate densities up to any fixed multiple of $n\log\log n$ edges; its validity range is larger than the range of strict improvement.
Data Structures and Algorithms.comment: 69 pages

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Properties of Concurrent Algorithms that Allow Asynchrony
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
In this paper, we investigate the conditions under which a concurrent system is able to guarantee convergence deterministically even without synchronization. In general, an algorithm is deemed asynchrony-tolerant iff the global states form a DAG even if the nodes can execute based on outdated/stale values from each other. In this paper, we show that the induction of a partial order (PO) among the local states visited by individual nodes is necessary and sufficient to allow asynchrony.
  There are certain problems for which the predicate that defines the problem, itself, induces a partial order among the local states (called \textit{PO-inducing problems}). On the other hand, \textit{non-PO-inducing problems} is another class of problems in which a predicate defining the problem cannot induce a partial order among local states. We introduce these classes of problems. We study example PO-inducing and non-PO-inducing problems, and provide example PO-inducing (in other words, asynchrony-tolerant) algorithms (algorithms under which any node traverses a partial order of local states) for all these problems.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Unique Decoding of Reed-Solomon and Related Codes for Semi-Adversarial Errors
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
Motivated by recent developments in coding theory, particular in list-decoding, we introduce a new error model which we call semi-adversarial errors. This error model bridges between fully random errors and fully adversarial errors by allowing some symbols of a message to be corrupted by an adversary while others are replaced with uniformly random symbols.
  We seek to understand optimal efficient unique decoding algorithms in the semi-adversarial model. For interleaved Reed--Solomon (IRS), folded Reed--Solomon (FRS) and univariate multiplicity codes, we design decoding algorithms running in near-linear time for most mixtures of random and adversarial errors. Our analysis matches the information-theoretic optimum for semi-adversarial errors.
  Our algorithm for interleaved Reed--Solomon codes is an improved implementation of the decoding algorithm by Bleichenbacher--Kiayias--Yung (BKY) for fully random errors. We use a monomial-tracking technique to analyze its performance in this new semi-adversarial errors. Inspired by the BKY algorithm, we use interpolations to extend our approach to the settings of folded Reed--Solomon and multiplicity codes, resulting in fast algorithms for unique decoding against semi-adversarial errors. Our new decoders for FRS and multiplicity codes replace the sophisticated root-finding step in traditional algorithms, such as the Guruswami--Wang algorithm, with a straightforward polynomial long division. Analysis of these algorithms requires more robust monomial-tracking arguments than IRS codes.
Data Structures and Algorithms.comment: 43 pages, full version to appear in IEEE Transactions on Information Theory

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Efficient Classical Algorithms for Ground Energy Estimation of Fermions with Conjugate-Pair Orbital Interactions
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: Estimating the ground energy of interacting fermions is central to quantum many-body physics, and recent quantum algorithms provide polynomial-time guarantees for some structured families. Classical approaches commonly rely on quantum Monte Carlo, where the sign problem is a major obstacle. However, even when a nonnegative expansion without sign problem is available, rigorous guarantees for rapid mixing are still far from well understood. In this paper, we give an efficient classical randomized algorithm for approximating the ground energy of fermionic Hamiltonians with conjugate hopping matrices and conjugate-paired orbital interactions, which includes the attractive Hubbard models. This guarantee not only holds without a physical spectral gap or a weak-coupling assumption, but also covers interactions beyond onsite density attractions. Technically, we first reduce ground-energy estimation to partition-function estimation and then use a discretization with controlled energy error to obtain a nonnegative weighted sum of squared determinant moduli and then apply the Chen--Liu log-concave counting theorem. In addition, we obtain a sharper arithmetic bound by controlling how many independent sampling runs and matrix updates are needed, and using sparse matrices to reduce the cost of each update.
Data Structures and Algorithms.comment: 41 pages, 1 figure

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Polylogarithmic Approximation for Packing Convex Polyhedra
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
We study translational packing of convex polyhedra in three dimensions. Given $n$ convex polyhedra in $\mathbb{R}^3$, we seek a placement with pairwise disjoint interiors that minimizes the volume of an axis-parallel bounding box. Constant-factor approximation algorithms are known when rotations are allowed, but no approximation guarantee was previously known for arbitrary convex polyhedra with fixed orientations.
  A central difficulty is that, unlike in the plane, the total volume and the coordinate extents of the objects do not provide a useful lower bound on the optimum: even objects with small total volume and small diameter may require a container of large volume. We overcome this difficulty using a better geometric lower bound based on a surprising connection to Wang and Zahl's celebrated recent proof of the three-dimensional Kakeya conjecture.
  Using this, we obtain a polynomial-time $n^{o(1)}$-approximation algorithm. A recent strengthening of Wang and Zahl's theorem claimed by OpenAI gives a polylogarithmic approximation ratio for the same algorithm.
  Our ideas extend to bin and strip packing: for any fixed $δ>0$, we obtain the same approximation guarantees for translational packing of convex polyhedra whose coordinate widths are at most a $1-δ$ fraction of the corresponding container widths.
Data Structures and Algorithms.comment: 28 pages, 8 figures

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Differentially Private Preconditioned Power Iteration Method for Principal Component Analysis that Adapts to the Coherence
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: In Principal Component Analysis (PCA), we are given as input a matrix $A\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d}$ and an integer $k\leq d$, and the goal is to find the top $k$ right-singular vectors of $A$. We consider the setting where each row of $A$ is the private data of an individual, and we design an $(ε,δ)$-differentially private algorithm whose utility guarantee improves with the coherence of the input matrix. Prior works were either restricted to the case $k=1$ or ensured significantly weaker privacy protections. Our algorithm is based on a preconditioned variant of the power iteration method that is designed to significantly reduce the noise needed to ensure privacy.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Exact guarantees and faster algorithms for $k$-rollercoasters
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
For $k\ge3$, a $k$-rollercoaster is a sequence of distinct values whose maximal increasing and decreasing runs all have length at least $k$. We discover the maximum guaranteed length $f_k(n)$ of $k$-rollercoasters appearing as subsequences of $n$-point permutations. In particular, letting $q=k-1$, we prove that $f_k(n)= \lceil n/q\rceil$ for $n\ge2q^2$, $f_k(n)= 2q-\lfloor \sqrt{2q^2-n}\rfloor$ for $q^2<n<2q^2$ and $f_k(n)= 0$ otherwise. We prove that the guarantees are tight by constructing an $n$-point permutation whose longest $k$-rollercoaster has exactly $f_k(n)$ points. Our proof extends Seidenberg's argument [Journal of the London Mathematical Society, 1959] for proving the Erdős--Szekeres theorem by representing points in a subsequence with respect to the lengths of longest monotonic (increasing and decreasing) subsequences that reach each point.
  The combinatorial proof yields a deterministic comparison-based algorithm that finds a rollercoaster of length at least $f_k(n)$ in $O(n\log f_k(n))$ time and $O(n)$ space for $n>q^2$. Independently, we give an $O(nk\log k)$-time, $O(nk)$-space algorithm for a longest $k$-rollercoaster, improving the previous $O(nk^2)$ bound. We use the dynamic program of Gawrychowski et al. [STACS 2019, Algorithmica 2022], and process its weighted predecessor queries through monotone subsequences with finger-search trees. Both algorithms return such subsequences.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Learning Multinomial Logits in $O(n \log n)$ time
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: A Multinomial Logit (MNL) model is composed of a finite universe of items $[n]=\{1,\dots,n\}$, each assigned a positive weight. A query specifies an admissible subset---called a slate---and the model chooses one item from that slate with probability proportional to its weight. This query model is also known as the Plackett--Luce model or conditional sampling oracle in the literature. Although MNLs have been studied extensively, a basic computational question remains open: given query access to slates, how efficiently can we learn weights so that, for every slate, the induced choice distribution is within total variation distance $\varepsilon$ of the ground truth? This question is central to MNL learning and has direct implications for modern recommender system interfaces. We provide both adaptive and non-adaptive algorithms for this task. Our first adaptive algorithm makes $O(\frac{n\log n}{\varepsilon^2})$ queries and learns every choice distribution in total variation distance $\varepsilon$. We also provide a second adaptive algorithm that with $O(\frac{n \log n}{\varepsilon^3})$ queries provides a stronger guarantee: each choice distribution is approximated to a multiplicative $1\pm\varepsilon$ error (except for subsets of mass smaller than $\varepsilon$). We complement these algorithms with lower bounds of $Ω(\frac{n\log n}{\varepsilon^2})$ for total variation distance and $Ω(\frac{n \log n}{\varepsilon^3})$ for the multiplicative error guarantee, showing the optimality of our adaptive algorithms. Our non-adaptive algorithm makes $O\left(\frac{n^{2}}{\varepsilon^{3}}\log n \log\frac{n}{\varepsilon}\right)$ queries to obtain guarantees under the multiplicative error notion. We complement this result with an $Ω(\frac{n^2 \log n}{\varepsilon^2})$ lower bound for any non-adaptive algorithm, showing that our algorithm is almost tight in $n$ (within a $\log n$ factor).
Data Structures and Algorithms.comment: We prove two new results. In particular, we provide a $O(n \log n / \varepsilon^2)$ algorithm for learning in $d_1$ error, which closes one of the main questions left open in the previous versions of the paper

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Approximation Algorithms for Asymmetric Multi-Path TSP
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
Asymmetric Multi-Path TSP is the generalization of the Asymmetric Traveling Salesperson Problem where we are looking for $k$ walks, each with prescribed start $s_i$ and prescribed end $t_i$, such that every vertex is visited by at least one of the walks. The objective is to minimize the total length of all walks. In general, it is NP-hard to find any approximation for this problem in polynomial time (even if the approximation factor is allowed to depend on the number of vertices). We show that one can obtain an $O(k)$-approximation in time $n^{O(k)}$, answering an open question by Friggstad [2013].
  For the special case where all tour start vertices $s_i$ are identical and all end vertices $t_i$ are identical, we obtain an $O(k)$-approximation in polynomial time, as well as an $(O(\frac{1}ε), 1+ε)$-bicriteria approximation. For the multi-depot setting, where $s_i =t_i$ for all $i$, we obtain a constant-factor approximation in polynomial time.
  Finally, our results imply improved constant-factor approximation algorithms for Asymmetric Regret-Bounded Vehicle Routing and unit-weight Path ATSP.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: SotSort: a stable quicksort with a tunable buffer
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: SotSort is a stable comparison sort whose single code path runs with anything from a fixed 16 KB buffer to a full n-element buffer. Its core is a stable quicksort that partitions blocks through the buffer and gathers them with rotations. This report summarises the design, states which parts are borrowed, and compares an implementation against blitsort, fluxsort, glidesort, driftsort, GrailSort and WikiSort. On one 2-vCPU machine, with 32- and 64-bit integers, the constant-memory mode takes between 0.32 and 0.82 of blitsort's time on 17 of 22 input classes and between 0.92 and 1.07 on the other five. With a comparator that rules out the vector partition it is slower than blitsort on 4 of 11 classes, by up to 2.3 times on sorted input. Against Virtual-Memory Powersort, on its authors' own harness and with the same auxiliary memory, the first measurement lost on most inputs; after three changes it located (one of them adopts that algorithm's paging scheme), SotSort is faster in 43 of 48 type and input combinations at n=10^6 on two machines. At n=10^7 on partially sorted integers it is between 7% faster and 7% slower depending on the machine, and on near-random input it is still slower: by 9% on integers at n=10^7, and by 5 to 17% at n=10^6 when comparisons are expensive. All numbers are preliminary.
Data Structures and Algorithms.comment: 5 pages. v2: comparison with Virtual-Memory Powersort on its authors' harness, two machines. Code, tests and raw measurements: https://github.com/sotomayorlucas/sotsort

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Tight Bounds for Distance-Unbiased Sorting
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: We study elitist randomized local search for sorting permutations. In this model, each iteration considers a possible exchange of two positions. The entries are exchanged if and only if they are in the wrong order. We introduce \emph{distance-unbiased} selection rules, which may choose an arbitrary distribution over exchange distances but sample uniformly among all pairs at each chosen distance. For static rules, we prove that the optimal worst-case high-probability runtime is $Θ(n(\log n)^2)$. This establishes the asymptotic optimality of the harmonic sorter within this class and partially resolves an open question of Olesker-Taylor. We then allow the distance distribution to change either according to a predetermined schedule or adaptively using the current permutation and the entire history. Matching upper and lower bounds show that both classes have optimal runtime $Θ(n(\log n)^2/\log\log n)$. Thus, scheduled adjustments of the distance distribution improve the optimal static worst-case runtime by a factor of $Θ(\log\log n)$, while full-information adaptation provides no further asymptotic improvement.
Data Structures and Algorithms.comment: Submitted to EvoCOP 2027

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Running-Time Lower Bounds under FPT $\neq$ W[1]
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: We revisit running-time lower bounds historically based on the Exponential Time Hypothesis. Our case study asks how much of their quantitative content can be recovered under the assumption FPT $\neq$ W[1]. The reductions encode the choice of a clique in few bits and control the target parameter in terms of that encoding. This makes a sufficiently fast algorithm for the target problem yield a fixed-parameter algorithm for deciding whether a graph has a clique of the requested size. We obtain twelve lower bounds for deterministic algorithms across graph, string, and integer feasibility problems, including bounds that hold under structural restrictions. In several cases the same function of the parameter appears in the exponent as in the historical bound, with the additional requirement that the cutoff for any prescribed saving in the exponent be computable.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Guided Cuckoo Filter: Full-Pipeline Insertion Optimization
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: Cuckoo filters are widely deployed as space-efficient alternatives to Bloom filters, supporting fast lookups, insertions, and deletions. However, their insertion cost grows steeply at high load factors because the standard insertion procedure is entirely unguided: it places each fingerprint into whichever candidate bucket happens to be tried first, and when both candidates are full, it displaces a random victim in a random walk. These blind random choices occur at two distinct stages of the insertion pipeline, the initial placement decision and the eviction victim selection, yet each stage can be independently replaced with a guided, informed decision. We propose the \emph{Guided Cuckoo Filter}, which optimizes the entire insertion pipeline by steering both stages. At the placement stage, the filter compares the occupancy of both candidate buckets and inserts into the less loaded one, applying the power-of-two-choice principle to reduce how often eviction chains are triggered. At the eviction stage, the filter preferentially displaces the most recently inserted element, whose alternate bucket carries latent randomness that shortens the resulting chain. Because these two guided decisions target orthogonal bottlenecks, eviction frequency and eviction chain length, their benefits compose multiplicatively. Experiments on cuckoo filters with $2^{22}$ slots confirm that the fully guided insertion reduces per-insertion kicks by up to $3.1\times$ at 96\% load and cumulative total kicks by 63\% at the practical capacity ceiling of 95\% load, with negligible computational overhead.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Below Three: A 2.8027-Approximation for Moldable Precedence Scheduling
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: We study makespan minimisation for nonpreemptive moldable jobs with arbitrary precedence constraints on identical processors. Each job runs on a chosen number of processors that remains fixed throughout its execution. Allocating more processors to a job can shorten its execution, but may increase total work and delay other jobs. We assume nonincreasing processing times, nondecreasing work, and a convex duration--work relation after dominated allocations are removed. This model includes jobs with concave speedup, for which Jansen and Zhang obtained a $3.291919\ldots$-approximation. Independently and concurrently with our work, Chen obtained a $3.016208\ldots$-approximation for the full convex model and a $2.973912\ldots$-approximation for concave speedup. We give a deterministic polynomial-time $2.8027$-approximation for the full convex model and every number of processors. Our result breaks the factor-three barrier for this model and also improves the approximation guarantee for concave speedup.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Fast Computation of Lowest Common Ancestor in Version Control Commit Graph
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
The problem of finding the lowest common ancestor in the commit graph arises when a user wants to merge two (or more) development branches: for example, to add their own development into a common branch. At that moment, the version control system must determine the merge base - the common ancestor of the latest commits of the branches, in order to show the mutual difference between the branches. The problem is complicated by the fact that the commit graph is not a tree but an arbitrary acyclic graph. Moreover, if there is no common ancestor, searching for one may require traversing the entire graph. Traversing a graph with several million vertices takes tens of seconds, which becomes noticeable to users.
  We show that the commit graph has additional structure - supporting branches - and that this can be used to speed up the algorithm. By extracting supporting branches, the graph can be preprocessed and the search for the lowest common ancestor can be significantly accelerated. Moreover, if removing the supporting branches decomposes the graph into connected components of bounded size, the lowest common ancestor query can be answered in time comparable to searching for a common ancestor within a single component only.
  We present an algorithm running in time $O(δ_Gm_c + n_s\log^2 n_s + m_s\log n_s)$ and requiring $O(d)$ preprocessed data per vertex, where $δ_G$ is the maximum out-degree of a vertex in $G$, $n_c$ and $m_c$ are the maximum numbers of vertices and edges in a connected component formed after removing the supporting branches, $n_s$ is the number of supporting branches, $m_s$ is the number of edges in the reachability graph between the supporting branches, and $d$ is the maximum number of supporting branches adjacent to any single component.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Improved Rank Aggregation under Fairness Constraint
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
Aggregating multiple input rankings into a consensus ranking is essential in various fields such as social choice theory, hiring, college admissions, web search, and databases. A major challenge is that the optimal consensus ranking might be biased against individual candidates or groups, especially those from marginalized communities. This concern has led to recent studies focusing on fairness in rank aggregation. The goal is to ensure that candidates from different groups are fairly represented in the top-$k$ positions of the aggregated ranking.
  We study this fair rank aggregation problem by considering the Kendall tau as the underlying metric.
