We systematically compare how categorical and continuous prediction shape learned dynamics under both next-token and iterative whole-frame generation. These choices are often bundled in approaches such as autoregressive token models and whole-frame flow matching. We design controlled 2D and 3D environments and evaluate dynamics validity, calibration, and visual quality. In 2D with lossless visual encoding, categorical models achieve higher rollout validity with less training compute, particularly for stochastic entities. Among categorical models, greedy decoding produces the highest rollout validity, while sampling from a next-token model yields the best-calibrated stochastic predictions. Failures in continuous models, such as disappearing game characters, echo those seen in more complex environments. Here, known dynamics let us measure their impact. In 3D, categorical models also achieve stronger long-horizon performance with less training compute. Even models with lossy tokenization remain competitive on semantic accuracy and FVD, despite lower next-frame RGB accuracy. Together, these findings make a strong case for categorical prediction as a compute-efficient route to learning world dynamics.

Machine Learning.title: Multi-Task Self-Evolving Harnesses with the Agent as Its Own Optimizer
Machine Learning.summary: A harness is the code around a language model agent that organizes prompts, calls tools, manages context, and controls execution. As models grow stronger, recent work has begun to let agents improve their own harnesses, a line of work known as self-evolving harnesses. In most existing methods, a separate proposer running on a human-designed harness modifies the solver's harness, and a separate harness is evolved for each benchmark. Real-world tasks come from many domains, so both the evolution and the evaluation of a harness should cover a diverse range of tasks. We propose a framework close to recursive self-improvement: the same frozen model, on the same version of the harness, first solves tasks as the solver and then, as the proposer, reads the complete run records and directly edits the harness that runs it. Each evolution batch draws tasks from five benchmarks in different domains. To measure generalization, training and held-out tasks are strictly separated, and we additionally evaluate on five out-of-distribution benchmarks not used in the first stage. The design borrows from deep learning training and has two stages, multi-task pretraining and continual training. Starting from a 49-line seed harness, the harnesses evolved by GLM-5.3 and GPT-5.6 Sol gain about 5 points on the in-distribution benchmarks. They are on par with Claude Code and Codex on these benchmarks, and the GPT-5.6 Sol harness is also on par with Codex on five out-of-distribution benchmarks. The weaker model of each family benefits less: GLM-5.3-Flash gains less than 2 points, and the harness evolved by GPT-5.6 Luna scores below the seed. Continued evolution on Claw-Eval in the second stage further improves GPT-5.6 Sol and GLM-5.3-Flash on its multimodal tasks. We also analyze where the gains come from and the mechanisms that emerged during evolution. Code: https://github.com/xqkkk/self-evolving-harness.

Machine Learning.title: Anchors That Move Without Collapsing: Exclusive-Region Anchor Routing for Vision Transformers
Machine Learning.summary: Anchor tokens let a vision transformer exchange global information through a few summaries, but nothing forces different anchors to summarise different things. On one shared backbone we show that a Perceiver-style pathway and an AnchorFormer pathway collapse to a single summary, the latter despite its mass normalisation (pooling-map similarity 0.99), while other soft pathways, including Representative Attention, stay partly redundant (0.59-0.79). These results concern the routing modules inside our block, not the full published models. An exclusive partition of the patch grid cannot collapse by construction, and matched component by component it is 2.4-3.6 points more accurate than Representative Attention on CIFAR-100. We then propose focus anchors, which place most anchors at the peaks of a learned importance map while all anchors keep one exclusive Voronoi partition. Focus anchors beat a fixed partition on a cluttered canvas (+1.5 points, 95% CI [0.5, 2.6]) but not on full-HD traffic-sign recognition. There, both variants match dense attention with local windows at about a fifth of its FLOPs, and the fixed partition also trains 1.5x faster per step than dense attention with FlashAttention, though both use more memory; a ViT on a downsampled input loses half its mean average precision. Hard exclusive assignment is the only region assignment we tested that is both stable and most accurate: softmax and Sinkhorn relaxations diverge, and Gumbel-softmax trains but is less accurate. We also report the limits: a ResNet-18 is more accurate on every task we trained it on in this from-scratch regime, and anchors train faster than FlashAttention only from about 1536x1536 pixels and never use less memory.

Machine Learning.title: La-JEPA: Compact Robot Policies with Latent World Modeling
Machine Learning.summary: World-action models adapt pretrained video generators, and vision-language-action models build on vision-language backbones, tying policy architecture and inference cost to large transformers designed for generation rather than control. While recent world-action models mostly scale the video backbone and its data, we argue that the choice of latent space is just as critical, and that the policy should be trained natively in that space. We introduce Latent Action JEPA (La-JEPA), a compact world-action model whose policy transformer is trained from scratch in the feature space of a pretrained V-JEPA 2.1 encoder; it predicts future features with actions during training and generates only actions at inference. Among policies without embodied pretraining, La-JEPA achieves state-of-the-art average RoboTwin 2.0 success under both clean-only and full training, and state-of-the-art LIBERO-Plus success with corrected instructions, while using far fewer parameters than the strongest competitors; with full training, its success scales with model size up to 2.1B. Its S and B policies run two to five times faster than Fast-WAM and Faster-WAM while outperforming both on LIBERO-Plus and RoboTwin 2.0, and La-JEPA outperforms the closest JEPA-based methods, LeapBot-WA and JEPA-WAM, without their pretrained policy backbones. On four real-robot tasks, its average success is comparable to $π_{0.5}$. A design study shows that JEPA features outperform video VAE latents, most clearly out of distribution, and that training-time future prediction improves the policy even when skipped at inference. Tailoring the policy's design, including its latent space, to control can thus matter more than the knowledge transferred from a pretrained generative backbone, suggesting that robot foundation models may benefit from architectures designed for control rather than inherited from generation.
Machine Learning.comment: 31 pages, 6 figures. v2: full-RoboTwin results with scaling to 2.1B parameters, leave-one-out ablation, revised figures and text. Code: https://github.com/mt-clemente/lajepa

Machine Learning.title: DistDNA: Language Model Fingerprinting under Stochastic Decoding
Machine Learning.summary: Behavioral fingerprints identify a large language model (LLM) from its responses to a shared set of prompts, enabling applications such as verifying whether a deployed model corresponds to the checkpoint it claims to be. Deployed models, however, are commonly served with stochastic decoding, under which the same model may produce different responses to an identical prompt, depending on an unknown temperature and top-$p$ setting. Existing representations such as LLM DNA provide limited treatment of this variation. A natural remedy is to characterize models by their response distributions, which, however, raises two challenges. First, each distribution must be estimated from only a small number of sampled responses. Second, a change in decoding setting can alter responses to the same extent as a change of checkpoint. Consequently, fingerprint distances alone provide an incomplete basis for model identity, and identification typically relies on a classifier trained jointly on fingerprints from many checkpoints. We propose DistDNA, which represents a model by its prompt-conditional response distributions and compares models by promptwise maximum mean discrepancy (MMD). The model under examination is assigned to the known checkpoint whose reference fingerprints, collected at several decoding settings, lie nearest to its own, without training a classifier. We show that finite sampling adds variance-dependent terms to the expected squared fingerprint distance, with these terms decreasing as $O(1/R)$ for equal response counts, where $R$ is the number of responses per prompt. Experiments across 115 model checkpoint entries demonstrate that DistDNA improves identification accuracy over the strongest baseline, LLM DNA, by 10.36%.

Machine Learning.title: Graph Signal Generation via Graph-Aware Diffusion Models
Machine Learning.summary: Many signals are defined on the nodes of a graph, such as traffic flow at road sensors or user purchases of related products. They are often partly observed, and learning their distribution enables imputing missing values and forecasting future ones. Diffusion models learn such distributions, but their forward noise is independent across nodes and does not depend on the graph. We introduce graph-aware diffusion (GAD), whose forward process is a heat diffusion on the graph driven by Gaussian noise. In the graph Fourier basis, the forward transition is a scalar Gaussian channel at each frequency. With a shared diffusion rate, high graph frequencies are attenuated faster than low ones. We propose Mode-Adaptive SNR Scheduling (MASS), which assigns each graph frequency its own diffusion rate and keeps all of them at the same SNR. For graph-stationary signals, MASS equalizes the normalized error of the optimal linear denoiser across frequencies. We bound reverse-SDE stiffness as a function of the (shifted) Laplacian's condition number, with a logarithmic upper bound for MASS and a linear lower bound for shared rates. GAD with MASS improves recommendation accuracy by 5-19%, reduces traffic-imputation RMSE by up to 7.8% with half as many reverse steps, and improves forecasting MAE and RMSE using only 3 reverse steps.
Machine Learning.comment: 19 pages, 2 figures, 9 tables. Under review at IEEE Transactions on Pattern Analysis and Machine Intelligence. Code: https://github.com/vimalkb7/SpectralAnalysisGAD

Machine Learning.title: Mixture of Latent Recursions for Low-Rank Adaptation
Machine Learning.summary: Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) performs task-specific adaptation using a fixed low-rank architecture, whose expressiveness is typically increased by enlarging or adding learnable modules with a proportional parameter overhead. We introduce Mixture of Latent Recursions (MoLR), an adaptive recursion framework that enhances adaptation expressiveness while preserving parameter efficiency. MoLR recursively refines the down-projected latent representation of each input using a shared transformation. A lightweight threshold-based router independently determines whether each token should undergo further refinement, while dynamically adjusted thresholds encourage balanced utilization across recursion depths. Extensive experiments across diverse language and vision tasks demonstrate that MoLR consistently outperforms representative LoRA variants with negligible parameter overhead over LoRA. Further analyses show that MoLR learns input-dependent recursion-depth allocation and enables a controllable inference-time compute-performance trade-off without requiring retraining. Code will be publicly available.

Machine Learning.title: Sampling non-abelian lattice gauge theories with diffusion models
Machine Learning.summary: We present gauge-equivariant diffusion models as samplers for lattice gauge theories (LGTs). Using lattice gauge-equivariant convolutional neural networks (L-CNNs) and the Metropolis-adjusted annealed Langevin algorithm (MAALA), we are able to accurately sample two-dimensional U(2) field configurations and show first promising results for four-dimensional SU(3). Our two-dimensional models extrapolate remarkably well to larger inverse couplings than originally trained on. We confirm this by comparing observables to analytically known values and to hybrid Monte Carlo results.
Machine Learning.comment: 7 pages, 4 figures, contribution to the Proceedings of the 22nd International Conference on QCD in Extreme Conditions (xQCD 2026), 14-17 July 2026, Busan, Korea

Machine Learning.title: Autonomous quantum machine learning via Riemannian gradient-based optimization
Machine Learning.summary: Quantum machine learning models typically rely on repeated quantum measurements and classical optimization during training, making the quantum-to-classical information-extraction process a fundamental bottleneck for scalability. We propose a framework for autonomous self-training quantum machine learning, based on Riemannian gradient optimization, in which the optimization proceeds entirely within the quantum domain without requiring quantum measurements or classical feedback. We derive the Riemannian gradient update rules for a broad class of learning tasks and identify sufficient conditions under which the resulting training dynamics can be realized fully autonomously. Within this regime, we establish an exponential convergence guarantee, in the training iterations, for sufficiently small step sizes, and further analyze the training cost in terms of the growth of the circuit depth. Importantly, we further show that the trained model can automatically discover symmetries hidden in the training data without $\textit{a priori}$ specification. For the canonical examples of quantum phase classification and unitary learning with a hidden symmetry, our numerical study indicates that learning can be achieved at low circuit depths with only a few distinct training examples. Our results thus establish autonomous quantum machine learning as a promising paradigm that removes the classical optimization loop while retaining strong theoretical guarantees and practical performances.

Machine Learning.title: Redesigning Neural Networks to Not be Confidently Wrong even to Strong Adversarial Attacks
Machine Learning.summary: Early deep learning models attempted to simulate visual perception using a neural hierarchy that alternated between two types of layer: one modelled on cortical simple cells (that was designed to increase selectivity), and one modelled on cortical complex cells (that aimed to increase tolerance). We show that such a neural network (NN) architecture, when implemented with novel components that are better able to learn selective and tolerant representations, is capable of accurate and robust image classification and improved alignment between the behaviour of the model and the perceptual abilities of humans. Firstly, the proposed models are shallow, fewer than ten layer-pairs, which is more consistent with the rapid feedforward object categorisation performed by the biological visual system. Secondly, they are far less prone to producing classification predictions with high confidence for samples from unknown classes or for image consisting of pure noise, and hence, like humans are not easily fooled into perceiving objects that are not present in the image. Thirdly, for the proposed NNs adversarial samples cause predictions with low confidence, enabling them to be accurately identified. In contrast to humans, our networks still do not correctly classify adversarial samples. However, the behaviour of our networks is a significant step towards human-like behaviour compared to standard DNNs that produce highly confident, but incorrect, classification predictions for adversarial samples. The increased robustness to adversarial and unknown samples is achieved while maintaining competitive performance in terms of generalisation to novel samples from the training categories. This enables models of this type to be competitive with state-of-the-art DNNs across multiple different evaluation metrics and benchmark tasks.

Machine Learning.title: Learning to Allocate Resources with Censored Feedback
Machine Learning.summary: We study the online resource allocation problem in which at each round, a budget $B$ must be allocated across $K$ arms under censored feedback. An arm yields a reward if and only if two conditions are satisfied: (i) the arm is activated according to an arm-specific Bernoulli random variable with unknown parameter, and (ii) the allocated budget exceeds a random threshold drawn from a parametric distribution with unknown parameter. Over $T$ rounds, the learner must jointly estimate the unknown parameters and allocate the budget so as to maximize cumulative reward facing the exploration-exploitation trade-off. We prove a worst-case regret lower bound $Ω(\sqrt{T})$ for the general model, even with known uniform threshold distributions. We then propose RA-UCB, an optimistic algorithm that leverages non-trivial parameter estimation and confidence bounds. When the budget $B$ is known at the beginning of each round and every arm receives a positive allocation at the optimum (interior optimum, with a known lower bound), RA-UCB achieves a regret bound of order $\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{T})$, and even $O(\mathrm{poly}\log T)$ under stronger assumptions. For unknown, round-dependent budgets, we introduce MG-UCB, which allows within-round switching and infinitesimal allocations, and matches the regret guarantees of RA-UCB; we also discuss an implementable discretization. We then validate our theoretical results through experiments on real-world datasets.

Machine Learning.title: SaturQ: Saturation-Aware Mixed-Precision Quantization
Machine Learning.summary: Mixed-precision quantization assigns each module of a language model its own precision format, such as NVFP4, FP8, or BF16, to minimize damage within a memory budget. Most allocators predict the damage of a configuration by summing per-unit sensitivities measured in unquantized networks. But the sensitivity of a unit \textit{saturates} as more units are quantized, so the sum overprices the heavily quantized configurations that tight budgets require. Assuming only that damage accumulates by an associative, increasing, continuous rule restricts it to the form $g\bigl(\sum_i b_i\bigr)$, with summed sensitivities as the case of linear $g$. We propose SaturQ, which uses a concave $g$, fits the per-unit parameters $b_i$ from a single Aumann--Shapley path integral, and allocates formats with a linear program. On Qwen3-30B-A3B, SaturQ lowers KL divergence to BF16 by 11--23\% relative to ModelOpt AutoQuantize at 4.2--6.0 effective bits, and it outperforms an interaction-aware allocator that measures up to 2{,}410 configurations while measuring only three. It also predicts the damage of unmeasured configurations with a median error of 6.9--11.4\%, lower than Gaussian-process and random-forest surrogates fit to 300 configurations, and served allocations of Qwen3.6-27B and GLM-5.2 (753B) run faster than vendor NVFP4 checkpoints at comparable accuracy.
Machine Learning.comment: 15 pages, 3 figures, 6 tables; presentation simplified and cleaned up

Machine Learning.title: SLP-Bench: Evaluating and Improving Acoustic Claims of Reasoning Audio Language Models on Clinical Speech
Machine Learning.summary: Audio language models (ALMs) can answer clinical questions from speech, outperforming baselines built on handcrafted acoustic features. Reasoning ALMs generate a chain of thought that refers to properties of the speaker's voice before predicting. Each statement the model makes about the voice needs to be checked against clinicians' perceptual ratings of the same recording. On clinical speech, existing evaluations score only the final answer. We introduce Speech Language Pathologist Bench (SLP-Bench), a benchmark grading each acoustic claim in the chain of thought against clinicians' perceptual ratings of the same recording. It covers five clinician-rated datasets and 25 perceptual dimensions, and assesses claims for factuality, stability under resampling, and consistency across reworded and different questions. Across ten open-weight reasoning ALMs evaluated zero-shot, claim balanced accuracy ranges from 0.52 to 0.58, claims change under resampling and rewording, and the most consistent models are not the most factual. Fine-tuning a 7B ALM with GRPO on a reward for claims that agree with clinicians raises its claim balanced accuracy from 0.54 to 0.60 and its mean kappa from 0.39 to 0.61, while preserving answer accuracy on per-dimension questions. SLP-Bench is available upon request, subject to approval by the providers of each dataset.
Machine Learning.comment: 5 pages, 4 figures, 2 tables, submitted to ICASSP 2027 workshop "Explainability, Robustness, and Controllability of Language Modeling for Speech and Audio"

Machine Learning.title: DOiT: Better Money-Flow Ranking Can Coexist with Worse Account Selection in Anti-Money Laundering Review
Machine Learning.summary: Anti-money laundering (AML) review selects suspicious accounts and reconstructs transfers. Downstream graph neural networks (GNNs) rank money-flow evidence but may also reorder the account queue. DOiT separates these decisions at equal review capacity: account selection determines where graph investigation starts. Across AMLWorld and AMLNet, GNN reordering harms higher-yield upstream orders but helps lower-yield ones. On AMLWorld, this harm coexists with higher transaction average precision (AP) in dimension-matched, per-run decoders, demonstrating separable ranking abilities. At small capacities, positive neighbors can displace a denser upstream prefix and lower yield; replacement costs fall as that prefix is exhausted, allowing the preferred order to reverse. A restricted-access synthetic benchmark informed by real transaction patterns reproduces this separation and validation-based upstream preservation. Capacity-matched combination protects upstream ordering while retaining GNN money-flow analysis, admitting GNN queue influence only where held-out evidence supports it.
Machine Learning.comment: 8 pages, 5 figures, 4 tables. Author-prepared version of the paper published in the Proceedings of the 7th ACM International Conference on AI in Finance (ICAIF 2026)

Machine Learning.title: $\mathtt{DistP}$: Scaling Local-Update Training with Zero-Shot Hyperparameter Transfer
Machine Learning.summary: Local-update methods offer a communication-efficient alternative to Distributed Data Parallelism ($\mathtt{DDP}$), but introduce additional hyperparameters that require costly tuning. For $\mathtt{DDP}$, zero-shot hyperparameter transfer reduces this cost by reusing settings tuned on smaller models, but its applicability to local-update training remains unclear. We propose $\mathtt{DistP}$, a theoretical framework extending existing transfer rules from $\mathtt{DDP}$ to local-update training with varying worker counts, local steps, and outer optimizers. With averaging as the outer optimizer, $\mathtt{DistP}$ supports learning-rate transfer across width and depth while improving model quality. The tuned inner learning rate also directly transfers across synchronization intervals, but follows two regimes when increasing the global batch size: square-root learning-rate scaling for larger local batches and a fixed reference rate for additional workers. We then generalize width and depth transfer to other outer optimizers, enabling stable scaling with $\mathtt{Adam}$. However, with momentum in the outer optimizer, changing batch size or local steps can require inner--outer learning-rate tuning, consistent with prior work. In language-modeling experiments at $823$M parameters, $\mathtt{DistP}$ reduces validation loss by $8.1\%$ and improves mean downstream accuracy by $10\%$ relative to baselines without retuning at the larger scale. Fitted scaling laws suggest that this advantage grows with the compute budget, reinforcing the benefits of $\mathtt{DistP}$ for communication-efficient training.

Machine Learning.title: SiMDex: Mining Similar Egocentric Videos for Cross-Embodiment Dexterous Manipulation
Machine Learning.summary: Recent years have witnessed an explosive trend of scaling ego-centric human videos for robot manipulation, yet it remains unclear which data actually benefits dexterous manipulation. We present SiMDex, a similarity-based data mining framework that casts human data selection for VLA post-training in dexterous manipulation as a recommendation problem. For each robot demonstration, SiMDex runs a recall-ranking-re-ranking cascade over ~32M egocentric human samples: two stages, recall and ranking, select a task-relevant subset in a morphology-agnostic action space, and re-ranking verifies it on pixels, with no change to VLA architecture or training. Against a strong baseline trained with an equal amount of randomly sampled human data, SiMDex uses only ~1.49M mined samples (<5% of the pool) yet improves the overall success rate from 47.7% to 61.7%, showing that selective curation outperforms indiscriminate data mixing.
Machine Learning.comment: 38 pages, 12 figures, 16 tables. Project page: https://lin-nie.github.io/SiMDex/

Machine Learning.title: $\varepsilon$-SegFormer: Multi-Resolution Vision Transformers for Sparsely Supervised Segmentation in Electron Microscopy
Machine Learning.summary: Segmenting organelles in electron microscopy (EM) volumes requires dense annotations that take experts months to produce, and every gain in imaging resolution adds to this cost. Sparsely supervised methods reduce this cost to a small fraction of labeled pixels, but the convolutional networks they build on see a limited neighborhood around each pixel, while the identity of an organelle often depends on context far beyond it. We introduce $\varepsilon$-SegFormer, a multi-resolution Vision Transformer for sparsely supervised semantic segmentation, which builds on the architecture of MuViT and extends the training method of $\varepsilon$-Seg. For each labeled pixel, $\varepsilon$-SegFormer samples views at three physical resolutions centered on it, embeds their patches into a single token sequence, and encodes every token's position in image coordinates, so that attention relates all views in one shared frame. A segmentation head classifies the pixel from the tokens around it; during training, the pixel's own token is hidden, so the label must be predicted from context rather than local appearance. The model is trained in a single stage, without pretraining, with an auxiliary reconstruction loss. On the BetaSeg FIB-SEM dataset, $\varepsilon$-SegFormer learns from about 10,000 labeled pixels among the 670 million voxels inside three cells, and, given the cell mask, segments nuclei, mitochondria and insulin granules in a slice of a fourth, unseen cell with an average Dice of 0.89 (0.91 after post-processing). Ablations show that coarser views improve accuracy and that a compact head on local tokens works best, with the wider context entering through attention in the encoder.

Machine Learning.title: AI Safety Considerations for Agents With Limited Time to Act
Machine Learning.summary: In the wake of the increasingly public discussion about AI alignment, recent work has tried to propose specific AI architectures that behave safely. However, the proposed arguments that seemingly demonstrate proved alignment mostly neglect the environment the agent needs to act in. We discuss theoretical bounds for agent-agnostic safety guarantees in environments that can only be partially observed and within which an action is required within limited time. We introduce two realistic scenarios, one with an infinite state space and one with signal mixture. In these scenarios, we prove that even a perfect agent cannot guarantee safe behaviour. It will be argued that for any proof of AI safety or alignment, the environment and associated safe actions need to be specifically considered together with the agent.

Machine Learning.title: Inpainting physics: self-supervised learning for context-driven fluid simulation
Machine Learning.summary: Neural surrogate models for computational fluid dynamics (CFD) are typically trained as forward operators that map explicit problem specifications, such as geometry and boundary conditions, to solution fields. This ties the model to the conditioning variables seen during training and limits reuse under boundary-condition shifts or local geometry changes. We propose to reformulate steady CFD inference as an inpainting problem: instead of training on explicit boundary conditions, we learn a self-supervised prior over velocity fields and impose boundary constraints only during inference by fixing known regions such as inlet, outlet or unchanged regions from previous simulations. To scale this idea to large 3D meshes, we introduce a local neighbourhood tokeniser that represents high-resolution velocity fields as compact spatial latent tokens and train latent flow-matching and masked-autoencoder models on these tokens. On simulations of intracranial aneurysm flow, our method reconstructs full velocity fields from sparse boundary context, outperforms supervised neural surrogates under boundary-condition and dataset shift and enables local geometry editing by reusing unchanged simulation context. These results suggest that viewing CFD inference as context-conditioned inpainting can turn neural surrogates from task-specific predictors into reusable flow priors. Code and demo are available at https://inpainting-physics.com.

Machine Learning.title: TopoPilot: Reliable Conversational Workflow Automation for Topological Data Analysis and Visualization
Machine Learning.summary: Recent agentic systems demonstrate that large language models can generate complex codebases from natural language prompts. Despite this progress, they present reliability concerns for scientific visualization due to invalid operations, subtle errors, and failure to resolve underspecified inputs. In this work, we introduce TopoPilot, a reliable and extensible agentic framework for automating complex scientific visualization workflows. We focus on topological data analysis and visualization as a primary use case, while designing the framework to generalize to broader visualization domains. TopoPilot employs a two-agent architecture: an orchestrator translates user prompts into workflows composed of atomic backend actions, while a verifier evaluates workflows prior to execution. Its modular design isolates components and supports new topological descriptors and domain-specific workflows without modifying the core system. It also employs numerous deterministic guardrails to ensure semantic consistency and accurate execution. To systematically improve reliability, we develop a taxonomy of failure modes and employ targeted safeguards for each class of error. Across 2,000 simulated multi-turn conversations spanning 100 prompts, including adversarial and infeasible requests, TopoPilot achieves a success rate exceeding 95%, compared with under 50% for a baseline without comprehensive guardrails and verification. We also show that TopoPilot outperforms Claude Code and Codex on similar prompts in terms of accuracy, completion time, and token usage.

Machine Learning.title: gHAWK: Structural Encoding for Scalable Training of Graph Neural Networks on Knowledge Graphs
Machine Learning.summary: Knowledge Graphs (KGs) are a rich source of structured data, and graph neural networks (GNNs) are the dominant tool for learning over them. However, existing message-passing GNNs struggle to scale to large KGs because they rely on the iterative message passing process to learn graph structure. This process is inefficient, especially under mini-batch training, where a node sees only a partial view of its neighborhood. In this paper, we address this problem and present gHAWK, a novel and scalable GNN training framework for large KGs. The key idea is to precompute structural features for each node that capture its local and global structure before GNN training even begins. Specifically, gHAWK introduces a preprocessing step that computes: (a) Bloom filters to compactly encode local neighborhood structure, and (b) TransE embeddings to represent each node's global position in the graph. These features are then fused with any domain-specific features (e.g., text embeddings), producing a node feature vector that can be used with any GNN backbone. Equipped with these structural priors, the GNN no longer needs to rediscover graph structure, significantly improving convergence and model accuracy with little memory overhead. Extensive experiments on large datasets from the Open Graph Benchmark demonstrate that gHAWK improves accuracy on both node property prediction and link prediction tasks. Remarkably, gHAWK enables simple GNNs to match or exceed more complex relation-aware ones, suggesting that careful preprocessing can substitute for architectural complexity in KG learning.

Machine Learning.title: Computation, Not Memory: Chain-of-Thought and State Tracking in LLM Agents
Machine Learning.summary: Language-model agents often reason before they act, and the value of monitoring that reasoning depends on how it relates to their actions. We ask how an agent's actions depend on its reasoning when the correct action depends on a changing state. In a small file-system task, background events announce which file's lock has been toggled but not its new value. The agent therefore has to reconstruct the current locks from its history before it can move files safely. With Qwen3-8B and Qwen3.5-9B, we separate two roles of reasoning: generating it before each action, and retaining earlier reasoning in the prompt. Most of the reduction in lock-violating commands comes from reasoning written at the moment of action. Retaining earlier reasoning adds little when the agent also reasons at each step, but it helps an agent that does not reason, and it helps in longer episodes. Retained notes have a limit: when a later event makes a note wrong, an agent without current reasoning responds little, while current reasoning makes the action follow the event. The benefit depends on what the reasoning says. Filler text, reasoning written for another history and an accurate table of the state do not reproduce it. When we give the agent reasoning written for a history that differs in one lock value, the agent acts on that reasoning even against its own history. For Qwen3-8B, this holds also when that value has since been toggled. Without reasoning, state readouts are less reliable after toggles, and Qwen3-8B's answers about the state favor the outdated value. The state answer and the action also depend on different parts of the prompt. In this setting, the benefit of reasoning for rule-following comes mainly from generating it at each step, where it makes the action respond to later events. The state that can be read out without reasoning is a limited guide to how the agent acts.
Machine Learning.comment: v2: adds retention without current reasoning and in longer episodes, tests of retained notes and current reasoning after a state change, explicit event labels, counterfactual pairs with a toggled lock, and readouts on outdated values

Machine Learning.title: DPMA: Learning to Compress Mixture-of-Experts Models
Machine Learning.summary: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architectures offer high computational efficiency, but storing all experts requires substantial memory and limits deployment on resource-constrained hardware. Most retraining-free MoE compression methods commit to either pruning or merging experts, often with a uniform compression ratio across layers. We introduce DPMA (Differentiable Prune Merge Absorb), which jointly learns compression operations and layer-wise expert allocation through gradient descent under a global expert budget. Separate learnable coefficients allow DPMA to prune experts, merge their parameters, and absorb their routing contributions by forwarding routing weights to retained experts. These coefficients and expert assignments are optimised to match the original model's outputs on calibration data while its weights remain frozen. Across four MoE models, eight multiple-choice benchmarks, and five compression ratios, DPMA achieves the highest accuracy averaged over benchmarks and compression ratios on each model among the evaluated methods. At $75\%$ expert reduction, it outperforms the strongest baseline on every model, with gains of up to $6.7$ percentage points.

Machine Learning.title: Budgeted Subset Selection with a Transferable Learned Value Model
Machine Learning.summary: Subset selection is a fundamental task in machine learning, statistics and combinatorial optimisation, with applications in active learning, band selection, input selection and experimental design. The utility of a subset depends on information revealed only after the selection, such as labels or responses, and on interactions among selected candidates. Existing approaches combine value estimation and redundancy control in application-specific ways, which limits their use in other domains. This paper introduces Subset Acquisition with Learned Value Estimates and Search (SALVES), a framework that decomposes subset selection into two components. First, a value model is trained by supervised learning on tasks where the hidden information is known. On a new task, it predicts the utility each candidate would add to the current selection. Second, a selection step chooses the subset from these predictions, typically by simulated annealing with a diversity term penalising redundancy. The value model transfers to new classes, pretrained networks, datasets and sensors, and from synthetic to real data. On the four applications, SALVES matches or outperforms application-specific baselines on average. It requires substantially fewer bands for equal accuracy and remains reliable in input selection where individual baselines fail.

Machine Learning.title: A Multi-Center Dataset and Benchmark for SYNTAX Segmentation of Coronary Angiograms
Machine Learning.summary: Dense pixel-level classification of coronary angiography is essential for automated cardiovascular diagnostics, yet the computer vision community lacks gold-standard protocols and robust datasets to tackle this topologically complex, heavily long-tailed domain. To bridge this gap, we introduce CARDIAG: a rigorous, multi-center benchmark dataset designed to evaluate deep learning architectures on fine-grained SYNTAX segment classification. Unlike prior efforts, CARDIAG systematically prevents patient- and center-level data leakage while providing an unprecedented suite of annotations: highly imbalanced multi-class labels, explicit catheter and stenosis masks, expert uncertainty maps, temporal sequence frames, and spatial metadata. Using CARDIAG, we conduct the most extensive architectural sweep in this domain, benchmarking 24 models spanning classic CNNs, Vision Transformers (ViTs), and State-Space Models (SSMs). Moving beyond naive overlap metrics, we evaluate topological preservation (clDice), vessel diameter error, and uncertainty error-detection. Our analysis reveals an insight: modern large-kernel CNNs (particularly ConvNeXt V2 with DeepLabV3+) still outperform recent ViTs and SSMs under a shared training recipe, establishing a Dice = 0.456. By ensembling complementary models, we push the baseline to Dice = 0.479. Through leave-one-center-out cross-validation and data efficiency analyses, we explore the current limits of out-of-distribution generalization. Ultimately, CARDIAG establishes a foundation for advancing medical computer vision for cardiology across many downstream tasks, including lesion detection, temporal frame interpolation, and 3D reconstruction.
Machine Learning.comment: Accepted to WACV 2027 Dataset available on Zenodo at https://zenodo.org/records/19958730, code available at https://github.com/cvlab-ai/cardiag-benchmark

Machine Learning.title: When Do Rankings Beat Signs? Gradient Direction Recovery under Even Nuisance
Machine Learning.summary: Comparison-based optimization minimizes an objective using only ordinal feedback without numerical values. Sign-based baselines evaluate symmetric perturbation pairs in isolation, retaining only within-pair signs and discarding cross-pair orders from the same ranked batch. We ask when complete batch rankings provably beat within-pair signs under an unknown differentiable even nuisance, such as quadratic curvature. We show that reversed cross-pair comparisons cancel shared nuisance offsets without estimating a Hessian, and introduce a geometric framework characterizing three nested direction sets, namely Mirror, Reverse, and Full. Rather than curvature magnitude or condition number, we identify relative shell variation $τ_a$, the nuisance range on a radius-$a$ sphere divided by $a\|g\|$ for gradient $g\ne 0$ in $d$ dimensions, as a key quantity governing localization. For target angular accuracy $\varepsilon$ in radians, whenever $τ_a\le c\varepsilon/\sqrt{d}$ for a small absolute constant $c$, one-round Reverse constraints from uniform directions localize every surviving direction within angle $\varepsilon$ of the gradient using $\widetilde{O}(d+\sqrt{d/\varepsilon})$ evaluations, versus $Θ(d/\varepsilon)$ for signs. This whole-cell guarantee needs no variation bound as input and matches a lower bound up to log factors. Conversely, over well-conditioned quadratics with unbounded curvature relative to gradient scale, rankings offer no minimax evaluation advantage over signs, even across multiple rounds. Experiments certify strict Full-over-Reverse separation, and on two ridge tasks under joint evaluation and round caps, although Full shows no established gain beyond reversed constraints, Reverse consistently attains lower terminal gaps than tuned Mirror and unit-normalized ZO-RankSGD.
Machine Learning.comment: This paper proves how black-box optimizers can reuse discarded batch rankings to cancel unknown curvature and recover accurate search directions with far fewer queries. (13 main pages; full proofs and experimental details in the appendices

Machine Learning.title: A Switching Mechanism for Selecting Environment-Adaptive Personalized Gains in Hearing Aids
Machine Learning.summary: Personalized amplification gains for hearing aids have been shown to be preferred over prescriptive gains. Since the preferred settings can vary depending on the background audio environment, this paper presents a switching mechanism or system that automatically selects personalized gains for a current background audio environment. To prevent foreground speech from interfering with background environment analysis, a one-class voice activity detector is designed to identify speech activity from speech mixed with noise. A consistency check is conducted to enable distinguishing foreground speech from background speech, preserving babble as a background environment of interest because hearing aid users often struggle to understand speech in background babble. Sound segments without foreground speech are then analyzed by an online discovery method combining Bayesian change-point detection with a memory of previously encountered environments. This discovery method detects changes, recognizes returning environments, and discovers new ones without a predefined number of environments. Experimental results show that three-seed mean macro-averaged F1 scores of 85.53%-91.98% across eight speech/background-corpus pairs covering 36 background noise types were achieved. Furthermore, the discovery method achieved adjusted Rand indices of 0.91 and 0.96 on two families of test streams. In the same-recording-return condition of audio streams combining speech with four background audio environments often encountered by hearing aid users, the switching mechanism selected the correct personalized gain profile after 105 environment changes, recalled the stored gain profile at every return, and made no switches to an incorrect gain profile.

Machine Learning.title: Beyond Math, Code, and Logic: Do Reasoning Models Transfer to Scientific Argumentation?
Machine Learning.summary: Scientific discourse depends on argumentative reasoning: identifying claims, evaluating evidence, and constructing coherent responses. While recent advances in reasoning-capable language models have demonstrated strong performance on mathematical, coding, and logical benchmarks, their ability to engage in scientific argumentation remains unclear. We present the first systematic evaluation of language models across seven tasks spanning argument mining, rebuttal generation, and discourse-level reasoning using research papers, peer reviews, and grant proposals. Our study reveals that even frontier models with strong general reasoning skills struggle with domain-specific argumentative tasks, highlighting a fundamental capability gap. To address this, we introduce a training framework that explicitly scaffolds the argumentative reasoning process in language models, substantially improving their competence in scientific discourse. The resulting compact models approach or exceed the performance of much larger proprietary systems and generalize to unseen conversational settings, demonstrating reasoning transfer beyond task-specific supervision. These findings underscore that effective scientific argumentation is not an emergent property of scale, but requires explicit reasoning-aware training, and they point toward practical pathways for building AI systems that can contribute meaningfully to scientific discourse.

Machine Learning.title: Decision Models for Multilingual Emotion Classification: A Comparative Study Against LLMs and Encoders
Machine Learning.summary: Decision models receive a question with a closed list of answers and return a probability for each answer instead of free text. They promise low latency and robustness to prompt wording, but no study has compared several of them with fine-tuned encoders across languages. We ask whether systems used without training on labelled data (zero-shot) can replace fine-tuning, and what the decision format adds over a general-purpose large language model (LLM). We compare three decision models (Jev, OpenAI Decisions, Strands Decider 2B) and two LLMs (GPT-6 Luna, Qwen3.5-2B), given Italian instructions, with two fine-tuned multilingual encoders (tabularisai, XLM-EMO) on four emotions (joy, sadness, anger, fear) in 10 social-media datasets in five languages, with paired difference and equivalence tests. The three best zero-shot systems (two decision models and one LLM) score on average about one macro-F1 point below an encoder fine-tuned on the target dataset; our test sets cannot exclude a gap of 4-5 points, and on single datasets either approach wins by up to 22 points. They beat encoders fine-tuned on another dataset by 8-15 points, though against XLM-EMO this may not extend to new datasets, and instructions in each text's language change their results by under 1 point. Exploratorily, they beat the strongest public emotion model used as is by about 6 points. OpenAI's decision endpoint matches GPT-6 Luna, the LLM it runs on, at a fifth of its median latency, and a 2-billion-parameter decision model beats a same-size general LLM by 10 points, owing to its training, not the decision format. The best zero-shot systems, the LLM included, have an SD of about 1 point across prompts. Without labelled data they are a strong default, and decision models add lower latency and, unlike generative LLM use, per-option probabilities. Fine-tuning won by a wide margin only on the largest dataset, GoEmotions.

Machine Learning.title: Solving the pre-image problem in kernel PCA: The reproducing property is all you need
Machine Learning.summary: Kernel PCA extends PCA to nonlinear dimensionality reduction by implicitly mapping data into a reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS) via the kernel trick, with applications ranging from image denoising to out-of-distribution detection. While its projection map is well understood, appropriately defining the associated reconstruction map is a longstanding challenge since projecting back from the RKHS to the input space is non-trivial. This is known as the pre-image problem. Existing approaches have tackled this problem by either relying on nonlinear optimization, which is prone to numerical instabilities and sensitive to initialization, or by solving a separate supervised learning problem, incurring additional computational overhead. Furthermore, although the projection map of kernel PCA reduces to that of standard PCA when a linear kernel is used, most of these approaches are not guaranteed to recover PCA's reconstruction map in this case, a consistency property that one would naturally expect to hold. In this paper, we leverage the reproducing property of the RKHS to derive a reconstruction map for kernel PCA that is provably consistent. Our derivations rely on the mild assumption that the RKHS either contains linear functions or the kernel is universal, which holds for standard kernels. We further extend the method to the random Fourier features (RFFs) approximation of kernel PCA by introducing a corresponding notion of RFF reproducing property. Numerical experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate that the proposed method performs comparably with state-of-the-art methods across kernel choices, while remaining more computationally efficient and maintaining consistent performance in settings where these baseline methods drastically fail.
Machine Learning.comment: This work has been submitted to the IEEE for possible publication. Copyright may be transferred without notice, after which this version may no longer be accessible

Machine Learning.title: On the Global Convergence of Gradient Descent for multi-layer ResNets in the mean-field regime
Machine Learning.summary: Finding the optimal configuration of parameters in ResNet is a nonconvex minimization problem, but first-order methods often find the global optimum when the network is overparameterized and the training algorithm is run for sufficiently many iterations. We study this phenomenon in the mean-field regime, where the network can be described approximately by an ordinary integral equation (OIE) and the training process of ResNet becomes a gradient-flow partial differential equation (PDE). Under the condition that the activation function is $2$-homogeneous or partially $1$-homogeneous, we show that this gradient-flow PDE converges to the global minimum. This result suggests that if the ResNet is sufficiently large, first-order optimization methods can find global minimizers that fit the training data as well. Further, by controlling the generalization error, we prove that the gradient-flow PDE is stable with respect to its cost function, implying that a finite-sized but sufficiently large dataset drawn from the underlying data distribution can exhibit the properties of the continuous limit. We give lower bounds on the depth and width of the network for the gradient-flow approximation to hold. We also lower-bound the size of the training data set needed to attain accurate approximation.

Machine Learning.title: TabularMath: Evaluating Computational Extrapolation in Tabular Learning via Program-Verified Synthesis
Machine Learning.summary: Standard tabular benchmarks reward interpolation: predicting values inside the data manifold, where local statistical smoothing works. However, much high-value tabular data, from pricing and financial rules to physical simulation, is produced by deterministic computations rather than noisy relationships. Can tabular models move from statistical interpolation to computational extrapolation, returning exact answers even beyond the range seen in training? We introduce TabularMath, a benchmark of 114 deterministic computations (233,472 rows) compiled from GSM8K and AIME problems into verified programs. We evaluate nine tabular methods, closed-form and symbolic regression baselines, and in-context learning with GPT-OSS-120B. On regression metrics, TabPFN v2.5 looks excellent: with 128 rows its median $R^2$ is 0.999 in-distribution, and it is the only tabular method whose median $R^2$ stays positive (0.76) when nearly every answer exceeds the training range. Exact answers tell a different story. Out of distribution (OOD), its accuracy falls from 39.5% to 7.8%, it answers no query correctly in 70 of 100 GSM8K tasks, and sixteen times more rows raise its OOD accuracy by only 0.4 points. Yet the answers are in the table: by construction, every label is a program's output on the row's inputs, and the training rows typically suffice to recover that program. Symbolic regression on the numbers alone recovers every OOD answer in 72 of 100 GSM8K tasks, and in-context learning with GPT-OSS-120B answers 39.2% of OOD queries. Tabular foundation models fit the trend but miss the computation, an inductive-bias gap that more data does not close. The competition-level AIME tasks remain open for every method.
Machine Learning.comment: 31 pages, 7 figures, 22 tables. Final version. A preliminary version appeared at the ICML 2026 AI4Math Workshop

Machine Learning.title: Disentangling Self-Distillation: Measuring and Modeling Acquisition and Retention
Machine Learning.summary: Self-distillation with privileged context adapts a language model from demonstrations by letting the model, once conditioned on a reference response, teach its context-free copy token by token. Our taxonomy reveals existing methods differ along three entangled axes: (i) the rollout source (student or teacher), (ii) the teacher coupling (frozen, or an exponential moving average of the student at some coupling rate) and (iii) the token-level divergence (here, reverse or forward KL), yet these axes are usually studied in fixed combinations and have led to conflicting conclusions. We formalize a unifying framework that covers both self-distillation and classic supervised fine-tuning: we train every combination of the three axes, on Qwen2.5-7B and Ministral-3-3B across ordinary and contradictory tasks, totaling 1,200 adaptation runs, to systematically investigate the impact of the above axes. We propose a controlled model of the same objective to interpret the resulting acquisition-retention trade-offs. We find that (i) the rollout source matters mostly where the task contradicts the pretrained behavior: there teacher rollouts raise acquisition (the accuracy gained on the new task) well above what student rollouts achieve, with almost no change in retention (the change in accuracy on general benchmarks); (ii) the teacher coupling changes acquisition most, on every task: acquisition rises with the coupling rate, then falls past a task-specific rate; (iii) switching the KL direction costs retention in one model but not the other, so which axis to tune first depends on the model. The controlled model reproduces the three trends.

Machine Learning.title: Chain of Operators: An Inference-Time Harness for In-Context Operator Learning
Machine Learning.summary: While scientific foundation models show immense promise in accelerating physical simulations and numerical forecasting, they remain notoriously brittle when encountering out-of-distribution (OOD) scenarios. Adapting these generalist models to complex OOD tasks typically requires expensive parameter fine-tuning. In linguistic AI, this bottleneck is bypassed using "harnesses", which serve as external scaffolding such as reasoning chains and tool use to adapt frozen weights to complex tasks, yet designing an equivalent harness for physical domains remains an open frontier. To bridge this gap, we introduce Chain of Operators (CHOP), a framework that guides a frozen foundation model through complex OOD tasks without updating a single weight. By exploiting the in-context learning capability of In-Context Operator Networks (ICON), CHOP systematically decomposes unfamiliar problems into a sequence of explicit, closed-form mathematical operations and multiple model calls, translating OOD queries back into the model's learned operating regime. Across diverse benchmarks, including canonical PDE problems and real-world air-quality forecasting, CHOP consistently and substantially reduces inference errors compared to direct model evaluation. Crucially, these modular operator chains remain fully interpretable and can generalize across entirely distinct families of physical equations. Ultimately, this work demonstrates how frozen scientific models can adapt through programmable inference, establishing a modular, potential paradigm for agentic scientific computing.

Machine Learning.title: Fast Training of Mixture-of-Experts for Time Series Forecasting via Expert Loss Integration
Machine Learning.summary: We propose a novel Mixture-of-Experts framework, referred to as Expert Loss Integration MoE (EliMoE), for time series forecasting. EliMoE addresses the optimization problem arising from small gating weights by incorporating expert-specific losses, which provide each expert with a direct learning signal independent of the gate-assigned weight. Specifically, the overall objective comprises the base forecasting loss and expert-specific losses, allowing individual expert prediction errors to directly influence parameter updates alongside the aggregate forecasting error. The framework also encourages different experts to learn from different temporal segments of the data. The proposed framework is further combined with a partial online learning strategy that enables efficient incremental updates of model parameters. By integrating expert-level loss information with partial online learning, EliMoE improves forecasting performance while retaining computational efficiency. Empirical results across five benchmark datasets from diverse application domains with different sampling frequencies show that the proposed approach generally outperforms state-of-the-art supervised neural forecasting models, including Transformer-based architectures such as PatchTST, as well as zero-shot time-series foundation models such as TimeMoE. Furthermore, ablation studies confirm the effectiveness of the expert-specific loss integration strategy, highlighting its contribution to enhancing predictive performance.

Machine Learning.title: Poisson-GENERIC Neural Operators: Exact Metriplectic Structure in Function Space via Casimir Entropies
Machine Learning.summary: Existing thermodynamically consistent neural operators enforce GENERIC degeneracy by projecting the reversible operator, introducing state dependence and generally forfeiting the Jacobi identity. We instead use the compatible Lie--Poisson pencil $L=αD+λ(uD+Du)$ for nonlinear transport and constant Poisson multipliers otherwise. Augmenting $u$ with a latent entropy density $s$ makes $S=\int s$ a Casimir, so $L\,δS/δz=0$ without projection. The energy combines a fixed mechanical quadratic, a learned gauge-free potential, and a convex internal energy; the friction operator $M=AA^{\!\top}$ enforces $M\,δE/δz=0$ pointwise and supports diffusion and damping through local Onsager fluxes. Skewness, positivity, and both degeneracies hold algebraically for any parameters; the continuum pencil satisfies Jacobi, with discrete residuals at machine precision on alias-free inputs. Closed-form heat and damped-wave friction operators are exactly representable, and a discrete-gradient integrator preserves the first and second laws. Across four PDEs in one and two dimensions and three backbones (FNO, Transolver, CNO), the model wins $62/72$ seed-level comparisons against unconstrained baselines at equal optimizer steps, recovers exact transport and wave symbols, matches heat and Burgers dissipation within $12\%$, and dissipates nothing on advection. At equal wall-clock time, the unconstrained FNO is more accurate over ten frames. Over one hundred frames, in and out of distribution, our model never increases physical energy and conserves it when dissipation vanishes, whereas the unconstrained FNO loses a quarter of conserved energy out of distribution and projected GENERIC-FNO often creates energy. Limitations include late-time heat under-damping and explicit-integrator divergence on waves.

Machine Learning.title: AECSF: Adaptive Ensemble Conditional Score Filtering for High-Dimensional Nonlinear Data Assimilation
Machine Learning.summary: In high-dimensional filters, particle weights can concentrate on a few members, while Gaussian updates can miss non-Gaussian posterior structure. A diffusion filter updates a forecast ensemble by gradually denoising particles in light of a new observation. Each noisy particle can correspond to several system states, and these states can have very different likelihoods. A score correction based on a single state can therefore misrepresent the posterior. We propose the Adaptive Ensemble Conditional Score Filter (AECSF), which uses the conditional Tweedie identity to express the required score through the mean state given the particle and the observation. All reverse particles share a set of proposals, but each assigns its own weights to estimate its conditional mean. As denoising proceeds, the reverse particles guide which proposals are resampled. We characterize when fixed proposals yield the exact noisy posterior score and bound the contribution of conditional-mean errors to the final sampling error. In controlled Gaussian experiments, AECSF samples the posterior more accurately than the tested likelihood-guidance rules. With 20 forecast members in 10,000-dimensional Lorenz-96, AECSF has lower RMSE and CRPS than the tested tempered SMC and kernel-density filters. On Kuramoto-Sivashinsky, the analysis ensembles also improve subsequent forecasts over the tested baselines at comparable cost. For Navier-Stokes flow, we learn a forecast prior that captures spatial dependence in vorticity and use it to reconstruct the full field from sparse velocity measurements.

Machine Learning.title: Geometrically Constrained Learning II: Agnostic Proper Learning of Lipschitz Functions
Machine Learning.summary:
We give a proper learner for Lipschitz functions over the Gaussian distribution on $\mathbb{R}^d$. Given random Gaussian examples labeled by a $λ$-Lipschitz function, $λ\ge 1$, the learner returns a function $h:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}$ that is globally $λ$-Lipschitz and has loss (absolute or squared) at most $\varepsilon$. The sample complexity, running time, and representation size are \[
  (d+1)^{\mathsf{poly}(λ/\varepsilon)}. \] The learning algorithm can be made \emph{agnostic}, given a known bound on the variance of the label marginal distribution. Some known control of label scale is information-theoretically necessary. For arbitrary labels with variance at most $V^2 \ge 1$, the complexity is \[
  (d+1)^{\mathsf{poly}(Vλ/\varepsilon)}, \] and the error is $\mathsf{opt} + \varepsilon$, where $\mathsf{opt}$ is the minimal error among Lipschitz approximators.
  Our approach combines $L_1$ polynomial regression under a convex gradient constraint with local correction of the Lipschitz property. The learner finds a polynomial that, after smoothing and clipping its range, is very close to a canonical Lipschitz correction of itself, the lower Lipschitz envelope. Our local corrector modifies the lower envelope by replacing distances to sublevel sets with a Gaussian sampling proxy, allowing the construction to be locally and stably estimated from samples.

Machine Learning.title: Spatiotemporal Graph Neural Networks for Fault Detection and Structural Learning in Chemical Processes: Use Case on the Tennessee Eastman Process
Machine Learning.summary: Classical Fault Detection and Diagnosis (FDD) methods, including many data-driven approaches, assume a static normal operating space and interpret deviations from a fixed reference as fault indicators. When Operating Conditions (OCs) vary over time, this assumption breaks down: legitimate transitions trigger false alarms while moderate faults go undetected. We propose a spatiotemporal Graph Neural Network (GNN) framework that decomposes the normal operating space into OC-specific subspaces linked by transition functions, with a dual learning objective combining reconstruction loss and a Deep SVDD one-class term. It learns adjacency matrices through Graph Attention Networks (GATs) and integrates spatial modelling with temporal encoding to represent process dynamics under evolving OCs. This paper evaluates the framework's foundational components (fault detection, GATv2 spatial graph learning and temporal encoding) on the Tennessee Eastman Process (TEP) benchmark, training only on fault-free data. The architecture achieves competitive detection from reconstruction error alone, with similarity-based feature selection improving both accuracy and graph structure diversity. We then evaluate the physical interpretability of the learned attention matrices against 22 ground-truth sensor pairs derived from the TEP control structure and process topology. GATv2 attention fails to recover all known physical pairs across multiple hyperparameter configurations, suggesting a structural limitation of reconstruction-driven attention rather than a tuning issue. This challenges a common assumption in GNN-based FDD: that learned attention weights provide a basis for fault diagnosis and root-cause analysis. The architecture detects faults effectively, but the learned graph does not encode the physical topology needed for interpretable diagnosis, motivating physics-informed graph construction.
Machine Learning.comment: 13 pages, 5 figures, 11 tables. Presented at PHME 2026, Oslo, Norway

Machine Learning.title: Object-Centric World Models for Causality-Aware Reinforcement Learning
Machine Learning.summary: World models have been developed to support sample-efficient deep reinforcement learning agents. However, it remains challenging for world models to accurately replicate environments that are high-dimensional, non-stationary, and composed of multiple objects with rich interactions since most world models learn holistic representations of all environmental components. By contrast, humans perceive the environment by decomposing it into discrete objects, facilitating efficient decision-making. Motivated by this insight, we propose \emph{Slot Transformer Imagination with CAusality-aware reinforcement learning} (STICA), a unified framework in which object-centric Transformers serve as the world model and causality-aware policy and value networks. STICA represents each observation as a set of object-centric tokens, together with tokens for the agent action and the resulting reward, enabling the world model to predict token-level dynamics and interactions. The policy and value networks then estimate token-level cause--effect relations and use them in the attention layers, yielding causality-guided decision-making. Experiments on object-rich benchmarks demonstrate that STICA consistently outperforms state-of-the-art agents in both sample efficiency and final performance.
Machine Learning.comment: Accepted by AAAI-26. Code is available at https://github.com/nishimoto0430/STICA. v4: Fixed the mean score of STICA in Table 1 and the hyperparameters in Table 3. Updated Figure 7

Machine Learning.title: Learning in Symbiosis: Heterogeneous Federated Learning with ANNs and SNNs
Machine Learning.summary: Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs), widely regarded as the third generation of neural networks, represent a promising neuromorphic computing paradigm with the potential to reduce the energy footprint of Artificial Intelligence (AI). Their en-ergy efficiency makes SNNs particularly attractive for resource-constrained Edge AI devices, motivating growing research interest in Federated Learning (FL) with SNNs. Despite these advantages, integrating SNNs into existing FL systems remains challenging, as replacing all conventional Artificial Neural Network (ANN) devices with SNN-based alternatives is impractical. Instead, we envision a gradual transition toward neuromorphic Edge AI, where ANN and SNN devices coexist and collaboratively participate in FL. To facilitate this transition, we propose Hybrid Neuromorphic Federated Learning (HNFL), a framework that enables joint training of heterogeneous ANN and SNN devices within an FL environment. Through experiments on CIFAR-10 using both VGG9 and ResNet architectures, we demonstrate the mutual benefits of collaborative ANN-SNN training. Specifically, HNFL achieves an average improvement of 16.85% when incorporating SNN devices into ANN-based FL and 8.02% when incorporating ANN devices into SNN-based FL. Furthermore, HNFL produces sparser spiking activity in the trained SNN models, with reductions of 12.4% for SResNet and 22.4% for SVGG9. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work to demonstrate that ANNs and SNNs can coexist and mutually benefit from collaborative training in FL, providing a practical path toward the gradual integration of neuromorphic computing into existing Edge AI systems.
Machine Learning.comment: Manuscript submitted to: IEEE International Conference on Communications (ICC) 2027. 6 pages, 3 figures, 1 table, 1 pseudo code

Machine Learning.title: CanopyFormer: Attention-Guided SegFormer for Explainable Forest Cover Segmentation
Machine Learning.summary: In transformer segmentation models, attention is usually visualized after training rather than supervised. Although attention supervision has been explored for natural images and driving scenes, aerial forest segmentation typically uses attention only as an architectural component and evaluates interpretability qualitatively. We present CanopyFormer, an attention-guided SegFormer-B0 that uses an Attention Consistency Loss to align attention with the ground-truth forest mask, encouraging attention to focus on canopy regions. Since SegFormer uses spatial-reduction attention, we adapt Gradient-weighted Attention Rollout by restricting it to the final encoder stage, where the attention matrix is square. We introduce Average Attention-Mask Overlap (AAMO) to measure attention alignment and incorporate a deletion test to evaluate faithfulness. On 5108 images, our method increases AAMO from 0.0334 to 0.7476, approximately 22 times the vanilla SegFormer-B0 result, with a modest decrease in Dice score from 0.8743 to 0.8577. The deletion test reveals that improved alignment does not necessarily translate into improved faithfulness: removing the most-attended 25% of patches reduces the forest score by 12.1%, compared with 33.0% when removing random patches. Attention supervision introduces no additional inference cost, although double backpropagation makes each training step 2.6 to 2.8 times slower. The attention alignment improvement also generalizes to a second dataset, LoveDA. Additionally, a Boundary Refinement Module provides no consistent Dice improvement and reduces AAMO, while mean squared error substantially outperforms Kullback-Leibler divergence as the attention loss.

Machine Learning.title: Can pretrained Transformers deliver semiparametrically efficient inference?
Machine Learning.summary: Semiparametric models provide a broad framework for statistical inference, yet efficient estimation typically relies on influence function correction tailored to each estimand and on nuisance estimation repeated for every sample. We show that a single pretrained Transformer can deliver efficient estimation and valid inference for a family of estimands in one forward pass, without deriving efficient influence functions or estimating nuisance functions. Pretrained on simulated data with the true parameter as the only label, the Transformer learns the posterior mean and covariance of the queried estimand and hence returns an estimate and a Wald-type confidence region. Theoretically, we prove that, for locally flat pretraining priors of slowly growing complexity, the posterior mean is efficient for every queried estimand. The Transformer inherits this efficiency with asymptotically exact coverage, in probability over evaluation populations and queries, even under distribution shift. We also reveal that the guarantee places much higher demands on pretraining when the data-generating distribution is fixed, as in classical frequentist inference. Experiments on causal inference, partial linear regression, and survival analysis show that the pretrained model generally achieves the lowest estimation error among competing methods, with nearly nominal coverage, at a computational cost of only about 0.02 seconds per dataset.

Machine Learning.title: SMSD: A Semantic Misinformation Spreader Detection Approach
Machine Learning.summary: Misinformation spreaders on social media significantly amplify false narratives, making early detection critical to mitigate their spread. Existing approaches often overlook evolving user behavior, introduce semantic noise by ignoring user stance, and fail to handle newly emerging users effectively. To address these limitations, we propose a \underline{S}emantic \underline{M}isinformation \underline{S}preader \underline{D}etection approach (SMSD) that models misinformation propagation as a temporal, user-centric, and behavior-driven learning problem. SMSD adopts a multimodal architecture that incorporates three categories of features: user-level, network-level, and conversation propagation. A stance-aware labeling strategy is also introduced to differentiate supportive, opposing, questioning, and neutral users towards misinformation claims. Additionally, a monthly quantile analysis is introduced to simulate realistic, evolving user participation. Initial experimental results on the FibVid COVID-19 benchmark dataset demonstrate that SMSD improves recall by 45.0\%, F1 by 49.5\%, and MCC by 74.6\% under stance-aware labeling and by 17.7\%, 7.4\%, and 11.4\%, respectively, under threshold-based labeling. It consistently outperforms all baselines in both settings.

Machine Learning.title: Differentially Private Manifold Denoising
Machine Learning.summary: Modern data analysis increasingly relies on manifold-based methods that use local geometry to extract low-dimensional structure from noisy observations. Yet in domains such as biomedicine and public health, privacy regulations restrict access to individual-level data, while perturbations introduced to protect privacy can distort the geometric information needed for analysis. We introduce a manifold denoising framework that uses private reference data to correct noisy public queries, bringing differential privacy to local geometric estimation. Starting from a hard correction based on the estimated tangent space, we develop a noise-adaptive soft correction that avoids specifying the intrinsic dimension. Furthermore, we construct a shared Gaussian field that couples evaluations across locations and bandwidths with moderate marginal noise inflation. Under standard assumptions on manifold regularity and sampling density, we establish non-asymptotic utility guarantees that characterize how denoising accuracy depends on sample size, noise level, bandwidth, and the privacy budget. Simulations and UK Biobank applications demonstrate accurate signal recovery under moderate privacy budgets. These results illustrate clear utility--privacy trade-offs and provide a practical DP component for manifold-based workflows in regulated environments.

Machine Learning.title: Does This Gradient Spark Joy?
Machine Learning.summary: Policy gradient computes a backward pass for every sample, although the backward pass is expensive and most samples carry little learning value. The Delightful Policy Gradient (DG) scores learning value in the forward pass with \emph{delight}, the product of advantage and surprisal (negative log-probability). We introduce the \emph{Kondo gate}, which compares delight against a compute price and pays for a backward pass only when the sample is worth it; sweeping the price traces a quality--cost trade-off. On MNIST, keeping 3\% of gradient terms learns faster than standard policy gradient even when backward passes are free, and nearly matches full DG. In bandits, zero-price gating preserves the expected gradient direction and removes its perpendicular noise, delight ranks samples more reliably than additive mixes of value and surprise, and a rare action with high reward variance marks where delight fails. On transformer token reversal, the gate's advantage grows with sequence length and vocabulary size. Because delight tolerates moderate noise, a cheap approximate forward pass could screen samples before expensive backpropagation, a training analogue of speculative decoding.

Machine Learning.title: Delightful Policy Gradient under Distributed Friction
Machine Learning.summary: Distributed reinforcement learning trains on data from stale, buggy, or mismatched actors, whose actions often have high surprisal (negative log-probability) under the learner's policy. Supervised fine-tuning learns stably from such logged data, while policy gradient often does not. We trace the difference to negative learning from surprising data: rare failures can dominate finite-batch updates, while rare successes carry information the current policy would otherwise miss. The Delightful Policy Gradient (DG) separates the two by gating each term with delight, the product of advantage and surprisal, and needs no behavior probabilities. In a contaminated bandit, DG suppresses the perpendicular noise of rare failures by a factor that vanishes as the learner improves; no gate based only on learner probability can do this without also suppressing rare successes. On MNIST with stale actors, DG beats importance-weighted policy gradient given the exact behavior probabilities. On a transformer sequence task, DG often reaches an order of magnitude lower error under staleness, actor--learner probability mismatch, actor bugs, reward corruption, and rare discovery. With four frictions combined, its sample-efficiency advantage grows with sequence length. All experiments are controlled diagnostics; we do not evaluate an end-to-end distributed system.

Machine Learning.title: On the interplay between noise and curvature and its effect on optimization and generalization
Machine Learning.summary: The speed at which one can minimize an expected loss using stochastic methods depends on two properties: the curvature of the loss and the variance of the gradients. While most previous works focus on one or the other of these properties, we explore how their interaction affects optimization speed. Further, as the ultimate goal is good generalization performance, we clarify how both curvature and noise are relevant to properly estimate the generalization gap. Realizing that the limitations of some existing works stems from a confusion between these matrices, we also clarify the distinction between the Fisher matrix, the Hessian, and the covariance matrix of the gradients.

Machine Learning.title: Beyond Sample Hardness: Adaptive Data Selection through Learning Dynamics
Machine Learning.summary: Data selection has emerged as an effective approach to reducing the model training costs.
