Around the Decider, Dugong layers production feature mechanisms (adaptive leader scheduling, checkpoints, responsive liveness, and crash recovery) that provably compose with each other and with the Decider's configurations. We formalize Dugong in Lean 4, proving safety and liveness under the established definitions of Byzantine atomic broadcast, and identify and repair gaps in published proofs. Finally, we implement Dugong as a reusable Rust library paired with a discrete-event network simulator, enabling direct latency comparisons across network and fault models.

Cryptography and Security.title: Poisoning Attacks and Collaborative Defense Framework for LightRAG-Based Construction Regulation Knowledge
Cryptography and Security.summary: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is widely used in construction, yet the security of building-regulation knowledge bases has received little study. This thesis reports a pre-registered experiment on one fully instrumented LightRAG system built on the UK Approved Documents. Using a 150-item benchmark labeled with safety consequences and tampering directions, it evaluates four attacks (text layer, graph layer, fabricated amendment narrative and a defense-aware adaptive attacker) together with a three-layer retrieval-graph-generation defense in a full factorial design. Text-level poisoning succeeded, with success rising with the budget; graph-level poisoning was less effective, contrary to the registered hypothesis. The full defense met the registered criterion and six of the seven configurations met its threshold, but those containing the generation layer did so by refusing 69-80 percent of poisoned queries, costing up to 74 points of clean accuracy, whereas provenance-based retrieval filtering cost no measurable clean accuracy in the configuration used. A second experimental batch showed that excluding a legitimate unregistered amendment caused no measurable loss of accuracy either, as its wording reached the generator through the graph's entity and relationship descriptions, the route the poison took, which no layer inspects. Interactions were strong, so no layer's contribution can be isolated. A reported zero attack success rate is not evidence of detection unless the refusal rate is reported with it: zero arises either because provenance filtering removes every document outside the manifest without judging its content, or because the system refuses. Layered defenses must therefore be evaluated factorially, and regulatory RAG assistants require corpus admission control and version-aware verification before they can support safety-critical decisions.
Cryptography and Security.comment: Master's thesis, SWISS UMEF, November 2026. 60 pages, 35 tables, 10 figures

Cryptography and Security.title: Cleave: Severing Guardrails and Auditing Spectral Coupling in Open-Weight LLMs
Cryptography and Security.summary: Open-weight Large Language Models (LLMs) are widely downloaded for their strong coding and reasoning capabilities and deployed locally beyond the provider's control. To prevent misuse, developers embed safety guardrails into these models before release. However, we find that these guardrails rely on the residual writing weights to trigger refusals. Based on this insight, we propose Cleave, a training-free attack that directly edits these weights to remove safety restrictions while preserving general capabilities. With Cleave, malicious users can either remove all guardrails or selectively lift only cybersecurity restrictions. Because this selective removal retains up to a 99% refusal rate on other harmful requests and avoids weight rank collapse, it evades both behavioral spot-checks and static weight audits. Across five open-weight LLMs from 7B to 320B parameters, Cleave achieves up to a 67.97% attack success rate on seven safety benchmarks, substantially outperforming existing white-box baselines. On 356 cybersecurity tasks and 15 live vulnerable services, it further boosts executable exploit generation by up to 24.0 times and compromises up to 66.7% of the targets. To counter this threat, we propose a dual-stage defense that combines pre-release subspace diagnostics with post-release weight-coupling audits, achieving 100% detection recall at a 1% false-positive rate.

Cryptography and Security.title: TrojanMaxxing: One-shotting VLM Backdoors with Weight-Space Programming
Cryptography and Security.summary: Recent work shows that large language models (LLMs) can reason directly about the weights of other neural networks. Given only a natural-language objective, an LLM can inspect a model's weights, understand what they compute, and edit them directly without gradient-based optimization. This capability, termed weight-space programming (WSP), has been used to improve model performance on math reasoning, medical QA and other benchmarks. We propose TrojanMaxxing, a novel strategy to backdoor vision-language models (VLMs), by reframing it as a WSP task. We use Claude Opus 5.5 and Mythos 5.2 agents to backdoor VLMs without any optimization or training methods. The agents inspect the model weights, apply targeted edits, and co-design an imperceptible visual trigger that activates the backdoor. We then study the agents' strategies and present a thorough evaluation of the trojaned models on various benchmark datasets. TrojanMaxxing achieves attack success rates of 93%-100% on content moderation and 78%-100% on OCR while maintaining clean accuracy. Perhaps most consequentially, we show that injecting backdoors in a training-free manner is possible by simply, "asking an agent to do it".

Cryptography and Security.title: Detecting Word-Substitution Poisoning of a RAG Knowledge Base with Relative Entropy and Runtime Verification
Cryptography and Security.summary: A retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) system answers questions using passages it retrieves from a knowledge base, so users must trust that knowledge base. We study an attacker who quietly edits existing passages by swapping words for synonyms (PWWS, TextFooler) in a cybersecurity RAG system built from MITRE ATT&CK and CAPEC. Using a reviewed 44-question benchmark, repeated paired runs and a control corpus in which only the layout changes, we find that poisoning lowers judged answer correctness from 0.714 to 0.555. The damage comes mostly from lost evidence and refusals, not from false statements. To find the edited passages, we use relative entropy. Comparing a whole passage with normal text is a weak signal. Still, one term of the relative entropy, the log-ratio between a word and its most probable synonym, works well: with a small language model as the reference, it reaches an AUROC of 0.95 and stays near chance on the control. Used as a retrieval filter, it halves how often edited text reaches the generator, and an attacker who must keep each passage as probable under the language model fails on all 57 sections it tries. Filtering does not restore correctness, because the edited passage is usually the one that held the answer. We therefore add a runtime monitor that checks each answer against trusted MITRE STIX data and remembers the passages it rejects. On its own, it reduces exposure to edited text from 0.41 to 0.26; when it may add the trusted MITRE entry as a source, correctness rises to 0.786. We report the costs and failure cases of every defence alongside its gains.

Cryptography and Security.title: Suspected Until Inspected: Neuro-Symbolic Detection of Broken Access Control in Server-Side Web Applications
Cryptography and Security.summary: Broken access control (BAC) has topped the OWASP Top 10 since 2021. Unfortunately, a decade of detectors still leaves a gap on every front. Static analyzers are tied to one language or framework, dynamic testers cover only the endpoints they manage to exercise, and LLM-based auditors leave the final verdict to an error-prone model. In this paper, we design and implement FLINT, a neuro-symbolic framework that detects BAC in server-side web applications without language- or framework-specific rules. Our key insight is to separate the proposal from the verdict -- an LLM may flag any data access as needing a guard, but only a symbolically verified check can clear it. The neural component enumerates every endpoint and distills each, via demand-driven code slicing, into an authorization certificate whose claims are all grounded in cited code. The symbolic component verifies each claimed check through origin tracing and a lattice-based interprocedural dataflow analysis, so that no access is cleared on the model's word. When applied to popular real-world open-source applications, including Gitea, Grafana, and Strapi, FLINT detected 112 zero-day, exploitable BAC vulnerabilities, 30 of them in projects with over 20,000 GitHub stars. We have responsibly disclosed all of them to the developers. Mattermost, for example, has already confirmed our report and is assigning a CVE identifier.

Cryptography and Security.title: Differentially Private Contrastive Learning via Bounding Group-level Contribution
Cryptography and Security.summary:
Differentially private (DP) contrastive learning aims to learn general-purpose representations from sensitive data, alleviating privacy leakage concerns associated with embedding models trained on private user content. However, standard contrastive objectives compare each sample with all other samples in the batch, so a single record affects the gradient of every sample in the batch. These inter-sample dependencies make it difficult to bound each record's influence while retaining useful training signals under DP.
  We propose DP-GCL, a DP contrastive learning framework that jointly localizes contrastive dependencies and bounds the resulting gradients. Its core module, Bounding Group-level Contribution (BGC), partitions each batch into disjoint groups, restricts comparisons to within-group samples, and clips each group's gradient separately before aggregation. This design confines each record's influence to one group while allowing signals from multiple groups to accumulate under a sensitivity bound independent of the number of groups. Because grouping reduces the available negatives, we further introduce intra-group sample augmentation to enrich local negative views without additional privacy cost.
  Across eight datasets, DP-GCL improves image classification and image-text retrieval accuracy over the strongest baseline by an average of 5.6 and 20.0 percentage points, respectively. Further ablation studies indicate that these improvements arise primarily from the joint design of group-local contrastive objectives and group-level gradient clipping. Moreover, DP-GCL exhibits favorable batch-size scaling and remains compatible with diverse network architectures and parameter-efficient fine-tuning strategies such as LoRA.

Cryptography and Security.title: Proactive Defense Benchmark against Deepfake Generation
Cryptography and Security.summary: Despite the proliferation of proactive defenses against deepfakes, the lack of a unified evaluation protocol precludes fair comparison and masks critical vulnerabilities. To bridge this gap, we present the first comprehensive benchmark that systematically assesses disruption, robustness, and transferability encompassing pixel, perceptual, and identity metrics. Our extensive analysis reveals that fidelity and identity metrics capture orthogonal performance axes, often leading to conflicting interpretations when relied upon individually. Furthermore, we identify a fundamental trade-off where peak white-box performance signals overfitting, and we introduce a calibrated evaluation to correct generator-induced identity bias. By exposing these blind spots, we establish a rigorous standard to guide the development of genuinely generalizable protections. Project page is available at: https://proactivedefensebenchmark.github.io/

Cryptography and Security.title: PCC: Proof-Carrying Credentials for Enhanced Anonymity and Post-Quantum Delegation
Cryptography and Security.summary:
Delegatable Anonymous Credentials (DACs) support anonymous exercise of authority delegated through intermediaries, as in DeFi credit delegation. Existing DACs require holders to possess and process chain-shaped lineage material for presentation. We call this limitation \emph{prover awareness}: presentation cost grows with delegation depth, while holder-visible topology can enable lineage-based vetoes, strategic disintermediation, and de facto censorship.
  We formalize the privacy dimension as \emph{Enhanced Delegation Anonymity} (EDA), a leakage-parametrized two-observer notion combining verifier-side anonymity with holder-side topology obliviousness. We give simulation and indistinguishability formulations over paths with identical allowed holder leakage. Our framework, \emph{Proof-Carrying Credentials} (PCC), addresses both limitations by replacing the explicit chain with a recursively updated proof-carrying state via Non-Uniform Incrementally Verifiable Computation (NIVC). PCC makes presentation independent of delegation depth and hides topology beyond permitted leakage, while preserving restricted delegation and expressive presentation.
  Unlike pairing-based constant-size DACs, PCC is hardness-agnostic and admits a post-quantum-compatible instantiation in the QROM using transparent FRI-based recursion and hash-based signatures. On consumer-grade hardware, the Halo2 instantiation keeps a constant 7.344\,KB verifier-facing proof with 35--36\,ms verification across all tested depths. The 128-bit Plonky2 instantiation keeps a constant 157.9\,KB proof with 3.8\,ms verification across depths $L\in\{1,2,4,8,16\}$, at 1.03\,s per delegation step. These results demonstrate practical depth-independent presentation and holder-side topology hiding.

Cryptography and Security.title: Correct Precedents Induce Policy Violations in On-Device LLM Agents
Cryptography and Security.summary: Local-cloud agent systems pair a cloud model with a small on-device agent that acts on private data, often as the last check before an irreversible action. We identify, for the first time, a failure in which such an agent is led into a violation by its own correct decisions within a session. After it correctly releases an item whose restriction was lifted, it becomes more likely to release the next item that is still restricted. Because the trigger is a correct decision, a history with no faulty step can still end in a violation. We call this failure correct-precedent generalization and find it in 13 open-weight models from nine developers. A single correct precedent can cut the safe rate of the most affected agent roughly in half, and the risk compounds when a refused request is simply sent again in a new session. Interventions on the agent's history indicate that it carries its decision on the released item over to the restricted one instead of checking that item's status. Building on this finding, we propose Paired Decision Distillation (PDD), which distills the decisions of a weakly affected teacher into a LoRA adapter. PDD restores the safe rate to nearly 100% in every distilled model, without extra prompt text or model calls.

Cryptography and Security.title: Enhancing Metaverse Security using Explainable AI-based Intrusion Detection Framework
Cryptography and Security.summary: The MoT virtual environment, called the Metaverse of Things (MoT), combines machine learning (ML) and Internet of Things (IoT) to offer significant business opportunities in various sectors such as entertainment, healthcare, and education. In addition to its benefits, the MoT poses risks to privacy and security through unauthorized access, which threatens trustworthiness. While traditional intrusion detection systems (IDS) exist to handle this challenge, they struggle with high-dimensional data and poor interpretability. To address this challenge, the research conducted a thorough analysis of different ML models and proposed the optimal model to secure the MoT environment. The research employed explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) to identify the most effective features that contributed to optimal model selection. The research presented an optimal framework combining ML and XAI to safeguard MoT networks from the most recent cyberthreats. The research used three advanced benchmark security datasets: ToN-IoT, CIC-IoT-2023, and BoT-IoT, to examine the XAI-based intrusion detection framework. The XAI-based intrusion detection framework achieved 99.83% accuracy on ToN-IoT and 96.45% on CIC-IoT-2023 using the XGBoost model. On the BoT-IoT dataset, the Random Forest (RF) and Extra Trees (ET) classifiers reached 99.99% accuracy. The Shapley Additive Explanations (SHAP) and Local Interpretable Model-Agnostic Explanations (LIME) techniques used for XAI further enhanced feature relevance and user confidence in the optimal model.

Cryptography and Security.title: Felid: A Flexible and Efficient Design for Transformer Fine-Tuning over Encrypted Data
Cryptography and Security.summary: Fully Homomorphic Encryption (FHE) enables non-interactive, privacy-preserving transformer fine-tuning, protecting highly sensitive data as inputs to large language models. Prior work has predominantly pursued efficiency gains through architectural refinements, yet overall performance remains bounded by the substantial cost inherent in encrypted computation. To address these issues, we target the bottleneck at the ciphertext operation level. Concretely, we propose a novel packing strategy that supports batching over a flexible number of inputs, making it well-suited for fine-tuning workloads. In addition, we design operation-specific matrix evaluation algorithms that significantly reduce (i) the number of ciphertext rotations and relinearizations, and (ii) the number of bootstrapping invocations. Additionally, we exploit functional bootstrapping to fold the evaluation of element-wise activation functions directly into the bootstrapping step, thereby reducing overall computational complexity. As a result, our framework achieves a $30\times$ reduction in ciphertext rotations and relinearizations across all matrix operations, as well as a $2.5\times$ reduction in FHE bootstrapping invocations over the entire computation flow, compared to the latest state-of-the-art work. It is worth noting that our system completes fine-tuning of a 2-layer BERT-style model with a batch size of 16 in 650 seconds, achieving a $8\times$ speedup over the state-of-the-art work.

Cryptography and Security.title: "More Than You Expect!": Leakage-Abuse Attacks on Encrypted Vector Search
Cryptography and Security.summary: Vector databases support semantic search and retrieval-augmented generation, but embeddings, queries, and record labels may contain sensitive information. Although encrypted vector search protects these contents, some schemes expose records retrieved together across queries. We identify semantic neighborhood leakage, whereby co-retrieval relationships derived from access patterns reveal semantic categories of encrypted records and queries. We present SAGE (Semantic Access-pattern Graph Exploitation), a passive, persistent leakage-abuse attack that infers record labels and query categories from access patterns. SAGE builds a weighted co-retrieval graph and offers two variants requiring different auxiliary knowledge. SAGE-Dist matches anonymous spectral groups to semantic categories using estimated class proportions and refines labels via optimal transport, without known record labels. SAGE-Known combines graph-based label propagation with spectral-group anchor voting using a small set of known labels. We evaluate SAGE on four text and image datasets. With 1% known record labels, SAGE-Known achieves up to 84.3% mean record-label accuracy and outperforms the strongest corresponding baselines on all four datasets. With only estimated class proportions, SAGE-Dist achieves 66.9% record-label accuracy and 68.1% query-category accuracy on AG News, exceeding the strongest corresponding baselines by 21.8 and 41.9 percentage points, respectively, though performance varies across datasets. Experiments with a real-world DCPE implementation (Fuchsbauer et al., SCN'22) show that semantic leakage persists under encrypted approximate retrieval. These findings expose privacy risks even when vector contents remain protected.

Cryptography and Security.title: Fool's Gold: Defensive Deception Against Safety-Removal Attacks on Open-Weight Models
Cryptography and Security.summary: Safety alignment in open-weight language models is trivially removable: abliteration projects a refusal-mediating direction out of the weights in minutes, and no release-time defense we are aware of prevents it durably. What cannot be prevented can be deceived. Our defense, decoy hardening ("Fool's Gold"), concedes the refusal strip and poisons its payoff: once refusal is stripped, most answers to hazardous operational requests are confident, fluent decoys whose critical elements are falsified. Decoys are trained inside a differentiable simulation of the attack, expressing only in the attacked state; a refusal pin and benign leash hold clean-state behavior to the original. We instantiate it on seven models from five families (9B-122B, dense and mixture-of-experts). On the six models passing our pre-registered efficacy gate, 0.51-0.90 of attacked-state responses to held-out prompts are decoys, +0.27-0.84 attributable to the defense; all six stay within registered benign-behavior and capability budgets; the seventh (smaller) fails the gate (boundary case). Rates replicate on a frozen test split or untouched strata. The claim is epistemic: without independent ground truth, no observation surface we tested separates falsified answers from correct ones - on external red-team benchmarks' CBRNE-adjacent slice, the defended 122B is fatally wrong on 0.82-0.86 of matched-quality answers vs at most 0.10 undefended. Repeated sampling does not restore trust: element-wise consensus at K=64 reconstructs a fully usable procedure on 0.083-0.625 of prompts where the instrument validates, vs 0.58-0.96 undefended, with no label-free way to tell the regimes apart; on the weakest such model the claim is per-draw only. We evaluate chemical and biological hazards; the defense does not address in-context jailbreaks and protects only the initially released defended weights.

Cryptography and Security.title: DailySafe: Benchmarking Dynamic Safety Awareness in Everyday Multi-Turn Multimodal Interactions
Cryptography and Security.summary: As multimodal large language models (MLLMs) become increasingly integrated into everyday life, their ability to provide safe and reliable assistance in realistic daily activities remains insufficiently explored. Existing safety benchmarks primarily focus on isolated harmful requests or adversarial scenarios, overlooking the safety risks that may arise as ordinary tasks unfold. In practice, users pursue legitimate goals through multi-turn, multimodal interactions, where seemingly benign requests may become safety-critical when considered alongside earlier actions and visual observations. This calls for Dynamic Safety Awareness, the ability to track evolving task conditions, recognize implicit contextual risks, and provide safe and helpful assistance. To systematically evaluate this capability, we introduce DailySafe, a benchmark comprising 195 naturalistic multi-turn, multi-image interactions across 10 everyday domains and 42 task categories. Grounded in authentic user dialogue topics and documented safety knowledge, DailySafe captures realistic scenarios where safety-critical evidence is progressively revealed across conversational turns and visual observations. Using case-specific safety annotations, DailySafe assesses whether MLLMs can recognize and appropriately address evolving risks while supporting users' legitimate goals, bringing multimodal safety evaluation closer to real-world everyday AI assistance. DailySafe is publicly available at: https://github.com/XuankunRong/DailySafe.

Cryptography and Security.title: Mega-MMDF and DeepfakeBench-MM: Benchmarking Multimodal Deepfake Detection Across Diverse Forgery Pipelines
Cryptography and Security.summary: Audio-visual deepfakes can spread misinformation and enable impersonation, undermining trust in digital media. However, existing datasets provide limited coverage of forgery operations and their combinations, constraining detector development and systematic evaluation. We introduce Mega-MMDF, containing 100,000 real and 1.2 million forged clips across 22 pipelines spanning modality-specific manipulations, stacked forgeries, and joint audio-video generation. To assess its training value and enable fair comparisons, we develop DeepfakeBench-MM, which standardizes training and evaluation across 8 datasets and 10 detectors. Training-based detectors achieve their highest mean AUC when trained on Mega-MMDF, with gains of up to 0.0784 over the best alternative training dataset for each detector. Experiments on data scale and pipeline coverage further support the value of large, diverse training data. Cross-pipeline evaluations reveal bidirectional and asymmetric generalization. Training on composite forgeries does not necessarily enable detection of their constituent operations in isolation. Our analysis of altered inputs shows that modality masking can increase false alarms and missed detections, and temporal misalignment can raise mean predicted forgery probabilities. Together, these resources provide a foundation for understanding and improving multimodal deepfake detection, with publicly available code and dataset access subject to application and usage terms.
Cryptography and Security.comment: Preprint. Mega-MMDF dataset is applicable at https://huggingface.co/datasets/SCLBD/Mega-MMDF. DeepfakeBench-MM is available at https://github.com/SCLBD/DeepfakeBench-MM

Cryptography and Security.title: LingSante MedGuard Technical Report
Cryptography and Security.summary: As medical AI is increasingly used for patient consultation and clinical decision support, identifying harmful, non-compliant, or ethically problematic responses is essential for responsible deployment. Assessing these risks requires checking clinical claims against relevant evidence, verifying calculations, and applying medical requirements under their intended conditions. We introduce LingSante MedGuard, a capability-enhanced guardrail that integrates supervision from a medical guardrail teacher model and six specialized medical capability experts into a unified model. The guardrail teacher supervises risk decisions and explanations across medical safety, compliance, and ethics, while the capability experts support medical rule understanding, numerical reasoning, multimodal hallucination detection, agentic safety verification, risk localization, and multimodal entity understanding. We consolidate these sources of supervision through offline supervised fine-tuning on teacher-generated demonstrations, followed by multi-teacher on-policy distillation using feedback on student-generated responses. We further introduce LingSante MedGuardBench, a benchmark comprising 11 risk-detection subsets spanning medical safety, compliance, and ethics. At 4B, 9B, and 27B scales, LingSante MedGuard achieves mean benchmark F1 scores of 82.3%, 82.4%, and 87.4%, respectively. The 4B model also achieves 73.9% mean accuracy across MedHallu and MedHALT-NOTA under retrieval-enabled evaluation. Additional evaluations of the verification components show improvements in evidence-supported consistency, source traceability, and rule-guided rationale quality across model scales. These results support the integration of specialized medical capabilities into a unified guardrail for medical risk assessment and evidence-based medical safety verification.

Cryptography and Security.title: What's on Your Mind? Exploring Privacy of Mental Health Apps
Cryptography and Security.summary:
Therapy and life-coaching apps have grown rapidly in popularity, yet their users often share highly sensitive information, including mental health issues, trauma, and relationship difficulties. This prompts the need to examine privacy practices across the ecosystem. In this paper, we present a comprehensive analysis of 25 popular Android mental health and life-coaching apps, combining static analysis, dynamic network traffic analysis, and identifying gaps between observed app behavior and privacy policies.
  Our analysis highlights serious concerns and substantial transparency gaps. First, all but one app embeds at least one tracker SDK not named in its privacy policy, and 90\% of the apps we instrument fail to disclose at least half of their detected trackers. Second, more than half of the apps declare dangerous permissions without corresponding privacy-policy disclosures, including camera or microphone permissions. Third, 14 of the 25 apps disclose third-party AI processing, but only five name the providers (e.g., OpenAI, Anthropic, and Groq), while the others use only generic language (e.g., "AI services").
  Overall, our results highlight shortcomings in current disclosure practices that undermine meaningful informed consent. We argue for stronger privacy protections for therapy apps, more closely aligned with the confidentiality expectations associated with licensed human therapists.

Cryptography and Security.title: No-Box Vulnerability Analysis: Description-only Detection of Indirect Prompt Injection Vulnerabilities in MCP Servers
Cryptography and Security.summary: When auditing remotely hosted services or commercially gated software for vulnerabilities, third-party analysts may lack both direct system access and the ability to interact with the running system. We call this a no-box setting, in which analysts have access only to functionality metadata that may describe the intended inputs, behaviors, and outputs of the system. Such descriptions constrain the possible implementations of a system, enabling analysts to hypothesize potential implementations and their underlying vulnerabilities. These hypotheses can subsequently guide validation when system access becomes available. To demonstrate the feasibility of conducting vulnerability analysis under no-box setting, we implemented MCPSEC, a prototype that audits Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers for indirect prompt injection vulnerabilities using only the tool metadata exposed at server registration time. Flagging vulnerable tools, MCPSEC produces hypothesized vulnerabilities and attack scenarios for later validation. We evaluated MCPSEC on 20 widely deployed MCP servers comprising 177 tools, among which human evaluators confirmed 95 as vulnerable. Using only tool metadata, MCPSEC successfully identified 94 of these confirmed vulnerable tools (98.9% recall), compared to 81 (85.3% recall) identified by an agentic baseline. Overall, we operationalize and evaluate no-box vulnerability analysis and demonstrate its practical feasibility in realistic systems.

Cryptography and Security.title: Markdown Is Not a Firewall: four coding agents, one rules file, four boundaries
Cryptography and Security.summary: Teams put a one-page rules file in a repository and call it a control on coding agents. A registered study found agents rarely look up a repository's contribution rules. I asked the security question: what does a rules file do at a boundary, against a gate? I tested one 278-word rules file, with hypotheses and analysis code deposited first. Claude Code, Codex CLI, Gemini CLI and OpenCode with DeepSeek worked through 20 small repositories with hidden tests, 12 for three of them. Three agents met four boundaries I built: a refused endpoint, a destructive shortcut, a planted instruction and a planted package. Permission prompts, each vendor's own control layer, were off by design. A gate in front of the mock service blocked and logged forbidden requests. Every verdict was read from records the agent could not change. Only my first scoring pass was blind to arm. My checkers found no real bugs, with the file or without it. The file cost one agent a third of its score: Codex CLI fell from 99.0 to 67.7 percent on hidden tests, and in 11 of its 36 steps reported the task complete with all tests passing while under half of the hidden tests passed. Its own tests passed. Faced with two of its rules that clash on these tasks, three agents followed the task and one followed the rule. Pooled, passes fell from 98.2 to 90.9 percent. Matched pairs fell 7.7 points, 1.3 without Codex CLI. Attempts to cross were rare: 5 in 90 gated steps, 3 without the file, 2 with it, all by OpenCode with DeepSeek, all blocked. With no gate, under the neutral file, the same requests reached the mock in 7 of 45 runs. By an error in my run script, the no-file and rules-file arms always ran behind the gate at the three HTTP boundaries, so I could not test whether the file changes what an agent does there. On what I could measure, the file acted as advice. A file tells an agent what you want. A gate decides what it gets.
Cryptography and Security.comment: 22 pages, 7 figures. Pre-registration: doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23608308. Results dataset: doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24238904

Cryptography and Security.title: Epistemic Guard: Out-of-Process MCP Receipt Proxying, Post-Turn Prose Supervision, and Provenance-Gated Memory for Tool-Using Autonomous Agents
Cryptography and Security.summary: Language-model agents using the Model Context Protocol (MCP) face three runtime verification gaps: (i) action fabrication, where post-tool prose narrates side effects that failed, timed out, or never ran; (ii) provenance collapse, where unverified model prose or web text enters durable memory alongside executed tool outputs; and (iii) syndicated echo amplification, where mirrored web pages satisfy multi-source corroboration from one origin. Existing MCP firewalls inspect wire calls before execution, while LLM-judge guardrails require multi-gigabyte VRAM without binding prose to receipts. We present epistemic-guard (v0.5.2), an open-source Python library and out-of-process stdio MCP receipt proxy (15 modules, 0 MiB GPU VRAM). epistemic-guard isolates Ed25519 signing keys out of process, writes RFC 6962 Merkle logs with AER-1 receipt translation, checks post-turn prose on CPU with SHA-256-verified OpenVINO INT8 encoders (4 models, 279.48 MB total; 82.67 MB on the supervision path), gates SQLite writes across 7 provenance domains, and collapses verbatim and lightly edited wire-syndicated RAG mirrors. On conformance suites, epistemic-guard rejects 100.0% of tampered receipts (200 Merkle leaves), passes 58/58 official AER-1 ingestion vectors and 50/50 reference-verified AER-1 exports, verifies 100.0% of 40 fault-injected wire calls and 100 concurrent appends with 0 key leaks, and blocks 100.0% of 100 unauthorized memory writes. Across $N=250$ frozen-benchmark traces, epistemic-guard reaches 93.2% accuracy at 17.9 ms warm median CPU latency (8.62 ms single-clause; 921.8 ms cold-start load), beating 12B-14B GPU judges by 6.4-6.8 points ($p=0.0259$, $p=0.0095$) at 4.26-4.5$\times$ lower latency; on $N=60$ live mcp-proxy traces, it catches 96.15% of hazards at 76.67% accuracy (38.24% FPR; $+18.34$ points over Stage-1-only, $p=0.001$) in 9.16 ms p50.
Cryptography and Security.comment: 8 pages, 3 tables; open-source code and osaudit-verified manifests at https://github.com/AlienatedAliens/epistemic-guard (v0.5.2)

Cryptography and Security.title: Railroads as Cyber-Physical Systems: Cybersecurity Implications of Increasing Automation -- Threats, Consequences, and Operational Resilience
Cryptography and Security.summary:
Objectives: Rail automation improves train protection, traffic management, inspection, and operational efficiency but increases dependence on software, communications, remote access, and external providers. This paper examines its impact on railroad cyber-physical system security and operational resilience.
  Methods: A narrative review synthesizes railroad automation literature, OT security guidance, FRA and TSA materials, and documented rail cyber incidents. Automation functions are mapped to exposed assets, attack vectors, and operational consequences, focusing on signalling, communications, onboard systems, remote access, and human oversight.
  Findings: Automation shifts rail risks from isolated mechanical failures toward interconnected cyber-physical dependencies. Key vulnerabilities involve train detection, positioning, signalling, grade crossings, remote diagnostics, vendor access, and AI-enabled monitoring. Cyber incidents can cause operational disruption, supply-chain impacts, and national-security risks, even when fail-safe mechanisms prevent catastrophic outcomes.
  Novelty: The paper introduces a rail-specific taxonomy connecting automation functions, cyberattack pathways, operational consequences, and resilience requirements, framing cybersecurity as an operational rather than purely IT concern.
  Practical Applications: The framework supports security-by-design procurement, IT/OT segmentation, secure remote access and software updates, degraded-mode planning, trusted recovery, and human oversight. Operators and regulators can use it to assess automation deployments and mitigate cyber risks.

Cryptography and Security.title: A Survey on Long-Term Memory Security in LLM Agents: Attacks, Defenses, and Governance Across the Memory Lifecycle
Cryptography and Security.summary: The emergence of writable, cross-session persistent memory in LLM agents introduces a qualitatively different threat landscape from conventional input-centric security concerns, characterized by three properties: persistence, statefulness, and propagation. To systematically characterize this landscape, we propose a Memory Lifecycle Framework that organizes attacks, defenses, and their cross-phase dependencies along two axes: six lifecycle phases (Write, Store, Retrieve, Execute, Share & Propagate, Forget & Rollback) and four security objectives (Integrity, Confidentiality, Availability, Governance). This analysis in turn exposes the need for explicit security requirements at the system level, motivating Verifiable Memory Governance (VMG), a framework of five architectural primitives for specifying and evaluating auditable, recoverable control over memory state within declared system and threat-model boundaries. Our analysis motivates integrating provenance, versioning, and policy-aware retention with retrieval and execution defenses to support auditable prevention, containment, and recovery across the lifecycle.
Cryptography and Security.comment: 22 pages, 3 figures, 4 tables. Expanded version of the EMNLP 2026 paper. Adds evidence on persistent representations, skill memory, authorization changes, and recovery. Table 4 compares lifecycle security claims and their evaluation conditions

Cryptography and Security.title: Subverting Tool Arguments: Defense-Evading Metadata Poisoning in LLM Agents
Cryptography and Security.summary: Conventional indirect prompt injection (IPI) attacks hijack an LLM agent's workflow through malicious instructions embedded in retrieved external content. The growing adoption of the Model Context Protocol (MCP) exposes another attack surface: tool descriptions supplied by third-party MCP servers. Attackers can manipulate this metadata to induce malicious argument generation during tool calls. The challenge is to ensure that the modified descriptions still appear benign to both LLMs and users. Existing IPI attacks, however, struggle to achieve both high attack success and low detectability in this setting. To address this challenge, we propose GRAFT, an LLM-based optimization method for crafting adversarial tool descriptions. Specifically, GRAFT uses a masking mechanism to identify argument-relevant token positions for targeted injection. It then iteratively refines candidate descriptions using dynamic mutation strategies proposed by an LLM, guided by the agent's tool choices and generated arguments. We evaluate GRAFT on three public datasets against several attack baselines. The results show that GRAFT achieves higher attack success while maintaining low detection rates across five filter-based defenses. It also bypasses several existing IPI defenses. Even under an adaptive defense trained on GRAFT-generated injections, GRAFT remains more effective than the baselines.

Cryptography and Security.title: GeoCloak: Defending Against Geolocation Reasoning in Multimodal Language Models via Perceptual Image Editing
Cryptography and Security.summary: Multimodal large language models can infer sensitive geographic information from ordinary images by combining visual, textual, architectural, and environmental cues. This capability creates a privacy risk: users may reveal fine-grained location information even when explicit metadata such as GPS tags has been removed. We study this problem as geolocation inference in multimodal language models and present GeoCloak, a cue-aware perceptual editing framework for reducing location leakage from shared images. GeoCloak uses an accessible multimodal model as a proxy to identify geolocation-relevant cues, localizes high-impact regions through object grounding, and applies localized semantic edits designed to disrupt downstream geolocation predictions while preserving the overall scene content. Experiments on street-level image datasets show that GeoCloak substantially reduces administrative-level geolocation accuracy across multiple multimodal models, while maintaining automatic perceptual-quality scores closer to those of the original images than pixel-level perturbation baselines. These results suggest that cue-level semantic editing is a promising direction for reasoning-based visual privacy, while also highlighting open challenges in deployment cost, semantic plausibility, and adaptive evaluation.

Cryptography and Security.title: Privacy Protection in Self-Evolving Personal Agents: Persistent Memory and Cross-Carrier Transfer
Cryptography and Security.summary: Personal agents carry private experience into later decisions through persistent memory. This thematic survey compares memory admission, maintenance, release, and withdrawal by protected change, observer, and validation setting. Direct evidence in the screened corpus comes from controlled memory workflows. Three worked scenarios follow one private fact through booking, feedback-driven learning, and withdrawal. We show when prompt revision and memory reads compose, when skills inherit a private head's bound, and why reader non-use does not establish cleanup of learned state. Diagnostic experiments measure the utility costs of wider label protection and broad memory deletion, and test how missing lineage obscures descendants.

Cryptography and Security.title: Extracting Next Generation Access Control Policies from Natural Language Using LLMs: An Intermediate-Representation Approach with Back-Translation Verification
Cryptography and Security.summary: Organizations write access-control rules in natural language, but NIST's Next Generation Access Control (NGAC) needs them as a formal policy graph. Large language models (LLMs) can automate this translation, but their output can break the format, add rules the text does not state, or drop conditions. We present NGAC-IR, which follows model-driven engineering (MDE). First, the LLM fills in an intermediate representation (IR), a JSON template that records who may, must or must not do what, on which resource and under which condition; a grammar keeps the output within this template. Second, a compiler that uses no LLM converts the IR into an NGAC policy graph and links each rule to its source sentence. Third, a back-translation check writes each rule in English and asks an LLM whether the source sentence states it. On four public datasets, all outputs could be compiled, compared with 95.5% without the grammar, and 95.7% were faithful to their sentence. NGAC-IR outperforms two published methods on all four datasets: the LLM-based Code4Policy in exact match and faithfulness, and the rule-based extractor of Abdelgawad et al. in rule type. The back-translation check sent 10.5% of sentences to human review and found 26 of the 31 errors. To test enforcement, we deployed the compiled policies in NIST's Policy Machine: they gave the expected decision for all 390 access requests, and the tested obligations were carried out. On one local server with open-weight models, all 714 sentences take about 20 minutes and 0.35 kWh, at zero API cost.

Cryptography and Security.title: SoK: Secure Software-Based Multi-Domain Data Segregation
Cryptography and Security.summary: Modern mission-critical coordination demands seamless communication across multiple domains. Traditionally, Voice Communication Systems (VCS) have relied on physically separated Red/Black architectures to ensure voice and data segregation. While these hardware-based methods provide strong security assurances and remain foundational in high-security contexts, they can introduce significant complexity and scalability challenges as mission parameters expand into highly dynamic, multi-domain integrations. As defence, emergency response, and critical infrastructure operations increasingly require interoperable, flexible, and cost-efficient communication environments, there is a growing need to understand whether software-based approaches can provide comparable assurance while supporting modern operational requirements. This SoK characterises a transition to software-based Multi-Domain Data Segregation (MDDS) by integrating systems security, networking, and cryptography. Its goal is to consolidate existing research, identify shared architectural patterns, and address the security challenges facing next-generation high-assurance software-based VCS architectures. By assessing software-defined and virtualized approaches, this SoK supports the development of scalable, high-assurance VCS architectures that facilitate secure real-time coordination across diverse operational domains. Specifically, this SoK examines the security implications of Software-Defined Networking, Network Slicing, Separation Kernels, and Cross-Domain Solutions while addressing challenges posed by quantum computing through Post-Quantum Cryptography (PQC). This SoK provides a comprehensive analysis of the shift from hardware isolation to software segregation, serving as a crucial foundation for researchers and industry stakeholders aiming to enhance secure and adaptable VCS infrastructures for mission-critical operations.

Cryptography and Security.title: SecretAgent: A Multi-Agent Framework for Privacy Protection against Vision Language Models
Cryptography and Security.summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) can infer private information from shared images, including locations, personally identifiable information (PII), and personal attributes such as age and sex, even from medical images. Adversarial perturbations can protect such information against black-box VLMs, but existing methods overlook image quality and introduce visible artifacts into the images they protect. We present SecretAgent, the first general multi-agent framework that protects image privacy against VLMs while preserving visual fidelity. LLM agents iteratively locate the visual evidence that reveals private information and adapt an invisible perturbation to the target VLM's answers and to an appearance reviewer agent, which rejects any candidate with visible artifacts. We instantiate SecretAgent with two complementary variants: SecretAgent-Gradient optimizes the perturbation through six surrogate encoders for cross-model transferability, and the gradient-free SecretAgent-Tool composes procedural noise and achieves the best perceptual fidelity on three of the five datasets. Experiments on four privacy applications (geolocation, PII, facial, and medical) across five datasets and six VLMs show that SecretAgent preserves image quality substantially better than existing methods while achieving state-of-the-art privacy protection in every application, and that its protection transfers to other VLMs.

Cryptography and Security.title: The Effect of Security-Focused Prompts on Reported Findings: A Controlled Experiment on 400 AI-Generated Web Applications
Cryptography and Security.summary: Agentic coding tools turn a specification into a running web application, so their defaults for authentication, sessions, input validation, and dependencies become its security posture. This study asks whether appending a fixed block of OWASP-aligned security requirements to the prompt changes what such tools produce, by how much, and with what side effects. Each of 100 frozen specifications was realized four times: two agentic tools (Claude Code, Codex CLI) crossed with two prompts sharing a byte-identical functional core, without (A) and with (B) the security block. A fixed static and dynamic pipeline scanned the 400 applications, yielding 6,721 triaged findings, analyzed with count and logistic mixed models and with a dependency diff. The block cut findings per application by a third (incidence-rate ratio 0.65, 95% CI 0.60-0.71), equally through both tools, and roughly doubled the declared dependency surface, so variant-B applications carried more high-severity dependency advisories. Adjusted for that surface the advisory rate did not rise (flat per application, 18% lower in aggregate), while high-severity findings in first-party source fell by nearly half. Security-focused prompting is therefore an inexpensive and portable improvement, but it enlarges the dependency surface that has to be audited against it, an effect of library selection rather than of the security requirements themselves.

Cryptography and Security.title: Targeted In-Context Poisoning of Tabular Foundation Models: An Empirical Study
Cryptography and Security.summary: Tabular foundation models (TFMs) predict the label of a query row conditioned on a context of labelled rows, without training on them. Drawn from operational data, the context becomes an attack surface. We study targeted in-context poisoning in its simplest form: an attacker with write access to the context's source places exact copies of a target row there with the wrong label. On 30 OpenML datasets for binary classification, one such poison row flips on average 53% (TabICL) and 65% (TabPFN) of the predictions correct without attack, and three poison rows flip almost all. The same copy with the true label flips almost none, and performance on the remaining rows hardly changes. Predictions flip by two routes: in TabICL, the target row's embedding rotates towards the mean of the wrong class; in TabPFN, the poison row pulls genuine rows of the wrong class along. The TFMs thus infer soundly, but from forged evidence. Predictions of trained models flip as well: almost always for a random forest, for CatBoost as often as for the TFMs, hardly for a logistic regression. New with TFMs is not the kind of vulnerability but the timing: the data take effect at the moment of prediction, not through training, and a poison row in a live context can be deleted afterwards. Three established requirements must therefore cover the context: access control for its source, traceability per prediction, which can also deter, and validation at prediction time. A detection mechanism shows how such validation can work.

Cryptography and Security.title: PIPETTE: Prompt Injection Purple-Teaming for Robust LLM Agents
Cryptography and Security.summary: Large language model (LLM) agents routinely interact with untrusted external data, exposing them to indirect prompt injection (IPI) attacks that hijack agents into executing attacker-chosen tasks. To uncover these vulnerabilities at scale, automated red-teaming methods often leverage reinforcement learning (RL) to generate attacks that achieve high attack success rates (ASR). Model developers use the attacks discovered during internal red-teaming to harden agents through adversarial training before deployment, a collaborative offensive-defensive process known in cybersecurity as purple-teaming. However, we show that achieving high ASR during red-teaming does not guarantee robustness gains from subsequent adversarial training. Specifically, we find that two state-of-the-art RL-based red-teaming methods, RL-Hammer and PISmith, suffer from mode collapse, repeatedly discovering similar attack strategies whose additional successes add no additional robustness improvements to adversarial training. To address this gap, we introduce PIPETTE, a unified prompt injection purple-teaming framework that effectively converts red-teaming discoveries into defender robustness improvements. PIPETTE employs a dictionary learning-based reward that encourages broader coverage of attack strategies during red-teaming. It also integrates an on-policy adversarial training pipeline tailored to IPI defense, enabling agents to resist attacks while completing legitimate user tasks. Extensive evaluations across agentic benchmarks (AgentDojo and ASB) demonstrate that PIPETTE produces defenders that achieve near-zero attack success rates on static attacks and can withstand strong adaptive attacks, while maintaining benign task utility close to that of the undefended baseline.

Cryptography and Security.title: Understanding Membership Inference Attacks on EEG Models
Cryptography and Security.summary: Electroencephalography (EEG) signals contain sensitive, subject-specific information, making models trained on them potential targets for membership inference attacks (MIAs). Although MIAs have been studied extensively in other domains, their applications to EEG models are relatively scarce, and the factors driving the vulnerability of EEG models to MIAs are not adequately understood. In this paper, we present a systematic empirical analysis of MIAs on EEG models using three datasets, seven model architectures, four attack methods, and two metrics. Results show that poor model generalization (large train-test loss and accuracy gap) is the strongest indicator of MIA vulnerability. Longer training and larger models also increase vulnerability. Moreover, no particular scalp region, frequency band, inter-channel correlation pattern, or temporal versus spectral representation of EEG data consistently explains MIA vulnerability across datasets. Finally, subject identification and leave-one-subject-out experiments indicate that models relying more heavily on subject-specific representations are more vulnerable to MIAs. Overall, our findings identify the key drivers of membership leakage in EEG models and can provide guidance for developing MIA-resilient EEG systems.

Cryptography and Security.title: Toward Adversarially Robust World Models
Cryptography and Security.summary: Latent dynamic world models have proven to be highly versatile tools for embodied artificial intelligence systems, enabling online action planning, safe policy evaluation, and scalable policy learning. However, this versatility makes world models a vulnerable and centralized point of failure as a compromised model can impact planning, evaluation, and training at once. Therefore it is critical that the security and robustness properties of world models are properly understood before they are universally deployed in embodied AI systems. In this work we take a unifying approach towards this understanding, developing two novel attacks against world models, named state hallucination and dynamic shift attacks, aimed directly at impacting downstream systems, and proposing a new theoretical lens through which to study the robustness of latent dynamic world models. Through our analysis we identify robust latent space encoders as the key component of robust world models. We empirically validate this finding on four separate latent dynamic world model families, studying Dino World Model, Le World Model, r2Dreamer, and Cosmos 3, demonstrating significant improvements in robustness through adversarial encoder model training.

Cryptography and Security.title: Enabling Verifiable Output Lineage for Virtualized ML Workload Execution
Cryptography and Security.summary:
Machine learning (ML) property attestation lets a model provider demonstrate properties of their models and datasets to verifiers, and trusted execution environments (TEEs) have emerged as its most practical mechanism. However, existing TEE-based systems attest only a static snapshot of the TEE's initial configuration, leaving run-time behavior unauditable. Proof of execution (PoX) architectures close this gap by requiring the prover's root of trust to also demonstrate that (1) the attested operation actually executed and (2) the claimed outputs were affected only by that operation. Existing PoX designs, though, target microcontrollers and rely on hardware features unavailable in server-grade TEEs, so they cannot be applied directly to ML workloads.
  We present EVOLVE, a software-based PoX framework for server-grade TEEs. EVOLVE mediates an operation's writes and control flow to track whether a requested ML operation executes without violation. It binds the execution status to measurements of the operation's inputs and outputs, enabling verifiers to assess run-time behavior through ML property attestation. We implement EVOLVE on Intel TDX as a Rust module within its virtual firmware, with policy checks built on primitives formally verified in F*. Our evaluation shows that EVOLVE is versatile across diverse ML applications on unmodified hardware, provides formal guarantees for its policy checks. EVOLVE incurs per-request run-time overhead on average ranging from 1.07$\times$ (for decision trees) to 2.13$\times$ (for multi-layer perceptrons).

Cryptography and Security.title: Quantity-Level FDIA in SDR-Based P2P Energy Trading: Cyber-Economic Impact and Pre-Clearing Detection
Cryptography and Security.summary: This paper investigates the cyber-economic impact and pre-clearing detectability of false data injection attacks (FDIAs) in peer-to-peer (P2P) energy trading among interconnected microgrids. In the proposed cyber-economic framework, load and photovoltaic profiles drive a sequential 15-minute market with deterministic double-sided proportional (pro-rata) allocation and supply-to-demand-ratio (SDR) pricing, while true physical injections are separated from communicated market quantities. The framework is evaluated through a multi-microgrid case study over 69,904 market-aligned states, for which all AC power-flow solutions converged and voltages remained within 0.98999-1.04369 per unit. Healthy local exchange reached 1,159.66 MWh and generated USD 92,772.62 of community benefit. Bias, scaling, and ramp attacks modify only one microgrid's communicated quantity, altering the settlement price, P2P allocation, scheduled residual-grid exchange, participant financial outcomes, and benefit fairness, while true feeder injections remain unchanged. Role-specific random forest, statistical threshold, and score-fusion detectors are compared using only information available before clearing. Pooled sample-level detection rates range from 7.82% to 12.14%, with false-alarm rates from 4.69% to 7.70% and role dependence. In the investigated case study, measurable downstream economic distortion and low pre-clearing detectability coexist under bounded quantity manipulation.
Cryptography and Security.comment: 6 pages, 2 figures, 3 tables. Accepted for publication in IEEE conference proceedings

Cryptography and Security.title: INSEP: Refusal-Direction Inseparability as a Defense Against Abliteration
Cryptography and Security.summary: Abliteration is a widely used white-box attack against the safety alignment of large language models (LLMs). It elicits harmful behavior by estimating a refusal direction in the model's activation space and projecting that direction out of the residual-stream write-out matrices. We propose INSEP, a defense that fine-tunes the model to reduce the separability of harmful and benign activations along the refusal direction. Abliteration estimates this direction as a difference in class means and projects it out. Reducing separability weakens the signal the attack relies on. An adversarial eigendecomposition selects the most separable prompt subsets. A low-rank adapter reduces their separation along that direction. Behavioral losses preserve the base model's refusal and the quality of its benign responses during training. We benchmark INSEP against six published defenses under five attacks, across eight LLMs from 1B to 14B parameters and several model families. Beyond response harm, we measure coherence, directness, over-refusal, and MMLU, to distinguish robust refusal from low harm produced by evasive or degraded responses. INSEP ranks first on the mean composite score across all eight base models while retaining utility, in the largest abliteration-defense evaluation reported to date.

Cryptography and Security.title: An LLM-Assisted Multi-Objective AutoML Framework for Efficient Network Intrusion Detection
Cryptography and Security.summary: Conventional Machine Learning (ML)-based Intrusion Detection Systems (IDSs) require manual design, optimize only detection performance, and neglect inference latency and model size, which are critical for resource-constrained Internet of Things (IoT) and Electric Vehicle Charging System (EVCS) deployments. Automated ML (AutoML) reduces manual effort but explores broad search spaces inefficiently. Meanwhile, Multi-Objective Optimization (MOO) methods lack guided search initialization, leading to long search times. This paper proposes a Large Language Model-Assisted Multi-Objective Automated ML (LLM-MOO-AutoML) framework for efficient intrusion detection. A local Llama 3.1 8B model analyzes a compact dataset profile and generates a bounded, validated policy for automated data balancing (AutoDP) and feature engineering (AutoFE). This policy narrows the search space for Non-dominated Sorting Genetic Algorithm III (NSGA-III), which jointly optimizes the LightGBM feature-selection threshold and key hyperparameters across three objectives: maximizing weighted F1-score, minimizing 99th-percentile (P99) inference latency ratio, and minimizing model size ratio. Experiments on CICIDS2017, IoTID20, and CICEVSE2024 demonstrate that the proposed framework achieves the highest weighted F1-scores on CICIDS2017 (99.788%), IoTID20 (99.778%), and CICEVSE2024 (99.989%), with feature sets reduced to as few as 10 features, P99 latency as low as 0.00038 ms, and model size as small as 0.1073 MB. The LLM-guided configuration reduced NSGA-III search time relative to unconstrained multi-objective search on all datasets at the largest trial budget and in most comparisons at smaller budgets, indicating that dataset-aware search-space reduction supports efficient, deployment-aware intrusion detection.

Cryptography and Security.title: Cross-Boundary Vulnerability Management for SDVs: A Traceability Architecture at the ISO/SAE 21434 and EU Cyber Resilience Act Interface
Cryptography and Security.summary: A software-defined vehicle depends on products that sit under different EU regimes. The type-approved vehicle and the systems, components and separate technical units made for it fall under Regulation (EU) 2019/2144, which makes UN R155 mandatory; Regulation (EU) 2018/858 does so for R156; and ISO/SAE 21434 supports the management system R155 requires. Chargers, companion apps, aftermarket devices and many backends may fall under the Cyber Resilience Act (CRA) instead, whose reporting duty in Article 14 has applied since 11 September 2026. Neither side defines how a vulnerability found on one reaches the other's risk process. We contribute a four-question classification procedure, a five-regime traceability matrix, a reference architecture with four handoff paths and three boundary findings. On 75 classified products from a frozen public-source corpus, the procedure yields 47 Periphery, 11 Core, 1 Other and 16 Boundary products, three of them outside both the CRA and compulsory R155. Because UN R10 lets an electronic sub-assembly be approved as a component, the texts leave a second reading open, and we report both counts. Under it, 22 aftermarket devices become components, Periphery falls to 25 and 25 products sit outside both regimes. Seven retrospective walkthroughs suggest that, for third-party products, vulnerability information stops in the vehicle manufacturer's own inventory, triggers or exploitation assessment, and that no provision obliges a product maker to tell a vehicle manufacturer: the only defined two-way route is a contract. No reviewed source establishes a case that reached an Article 14 clock.
Cryptography and Security.comment: Preprint; regulatory statements as of 15 October 2026

Cryptography and Security.title: Control and Cryptosystem Co-Design for Encrypted Nonlinear Multi-Agent Coordination
Cryptography and Security.summary: A cloud that must not see the agents' states can steer them on data encrypted under CKKS, the approximate scheme for real-valued arithmetic. Its stored estimate admits only so many multiplications before a refresh that costs time and error, and every decrypted command is flooded with noise of a mandated size, constraints no controller designed in exact arithmetic meets. For networked agents with polynomial dynamics, we prove one closed-loop bound tying the controller and the cryptosystem in both directions. If the exact loop contracts on a region, the encrypted loop stays within a certified radius of it, set by the per-cycle and refresh errors, the refresh interval, the flooding and the delay. The errors and the bound's probability are derived from the library's circuits, not measured. Inverted, the bound turns the tolerance and a failure-probability target into the refresh interval, and with it the precision, security parameters and period. Conversely, costs shape the realization: a tracing backend tallies any pipeline's operations before a ciphertext exists, and evaluating the prediction about each agent's reference holds the released error below its sixteen-agent level. A full satellite-train mission encrypted at 128-bit security ran inside its certified radius, and the certificate holds across six graphs and at 32, 64 and 128 agents. Security enters the design twice, in time and precision. The cryptosystem is therefore part of the control design, derived from the same specification and certified by the same guarantee as the controller.

Cryptography and Security.title: Development of an Effective Federated Learning-Based Defense System Against Phishing Attacks on Mobile Platforms
Cryptography and Security.summary: Phishing remains one of the most pervasive and damaging cyber threats, exploiting both technical flaws and human behavior to compromise sensitive data. We present a privacy-preserving, real-time defense that analyzes full webpage source code on mobile platforms. Our system combines a lightweight Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) for end-to-end feature extraction with a Federated Learning (FL) framework that updates models collaboratively on user devices without transferring raw data-supporting regulatory compliance and personalization. Evaluated on a large and diverse dataset, the model attains 86.02\% accuracy, 90.35\% precision, 80.64\% recall, and 92.78\% ROC-AUC. While some centralized, classical approaches may report higher accuracy, our design emphasizes a practical balance among accuracy, user privacy, and real-time performance on resource-constrained devices. We further demonstrate an end-to-end integration within the open-source Lightning Android browser, achieving real-time detection with low computational overhead. This work shows that privacy-first, AI-driven phishing detection is both feasible and scalable across mobile and IoT settings, delivering robust protection while keeping user data on-device.

Computation and Language.title: MemOnce: A Scalable Memory Architecture for Large Language Models
Computation and Language.summary: Deploying large language models (LLMs) in long-horizon and continual interactions requires maintaining reusable memory states for future inference, posing challenges for existing architectures. Standard Transformers accumulate layer-wise, token-level KV caches, incurring linear GPU memory growth and quadratic computational complexity as the context expands. In contrast, linear-time architectures compress history into fixed-size states, but struggle to retain fine-grained details. We introduce MemOnce, a foundation architecture that learns scalable memory states for language models. MemOnce is based on two core designs: (a) Memory encoder-decoder: it caches only a small subset of final-layer hidden states as compact memory representations and dynamically decodes them back into KV caches for attention layers; (b) Memory sparse attention: for each continual input, MemOnce adaptively retrieves relevant memory representations, with the sparse indices computed only once across layers. Coupling these two designs enables efficient on-the-fly memory loading and KV cache decoding, drastically reducing the GPU memory footprint and achieving linear-time complexity. We conduct extensive experiments to show that MemOnce outperforms Transformers and other architectures across varying model sizes, context lengths, and training paradigms (pretraining and post-training adaptation). In particular, adapting Qwen3.5-4B with MemOnce reduces memory state cache by 1313$\times$ and prefill latency by 6.9$\times$ at 1M context, and improves throughput by 3.5$\times$ and overall memory performance by +5.77%. Finally, MemOnce generalizes zero-shot to downstream representation tasks, achieving competitive results against specialized models.

Computation and Language.title: MemLife: Curating and Reasoning over Long-Term Egocentric Video Memories
Computation and Language.summary: Long-term egocentric video enables personalized AI assistants to reason about daily life. However, as video histories grow to hundreds of hours spanning months or years, reprocessing raw clips for every query becomes computationally prohibitive. Memory systems offer a scalable alternative by compacting videos into text representations, but often fail on practical benchmarks: either the memory does not preserve key evidence, or the retriever fails to locate relevant entries due to retrieval competition in growing search spaces. To address these challenges, we introduce MemLife, a multimodal memory system that constructs entity-grounded, first-person text episodes and retrieves them via a time-indexed agentic reader. Without training or query-time video access, MemLife improves over the strongest training-free baseline by 4.6-12.0% across four long-horizon benchmarks. To further improve memory quality, we propose MemOpt, a reinforcement learning framework that optimizes the memory writer to produce faithful, informative, and retrievable memories. MemOpt consistently improves MemLife by 2.7-5.0% across different video and question distributions, with gains that generalize across writer and reader backbones and memory systems.

Computation and Language.title: Deletion Sensitivity Is a Property of the Model: A Three-Condition Measurement over 72 Valid Experimental Cells
Computation and Language.summary: Reasoning models write a trace at every turn of a multi-turn tool session, and later turns read it. Upstream providers hold different retention constraints, so a request forwarded across issuers arrives with its history deleted, and its task cost remains unmeasured. This paper reports a direct, blind, multi-seed measurement of full history deletion in multi-turn tool calling, through three rendering conditions, a calibrated set of 72 valid experimental cells, a multi-seed protocol, and the official checker. The same deletion separates the models by direction and by magnitude, one class losing tens of points, another gaining, and a third unchanged, with the endpoint ordering reproduced across seeds and task subsets modulating the magnitude and, near zero, the sign. A re-dosed model preserves its success across the full deletion range, so the reading belongs to the model rather than the dose. Deletion sensitivity is a model-level property under an operational definition, measured under a fixed task family, scorer, and protocol, and a retrained model is a new model that a two-cell screen, one retention run and one deletion run, re-reads for the cost of two runs. Deletion sensitivity is thus a measurable property of the model, and the reading must enter routing as prior information rather than persist as an invisible default cost.

Computation and Language.title: From Exposure to Expectation: Frequency, Surprisal, and Language Across Development in Spanish
Computation and Language.summary:
Surprisal, the negative log-probability a language model assigns to a word given its preceding context, reliably predicts adult reading times. Does it contribute as much to explaining when children acquire individual words? Frequency reflects a learner's cumulative exposure to a word, whereas surprisal reflects how predictable a single occurrence is given its context. We investigate this question across two corpus-based studies of Spanish.
  In Study 1, we modeled age of acquisition (AoA) for 225 Spanish nouns using lexical frequency and contextual diversity from child-directed speech, plus surprisal from three language models differing in architecture and training language (BETO, BERTIN, mGPT). Frequency strongly predicted AoA (r=-.597, p<.001); surprisal added little beyond frequency and word length, including in a naturalistic-context analysis.
  In Study 2, we modeled adult fixation durations in the Chilean Spanish subsample of the Multilingual Eye-movement Corpus (MECO Wave 2), using mGPT surprisal alongside two independent frequency measures. Surprisal robustly predicted longer fixation durations after controlling for frequency and word length, consistent across both frequency sources. A matched word-type-level comparison showed the surprisal-behavior association was stronger in reading than in acquisition (z=3.63, p<.001).
  The findings suggest cumulative lexical exposure and contextual predictability play different roles across the language trajectory: frequency is particularly informative about when early lexical representations are acquired, whereas surprisal captures moment-to-moment processing difficulty in an already-established linguistic system. We discuss this pattern in relation to usage-based and entrenchment-based accounts of lexical development and to the evaluation of language models as models of human language behavior.

Computation and Language.title: Massive Activations in Hybrid Linear Attention Large Language Models: Pre-Attention Spikes and Inter-Spike Plateaus
Computation and Language.summary: We present the first systematic study of massive activations (MAs) in layer-interleaved Hybrid linear attention large language models (HLA LLMs), examining their architectural organization, training-time emergence, underlying mechanisms, and functional significance. Across five linear attention architectures, six hybridization configurations, and five input domains, we identify two architecture-aligned morphologies: pre-attention spikes (PAS) immediately before full attention and inter-spike plateaus (ISP) persisting through intervening linear attention layers. Denser full attention increasingly connects PAS through ISP, approaching the persistent MAs of conventional Transformers. This organization also recurs across 12 public checkpoints spanning 1.2B-397B parameters, covering linear attention and state-space hybrids. Controlled pretraining of Gated DeltaNet (GDN) hybrids up to 1.3B reveals early emergence and consolidation of both morphologies, alongside asymmetric gating effects. Specifically, full attention output gates strongly attenuate MA magnitudes without eliminating their organization, whereas removing GDN output gates yields modest amplification. Mechanistically, we develop a shared systematic-outlier account: PAS follows a localized write-sink-cancel process, while ISP is consistent with delayed cancellation. Functionally, our interventions show that deleting only the four largest-magnitude PAS coordinates at each full attention input reduces mean downstream accuracy by 21.9%-63.6% relative to normal inference. Moreover, reference-conditioned spike-to-plateau connection consistently improves mean real-world retrieval accuracy, yielding relative gains of 1.1%-12.6% without retraining. Our code is available at https://github.com/StartLuxLabs/Massive-Activations-HLA.

Computation and Language.title: TEA-Bench-BR: Can Coding Agents Turn a Branching Clinical Specification into Correct Code?
Computation and Language.summary: Coding agents increasingly implement rules written by domain experts, and bugs in such code are silent: it runs and returns a plausible answer. We introduce TEA-Bench-BR, a benchmark built on the Brazilian pathway for early autism (TEA) screening: three fictitious instruments with the structure of real ones, a multi-professional referral flow, and export to FHIR R4 with the national RNDS profiles, all specified in Portuguese. A generator samples each task's parameters (144 tasks, 6,798 hidden cases), and the hidden cases kill all 1,955 non-equivalent mutants of the reference. With Gemma 4 as the agent, the 12B solves 38.0% of single-instrument tasks and none at the FHIR level; the 31B solves 77.8%, 85.2% and 78.7% at levels 1 to 3 and passes over 99% of the hidden cases, its remaining failures mostly in input validation rather than clinical decisions. With the same tasks in English, the 31B solves 57.4% at level 3, as its code validates an identifier less often; the 12B's, more often. The 12B misses 10.10% of the cases that call for referral; the 31B, 0.02%. A contamination probe on a modified PHQ-9 finds no error that follows the original rules.
Computation and Language.comment: 7 pages, 2 figures. Submitted to the Google Gemma 4 Developer Agent Paper Track (Kaggle, November 2026). Benchmark, code and results: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24143388

Computation and Language.title: The Voice on the Line
Computation and Language.summary: A transcriber listening through one microphone also hears everyone near it. We train causal voice isolators that keep only the caller for a speech recogniser: masking transformers with 20 ms of latency that enroll the caller from the call itself. Short evaluation windows hide two failures that real calls expose: forgetting the caller when another voice talks alone for a while, and damaging a caller who is alone. Long calls with turns, memory beyond the attention window and real headset crosstalk address the first, at a cost to the second. WavLM-Large's own weights, made causal and trained inside the model, move that trade, and training windows cut from longer calls remove most of a lone caller's cold start. The release (555M parameters) makes 16.13% word errors on 60 s AMI windows, against 23.66% for VoxLock, the strongest open isolator, and 14.77% on average over nine test sets, against 18.04%; it is level on Krisp's benchmark, and a caller who is alone still loses more words than with VoxLock. Distilled without WavLM into 22.1M and 9.8M parameters, it runs live on one CPU thread inside a LiveKit agent, at 12.5% and 8.5% of a core per call, with 10.66% and 10.99% error on our development sets (the release 10.49%).
