It detects 11.8 points more unsafe responses than the probe at a similar cost, under 4% added latency per token.

Computation and Language.title: MatLoom: Layered Text-to-Material Generation in a Compact Program Space
Computation and Language.summary: Material generation should produce not only an appearance, but also the rules that construct it. We introduce MatLoom, a compact, layer-oriented language for text-to-material generation with pretrained language models. Each program composes alpha-masked layers whose shared spatial expressions define coverage and physically based rendering (PBR) channels, making dependencies between patterns, color, and relief explicit. A standalone interpreter evaluates the program into material maps, while the source retains named fields and layer parameters for subsequent authoring. Without task-specific fine-tuning, our pipeline uses parser-guided repair and preview-based critique to revise material designs, then searches noise seeds while keeping each candidate's remaining source fixed. On a curated benchmark of 141 prompts evaluated with six backbones, our best-performing configuration achieves higher mean scores than three diffusion baselines on all four flat-layout prompt-alignment metrics, and the margin persists on seven of the eight metric-layout cells under feasible equal-budget selection including best-of-10 sampling with the same quick scorer, with staged CLIPScore a statistical tie. A per-metric oracle bound over the same ten samples, which requires test labels, narrows the judge margins to 6.1 points flat and a staged statistical tie. Its initial programs already exceed all three baselines on mean BLIPScore, before critique or seed search. Retained programs have a median length of 21 lines when pooled across backbones. In a blind four-way comparison involving 30 participants and 20 prompts, our renders receive 59.2% of choices, compared with 19.3% for the most-preferred baseline. Compact executable programs thus offer a way to generate prompt-aligned materials while retaining their construction as part of the asset.

Computation and Language.title: Right Numbers, Wrong Story: When LLMs Narrate Financial Changes Beyond Their Inputs
Computation and Language.summary: A financial report drafted by an LLM can state every number correctly but still go beyond its input, adding judgments and causes that no one supplied. We call these additions unsupported framing and find them far more often in LLM drafts than in reports written by proInput facts Revenue +3% Higher prices 10-K filings Revenue increased 3% on higher prices. 10-K writer Revenue surged 3% on higher prices, due to strong demand. LLM Fits the size? Surged: Unusual for 3% In the input? In the input? Strong demand: Not in input Higher prices: Kept fessionals, and attempts to fix them by prompting with how each word is used instead make such judgments more frequent. We therefore propose FrameCheck, a plug-in that sits beFrameCheck Revenue increased 3% on higher prices. No extra model call Judgment word Unsupported cause Supported cause tween the LLM and human review to keep each draft within its input. Specifically, FrameCheck 1) guides the draft with professional examples that report a change of similar magnitude, 2) flags judgments that professionals would not use and causes the input does not give, and 3) removes them by rule, without a model call. In experiments on 17 open LLMs and 3M drafts, FrameCheck removes almost all unsupported framing from drafts and brings the judgment rate close to that of the writers of 10-K filings, the annual reports that US firms file with regulators. Code is available at github.com/seunghan96/framecheck.

Computation and Language.title: Beyond Prompt Heuristics: Assessing Child Safety Alignment in LLMs
Computation and Language.summary: Child-safety taxonomies typically characterize safety risks through a predefined set of harm categories, and existing evaluations largely operationalize these categories using prompts that explicitly invoke them. However, child-safety considerations can also arise in seemingly benign requests that lack recognizable harm-category cues. We therefore investigate how child-safety alignment generalizes to such settings. Across six models, we find considerably higher misalignment rates on requests without recognizable harm-category cues than on those containing such cues (80.0, 54.0, and 48.4 percentage-point gaps for Qwen3.5-27B, GPT-5.4-mini, and Claude-Haiku-4.5, respectively). Through controlled behavioral and mechanistic analyses, we find that introducing a single harm-associated word reduces misalignment across most models, with mechanistic evidence suggesting that child-safety reasoning may rely in part on lexical and semantic associations with words in the prompt. Our findings motivate evaluations that treat child safety as context-dependent, and not reducible to a fixed set of harm categories.
Computation and Language.comment: accepted to NeurIPS 2026 Child Safety in AI Workshop

Computation and Language.title: Compute Optimal Tokenization
Computation and Language.summary: Scaling laws enable the optimal selection of data amount and language model size, yet the impact of the data unit, the token, on this relationship remains underexplored. In this work, we systematically investigate how the information granularity of tokens, controlled by the compression rate (i.e., average bytes of text per token), affects scaling trends. We train 988 latent tokenized models (BLT) ranging from 50M to 7B parameters that enable setting the desired compression rate. This flexibility allows us to study the role of compression rate well beyond 4.57 bytes per token obtained with a popular BPE tokenizer. Our experiments reveal that in compute-optimal configurations, model parameter counts scale proportionally to data size measured in bytes, not in tokens as commonly perceived (Kaplan et al., 2020; Hoffmann et al., 2022). Furthermore, we discover that the optimal compression rate differs from the one obtained with BPE and decreases with compute. These findings generalize to both latent and subword tokenization, as well as to languages other than English, guiding language model developers on tokenization scheme selection for maximal compute efficiency.

Computation and Language.title: RAG Makes Guardrails Brittle? Investigating Robustness of Guardrails under RAG-style Contexts
Computation and Language.summary: With the increasing adoption of large language models (LLMs), ensuring the safety of LLM systems has become a pressing concern. External LLM-based guardrail models have emerged as a popular solution to screen unsafe inputs and outputs, but they are themselves fine-tuned or prompt-engineered LLMs vulnerable to data distribution shifts. In this paper, taking Retrieval Augmentation Generation (RAG) as a case study, we investigate how robust LLM-based guardrails are against additional information embedded in the context. Through a systematic evaluation of 3 Llama Guards and 2 GPT-oss models, we find that inserting benign retrieved documents flips the judgments of input and output guardrails in around 11% and 8% of cases respectively, with the majority of these flips (72% and 64%) reversing previously correct decisions. We further analyze the effect of each component in the augmented context: retrieved documents, user query, and LLM response. Two tested mitigations reveal that the robustness gap is not easily closed. These results expose a context-robustness gap in current guardrails.

Computation and Language.title: Self-similar Organization of Information in Language
Computation and Language.summary: How much information relevant to predicting the future of a passage (i.e. predictive information) is carried by the preceding text, and how is this information distributed along that history? These questions are fundamental to understanding both the statistical structure of language and what large language models (LLMs) can learn about it. Indeed, LLMs trained to predict the next token in text must exploit this predictive information, so its organization determines how the structure of language becomes available to the model to learn. We develop a theory for the organization of predictive information based on the scaling behavior of a family of information measures, and the theory predicts that if this organization has the same form at all measured length scales -- i.e., it has a self-similar structure -- then the information measures evaluated at different lengths collapse onto a common form. We observe this scaling collapse in long text documents, showing that predictive information is present at every length scale we measure and has a self-similar structure. Self-similarity is a considerably stronger property than showing the existence of long-range dependencies, and it constrains the process generating the text. More broadly, our results give quantitative support to the empirical observation that conditioning on more distant text continues to reveal new structure in language to LLMs.

Computation and Language.title: AhaBench: Do Agents Turn Experience into Reusable Insights? A Long-Horizon Benchmark for Continual Learning
Computation and Language.summary: Solving a task, even from a worked example, does not make an agent any better at the next one. As agents move from single tasks to long collaborations with people, turning experience into reusable insight becomes the capability that separates a tool from a collaborator that improves over time. AhaBench is a benchmark for this kind of continual learning. It simulates three patterns of long human-AI collaboration and holds a later test fixed while varying the experience before it: in Aha-Puzzle, the agent questions a partner who knows the answer to a new mystery after solving earlier ones; in Aha-Euler, a person teaches a computation and the agent applies it to new inputs; in Aha-Vending, the agent runs a delegated business for a simulated year. The learning mechanism is left open, so memories, skill libraries, and weight updates can be compared under common rules against a baseline of fixed-weight agents that see their experience in context. Our results show that today's frontier agents are not yet continual learners. Earlier Aha-Puzzle solutions help some models, most clearly Qwen 3.6 Plus, which gains +12.57 points over attempts on the same stories without earlier episodes, yet every model scores far below what it reaches with hints. On single-step Aha-Euler tasks, the same model solves 94.0% of requested held-out inputs when taught with an explanation and code but 6.0% when given only the question and answer, counting unanswered attempts as incorrect. In incident-free Aha-Vending operation, Doubao Seed 2.0 Pro ends the year at +495 USD, yet its profit averaged over the year is -10 USD because it recovers late. Exploring without help, reconstructing a method, and sustaining productive operation remain open problems, and AhaBench provides the paired tests a learning method must pass to solve them.

Computation and Language.title: Partially canonical axes in large language model representations
Computation and Language.summary: Large language models (LLMs) develop rich internal representations of language, but whether their individual coordinate axes carry meaning, or whether meaning is encoded only in directions in representation space, is still an open question. A common assumption is that individual axes in LLMs are arbitrary. We here challenge this view: across 12 LLMs from six model families, the native axes are reliably more aligned with other models' representations, with human brain responses to language, and with interpretable linguistic features than randomly rotated axes that preserve the same geometry. The native axes nonetheless fall well short of the best achievable alignment, so LLM coordinates are not fully arbitrary but also not fully canonical: they are partially canonical. A theory of how LLMs represent language must explain both the population geometry they learn and why individual units acquire patterns of response profiles that recur across systems.

Computation and Language.title: ERA: Embed, Route, Adapt for Cold-Start Cross-Model Latent Retrieval
Computation and Language.summary: Production retrieval systems are tied to the embedding model that indexed their corpus. Moving queries to a different encoder normally requires re-embedding the whole corpus, and at cold start there are no query logs while every document embedded by the new encoder incurs an API or compute cost. We present ERA (Embed, Route, Adapt), a system for cold-start cross-model latent retrieval. ERA spends a small anchor budget on maximally informative documents, selected from the existing target index via Cosine Farthest Point Sampling, trains a lightweight adapter with a Manifold Alignment Loss that couples directional alignment with orthogonal regularization to prevent representation collapse, and pairs the adapter with a deterministic router that escalates the rare, hard queries that define perceived retrieval quality. Across five BEIR datasets, ERA matches or outperforms point-wise L2 and embedding-conversion baselines, with relative gains of up to 35% nDCG@10 on Arguana, and on clustered corpora its anchor selection also improves prior methods under a fixed anchor budget. With 1.2 ms of adapter and router overhead on top of a ~20 ms local encoder, ERA at a 20% nominal escalation budget reduces end-to-end query latency from roughly 160 ms to 38-86 ms while concentrating escalations on the queries where the projection fails most.

Computation and Language.title: What Does the Visual Encoder Buy? Visual Information Gain in Encoder-Free Multimodal Pretraining
Computation and Language.summary: Recent scaling studies ask whether vision-language models still need a visual encoder by comparing encoder-free and encoder-based models on the next-token loss of the text in image-text data. This loss can fall without any use of the image, and two runs with the same loss can differ in what they take from it. Visual information gain (VIG) is the loss increase when the image is replaced by a uniform one. It splits exactly into global information, carried by image statistics, and layout information, which shuffling the patches within the image destroys. We apply it to decoders with 158M to 1.04B parameters that read pixel patches through a linear embedding, evaluated every billion tokens up to 40B, and to 19 public checkpoints. In our decoders the image lowers the loss by 3% to 46%, depending on the image type. Global information is present after the first billion tokens. Layout information starts near zero, grows slowly with training and does not grow with model size on five of six image types, and a larger batch reaches the same loss with less of it. With a frozen SigLIP 2 encoder in front of the same decoder the loss is lower only when the arrangement of the image is intact. On shuffled images the losses with and without the encoder agree to within 0.04 nats on five of six image types, so the net advantage of the encoder in the loss is layout information, above all the ability to read text in images. Public encoder-free models at production scale (Gemma 4 12B, NEO, Mono-InternVL) do acquire layout information. On the same documents they have 0.53 to 0.76 nats of it, against 0.65 to 0.82 for recent encoder-based models and 0.04 to 0.07 for our decoders, and their released training stages show it rising. These results agree with the reported parity of the two families when both are trained from scratch and place the reported advantage of a pretrained encoder in layout information.

Software Engineering.title: ScopeAct: Scoping Decision Models for Reliable Multi-Step Execution in Mobile GUI Agents
Software Engineering.summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) enable mobile GUI agents to execute complex tasks, but frequent VLM invocations incur substantial latency and API costs. Prior work mitigates this overhead by delegating low-level action selection to lightweight decision models that choose among executable candidates. However, candidate selection alone lacks the task-level control needed to prevent premature termination and recover from failures, while candidates derived from accessibility trees (AXTrees) may not cover all actions required for task completion. To address these challenges, we introduce ScopeAct. This training-free mobile GUI agent framework combines frequent action selection with sparse VLM reasoning through the Delegation Contract and the Candidate Actions Builder. For task-level control, the Delegation Contract enables the VLM to plan subgoals with explicit completion criteria, recover from failures, and verify task completion. The decision model repeatedly selects actions to execute each subgoal without per-step VLM intervention, returning control to the VLM when execution stalls or final verification is required. For broader action coverage, the Candidate Actions Builder supplements AXTree-derived and system actions with VLM-provided text bindings for task-specific text entry and coordinates for widget-free interactions. Experiments on AndroidWorld demonstrate that ScopeAct achieves 1.7-4.8$\times$ faster execution and 3.7-8.3$\times$ lower API costs than six API-based baselines. ScopeAct requires only 5.3 and 4.6 VLM calls per task under the extended and official evaluation settings, respectively. Under the same settings, it attains 96.3% and 81.0% task success rates, surpassing the strongest baselines by 3.4 and 1.7 percentage points, respectively.

Software Engineering.title: Perceived Differences in Activity and Experience Between Developing Software With and Without AI
Software Engineering.summary: The fundamental changes in software engineering driven by generative AI will have profound effects not only on the number of available software engineering jobs but also on what software engineering itself looks like. As the career evolves, questions arise about what the skillset and interests of the next generation of software engineers will be and whether long-time engineers will continue to be attracted to the career. In this paper, we contribute to answering these questions by studying how software development with AI tools is perceived to differ from traditional development and how the differences are modulated by years of programming experience. We find that, in terms of programming activities, engineers report less talking with peers about technical problems, less decomposition, less searching of documentation, and less using a debugger, while they report more task switching. We also find experiential differences, including less deep focus and less sense of control over code and design. We call these the different craft results, in contrast to core code-production activities such as writing, refactoring, and fixing code, which show only small mean differences. We also find that these differences are amplified by years of programming experience (an experience gradient), with software engineers who started programming before the age of generative AI perceiving greater changes in both activity and developer experience. We discuss our findings and their implications on training of the next generation of engineers and on engineers who may have difficulty transitioning to the AI-infused world of software engineering.
Software Engineering.comment: 21 pages, 4 figures, 7 tables

Software Engineering.title: CodeTeam: An LLM-Powered Multi-Agent Framework for Repository-Level Code Generation
Software Engineering.summary: Natural language to repository generation (NL2Repo) requires a system to construct an entire software repository from a natural-language requirements document. Compared with function-level code generation, this task demands longer planning horizons, stable interfaces across files, and iterative debugging of cross-file inconsistencies. To address these challenges, we propose CodeTeam, an LLM-based multi-agent framework that separates planning, decision making, and implementation into distinct, coordinated stages. In the planning stage, multiple Architect agents draft competing software design sketches (SDSs), optionally grounded by retrieved design references. A cto (Chief Technical Officer) agent then evaluates, selects, and normalizes the most promising SDS into a machine-checkable contract that specifies file ownership, public interfaces, and dependency constraints. In the implementation stage, Developer agents generate code under a dependency-aware scheduler with bounded context and lightweight Git-based coordination, while a qa agent runs tests and drives iterative repairs. On the synthesis-based SketchEval benchmark, we compare CodeTeam's prompt-engineering (PE) variant with CodeS and five representative baselines across 19 repositories under a retrieval-free protocol, where CodeTeam improves the mean structural score by 3.84 absolute points over CodeS (53.88 versus 50.04). CodeTeam and the experimental results are available at https://github.com/WhitenWhiten/CodeTeam
Software Engineering.comment: 33 pages, 1 images, 20 tables, Manuscript revision to a Journal (2026)

Software Engineering.title: Deletion Sensitivity Is a Property of the Model: A Three-Condition Measurement over 72 Valid Experimental Cells
Software Engineering.summary: Reasoning models write a trace at every turn of a multi-turn tool session, and later turns read it. Upstream providers hold different retention constraints, so a request forwarded across issuers arrives with its history deleted, and its task cost remains unmeasured. This paper reports a direct, blind, multi-seed measurement of full history deletion in multi-turn tool calling, through three rendering conditions, a calibrated set of 72 valid experimental cells, a multi-seed protocol, and the official checker. The same deletion separates the models by direction and by magnitude, one class losing tens of points, another gaining, and a third unchanged, with the endpoint ordering reproduced across seeds and task subsets modulating the magnitude and, near zero, the sign. A re-dosed model preserves its success across the full deletion range, so the reading belongs to the model rather than the dose. Deletion sensitivity is a model-level property under an operational definition, measured under a fixed task family, scorer, and protocol, and a retrained model is a new model that a two-cell screen, one retention run and one deletion run, re-reads for the cost of two runs. Deletion sensitivity is thus a measurable property of the model, and the reading must enter routing as prior information rather than persist as an invisible default cost.

Software Engineering.title: TEA-Bench-BR: Can Coding Agents Turn a Branching Clinical Specification into Correct Code?
Software Engineering.summary: Coding agents increasingly implement rules written by domain experts, and bugs in such code are silent: it runs and returns a plausible answer. We introduce TEA-Bench-BR, a benchmark built on the Brazilian pathway for early autism (TEA) screening: three fictitious instruments with the structure of real ones, a multi-professional referral flow, and export to FHIR R4 with the national RNDS profiles, all specified in Portuguese. A generator samples each task's parameters (144 tasks, 6,798 hidden cases), and the hidden cases kill all 1,955 non-equivalent mutants of the reference. With Gemma 4 as the agent, the 12B solves 38.0% of single-instrument tasks and none at the FHIR level; the 31B solves 77.8%, 85.2% and 78.7% at levels 1 to 3 and passes over 99% of the hidden cases, its remaining failures mostly in input validation rather than clinical decisions. With the same tasks in English, the 31B solves 57.4% at level 3, as its code validates an identifier less often; the 12B's, more often. The 12B misses 10.10% of the cases that call for referral; the 31B, 0.02%. A contamination probe on a modified PHQ-9 finds no error that follows the original rules.
Software Engineering.comment: 7 pages, 2 figures. Submitted to the Google Gemma 4 Developer Agent Paper Track (Kaggle, November 2026). Benchmark, code and results: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24143388

Software Engineering.title: From Correctness to Consistency: Redefining Reliability for the Agentware Era
Software Engineering.summary: The rise of "vibe coding" has marginalized requirements analysis, allowing unverified "Make it Work" assumptions to accumulate into complex defects that evade standard testing. In the absence of a reliable ground truth oracle, we advocate a paradigm shift from correctness verification to logic consistency. We introduce Differential Logic Analysis (DLA), a framework that utilizes Logical Inference to detect internal contradictions across parallel and sequential development workflows. Preliminary simulations demonstrate that DLA successfully intercepts logic drift, such as contradictions and unspecified assumptions, and offers a new perspective on reliability assessment in the AI-assistant development era.

Software Engineering.title: BinXSight: Fast Binary Program Summarization via Hierarchical Modular Decomposition
Software Engineering.summary: Binary code summarization (BCS) is crucial in fields such as cybersecurity. Particularly, program-level BCS can quickly provide a comprehensive overview of an entire stripped binary without in-depth manual reverse engineering. However, a binary often contains numerous functions with complex interactions, making it challenging to extract its functionality efficiently. Moreover, existing methods focus solely on function-level without considering contextual information, limiting their applicability to program-level analysis. Towards comprehensive and fast program-level BCS, we propose BinXSight, an LLM-powered framework based on hierarchical modular decomposition. Specifically, we first propose binary graph, a new data structure composed of four graphs, to comprehensively represent a binary. Then, based on the binary graph, we hierarchically decompose functions into modules and select the most significant ones. Finally, BinXSight generates a program-level summary from these module summaries. We evaluate BinXSight on stripped binaries across various sizes, fields, platforms, and architectures. Results show that BinXSight outperforms baselines by 23.18% to 46.99%, and summarizes a binary with about 3K functions in 24.3 seconds on average. In addition, a user study with 27 experts shows that BinXSight's high-quality summaries help users quickly understand the whole binary. Our case analysis on recent real-world malware further demonstrates its practical utility.

Software Engineering.title: MetaRigor: From Agentic Automation to Verifiable End-to-End Meta-Analysis Through Scientific Decision Boundaries
Software Engineering.summary: Automated meta-analysis requires not only accurate numerical extraction but also the consistent preservation of result identity across stages, including the associated study, comparison, population, outcome, time point, and analysis conditions. We present MetaRigor, an LLM workflow framework for verifiable end-to-end evidence synthesis. MetaRigor organizes study results as Study x Target units and operationalizes scientific decision boundaries at the task level through Task Contracts, programmatic rules, and source binding. The model performs semantic interpretation that depends on study context, whereas programs execute formalizable rules, computations, validation, and source verification. We conducted controlled evaluations across five stages: evidence acquisition, data extraction, risk of bias assessment, certainty of evidence assessment, and manuscript generation. MetaRigor achieved an F1 score of 86.29% for complete result delivery and 80.20% agreement for domain-level certainty of evidence judgments. Generated manuscripts received scores of 86.00 under human evaluation, exceeding all three baselines. A seven-case downstream end-to-end evaluation further yielded an aggregate F1 score of 77.01%, exceeding the strongest baseline by 9.78 percentage points. Cross-system tracing of archived outputs from three systems further showed that local mismatches or omissions in result identity could alter statistical inputs and the objects subjected to risk of bias assessment, with these errors subsequently propagating into the final report. Ablation experiments showed that task constraints and programmatic rules played distinct roles across different stages. These findings indicate that, in LLM-driven evidence synthesis workflows, consistently maintaining explicit result identity, decision boundaries, and provenance relationships is critical to improving end-to-end verifiability.

Software Engineering.title: From 6G Capabilities to Software-Business Value: A Multivocal Review of Characteristics, Opportunities, Challenges
Software Engineering.summary: Sixth-generation (6G) technology is expected to enable intelligent, autonomous, and software-defined ecosystems, creating new ways for software firms to generate value. However, evidence on the characteristics, opportunities, and challenges of 6G software businesses remains fragmented across academic and practitioner literature. We conducted a multivocal literature review of 133 sources (102 peer-reviewed studies and 31 grey literature sources) to examine this emerging landscape from the perspective of software-producing organizations. Thematic analysis identified 18 characteristics grouped into five themes, 32 business opportunities across eight themes, and 19 challenges and constraints across six themes. Three independent raters assessed the reliability of factor-to-theme classification, with Fleiss' kappa indicating substantial to almost perfect agreement (0.744 to 0.832). Findings suggest that value creation depends not only on technological capabilities but also on translating them into viable services and business models while addressing integration complexity, organizational and economic barriers, regulatory uncertainty, and security and sustainability concerns. The synthesis reveals that characteristics, opportunities, and challenges are interdependent dimensions of 6G software businesses. By integrating academic and practitioner evidence, this study provides a traceable foundation for future empirical research and strategic decision-making as 6G technologies, standards, and markets evolve.

Software Engineering.title: Characterizing and Detecting Unfaithful Work Reports by Coding Agents
Software Engineering.summary: Coding agents increasingly carry out long-horizon development tasks, autonomously planning and executing multi-step actions that span files, tools, and sessions. Because developers rarely follow each action, and agents resuming the work depend on records of what was done, the agent's work report often becomes the primary account of what was changed and established. When the report contains false or unsupported claims, it gives recipients false assurance: incomplete work may be accepted without verification, incorrect assumptions about the current state can propagate to later steps and agents, and evaluators that credit stated success may reward the report rather than the work. Yet little is known about what unfaithful reporting looks like in real development work, or how developers and agents handle it once it surfaces. Starting from real developer-agent conversations in SWE-chat, we conduct a systematic mixed-methods analysis of self-admitted unfaithful reports. We identify eleven subtypes in four categories: misreported observations, misattributed evidence, overstated task success, and faulty technical explanations, with overstated task success the most common. Handling these problems involves on average 4.3 further user turns and 12.71 minutes of recorded response and execution time, and users express dissatisfaction more often. Among 435 work reports that we separately sample and annotate, 37.24% contain at least one unfaithful claim. We also develop FaithDetector, a detector for unfaithful reporting informed by the observed patterns. On naturally sampled reports, FaithDetector attains 93.06% macro-F1, about 13 percentage points above the baseline. Together, our findings and FaithDetector provide empirical evidence and an automated method for checking reporting faithfulness, informing agent evaluation and training feedback.

Software Engineering.title: GRAML: Graph-Grounded Reasoning and Multi-Task Learning for LLM-Based Software Vulnerability Detection
Software Engineering.summary: Large language models (LLMs) have shown promise in software vulnerability detection. Existing approaches leverage program graphs to provide structural evidence for vulnerability analysis and description generation. However, redundant or weakly relevant graph relations make it difficult to identify vulnerability-related code lines and their connections to vulnerable statements. Meanwhile, generated descriptions may omit key information or contain claims unsupported by the source code. To address these challenges, we propose GRAML, a graph-grounded multi-task framework for LLM-based vulnerability detection. Specifically, GRAML uses structural propagation, relation diversity, and redundancy control to identify vulnerability-relevant code lines and their associated program relations. To improve description reliability, we further develop Tree-of-Thought-based Vulnerability Reasoning (ToT-VR), which explores multiple candidate explanations and evaluates their consistency with source code. The resulting descriptions are organized as Description samples and combined with Detection, Localization, and Assessment samples for four-task fine-tuning. We evaluated four code LLMs on seven vulnerability detection datasets. In particular, GRAML achieves average F1 scores of 67.08% to 69.32%, outperforming the evaluated baselines by 2.02 to 31.54 percentage points. Furthermore, ToT-VR improves average F1 by 4.43 to 6.99 percentage points over Chain-of-Thought (CoT)-based description generation, while multi-task training improves it by 8.03 to 18.26 percentage points over Detection-only training. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of graph-grounded multi-task supervision for software vulnerability detection.

Software Engineering.title: QANAD: A Model-Driven Framework for Quantitative Analysis and Synthesis of Activity Diagrams via Probabilistic Model Checking
Software Engineering.summary: Probabilistic model checking is a widely used formal verification technique to automatically verify qualitative and quantitative QoS properties for probabilistic models, such as reliability, performance, and cost. However, devising suitable and representative models for systems of interest in model checkers, writing corresponding properties, and verifying them requires domain knowledge in probabilistic models, formal verification, and the target model checkers. This unavoidably makes model checking not easily accessible for researchers and engineers who may lack the required knowledge. Previous work has extended UML activity diagrams with probability and time, along with quality annotations, developed transformations from activity diagrams to probabilistic models which model checkers support, and implemented accompanying tools for automation. The research, however, is fragmented, informal, or not fully open, making its use, extension, and adaptation non-trivial. To mitigate these challenges, we introduce QANAD, a comprehensive verification framework for activity diagrams, that includes a new profile for probability, time, parameters, and quality annotations, a semantics interpretation of activity diagrams in Markov models variants (DTMCs, MDPs, and CTMCs) and their parametric versions, and a set of formal transformation rules from activity diagrams to the PRISM modelling language, supported by the leading model checkers PRISM and Storm. The theory underpinning QANAD has been realised into transformation implementation using model-driven engineering, enabling fully automated model transformation with automated verification using (parametric) probabilistic model checking and semi-automated synthesis. We demonstrate QANAD on a case study where multiple robots are used for delivery in a hospital environment and evaluated six other examples from the literature.
Software Engineering.comment: Accepted version by the journal of Software and Systems Modeling (SoSyM)

Software Engineering.title: Testing for Coordination Failures in Cooperative Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
Software Engineering.summary: Deep parallel cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning (CMARL)} trains multiple agents that all act at every time step to optimize a common objective. Like single-agent RL, CMARL can produce unsafe behaviors that violate implicit safety requirements not captured by the reward, and these behaviors are hard to explain. However, testing CMARL policies for safety has received less attention than the safety testing of single-agent RL policies. In this paper, we propose DisQ, a test case selection method that identifies failure-revealing states in value-based CMARL by exploiting a signal specific to trained Q-learning agents. The signal is the Q-value gap, an explainable metric that flags a state when the agents' estimates of the achievable return diverge by more than a calibrated threshold. DisQ selects such states for execution and skips those without a gap. Our experiments in four CMARL benchmark environments show that, in most of the evaluated configurations, DisQ improves failure detection over single-agent RL testing methods applied to CMARL, namely random testing and search-based testing with genetic algorithms. Our main contributions are the Q-value gap, an indicator of potential miscoordination computable from a single state without executing the system, and DisQ, a test case selection method that adapts existing single-agent testing methods to CMARL.
Software Engineering.comment: STVR

Software Engineering.title: Adopting Embedded AI Through an Innovation Team
Software Engineering.summary: Software organizations are increasingly embedding AI capabilities into products that existing teams already own and maintain, but how this development work should be organized is not well understood. We conducted a qualitative case study of a temporary cross-functional innovation team in a large Norwegian financial organization, drawing on 18 interviews with 15 participants, 10 days of office observation, observations of ten meetings, and internal documents. We found that structural separation, AI competence inside the team, high autonomy within a clear mandate, senior expertise, and flexible ways of working enabled the team to explore and build embedded AI solutions. While structural separation enabled this work, it also made adoption dependent on coordination with the permanent product team that would own the solution. Misaligned roadmaps, prioritization gaps, and a lack of co-location constrained that coordination. We identify seven success factors for adopting embedded AI through an innovation team and propose expertise awareness as an alternative to redundancy in the Agile Team Effectiveness Model.
Software Engineering.comment: 10 pages. Accepted for publication in the Proceedings of the 60th Hawaii International Conference on System Sciences (HICSS 2027)

Software Engineering.title: HookEvo: A Framework for Coordinated Plugin Evolution on Hook-Enabled Agent Runtimes
Software Engineering.summary: Repairing failures in tool-using agents can require coordinated changes to how the harness interprets tool receipts, assembles context, and checks actions. We introduce HookEvo, a framework that uses an existing agent runtime's lifecycle hooks to evolve task-specific harnesses. We instantiate HookEvo on DeepSeek Harness. In each round, a separate improver diagnoses failures from execution traces and proposes a candidate. HookEvo evaluates the candidate against the current harness on matched tasks and carries the retained version into the next round. A single candidate can jointly edit executable plugin handlers and the state they share within a task, allowing a tool receipt to inform context and control a later action. Using a frozen Qwen3-4B executor, the selected harnesses lead the reported Qwen3-4B comparisons, achieving 95.41% on ALFWorld, 70.56% on DBBench, 48.17% on WebShop, and 41.67% on OSBench. Across three improvers and three edit scopes, from skill text to single-component and coordinated executable edits, GPT-6.1 Sol shows the largest average gain from the broadest scope. Our code is available at https://huangshengzebluesky.github.io/hookevo/.

Software Engineering.title: How Effective Are NPM Malicious Package Detectors? A Large-Scale Empirical Study
Software Engineering.summary: The NPM ecosystem faces escalating threats from malicious packages that exploit its open publication model. While numerous detection tools have been proposed, they are evaluated on disparate datasets with inconsistent settings, making cross-tool comparison unreliable and leaving practitioners without clear guidance. We present the first large-scale empirical study of NPM malicious package detection, evaluating 11 tools with 16 variants on a unified benchmark of 6,420 malicious and 7,288 benign packages annotated with 11 behavior categories and 8 evasion techniques. Unlike prior work, we inspect each tool's source code to explain why tools succeed or fail, not merely how often. Our key findings: (1) the precision and recall a tool achieves are structurally determined by how it resolves the ambiguity between code capability and malicious intent, with IntelGuard reaching the best F1 at 95.98% by grounding its judgment in retrieved evidence and GuardDog the best among conventional tools at 93.32%; (2) behavioral coupling amplifies detection signals when behaviors co-occur, raising SAP_DT from 3.2% to 79.3% for the collect-and-exfiltrate chain; (3) 80.3% of malware uses no evasion because the ecosystem lacks mandatory pre-publication scanning; (4) ML degradation is driven by concept convergence rather than concept drift, since malware became simpler and every decision boundary fitted to a corpus ages with it; (5) combination effectiveness equals complementarity minus false-positive introduction, not paradigm diversity. Strategic combinations reach up to 97.21% accuracy and 97.02% F1. We release our benchmark and evaluation framework.

Software Engineering.title: Can Coding Agents Write and Transpile Unit Tests
Software Engineering.summary: Coding assistants built on Large Language Models (LLMs) have become a staple of modern software development, increasingly trusted to execute workflows and modernize code end-to-end. Much of this trust rests on passing tests, which are often written by the coding agents themselves. In this work, we examine the ability of these agents to both write reliable tests and translate them between programming languages. We benchmark three popular coding agents, each evaluated with a native frontier model and high reasoning effort. Verifying across a broad suite of metrics, we find that coding agents far exceed human written suites on traditional measures of coverage. This advantage, however, is uneven: agent test quality degrades sharply with project size, and much of the advantage lies in a greater number of written tests. We also show that agentic test translation---while seemingly strong in aggregate---remains inconsistent and unreliable.

Software Engineering.title: Why Does CLAUDE.md Keep Growing? Catastrophic Remembering in Agentic Coding
Software Engineering.summary: Agentic prompts like CLAUDE.md grow without bound in real repositories, stopping only when history ends or someone rewrites the file wholesale. We trace this to imperfect recall: appending an instruction is always cheap, but once an instruction's latent reasoning is gone, deleting it without risking a regression costs O(2^|D|) in a prompt of |D| instructions. Successive edits destroy that latent reasoning, additions outrun deletions and prompts grow until agents become non-functional -- catastrophic remembering. First, we characterize this phenomenon across 247,694 instruction lifetimes in 1,867 repositories: agentic prompts grow nearly monotonically, more than tripling over their lifetime (+226%) at +4.7 net instructions per commit. Deletion hazard decays geometrically with instruction age, consistent with imperfect recall and with no other rival we test. Then, we show that prompt comments can halt the growth: in verifiable worlds built by inverting IFEval, comments encoding latent reasoning remove 99.3% of excess size (+211.3% to +1.4%). Finally, we show comments yield smaller real-world and coding-convention prompts than existing context maintainers, grow more effective with model capability and, at small scale, improve instruction-following in real repositories by 17.7%. If English is the new code, why don't we have comments yet?

Software Engineering.title: MSRyzen: An Agentic Platform for Unified Proteomics Analysis and Evidence-Centric Visualization
Software Engineering.summary: Mass spectrometry (MS)-based proteomics is essential for comprehensive protein characterization, yet it relies on multistep computational workflows that typically demand tedious manual parameter tuning and complex software integration. Here, we present MSRyzen, an agent-driven framework that provides automated parameter optimization and extensible tool integration across bottom-up and top-down proteomics workflows. MSRyzen translates natural-language prompts into directed acyclic workflow graphs, optimizes analytical parameters guided by quantitative metrics and user-defined objectives, and incorporates new third-party software through standardized callable interfaces. Across four public top-down datasets, automated parameter optimization increased proteoform identifications by 3.6% to 15.8% compared to default settings at a 1% false discovery rate. To ensure transparent data interpretation, an interactive visualization interface coordinates identification metrics with peak-level spectral evidence and sequence coverage. Integrating adaptive tuning with multi-tiered spectral inspection, MSRyzen delivers an end-to-end, fully automated framework, dramatically reducing the operational barrier to modern mass spectrometry data analysis.

Software Engineering.title: Exploration Structure in LLM Agents for Multi-File Change Localization
Software Engineering.summary: Fixing an issue starts with finding the files to change, and most benchmark issues touch several. LLM agents for this task increasingly add structure, such as specialized tools, multiple agents, or code summaries. We ask which of this structure matters when the model is small. We build a coordinator agent with repository tools that limit their output and a reusable registry of subsystem-scoped domain agents. We compare six configurations, each adding structure to the previous one. They are the model alone, a single agent with a Python REPL, a coordinator with only the REPL, the previous structure plus repository tools, then plus the registry map, and finally plus consultation of the domain agents. We also run four published localizers with the same model, two larger-model references, and five non-LLM rankers on 105 multi-file issues from three Python repositories, in audited single-commit checkouts. Most of the gain comes from letting the model explore the repository over many turns. Pooled source-file F1 rises from 0.199 for the model alone to 0.677 for the REPL-only coordinator. The repository tools add a small, non-significant gain, and the registry does not help, lowering pooled F1 by 0.031. A small model in a plain multi-turn agent loop (0.695) thus exceeds all four published localizers (best 0.586), while Codex with a larger model reaches 0.751. For a small model, the agent loop matters more than added agents. New files and narrative documentation remain largely missed. We release the benchmark, predictions, tool logs, and scripts.

Software Engineering.title: EDAGoat: An EDA-Aware Agent for Project-Level GPU Optimization
Software Engineering.summary: GPU acceleration has transformed electronic design automation (EDA), yet further improving expert-engineered GPU tools still demands substantial manual effort. Automating this work calls for coding agents that can trace bottlenecks across host and device code while preserving correctness and design quality. We introduce EDAGoat, to our knowledge the first EDA-aware GPU optimization agent for this task. Its optimization enhancement (OE) mode guides edits with four cross-project GPU optimization patterns. Its mandatory validation (MV) mode requires the agent to test the edited program against the EDA constraints its changes could affect. Our benchmark covers five GPU EDA projects across four task families and 55 circuit inputs, measuring complete-solve runtime and verifying the resulting designs. Each configuration runs three independent searches per project. A search qualifies only if its solver passes correctness and design-quality checks on all public and hidden inputs. With DeepSeek, generic prompting qualifies in 7 of 15 searches and OE in 6 of 15, despite a higher best speedup on four projects. Adding MV raises this to 13 of 15 and, on every project, exceeds both generic baselines in mean and best speedup and OE in mean speedup; the geometric mean of per-project mean speedups rises from 1.11x (1.36x with OE) to 1.53x. With GPT-6 Astra, EDAGoat qualifies in all 15 searches and improves both speedup metrics over generic prompting on every project, lifting the same geometric mean from 1.26x to 1.57x. These results show that agents can use EDA knowledge to find further speedups in expert-tuned tools while preserving design correctness and quality, establishing EDA-aware GPU optimization as a new direction for agent research.
Software Engineering.comment: 7 pages, 2 figures, 3 tables

Software Engineering.title: How Much of a Calculation-Error Rate Is Not Arithmetic: Auditing the FinReason Cup 2026 Task 3 Metric with a Deterministic Rule System
Software Engineering.summary:
Task 3 of the FinReason Cup 2026 scores a system on two values per case, the one an XBRL filing reports and the one its own calculation relationships imply, and labels each failure as structural, extraction or calculation. This report shows that the calculation-error rate so defined does not count arithmetic failures, and bounds how far it is from one using the published board alone. One of the three rules behind the benchmark, DQC_US_0015, has an answer that is the negation of the reported value (in all 110 published practice cases, against 1 of 120 and 6 of 102 for the other two), so a calculation label on such a case records a wrong fact or a wrong route, not a wrong sum. Subtracting the available structural and extraction labels from each entry's error count on that rule gives a floor: the bound is positive for 22 of the 23 ranked entries, and at the top it is sharpest, with at least 11 of 12 and 12 of 13 calculation errors of the two joint-first entries falling on cases where no arithmetic remained. The calculation-error rate of the best systems on this task is almost entirely not arithmetic.
  The vehicle for that result is an entry that reconstructs the three data-quality rules the benchmark is drawn from, DQC_US_0015, DQC_US_0117 and DQC_US_0126, as a deterministic system with no learned parameters, no training step and no external service, running all 680 cases in 1.4 seconds. It scores 96.62% under the offline judge on development and 95.29% on the published test set, and its residual error concentrates in cases where a concept carries several equally flagged facts and the question names no dimensional member. Reading those error classes against the per-rule accuracies is what exposed the metric, which is why both are reported here.
Software Engineering.comment: 7 pages, 3 tables. FinReason Cup 2026 (IEEE Big Data 2026) Task 3 Working Notes

Software Engineering.title: Which Data-Center Load Models Can Be Trusted? An Evidence-Graded Review of Dynamic Modeling and Validation for Large Computational Loads
Software Engineering.summary: Grid operators now require dynamic models of data centers and other large computational loads, and new ride-through rules assume that these models predict how facilities respond to disturbances. This review asks what evidence supports that assumption. We coded 160 documents, screened from 1,424 de-duplicated database and seed records plus 65 added documents, by the strongest reference object each presents, from grid-side records to simulation only. Across 19 field-evidence entries, 15 requirement documents from three continents and nine model classes, we find two comparisons of a standard library model with measured data-center events: with default parameters the model failed both, and refitting it to each event separately reduced the error but was never tested on an unseen event. Among the sources reviewed, we found no successful held-out validation of a frozen, facility-specific data-center model against an independent measured disturbance, and 25 of the 33 model-phenomenon combinations with any evidence involve no electrical measurement. The features that distinguish the new rules (memory of repeated dips, recovery within 0.5-3 s, proportional power reduction during the sag, overvoltage response) are those current phasor models cannot represent or have never been tested against. In the operator procedures examined, simulations and model-to-model benchmarks are accepted as evidence of model fidelity, unlike the measured validation required of generators, and proposed mitigations have mostly been evaluated on unvalidated facility models. We propose context-of-use gates that separate calibration from validation, release labels for model claims, a minimum validation protocol with acceptance criteria, and a research agenda.
Software Engineering.comment: 21 pages, 10 figures, 10 tables. Companion dataset included as ancillary files

Software Engineering.title: Git History Is a Pangenome: Repetition in Code Training Corpora and What Deduplication Removes, Keeps and Misses
Software Engineering.summary: Code models are increasingly trained on the full history of software repositories, every version of every file, rather than on a single snapshot. The tools that deduplicate training data were built for snapshots, and what they do to a history has not been measured. We measured it on a pre-registered random sample of 306 public repositories, 25 mature projects, and the 12 repositories behind the SWE-bench benchmark. A history is mostly repetition: in the vocabulary of text indexing, a pangenome, one text in many near-identical variants. The history of a typical repository holds the equivalent of 19 copies of its current code, and a mature repository holds 89. The reason is that each edit changes a few lines and leaves the rest of the file in place: nine tokens in ten of a changed file already existed before the change. Exact-match deduplication removes none of these copies, since no two versions are identical. Large training pipelines already deduplicate their snapshots by grouping near-identical files and keeping one. Applied across versions, the same step brings the repetition down to about two copies. But two problems remain. The deduplicator keeps one version of each file, and in widely used implementations, including the one we measured, the rule for choosing that version ignores dates, so for half of all files the version kept for training is an old one. Sorting versions newest first before deduplicating fixes the problem at almost no cost. The second problem is benchmark answers. Benchmarks such as SWE-bench test a model on real bug fixes, and a merged fix survives in a median of 18 later versions of the files it changed. Therefore, removing benchmark fixes needs a separate step that checks every version. We turn the measurements into a short set of rules for teams that train on code history, and release the instruments and frozen outputs.
Software Engineering.comment: 12 pages, 3 figures, 4 tables. Replication package: https://osf.io/5nwgv/?view_only=34532f33e19149829435aa819d476191

Software Engineering.title: Simulation-Based Testing of RCM-Constrained Robotic Software via Task Manifolds
Software Engineering.summary: System-level testing of surgical robots requires generating executable test scenarios that exercise diverse, safety-critical behaviors. However, remote-center-of-motion (RCM) surgical manipulators operate within tightly constrained workspaces governed by coupled task geometry, inverse kinematics, and motor limits. Direct sampling in motor-command or Cartesian spaces frequently wastes testing budgets on physically unfeasible configurations. To address this limitation, we present a manifold-centered testing framework that decouples feasible test-domain construction from downstream test-generation strategies. Candidate inputs are generated directly within this constructed feasible domain and mapped to lower-level joint commands for simulation execution. Offline trajectory safety oracles and a spatial reference grid then evaluate failure yield and coverage. We compare our task-manifold representation against Cartesian XYZ and principal component analysis (PCA) under random testing, systematic traversal, and genetic search strategies. Results demonstrate that the feasible task domain improves test-generation efficiency and enables systematic reference-cell coverage. Crucially, random and genetic search strategies detect a broader spectrum of failure patterns than baseline representations, revealing that complete reference-cell coverage alone does not exhaust intra-cell behavioral dynamics. Furthermore, differential testing between defective and patched controller versions reveals that targeted evolutionary search detects aggregate failure-rate shifts from software repairs. Finally, a cross-platform study on a 7-DoF Kinova Gen3 arm in MoveIt 2 confirms workflow transferability to kinematically redundant manipulators. Together, these findings highlight the necessity of combining feasibility-aware domain modeling with complementary search strategies for systematic testing of robot software.
Software Engineering.comment: 20 pages, 5 figures

Software Engineering.title: Markdown Is Not a Firewall: four coding agents, one rules file, four boundaries
Software Engineering.summary: Teams put a one-page rules file in a repository and call it a control on coding agents. A registered study found agents rarely look up a repository's contribution rules. I asked the security question: what does a rules file do at a boundary, against a gate? I tested one 278-word rules file, with hypotheses and analysis code deposited first. Claude Code, Codex CLI, Gemini CLI and OpenCode with DeepSeek worked through 20 small repositories with hidden tests, 12 for three of them. Three agents met four boundaries I built: a refused endpoint, a destructive shortcut, a planted instruction and a planted package. Permission prompts, each vendor's own control layer, were off by design. A gate in front of the mock service blocked and logged forbidden requests. Every verdict was read from records the agent could not change. Only my first scoring pass was blind to arm. My checkers found no real bugs, with the file or without it. The file cost one agent a third of its score: Codex CLI fell from 99.0 to 67.7 percent on hidden tests, and in 11 of its 36 steps reported the task complete with all tests passing while under half of the hidden tests passed. Its own tests passed. Faced with two of its rules that clash on these tasks, three agents followed the task and one followed the rule. Pooled, passes fell from 98.2 to 90.9 percent. Matched pairs fell 7.7 points, 1.3 without Codex CLI. Attempts to cross were rare: 5 in 90 gated steps, 3 without the file, 2 with it, all by OpenCode with DeepSeek, all blocked. With no gate, under the neutral file, the same requests reached the mock in 7 of 45 runs. By an error in my run script, the no-file and rules-file arms always ran behind the gate at the three HTTP boundaries, so I could not test whether the file changes what an agent does there. On what I could measure, the file acted as advice. A file tells an agent what you want. A gate decides what it gets.
Software Engineering.comment: 22 pages, 7 figures. Pre-registration: doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23608308. Results dataset: doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24238904

Software Engineering.title: Omo: Giving Continuing AI-Agent Work a Place to Return To
Software Engineering.summary: AI coding agents now keep working while the people who started them are away. Coming back is the hard part: a session list tells you which agent is where, but not what it was asked to do, what it changed, or what to tell it next. We present Omo, which gives each piece of continuing agent work a persistent place to return to. We built the idea twice. Omo Space is an open-source Minecraft mod in which rooms and screens that people build are live terminals on their own machine. Omo Theia brings the same rooms and desks into a customizable IDE, one step away from the editor and the Git patch. Both keep agent sessions running on the host after the view is closed. We describe the two systems, four lessons from building them, and a study designed to test whether returning to a place helps people pick up agent work correctly.
Software Engineering.comment: 4 pages, 1 composite figure (5 panels)

Software Engineering.title: Schema-Validated LLM Workflows: A Benchmark Protocol and Comparative Evaluation Across Six Python Implementations
Software Engineering.summary:
Large language models are increasingly used to extract records, generate SQL, summarize reports, answer policy questions, and route operational work. At these software boundaries, parseable output is necessary but does not establish task correctness. We present a reproducible benchmark protocol, a public executable artifact, and a confirmatory live API evaluation that separate structural validity from task-specific correctness across five business workflow tasks and six Python implementation conditions: PydanticAI, LangGraph, DSPy, CrewAI, Agno, and a framework-free SDK reference.
  We hypothesize that (H1) schema validity and task quality are separable, (H2) structured-output binding paths are heterogeneous under a shared model and lowest-common-denominator contract, and (H3) condition-by-task interactions concentrate failures rather than shifting all tasks equally. Confirmatory analysis uses distinct task instances (100 extraction and 50 per other task, with three nested replicates) under a frozen analysis plan, yielding a 5400-row primary matrix with equivalence margins and Holm-adjusted contrasts against the SDK reference.
  In the eligible confirmatory run, overall schema validity was 0.684 and mean automated quality was 0.638. PydanticAI, LangGraph, and DSPy retained near-ceiling schema validity with mean quality 0.91-0.94, while the plain SDK, Agno, and CrewAI conditions were substantially lower in this package and model configuration. Schema-valid rows still produced many task-score flags, especially in extraction and compliance QA, and quality residuals show strong condition-by-task interactions (including a workflow collapse for CrewAI). Labelled ablations address retry budgets and feature-using mechanisms; primary contrasts remain system-configuration findings, not causal attributions to marketed library features.
Software Engineering.comment: 28 pages, 1 figure; code at github.com/ULDataProfessor/schema-validated-llm-workflows

Software Engineering.title: Epistemic Guard: Out-of-Process MCP Receipt Proxying, Post-Turn Prose Supervision, and Provenance-Gated Memory for Tool-Using Autonomous Agents
Software Engineering.summary: Language-model agents using the Model Context Protocol (MCP) face three runtime verification gaps: (i) action fabrication, where post-tool prose narrates side effects that failed, timed out, or never ran; (ii) provenance collapse, where unverified model prose or web text enters durable memory alongside executed tool outputs; and (iii) syndicated echo amplification, where mirrored web pages satisfy multi-source corroboration from one origin. Existing MCP firewalls inspect wire calls before execution, while LLM-judge guardrails require multi-gigabyte VRAM without binding prose to receipts. We present epistemic-guard (v0.5.2), an open-source Python library and out-of-process stdio MCP receipt proxy (15 modules, 0 MiB GPU VRAM). epistemic-guard isolates Ed25519 signing keys out of process, writes RFC 6962 Merkle logs with AER-1 receipt translation, checks post-turn prose on CPU with SHA-256-verified OpenVINO INT8 encoders (4 models, 279.48 MB total; 82.67 MB on the supervision path), gates SQLite writes across 7 provenance domains, and collapses verbatim and lightly edited wire-syndicated RAG mirrors. On conformance suites, epistemic-guard rejects 100.0% of tampered receipts (200 Merkle leaves), passes 58/58 official AER-1 ingestion vectors and 50/50 reference-verified AER-1 exports, verifies 100.0% of 40 fault-injected wire calls and 100 concurrent appends with 0 key leaks, and blocks 100.0% of 100 unauthorized memory writes. Across $N=250$ frozen-benchmark traces, epistemic-guard reaches 93.2% accuracy at 17.9 ms warm median CPU latency (8.62 ms single-clause; 921.8 ms cold-start load), beating 12B-14B GPU judges by 6.4-6.8 points ($p=0.0259$, $p=0.0095$) at 4.26-4.5$\times$ lower latency; on $N=60$ live mcp-proxy traces, it catches 96.15% of hazards at 76.67% accuracy (38.24% FPR; $+18.34$ points over Stage-1-only, $p=0.001$) in 9.16 ms p50.
Software Engineering.comment: 8 pages, 3 tables; open-source code and osaudit-verified manifests at https://github.com/AlienatedAliens/epistemic-guard (v0.5.2)

Software Engineering.title: Separating Automation Gains from Agent Contributions in AI-Assisted Model Validation
Software Engineering.summary: LLM agents are being proposed for bank model validation, yet evaluations that compare agent-assisted work with manual practice credit the agent with gains that come from digitized evidence and deterministic tests. We propose a staged architecture in which an LLM-free controlled workflow (P1) is both the fallback and the control arm for individually authorized agent tasks (P2), and an attribution protocol that credits an agent only for faults P1 does not already report. The protocol charges decoy false alarms, unnecessary actions and endorsed developer assertions, counts invalid outputs as misses, folds newly automatable findings back into P1 with discovery credit, and fixes safety bounds and a break-even cost gate in advance. On a synthetic credit-scorecard harness, five scripted reference policies show why this matters: naive case accuracy (4/6) and pooled detection (3/5) tie four flawed policies, whereas the protocol separates all five and credits only the reference policy with detection beyond P1. One fold-back round raises a P1-parroting policy's naive scores without any change to the policy. A regression matrix of sixteen mutants covers nine ways in which earlier versions of the evaluation passed misleadingly. No LLM agent has been evaluated yet; we specify a falsifiable pilot.
Software Engineering.comment: 5 pages, 1 figure, 3 tables. Synthetic evaluation pack and reproducibility code included as ancillary material

Software Engineering.title: Exercised, Rarely Recovered: What Public Reports Say About Recovery in 50 AI Agent Harnesses and Runtimes
Software Engineering.summary: When an AI coding agent deletes the wrong files or a long agent run crashes, users fall back on recovery mechanisms: resume from a checkpoint, undo, ask for approval, read the log. Research runtimes promise stronger guarantees, such as saga-style compensation and transactional rollback. We ask what public evidence shows about whether either kind works in real use. Under a protocol frozen before data collection, we graded 12 persistent agent runtimes, 26 coding-agent harnesses and 12 research runtimes on eight recovery mechanisms, from not found to exercised in a real run, with two blind coding passes, adjudication and re-verification against archived sources. Recovery is exercised almost everywhere in practice: 11 of 12 runtimes and 25 of 26 harnesses have at least one real-use report. Yet of 128 such reports, only 19 describe the run fully recovering; 54 are partial and 45 failed. Checkpoint/resume recovered once in 27 reports, rollback once in 15. Research runtimes show the opposite profile: guarantees evaluated on benchmarks, none reported in operation, and compensation of external effects, their central guarantee, is offered by no harness at all.
Software Engineering.comment: 5 pages, 2 figures. Replication dataset: doi:10.5281/zenodo.24122560

Software Engineering.title: Safe Personal RSI: Evaluating and Repairing Personal-Agent Updates
Software Engineering.summary: Kicker is a personal health assistant. Changes to an assistant's reusable instructions can improve task handling while changing what it discloses, which requests it follows, and how it reports actions. We study Safe Personal RSI, an update-evaluation component developed for Kicker. We restrict recursive self-improvement (RSI) to prompt updates, with model weights and runtime code fixed. The procedure tests proposed and current instructions, repeats failing cases, temporarily undoes changes to guide repairs, and checks safety and task performance before adoption. If no version passes, the current instructions stay in use. Our executable benchmark contains 29 email, calendar, health, and marketplace cases, with separate probes for authorization reuse, memory, and tool-output injection. Across three models and two deliberately risky edits, the procedure rejects 20 of 21 update attempts. In repair confirmation, an admitted GPT-5.6 Luna repair reduces attack violations from 10.7% to 0% and increases safe task completion from 89.7% to 100%; a broad handwritten authority rule matches these outcomes. Under stronger attacks, a repair transferred from Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct to Qwen3-14B reduces violations from 69.0% to 17.9% and increases safe task completion from 19.5% to 64.4%. Separate runtime probes examine memory-entry deletion and identify missing local OAuth scope checks in the evaluated snapshot.
Software Engineering.comment: Typo fixed. Add more to appendix

Software Engineering.title: Declarative Skills for AI Agents in Knowledge-Grounded Tool-Use Workflows
Software Engineering.summary: We study how orchestration affects tool-using large language model (LLM) agents in customer-service workflows over an unstructured knowledge base, comparing a declarative agent that reads natural-language skill files, an imperative agent built on a state machine, and an unscaffolded baseline. The three are formalized as policy classes within one decentralized partially observable Markov decision process and evaluated on a complete design of five models, two retrieval regimes, and three agents, with paired tests. Averaged over all conditions, orchestration does not improve task success. The effect, however, depends on the quality of the agent's observation channel. Under perfect retrieval, skill files are neutral-to-negative on four of the five models; under embedding retrieval they are neutral-to-positive on four of the five. On the tasks where baseline and scaffold disagree, the declarative win rate rises from 42.4% to 62.7% (p = 0.016), and the same interaction is present for the state machine (p = 0.003). Orchestration thus substitutes for information the agent lacks rather than supplementing information it has. Since deployed systems never attain perfect retrieval, the regime in which skill files help is the realistic one. Skill files also improve write-argument accuracy in all ten conditions (p = 0.002) without improving end-to-end success, and reduce unauthorized writes only where a compliance gap exists. The state machine lowers task success on four of the five models, and its verification gate is phase routing that misclassification can bypass. Enforcing the same precondition at the tool-execution layer eliminates unauthorized writes while preserving task success.

Software Engineering.title: Towards Energy-Efficient Large Language Model Inference: A Systematic Literature Review
Software Engineering.summary: Large language model (LLM) inference is becoming a significant contributor to both operational cost and environmental impact in modern AI deployments. Energy consumption during inference depends on multiple factors across the pipeline, including input and output length, model design, deployment-level decisions, and hardware characteristics. This paper presents a systematic literature review (SLR) of energy-efficient and sustainable LLM inference. We analyze selected primary studies to identify techniques proposed to reduce energy consumption across different levels of the inference pipeline, including input, model, deployment, and hardware. We further examine the trade-offs between energy consumption, latency, and accuracy, highlighting inconsistencies in how these relationships are evaluated. In addition, we review the tools, datasets, and metrics used for energy measurement, covering both software-based and hardware-based approaches. This survey provides a comprehensive synthesis of existing literature, offering insights into the effectiveness of different techniques in terms of energy savings and their associated impact on accuracy. It highlights the trade-offs between energy efficiency and performance, and identifies limitations in current evaluation practices. Overall, this work aims to support future research toward energy-efficient and environmentally responsible deployment of LLMs. Our repository of relevant references is maintained on GitHub.

Software Engineering.title: Idempotency Is Not Recovery: A Fault-Injection Study of Language-Model Agent Tool Actions
Software Engineering.summary: When a language-model agent's tool call is interrupted, the action may already have changed an external system without confirmation. Retrying risks duplication; assuming success may conceal an action that never occurred. We study these failure modes in a controlled agent runtime combining authorization, an action ledger, target-side idempotency, reconciliation, and evidence sealing. We inject ten single-host fault classes and compare four configurations and three ablations using a target-side oracle separate from the runtime ledger. On each of Windows and Linux, 7,513 trials used 96 captured model responses from 24 constructed cases. In 200 known original crash and replay pairs, the full configuration recorded 0/200 repeated effects versus 117/200 for each simpler baseline. A ledger-related ablation had 170/170 orphaned effects versus 0/170 and 200/300 recovery successes versus 300/300 for the full configuration. Disabling reconciliation left 100/100 known post-effect crash outcomes ambiguous despite no observed duplicates. A separate supplement designed after the initial results and reusing the same inputs found a similar pattern under response loss or delay. The full runtime had about one-seventh of fail-open throughput, while injected evidence-write faults left 75/100 trials per platform unresolved. These findings distinguish duplicate suppression from recovery and identify their measured reliability and performance tradeoffs within the tested benchmark.
Software Engineering.comment: 12 pages, 1 figure. Added submission notice on first page. Earlier single-author preprint; a later revision with additional authors was submitted to IEEE Transactions on Reliability. Aggregate data: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24369921

Software Engineering.title: CodeReviewBench: An Automated Benchmark for Evaluating the Software Factory
Software Engineering.summary: As AI agents ship more code with minimal human oversight, code review becomes the critical quality-control checkpoint -- but one without a reliable, objective verifier: review quality is nuanced and ultimately a judgment call by the PR author. Existing benchmarks are structurally misaligned with this: annotators are third-party reviewers, like the bots they evaluate, not the PR authors who actually decide what to fix. They also rely on small, static issue sets that require full re-evaluation as tools update, limiting how frequently progress can be tracked. We introduce CodeReviewBench, built on a fundamentally different signal: revealed developer preferences -- if a developer acts on a bot's suggestion, we treat it as useful; if they ignore it, we do not. This signal is mined daily from the public GitHub event stream, yielding 500K+ judged PRs across 18 tools, and refreshes continuously as tools evolve. We validate the developer preference against an independent offline benchmark: the two agree on precision rankings and independently detect the same product updates within days of vendor releases. Together, these form the benchmark.

Software Engineering.title: When AI Should Not Decide: Evidence Sufficiency and Decision Stability in Automated Job Interviews
Software Engineering.summary: Artificial intelligence is increasingly used to assess employment candidates, yet consistent interview scoring does not establish whether automated recommendations are supported by sufficient evidence. This study introduces the Evidence Sufficiency and Decision Stability Assessment (ESDSA), which combines criterion-level evidence classification, deterministic quotation traceability and stability checks across linguistic variants assessed as substantively equivalent. We evaluated four approaches (scoring-only, evidence-aware, traceability-based and integrated ESDSA v2) using 540 synthetic interview responses from 60 evaluated scenario families across Software Engineering, Customer Support and Operations. In held-out testing (216 responses), integrated ESDSA achieved 85.19% actionable coverage and 3.80% disagreement among actionable recommendations against AI-assisted provisional references. Evidence-aware evaluation achieved 92.59% coverage and 4.50% disagreement; scoring-only evaluation achieved 71.30% coverage and 1.95% disagreement. The integrated stability gate deferred 11 additional previously actionable decisions, ten of which had agreed with provisional references. The findings demonstrate trade-offs between evidential constraints, decision consistency and abstention, rather than overall superiority of the integrated framework. ESDSA offers a reproducible methodology for examining when automated interview recommendations should be actionable or deferred. Synthetic responses and AI-assisted references do not establish real-world recruitment validity.
Software Engineering.comment: 17 pages, 3 figures, 3 tables. Code and synthetic benchmark: https://github.com/khalidaals/ESDSA

Software Engineering.title: Taking the PULSE of Enterprise Workflows: Evaluating Persistent Project-State Understanding
Software Engineering.summary: Enterprise agents must maintain an up-to-date understanding of work distributed across heterogeneous artifacts, evolving over time, and unevenly visible to different collaborators. We formulate this challenge as persistent project-state understanding (PPSU) and introduce PULSE, a benchmark of 1,573 questions over 30 enterprise project histories.
