Captured with multi-sensor glasses, it contains 41,909 training hand-instance rows across 55 procedure recordings and 9,476 human-validated evaluation rows across 13 held-out recordings, spanning 13 tasks, 3 glove colors, and 4 trainees from first-year medical student to third-year resident. Each frame carries a multi-sensor stack: intrinsics, hand landmarks with per-hand confidence, timestamps, and eye gaze, plus SLAM extrinsics where SLAM succeeded. Evaluation labels combine sensor-fused pseudo-ground truth, human cross-review of every frame, surgeon adjudication of flagged cases, and an independent multi-view triangulated reference. Alongside the within-corpus, procedure-disjoint split, a leave-one-wearer-out protocol tested unseen trainees. Across eight methods evaluated zero-shot, from MANO-based reconstructors to the two-hand IntagHand and the keypoint-only MediaPipe Hands, egocentric pretraining was associated with stronger transfer on every held-out wearer. WildHands and JointTransformer had 18\% and 40\% lower PA-MPJPE, respectively, than the non-egocentric HaMeR. JointTransformer was the best performing model with an error of 14.95 mm. A substantial surgical domain gap remains, and the widely deployed MediaPipe Hands detected a hand in only 24.1\% of evaluation rows. As a baseline, a 58K-parameter residual corrector (JRN) on frozen backbones reached 10.96-14.85 mm PA-MPJPE on held-out wearers for the two ego-pretrained backbones. We release the dataset and benchmark code at https://egosurghands.github.io
Robotics.comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026. Code, dataset, and benchmark leaderboard available at https://egosurghands.github.io

Robotics.title: PACE: Policy Augmentation and Compensation With Explicit Disturbance Estimation for Robust Locomotion
Robotics.summary: Reinforcement learning has made quadrupedal locomotion remarkably robust. To handle unmodeled dynamics and external disturbances, domain randomization is usually employed to make a policy hedge against every condition it might meet. However, maintaining accurate tracking across varying dynamics and generalizing beyond the sampled range remain challenging. Here we show that explicitly estimating the disturbance and feeding the resulting estimation back into both the policy and the controller can relax this compromise. We introduce Policy Augmentation and Compensation with Explicit disturbance estimation (PACE). The framework lumps payload variations, center-of-mass (CoM) shifts, actuator degradation, and external forces into one joint-space disturbance. A nonlinear observer subsequently recovers this disturbance online without requiring joint acceleration measurements. The disturbance estimation provides feedforward torque compensation as the foundational control pathway and further augments the policy observation to enable disturbance-aware action generation. Considering the learning difficulty of fast-varying contact effects, we further provide an analytical contact estimation approach from joint and inertial measurements, without demanding force sensors. Across eleven simulated dynamics conditions, PACE reduces velocity-tracking error by 18.1% to 57.0% against state-of-the-art baselines, and maintains improved tracking under out-of-distribution (OOD) commands. Notably, in real-world experiments, the deployed real robot carried an 11.5 kg payload, nearly equal to its own mass. It also negotiated unseen 16 cm step-downs and crossed five outdoor terrains. The policy was trained exclusively on flat ground in simulation with at most 3 kg of added mass.

Robotics.title: A Learning-Enhanced Control Scheme for Aerial Manipulator Under Composite Disturbances
Robotics.summary: Achieving high-precision dynamic tracking in aerial manipulators remains fundamentally challenging due to strong coupling effects and external disturbances. Existing approaches are typically limited to compensating first-order coupling term, leaving higher-order nonlinearities unaddressed. Building upon the philosophy of learning-for-control, this paper proposes a composite control scheme that combines learning-based approximation with observer-based compensation in a complementary manner. Based on the polynomial decomposition theorem, the unknown high-order term is decomposed into a shared constant basis matrix, a state-related polynomial matrix, and a task-related parameter vector. A bilevel optimization formula is first established to extract the task-invariant shared information, enabling efficient knowledge reuse across different operation conditions. By leveraging the learned shared basis, an adaptive law is designed to update the task-dependent parameter vector online. Furthermore, an observer is introduced to compensate for the inevitable approximation residual and external disturbances. The resulting framework leads to a concurrent attainment of the stable transient response and high-precision steady-state tracking performance. Extensive real-world experiments on an aerial manipulator across four representative scenarios demonstrate the effectiveness and robustness of the proposed approach.

Robotics.title: BeyondEgo: Learning to Act Beyond Egocentric Perception via Humanoid Ego-Exo Foresight
Robotics.summary: Humanoid loco-manipulation requires coordinating whole-body motion to perform manipulation tasks in complex environments. Yet egocentric vision-language-action (VLA) policies can miss critical body--scene relationships, and action imitation alone provides no explicit supervision for future scene evolution. We propose BeyondEgo to extend VLA perception in space and time. Spatially, we encode a synchronized exocentric view with frozen DINOv3 and concatenate the resulting tokens with egocentric VLM tokens to condition the action expert. Temporally, we use future observations from both views as privileged supervision for a residual adapter on task-conditioned VLM features. A foresight expert regresses DINOv3 representations of both views 0.6s ahead. At deployment, the foresight expert is discarded and the 4.2M-parameter adapter is retained. We also introduce HELM, to our knowledge, the first closed-loop humanoid loco-manipulation benchmark with synchronized egocentric and exocentric views across five whole-body tasks.On HELM, BeyondEgo improves success from 48.0% to 92.0% in distribution and from 23.5% to 65.0% on 200 held-out scenes with layout, asset, material, and lighting shifts. Ablations show that dual-view DINOv3 foresight yields the best transfer results.

Robotics.title: RoboColiseum: Co-evolution of Simulation, Evaluation, and Models
Robotics.summary: Simulation-based evaluation of embodied models requires calibrated interactions, diverse tasks, and explicit execution constraints. We present RoboColiseum, a platform combining system identification, composable physics and rendering, and multidimensional benchmarking. Recorded-command replay characterizes robot dynamics and object interactions, while a shared interface connects rigid and deformable simulation to rendering. Across 22 paired real--simulation robot--task configurations, task scores have a reported Pearson correlation of 0.9686. Eight evaluation tracks span instruction following, spatial reasoning, general manipulation, robustness, dexterous manipulation, precision manipulation, whole-body coordination, and execution across robot embodiments. Budget-aware scoring combines task progress, resource use, and completion rewards. We report 12 selected Season~I policies and all 11 systems on the public Season~II leaderboard, comprising eight Agent systems and three VLA policies. Agent2Act connects language models to robot-control execution; the VLA study uses mixed-task supervised fine-tuning. The results reveal substantial variation across tracks within each evaluation category. RoboColiseum connects simulation development with capability-oriented evaluation and provides a foundation for extending robot interactions and model assessment.
Robotics.comment: 11 pages, 8 figures. The first eight authors contributed equally. Maoqing Yao and Qian Wang are the corresponding authors

Robotics.title: WorldFlow: Joint Video and 3D Motion Prediction via Large-Scale Pretraining
Robotics.summary: Predicting future physical states stands as a central challenge in embodied intelligence. Existing video world models leave 3D dynamics implicit, action-based formulations remain tied to specific robot configurations, and 3D motion prediction models use flow-only supervision, providing a limited learning signal for physical dynamics. To circumvent these limitations, we introduce \method{}, a generative world model that jointly predicts future video and query-based 3D trajectories. By parameterizing 3D motion as continuous displacement tokens aligned with the video grid, a unified Mixture-of-Transformers (MoT) backbone jointly denoises both modalities under a rectified-flow objective. This formulation couples explicit geometric dynamics with visual evolution, effectively unlocking the physical commonsense embedded within pretrained video models. To empirically scale and validate this unified architecture, we train \method{} on a heterogeneous mixture of 1.44 million object-level samples spanning simulated and real-world domains. We further introduce WorldFlowBench, comprising 1,678 evaluation samples from 11 data sources across simulated and real-world interactions, including spatial reasoning tasks. Across all three evaluation sets, WorldFlow achieves the lowest average displacement error (ADE) and final displacement error (FDE) among the evaluated learning-based methods. Notably, on the challenging SpatialCog set, WorldFlow achieves an ADE of 0.060 m, a 54.2\% reduction compared with the strongest external baseline. It also reduces ADE and FDE by 55.9\% and 68.5\%, respectively, compared with its flow-only variant. Project page: https://roboscience-ai.github.io/worldflow-page/.

Robotics.title: Many Plans at Once: Diverse Top-Quality Planning in Continuous Time
Robotics.summary: Planners for physical systems usually return a single trajectory, which leaves no alternative when an unmodeled constraint invalidates the chosen route or downstream preferences change. A set of plans computed in advance provides ready-made alternatives and warm-starts for fast adaptation, but only if the plans are both low-cost and mutually distinct. Discrete planning addresses this with top-quality and diverse planning, but these ideas do not transfer to continuous time, where every valid trajectory has infinitely many valid near-copies, and existing trajectory planners converge to one or a few solutions. We present Many Plans at Once (MPAO), which treats every plan it finds as a reason to search elsewhere: it samples untrained neural networks whose outputs meet the boundary conditions by construction, trains corrections shared by networks from the same distribution, stores every validated plan, and adapts its sampling to what it has found, which makes it anytime. We define the goal by bringing the cost bound of top-quality planning and the distinctness threshold of diverse planning to continuous time. Under equal budgets against five baselines, MPAO is the only method that solves all 40 instances across four domains. On contact-rich manipulation, it is the only method with plans within 25% of the best known cost on one task, and returns about ten times as many such plans as the strongest baseline on the other two.

Robotics.title: FoRe: A Force-Guided Framework for Autonomous Grasp Recovery in Vision-Language-Action Models
Robotics.summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) models have demonstrated strong performance in grasp-based manipulation, yet reliable recovery from local grasping failures remains challenging. Specifically, in pick-and-place tasks, policies may continue transport after a failed grasp instead of retrying, potentially reflecting overreliance on proprioceptive cues for stage progression and limited retry supervision. Existing recovery approaches typically rely on deployment-time guidance or demonstration augmentation. We introduce Force-guided Recovery (FoRe), a framework for autonomous recovery from local grasping failures. Using force feedback, FoRe partitions demonstrations into approach-grasp and transport-placement stages to train separate policies. To supplement limited retry supervision, FoRe then initializes a dedicated retry policy from the approach-grasp policy and refines it through local reinforcement learning (RL) from post-failure states. To avoid inappropriate stage progression, a controller combines force feedback with grasp-command status at inference to coordinate the stage policies, detect grasp failures, and invoke the retry policy. We also construct LIBERO-SUCTION, a force-augmented suction manipulation benchmark adapted from LIBERO, with complete demonstration trajectories for policy training. FoRe consistently improves task success rates for VLA-Adapter and $π_{0.5}$ on LIBERO-SUCTION, LIBERO, and real-world tasks. On LIBERO-SUCTION, average absolute gains are 18.4% and 6.5%, respectively. The corresponding real-world absolute gains are 25.0% and 21.7%. FoRe also remains effective with only one demonstration per task on both simulation benchmarks.

Robotics.title: PonderPounce-WM: When Does Predicting the Future Help Context-Dependent Robot Control?
Robotics.summary: How does future prediction affect context-dependent robot control? We introduce PonderPounce-WM, extending PonderPounce with three future tokens supervised to predict visual-feature changes. Its pretrained MLLM, Ponder, integrates history and demonstrations into continuous cognition for the action model, Pounce. We investigate token ordering and delivery to distinguish predictive supervision from direct future conditioning. On RoboMME, cognition-first ordering with cognition-only delivery improves success from 60.83% to 67.42%. With the same ordering, direct future-token delivery yields 64.00% success. Probes show increased future information in cognition while the tested past-event attributes remain largely decodable. Across four real-robot tasks, PonderPounce-WM achieves 67.44% mean success under asynchronous execution, compared with 60.98% for PonderPounce. These results suggest that future prediction can improve context-dependent control through auxiliary supervision without delivering future tokens to the action model.

Robotics.title: Geo-Force: A Theory of Force Sensing from Object Geometry
Robotics.summary: Robots need contact forces to handle delicate objects, but tactile sensors are fragile and hard to integrate, whereas depth sensors, such as RGB-D cameras, are widely available. A virtual touch sensor that keeps the sensing surface of a tactile sensor but replaces its electronics with a touch signal predicted from the target object's geometry, as measured by a depth sensor, could close this gap, yet it is unclear what such a virtual sensor computes and when its output can be trusted. We give a formal answer. We define the Geometric Force as the force on each taxel of a virtual touch sensor, computed in three steps: rendering the surface to be touched as seen from the virtual sensor, predicting the touch signal with a touch map, learned or simulated, and estimating the force from that signal. We prove three properties of the Geometric Force. First, its force vectors only rotate under a change of coordinate frame. Second, it vanishes when the rendered surface does not touch the virtual sensor. Third, it is stable: its error grows at most linearly with the errors of the three steps for Lipschitz maps. The rendering error, in turn, depends on how well the surface is sampled or reconstructed and how accurately the sensor is placed. We then show a fundamental limit: geometry does not reveal the object's stiffness, so no touch map can predict touch exactly for objects of the same shape and different stiffness. Under an elastic contact model, all object-specific knowledge resides in the touch map. From these results, we derive requirements on the depth sensor and the objects, design rules, and the conditions under which such a virtual sensor fails.

Robotics.title: PRISM-SLAM: Probabilistic Ray-Grounded Inference for Scale-aware Metric SLAM
Robotics.summary: Monocular SLAM historically suffers from scale ambiguity and tracking failure in dynamic environments. While recent vision foundation models (VFMs) provide remarkable zero-shot depth priors, naively integrating these deterministic predictions ignores predictive uncertainty and frame-to-frame scale inconsistencies. We propose PRISM-SLAM, a real-time framework that rigorously integrates VFM priors into a structured Bayesian factor graph to achieve scale-aware, metric-consistent localization and mapping. Specifically, we introduce a Plücker Ray-Distance Factor to anchor monocular observations in absolute space within a globally consistent metric coordinate system, mathematically resolving scale drift by making the metric scale Fisher-identifiable. To handle environmental dynamics, we derive an epistemic uncertainty proxy from temporal depth consistency and formulate a Dynamic Scene Uncertainty Gating (DSUG) mechanism. This soft-gating approach probabilistically down-weights dynamic distractors without incurring the heavy computational overhead associated with traditional semantic segmentation masks. By employing a multi-process architecture that asynchronously processes VFM inference and geometric tracking, PRISM-SLAM provides verified metric output at 30 FPS using solely RGB input, bridging the gap between foundation models and real-world robotic applications. Evaluated on the TUM RGB-D and 7-Scenes benchmarks, PRISM-SLAM achieves a metric $SE(3)$ Absolute Trajectory Error (ATE) nearly identical to its oracle-aligned $Sim(3)$ error. This demonstrates that our system can produce deployment-ready metric trajectories by delivering robust metric SLAM solutions without any post-hoc scale correction. Project page: https://prismslam-cmd.github.io/prismslam_pr/

Robotics.title: RoboPRO: A Perturbation-Resilient and Obstacle-Aware Benchmark for Robotic Manipulation
Robotics.summary: Object manipulation in the real world requires robotic policies to be robust to contextual perturbations and capable of safe planning in cluttered scenes. However, the majority of existing robotics benchmarks contain clean tabletop environments with success rate as the sole metric, leaving two critical deployment questions unanswered: does the policy manipulate safely under real conditions and what does lead to its failure? To this end, we present RoboPRO, a Robotics benchmark for Perturbation-Resilient and Obstacle-aware planning, which unifies various axes of robustness in manipulation. RoboPRO comprises 80 diverse bimanual atomic and compositional tasks across four furnished indoor environments, with a total of 16,000 demonstrations and 5.6K diverse language instructions. The scenes are populated with different numbers of distractors (non-targets), ranging from clean, involving only target objects, to densely populated to impose both visual and operational clutter. Moreover, we propose two safety-aware event metrics to determine unsafe contact between the robot and the environment or distractors. Our evaluation protocol consists of a per-factor analysis of three key perturbations, namely visual, linguistic, and object-level, with different levels of distractor densities. We conduct extensive experiments on RoboPRO using state-of-the-art manipulation policies to analyze the impact of visual and operational clutter, perturbations, and instructional diversity. Our findings indicate clutter can drastically reduce success and increase non-target collision, different perturbations have different effects on the performance, and that training data composition affects overall performance. Our findings highlight the key challenges for manipulation in real-world conditions and motivate future research in this domain. Project page: https://robopro-bench.github.io/RoboPRO/
Robotics.comment: 8 pages, 8 figures, 5 tables. Project page: https://robopro-bench.github.io/RoboPRO/

Robotics.title: RoboDyna: A Benchmark for Evaluating Robotic Manipulation under Physically Grounded Dynamics
Robotics.summary: Object manipulation in the dynamic real world requires understanding how the environment functions and evolves, and acting accordingly. Existing benchmarks, however, do not adequately address these needs. Physics-oriented benchmarks evaluate predictive fidelity but not closed-loop action. Dynamic robotic manipulation benchmarks often use simplified, physically implausible object motions, limiting evaluation of reasoning and action under realistic dynamics. Evaluation is also typically synchronized, freezing the environment during inference and making computation time irrelevant to task outcomes. To this end, we propose RoboDyna, a benchmark for evaluating the physical understanding and action capabilities of manipulation policies in dynamic scenes. RoboDyna comprises 20 conceptual dynamic tasks spanning five capability categories, with simple objects and minimal scene clutter, under a two-factor difficulty design, and 10 household tasks that instantiate the same capabilities in visually and semantically richer simulated real-world environments. RoboDyna provides 3,500 expert demonstrations, paired synchronous and asynchronous evaluation protocols, metrics for task success and partial completion, and interactive tools for human baseline evaluation. Evaluating vision-language-action models and a world-action model across 5.4K episodes, we find that all policies achieve success rates below 20%, revealing substantial limitations in dynamic manipulation. The world-action model captures simple physical dynamics but struggles with complex interactions, and its prediction fidelity does not consistently align with task success. Sync-async comparisons show that inference latency flips 5-12% of episode outcomes while changing average success rates by at most 3%. Human baselines substantially outperform all policies under matched conditions. Project page: https://robodyna.github.io/robodyna/
Robotics.comment: 8 pages, 9 figures, 2 tables. Project page: https://robodyna.github.io/robodyna/

Robotics.title: LF-GICP: Parameter-Free Degeneracy-Aware LiDAR Odometry via a Voxel-Normal Localizability Field
Robotics.summary: Scan-to-map LiDAR odometry drifts unboundedly along the unobservable axes of geometrically degenerate environments like tunnels and corridors, and existing degeneracy handling requires environment-specific parameter tuning. This paper presents a parameter-free approach. We show that in voxelized GICP the Gauss--Newton (GN) Hessian masks translational degeneracy, because covariance regularization keeps the translation block artificially well-conditioned. We bypass this with a regularization-free voxel-normal localizability field and two of its statistics: a normalized fraction $f_0$ detecting directional anisotropy, and an absolute per-voxel mass $λ_0$ distinguishing information absence (tunnels) from dilution (dense open scenes). A temporal-median gate combines both to trigger Fisher-information correspondence weighting. Calibrated once by fixed rules on two short sequences and then frozen, LF-GICP achieves the lowest KITTI relative translation error ($0.865\%$) under an identical evaluation protocol against re-run baselines, outperforms them on GEODE tunnels and MulRan, leads the HeLiPR mean, and generalizes across four sensor types without re-tuning. We further demonstrate empirically that straight, uniform tunnels remain unobservable along their axis for LiDAR-only registration.

Robotics.title: Mechanistic Analysis of Unified Proximity-Tactile Observation by a Capacitive Fingertip Array Constrained by a Metal Phalanx
Robotics.summary: A capacitive fingertip array on a metal phalanx under thin silicone skin senses centimetre-scale conductive targets by fringing fields and contact force by dielectric compression. Electrode-to-body parasitics exceed the useful proximity increment by one to three orders of magnitude, and crosstalk and time-division-multiplexing (TDM) settling prevent identifying the capacitance-to-digital converter (CDC) reading with the electrode-target capacitance. The array is modelled as a multi-conductor system (sensing electrodes, driven-shield nodes, phalanx ground and an external target). The CDC measurand follows from the Maxwell capacitance matrix, with each inactive termination in the observation operator. Three mechanisms are examined: driven-shield hiding of shield-branch current and gain/phase-mismatch leakage; distinct far- and near-field operators; and TDM settling as a frame-rate limit set by shield load. A single layer used for both proximity and force reads Delta C = Delta C_force + Delta C_dielectric(epsilon_target), so its force map cannot be material-independent. A dual-array stack is analysed: the outer array is grounded as a Faraday screen during contact, and the inner array reads silicone-gap compression. FEM simulations give a monotonic, nonlinear contact response (4.6 fF at 0.05 mm to 370 fF at 0.5 mm on a 1.08 pF base), a nylon-versus-metal difference of at most 0.3 fF at exported-matrix resolution (not mesh-converged), mutual-term cancellation under driven-shield readout, and about 1 fF crosstalk on the coarse mesh. In proximity mode, electrode-shield coupling of 1.47 pF makes 10^{-3}-10^{-4} mismatch a quantitative gate: a 15.9 fF increment at 5 mm equals the leakage at |epsilon_A| ~ 10^{-2}. Force map, mechanical crosstalk and all bench quantities remain unvalidated; the equations and FEM evidence are a baseline for prototype calibration, not measured performance claims.
Robotics.comment: Mechanistic analysis with electrostatic FEM; no bench force map. 14 figures

Robotics.title: Analysis of Multi-Client Inference Techniques for Vision-Language-Action Models
Robotics.summary: Vision-Language-Action models (VLAs) are a new class of machine learning model for generalizable robot control. While they enable robots to perform complex tasks in unseen environments, serving VLAs leaves hardware idle between inference passes and under-utilized during inference. Serving multiple clients at once can improve utilization, but fundamental multi-client techniques such as batching and co-execution have not been characterized for VLAs. We therefore characterize the trade-offs these known techniques impose across latency, throughput, power, and hardware utilization. Our findings inform trade-offs and challenges for future multi-VLA serving systems.

Robotics.title: RoboCap-10k: A Metrically Accurate Egocentric Dataset for Robot Learning
Robotics.summary: Egocentric video is the most scalable source of manipulation data for robot learning, but its difficulty lies in producing high-quality supervision. Existing large corpora lack metric 3D labels or rely on heterogeneous devices, motion-capture labs, or a headset's built-in real-time tracker, whose accuracy is not reported for the released data. We introduce RoboCap-10k: 10,000 curated hours of unscripted manipulation recorded during workers' paid shifts in 11 countries, spanning 18 task families, 200 task types, and 2,000 tasks. Every hour is captured on one device, the RoboCap, a 250 g hat with six synchronized global-shutter cameras and dual IMUs. Online calibration brings every device below 1 px of epipolar error, visual-inertial SLAM yields gravity-aligned 6-DoF head trajectories, and a multi-view hand tracker yields metric cm-precise hand poses. Each episode is annotated with task and sub-task language captions. Project page: https://robocap10k.com
Robotics.comment: 24 pages, 9 figures, 11 tables. Project page: https://robocap10k.com

Systems and Control.title: What Graph Unlearning Cannot Erase: Physics-Induced Leakage of Cyberattack Information in Electric Vehicle Charging Networks
Systems and Control.summary: Electric vehicle charging stations (EVCSs) can expose distribution feeders to cyberattacks. While machine learning methods, including graph neural networks (GNNs), can localize which bus is compromised, significant challenges remain in data sharing and model training. For example, data-sharing agreements grant EVCS operators the right to withdraw their charging power for privacy or security reasons from a deployed model, yet retraining from scratch on every request would repeat the full-retraining (FR) cost. To address this, we study graph unlearning (GU) for EVCS cyberattack localization, formulated as a feature-level unlearning problem on a graph-level multi-label classification task. We benchmark fine-tuning (FT) against two GU baselines on the IEEE 34-bus, 123-bus, and 8500-node distribution networks across three GNN backbones and cumulative unlearning scenarios. Experiments show that a GNN unlearned or retrained without the withdrawn power still localizes cyberattacks at the forgotten EVCSs. This physics-induced leakage floor arises because a cyberattack on an EVCS also shifts the voltages of electrically coupled buses. The distribution system operator can thus promise an EVCS operator that the deployed GNN model no longer uses its charging power data, but the voltages still reveal cyberattacks at its EVCS.

Systems and Control.title: Load-Following Dynamics of an SMR-Powered All-Electric Ship with Battery Energy Storage
Systems and Control.summary: Small modular reactors (SMRs) are being considered as compact, high-energy-density power sources for future all-electric ships. In such systems, propulsion-load variations can propagate through the electrical network, turbine-generator set, steam generator, and reactor, producing coupled nuclear, thermal, mechanical, and electrical transients. This paper presents an integrated dynamic load-following analysis of an SMR-powered all-electric ship with and without battery energy storage system (BESS) support. The model couples an integral pressurized water reactor, a once-through moving-boundary steam generator, a simplified turbine model, a synchronous generator, an AC shipboard electrical network, an asynchronous propulsion motor, and a grid-connected BESS. A propulsion-load reduction is applied through the motor torque command, and the responses of the SMR-alone and SMR+BESS configurations are compared. The results show that, without BESS support, the sudden decrease in propulsion motor power creates a temporary surplus between turbine mechanical power and electrical demand, causing a large over-frequency transient and rapid steam-cycle adjustment. With BESS support, the battery absorbs excess electrical power during the transient, reducing the frequency peak from approximately 61.1 Hz to about 60.06 Hz. The BESS also indirectly smooths the upstream steam-cycle and reactor responses, including steam flow, steam-generator pressure, feedwater flow, coolant temperature, reactivity, reactor thermal power, and steam-generator region lengths. These results demonstrate the importance of modeling nuclear-powered electric ships as coupled multi-domain systems and show that BESS integration can improve short-term load-following performance.

Systems and Control.title: Terrain-Aided Navigation Without Raycasting: A Sliding Grid Approach for Point Cloud Processing
Systems and Control.summary: We investigate the use of a point cloud measurement in terrain-aided navigation. Our goal is to aid an inertial navigation system, by exploring ways to generate a useful measurement residual for effective nonlinear state estimation. We compare two such measurement models that involve the scanning of a digital terrain elevation model: a) one that is based on typical ray-casting from a given pose, that returns the predicted point cloud measurement from that pose, and b) another computationally less intensive one that does not require raycasting and we refer to herein as a sliding grid. Besides requiring a pose, it requires the pattern of the point cloud measurement itself and returns a predicted point cloud measurement. We show that the sliding grid achieves comparable accuracy to raycasting, especially at higher altitudes, while being orders of magnitude faster computationally. By eliminating the need for raycasting, the sliding grid removes the dependency on dedicated GPU hardware or high-performance CPUs, making it well-suited for real-time terrain-aided navigation on resource-constrained embedded platforms.

Systems and Control.title: Bayesian Bias Learning-Enabled Probabilistic Voltage Estimation with Unknown Uncertainty Modeling of DERs in Distribution Grids
Systems and Control.summary: One key challenge in distribution system state es- timation is unknown input statistics from the growing inte- gration of distributed energy resources (DERs), which may largely deviate from Gaussian uncertainty. Existing model-based estimators often rely on the assumption that all inputs follow known Gaussian distributions, while data-driven methods suffer from overfitting and failure in out-of-distribution scenarios. This paper proposes a Bayesian bias learning (BBL)-enabled probabilistic voltage estimation method in distribution systems with unknown DER generation statistics. The proposed learning- enabled method consists of two stages: probabilistic uncertainty inference and computationally efficient voltage estimation. First, a physics-constrained probabilistic density inference network is developed to learn Gaussian mixture representations of DER generation from historical data. Then, the resulting probabilistic representations, treated as pseudo-measurements, are integrated into a BBL-enabled voltage estimator via a decomposition- and-parallelization mechanism. Furthermore, utilizing a linear analytical solution, the proposed BBL-enabled voltage estimator efficiently captures linearization-induced biases and attains ac- curate probabilistic estimation. By integrating learning-enabled probabilistic uncertainty modeling into the parallel estimation structure, the proposed method achieves uncertainty-aware scal- able voltage estimation. Case studies on two unbalanced IEEE distribution networks show that the proposed estimator achieves significantly higher accuracy and computational efficiency under unknown uncertainty, outperforming recent data-driven and model-based methods.

Systems and Control.title: Simplifying Gas-Phase Kinetic Measurements with a Dual-Arm Flow Tube
Systems and Control.summary: We demonstrate a simple dual-arm flow tube reactor that provides well-defined reaction times ranging from one second to several minutes for gas-phase kinetic measurements near ambient temperature and pressure. Constructed entirely from standard tubing, the flow tube reactor eliminates the need for injector translation. It operates in two configurations: a variable-length configuration, in which the tube length is changed at fixed flow, and a variable-flow configuration, in which an exhaust branch allows the flow through the reaction section to be adjusted while maintaining constant reactant inlet flows. With 3.96 mm i.d. tubing, the measured tracer pulses had a typical full width at half maximum of about $10\%$ of their mean arrival time. A kinetic demonstration using the ozonolysis of 2,3-dimethyl-2-butene (TME) yields an apparent rate coefficient for TME loss $k_{\mathrm{app}} = 2.0(5) \times 10^{-15}\,\mathrm{cm}^{3}\,\mathrm{molecule}^{-1}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}$. Fitting the same kinetic data with a reaction network including secondary OH and peroxy-radical chemistry yields $k = 1.18(19) \times 10^{-15}\,\mathrm{cm}^{3}\,\mathrm{molecule}^{-1}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}$ at 293 K for TME + $\mathrm{O}_{3}$, consistent with the IUPAC recommendation. This compact, low-cost reactor provides an alternative to conventional movable-injector flow tubes for atmospheric chemistry, fundamental kinetics, and gas-liquid or gas-solid uptake studies.

Systems and Control.title: Energy-preserving Bayesian model reduction: closed-form structured posteriors and probabilistic stability certificates for quadratic operator inference
Systems and Control.summary:
Bayesian operator inference learns reduced-order models (ROMs) with polynomial structure from state data and returns a closed-form Gaussian posterior over the reduced operators. That posterior is unconstrained, so it gives positive probability to operators with unbounded dynamics, and current practice controls this only through finite-horizon simulation tests on a few samples. We show that energy preservation of the quadratic operator is a set of linear equality constraints, which can be imposed exactly inside the Bayesian formulation without losing the closed form. In particular, the constrained posterior follows from one Kalman-type update of the unconstrained one, and its samples are obtained exactly, by the same correction applied to unconstrained draws. Under this structure, global boundedness for all initial conditions and bounded inputs reduces to a linear matrix condition on the symmetric part of the linear operator. The simulation test is then replaced by a probabilistic stability certificate: the posterior probability that the ROM is globally bounded, estimated with exact confidence bounds; the posterior restricted to certified models is then sampled exactly by rejection. For energy-conserving systems, the linear part can be constrained to be skew-symmetric as well: every draw then grows at most linearly in time, and conserves energy exactly when unforced.
  On a forced viscous Burgers' equation, the Korteweg-de Vries equation and a two-dimensional viscous Burgers' equation, every sample of the constrained posterior integrates to a bounded trajectory, where up to all unconstrained draws diverge, and beyond the observation window the former is also the more accurate of the two.

Systems and Control.title: Fault-Geometry-Aware Control Allocation for Emergency Quadrotor Landing under Single-Motor Loss of Effectiveness
Systems and Control.summary: Partial single-motor loss of effectiveness (LoE) changes the remaining control-authority geometry of a quadrotor and can change which control allocator performs best during emergency landing. We compare three allocators in Crazyflie software-in-the-loop simulation: bounded weighted least squares (reported as PINV), a finite-candidate residual allocator (QP-lite), and the same residual allocator with scoring parameters tuned offline by the Cross-Entropy Method (CEM). For this study, fault geometry is represented by the known failed-motor index. At $η= 0.496$ remaining effectiveness, matched development trials select CEM for M1, M3, and M4 and PINV for M2; the M3 selection is a one-trial margin (29/30 versus 28/30). After freezing this routing map, the policy achieves 117/120 safe first-contact touchdowns on fresh seeds and 115/120 in a separate randomized-order integrated-supervisor evaluation. For the critical M2/PINV branch, Firth regression gives a nominal $η_{50} \approx 0.4956$ with a within-model 95% bootstrap interval of approximately $[0.4955, 0.4956]$. One-factor-at-a-time $\pm 10\%$ plant perturbations shift $η_{50}$ by up to $0.05495$ for thrust coefficient and $0.04974$ for mass; the most frequent violated first-contact criterion also changes from vertical speed in many conditions to angular rate for mass $-10\%$ and thrust-coefficient $+10\%$. At fixed $η= 0.496$, PINV has a higher M2 safe count than frozen CEM in 9/11 tested plant states and ties in 2/11; the two ties are both 0/30. The experiments therefore distinguish motor-conditioned allocator selection from sensitivity to plant-model mismatch.
Systems and Control.comment: 6 pages, 7 figures, 1 table

Systems and Control.title: Optimal Uniform Pricing for Multi-Interval Dispatch without Make-Whole Uplifts
Systems and Control.summary: In a network with ramp-limited generators and inaccurate net-demand forecasts, practical rolling-window dispatch can drive locational marginal prices (LMPs) below generators' bid-in offers. In such cases, out-of-market (OOM) settlements are used to compensate generators and maintain dispatch-following incentives, but OOM can have negative consequences, including nontransparent real-time price signals, discriminatory compensation, and incentives for untruthful bidding. This paper presents an optimal uniform pricing rule that minimizes demand payments, eliminates OOM make-whole payments, preserves LMP-based congestion charges, and ensures revenue adequacy. We derive the proposed pricing rule in closed form and relate it to existing pricing schemes. Numerical comparisons demonstrate favorable generator profits and reduced price volatility. However, higher generator profits are accompanied by increased demand payments, reflecting the in-market, uniform allocation of ramping costs while preserving the LMP-based congestion charges widely used in real-time market settlements. The numerical results also show that, under LMP with OOM settlement, a price-taking generator has an incentive to inflate its offer, whereas this incentive is absent under the proposed pricing rule within the tested bid range.
Systems and Control.comment: 7 pages, 7 figures, 4 tables. Accepted for presentation at the 2027 IEEE PES International Meeting

Systems and Control.title: Eliminating Make-Whole Uplifts with a Minimum-Cost Uniform Price Adder
Systems and Control.summary: Co-optimizing energy and flexible ramping reserves may dispatch generators at locational marginal prices (LMPs) below their submitted energy offer prices, necessitating out-of-market make-whole payments. Such payments create discriminatory settlements among generators and may incentivize strategic bidding for higher profits. This paper proposes LMP+U, an in-market uniform price adder to LMP for transmission-constrained networks, which minimizes demand payments subject to zero out-of-market make-whole uplift, preserves LMP-based congestion charges, and provides locally truthful bidding incentives for price-taking generators. We also identify conditions under which a price-taking generator can increase its profit by inflating its energy offer under conventional LMP with make-whole uplift. Numerical simulations illustrate the properties of LMP+U and its advantages over conventional LMP in congested networks.
Systems and Control.comment: 5 pages, 3 figures, 2 tables

Systems and Control.title: Iteration-Dependent Temporal Resilience in Diffusion Models for Approximate Computing
Systems and Control.summary: This paper empirically analyzes iteration-dependent resilience in diffusion models by replacing MACs with efficient SAC approximations. Results on Q-Diffusion show early steps are highly sensitive while later steps are robust, enabling iteration- aware approximation that improves efficiency and reduces hardware cost with minimal quality loss.
Systems and Control.comment: Accepted for publication at ICSEE 2026

Systems and Control.title: On Robust Strictly Positive Real Synthesis for High-Order Interval Polynomials
Systems and Control.summary: We establish two complementary results on common strictly positive real (SPR) numerators for Hurwitz-stable interval polynomial families. First, for every order $n \ge 10$, we construct a monic Hurwitz-stable interval polynomial family with rational endpoints and positive width in every nonleading coefficient such that every nonzero real numerator of degree at most $n$ produces a strictly negative real part at some member and some positive frequency. In particular, robust Hurwitz stability alone does not guarantee equal-degree SPR synthesis in high orders. Second, for every order $n \ge 1$, we prove that a common real SPR numerator of exact degree $n$ always exists whenever the lower endpoint of each interior coefficient interval is at most $10^{-5}$ times its upper endpoint, while the constant and leading coefficients vary over arbitrary compact positive intervals.

Systems and Control.title: Hierarchical Agentic Mid-Band Agility for Reliable Low-Latency Space-Air-Ground Integrated V2X Networks
Systems and Control.summary: Upper-mid-band spectrum offers bandwidth opportunities for the integrated networks of ground vehicles, unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs), and low Earth orbit (LEO) satellites to support 6G wide-area vehicle-to-everything (V2X) connectivity. However, V2X services' latency and reliability are sensitive to the mid-band selection due to frequency-dependent propagation and rain attenuation. This paper investigates environment-aware spectrum agility over candidate frequency range 3 (FR3) bands within 7.125-24.25 GHz, jointly with end-to-end (E2E) multi-path traffic splitting and transmit power control. Each data packet is partitioned into non-overlapping subflows over direct and UAV-assisted paths, with failed sky-link subflows selectively retransmitted subject to retransmission and freshness constraints. We formulate latency- and reliability-oriented problems, followed by a unified sequential optimization problem incorporating band-switching costs and average quality-of-service (QoS) violation budgets. To coordinate optimization decisions across heterogeneous timescales, we develop an agentic AI-assisted hierarchical multi-agent reinforcement learning (AA-HMARL) framework. A high-level agentic supervisor integrates recurrent memory, analytical evaluation of candidate bands, and event-triggered replanning to coordinate slow environmental adaptation with fast channel and retransmission dynamics, while distributed ground vehicles and UAV agents optimize data splitting and power using constrained MAPPO. Simulation results demonstrate an adjustable reliability-latency trade-off. Particularly, AA-HMARL reduces the mean E2E completion latency and the mean number of retransmission rounds among successfully delivered updates by 17.8-25.5% and 57.6-61.5%, respectively, and reduces the mean age of information (AoI) by 12.7-14.6% relative to fixed-band MAPPO across two traffic types.
Systems and Control.comment: This work has been submitted to the IEEE for possible publication. 13 pages, 9 figures

Systems and Control.title: Planar Formation Control with Minimal Sensing and No Common Orientation: An Almost-Global Result
Systems and Control.summary: Formation control based on geometric constraints often requires either rigid interaction graphs or a common orientation reference. This paper investigates whether a prescribed planar formation can instead be achieved using only $N-1$ pairwise interactions while preserving global rotational freedom. To this end, a guiding-vector-field-inspired framework is developed in which each selected distance relation is represented by a parameterized circular manifold and the remaining geometric freedom is coordinated through relative virtual phases, based on which, a distributed controller is then constructed. The closed-loop system is shown to possess only the desired equilibrium set and a degenerate undesired equilibrium set corresponding to collapse of the central edge. The latter is proved to form a saddle-type equilibrium manifold with a measure-zero stable set, yielding almost-global convergence to the desired formation. In addition, the controller admits an implementation under mutually misaligned local frames using locally expressed relative measurements and scalar phase information.

Systems and Control.title: Unlocking Heterogeneous Accelerator Flexibility in AI Data Centers: Sizing and Workload Allocation
Systems and Control.summary: AI data centers are an emerging electricity demand, but limited local grid capacity could delay their connection and expansion. While existing operational strategies consider spatio-temporal workload flexibility, few studies address the strategic sizing and allocation of diverse accelerator archetypes with different capital and energy-efficiency trade-offs. This paper unlocks the flexibility potential of heterogeneous accelerators by jointly sizing and allocating different AI workloads (training, delay-tolerant batch work, and online inference requests) across sites and hours to meet the time-varying grid constraint at minimum cost. Workload-specific throughput and energy coefficients link these decisions to facility power. In a representative two-site case, heterogeneous sizing reduces daily cost by 6.5% relative to spatio-temporal scheduling with fixed capacity. When evaluated using workload-specific performance, a capacity design based on workload-averaged hardware coefficients costs 7.7% more than the proposed design. The proposed design also eliminates the envelope violations of an unconstrained design at a 0.25\% daily cost increase. These results show how hardware heterogeneity and workload flexibility jointly shape economical, grid-compliant capacity plans.

Systems and Control.title: Incentive-Based Regulatory Mechanism for Tariff Design in District Heating and Cooling Networks
Systems and Control.summary: Low-temperature district heating and cooling networks exchange heat bidirectionally at near-ambient temperatures. When one supplier owns the shared loop, it controls both the tariff and the network temperature that sets every user's conversion efficiency. Existing price-cap and cost-based rules leave this non-price instrument unregulated and reach neither the first-best dispatch nor an explicit division of gains. This paper proposes a two-part, incentive-based tariff that anchors the supplier's lump-sum fee, per building and hour, to an audited outside alternative and divides the participation gains through one regulated share. We model a mixed-integer bilevel Stackelberg game in which the supplier sets hourly tariffs and the temperature regime, anticipating the buildings' co-optimization of electricity and thermal exchange. We prove that the mechanism attains the first-best welfare, posts the shadow price of the efficient dispatch as its tariff, keeps every building at or above its outside option every hour, and keeps the supplier solvent whenever operation adds surplus. A Belgian case study confirms these properties. The mechanism reproduces the centralized welfare whenever operation is worthwhile, declines to operate otherwise, holds the loop at its first-best temperature, and outperforms cap-based regulation and Ramsey pricing in welfare, user protection, and cost recovery.

Systems and Control.title: Uncertainty-Aware Hybrid Offline Reinforcement Learning with Online Action Selection Enabled by Sparse Gaussian-Process Critics
Systems and Control.summary: Start-ups and grade changes remain largely operator-driven, while developing and maintaining dynamic models for model-based control requires substantial engineering effort. Hybrid Offline Learning and Online Optimisation (HOFLON) uses one-step offline reinforcement learning to select actions from historical transition data. In its original implementation, the online objective combines the predicted return from a tree-ensemble critic with an adversarial-autoencoder (AAE) penalty for unfamiliar state-action pairs. We examine the effect of this penalty and replace the critic and AAE with a sparse variational Gaussian-process (sGP) critic. Actions maximise $μ- κσ$, an uncertainty-adjusted estimate of the return from one action followed by the historical operating practice. On the HOFLON polymerisation-reactor benchmark, removing the AAE from HOFLON led to 4 failed start-ups in 15 runs over five critics. At its published weight, the variation in the AAE penalty is four orders of magnitude smaller than the variation in the tree-ensemble critic. Nevertheless, it changes actions when the predicted returns of competing candidates are nearly equal, and paired runs with and without the penalty diverged from the first move. With a Matérn-5/2 sGP critic, $κ= 0$ led to failure in 13 of 15 runs, whereas with $κ= 3$ none of 15 runs (five critics, three noise realisations) failed. The median and lowest returns were 13,464 and 13,398 (HOFLON: 13,393 and 12,411). A squared-exponential sGP critic with learned inducing inputs needed $κ\geq 3$ to remain within the empirical data support in steady state, and then settled with a temperature offset of 2.0 K.
Systems and Control.comment: 8 pages, 5 figures, 1 table. Submitted to the 2027 European Control Conference (ECC 2027)

Systems and Control.title: Where Delay Compensation Belongs in a Decentralized Mean-Field-Game Swarm with a Control-Barrier Safety Filter
Systems and Control.summary: Large robot teams are often run as a plan-then-execute stack. We study a decentralized instance for drone swarms, a mean-field-game (MFG) routing field with a per-agent control-barrier-function (CBF) safety filter, when communication is limited by a shared TDMA channel. Neighbors are known only through noisy range and bearing measurements exchanged in round-robin slots, so the frame, and with it the age of every estimate, grows with swarm size. In simulation this delay reaches both layers but breaks only the safety layer. Without delay, swarms of up to 100 agents do not collide, even with each measurement's noise held for a whole frame; with it, stale estimates at the CBF cause collisions beyond a frame period of 125 to 175 ms, or 75 to 100 ms at 100 agents with held noise, and swarm size sets where that limit lies and how steeply collisions rise. At the MFG, staleness makes the local density noisier without biasing it, and throughput drops by at most a tenth. We then compensate with lightweight on-board predictors, from constant-velocity fits to a small learned network, that estimate each neighbor's position from its last broadcasts. A layer-split experiment shows where prediction is needed: at the CBF it restores safety and extends the tolerated frame period by 1.4 to 1.7 times with an untrained constant-velocity fit and about 2.3 with the learned network when the noise is redrawn each step; with noise held for a frame the two extend it about equally, while at the MFG it only refines the congestion correction. A constant wider safety margin, the simplest alternative, makes collisions more frequent in a bottleneck. With the routing solved offline, that layer is robust to the delay because it sees neighbors only through a crowd average; compensation belongs in the safety filter, switched on only above the uncompensated limit, since below it the predictor's own error adds collisions.
Systems and Control.comment: 9 pages, 3 figures, 2 tables. Submitted to the 8th International Workshop on Multi-Agent Path Finding (WoMAPF) at AAAI-27 (non-archival workshop)

Systems and Control.title: Efficient Natural Language to Temporal Logic Translation for Real-Time Physical AI
Systems and Control.summary: Robots can be controlled to perform tasks with guaranteed correctness when the task instructions are stated in a formal language. Large language models (LLMs) have been widely used to allow users to provide such instructions in natural language (NL), by translating NL into formal language. When deploying such translators on a robot, however, we face limited computing and energy resources, while offloading computation or data to the cloud may be infeasible or undesirable. Yet an LLM is a general-purpose text generator, whereas a formula in a fixed formal language fragment follows a well-defined syntax. We therefore ask whether text generation is needed at all. For the formal language of linear temporal logic (LTL), we show that this translation can instead be broken down into answering a set of questions with pre-defined answers. We then construct a System-One model, a recent class of NL-based classifier, to provide such answers and enable us to translate a natural language instruction into an LTL instruction. On three benchmarks, our translator matches or exceeds the accuracy of the best local LLMs available, at up to one order of magnitude lower runtime and energy consumption. We show that it generalizes to unseen atomic propositions and temporal patterns.
Systems and Control.comment: 24 pages, 5 figures

Systems and Control.title: Incentive-based Fleet Rebalancing in Vehicle-Sharing Systems via Equilibrium-Constrained Optimal Control
Systems and Control.summary: We propose an incentive-based fleet rebalancing scheme for vehicle-sharing systems that uses fare discounts to steer users toward alternative pick-up locations. The discounts solve an optimal control problem that trades off users leaving the service against incentive costs over a day of operation. Users' responses to incentives are modeled as a Nash equilibrium of logit models coupled through shared vehicle-availability constraints, which makes the control problem a mathematical program with nested equilibrium constraints. We develop a first-order algorithm that backpropagates through the equilibria via nonsmooth implicit differentiation and enjoys convergence guarantees. In a case study that uses Helsinki bike-sharing data, our scheme reduces the number of leaving users by up to 99% relative to no incentives, and outperforms heuristic policies while using up to 52% less incentive.
Systems and Control.comment: 10 pages, 4 figures. Extended version of a paper submitted to the 2027 European Control Conference (ECC 2027). Code and data: https://github.com/tihanyidani/vehicle-sharing

Systems and Control.title: Binary Decision Process in Pre-Evacuation Behavior
Systems and Control.summary: In crowd evacuation the time interval before decisive movement towards a safe place is defined as the pre-evacuation phase, and it has crucial impact on the total time required for safe egress. This process mainly refers to situation awareness and response to an external stressors, e.g., fire alarms. Due to the complexity of human cognitive process, simulation is used to study this important time interval. In this paper a binary decision process is formulated to simulate pre-evacuation time of many evacuees in a given social context. The model combines the classic opinion dynamics (the French-DeGroot model) with binary phase transition to describe how group pre-evacuation time emerges from individual interaction. The model parameters are quantitatively meaningful to human factors research within socio-psychological background, e.g., whether an individual is stubborn or open-minded, or what kind of the social topology exists among the individuals and how it matters in aggregating individuals into social groups. The modeling framework also describes collective motion of many evacuee agents in a planar space, and the resulting multi-agent system is partly similar to the Vicsek flocking model, and it is meaningful to explore complex social behavior during phase transition of a non-equilibrium process.
Systems and Control.comment: 7 pages

Systems and Control.title: Readiness Barrier Functions: Forward-Invariant Control Authority for Overactuated Multirotor Allocation
Systems and Control.summary: Allocators that greedily maximize a readiness metric over the actuator fiber bundle of an overactuated multirotor jump between disconnected optimal strata, demanding actuator rates no motor can deliver; effort-minimizing allocators are continuous but cannot keep wrench-rate authority above any certified level. We reconcile the two by treating authority as a forward-invariant quantity: a control barrier function on the log-determinant of the drag-aware authority co-metric, enforced at torque level by a quadratic program in the allocation null space. A single design inequality makes the certified set compact and strictly interior to the actuator box; the readiness cost of a rotor deactivation is $\ln(n/(n{-}m))$ for symmetric designs. An alignment ratio states when tracking stays exact, otherwise the wrench error is $\mathcal{O}(ρ^{-1/2})$, and a robust variant handles motor-parameter uncertainty with a closed-form floor shift independent of the airframe matrix. On a hexarotor and a fully-actuated octorotor the closed-form gap matches simulation to machine precision. Over $300$ randomized missions, greedy maximization violates the certified floor in up to $51\%$ of authority-scarce missions, while the proposed filter never leaves the certified set and, in the hardest moment reversal, commits a $79\times$ smaller wrench error. The robust variant holds the floor on all $150$ perturbed plants. A high-fidelity simulation with measured propeller and motor data shows where the floor holds under unmodeled aerodynamics, electrical limits, and delay, and where it stops applying.
Systems and Control.comment: Accepted for publication in IEEE Robotics and Automation Letters

Systems and Control.title: Beyond Scalar Inertia: Frequency-Response-Based Assessment of Finite-Duration Inertial Support in Grid-Forming Converters
Systems and Control.summary: Conventional scalar inertia characterizes only the low-frequency terminal behavior of grid-forming converters (GFMs) and cannot fully predict inertial energy delivery during short-duration frequency disturbances. This letter proposes a frequency-response-based method to assess finite-duration inertial support using complex terminal power--frequency responses, such as those provided by Network Frequency Perturbation (NFP) plots. For GFMs with nonzero steady-state droop, a duration-dependent energy-equivalent inertia is defined after subtracting the ideal static-droop contribution. An exact spectral relationship is established, expressing this metric as a duration-weighted integral of frequency-dependent inertia, without requiring knowledge of the internal controller structure and parameters. The duration dependence of the metric is further shown to encode observable oscillation frequencies and damping ratios. A coefficient-decoupling GFM control with identical scalar inertia and droop across different settings is used for verification.
Systems and Control.comment: This paper has 8 pages with 8 figures

Systems and Control.title: Learned Network Dynamics for Model Predictive Traffic Signal Control under Incidents
Systems and Control.summary: Model predictive control (MPC) of urban traffic signals relies on a model of how queues respond to signal decisions, which is hard to specify and calibrate in heterogeneous networks, particularly when incidents change capacities and turning shares. Measurements add a second limitation: the controlled lanes at the stop line are often short, so queues extending upstream of them fall outside lane-level measurements. We propose GNN-MPC, a receding-horizon controller that plans with action-conditioned network dynamics learned by graph neural networks. Phase sequences are coordinated across intersections by approximate best responses, with an acceptance test that keeps the predicted cost no higher than that of the initial plan. In microscopic simulation under non-recurrent incidents, GNN-MPC reduces travel time and increases completed trips relative to all tested controllers, on a homogeneous grid and a heterogeneous 21-intersection network. Controlled comparisons on the heterogeneous network distinguish the roles of observation and prediction. With nearly as many vehicles entering the network, GNN-MPC reduces travel time by 13% relative to MaxPressure with the same upstream measurement, and GNN-MPC without the upstream representation does not reproduce its performance. Under the same traffic measurements, planner and objective, replacing the learned dynamics with calibrated store-and-forward predictors increases travel time by 31-34%. Observing hidden demand and predicting its response to control are thus complementary requirements of network-level predictive control.
Systems and Control.comment: 13 pages main manuscript, 26 pages supplementary material (39 pages total)

Systems and Control.title: Linear Quadratic Control With Event-Based Control Actions: Performance Beyond Periodic Control
Systems and Control.summary: This paper investigates linear quadratic (LQ) control for discrete-time stochastic systems to balance control performance and actuation rate. In our framework, the control input is sparse in time, and the actuation timings are determined in an event-based manner. We examine two types of problems: A sparsity-promoting regularization problem and a hard-constraint problem with a prescribed average actuation rate. Due to the combinatorial nature of these problems, finding optimal solutions is generally hard. Inspired by rollout algorithms in the context of dynamic programming, we develop a rollout-based approach to obtain tractable suboptimal policies. We show closed-loop stability and establish theoretical performance guarantees with respect to classical periodic control. Moreover, under additional conditions, we quantify the performance improvement over periodic control and prove that this improvement is strictly positive. A numerical example demonstrates the effectiveness of the proposed method in balancing control performance and actuation rate.
Systems and Control.comment: 16 pages. Submitted to IEEE Transactions on Automatic Control

Systems and Control.title: Active Learning of Flows from Curve Observations using Gaussian Processes
Systems and Control.summary: The active learning of real control systems requires informative roll-outs of controls. In this paper, we present a local optimization algorithm that finds the trajectory that most reduces uncertainty about the flow of a control system modeled by a Gaussian process. Therefore, we derive an approximation scheme for the posterior kernel of the Gaussian process after observing it on an entire continuous-time trajectory and establish a Pontryagin-type necessary condition for the optimizer. As the flow is unknown, the actual trajectory can deviate from the planned trajectory. We propose a trajectory planner that searches for the most informative control within a maximal allowed deviation horizon instead of a fixed time horizon. We show by trajectory-wise time rescaling that the underlying optimal control problem is equivalent to a fixed end time optimal control problem. Finally, we study both the fixed end time planner and the fixed maximum deviation planner in a numerical example and compare them with benchmarks.

Systems and Control.title: Network Traffic Dynamics in Urban Low-Altitude Air Transport with Projected-Space Macroscopic Fundamental Diagrams
Systems and Control.summary: The growth of Low-Altitude Air Transport (LAAT) systems calls for effective macroscopic modeling tools to manage dense drone traffic. The Macroscopic Fundamental Diagram (MFD) offers a promising framework for this purpose, but its conventional formulations do not directly account for the three-dimensional interactions and path deviations that characterize drone operations. To address this challenge, we introduce a projected-space framework that represents drone motion using projected speed and shortest origin-destination (OD) distances, eliminating the dependence on realized trip lengths that are unknown at trip generation. Under suitable assumptions, we prove the steady-state exactness of the projected-space accumulation-based model and establish deterministic finite-window error bounds for the trip-based estimator. The projected-space accumulation-based formulation is further extended to heterogeneous multi-class systems to accommodate different drone characteristics and operational priorities. Microscopic simulations validate the projected-space formulations under stationary and transient traffic conditions, including hysteresis. Moreover, simulations involving heterogeneous priority classes demonstrate that mixed-priority operations can improve network outflow under the investigated scenarios. These findings establish a theoretical foundation for projected-space macroscopic modeling of LAAT systems and support its application to real-time traffic estimation and future airspace management and control.

Systems and Control.title: On the Existence of Koopman Linear Embeddings for Controlled Nonlinear Systems
Systems and Control.summary: Koopman linear representations have become a popular tool for control design of nonlinear systems, yet it remains unclear when such representations are exact. In this paper, we establish sufficient and necessary conditions under which a controlled nonlinear system admits an exact Koopman linear representation in both infinite-dimensional and finite-dimensional settings. We show that such a system must be transformable into a special control-affine preserved (CAP) structure, which enforces affine dependence of the state on the control input and isolates all nonlinearities into an autonomous subsystem. We further prove that a finite-dimensional representation additionally requires this autonomous subsystem must itself admit a finite-dimensional Koopman linear model with a sufficiently-rich Koopman invariant subspace. Finally, we introduce a symbolic procedure to determine whether a given controlled nonlinear system admits the CAP structure, thereby elucidating whether Koopman approximation errors arise from intrinsic system dynamics or from the choice of lifting functions.

Systems and Control.title: Strong Functional Observability and Strong Functional Detectability: Applications to Functional Observer Design for Systems with Unknown Inputs
Systems and Control.summary: This paper investigates strong functional observability, strong functional detectability, and strong$^*$ functional detectability for continuous-time linear systems with unknown inputs in both the state and measurement equations. Extending Kratz's finite algebraic approach \cite{26}, zero-output trajectories are characterized through the projected kernel of a finite matrix, without differentiating the unknown inputs. This characterization yields a necessary and sufficient rank condition for strong functional observability. For strong functional detectability, a frequency-dependent rank criterion involving only the original system matrices is derived, along with an equivalent finite test based on reduced zero-output dynamics. Strong$^*$ functional detectability is then characterized by an additional algebraic rank condition, and its relationship with the existence of stable functional observers is examined. A constructive observer design procedure based on constrained Sylvester equations is also developed. Particular cases and a numerical process example illustrate the theoretical results.

Systems and Control.title: Error-Corrected Physics-Informed Neural Operator for Optimal Control of Unmanned Aerial Vehicles under Uncertainty
Systems and Control.summary: We solve open-loop optimal control problems under parametric uncertainty using a physics-informed DeepONet that returns trajectories for all sampled scenarios in one evaluation. Trained only on the residual at generic controls, the operator is reused across targets and horizons. Because a gradient-based optimizer exploits surrogate errors, we correct the prediction by one Newton step on the dynamics, computed for all scenarios and times by one parallel scan. The corrected state has a second-order error bounded by the residual alone, and the corrected cost is honest for every control up to the sampling error. On a fixed-wing UAV benchmark, the corrected operator matches the accuracy of a batched Adam solver and an Ipopt solver at equal sample size and is 8 times faster than the Adam solver on the same GPU at a few hundred scenarios and 15 times faster than Ipopt on a CPU.
Systems and Control.comment: 26 pages including appendices, 2 figures, 10 tables

Systems and Control.title: Recursive Bayesian Monitoring of SLAM Failures for LiDAR-Based UAV Navigation
Systems and Control.summary: SLAM failures remain difficult to avoid in autonomous robotic systems, and undetected failures can propagate to unsafe planning, control, and mission-level decisions. Existing monitoring strategies often depend on prior maps, estimator-internal variables, or redundant sensing, which limits their applicability to deployed and resource-constrained robots. This paper presents a scene-geometry consistency monitor for detecting geometry-manifested SLAM failures using only the geometric output of the SLAM backend. The targeted failures include cumulative drift-induced failures, abrupt misregistration failures, and backend map corruption when they become observable as inconsistency in reconstructed scene geometry. The proposed method represents revisited local regions with recursive latent voxel geometry and evaluates each current observation against a trusted continuation explanation and a weak non-propagated reference explanation. The resulting voxel-wise evidence contrasts are aggregated into a fixed-boundary monitoring signal for online failure declaration and downstream safety response. Experiments on self-collected sequences, GEODE benchmark sequences, multiple robotic platforms, and different SLAM backends show that the monitor responds to failures when they are manifested in backend scene geometry. It achieves 4/4 valid post-onset declarations with no pre-onset alarms on four self-collected sequences, detects geometry-manifested failures in all five corrupted GEODE runs while remaining alarm-free in five geometrically consistent runs, adds only 0.1--0.2\% absolute CPU load, and supports a closed-loop UAV detect--isolate--recover workflow.

Systems and Control.title: Which Data-Center Load Models Can Be Trusted? An Evidence-Graded Review of Dynamic Modeling and Validation for Large Computational Loads
Systems and Control.summary: Grid operators now require dynamic models of data centers and other large computational loads, and new ride-through rules assume that these models predict how facilities respond to disturbances. This review asks what evidence supports that assumption. We coded 160 documents, screened from 1,424 de-duplicated database and seed records plus 65 added documents, by the strongest reference object each presents, from grid-side records to simulation only. Across 19 field-evidence entries, 15 requirement documents from three continents and nine model classes, we find two comparisons of a standard library model with measured data-center events: with default parameters the model failed both, and refitting it to each event separately reduced the error but was never tested on an unseen event. Among the sources reviewed, we found no successful held-out validation of a frozen, facility-specific data-center model against an independent measured disturbance, and 25 of the 33 model-phenomenon combinations with any evidence involve no electrical measurement. The features that distinguish the new rules (memory of repeated dips, recovery within 0.5-3 s, proportional power reduction during the sag, overvoltage response) are those current phasor models cannot represent or have never been tested against. In the operator procedures examined, simulations and model-to-model benchmarks are accepted as evidence of model fidelity, unlike the measured validation required of generators, and proposed mitigations have mostly been evaluated on unvalidated facility models. We propose context-of-use gates that separate calibration from validation, release labels for model claims, a minimum validation protocol with acceptance criteria, and a research agenda.
Systems and Control.comment: 21 pages, 10 figures, 10 tables. Companion dataset included as ancillary files

Systems and Control.title: Adaptive Collective Decision-Making in Signed Networks
Systems and Control.summary: Collective decision-making often unfolds in networks where cooperation and antagonism coexist. Such signed interactions arise in social, biological, and robotic systems, and can lead to qualitatively different collective outcomes: consensus, polarization, or clustering. Existing signed network models typically explain these outcomes separately, leaving open how they can emerge within a single dynamical framework. Here, we introduce a generalized Laplacian flow for bi-partitioned signed networks, a class of networks that allows cooperative and antagonistic interactions both within and across two prescribed groups. The proposed model includes an adaptive social effort state, interpreted as a leaky memory of persistent signed network disagreement, which enables bounded and nontrivial steady-states beyond classical signed Laplacian flows. We derive conditions that determine whether the network reaches consensus, polarization, or clustering based on the spectral structure of the generalized Laplacian and effective resistance matrices. The framework applies beyond structurally balanced, weakly balanced, and quasi-structurally balanced networks, and reveals how changes in signed interaction strengths can shift a network between collective decision regimes. We validate the theory on stochastic block model networks, a judicial voting network, and a U.S. senate bill co-sponsorship network. Altogether, our results provide a structural and dynamical account of how mixed cooperative and antagonistic relationships shape emergent collective behaviors.

Systems and Control.title: Performance guarantees for optimization-based state estimation using turnpike properties
Systems and Control.summary: In this paper, we develop novel accuracy and performance guarantees for optimal state estimation of general nonlinear systems (in particular, moving horizon estimation, MHE). Our results rely on a turnpike property of the optimal state estimation problem, which essentially states that the omniscient infinite-horizon solution involving all past and future data serves as turnpike for the solutions of finite-horizon estimation problems involving a subset of the data. This leads to the surprising observation that MHE problems naturally exhibit a leaving arc, which may have a strong negative impact on the estimation accuracy. To address this, we propose a delayed MHE scheme, and we show that the resulting performance (both averaged and non-averaged) is approximately optimal and achieves bounded regret with respect to the infinite-horizon solution, with error terms that can be made arbitrarily small by an appropriate choice of the delay. In various simulation examples, we observe that already a very small delay in the MHE scheme is sufficient to significantly improve the overall estimation error by 20-25% compared to standard MHE (without delay). This finding is of great importance for practical applications (especially for monitoring, fault detection, and parameter estimation) where a small delay in the estimation is rather irrelevant but may significantly improve the estimation results.
Systems and Control.comment: replaced with accepted version

Systems and Control.title: Geometry-Preserving Neural Architectures on Manifolds with Boundary
Systems and Control.summary: A growing number of neural architectures have been developed to enforce geometric constraints, including projection-based networks, exponential-map updates, and manifold neural ODEs. In this paper, we study several such architectures, with the goal of understanding their approximation-theoretic properties and trade-offs. We distinguish between architectures that enforce constraints at intermediate layers and those that enforce constraints only at the output. For projected neural ODEs on uniformly prox-regular sets, we establish stability estimates and derive universal approximation results on compact smooth manifolds, including manifolds with boundary. In particular, we establish universal approximation of measurable manifold-valued maps in the $L^2$ topology.
