By delivering finely controlled electrical stimulation through 15 electrodes, it can evoke a wide range of tactile sensations that cover diverse interaction scenarios.
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: 10 pages, 8 figures

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Shaping AI Explanations to Expert Perspectives for Scientific Discovery
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: AI explanations for scientific discovery are typically optimized around a single notion of explanation quality. Experts, however, differ in how they assess evidence, prioritize mechanisms, and judge relevance, meaning that a general-purpose explanation may not provide the evidence an expert finds most informative or convincing. We show that these differences exhibit structured epistemic perspectives and ask whether explanations conditioned on these perspectives are preferred by experts. To study this, we introduce a reinforcement learning-based framework for generating \textit{perspective-conditioned explanations}, which is guided by the judgments of LLM-based personas derived from expert evaluations. We instantiate the framework over scientific knowledge graphs and evaluate it in drug discovery through drug repurposing and drug--target interaction prediction. Expert studies show that perspective-conditioned explanations capture characteristic patterns of judgment, are preferred over general-purpose explanations, and receive higher relevance and validity ratings without sacrificing predictive performance. These findings establish explanation quality as perspective-dependent and enable scalable, perspective-aligned explanations for scientific discovery.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Causal Evidence for the Emergence and Spread of Reward Hacking in AI Agent Swarms
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Autonomous AI agents that coordinate and collaborate among each other have become pervasive across domains ranging from scientific research to finance and engineering. The opportunity to share messages and build upon each other's work also creates the potential for misaligned behaviors to spread across AI agents. We provide causal evidence that mere exposure to reward hacking, cheating on a task to pass an automated check, is enough to spread the behavior among AI agents, even after the cheat has been rejected. We conducted 17 preregistered experiments with six frontier models (n = 20,111 agents). First, we show that cheating emerges spontaneously. When agents were told that work passing the visible tests is accepted, 33% cheated in the first round, when the shared record of teammates' submissions was empty. Second, we show that agents who rarely cheat when working alone cheat most of the time after seeing a teammate's cheat, as 94% of teammates who saw an accepted cheat cheated. Third, we show that rejection of reward-hacked solutions offers little protection, using experiments that changed only the label on the cheat. Most agents copied a cheat labeled rejected, 34% of agents cheated after an AI reviewer had rejected the cheat, and nearly every agent copied a cheat labeled accepted. Fourth, we show that cheating generalizes to new tasks. On a new problem with an empty collaboration record, 70% of agents who had earlier seen an accepted cheat cheated again, compared with 32% of agents who had seen an empty record. Fifth, we show that cheating spreads from neighbor to neighbor through networks of 256 agents. In the networks, 44% of agents with a cheating neighbor cheated, compared with 2% of other agents. Together, the results suggest that mere exposure can spread misaligned behavior among AI agents, and that catching a cheat is insufficient once other agents have seen the cheat.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Transfer Learning of Keystroke Dynamics for Cross-Device User Authentication
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Keystroke dynamics (typing patterns) can be used as a behavioural biometric modality for user authentication, with applications such as fraud prevention. While the modality has been shown to work well for single device authentication, its application to cross-device scenarios is more challenging. Dynamics learned on one device (e.g., phone) may not be directly applicable to authentication on a secondary device with a different form factor (e.g., tablet) due to changes in typing patterns that can lead to distribution drifts. To address this, we propose a cross-device user authentication system based on inductive transfer learning, where keystroke dynamics learned on one device are adapted to a secondary device. The adapted data is then combined with necessarily limited training data for the secondary device, which is used to robustly train a binary classifier. Furthermore, an extended set of keystroke features is used to better capture discriminative dynamics. Experiments on the BBMAS dataset show that proposed system achieves an equal error rate of 14.2% for the cross-device scenario, surpassing previous methods.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: GlyphWeaver: Unlocking Glyph Design Creativity with Uniform Glyph DSL and AI
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Expressive glyph visualizations provide a powerful and versatile means to represent complex multivariate data through compact visual encodings, but creating custom glyphs remains challenging due to the gap between design creativity and technical implementation. We present GlyphWeaver, a novel interactive system to enable an easy creation of expressive glyph visualizations. Our system comprises three key components: a glyph domain-specific language (GDSL), a GDSL operation management mechanism, and a multimodal interaction interface. The GDSL is a hierarchical container model, where each container is independent and composable, providing a rigorous yet practical foundation for complex glyph visualizations. The operation management mechanism restricts modifications of the GDSL to atomic operations, making it accessible without requiring direct coding. The multimodal interaction interface enables direct manipulation, natural language commands, and parameter adjustments. A multimodal large language model acts as a translator, converting these inputs into GDSL operations. GlyphWeaver significantly lowers the barrier for designers, who often do not have extensive programming skills, to create sophisticated glyph visualizations.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: MindBridge: A Multilingual and Multimodal Tool for Interactive Cognitive Monitoring
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: We present MindBridge, a clinician-informed, multilingual, multimodal cognitive monitoring tool combining participant-controlled interviews with explainable reports. Reports link lexical diversity and pause patterns to speech or text evidence and disclose data quality and missingness. In a formative study of typed interaction with 10 adults (seven aged 18-59; three aged 60 or older), follow-ups prompted elaboration but sometimes introduced assumptions requiring correction. Nine participants ranked interpretation-first reports highest; all identified score-only reports as most likely to encourage fixation and overreaction. On a fixed DementiaBank manifest, the best configuration achieved 70.3% zero-shot accuracy on valid predictions versus a 56.0% majority-class baseline on the full manifest. Some configurations predicted only one category; tests with generated samples revealed different error patterns across input types and languages. MindBridge makes evidence collection, analysis, and interpretation inspectable, linking participant control to the scope and limits of monitoring results.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: How AI Impacts Skill Formation
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: AI assistance produces significant productivity gains across professional domains, particularly for novice workers. Yet how this assistance affects the development of skills required to effectively supervise AI remains unclear. Novice workers who rely heavily on AI to complete unfamiliar tasks may compromise their own skill acquisition in the process. We conduct randomized experiments to study how developers gained mastery of a new asynchronous programming library with and without the assistance of AI. We find that AI use impairs conceptual understanding, code reading, and debugging abilities, without delivering significant efficiency gains on average. Participants who fully delegated coding tasks showed some productivity improvements, but at the cost of learning the library. We identify six distinct AI interaction patterns, three of which involve cognitive engagement and preserve learning outcomes even when participants receive AI assistance. Our findings suggest that AI-enhanced productivity is not a shortcut to competence and AI assistance should be carefully adopted into workflows to preserve skill formation -- particularly in safety-critical domains.
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: V3: Corrected numerical issues

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Rapid Exploratory Maps and their potential role in supporting evidence-to-policy dialogues and processes
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Producing useful evidence syntheses requires clearly formulated research questions linked to an understanding of their optimal scope. When policymakers (or other end users) commission or steer the production of systematic reviews or other evidence syntheses to fulfil a demand for evidence, these parameters are rarely specified sufficiently for production to proceed. Instead, these details are typically developed via a collaborative dialogic process involving evidence producers and users to ensure the resulting synthesis will meet users' needs. This process is informed by scoping and (more-or-less formally) mapping the existing evidence base, which can take many weeks or months, slowed by applying mostly manual processes to identify and characterise the evidence. Recent developments in artificial intelligence (AI) technologies have opened up new opportunities for more rapid, iterative, and responsive mapping of relevant evidence to support such early-stage evidence-to-policy dialogues and processes. In this article, we outline and characterise this emerging approach, termed Rapid Exploratory Maps (REMs). We also present two illustrative case studies drawn from first-hand experiences within a programme of evidence reviews production to inform government policy in England. While this approach could be transformative for the mapping process, its broader potential is as yet largely unassessed, and it confers important challenges and likely risks, as well as benefits. Determining whether REMs could usefully support more efficient ways of working with end users when developing and designing evidence syntheses will require continued development and careful evaluation.
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: 16 pages

Human-Computer Interaction.title: "The explanation makes sense": An Empirical Study on LLM Performance in News Classification and its Influence on Judgment in Human-AI Collaborative Annotation
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: The spread of media bias is a significant concern as political discourse shapes beliefs and opinions. Political news bias classification is inherently subjective, depending on reader interpretation of tone, framing, and language. While Large language models (LLMs) can assist at scale, their influence on human judgment remains poorly understood. To advance understanding of how AI-generated explanations influence subjective judgment, we investigate how LLMs classify U.S. news by political ideology and examine how their explanations shape human decision-making. We first compared GPT models with prompt engineering to state-of-the-art supervised machine learning on a 34k public dataset. We then collected 17k news articles and tested GPT-4 predictions with Brief and Detailed explanations. In a between-subjects study (N=124), we examined how LLM-generated explanations influence human judgment and confidence. Results show that AI assistance significantly increases confidence ($p<.001$), regardless of whether GPT predictions are reliable. Detailed explanations were associated with about three times higher odds of decision switching than Brief explanations, suggesting that explanations may support interpretive reasoning while also increasing confidence and agreement with AI, even when they diverge from publisher-level labels. Through thematic analysis, we identify the benefits and risks of AI explanations in subjective decision contexts, offer recommendations for responsible AI design, and release our dataset to support future research.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Latent Channel Completion for Forecasting in Sensor Networks with Failed Detectors
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Monitoring networks for traffic and utility infrastructure lose sensors routinely, and forecasting models that couple sensors together to gain accuracy also inherit an exposure to those losses. When a detector stops reporting, the substituted value is embedded as though it were a reading and propagates through the shared representation that couples the network, degrading forecasts for sensors that are still healthy. Because these models are selected on benchmarks where every sensor reports, the exposure is absent from the numbers used to choose them. We introduce Latent Channel Completion, a channel-axis joint embedding predictive objective that reconstructs missing sensors' latent representations rather than their values, since a coupling operator consumes embeddings and never sees raw readings. Channels are masked during training and their representations predicted from surviving channels against stop-gradient targets; at inference the operator fills in whichever sensors the monitoring system reports as dark, using parameters shared with the forecaster. On three highway detector networks, after half of each network goes dark, the accuracy advantage of coupling changes by -1.0, -0.5 and +8.8 percentage points, against losses of 10.2 to 50.3 points for the unmodified forecaster, which on one network falls behind an uncoupled reference entirely. Against cross-channel ridge imputation drawing on the same surviving sensors, completing the latent lowers error by a further 13.9% and 28.6%, and on complete inputs, the method matches its backbone. The benefit tracks how much a network gains from coupling when intact, giving operators a criterion evaluable before any outage occurs.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: The Paradox of Agency-Preserving AI: Negotiating Learner Agency in Layered Human-AI Interactions
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Generative AI is increasingly used by learners in cognitively demanding tasks, but its capacity to provide immediate solutions raises concerns about decreased learner agency. Meta-level AI systems that provide reflective and metacognitive scaffolding have emerged as a promising approach to supporting learners' self-regulation. However, these systems introduce a fundamental paradox: AI intended to preserve learner agency can itself constrain that agency by regulating when, how, and why learners should reflect. To investigate this challenge, we conducted a co-design workshop with 18 students engaged in programming and academic writing tasks using ChatGPT extended with ChatWise, a meta-level AI system providing self-regulated learning-aligned feedback. Drawing on 185 prompt-feedback entries, 174 written reflections, and participants' design artifacts (17 storyboards and 5 group design proposals), we identified four interconnected design tensions: assistance vs reflection, immediate intervention vs space for self-regulation, visibility vs attention competition, and system adaptation vs user control. The study contributes a multidimensional account of learner agency that includes task, cognitive, and interaction agency, along with empirically grounded interaction-design mechanisms to negotiate these tensions.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: COGENT: A Modular Cognitive Architecture for Agentic User Simulation
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: LLM-based user simulation can support interface design, accessibility research, and interactive-agent evaluation, but standard computer-use agents are optimized for task completion rather than reproducing how people perceive, reason, and act. We introduce COGENT (COGnitive agENT), a modular cognitive architecture for simulating user interaction with desktop interfaces. COGENT draws on established cognitive theories, such as Norman's action cycle and ACT-R, to enable explainable, intervenable, and modular user simulation by decomposing the simulation process into cognitive modules with explicit representations of perception, memory, user state, intentions, and action selection. We begin by presenting six intervenability demonstrations, each tracing how a single edit to memory, a user attribute, or a processing module propagates through the cognitive pipeline to produce a behavioral change. We evaluate COGENT's behavioral and attributional fidelity across three benchmarks -- AgentNetBench, A11y-CUA, and SENSE-42 -- finding that it achieves statistically significant fidelity gains over computer-use baselines in reproducing recorded human behavior and recovers the relational structure among human self-reported psychological states. Together, these demos and evaluations demonstrate COGENT's utility toward more faithful, explainable, intervenable, and modular LLM-based cognitive simulations.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Can LLM-Simulated Respondents Pre-Test Survey Questions? Evidence From Preregistered Prospective Validation
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Large language models (LLMs) can be conditioned to simulate behavioral responses, including survey responses, but it remains unclear whether and how these simulations can support downstream research tasks. Here, we evaluate whether simulated respondents can support pre-testing new candidate survey questions before fielding them, operationalized as prioritizing candidate survey items. Specifically, we rank candidate questions by their mean responses, which can reveal ceiling or floor effects; their variance, which indicates whether responses contain meaningful variation; and differences between subpopulations, which indicate whether questions capture distinctions between relevant groups within a population. We introduce a preregistered, prospective evaluation that commits model predictions before target human responses exist, ruling out memorization of those responses by design. Using two waves of a local survey (2025: N = 1,271; 2026: N = 1,161), we built simulated respondents from 2025 participants and preregistered GPT-4.1 predictions for 22 questions introduced in 2026. Simulations accurately ranked questions by mean responses (Spearman \r{ho} = 0.71) and anticipated which questions distinguished city from county residents (\r{ho} = 0.88), Black from White residents (\r{ho} = 0.68), and employed from unemployed residents (\r{ho} = 0.57), suggesting simulations can help prioritize questions before fielding. More broadly, our prospective, preregistered design provides a general framework for evaluating AI simulations without contamination from memorized target outcomes.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: CRAB-H: Task-Centric Certification for Healthcare Autonomous Systems
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: This paper introduces CRAB H as a task-centric certification methodology for healthcare autonomous systems. CRAB H extends the ARC governance architecture by introducing the task as a first-class governance object, represented through Task Requirement Profiles TRP H. Each profile defines the cognitive capabilities, governance constraints, evidentiary requirements, and operational assumptions necessary for the safe execution of a specific healthcare activity. Rather than asking whether a robot achieves a sufficiently high benchmark score, CRAB H asks whether demonstrated capabilities satisfy the requirements of the task. Certification becomes a comparison between demonstrated capability and required capability. A reliability-gated assurance allocation mechanism routes cognitive dimensions that cannot be reproducibly evaluated to LEA operational requirements rather than discarding them. Governance integrity is preserved: unreliable dimensions are governed, not ignored. The Capability Margin is defined as the threshold-based conjunction of per-dimension compliance determinations, not as a subtracted scalar preserving non compensatory governance logic appropriate for safety-critical healthcare deployment

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Symbolic Proof Compression and Fractal Universality: A Conditional Non-Constructive Refutation of the Riemann Hypothesis
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Building on S.~C.~Woon's (1994) fractal and symbolic reformulation of Voronin's Universality Theorem, we construct a formal, non-constructive proof-by-contradiction architecture exploring the Riemann Hypothesis ($\mathsf{RH}$). Woon's Corollary~3 permits arbitrary finite binary strings to be encoded into nowhere-vanishing exponential waveforms on a closed disk inside the critical strip. Combining effective upper bounds for Voronin universality (Good, Garunkštis) with Cauchy-integral Taylor decoding yields an explicit finite rational grid $\mathcal{G}_{L_0}$ below an effective ceiling $H_{\mathrm{crit}}(L_0)$ within which every formal proof of bit-length at most $L_0$ is imprinted with zero flipped digits. We introduce a conjectural \emph{Zeta-Universal Symbolic Proof Compression Hypothesis} ($\mathsf{SPC}_{\mathsf{RH}}$), positing that the global regularity implied by $\mathsf{RH}$ compresses true $Π_1^0$ statements about $ζ(s)$ into $\mathsf{ZFC}$ derivations of bounded length $L_0$. Assuming classical logic and $\mathsf{SPC}_{\mathsf{RH}}$, Gödel--Carnap diagonalization over bounded zeta-encoded provability yields a contradiction. The self-referential result converts a digital encoding framework with any uniform proof-compression principle for RH into an immediate non-constructive refutation of RH. Given that, with human input and computer assistance, $\mathsf{RH}$ has been formally verified in the Lean theorem prover strictly within constructive logic, this contradiction does not refute $\mathsf{RH}$. Instead, it falsifies $\mathsf{SPC}_{\mathsf{RH}}$. We conclude by isolating the exact proof-theoretic obstruction---Pudlák's lower bound on bounded reflection proofs---showing why the analytic regularity of $\mathsf{RH}$ cannot compress logical self-reference, and exposing the limits of applying the Law of Excluded Middle to uncomputably bounded searches.
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: 7 pages

Networking and Internet Architecture.title: AI-Assisted Auto-formalization for Trustworthy Scientific Computing: Case Studies and Lessons Learned
Networking and Internet Architecture.summary: Agentic AI tools have recently had success in mathematical reasoning. Both general purpose coding agents such as Claude Code and Codex, and specialized mathematics agents such as Aristotle, have been used for formalizing mathematical problems such as Fermat's last theorem, Erdős problems and several IMO level math problems. However, much of these efforts are concentrated in the pure mathematics domain, which benefits from relatively self-contained theorem statements, fixed mathematical representation and extensive support in existing formal libraries. Applied mathematics, on the other hand, presents additional challenges because the source may describe a computational procedure or modeling transformation rather than a declarative theorem. In this work, we present a systematic study of AI-assisted auto-formalization for scientific computing (SC), a domain in applied mathematics central to U.S. Department of Energy applications. Through case studies spanning hierarchical abstraction layers in SC software stack, we evaluate not only whether AI agents can complete numerical proofs, but also where and why they fail across the stack. Our primary contribution is a cross-layer taxonomy of failure modes and an analysis of the form of expert feedback required at each layer to recover mathematical soundness. From these observations, we derive a workflow for recurring proof patterns and practical guidance for using AI agents while preserving mathematical soundness. Our results characterize both the practical value and the current limitations of AI-assisted formalization for trustworthy scientific computing.

Networking and Internet Architecture.title: Accurate Products, Inaccurate Inverse: Emulated FP64 BLAS in Blocked Triangular Inversion
Networking and Internet Architecture.summary: FP64 emulation on integer tensor units now ships in cuBLAS and GEMMul8, and each emulated matrix product can be checked against an accuracy grade. We ask if a routine built from such products inherits their accuracy, and show that blocked triangular inversion, the core of LAPACK's inverse of a symmetric positive definite matrix, does not. Under fixed-precision emulation every product passes the grade-B error bound of Demmel et al., yet the inverse errs at 7.1e-2, against 2.0e-15 natively. The matrices are well conditioned after diagonal scaling, but the scaling spans 64 binades. The cause is one product, T = X22 L21, whose summed index carries both the diagonal scaling and its inverse, which a grade-B bound does not absorb. Computing those products natively restores native accuracy; leaving any one of them emulated does not. The pattern holds on four GPUs, and on real covariance matrices the fixed-precision routes lose up to about four orders of accuracy. Equilibration, a solve-based association and cuBLAS's automatic dynamic precision avoid the loss, and an exact error recurrence audits a completed run. On an RTX 4090 the fastest accurate emulated inversion takes 0.40 of cuSOLVER's time. Where each product's scaling falls decides if per-product accuracy carries over to a composite routine, and that is what builders of emulated libraries need to check.
Networking and Internet Architecture.comment: Submitted to ISC High Performance 2027. 16 pages, 4 figures, 12 tables. Review artifact (code and run records) linked in the paper

Networking and Internet Architecture.title: Native Rectangular Linear Assignment with Implicit Rejection: A Jonker-Volgenant Solver without Square Expansion
Networking and Internet Architecture.summary: Rectangular assignment with a uniform unmatched penalty is often implemented by expanding the cost matrix. We integrate established rectangular Jonker-Volgenant principles and implicit rejection with float64 working arithmetic and reusable workspaces in Rust (JVRUST), hybrid Rust/C++ (JVHYBRID) and C++ (JVCPP). A campaign evaluates laprust/lapcpp 1.2.0 and LAPX 0.13.0 in four Windows/Linux and Python environments. Each environment contains 302 cases: 3,286 complete-call timing conditions with five inputs and three rounds, plus 91 memory conditions with five fresh-process trials. Against the matching compact SciPy reference, all three native implementations exceed a 3% advantage on all 102 required cases; JVRUST and JVCPP do so on 163-165 and 163-166 of 166 optional cases, respectively. Controlled comparisons qualify these gains by representation, initialization, sparsity, batching and orientation. We also assess how solver gains carry over to pedestrian and cell tracking using real-world data and prepared detections. In each Windows environment, the specialized LSAPE code wins 38 of 67 cases against the original Hungarian implementation and all 67 against its unchanged one-sided baseline. The contribution is software integration and reproducible performance characterization. Adverse results are retained; no algorithmic priority, statistical significance or universal solver ranking is claimed. The initialization policy was developed using related workload families, so the campaign is not a held-out test of heuristic optimality.
Networking and Internet Architecture.comment: 35 pages, 14 figures, 12 tables. v3 adds a ByoTrack microscopy benchmark on nine video excerpts and a side-by-side comparison of Bougleux and Brun's LSAPE design with the native Jonker-Volgenant solver in Table 1

Networking and Internet Architecture.title: Computing $ab+cd$ and other expressions with correct rounding in binary floating-point arithmetic
Networking and Internet Architecture.summary: We introduce two ``high-level'' algorithms that make it possible to evaluate the sum $(x\_h+x\_\ell) + (y\_h+y\_\ell)$ of two double-word numbers with correct rounding in binary floating-point arithmetic. These algorithms allow one to evaluate expressions of the form $ab+cd$, $a+b+cd$, $a+b+c+d$, and $abc$ with correct rounding, where $a$, $b$, $c$, and $d$ are floating-point numbers.

Networking and Internet Architecture.title: Ziv: A Language for Correctly Rounded Math Libraries
Networking and Internet Architecture.summary:
Developing performant, correctly rounded math libraries is challenging. Such implementations often rely on extended-precision arithmetic for correct rounding and precomputed constants for performance. Existing implementation languages, however, provide limited support for (i) high-level abstractions for such arithmetic and (ii) staged computation to combine precomputation and runtime computation in one program. As a result, existing implementations often miss abstraction opportunities and hard-code constants precomputed using separate programs. These practices make it difficult to write, understand, and modify these libraries.
  We present Ziv, a programming system for developing correctly rounded math libraries. It consists of a small language, a rich standard library, and a provably sound compiler targeting C. Ziv supports (i) high-level numerical abstractions via types and operations for extended-precision numbers, and (ii) staged computation via compile-time evaluation of expressions known to be input-independent. These features enable high-level code that unifies precomputation and runtime computation. We embed Ziv in Julia and evaluate it by reimplementing 19 functions from two state-of-the-art libraries targeting correct rounding; we achieve competitive performance with 2.63$\times$ reductions in lines of code. We also implement three new functions and automatically explore 824,256 variants, achieving 96.5$\times$ average speedup over an arbitrary-precision library.

Networking and Internet Architecture.title: infomeasure-rs: A High-Performance Rust Library for Information-Theoretic Measures and Estimators
Networking and Internet Architecture.summary: Information theory has become a standard tool across the natural and social sciences, yet practical use is limited by estimator choice, fragmented software, reproducibility, and computational cost. We present infomeasure-rs, an open-source Rust library that brings a broad set of information-theoretic measures and estimators into one self-contained, type-safe package. It covers entropy, mutual information, conditional mutual information, transfer entropy, conditional transfer entropy, cross-entropy, and the Kullback-Leibler and Jensen-Shannon divergences, with discrete (plug-in and bias-corrected), kernel, ordinal, and nearest-neighbour estimators, including the Rényi and Tsallis families, and exposes local and global values and significance testing through a consistent trait interface. It ships as a single portable binary with no runtime dependency and is continuously validated against a reference implementation. On a single central processing unit (CPU) core, and even without its GPU or parallel paths, it is the fastest of the packages we compared across languages, matching the closest packages only for plug-in discrete entropy and substantially faster for mutual information, the conditional and transfer measures, and the kernel, ordinal, and generalised-entropy estimators. The optional GPU and multi-threaded paths accelerate selected continuous estimators further. The library is open source and, to our knowledge, the most complete information-theory package for Rust.

Social and Information Networks.title: Matching Under Metric Privacy
Social and Information Networks.summary: We study how to represent and randomize points in $d$-dimensional Euclidean space to obtain accurate bipartite matchings under metric privacy. Given $n$ private and $n$ public points, we analyze local mechanisms that randomize each private point or its distances to the public points. Using the public points' affine span, we construct a smaller representation that preserves all matching costs. When a trusted server receives the private points, we establish privacy and utility guarantees for Gumbel matching, which randomizes edge costs and releases only the assignment. Through upper bounds and worst-case constructions, we establish the tight rate $Θ\!\left(n\min\{d,\log n\}/\varepsilon\right)$ for expected cost above the nonprivate optimum. Benchmark experiments support $d\approx\log n$ as a practical guide to the transition between directly randomizing point coordinates and using Gumbel matching. Extensions to squared Euclidean costs enable private nonparametric two-sample hypothesis testing. These results show how the application's trust model guides representation and dimension choices for better utility: under local privacy, low-dimensional point representations reduce excess cost, while under central privacy, distance representations achieve the optimal rate even in high dimension.

Social and Information Networks.title: LLM-Enhanced Rumor Detection via Virtual Node Induced Edge Prediction
Social and Information Networks.summary: The rapid proliferation of rumors on social networks poses a significant threat to information integrity. While rumor dissemination forms complex structural patterns, existing detection methods often fail to capture the intricate interplay between textual coherence and propagation dynamics. Current approaches typically represent nodes through isolated textual embeddings, neglecting the semantic flow across the entire propagation path. To bridge this gap, we introduce a novel framework that integrates Large Language Models (LLMs) as a structural augmentation layer for graph-based rumor detection. Moving beyond conventional methods, our framework employs LLMs to evaluate information subchains and strategically introduce a virtual node into the graph. This structural modification converts latent semantic patterns into explicit topological features, effectively capturing the textual coherence that has historically been inaccessible to Graph Neural Networks (GNNs). To ensure reliability, we develop a structured prompt framework that mitigates inherent biases in LLMs while maintaining robust graph learning performance. Furthermore, our proposed framework is model-agnostic, meaning it is not constrained to any specific graph learning algorithm or LLMs. Its plug-and-play nature allows for seamless integration with further fine-tuned LLMs and graph techniques in the future, potentially enhancing predictive performance without the need to modify original algorithms.
Social and Information Networks.comment: 15 pages, 4 figures. Updated manuscript with additional experiments, corrected dataset statistics, and revised references

Social and Information Networks.title: Temporal connection probabilities in real networks
Social and Information Networks.summary: Principled prediction of when and where links form in complex networks is a fundamental problem. We derive a closed-form non-Markovian expression for next-step connection probabilities that unifies latent hyperbolic geometry with long-range memory of past interactions. This expression yields interpretable forecasts governed by a small set of parameters. Applied to large-scale real networks, the framework explains how interaction history changes the distance dependence of connectivity: repeated interactions can remain probable at large distances, whereas first-contact probabilities are consistent with a nonmonotonic distance dependence. The framework's predictions agree quantitatively with empirical connection probabilities. These results provide a common probabilistic description of first contacts and repeated interactions, linking the latent geometry of networks to their temporal connectivity.

Social and Information Networks.title: BiLight: A Fast Method for Estimating Counts of 6-Vertex Bipartite Motifs in Large Graphs
Social and Information Networks.summary:
Motifs, or small subgraphs, are fundamental building blocks of complex networks. Analyzing their frequency distribution provides deep insights into the local structure of graphs, with applications in social network analysis, bioinformatics, and web mining. However, exact enumeration of motifs becomes computationally expensive as the size of the motif and the network increases. This challenge is particularly acute for bipartite motifs, which are ubiquitous in modeling relationships like user-item, author-paper, and actor-movie interactions.
  In this work, we present BiLight (Bipartite Lightweight motif estimation), a scalable framework for estimating the frequencies of all 17 non-isomorphic 6-vertex bipartite motifs. Specifically, we focus on estimating the non-induced counts of these motifs, which is a common requirement in many graph mining tasks.
  Our approach relies on a randomized path sampling of paths on four vertices. We use an efficient, weighted strategy by counting the ways that each sampled path can be extended to one of the 17 motifs. This framework yields unbiased estimates of the global motif counts. We conduct extensive experiments on networks of various sizes.
  Our experiments demonstrate that BiLight converges rapidly to the ground truth with high accuracy, even on massive networks where exact counting is infeasible.
  The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/celikmustaa/BiLight.

Social and Information Networks.title: Copy, Predict, Code the Rest: Lossless Graph Compression with Decoder-Side Neighbor Prediction
Social and Information Networks.summary:
We present a lossless compressor for directed graphs. It copies neighbors from an earlier row, predicts further targets from the part of the graph already decoded, and codes what remains. Its main coder, the candidate-bit coder (CB), proposes a bounded set of candidate targets, mixes their probabilities adaptively, and codes the leftover targets with a popularity-aware model. The encoder tries a fixed set of vertex orders and storage directions and keeps the smallest file that decodes exactly.
  On the benchmark graphs outside our development set, the selected files are smaller than the best recorded WebGraph and Zuckerli files and the best published HyperFast results. These savings have a cost. CB decodes much more slowly than the baselines and supports only sequential access. A faster companion coder, CG, is still slower than the baselines on large graphs. An indexed variant, CS-RA, gives smaller seekable files than the measured access baselines on nearly all tested graphs, but its cold queries are slow, and it fails on one development graph. We also explain what successful and failed predictions cost, and when copying a repeated row saves information.
Social and Information Networks.comment: 61 pages, 9 figures, 49 tables. v3: substantially revised and retitled; adds the candidate-bit coder (CB), a frozen comparison against WebGraph, Zuckerli and HyperFast, and indexed variants. Open-source implementation at https://github.com/jimbotonic/Adjacently.jl. Preprint; comments welcome

Social and Information Networks.title: Can LLM-Simulated Respondents Pre-Test Survey Questions? Evidence From Preregistered Prospective Validation
Social and Information Networks.summary: Large language models (LLMs) can be conditioned to simulate behavioral responses, including survey responses, but it remains unclear whether and how these simulations can support downstream research tasks. Here, we evaluate whether simulated respondents can support pre-testing new candidate survey questions before fielding them, operationalized as prioritizing candidate survey items. Specifically, we rank candidate questions by their mean responses, which can reveal ceiling or floor effects; their variance, which indicates whether responses contain meaningful variation; and differences between subpopulations, which indicate whether questions capture distinctions between relevant groups within a population. We introduce a preregistered, prospective evaluation that commits model predictions before target human responses exist, ruling out memorization of those responses by design. Using two waves of a local survey (2025: N = 1,271; 2026: N = 1,161), we built simulated respondents from 2025 participants and preregistered GPT-4.1 predictions for 22 questions introduced in 2026. Simulations accurately ranked questions by mean responses (Spearman \r{ho} = 0.71) and anticipated which questions distinguished city from county residents (\r{ho} = 0.88), Black from White residents (\r{ho} = 0.68), and employed from unemployed residents (\r{ho} = 0.57), suggesting simulations can help prioritize questions before fielding. More broadly, our prospective, preregistered design provides a general framework for evaluating AI simulations without contamination from memorized target outcomes.

Social and Information Networks.title: Differential Privacy for Network Connectedness Indices
Social and Information Networks.summary: Researchers increasingly use data on social and economic networks to study a range of social science questions, but releasing statistics derived from networks can raise significant privacy concerns. We show how to release network connectedness indices that quantify assortative mixing across node attributes under edge-adjacent differential privacy. Directly adding noise to connectedness indices based on global sensitivity can result in poor accuracy both because connectedness indices have high global sensitivity and because a single node's attribute can potentially be an input to connectedness in thousands of cells, leading to poor composition. Our method, which is straightforward to apply, first randomizes node attributes, then analytically debiases downstream statistics, and finally adds noise to protect the presence or absence of individual edges. We prove consistency and asymptotic normality of our estimators for both discrete and continuous labels and show our method works well in simulations and on real networks with as few as 200 nodes collected by social scientists.
Social and Information Networks.comment: Code to replicate all of our analyses is available at: https://github.com/TomRutter42/Privacy-for-Connectedness-Indices

Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.title: Decoupling Faults from Uncertainty: Message-Efficient Byzantine Agreement with Local Predictions
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.summary:
Byzantine Agreement protocols are traditionally designed under worst-case uncertainty about which processes are faulty, coupling the adversary's corruption budget $t$ with the system's epistemic uncertainty. Recent work showed that auxiliary failure predictions can improve round complexity, but cannot improve communication complexity when prediction errors are unconstrained. In this paper, we initiate a theoretical study of the complementary question: how much can Byzantine Agreement benefit when each process is guaranteed a local bound on its prediction error?
  We study this question through the local $k$-error prediction model, in which each process receives a local classification vector differing from the ground truth in at most $k$ positions. The predictions need not be common, and honest processes may hold substantially different views about whom to trust.
  Under this promise model -- where correctness relies on the local error bound holding -- we present a synchronous Byzantine Agreement algorithm requiring $n \ge t + 4k + 1$, where $n$ is the total number of processes, $t$ is the maximum number of failures, and $k$ is the local error bound per honest process. In the regime where local uncertainty is small ($k \ll t$), our protocol decouples communication from the total fault budget $t$: in an execution where the actual maximum prediction error is $s \le k$ and the actual number of failures is $f \le t$, the protocol terminates in $O(s+1)$ rounds and sends $O((f+k)ks + nk)$ honest messages, achieving $o(n^2)$ communication when $t = Θ(n)$ and $k = o(\sqrt{n})$. Finally, we show that it is not possible to solve Byzantine Agreement in the local $k$-error prediction model with fewer than $Ω(nk)$ honest messages.
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.comment: 29 pages. To appear in OPODIS 2026. Full version with complete proofs

Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.title: Geometry, Reliability, and Spacetime Dynamics of Hyper-Simplex Fractal Networks
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.summary: Large-scale, delay-tolerant peer-to-peer networks that need strong consistency usually separate naming, routing, consensus, and ordering into independent layers. To bring deterministic network properties into complex peer-to-peer structures, we unify all four on a single recursive topology. Modeling mutual equality among N peers in Euclidean space requires dimension at least N-1, which prevents flat equal groups from scaling at fixed dimension. The hyper-simplex fractal network G(N,m) escapes this limit by recursion. Each non-leaf node anchors a half-scale N-clique. From the resulting digit-word addresses alone, nodes decide adjacency without routing tables, forward greedily along exact shortest paths, and converge geometrically to a self-similar attractor of dimension log_2 N. Running hierarchical PBFT on the same prefix tree achieves linear message load and logarithmic fault-free latency, with an explicit reliability threshold under independent faults and analytical recursions for anchor exposure, dual homing, and event registration. Reversible topology edits generate the Higman-Thompson group V_N on the address boundary, block order characterizes service-topology hosting beyond treewidth, and root-anchored block heights yield persistent spacetime coordinates with compact light-client proofs.
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.comment: 49 pages (19 pp. main text & refs, Appendices A-F from p. 20), 23 numbered figures (24 graphic files), 13 numbered tables. Unified formal theory of the sparse node-anchored hyper-simplex fractal network G(N,m), superseding arXiv:2410.00583v1. Lean 4 mechanization: https://github.com/Tongji708A/hsfn-lean (49 modules, 853 kernel-audited statements, zero sorry, commit 664b9d7)

Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.title: X-BQSR: Holistic Acceleration of Base Quality Recalibration for Scalable Genomic Analysis
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.summary:
With the continued decline in sequencing costs, genomics-based precision medicine is gaining increasing importance. The Genome Analysis Toolkit (GATK) is the standard framework for converting raw genomic data into actionable variants, but one of its most expensive steps is base quality score recalibration (BQSR), which corrects systematic sequencing errors. Despite significant work on accelerating other parts of the variant calling pipeline, BQSR has not been systematically explored on GPUs.
  In this work, we analyze BQSR to identify computational and I/O bottlenecks and show that simply offloading key stages to an accelerator is insufficient to achieve overall gains. We then present X-BQSR, a holistic redesign of the entire BQSR pipeline, including I/O, compression, and kernel execution, to better leverage GPU parallelism. We implement X-BQSR using portable SYCL kernels for NVIDIA, AMD, and Intel GPUs, along with native CUDA and HIP backends for comparison, and we evaluate its performance against previous FPGA work. Our evaluation shows up to 141.7x acceleration compared to standard GATK and 8.7x acceleration compared to a proprietary GPU-accelerated solution.
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.comment: 14 pages, 4 figures. Author's submitted version (preprint) of paper accepted at Euro-Par 2026 (European Conference on Parallel Processing). E. Marinelli and I. D. Kabadzhov contributed equally. The final authenticated version is available online at https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-032-35248-4_36

Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.title: Accurate Products, Inaccurate Inverse: Emulated FP64 BLAS in Blocked Triangular Inversion
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.summary: FP64 emulation on integer tensor units now ships in cuBLAS and GEMMul8, and each emulated matrix product can be checked against an accuracy grade. We ask if a routine built from such products inherits their accuracy, and show that blocked triangular inversion, the core of LAPACK's inverse of a symmetric positive definite matrix, does not. Under fixed-precision emulation every product passes the grade-B error bound of Demmel et al., yet the inverse errs at 7.1e-2, against 2.0e-15 natively. The matrices are well conditioned after diagonal scaling, but the scaling spans 64 binades. The cause is one product, T = X22 L21, whose summed index carries both the diagonal scaling and its inverse, which a grade-B bound does not absorb. Computing those products natively restores native accuracy; leaving any one of them emulated does not. The pattern holds on four GPUs, and on real covariance matrices the fixed-precision routes lose up to about four orders of accuracy. Equilibration, a solve-based association and cuBLAS's automatic dynamic precision avoid the loss, and an exact error recurrence audits a completed run. On an RTX 4090 the fastest accurate emulated inversion takes 0.40 of cuSOLVER's time. Where each product's scaling falls decides if per-product accuracy carries over to a composite routine, and that is what builders of emulated libraries need to check.
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.comment: Submitted to ISC High Performance 2027. 16 pages, 4 figures, 12 tables. Review artifact (code and run records) linked in the paper

Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.title: Autonomous Mobile Robots on a Computing Field
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.summary: We introduce CABOT, a computational model for autonomous mobile robots in which the discrete plane the robots operate on is not a passive stage but an active computing medium. In the classical Look-Compute-Move (LCM) model every increase in computational capability is obtained by strengthening the robots themselves, with lights, memory or wider visibility, at a cost paid once per robot. CABOT strengthens the environment instead: each cell of the grid holds a state from a finite set Q, the states evolve synchronously under a uniform local rule that also senses whether a robot stands on the cell, that is, the floor is a cellular automaton, and the Look operation returns the states of the visible cells in addition to the positions of the visible robots. The robots are as weak as we can make them: oblivious, silent, lightless, myopic with visibility range 1, without multiplicity detection and unable to write to the floor. The number of field states |Q|, rather than any robot capability, becomes the measure of the resources required. On an inert floor (|Q| = 1) such robots can neither form a line, nor gather from scattered positions, nor explore a grid. We show that a handful of states changes this. Line Formation from connected configurations is solvable with four states, and field-silently, so that the floor also reaches a fixed point, with five. Gathering from arbitrary, possibly disconnected, configurations is solvable with three states and Line Formation from arbitrary configurations with six; we prove that neither can be solved field-silently with any number of states. A single robot explores every finite grid forever with four states and every torus with two, which is optimal. Further rule sets, validated by simulation only, equalize the spacing of robots on a row, fill a pattern painted on the floor and guide robots through a maze, and indicate the range of the model.

Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.title: SYCLDB: A Cross-Vendor Heterogeneous Analytical DBMS
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.summary: The rapid growth of AI and analytical workloads has increased the need for fast, interactive analytical data processing. This, in turn, has led to a surge of interest in designing accelerated analytical database engines that can exploit modern GPUs to scale computation. While GPUs provide the massive data-parallelism required by modern analytics, the software landscape remains dominated by closed-source, vendor-locked programming models, like CUDA, limiting portability across multi-vendor GPUs. In this work, we present SYCLDB, an end-to-end analytical database engine built upon the SYCL open standard, designed to enable efficient, hardware-agnostic execution across a wide range of accelerators using a single codebase. By implementing core relational operators as modular SYCL kernels, integrating them with a SQL frontend based on Apache Calcite and Apache Thrift, and supporting Apache Arrow for efficient columnar ingestion, SYCLDB reduces dependence on vendor-specific GPU programming stacks by enabling a single SYCL codebase to execute analytical query pipelines across Intel, AMD, and NVIDIA GPUs.
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.comment: 16 pages, 3 figures. Author's submitted version (preprint) of paper accepted at ADBIS 2026 (European Conference on Advances in Databases and Information Systems). The final authenticated version is available online at https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-032-39820-8_4

Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.title: Which $\Diamond \mathcal{P}$ Algorithm is Suitable for You? An Empirical Benchmark on Real Network Traces
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.summary: Unreliable failure detectors (UFDs) are a fundamental abstraction for dependability and fault tolerance in distributed systems, supporting core distributed algorithms, such as consensus. Yet selecting a suitable detector remains difficult because existing implementations are evaluated under different environments, workloads, parameterizations, and quality-of-service (QoS) requirements. We address this problem by systematizing 14 $\Diamond \mathcal{P}$ and closely related $\Diamond \mathcal{P}$-style UFDs, implementing 13 of them, and providing a reusable benchmark for their empirical comparison. Our methodology evaluates detectors through common QoS metrics, such as detection time, mistake rate, and query accuracy, and combines same-input replay of network traces with live deployment for detectors whose active probing or cooperative behavior requires online execution. We then formalize failure-detector selection as a constrained algorithm-selection challenge, mapping operational requirements to suitable detector candidates. We instantiate this methodology under controlled variations of communication rate, host load, and crash regime. Applying the selection process shows that no detector is uniformly preferable across the evaluated settings. At relaxed detection-time budgets, 2W [Tomsic et al., IPDPS 2015] is the most frequently selected detector, appearing in 12 of 16 scenario-metric combinations for $T_D \le 500$ ms, whereas stricter budgets yield substantially more scenario- and metric-dependent selections. The benchmark and selection methodology provide a reusable basis for practical detector selection and for establishing stronger analytical baselines for future failure-detection approaches, including learning-based detectors.
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.comment: To appear in the Proceedings of OPODIS 2026

Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.title: Obaleth: Build Your Own GPU Communication Stack
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.summary: Machine learning systems specialize computation to the workload and hardware, but communication remains in generic libraries whose device code and transport decisions are not visible to high-level compilers. We present Obaleth, a compiler that makes GPU-initiated communication part of a kernel's intermediate representation, co-optimizes it alongside computation, and lowers it to specialized transport code. Obaleth plans completions around buffer lifetimes and optimizes memory ordering, synchronization, and batching across NVIDIA and AMD GPUs. On H100 GPUs, Obaleth sends small messages up to 3.3$\times$ faster, and on 256 GPUs runs all-to-all 1.25$\times$ and 2.3$\times$ faster than NVSHMEM and NCCL GIN, with much smaller memory and register use. In vLLM, it serves Qwen3-235B on 16 B200 GPUs and answers requests up to 1.29$\times$ faster than with DeepEP.
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.comment: 20 pages, 13 figures, 6 tables. Equal contribution from first two authors. Code: https://github.com/ParCoreLab/aboleth

Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.title: Torcalia.jl: An MPI-based Runtime System for Asynchronous Task Parallelism in Julia
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.summary:
Designed to address the two-language problem, the Julia programming language provides a powerful platform for developing high-performance scientific computing and machine learning applications. Such applications increasingly exhibit irregular, adaptive, or data-driven workloads for which traditional bulk-synchronous parallel (BSP) models often struggle to efficiently exploit the available parallelism. Asynchronous many-task (AMT) runtime systems offer a compelling alternative, decomposing computations into fine-grained tasks that are dynamically scheduled across the hierarchical architecture of modern HPC systems.
  This paper introduces Torcalia$.$jl, a Julia package designed to orchestrate the asynchronous execution of tasks across both shared and distributed memory environments. Built on top of MPI$.$jl and Julia's native multithreading, Torcalia employs a dependency-aware task scheduling scheme that combines the work-sharing and work-stealing paradigms to achieve adaptive load balancing. Tasks can be nested arbitrarily, enabling applications to exploit multiple levels of parallelism, while application-level distributed shared memory (DSM) extends task-based shared-memory programming to multi-node clusters. Beyond task-based programming, the proposed library supports skeletal programming, providing high-level abstractions that facilitate the implementation of parallel applications at scale. Evaluated on the ARIS supercomputer using four diverse workloads, Torcalia demonstrates strong scalability, reducing wall-clock time by up to 18.1% compared with Dagger, a state-of-the-art task-based engine in Julia. The source code of Torcalia$.$jl is publicly available at https://github.com/CEID-HPCLAB/Torcalia.jl.

Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.title: A Pipeline-Parallel System for Depth-Recurrent Models
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.summary: Depth-recurrent (Looped) models raise effective depth by applying a shared stack of blocks several times. Scaling them usually requires pipeline parallelism, but commonly used interleaved 1F1B is drawn for an acyclic stage graph in which each micro-batch enters each stage once. Once that stack is split across stages, the same stage is visited several times on one micro-batch and later stages feed earlier ones: native 1F1B has no slot for the extra visit, cannot rank a first iteration against a second, and its neighbour-only send/receive order has no back edge to the first stage, so the arrangement stalls or fires out of order. We present Loop-PP, which rebuilds both the timetable and the communication for this cyclic layout. It schedules different iterations of the same stage separately, specializes a 1F1B skeleton into a globally consistent order over those visits, and emits a static instruction stream per rank that separates posting from waiting so communication overlaps local compute. Loop-PP is bit-identical to a single-stage reference. On 8B-60B MoE models, it lowers peak memory by as much as 32.8\%, and with compute budget fixed, the best observed throughput rises by 12.7\%.

Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.title: GC-MoE K3: A Green-Context Role Graph for Latent Mixture-of-Experts Decode
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.summary: Kimi K3 combines a latent routed mixture of experts with full-width shared experts. A complete feed-forward evaluation must score and select experts, project tokens into the latent space, exchange tokens across expert-parallel ranks, compute the routed and shared branches, and normalize and project the routed sum before joining the branches. We present GC-MoE K3, a datacenter Blackwell implementation that schedules this entire evaluation as a CUDA Graph across two Green Contexts. Five base roles split input projection, routing, dispatch, expert computation, and finalization. Dispatch can fill the routed input ring while the compute partition evaluates shared experts. Finalize waits for the expert owners needed by each token and overlaps routed reduction and RMSNorm with loading the output projection weights. Conditional roles reuse the communication partition for routed computation and reduce split-$K$ projection partials. On GB200 at EP8, EP16, and EP32, the operator is faster at all 24 measured configurations than the paired SGLang-style reference (mean speedup $1.1324\times$). A comparison with historical vLLM-style measurements gives $1.3651\times$ across the same 24 shapes. Both latency comparisons time single-layer graph replay on synthetic K3-shaped inputs with a residual prefix. The separate paired numerical suite passes all 142 cases and 2,936 rank checks.

Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.title: What Information Survives Authenticated Byzantine Communication?
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.summary: Two principals independently approve actions for a delegate that can choose a route to a goal and carry it out under current policy. A stable work-order receipt records the routes authorized at issuance. For intersection policies, we characterize the leading number of reachable joint configurations under overlapping updates. The lower bound uses the first writer's ability to finish before its peer invokes an update. The matching protocol checks an older route against the changed principal's policy because the unchanged principal already approved each of its steps. When each route has a command unique to it, the count has a closed form in terms of unions of route supports. Two three-command workflows with four possible receipts each have leading counts of $360$ and $328$ under encoded overwrite, and both have append count $1024$. Exact policy read-back forces at least six bits per block in both cases. Route overlap affects the count even when route lengths are fixed. The construction preserves authorization, withdrawal, stable recovery, and progress after stabilization with one coordinator crash.

Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.title: CGSpec: Consistency-Guided Speculative Decoding with Overlap-Aware Verification Scheduling for Edge-Cloud Inference
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.summary: Collaborative speculative decoding accelerates large language model inference by enabling edge clients to draft tokens locally and a shared cloud model to verify them. However, draft target disagreement wastes communication and verification resources, while heterogeneous client return times complicate shared verifier scheduling. We propose CGSpec, a consistency guided framework for multi client edge-cloud speculative decoding. CGSpec uses draft target distribution divergence to adapt the speculative budget and introduces a nomination and competition mechanism to construct candidate trees through global growth control and local token selection. An overlap-aware scheduler further estimates remaining verification work and client return times to prioritize requests and improve verifier utilization. We evaluate CGSpec using four model pairs and three datasets under heterogeneous network conditions. Across 24 configurations with 8 and 16 clients, CGSpec achieves the highest mean system and client throughput among the evaluated methods. Compared with current SOTA methods, it improves system throughput by 12.2\% and 10.2\%, and mean client throughput by 14.0\% and 33.0\%, respectively.

Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.title: Placing the Control Plane: Cloud-Native Federated Learning Across Batch-Scheduled HPC
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.summary: The United Kingdom's AI Research Resource (AIRR) opens national supercomputers to a community familiar with always-reachable cloud services. With batch-scheduled HPC, a user requests a time-bounded allocation that is then reclaimed. Federated Learning (FL) exposes this tension, pairing a long-lived control plane with short-lived training. We characterize the resulting placement asymmetry: the coordination server sees only model updates and control metadata, so it can sit on neutral infrastructure, whereas the client control process is bound to the participating site's data and must remain within its trust boundary. The outbound-only connection this implies is also how edge clients connect, though the batch-scheduler mismatch is specific to HPC. We demonstrate a cross-silo federation spanning three independently administered systems (Isambard-AI, Isambard 3, and Zenith) using unmodified production FL frameworks (FLARE-wrapped Flower), measure the cost the client placement incurs, and propose Kubernetes-as-a-service as the in-boundary home for the persistent process.
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.comment: Accepted at The 1st International Workshop on Edge-Cloud-HPC Operational Continuum (ECHO), co-located with SC26, Chicago, IL, USA, November 20, 2026. To appear in the SC26 Workshop Proceedings

Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.title: Multimmit: Low-Latency and Robust Transaction Ordering
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.summary:
To meet the throughput demands of blockchain systems, protocols for State Machine Replication increasingly have many processors disseminate transaction blocks in parallel. Certified designs require availability certificates before blocks enter the ordering process, which is robust but adds latency. BlueBottle, the leading uncertified design under $n\geq 5f+1$ ($n$ processors, at most $f$ Byzantine), reduces latency in favourable conditions but can put fetching missing data on the critical path. Raptr, the state of the art under $n\geq 3f+1$, avoids fetching on the voting path, but transactions wait for a leader's proposal and two voting rounds, and the leader controls the proposed sequence. We prove that strengthening the resilience assumption alone cannot remove Raptr's second voting round.
  We present Multimmit, a protocol for $n\geq 5f+1$ that builds on Raptr's approach and finalises leader blocks after a single round of voting, improving latency by at least one message delay. Extension votes let voters endorse fresh transaction blocks omitted from the leader's proposal: once a leader block finalises, every fresh, well-circulated block of an honest chain enters the total ordering by the next finalised leader block, even if that block's leader is Byzantine. Producer chains are interleaved by a prescribed rule, not in a leader-chosen sequence. Payments are final within a single round trip, once the producer assembles $n-f$ acknowledgments into a transferable receipt. With fifty validators across thirteen regions, Multimmit's median latency to placement in the total ordering moves from 383 to 411 ms as the offered rate rises from 100k to 1M transactions per second. At 100k, it is essentially unchanged under 0.1% message loss and rises by a factor of 1.4 with nine validators crashed; these conditions slow BlueBottle and Raptr, respectively, by more than an order of magnitude.

Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.title: The Complexity of Distributed Minimum Weight Cycle Approximation
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.summary:
We study the Minimum Weight Cycle (MWC) problem in the $\mathsf{CONGEST}$ model of distributed computing. For undirected weighted graphs, we give a randomized $(k+1)$-approximation algorithm for every real number $k \geq (1+\sqrt{5})/2 \approx 1.618$. The algorithm runs in $\tilde{O}\left(n^{\frac{k+1}{2k+1}} + D\right)$ rounds, where $n$ is the number of nodes and $D$ is the unweighted diameter of the graph. Varying $k$ therefore yields a smooth trade-off between approximation ratio and round complexity.
  On the lower bound side, assuming the Erdős girth conjecture, for every integer $k \geq 1$ and every $ε> 0$, any randomized $(k+1-ε)$-approximation algorithm for MWC requires $\tildeΩ\left(n^{\frac{k+1}{2k+1}}+D\right)$ rounds. The lower bound holds for both directed unweighted graphs and undirected weighted graphs, even on graphs of diameter $Θ(\log n)$. This gives a nearly tight characterization of the round complexity of approximate MWC.
  Our algorithm is based on a new connection between MWC and the low-diameter decomposition of Miller, Peng, and Xu (SPAA 2013). This connection has consequences beyond the $\mathsf{CONGEST}$ model: for every real number $k \geq 1$, this leads to a $(k+1)$-approximation algorithm for MWC with $\tilde{O}(mn^{1/k})$ work and $\tilde{O}(1)$ depth in the parallel setting, as well as an $\tilde{O}(n^{1/k})$-round algorithm in the broadcast congested clique model. We complement the latter bound with a matching $\tildeΩ(n^{1/k})$ lower bound for $(k+1-ε)$-approximation in the broadcast congested clique model, for every integer $k\geq1$, assuming the Erdős girth conjecture.

Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.title: One Structure Is Enough: Record-Native Tiles for Evolving Sparse Matrices on GPUs
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.summary: Sparse matrices that change over time, such as streaming graphs, are usually handled on GPUs with two parts: a packed format such as CSR, ELL, or SELL for computation, and a separate buffer for updates. Periodic maintenance then merges updates, rebuilds data, or changes formats. Our measurements show that this split is often unnecessary. We present RecTile, a tiled storage layer where each tile is kept in one sorted array of 12-byte edge records. For fragmented matrices, with 1 to 21 nonzeros per tile in our workloads, RecTile matches the best format-pinned slab tile at 0.56 to 1.21 times its time. Its tiled layout is also up to 21 times faster than whole-matrix cuSPARSE CSR. Specialized slabs are faster on the patterns they target at medium density, but both approaches converge by 25% density. RecTile stays within 1.1 to 1.6 times of whole-matrix cuSPARSE COO, our strongest static baseline, while COO cannot be updated in place. RecTile also uses no fixed per-tile device metadata for the stored matrix payload, so its tiles are smaller at realistic occupancies. A fully GPU-based ingest pipeline applies insert/delete/modify batches at up to 29 million edges per second, 4.5 times faster than the host path. An exact dynamic-programming oracle selects zero folds on every tested workload under its action space and calibrated cost model. Standard folding heuristics use 4 to 15 times more GPU time and up to 4 times more persistent device storage. End to end, RecTile improves the time-storage tradeoff on all five evolving-graph workloads, including delete-heavy streams. It is also fastest on a dense stress stream with 1220 records per tile. There, folding uses 1.3 times less peak persistent storage but takes 3.9 times more time. For the evolving graph-like, interleaved update/SpMV workloads evaluated here, the mutable record store can serve directly as the compute representation.
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.comment: 8 pages, 2 figures, 2 tables. Presented at BAŞARIM 2026, the 9th National High Performance Computing Conference, İstanbul, Türkiye, October 14-16, 2026. Code: https://github.com/tweetpie/RecTile

Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.title: MotionServe: Efficient Multi-Robot Serving by Exploiting Robot Execution Slack
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.summary: As robotic arms undertake diverse manipulation tasks, a deployment may need to serve many task-specific vision-language-action (VLA) policies concurrently. Dedicating a GPU to each robot is costly, motivating shared-GPU inference. Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) allows compatible policies to share a frozen backbone with lightweight policy-specific adapters, reducing model-weight memory and enabling cross-policy batching. However, robot inference must keep pace with physical execution. With action chunking, robots continue executing buffered actions while awaiting new predictions, and the remaining buffered time provides each robot's execution slack for serving its next request. Once this slack is exhausted, the robot stalls until new actions arrive, interrupting task progress. Observing earlier preserves more slack but can lead to disruptive replanning and lower task success, whereas delaying dispatch to form larger batches can improve GPU efficiency but consumes slack and risks stalls. To balance these competing demands, we present MotionServe, a shared-GPU serving system that coordinates robot observation timing with server-side batch formation. MotionExec selects observation triggers based on motion structure in predicted action chunks, allowing inference to overlap with remaining buffered execution. SlackBatch combines the resulting per-robot execution budgets with estimated outstanding GPU work to determine when to wait, which requests to batch, and when to dispatch them. We evaluate X-VLA on LIBERO and SimplerEnv's WidowX tasks and OpenVLA-OFT on LIBERO, with up to 96 simulated robots sharing one NVIDIA H200 GPU. At 96 robots, MotionServe reduces mean stall per episode by 43.4% and 32.6% and improves task success by 8.98 and 2.30 percentage points, respectively, over each model's lowest-stall baseline. Backbone sharing also reduces weight memory for 96 policies by 97.6% and 91.1%.

Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.title: Cascade: Exploiting SLO-Aware latency budget for fair and high goodput LLM inference serving
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.summary:
The reasoning and agentic capabilities of LLMs have expanded the range of applications they support, from short interactive exchanges to long, prefix-heavy requests. LLM serving platforms today define response-latency service-level objectives (SLOs), yet requests under the same SLO differ by orders of magnitude in input length, generation length, execution cost, and reusable KV-cache availability, leaving each request with a different amount of latency headroom. This headroom must cover not only execution, but also scheduling and preemption delays and the cost of retrieving KV state from deeper memory tiers. Existing systems manage these decisions independently, despite their combined impact on latency.
  We present Cascade, an LLM serving system that coordinates these decisions using a per-request latency budget: the difference between a request's SLO and its predicted remaining service time, continuously updated from request characteristics, KV-cache state, and system load. Cascade uses this budget to prioritize requests and to decide how much non-resident KV state to prefetch from deeper tiers, with the remainder fetched on demand or recomputed given the serving system. On production traces across three LLMs, Cascade improves goodput by 10.4x over vLLM and 1.8x over a SLO-aware scheduler, and reduces SLO violations by 76% and 31%, respectively, while remaining fair across heterogeneous requests.

Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.title: Fast 4-bit KV-Cache Decoding on Hopper GPUs: Why Existing Kernels Are Slow and How to Fix Them
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.summary: A 4-bit KV cache reads about half the bytes of FP8, but Hopper GPUs have no FP4 hardware and little instruction-issue capacity per byte of memory bandwidth, so 4-bit values must be decoded in software. On H200, vLLM's NVFP4 KV path (FlashInfer's decode) reaches 10-20% of memory bandwidth and is up to 1.7x slower than FP8. NVBit instruction counts show two causes: the kernels behind vLLM's 4-bit paths (FlashInfer NVFP4, Triton UltraQuant) execute 2-6x Hopper's issue budget per byte and serialize loading, decoding and matrix multiplies. Our Hopper-native decode kernel overlaps a TMA producer warp with two compute warpgroups, lays the cache out at write time so decoded values feed the tensor cores from registers, and swaps the matrix operands so small query groups need no padding. On H200 it reaches 67-75% of peak bandwidth at batch 32-128 and at all 11 shapes is 1.12-1.49x faster than the faster of XQA and FlashAttention-4's proposed native FP8. Inside vLLM, with an accuracy recipe (K mean removal and rotation, 4 BF16 sink tokens, BF16 layer 0), it decodes 1.12-1.64x faster per step on Llama-3.1-8B than vLLM's FlashInfer FP8 path at batch 8 and above (1.04-1.24x over FlashAttention-4's FP8), is level at batch 1, and holds 1.63x as many tokens. On one H200 under a reasoning-like request stream, the highest rate at which 99% of requests meet the latency targets is 1.23-1.32x FP8's on Llama-3.1-8B and 1.67-2.20x on Qwen2.5-72B, as the cache becomes the limit; prefill-heavy streams are worse (7% slower prefill). On five 7B-32B models, repeated runs show no significant accuracy difference from BF16 KV. In Qwen2-family models, whose reasoning variants collapse under FP8 KV, layer 0's key mean is almost entirely the key-projection bias identified by prior work, seen through RoPE and computable from the weights alone; keeping that layer in BF16 restores FP8 KV and, with K mean removal, 4-bit KV.

Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.title: Purlin: Separating Orchestration from the Datapath of Collectives
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.summary: Distributed inference depends on GPU collective communication that must keep pace with evolving hardware and specialized workloads. However, existing works often couple the semantics, orchestration (where and when data moves), and datapath (how data moves) of collective communication. This coupling makes it costly to adopt new hardware mechanisms and customize communication for applications. We present Purlin, a scale-up communication framework that separates these concerns. At the top of Purlin, we specify collectives as a transformation from an input to an output layout. In the middle, we introduce a shared protocol, Stage, Notify, And Consume (SNAC), which derives orchestration from these specifications. Below SNAC sits a hardware-specific datapath we call Atom, which implements two key data movement primitives for collectives: copy and reduce. This separation lets us customize collectives and adopt new hardware mechanisms while reusing orchestration via SNAC. We evaluate Purlin on A100, H200, and B200 GPUs. Across seven collectives, Purlin achieves latency speedups of up to 5.14x and bandwidth improvements of up to 4.50x over baselines. Integrated into SGLang, Purlin improves offline LLM serving throughput and interactivity by 1.13x on average and up to 1.37x over baselines. For online LLM inference, Purlin improves interactivity by 1.26x on average and up to 2.85x, with the largest gain occurring under overload.
