StableToolBench calls some of its test groups tests on "unseen" tools, yet the ToolBench instruction pool, which retrievers and experience-sharing methods learn from, contains every test query and labels every gold tool of the two single-tool groups among them. We release STUN-Bench (StableToolBench, Truly UNseen), a split whose experience pool has no item that labels or names 172 held-out tools. Unseen here means absent from shared experience and retriever training data, not from pretraining. On the split we find crowding: experience pooled from five simulated clients, added to an index of tool descriptions, outranks the descriptions of tools no client has used, which then often drop out of the candidate list. Under the Jina-v2 retriever, routing accuracy on held-out tools falls from 0.534 to 0.278. Retrievers trained for tool retrieval lose much less, and keeping experience in a separate index recovers most of the loss under Jina-v2. The split also reverses a conclusion: with every test tool labeled in the pool and our default leak filter applied, shared experience beats descriptions alone; on STUN-Bench it falls below them. The split, leak filter and evaluation harness are available at https://github.com/<org>/STUN-Bench.

Software Engineering.title: OWE-Bench: A long-horizon benchmark for measuring real-world engineering
Software Engineering.summary: We present OWE-Bench (OpenWorldEngineer-Bench), a benchmark of 26 long-horizon engineering tasks written by domain experts in software engineering, physical engineering, machine learning, and scientific computing. Tasks range from optimizing kernels and designing an aircraft, to identifying the faults responsible for an earthquake. Each task requires significant domain knowledge and engineering work, with models averaging hundreds of millions of tokens per task. Solutions are scored on practical measures such as speed, cost and accuracy, both on provided cases the agent could test against and on hidden cases that an engineer would expect from the task description. The best-performing frontier model so far, Claude Fable 5.2, scores 54.6% and averages 211 million tokens per task. We highlight two findings. First, when models are given more time, they use more test-time compute and achieve higher scores. Models also scale differently with test-time compute: GPT-6 Astra achieves higher scores at shorter time limits and at equal token use, while Claude Fable 5.2 uses more tokens at longer limits to achieve the highest overall score. Second, each model scores lower on hidden cases than on the provided cases, by an average of 18 points, which we call the deployment gap. Models also fail to predict the deployment gap, overestimating their performance on hidden test cases by an average of 21 points. We hope that OWE-Bench grounds progress toward agents whose engineering solutions perform as well in deployment as they do in testing.
Software Engineering.comment: 35 pages, 14 figures, 9 tables. Code: https://github.com/Mercor-Intelligence/OpenWorldEngineer ; data: https://huggingface.co/datasets/mercor/OpenWorldEngineer ; leaderboard: https://openworldengineer.mercor.com

Software Engineering.title: LLM-Assisted Software Migration: from Module-Level Transformation to Repository-Level Integration
Software Engineering.summary: Software migration adapts an existing implementation to a new language, version, API, framework, or platform while preserving its behavior. Large language models (LLMs) succeed on individual functions and modules, but this success does not readily carry over to entire repositories, particularly deployable applications. This survey reviews LLM-assisted migration from module-level transformation to repository-level integration, culminating in the delivery of complete applications. We analyze 96 sources---including 46 direct migration papers---across four perspectives: (1) supported software engineering activities, (2) model roles as editors or orchestrators, (3) orchestration workflows (agentless, single-agent, or multi-agent), and (4) enabling techniques including knowledge engineering, project context, environment feedback, and model adaptation. We then compare evaluation practices and benchmarks. Although 30 of the 46 studies target repositories, most acceptance evidence relies merely on build success, supplied tests, or static and model-based proxies. Moreover, compilation, visual similarity, test outcomes, and runtime behavior capture fundamentally distinct properties and cannot be conflated into a single success rate. We also identify critical gaps in requirements engineering support and in controlled comparisons of agent architectures. Finally, we discuss six open problems: application integration, platform differences, non-functional properties, generalization, attribution of gains, as well as cost and maintenance.

Software Engineering.title: Articulating Assumptions in AI-Generated Scientific Analyses through Task Decomposition
Software Engineering.summary: Scientific results produced by LLM generated analysis code must be understandable and reproducible. However, uncertainty can arise at different stages of the process, both in the original natural language specification and in the generated implementation. As a result, even executable code may not provide a clear understanding of which quantities are being computed or which assumptions determine the final results. To address this challenge, we introduce quantity grounded semantic differencing, a multi-agent framework for analyzing and comparing scientific programs generated by LLMs. The framework assigns code generation, execution, tracing, and validation to separate agents, allowing it to reconstruct how key output quantities are produced and to identify differences between the intended analysis and the implemented code. We also introduce a module that inspects ambiguities in the initial user instruction and suggests alternative rewrites before code generation. Its modular design enables application to different scientific domains by replacing domain specific resources while preserving the same workflow. We validate the framework on representative collider physics analyses. The results demonstrate that the modular task decomposition enhances both transparency and reliability relative to the previous single prompt approach, while enabling substantially smaller models to execute the complete workflow.
Software Engineering.comment: Published version

Software Engineering.title: Does the Agent's Map Match the Territory? Architectural Claims in AI Agent Context Files and Their Fit with the Code
Software Engineering.summary: AI coding agents start every session without memory of how a system is built. Developers fill this gap with context files, such as CLAUDE.md and AGENTS.md. Agents treat these files as true, so it matters whether they match the code. We study two kinds of architectural claims that can be checked against a repository: path claims, which name folders and files, and dependency rules, which say what may import what. We check 41,090 path claims and 184 dependency rules from 3,602 context files in 3,346 open-source projects against the code and its history. About 5% of path claims point to paths we cannot find, but we estimate that only 2.2% are real errors, similar to READMEs (3.5%). When code moves, 61% of claims that became stale are fixed, most in the same commit. Dependency rules behave differently: 33 of 184 (18%) were confirmed broken on the day they were written, usually by older code, and nearly all stayed broken. Context files are good maps but less reliable rulebooks: their rules often describe the architecture a team wants, not the one it has. In an exploratory comparison of 7,480 commits, new rule breaks were rare. Agent-assisted commits broke rules about 1.8 times as often as other commits (0.29% vs. 0.16%), but with only 14 breaks this is not significant: an early signal, not evidence of a difference or of its absence. We used an LLM with human review at each step, and discuss what this offers and risks for mining studies.

Software Engineering.title: Enhancing Code Consistency in AI Research with Large Language Models and Retrieval-Augmented Generation
Software Engineering.summary: Ensuring that code accurately reflects the algorithms and methods described in research papers is critical for maintaining credibility and fostering trust in AI research. This paper presents a novel system designed to verify code implementations against the algorithms and methodologies outlined in corresponding research papers. Our system employs Retrieval-Augmented Generation to extract relevant details from both the research papers and code bases, followed by a structured comparison using Large Language Models. This approach improves the accuracy and comprehensiveness of code implementation verification while contributing to the transparency, explainability, and reproducibility of AI research. By automating the verification process, our system reduces manual effort, enhances research credibility, and ultimately advances the state of the art in code verification.

Software Engineering.title: Context-Aware Proactive Self-Adaptation: A Two-Layer Model Predictive Control Approach
Software Engineering.summary: In self-adaptive software systems, the role of context is paramount, especially for proactive self-adaptation. Current research, however, does not fully explore context's impact, for example on priorities of the requirements. To address this gap, we introduce a novel contextual goal model to capture these factors and their influence on the system. Using this, we propose a two-layer control mechanism with a context-aware model predictive control to achieve proactive adaptation for the software system and adaptation for the controller itself. By contextual prediction and a more accurate system model, our approach utilizes model predictive control to facilitate timely and efficient system adaptations, improving both performance and adaptability. Meanwhile, we perform requirement adaptation to update the contextual goal model, which in turn updates the objective function and constraints of the controller. Our experimental evaluations across two scenarios demonstrate the significant benefits of our approach in enhancing system performance.
Software Engineering.comment: Author's version of an article published in ACM Transactions on Autonomous and Adaptive Systems (TAAS), vol. 21, no. 2, Article 13, 2026. 36 pages

Software Engineering.title: Landscape and Taxonomy of Prompt Engineering Patterns in Software Engineering
Software Engineering.summary: Advancements in large language models (LLMs) have enhanced their ability to handle ambiguous user instructions. However, effective prompt patterns remain crucial for usability and comprehension. This article presents a taxonomy of prompt engineering patterns for software engineering. It is based on a systematic literature review that was conducted in early 2023, when LLMs still faced significant limitations in context length and inference capabilities. Our study explores techniques that enhance the usability and reliability of LLMs, emphasizing the ongoing importance of well-designed prompts in optimizing task performance. Our findings highlight the critical role of prompt patterns in maximizing LLM's potential, even as their capabilities continue to evolve.
Software Engineering.comment: Published in IEEE IT Professional, vol. 27, no. 1, pp. 41-49, 2025. Recipient of the IT Professional 2025 Best Paper Award. 8 pages, 2 figures

Software Engineering.title: SWE-Proof: Can Language Models Resolve Real-World Issues with Machine-Checked Proofs?
Software Engineering.summary: Ensuring the correctness of LLM-generated code is a core challenge for modern software engineering. Benchmarks for agentic code generation check correctness with held-out test suites, which are inherently incomplete and increasingly susceptible to memorization. Formal verification avoids both problems, but existing work covers only standalone tasks whose specifications are given as input, not real issues, which touch large repositories and state intent in vague natural language. We present BenchProofer, a pipeline that turns a coding task with a known correct patch into a formally verified one: it writes a specification for the new code, summarizes the existing functions that code calls with axioms, and admits an instance only after mechanical and adversarial gates agree. Applying it to SWE-bench Verified yields SWE-Proof, 500 real issues whose correctness is formally verified rather than tested, and it extends to SWE-bench Pro. Evaluating Claude Opus 4.8, we find that verification catches what tests miss: nearly a third of test-passing patches admit counterexamples, which a structured natural-language specification does not fix, while a correct formal one lifts resolution from 85% to 95%. Writing that specification is the hard part: an agent that must write its own gains nothing over an unaided baseline, and only 56% of those specifications pass our audit. The usual failure is faithfulness, where a specification constrains part of the required behavior and leaves the rest free. Specification quality also tracks the outcome, failing on 92% of unresolved instances against 51% of resolved ones, making faithful specification synthesis a concrete open problem. Code is available at https://github.com/amazon-science/BenchProofer.

Software Engineering.title: GoldiBench: Right Tools, Wrong Amount -- Benchmarking Agents on Effect Judgement in Professional Editing
Software Engineering.summary: Real editing requests describe a look, not the steps to reach it, so an agent that serves them must judge how much of each tool the look takes. Existing benchmarks do not measure this: their tasks either state the tools and values, or leave the amount open and are scored by VLM judges that pass more than half of half- and triple-strength results. We introduce GoldiBench, a benchmark of 500 editing tasks in five professional applications (darktable, RawTherapee, GIMP, Inkscape, Blender), solvable by writing a program or by operating the GUI. Each task pairs a START image with a TARGET rendered from a hidden program, so the amount is fixed by a known target; the agent's edit is re-rendered and compared with TARGET, and the same task is posed with the tools and values, the tools only, or the goal only, separating operation from effect judgement. Across 25 open, GUI and closed models, agents operate well (99-100% with programs from 4B up when told the values) but fall off a cliff when they must judge the amount: given only the tools, the best model passes 19% of the tasks with programs and 33% through the GUI, and scale does not close the gap. Manuals barely help; the measured TARGET-START difference more than doubles the pass rate, but the same difference shown as an image does not for open models. Allowed four renders, agents almost always stop after the first; forced to compare, the strong models double their pass rate. Agents know the tools, but neither read nor check the amount.
Software Engineering.comment: 20 pages. Project page: https://uservan.github.io/GoldiBench

Software Engineering.title: Agent Recovery Gone Wrong: Measuring Harm Beyond Duplicate Calls
Software Engineering.summary: Code-executing LLM agents submit blocks of code that issue several API writes. If a block fails after some of its writes have taken effect, the agent rewrites the block and continues. It is unknown how often such a recovery harms the external state when the failure occurs naturally in the code written by the agent. In this paper, we measure it on recorded trajectories of AppWorld agents. In a stratified random sample of 200 candidate episodes across ten models, 145 are partial executions confirmed by the database state. In the sample, 30 of 143 confirmed partial executions with a determinable outcome are followed by a harmful recovery, and its violation remains at the end of the run, which gives a stratification-weighted estimate of 24.6%. Two thirds of the harmful recoveries duplicate an effect, and the rest delete user data or make a wrong first-time write, e.g., an order of a wrong product. A rule that searches for repeated calls finds 75% of duplications but only 41% of all harm. We also examine two sources of operation identity for an idempotency contract. In a small pilot (17 episodes, one local model), identifiers supplied by the model do not detectably reduce harm, because the model issues a new identifier for the same operation. Identity derived from the call content, evaluated counterfactually on the sample, would have matched every harmful write in 14 to 18 of the 30 harmful recoveries, but in none of those with a wrong first-time write, and it would also have matched writes required by the task in 30 episodes. Based on these results, we outline design requirements for safer agent recovery.
Software Engineering.comment: 5 pages, 1 figure, 4 tables. Data, labels, and scripts: https://github.com/flame-stream/agent-recovery-harm

Software Engineering.title: Below the Stopwatch: Checking the Performance Claims of Coding Agents in the Kernel
Software Engineering.summary: Coding agents open many pull requests (PRs) that claim to make software faster. Most such claims also give a reason, such as "cache the result" or "read the file once". A stopwatch can show that code got faster, but not that it got faster for the stated reason. We present Below, a pipeline that checks these reasons at the kernel level. From 1,343 runtime-performance PRs in the AIDev dataset, Below extracts the mechanism each PR claims and maps it to the kernel and hardware signals that must change if the claim is true. A build agent that never sees the claim rebuilds the code before and after each PR. Below then measures both versions with plain timing runs, hardware counters and LTTng kernel traces. Most claims are not measured: 57.3% of the PRs offer only reasoning or no evidence, and only 31.4% state an effect size. Of 82 analyzed PRs, 32 ran faster, 28 showed no clear change and 22 ran slower. The expected signal of the claimed mechanism appeared in 34 PRs (20 in kernel-trace signals alone), and 42 PRs also changed their output. Kernel signals move about 1.7 times as often for a faster PR's claimed mechanism as for mechanisms it did not claim; the instruction count barely separates them (1.15 times).
Software Engineering.comment: Short paper for the AGENT 2027 workshop at ICSE 2027. 5 pages, 2 figures, 4 tables

Software Engineering.title: CrossCheck II: A Compiler Plugin for Certified Cost Bounds of Real-Time C and C++ Code, and its Evaluation
Software Engineering.summary: We describe a plugin for the Clang compiler that bounds the cost of C and C++ functions intended for real-time use, and rejects at compile time the functions that allocate, throw, call through pointers, or contain a loop or a recursion for which no bound is found. Loops are bounded by affine ranking potentials synthesized with an SMT solver through Farkas' Lemma, or by logarithmic ones, recursion by depth and size potentials, and callees are analyzed in the calling context in which they are used. For functions in a linear fragment, the plugin emits a cost certificate that a checker, compiled from a Lean~4 definition proved sound in a companion paper, validates with integer arithmetic only; the bound then depends neither on the analyzer nor on the solver. On the 29 kernels of the TACLeBench collection, without annotations, the plugin bounds 142 of 220 loops in the calling contexts of the programs, 131 of them exactly as the benchmarks' flow facts, and 161 of the 165 bounded functions receive a certificate that the checker accepts, 152 of them also validated against an independent description of the source. On the CMSIS-DSP library for Cortex-M (786 functions), with assumed input ranges, it bounds 616 functions. We compare the loop bounds with loop counts observed by running the kernels and with five existing analyzers (LLVM's ScalarEvolution, KoAT2, CoFloCo, Infer and oRange), and the plugin with KoAT2 and CoFloCo on the C programs of the Termination and Complexity Competition: without annotations, 147 of 553 programs receive a certified bound that holds for all inputs, where the two tools bound 288 and 264. Loop bounds, exported annotations and the checker program are also tested on random programs and on mutated certificates.
Software Engineering.comment: 23 pages. Companion of "CrossCheck I" (doi:10.5281/zenodo.24444576), which holds the theory and the Lean proofs. Code, benchmarks and Lean formalization: doi:10.5281/zenodo.24425070

Software Engineering.title: Decision Models for Definition-Driven GitHub Actions Workflow Smell Detection
Software Engineering.summary: GitHub Actions workflows automate continuous integration and delivery (CI/CD), and workflow smells are recurring configuration patterns that may weaken security, hinder maintenance, or waste resources. Extending static analyzers to new smells requires encoding constructs, applicability conditions, and exceptions in detection rules. We investigate definition-driven detection, in which models assess workflows against reusable natural-language smell definitions, focusing on decision-oriented models that return scores for bounded questions. We compare them with generative models and a static analyzer, and examine their score reliability, repeatability, and robustness. We evaluate three decision-oriented and two generative configurations on 1,710 manually validated workflow-smell pairs covering 19 smells, 903 workflows, and 559 repositories. Effectiveness depends strongly on the decision policy: JEV 1.13 achieves 79.69% micro-F1 at threshold 0.5 and 85.43% with thresholds selected on separate repository folds, but global thresholds selected on the benchmark lower micro-F1 on a historical comparison set. Generative GPT-6 LUNA achieves comparable effectiveness on the pairs it classifies but leaves 247 unresolved. Repeatability does not ensure robustness: two decision models agree across three identical-input runs yet change more than 3% of their predictions after label-preserving transformations, despite nearly unchanged aggregate F1. On 46 reconstructed workflows, a static analyzer outperforms JEV 1.13 (87.8% versus 76.4% micro-F1). With a median latency of 0.675 seconds per workflow and about US$0.22 in API charges for the benchmark, JEV 1.13 makes frequent model-assisted checks operationally plausible, but deployment requires validated decision policies, and effectiveness on new criteria remains to be evaluated.

Software Engineering.title: Diffs Are Cheap, Show Me the Trajectory: An Empirical Study of Trajectory-Informed Code Review
Software Engineering.summary: Code review typically starts from the final diff. However, the diff reveals little about how the code was developed. Coding-agent trajectories preserve intermediate decisions, failed attempts, and validation evidence that may assist code review. We systematically investigate whether and how these trajectories can help independent review agents identify problems in the resulting code, beyond inspecting the final diff and repository. We develop a procedure that generates review comments by comparing the initial and merged versions of pull requests, and assess it against withheld human review comments. Using held-out reference implementations as comparison targets for agent-produced code, we construct a dataset linking 339 implementations of 113 DeepSWE tasks with their trajectories and 882 synthetic reference review comments. Across three coding-agent configurations and two review harnesses, we compare diff-only review, full-trajectory access, and four alternative ways of presenting and using trajectories. Full-trajectory access raises mean reference recall from 23.03% to 25.87%, but improves recall in only four of six configurations. All four alternatives improve mean reference recall over diff-only by between 4.05 and 7.32 percentage points. The gains also extend to review comments that explain task-verifier failures. Higher recall can require more tokens and longer review time, while simpler trajectory views remain competitive. These results support development trajectories as an additional source of code-review context and show that their benefits and resource costs depend on how they are presented and used.

Programming Languages.title: Hereditary permutations for simple types revisited: A baby case for University Algebra
Programming Languages.summary: It is a classical result that the definable isomorphisms of the simply typed $λ$-calculus with function types are exactly the hereditary permutations, and that they are generated by $A \to B \to C \cong B \to A \to C$ and congruence. We give a new proof of this result that stays inside $β$-normal $η$-long typed terms and uses no completeness theorem: an induction that descends through both components of an isomorphism at once. It proceeds by showing that both components are linear terms: relevance follows from one of the inverse equations, and no copying from relevance of the other component. We then go one level up and prove a coherence theorem: two derivations of an isomorphism denote the same isomorphism if and only if they are equal modulo an explicit list of equations (groupoid laws, functoriality, involution, naturality and the braid equation), so these equations present the groupoid of isomorphisms, a hereditary version of the Coxeter presentation of the symmetric groups. All results are formalised in Agda, on intrinsically typed syntax with hereditary substitution, without postulates. The work is a case study for the syntactic completeness conjecture of University Algebra, a proposed solution of Tarski's high school algebra problem using dependent types, whose semantic counterpart is open. We explain the motivation and which parts of the method we expect to carry over.
Programming Languages.comment: v2: characterisation proved via linearity (relevance and no copying); Agda code tagged v2.0 at https://github.com/txa/stlc-iso"

Programming Languages.title: Obaleth: Build Your Own GPU Communication Stack
Programming Languages.summary: Machine learning systems specialize computation to the workload and hardware, but communication remains in generic libraries whose device code and transport decisions are not visible to high-level compilers. We present Obaleth, a compiler that makes GPU-initiated communication part of a kernel's intermediate representation, co-optimizes it alongside computation, and lowers it to specialized transport code. Obaleth plans completions around buffer lifetimes and optimizes memory ordering, synchronization, and batching across NVIDIA and AMD GPUs. On H100 GPUs, Obaleth sends small messages up to 3.3$\times$ faster, and on 256 GPUs runs all-to-all 1.25$\times$ and 2.3$\times$ faster than NVSHMEM and NCCL GIN, with much smaller memory and register use. In vLLM, it serves Qwen3-235B on 16 B200 GPUs and answers requests up to 1.29$\times$ faster than with DeepEP.
Programming Languages.comment: 20 pages, 13 figures, 6 tables. Equal contribution from first two authors. Code: https://github.com/ParCoreLab/aboleth

Programming Languages.title: Sheaf Semantics of Probabilistic Programs
Programming Languages.summary:
Finding denotational models of probabilistic languages that support sampling from continuous distributions is difficult: the existence of continuous distributions means that measure-theoretic objects are needed to define the semantics. A challenging task on top of this is logical reasoning with respect to the semantic model: in the case of probabilistic programs, the desired properties to reason about include the distributions, expected value and the probabilistic (in)dependence of outputs.
  This paper introduces a monadic semantics for higher-order probabilistic programs with continuous distributions based on Simpson's theory of probability sheaves and the internal logic of atomic sheaves. We prove that our semantics forms a model of the $ν$-calculus. Furthermore, using the well-behavedness of the semantic domain and the internal logic of the topos, we derive the first higher-order probabilistic Hoare logic with rigorous treatment of continuous random variables, higher-order functions, and independence.
Programming Languages.comment: Accepted to POPL 2027

Programming Languages.title: Ziv: A Language for Correctly Rounded Math Libraries
Programming Languages.summary:
Developing performant, correctly rounded math libraries is challenging. Such implementations often rely on extended-precision arithmetic for correct rounding and precomputed constants for performance. Existing implementation languages, however, provide limited support for (i) high-level abstractions for such arithmetic and (ii) staged computation to combine precomputation and runtime computation in one program. As a result, existing implementations often miss abstraction opportunities and hard-code constants precomputed using separate programs. These practices make it difficult to write, understand, and modify these libraries.
  We present Ziv, a programming system for developing correctly rounded math libraries. It consists of a small language, a rich standard library, and a provably sound compiler targeting C. Ziv supports (i) high-level numerical abstractions via types and operations for extended-precision numbers, and (ii) staged computation via compile-time evaluation of expressions known to be input-independent. These features enable high-level code that unifies precomputation and runtime computation. We embed Ziv in Julia and evaluate it by reimplementing 19 functions from two state-of-the-art libraries targeting correct rounding; we achieve competitive performance with 2.63$\times$ reductions in lines of code. We also implement three new functions and automatically explore 824,256 variants, achieving 96.5$\times$ average speedup over an arbitrary-precision library.
Programming Languages.comment: 44 pages, 23 figures, 3 tables, including appendices

Programming Languages.title: What Field Enumeration Costs to Compile in C++26: Native Reflection, Structured-Binding Packs, Reflection Libraries and Hand-Written Serializers on GCC 16
Programming Languages.summary: C++26 adds standard ways to enumerate a struct's fields, among them static reflection (P2996, with P3394 annotations) and structured-binding packs (P1061), alongside hand-written code, X-macros and libraries (Boost.PFR, reflect-cpp, Glaze) that now ship pre-C++26 and C++26 paths. We time each in a struct serializer with byte-identical output on GCC 16.2.0, at the front end and at -O2, in randomized interleaved rounds with code-level checks of every single-factor contrast. At the front end, inline native enumeration in the form used in several of P2996's own examples, an expansion statement over the std::span of define_static_array, costs about as much per struct of 16 scalar fields as Boost.PFR and 7.96x a P1061 pack, itself about as cheap as hand-written code. The same loop over a constant array costs 0.47x as much: about half of the span form's cost comes with the span. The ratio to P1061 shrinks on a heterogeneous type graph and at -O2. In a whole translation unit at the front end the library outweighs the mechanism: 200 structs take 0.59 s with inline native enumeration, 0.56 s with Boost.PFR and 3.86-4.13 s with the C++26 paths of reflect-cpp and Glaze, whose visitors also compute field names. Per type, each library's C++26 path is cheaper than its pre-C++26 path at 16 fields, but Glaze's gain reverses at 128 fields (pinned release v9.1.0); Boost.PFR's C++17 path grows almost quadratically with the number of types. Hand-written serializers sharing one overloaded name grow superlinearly with the number of types. The -freflection flag alone makes reflection-free code up to 1.264x costlier per type on GCC 16.2.0 and up to 2.578x on 16.1.0, so comparisons between mechanisms depend on the point release. Part of the span form's cost grows with the number of structs, which we trace to GCC registering block-scope statics in quadratic time (reported as GCC PR128928).
Programming Languages.comment: 21 pages, 5 figures, 6 tables. Code, raw per-run data and analysis scripts: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24443567 (GitHub: https://github.com/DenysKachalenko/CPP26FieldEnumerationCompileCostArtifact)

Programming Languages.title: Tenon: A Unified Programming Framework for Retargetable PIM Compilation
Programming Languages.summary: Processing-in-memory (PIM) is emerging as a building block of heterogeneous systems for memory-bound workloads, and commercial prototypes now span near-bank SIMD engines, bank-level GDDR accelerators, programmable DRAM cores, and bit-level in-SRAM processors. Their programming stacks are fragmented: no abstraction or compiler is shared across vendors, and per-device models range from instruction sequences to C-like languages. Data layout further complicates the problem: tight compute-memory integration makes data layout a first-order optimization, yet existing PIM compilers lack a unified way to represent and optimize it. A key observation is that PIM compilation targets can be modeled as nested grids of compute and storage units connected by legal data-transfer paths. We present Tenon, a unified programming framework for retargetable PIM compilation. It decouples workload, compilation target, and cost specifications, so a workload is expressed once and compiled through a unified programming framework. Tenon generalizes the $\mathbb{F}_2$ linear layout algebra from GPU compilers to map logical work and data onto these compute and storage grids. It automatically constructs a minimum-movement data layout given a workload and a target specification. We evaluate Tenon on six PIM backends: five commercial backends and AttAcc, a state-of-the-art academic HBM-based PIM architecture. Across the commercial backends, it matches or outperforms vendor, expert, and compiler baselines, with geometric-mean speedups of up to $1.20\times$ and individual speedups up to $3.65\times$. For end-to-end GPT-13B decoding on AttAcc, Tenon-compiled workloads run $1.2$--$1.3\%$ faster than those compiled by DCC, a state-of-the-art PIM compiler, across all three batch-4 configurations. Together, these results demonstrate Tenon's performance portability across diverse PIM target families.
Programming Languages.comment: HPCA 2027

Programming Languages.title: StatClaim: Study Designs as Types, Protocols as Programs and Statistical Claims as Proof Obligations
Programming Languages.summary: Statistical guarantees depend on the compatibility of a study's model, hypotheses, sampling plan and analysis. StatClaim is a declarative domain-specific language for encoding research protocols and statistical analysis plans as programs built from objects whose types encode their statistical roles within the study design. The compiler checks type compatibility and applies contracts to check additional requirements on the values and relationships of these objects. When verification is requested, StatClaim's backend constructs and checks proofs of supported statistical claims using Lean under stated assumptions. These claims concern Type I error, familywise error, power and interval coverage, including supported combinations of analyses and procedures with planned stopping rules. Reports distinguish formally proved, conditional, cited and author-declared guarantees and provide replayable certificates for verified claims. The same specification supports sample-size searches, power calculations and interval-precision assessment using exact calculations, analytical approximations or reproducible simulation. A command-line interface, editor integration and graphical block editor use a shared compiler and execution layer. Validation reproduces 102 optimal and minimax two-stage designs from Simon's published tables and verifies their error and power bounds in Lean. A clinical trial case study illustrates partial encoding of a published analysis plan using cited methods and conditional proofs. The open-source implementation includes runnable tutorials and examples for specifying and checking study designs before outcomes are collected.
Programming Languages.comment: 26 pages, 2 figures, 9 tables. Includes ancillary example programs and replication helpers

Programming Languages.title: Compositional Symbolic Execution à la Carte (Extended Version)
Programming Languages.summary: We introduce compositional symbolic execution à la carte, a modular approach for building compositional symbolic execution (CSE) tools, powered by combinator-based design of key components, including memory models, management and automation of user-defined predicates, and bi-abductive analysis. Our approach is grounded on meta-theory mechanised in the Rocq proof assistant and allows tool developers to easily build correct-by-construction CSE tools for symbolic analysis of their programming languages of choice, with minimal implementation and proof effort. We show how our approach scales to real-world languages by implementing it in Gillian, a state-of-the-art CSE tool, and using it to capture the intricacies of the memory models of C, JavaScript, and Rust. We evaluate our approach by running all of the relevant previous case studies of Gillian, showing no unexpected behaviours and comparable performance.
Programming Languages.comment: Extended version, with appendices, of the corresponding POPL'27 paper

Programming Languages.title: Omnidirectional type inference for ML: principality any way
Programming Languages.summary:
The Damas-Hindley-Milner (ML) type system owes its success to principality, the property that every well-typed expression has a unique most general type. This makes inference predictable and efficient. Unfortunately, many extensions of ML (GADTs, higher-rank polymorphism, and static overloading) endanger princpality by introducing _fragile_ constructs that resist principal inference. Existing approaches recover principality through directional inference algorithms, which propagate _known_ type information in a fixed (or static) order (e.g. as in bidirectional typing) to disambiguate such constructs. However, the rigidity of a static inference order often causes otherwise well-typed programs to be rejected.
  We propose _omnidirectional_ type inference, where type information flows in a dynamic order. Typing constraints may be solved in any order, suspending when progress requires known type information and resuming once it becomes available, using _suspended match constraints_. This approach is straightforward for simply typed systems, but extending it to ML is challenging due to let-generalization. Existing ML inference algorithms type let-bindings (let x = e1 in e2) in a fixed order: type e1, generalize its type, and then type e2. To overcome this, we introduce _incremental instantiation_, allowing partially solved type schemes containing suspended constraints to be instantiated, with a mechanism to incrementally update instances as the scheme is refined.
  Omnidirectionality provides a general framework for restoring principality in the presence of fragile features. We demonstrate its versatility on two fundamentally different features of OCaml: static overloading of record labels and datatype constructors and semi-explicit first-class polymorphism. In both cases, we obtain a principal type inference algorithm that is more expressive than OCaml's current typechecker.
Programming Languages.comment: updated to reflect the final TOPLAS version; 46 pages + appendices

Programming Languages.title: CrossCheck II: A Compiler Plugin for Certified Cost Bounds of Real-Time C and C++ Code, and its Evaluation
Programming Languages.summary: We describe a plugin for the Clang compiler that bounds the cost of C and C++ functions intended for real-time use, and rejects at compile time the functions that allocate, throw, call through pointers, or contain a loop or a recursion for which no bound is found. Loops are bounded by affine ranking potentials synthesized with an SMT solver through Farkas' Lemma, or by logarithmic ones, recursion by depth and size potentials, and callees are analyzed in the calling context in which they are used. For functions in a linear fragment, the plugin emits a cost certificate that a checker, compiled from a Lean~4 definition proved sound in a companion paper, validates with integer arithmetic only; the bound then depends neither on the analyzer nor on the solver. On the 29 kernels of the TACLeBench collection, without annotations, the plugin bounds 142 of 220 loops in the calling contexts of the programs, 131 of them exactly as the benchmarks' flow facts, and 161 of the 165 bounded functions receive a certificate that the checker accepts, 152 of them also validated against an independent description of the source. On the CMSIS-DSP library for Cortex-M (786 functions), with assumed input ranges, it bounds 616 functions. We compare the loop bounds with loop counts observed by running the kernels and with five existing analyzers (LLVM's ScalarEvolution, KoAT2, CoFloCo, Infer and oRange), and the plugin with KoAT2 and CoFloCo on the C programs of the Termination and Complexity Competition: without annotations, 147 of 553 programs receive a certified bound that holds for all inputs, where the two tools bound 288 and 264. Loop bounds, exported annotations and the checker program are also tested on random programs and on mutated certificates.
Programming Languages.comment: 23 pages. Companion of "CrossCheck I" (doi:10.5281/zenodo.24444576), which holds the theory and the Lean proofs. Code, benchmarks and Lean formalization: doi:10.5281/zenodo.24425070

Programming Languages.title: CrossCheck I: Cost Bounds of Imperative Programs as Constrained Optimization, with a Sound Cost Logic and a Verified Certificate Checker
Programming Languages.summary: Static analysis of imperative programs often relies on iterative fixed-point approximations or concrete path exploration. We show that structured imperative control flow---while loops, linear recursion and branching recursion---can be mapped into constrained optimization problems over the free monoid of execution traces and the free algebra of computation trees. Ordering traces and trees by an intensional \textit{order-by-composition} ($\sqsubseteq$), halting is characterized as finding the minimal trace or tree that satisfies the exit condition, and we prove that this characterization coincides with the standard big-step semantics. Exact state recurrences are undecidable in general, so we relax them into cost envelopes, using ranking potentials and the tropical $(\max,+)$ reading of the timing schema, and obtain sound upper bounds on execution cost. The bounds compose over whole programs in a cost logic for a small language with nondeterministic actions, procedures, recursion and assumed contracts, which we prove sound for terminating and non-terminating executions. A linear instance of the logic has certificates---programs annotated with invariants, potentials and Farkas multipliers---and a checker that validates them with integer arithmetic only; an accepted certificate bounds the cost of every execution. All results, the checker and the worked examples are machine-checked in Lean~4. A companion paper describes a Clang plugin that produces such certificates and its evaluation.
Programming Languages.comment: 43 pages. Lean 4 formalization and code: doi:10.5281/zenodo.24425070

Formal Languages and Automata Theory.title: Complete Test Suites for Effectful Automata
Formal Languages and Automata Theory.summary:
Complete test suites for automata are (finite) sets of words that enable testing an implementation against a specification: when a (black-box) automaton passes the test suite, completeness guarantees that it is equivalent to the specification on all (infinitely many) words. A well-known method for constructing complete test suites for deterministic automata is the W-method, used in conformance testing and automata learning.
  Based on a recent categorical generalisation of the W-method, we propose a framework for~the construction and analysis of test suites for a certain class of effectful automata defined by commutative monads. By working in the Eilenberg-Moore category of the associated monad at hand, we obtain a generic notion of effectful W-method, together with a completeness theorem. We show how to apply the framework and derive complete test suites for non-deterministic and weighted automata.

Formal Languages and Automata Theory.title: Complexity of the Infinity and the Modulo-Counting Quantifiers in Automatic Structures
Formal Languages and Automata Theory.summary: Automatic structures allow us to decide their first-order theory using automata-theoretic techniques. The complexity of this decision problem for formulas in prenex normal form depends on the quantifier alternation depth, e.g., it is PSPACE-complete for formulas with quantifier-prefix $\exists\exists\cdots\exists$. Blumensath observed that the decidability also holds if one extends first-order logic with the infinity quantifier. His decision procedure introduces many more quantifier alternations such that, even for formulas with quantifier prefix $\exists^\infty\exists^\infty\cdots\exists^\infty$ of length $n$, his decision procedure runs in $(2n-1)$-fold exponential space. We show that this is not necessary. To be more precise, we prove that handling the infinity quantifier is not more costly than handling the existential quantifier. On the other hand, we also show that addition of the modulo-counting quantifier to first-order logic results in a much higher complexity.
Formal Languages and Automata Theory.comment: Appears in the Proceedings of the 52nd International Conference on Current Trends in Theory and Practice of Computer Science (Sofsem 2027)

Formal Languages and Automata Theory.title: Characterizing normality via automata and random matrix products
Formal Languages and Automata Theory.summary: For a fixed alphabet A, an infinite sequence X is said to be normal if every word w over A appears in X with the same frequency as any other word of the same length. A classical result relates normality to finite automata as follows: a sequence X is normal if and only if all gambling strategies implementable with finite deterministic automata lose all their capital when trying to predict the next bit of X after seing the ones before. More precisely, Schnorr and Stimm (1972) proved that the capital goes exponentially fast to zero unless the automaton represents the gambler that never bets, in which case the capital remains constant. In this paper we show that an analogous result holds when considering probabilistic automata: a sequence X is normal if and only if for any gambling strategy implementable with probabilistic finite automaton it holds that the expected value of the capital of the gambler converges exponentially fast to a finite value when playing against X. To obtain this result, we show a more general statement related to the convergence of martingales given by finite sets of non-negative matrices {M a } a$\in$A . In particular, we show that X is normal if and only if ||vM X[1] . . . M X[n] || converges exponentially fast to a finite value for any non-negative starting vector v. Moreover, we distinguish three distinctive behaviours that this sequence can attain, and prove that the problem of recognizing, given a family of matrices, to which case it belongs, is decidable.

Formal Languages and Automata Theory.title: Constant-Coin Complete-Information Debates for $\mathsf{P}$ with Arbitrarily Small Strong Error
Formal Languages and Automata Theory.summary: We study complete-information debate systems in which a probabilistic finite-state verifier reads the alternating messages of a prover and a refuter. Demirci, Say, and Yakaryılmaz showed that every language in $\mathsf{P}$ has such debates checkable with a constant number of random bits and arbitrarily small weak error. Their strong-error construction, which also counts nontermination as failure, did not permit arbitrary error reduction. We close this gap: for every $L\in\mathsf{P}$ and every $\varepsilon>0$, there is a constant-space verifier using a constant number of private coin tosses that has perfect completeness and strong error at most $\varepsilon$. The verifier simulates a polynomial-time alternating multihead finite automaton, privately spot-checking one of its input heads. The key observation is that, on a nonmember, the refuter may concede any round in which the prover first misreports a head reading. This ensures termination against every prover when the refuter follows the specified strategy, and permits strong-error reduction by repetition.
Formal Languages and Automata Theory.comment: Appears in the Proceedings of the 52nd International Conference on Current Trends in Theory and Practice of Computer Science (Sofsem 2027)

Formal Languages and Automata Theory.title: A characteristic-graph reduction for deterministic L-system inference with classical and quantum-heuristic solvers
Formal Languages and Automata Theory.summary: L-systems are widely used to model and simulate biological growth processes, including plant development. Motivated by the broader goal of automating L-system construction, this paper studies the formal deterministic context-free L-system (D0L-system) inference problem in which the input is a finite, noise-free sequence of strings. We introduce the characteristic graph of a string sequence and prove that the existence of a compatible D0L-system is equivalent to the existence of an independent set of a prescribed size in this graph. This gives polynomial reductions from D0L inference to maximum independent set (MIS) and SAT, and hence an exact classical decision route when combined with an exact MIS or SAT solver. We also describe a Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA)-based quantum heuristic for generating candidate independent sets. This heuristic is not a decision procedure for D0L inference, and failure of the heuristic is inconclusive rather than a certificate of nonexistence. We include computational validation on $22$ generated D0L traces and $8$ negative controls, explicitly incorporate known fixed-identity symbols, and report small statevector QAOA simulations. The quantum component is presented as a proof-of-concept candidate generator, not as a claimed quantum speedup; the immediately useful contribution is the characteristic-graph reduction and the exact classical/SAT decision framework it enables.
Formal Languages and Automata Theory.comment: 26 pages, 1 figure, 4 tables. Published in Research in the Mathematical Sciences (2026)

Symbolic Computation.title: Quasilinear multiplication in the Cayley-Dickson tower
Symbolic Computation.summary: Direct evaluation of the defining product of the Cayley-Dickson algebra $A_n$ of rank $N:=2^n$ requires a quadratic number of arithmetic operations. This paper gives a uniform bilinear algorithm that computes multiplication in $A_n$ over a unital commutative ring $R$ in which $2\in R^\times$ using $O(N\log N)$ arithmetic operations and $O(N)$ auxiliary storage, given $A_n$ is defined with doubling parameters that are units with square roots in a fixed commutative algebra finitely generated as an $R$-module admitting a linear surjection onto the base ring preserving the identity. These conditions are satisfied by every Cayley-Dickson tower over $\mathbb{R}$ and over finite fields of odd characteristic, where the tensor rank of multiplication in $A_n$ is at most $(36n-69)2^{n-3}+10$ for $n\ge4$. To the author's knowledge, this is the first uniform subquadratic algorithm for multiplication in $A_n$. In single-core benchmarks over $\mathbb{R}$, an open-source implementation in the library fastCD is approximately $17$ times faster than direct multiplication at $N=1024$.
Symbolic Computation.comment: 43 pages, 7 tables. v5: Updated the abstract; added content to the applications paragraph in the introduction; updated data and fastCD version in Section 5; updated disclosures in Section 7 and added a statement on code availability. Code: https://git.tanuki-cd.com/algebraity/fastCD

Symbolic Computation.title: So Many Ways to Multiply $3\times3$ Matrices: A Large Dataset of Rank-23 Schemes
Symbolic Computation.summary: A publicly available dataset of 62029 rank-23 schemes for $3\times3$ matrix multiplication is presented. Every scheme in it has its own rank pattern, an invariant formed by the ranks of the factor matrices of a scheme, so all schemes are pairwise inequivalent. The schemes were obtained by a numerical method combining gradient descent with alternating least squares and by flip graph search, and have ternary, integer or rational coefficients. Rank 23 is the best known for this format and is optimal for schemes with integer coefficients, but the number of essentially different schemes of this rank was poorly understood: the existing collections of Heule et al. and Mårtensson et al. contain many schemes that share only a small number of rank patterns (17376 schemes with 387 patterns and 15316 schemes with 568 patterns respectively). The dataset shows that the number of different rank patterns is much larger than previously known.

Symbolic Computation.title: Vitrify Exact Learning: exact differential equations, changes of variable and closed forms from numerical data
Symbolic Computation.summary: Symbolic regression searches a space of expression trees for a formula that fits data. Many functions of the sciences have no finite expression over the usual operations and still satisfy a linear differential equation with polynomial coefficients. Vitrify Exact Learning takes nu- merical values of a function and proceeds in three steps. It assumes that the function, in its own variable or after a change of variable or a pushforward of a density, is annihilated by an operator with polynomial coefficients. It finds that operator as the null vector of a matrix of weak-form measurements, in which the data are integrated against test functions and never differentiated, makes the coefficients exact, and tests the exact operator on data that the fit did not read against a noise level propagated from the data. It then solves the exact operator symbolically and keeps the closed form that matches the data. Each step has precedent; the combination takes values on an interval, from a quadrature, a float64 table or a sample, to an exact equation and a closed form. On noise-free benchmarks it recovers 45 of 53 classic targets, 108 of the 120 AI Feynman equations and 74.1% of the Feynman problems of SR- Bench, against 33, 69 and 55.8% for the best other programs, and 50 of 132 special-function targets generated after its code was frozen, against 23. From 40-digit values it returns Meijer G densities, hypergeometric forms for the deflection of light by a black hole, and Appell and Lauricella functions of two variables. With noise in several variables, with sparse data and for equations above fourth order it mostly returns no model.

Symbolic Computation.title: Parallelizing Complex Matrix Multiplication: The 3M Solution
Symbolic Computation.summary: We consider the problem of computing the product of two matrices with complex entries, a kernel used in quantum chemistry, electromagnetic simulation, quantum circuit simulation, and FFT-based methods. Standard practice already restructures the local computation using the classical \emph{3M} (Gauss/Karatsuba) identity, computing the product from three real matrix multiplications instead of four, dropping arithmetic by $25\%$ unconditionally but leaving communication unchanged. We show that whether 3M is worth doing at all, and whether it is additionally worth restructuring communication to get more of it by computing the three products \emph{in parallel} on disjoint processor groups, are independent questions, and we answer each in closed form under a standard $α$-$β$-$γ$ communication model. Under this model, for 2D layouts, in the large-$P$ limit, parallelizing the split reduces bandwidth by $13.4\%$ and latency by $1-1/\sqrt3\approx42.3\%$, the latter independent of the underlying algorithm's arithmetic exponent; neither reduction is achieved for 3D. For Strassen's algorithm the arithmetic picture reverses: restructuring locally is $7.1\%$ \emph{worse}, not better. We further generalize to Toom-Cook-$k$, giving a closed-form condition, increasing in $k$, under which higher-order splits rescue 3D layouts entirely: for instance, $k=3$ already makes 3D favorable for classical matrix multiplication, where the ordinary $k=2$ split never does.

Symbolic Computation.title: Ramanujan Challenge Results: AI-Assisted Evaluation Pipeline for Multi-Format Proofs
Symbolic Computation.summary: As AI's mathematical capabilities rapidly improve, meaningful benchmarks are shifting from university-level problems and math olympiads to research-level mathematics. The Ramanujan Challenge is a benchmark comprised of research-level problems in number theory, including unpublished results and open conjectures. It presented concrete formulas for mathematical constants whose correctness can be checked numerically, while their proofs may require non-obvious mathematics. Here, we analyze the Challenge submissions, measuring the relative success of different AI models, Computer Algebra Systems (CAS), and formal tools. We find correct submissions that are conceptually distinct from the official solutions, and a proof of one of the published open conjectures. Evaluating the submissions exposed a second challenge: judging complex proofs reliably at scale. We introduce an AI-assisted evaluation pipeline for natural language proofs, CAS code, and Lean formalizations that assesses semantic and logical correctness. Compared with the conventional one-shot LLM judgment, our pipeline reduces false-positive verdicts on natural language proofs from 23% to 6% and improves judgment accuracy on supporting code from 46% to 58%. This approach provides a methodology for evaluating research-level mathematics at scale, with potential applications across mathematics and AI for science.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: Pruning Autonomous Driving VLAs: What to Preserve for Reasoning and Action
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Reasoning vision-language-action (VLA) models for autonomous driving use chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning to guide action generation, but incur substantial memory and computational costs. We study structured pruning for these models, focusing on preserving both scene understanding and trajectory prediction. Our analysis of Taylor importance in Alpamayo-1.5-10B shows that reasoning and trajectory objectives assign different importance to the same vision-language model (VLM) structures. In the action expert, MLP channels exhibit more stable importance rankings across denoising steps than query heads, and a small fraction of channels accounts for most of the measured importance. Based on these findings, we propose MoOP, which combines importance ranks from both objectives for VLM pruning and aggregates stepwise importance to select a fixed subset of expert MLP channels. At 24.0% total parameter reduction, VLM-only pruning with MoOP performs comparably to or slightly better than the strongest baselines in driving, while retaining 94.0% of the dense model's LingoQA score, far above all other methods. At a higher reduction of 30.0%, MoOP degrades much less than every other method, as it is the only one whose reasoning does not collapse. Removing 93.75% of expert MLP channels increases total parameter reduction to 39.4%, with nearly unchanged open-loop errors relative to VLM-only pruning and competitive closed-loop performance. The resulting model achieves a 1.37x end-to-end inference speedup and 36.6% lower peak memory than the dense model, without post-pruning fine-tuning.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: Super-resolved digital terrain models for GEDI geolocation correction: agreement with airborne LiDAR DTM-based corrections at the beam level, not the footprint level
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: The Global Ecosystem Dynamics Investigation (GEDI) mission measures three-dimensional forest structure with a LiDAR instrument aboard the International Space Station. GEDI observations have geolocation errors of about 10 m, which cause misalignment with other remote sensing data and reduce the accuracy of downstream tasks. Matching GEDI ground elevations against high-resolution digital terrain models (DTMs) from airborne LiDAR is one way to correct these errors, but such DTMs exist in few regions. To widen this method's applicability, we super-resolved a more widely available low-resolution DTM for elevation matching. We ask whether a super-resolved DTM yields the same correction as a 1 m-resolution airborne LiDAR DTM and, if not, why. In steep forests of western Japan, we super-resolved an existing 10 m-resolution DTM to 1 m. Additionally fusing a global 30 m-resolution DTM from a different source substantially improved the accuracy. Using the resulting DTM, we corrected GEDI observation positions first by a single offset per ground track, then point by point. For most tracks, the per-track corrections nearly agreed with those from the airborne LiDAR DTM. Point-by-point corrections, however, did not agree. This was because the error of the generated DTM was close to the elevation differences that point-by-point correction must resolve, and most of this error lay at scales that even a 10 m-resolution DTM can represent. Under similar conditions, a super-resolved DTM may be usable in place of a 1 m-resolution DTM for per-track correction, but improving the accuracy, or using it for point-by-point correction as well, requires reducing the error at these scales rather than reproducing fine relief.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: Lyris: Layout-Guided Long Video Generation with Persistent 3D Memory
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Exploring a scene from as little as a single photo requires generating a long, camera-controlled walkthrough that extends far beyond what was captured, yet remains consistent upon return. Memory-based video generation methods preserve what they have already seen, but have no anchor beyond it, where the camera drifts from its path and a text prompt can name objects but not place them. Layout-conditioned methods provide such an anchor and precise control over what appears where, but rely on layouts that are typically authored by hand. Both limitations arise because, beyond what was captured, nothing anchors the video model unless a human authors one. To overcome both, we propose Lyris, a long video generation framework that never leaves the video model without an anchor: a persistent point-cloud memory where the scene has been observed or generated, and a 3D layout that a vision-language model authors where it has not. Our key insight is that the interface between the two models can be surprisingly coarse. A layout of one labeled 3D box per object is simple enough for a vision-language model to author (and for a user to edit), yet expressive enough for a video model to follow once rendered along the camera path. We demonstrate walkthroughs of over three minutes and 50 meters from a single photo, passing through doorways into rooms it never shows. When evaluated on minute-long round trips across four datasets, Lyris outperforms state-of-the-art methods by a wide margin, reducing camera error by 3.8x and improving consistency upon return by 22% on average.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: Modern Self-Supervised Vision Transformers Are Pareidolic
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: In human perception, pareidolia is the tendency to perceive a meaningful pattern, such as a face, in a random or ambiguous stimulus.We find a similar phenomenon in modern self-supervised Vision Transformers (ViTs): on white noise, which contains neither objects nor spatial structure, a few directions of their features still form spatially coherent patterns across the patches, imposed by the features themselves.We call this behavior pareidolia, and the span of these directions the pareidolic subspace.On natural images, it holds most of the feature variance in DINOv2 and DINOv3 but little in DINO.This excess explains why DINOv2 and DINOv3, despite stronger dense features, fall far behind DINO in object emergence, the hallmark ability of self-supervised ViTs to identify the patches of an object on their own.Our experiments further show that scaling down their pareidolic subspaces steadily restores their ability to discover objects, so their object emergence is hindered rather than lost.These findings naturally lead to a training-free calibration: Pareidolia Subspace Calibration(PSC) measures the pareidolic subspace only on a noise input and then calibrates the features of natural inputs by scaling its directions down to the variance level of the remaining directions.Across diverse object emergence tasks, PSC improves DINOv2 and DINOv3 by up to 31.7 CorLoc on object discovery, 30.2 maxF on saliency detection and 59.9~$\mathcal{J}$ on video object segmentation.To identify the cause of pareidolia, we trace it block by block and find that it forms in the middle blocks of every self-supervised model we examine but stays strong to the last block only in models trained with a patch-level loss; controlled training confirms that an image-level loss alone lets it fade.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: Let Vision-Language Models Generate Images through Their Representations
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Recent unified multimodal models aim to combine visual understanding and generation within a single model, yet effectively integrating the two capabilities remains challenging. Leveraging pretrained vision-language models offers a way to build on already learned multimodal knowledge, but making this knowledge effectively accessible to visual generation remains nontrivial. We find that a central challenge lies in the heterogeneous visual representations used for understanding and generation. To address this challenge, we introduce Integral, which converts a pretrained vision-language model into a unified multimodal model by constructing a shared visual representation space across the two capabilities. Integral implements this design through two complementary components. Abstraction Fusion constructs shared visual tokens by aggregating hierarchical representations from the frozen vision encoder, while Block-wise MoT introduces a lightweight generative stream that interacts with the vision-language model only at block boundaries. Our approach effectively preserves the pretrained understanding capability while extending it to strong visual generation. Controlled comparisons further demonstrate that sharing visual representations between understanding and generation substantially improves generative learning compared with using a separate visual representation space, despite comparable reconstruction fidelity. These results suggest that representations learned by pretrained vision-language models already provide an effective foundation for visual generation.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: TowerBridge: Bridging the Dual-Encoder Modality Gap via Weight-Space Programming
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: CLIP-style dual encoders map images and text through two separate towers into a shared embedding space, where the two modalities occupy distinct regions separated by a modality gap. Retrieval fails when wrong matches, or hard negatives, outrank the correct one, and the gap is the usual suspect. Yet removing it post hoc degrades retrieval on every CLIP checkpoint we test. We introduce a paired statistic that identifies directions where the two towers agree more on hard negatives than on matched pairs. Mildly attenuating these directions improves retrieval while largely preserving the gap. We arrive at this correction through weight-space programming: guided by the statistic, an LLM agent inspects both towers and writes closed-form weight edits without backpropagation. Free to edit any component, the agent improves COCO test retrieval on all 13 CLIP checkpoints and edits an output projection in 12 of the 13. We distill and refine its recurring correction into TowerBridge, a closed-form recipe motivated by a first-order analysis of the hard-negative margin. Computed in seconds from 25,000 labelled pairs, it requires no model-specific tuning and leaves the architecture and inference cost unchanged. TowerBridge improves COCO test retrieval by 16.8 RSUM and Flickr30k test retrieval by 6.6 on average across all 21 evaluated CLIP checkpoints, including 8 unseen by the agent, while limiting any drop in ImageNet zero-shot accuracy to 0.5 points. It also reduces hubness on all 21 checkpoints and improves retrieval on 4 of 5 dual encoders from other families.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: Self-Supervised Dataset Distillation via Mutual Information Maximization
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Dataset distillation (DD) aims to compress a large dataset into a small synthetic one that remains effective for training neural networks. Despite its success in supervised learning, DD remains underexplored in self-supervised learning (SSL), where distilled data must preserve the information needed to learn representations that remain consistent across augmentations. To bridge this gap, we introduce Mutual Information Prototype Alignment (MIPA), an efficient SSL dataset distillation approach that optimizes synthetic images to preserve augmentation-invariant information. Specifically, MIPA treats synthetic images as learnable prototypes and uses a frozen encoder to assign real samples to them based on feature similarity. A synthetic dataset that preserves such augmentation invariance should yield stable prototype assignments across multiple augmented views of the same real image. MIPA encourages this by maximizing mutual information between cross-view assignments while avoiding trivial solutions in which all real samples are assigned to only a few synthetic prototypes. Evaluations on image classification benchmarks show that synthetic data generated by MIPA yield higher-quality representations than existing distillation approaches while reducing time and storage demands during distillation.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: CTLink: A Text-Prompted Segmentation Model for Linking Radiology Report Findings to 3D Chest CT Scans
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Radiology reports describe findings in text only, without visually marking them on the scan, so readers cannot directly see which abnormality each reported finding refers to. We introduce CTLink, a text-prompted 3D segmentation model that segments findings described in a chest CT report. CTLink was trained on 4123 noncontrast chest CT scans with 9547 segmented report findings, including ReXGroundingCTv2, a newly annotated dataset of 1134 scans and 1895 findings with every instance of each finding segmented. On the 200 ReXGroundingCT validation scans, CTLink achieved a hit rate of 0.816, an instance F1 score of 0.456, and a mean Dice score of 0.400, compared with 0.533, 0.175, and 0.234 for VoxTell, a publicly available text-prompted segmentation model (P < .001 for all). On the test set of the MICCAI 2026 ReXGrounding challenge, an ensemble of seven CTLink models achieved the highest hit rate (0.782) and instance F1 score (0.386) of all 48 participating teams. On 50 test scans segmented twice by independent radiologists, CTLink matched or exceeded inter-rater agreement. Diffuse non-focal findings remained the main limitation, partly because their extent is outlined inconsistently even between radiologists. The CTLink model weights are available at https://huggingface.co/rajpurkarlab/CTLink, and the dataset at https://huggingface.co/datasets/rajpurkarlab/ReXGroundingCT.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: LeJEPA Features Are Not Isotropic, and Should Not Be
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: The SIGReg term in LeJEPA regularizes features to have an isotropic Gaussian distribution. Our first result is to show that this regularizer, in practice, cannot achieve its goal. We design a modified regularizer to enforce the objective better. This leads to slightly improved performance. For example, on ImageNet-100, our modified regularizer reaches the final accuracy of SIGReg in 1.3$\times$ fewer epochs. Our second result argues that self-supervised encoders should not have isotropic Gaussian features. We show that the alignment term in LeJEPA conflicts with SIGReg, because it couples the magnitude of the features with their directions. In contrast, isotropic Gaussian features would entail independent magnitude and directions. Features obtained with LeJEPA are, in fact, not isotropic. So LeJEPA has two issues. Its regularizer is weak, and the isotropic Gaussian target is too strict. Our third result is about reformulating the isotropic Gaussian regularizer to enforce only the marginal distributions of the magnitude and direction, without enforcing independence. This leads to a simple regularization term, PolarReg, that can be optimized reliably across many different datasets, batch sizes and embedding dimensions without any hyper-parameter changes. On ImageNet-1k, our technique matches the accuracy of LeJEPA and its variants in 4.7$\times$ fewer epochs. It improves the final accuracy by 1.8 points.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: Neural Field Thermal Tomography: A Differentiable Physics Framework for Non-Destructive Evaluation
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Inverse problems for stiff parabolic partial differential equations (PDEs), such as the inverse heat conduction problem (IHCP), are severely ill-posed: the forward map rapidly damps high-frequency interior structure before it reaches the boundary. Soft-constrained physics-informed neural networks (PINNs), which embed the PDE as a residual penalty, decouple the diffusivity from the surface data in their standard two-network inverse formulation, and the evaluated variants fit boundary measurements while leaving the interior field essentially untouched. We propose Neural Field Thermal Tomography (NeFTY), a hard-constrained neural field framework for label-free three-dimensional inverse heat conduction. NeFTY represents the unknown diffusivity as a continuous coordinate-based neural network, and at every optimization step passes the candidate field through a differentiable implicit-Euler heat solver with harmonic-mean interface flux, so that the simulated temperature satisfies the discretized heat equation up to the solver tolerance. Adjoint gradients propagate the surface reconstruction error back to the network weights at solver-level memory cost, making test-time inversion tractable on a single GPU. Across synthetic 3D benchmarks, NeFTY outperforms soft-constrained PINN variants, a voxel-grid baseline, and classical L-BFGS voxel inversion through the same solver on label-free volumetric recovery, and it transfers to real thermography data, surpassing classical signal-processing baselines in both defect segmentation and depth estimation. Additional details at https://cab-lab-princeton.github.io/nefty/

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: WorldLatent: A Unified 4D Latent Space for World Perception and Generation
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Generative Pre-Training (GPT) represents a profound milestone in natural language processing, serving as the foundation for most of today's state-of-the-art large language models. By casting diverse understanding and generation problems into a shared token representation, GPT enables a single architecture and unified optimization loop to master heterogeneous tasks across massive corpora, giving rise to powerful foundation models for natural language. In contrast, 4D spatiotemporal vision lacks a common representational protocol: perception (such as depth and camera estimation) and generation are either handled by separate one-way pipelines or bolted together from unaligned single-modality spaces. In this work, we introduce WorldLatent, a framework that formulates a unified 4D latent space as a common protocol for both world perception and generation. Rather than relying on fragmented, task-specific models or stacked single-modality representations, our framework proposes a multimodal VAE architecture that compresses and fuses complex 4D visual appearance, geometry, and dynamics into a single structured latent representation. Within this formulation, perception and generation operate as complementary denoising processes over the same latent space, enabling one generative model to learn both capabilities simultaneously within a single training loop. Experiments across representative 4D benchmarks verify that our fused latent protocol achieves specialist-level zero-shot 4D perception, coherent 4D generation, and controllable editing from a single model. By demonstrating that diverse 4D tasks can be seamlessly unified under a shared representational protocol, our work provides a scalable foundation for general-purpose 4D spatial intelligence.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: ToolSmith: An Automatic Tool-Generation Framework for Multimodal Search Agents
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Recent multimodal search agents use reasoning, vision, and live web search across many turns to answer questions beyond parametric knowledge by orchestrating a small library of hand-crafted search and visual tools. However, the library is laborious to create and maintain, and frozen when new query types, evidence formats, and failure modes are encountered in the wild. Human practitioners, by contrast, cope with insufficient tools by fashioning new ones from familiar parts and reusing them across tasks. Inspired by this, we propose ToolSmith, an automatic tool-generation framework that grows and reuses modules on top of a lean base tool library. We evaluate ToolSmith on three in-domain multimodal search benchmarks and ten out-of-domain benchmarks under a VLM-as-a-Judge protocol. ToolSmith consistently improves over the base library across deployed agents of varying scales, with larger backbones reaping greater gains, demonstrating the scalability of the approach. Our code and data are available at https://threesr.github.io/toolsmith/.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: EditThinker: Enhancing Image Editors via Iterative Reasoning with a Plug-and-Play VLM
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Image editors can produce realistic images while still failing to satisfy the requested changes. Improving their instruction following requires identifying these failures and translating visual feedback into instructions that the editor can execute. We introduce EditThinker, an 8B vision-language model (VLM) that enhances existing image editors through iterative reasoning while keeping their weights fixed. EditThinker jointly critiques semantic consistency and visual quality, reasons about editing failures, and refines the instruction in a structured response.
