Compared with Action Loss OPD and Teacher-rollout SFT, it achieves absolute success-rate gains of 6.4-9.5% on LIBERO-40, 9.7-18.3% on CALVIN, and 3.2-4.2% on Meta-World MT50. Analysis by sequence length further shows larger success-rate gains on longer CALVIN sequences. These results demonstrate effective multi-domain capability consolidation through two-level on-policy supervision, with a single student deployed across domains.
Robotics.comment: 13 pages, 6 figures, 4 tables. Includes supplementary material

Robotics.title: Beyond Which: Where, How, and When in Vision-Language-Action Models
Robotics.summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) models typically rely on vision-language model (VLM) features as the primary perceptual source for action prediction, showing strong generalization across diverse robotic manipulation tasks. Although VLM features can identify which entities are relevant to action prediction, precise manipulation also requires understanding where task-relevant entities are located within the spatial layout, how their geometric structure constrains physical interaction, and when spatial or geometric information should make a greater contribution to action prediction. To this end, we introduce {\mathcal{W}^{3}\mathcal{H}}-VLA to organize VLA perception and action prediction around which, where, how, and when. Specifically, {\mathcal{W}^{3}\mathcal{H}}-VLA retains VLM-based semantic entity perception which and further introduces spatial distance perception where and geometric structure perception how with adaptive spatial-geometric guidance when to enrich the perceptual information available for action prediction. Experiments across real-world settings and simulation benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness and superior performance of {\mathcal{W}^{3}\mathcal{H}}-VLA.

Robotics.title: SGPC: Safety-Guiding Policy Constraint for Stable Off-Policy Safe Reinforcement Learning
Robotics.summary: Off-policy safe reinforcement learning (RL) faces a challenging trade-off between task optimality and constraint feasibility. In primal-dual methods, the coupled optimization of cumulative reward and constraint penalties through adaptive Lagrange multipliers may induce oscillatory policy updates near the safety boundary and amplify the effect of unreliable reward estimates outside the safe set. To address these issues, we formulate a new constrained optimization problem (COP) for safe RL by introducing a Safety-Guiding Policy (SGP) and a corresponding Safety-Guiding Policy Constraint (SGPC). The proposed COP augments the standard COP in safe RL with a conditional safety-guidance constraint. During actor updates, the current actor is evaluated using the learned cost critic. If it is predicted to be outside the safe set, SGP provides a nearby lower-cost training reference, and SGPC guides actor optimization toward this reference. Once the policy enters the safe set, the added constraint becomes inactive, and the formulation reduces to the original COP. This formulation leads to a plug-in actor-training constraint that can be integrated into off-policy safe RL algorithms. By applying primal-dual optimization to the auxiliary COP, we finally derive an SGPC-based off-policy safe RL algorithm and implement it in two representative off-policy algorithms, yielding SAC-SGPC and TD3-SGPC. Experiments on multiple Safety-Gymnasium benchmarks demonstrate that SGPC achieves a better optimality-safety trade-off by substantially reducing constraint violations and cost oscillations while maintaining competitive or better task returns.

Robotics.title: Skill-Adaptive Noise Scheduling for Diffusion Policies
Robotics.summary: Recent advances in diffusion policies have demonstrated strong effectiveness when integrated into hierarchical skill-based learning frameworks, leveraging offline data to capture multimodal and temporally abstracted behaviors. However, prior approaches have rarely considered the diffusion process as a learnable component, adopting fixed noise schedules applied uniformly across skills, regardless of their distinct behavioral contexts. Such a design fundamentally limits the achievable performance, particularly for contact-rich and dexterous manipulation tasks where different skills exhibit distinct couplings between action dimensions. In this paper, we present a skill-adaptive noise diffusion framework (SaND) which introduces a learnable, skill-conditioned noise schedule that modulates the diffusion process per action dimension, adapting the noising dynamics to each skill. To prevent the learned noise schedule from collapsing into trivial solutions, we employ an auxiliary inverse objective that reconstructs the skill embedding from the Legendre coefficients of the derivative of the noise schedule, encouraging the schedules to remain skill-discriminative. This formulation naturally enables adaptive control over the denoising steps for each skill, where noise schedules are clustered in the Legendre coefficient space, and the appropriate number of denoising steps is determined at the point where reconstruction error abruptly increases. At inference, we identify each skill embedding's cluster from its noise schedule and apply the corresponding number of denoising steps, dedicating more compute to skills requiring fine-grained control and less to simpler ones. In simulation and on real robot hardware, SaND outperforms existing skill learning and planning baselines on contact-rich and dexterous manipulation tasks, achieving higher success rates while requiring fewer denoising steps.
Robotics.comment: 40th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026)

Robotics.title: Innata-0: A Native Embodied World System with Model-Agent Co-Design
Robotics.summary: The physical world is open-ended, dynamic, and partially observable. While foundation models have advanced embodied intelligence, standalone models struggle with long-horizon execution, and simply integrating models with agents may lead to inconsistencies between planning and physical control. To support reliable and adaptive behaviors in the physical world, we introduce Innata-0, a native embodied world system. Innata-0 jointly designs an embodied world-action model and an agent to combine their complementary strengths. The model, Innata-0-WAM, adopts a tri-tower Mixture-of-Transformers architecture that integrates understanding, prediction, and action generation. The agent, Innata-0-Agent, coordinates long-horizon execution through memory, verification, and recovery. A co-design protocol is further proposed to align model training with agent execution and leverage validated experiences to support subsequent adaptation and model improvement. Extensive evaluations demonstrate strong embodied capabilities across understanding, world prediction, and robotic manipulation. Innata-0 represents our first step toward physical intelligence, and we see it as the beginning of a much longer journey.

Robotics.title: RankFormer: A Propose-then-Select Transformer for Multi-Agent Multimodal Trajectory Prediction
Robotics.summary: Predicting traffic agent trajectories plays an important role in autonomous driving, traffic operations, transportation safety analysis, etc. Although many deep learning algorithms are devised to predict future agent trajectories, the trajectory prediction problem is still challenging due to the complexity of decision-making process, interactions with surrounding vehicles, and the existence of multiple possible intentions for the traveling agents even under similar scenarios. Most existing methods are limited by the requirement of graph structures (e.g., Graph Neural Network) or the requirement of manually labeled intentions. In this study, we propose a pure Transformer-based deep learning model for multi-modal trajectory prediction considering temporal dependencies and agent-agent spatial interactions. After encoding the historical trajectories, two parallel decoders are employed to generate trajectories and probabilities on separate decoder tracks. The model is evaluated on two real-world datasets, one highway dataset and the other pedestrian dataset with solid performance. One important insight is that following a ``propose-then-select'' strategy, the agent-agent spatial interactions are only considered for probability estimation instead of trajectory generation. In summary, the proposed model provides a potential direction to design more robust and effective multi-modal trajectory prediction models.

Robotics.title: Neural 3D Object Reconstruction with Small-Scale Unmanned Aerial Vehicles
Robotics.summary: Miniaturized Uncrewed Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) can access indoor and hard-to-reach spaces, but severe constraints on payload and autonomy have limited their use in demanding tasks such as high-quality 3D reconstruction. We introduce a novel system architecture that enables autonomous, high-fidelity 3D scanning of static objects with sub-100 gram UAVs. Our core innovation lies in a closed-loop active viewpoint selection framework specifically tailored for ultra-constrained micro-platforms, advancing beyond standard static or offline active reconstruction methods. The framework establishes a dual-reconstruction pipeline that creates a real-time (RT) feedback loop between data capture and flight control. A near-RT process uses Structure-from-Motion (SfM) to generate an instantaneous point-cloud of the object. A systematic trajectory adaptation algorithm analyzes the model quality on the fly and dynamically adapts the UAV's trajectory based on parameterized spatial partitioning to intelligently capture new images of poorly covered areas, ensuring comprehensive acquisition. For the final, high-fidelity output, a non-RT pipeline employs a Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF)-based Neural 3D Reconstruction (N3DR) approach, fusing SfM-derived camera poses with precise external location data, evaluated across both radio-based Ultra Wideband (UWB) and visual motion-capture setups, to correct sensor noise and achieve superior accuracy. We implemented and validated this architecture using Crazyflie 2.1 UAVs. Our experiments, conducted in both single- and multi-UAV configurations show that algorithmic dynamic trajectory adaptation consistently improves reconstruction quality over static flight paths. This work demonstrates a scalable and autonomous solution that unlocks the potential of miniaturized UAVs for fine-grained 3D reconstruction, a capability previously reserved for much larger platforms.

Robotics.title: RoboAda: Adapting Frozen Robot Policies at Test Time to Physics They Cannot See
Robotics.summary: Pretrained robot policies decide what to do from camera images, yet some of the physics that decides whether their plans succeed is not visible. An object may look light but be 100 times heavier, and a weakened joint or a lagging controller leaves no trace in the image. When the physics at deployment differs from training, the plan is often still right but is executed as if nothing had changed. Training on such variations in advance cannot handle unseen changes, while adapting once deployed either changes the plan, leaving the miscalibrated commands in place, or updates a robot model by gradient steps that do not know how reliable they are and can make the robot worse even when nothing has changed. We propose RoboAda, which keeps the policy and its plan unchanged and corrects the commands that carry it out by inferring at test time how the robot turns commands into motion. The key observation is that the robot's own motion reveals the change: after each action chunk, an inverse-dynamics model of the original robot converts the observed motion into the commands it would have needed, yielding free labels at every step. Competing hypotheses of how the robot responds, including that nothing has changed, are weighted by how well they predict these labels, and the next chunk is sent with the commands that best realize the plan under them. RoboAda needs no reward, no gradient step and no data from the changed robot. We evaluate RoboAda with five frozen policies on LIBERO, two world action models and three vision-language-action models. Under eleven physical shifts, it more than doubles their average success, from 27.8% to 62.9%. It beats the best of seven test-time adaptation methods by 17.3 points on Cosmos Policy, and largely preserves the policies' success when nothing has changed. On bimanual RoboTwin 2.0 in joint space, it raises success under joint-target offsets from 24.9% to 78.8%.

Robotics.title: Counterfactual Velocity Steering for World Action Models
Robotics.summary: Flow-based robot policies generate actions by repeatedly evaluating a conditional velocity field, so test-time bias correction seems simple: query the action expert under a task-agnostic condition and subtract that velocity from the task-conditioned prediction. We show this is often wrong. On Fast-WAM across 50 RoboTwin 2.0 tasks, mean-instruction predictions align strongly with task-conditioned velocities (cosine approximately 0.94-0.95). Averaging eight completed-state references barely cancels this direction: their mean norm is 98.3% of the mean individual norm. References thus contain a large shared transport component, not only harmful bias, and aggressive subtraction damages generation. We propose a same-state diagnostic and shrinkage analysis showing that the optimal correction scale depends on reference signal-to-noise. This motivates geometry-calibrated action debiasing, which removes only the component orthogonal to the task velocity and predicts a small task-dependent scale from instruction geometry. In controlled RoboTwin experiments, corrupting instructions still permits 25.1% success (50 tasks, 20 episodes), whereas dynamic visual corruption nearly eliminates success. A fixed centered orthogonal correction reaches 92.7% versus a 92.1% baseline in one randomized 1000-trial sweep, but gains are non-monotonic and within run-to-run variation. An angular scale pilot has an offline oracle-gated bound of 94.5%; its best learned online realization reaches 92.5%. These results identify shared flow and train-serve mismatch as central obstacles and provide a reproducible foundation for conditional correction.

Robotics.title: Calibrating World Action Models: From Adaptive System 2 Takeover to Self-Evolution
Robotics.summary: World action models (WAMs) deliver fast visuomotor control, yet degrade sharply in challenging scenes and act blindly when about to fail; conversely, foundation-model-based agents generalize and recover reliably, but incur prohibitive latency and cost when queried at every step. To achieve both WAM (System 1)-level speed and agent (System 2)-level reliability--- we propose \textbf{\oursfull (\ours)}, a framework that calibrates WAMs' confidence--- adaptively triggering System~2 only when necessary, and distilling System~2's knowledge to form an evolving System~1. First, \ours equips a frozen WAM with \textbf{calibrated self-assessment}: a single lightweight judgment token reading internal video--action features is trained via our proposed \textbf{cross-fitted temporal-difference (TD) learning} using only binary rollout success/failure signals. It can predict a \textbf{calibrated success probability} at negligible overhead without affecting action predictions. Second, this calibrated success probability schedules control chunk by chunk---invoking System~2 to resolve bottlenecks when confidence drops, and handing control back to the WAM once confidence recovers, preserving WAM-like speed while approaching System~2 reliability. Third, as System~2 intervenes only when the WAM lacks confidence, its takeover trajectories directly capture the WAM's capability gaps. JiL distills these takeovers into the WAM to repair those gaps so System~1 can operate standalone without System~2 at test time, while our mastered-skill anchoring and dynamic confidence gating prevent degrading existing capabilities.

Robotics.title: Stubborn: A Streamlined and Unified Reinforcement Learning Framework for Robust Motion Tracking and Fall Recovery for Humanoids
Robotics.summary: Recent reinforcement learning approaches have shown great promise in improving humanoid motion tracking performance and achieving fall recovery under disturbances. However, most existing works treat motion tracking and fall recovery as different tasks and require multi-stage training with specialized recovery rewards and/or separate recovery policies. Moreover, existing reinforcement learning-based methods often terminate training episodes immediately after severe tracking failures, limiting recovery-oriented exploration in unstable or fallen states. To address the above issues, we propose Stubborn, a streamlined and unified reinforcement learning framework to achieve robust humanoid motion tracking and fall recovery. Specifically, Stubborn uses an asymmetric Actor-Critic architecture and consists of three major components. First, a yaw-aligned tracking representation is adopted to reduce sensitivity to global drift and heading disturbances while preserving gravity-related balance information. Second, we introduce a Bernoulli-based probabilistic termination mechanism that enables the policy to encourage exploration of fall-recovery behaviors under varying failure modes. Third, we propose a probabilistic termination and tracking-error-driven strategy that dynamically reshapes the sampling distribution based on tracking performance, increasing the training efficiency for difficult motion segments and unstable states. Extensive comparisons with SOTA methods and ablation studies show that Stubborn achieved competitive performance and avoided the reward-hacking tendency of baseline methods, and the proposed probabilistic termination mechanism and adaptive sampling strategy contributed to the performance and robustness gains. For real-world demonstrations, please refer to the project page at https://aislab-sustech.github.io/Stubborn/.

Robotics.title: OmniSLAM: Evidence-Authorized Revision of Persistent Object Maps
Robotics.summary: Persistent object maps must incorporate new surfaces while retaining valid identities and correcting earlier associations. We present a map-revision module that separates historical identity changes from new-surface admission. Proposed merges are tested against shared and separate mask explanations across views; a merge is allowed only if its evidence margin remains positive after removing any one observed frame. New measured points are assigned through local identity competition, with a mask witness and a seed-frame stability check. On two preselected KITTI-360 windows, the fixed method increases mean building/car instance AP50:90 from 17.259 to 18.762 under a local evaluation protocol. Controlled output interventions attribute the gains to fragment consolidation, protection against harmful overwrites, and local assignment of new points. Four additional spatial holdouts increase mean AP from 20.263 to 23.171, although unconditional revision is slightly higher at 23.251. The extra seed-frame check yields no AP gain over nearest-seed assignment in either set. A 330-frame garage recording demonstrates offline integration with LiDAR--inertial--visual odometry. These results identify where observation-supported revision improves object maps and where conservative decisions still limit recovery.

Robotics.title: StereoVLM: Binocular Vision-Language Models for Metric 3D Spatial Reasoning
Robotics.summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) exhibit strong semantic understanding but remain limited in their ability to reason about metric 3D space in the physical world. Existing VLMs typically infer 3D scene structure from one or more images without known camera calibration or cross-view geometric constraints. This makes metric 3D inference inherently ambiguous and leaves it unclear whether their spatial predictions are grounded in visual evidence or driven primarily by semantic priors. In contrast, calibrated stereo provides explicit cross-view geometry that resolves this ambiguity and offers a more reliable foundation for metric 3D perception and geometric generalization. We investigate how VLMs can learn transferable 3D representations directly from calibrated binocular observations. To this end, we introduce StereoVLM, the first geometry-aware binocular VLM for metric 3D spatial reasoning. StereoVLM follows a hierarchical learning paradigm spanning from cross-view correspondence and disparity estimation to calibration-conditioned metric depth perception and semantic spatial reasoning. We further find that disparity supervision generalizes substantially better than direct binocular depth supervision on unseen environments. To evaluate these capabilities, we introduce Stereo3D-Bench, a comprehensive benchmark across three levels, from point-level geometry to object-level spatial reasoning. StereoVLM-8B achieves 95.17% depth accuracy ($δ_1$) and a 66.98 average object-level score on Stereo3D-Bench. Intervention results further indicate that the model's performance on Stereo3D-Bench benefits from valid cross-view geometry and cannot be explained solely by additional visual tokens or semantic priors. Hierarchical geometric supervision also yields average gains of 3.54 points across five spatial benchmarks and 4.3 percentage points in RoboCasa manipulation success.

Robotics.title: Trustworthy agentic lunar robotics: safety-constrained contingent planning with a foundation-model planner
Robotics.summary: Sustained lunar-base operations require robots that restore equipment and deliver cargo under conditions unforeseen before deployment. Flown space autonomy executes pre-validated procedures and enters a safe hold outside their scope, whereas foundation models synthesize plans on site that cannot be verified before execution. We formulate these operations as safety-constrained contingent planning with irreversible actions, erroneous records, three-valued physical evidence, and costly, deadline-constrained sensing. We propose asymmetric knowledge-level replanning (AKR), which treats the planner as an untrusted black box: reversible actions run on the planner's assumptions, and irreversible actions run only after a minimum-cost sensing cover verifies every precondition. Under sound measurements, no irreversible action executes on a false precondition for any planner or record, the sensing cost before an irreversible action is bounded below for every sound knowledge-based policy, and execution with a complete planner ends in a verified goal or a certified hold. AKR executed no hazardous action in 21,000 Monte Carlo trials with sound observations or in 58 full-stack runs; the FF-Replan acting rule executed one in 7% of those trials. The median AKR run took 1.10 times the fastest run on the same mission, against 1.50 under the K-replanner acting rule. AKR completed 20 of 21 contingency and sequential-fault runs with an unchanged task model; the original PLEXIL and EUROPA$\rightarrow$PLEXIL procedures completed none.

Robotics.title: Quantizing in the Loop: Drift-Aware Ultra-Low-Bit Vision-Language-Action Models
Robotics.summary: Deploying large vision-language-action (VLA) models on resource-constrained robots demands extreme compression, yet existing post-training quantization (PTQ) methods frequently collapse at ultra-low bit-widths ($\le$ 2 bits). We trace this failure to two mismatches in standard pipelines. First, calibrating on static offline demonstrations induces distribution shift: minor quantization perturbations drive the policy into unseen states where uncalibrated errors compound. Second, minimizing the layer-wise weight reconstruction error is a flawed proxy, as action generation depends only on the representations consumed by the action head. We present LoopQ, an on-policy ultra-low-bit quantization framework. LoopQ closes the loop by calibrating on states from the quantized policy's own rollouts. It then adds readout-aligned fine-tuning, which freezes the trellis codes and optimizes only lightweight lookup tables and scaling factors to align the backbone readout with the full-precision teacher. With all linear layers at 2 bits, LoopQ achieves a 60.4% success rate on LIBERO-Plus with GR00T N1.7, close to the 61.8% of full precision. Even at 1 bit per weight, $π_{0.5}$ still completes 80.0% of LIBERO tasks. With 8-bit activations, the 2-bit $π_{0.5}$ runs on integer kernels on an embedded NVIDIA Jetson AGX Thor, with 4.1$\times$ smaller weights and 44% less memory. On a real AgileX Piper arm, it stays within one success of full precision on each of three tasks. Code and checkpoints are available at https://github.com/ForeverBlue816/LoopQ
Robotics.comment: The paper is currently under review. Code and models: https://github.com/ForeverBlue816/LoopQ

Robotics.title: Confidently Lost: Silent Failure and Edge Deployment of Dense Visual SLAM under Photon Starvation
Robotics.summary: Dense visual SLAM built on learned two-view geometry is evaluated in good light; in low light it fails silently. Two frames of 9-level quantized noise, no scene at all, give MASt3R-SLAM's network a cross-view geometric self-consistency of 0.936; a real dark frame pair gives 0.935. Starved of structure, the network invents the same geometry for both views and the system trusts the agreement: on a dark sequence it consumes 1,605 frames, emits 7 keyframes, rejects no factor-graph edges and reports full frame rate, while over 95% of the correspondences it accepts violate the ground-truth epipolar geometry. One inflated statistic is read by two subsystems against thresholds in opposite directions, so keyframing starves while relocalization accepts almost every candidate. The same statistic, read at keyframe-pair baselines, separates the confident collapse from working runs on the ETH3D dark sequences without ground truth or extra computation (in-sample). Low-light-adapted weights take tracked trajectories from 1/6 to 5/6, as does retuning two thresholds; neither yields accurate ones, because the adaptation withdraws confidence from wrong geometry rather than finding right geometry. Replayed on a Jetson AGX Orin carried by a legged robot, the mechanism's signature reproduces on the two darkest of four routes, and which of its faces appears varies with route geometry and sensor encoding. The network does not lose confidence in the dark; it manufactures it.
Robotics.comment: 8 pages, 7 figures. Submitted to IEEE ICRA 2027

Robotics.title: Toward Open Room-Scale Scanning with Consumer LiDAR via Depth-Inertial Odometry
Robotics.summary: Room scanning with consumer LiDAR today depends on ARKit, whose tracking and map update are a black box: an application receives depth and poses but cannot inspect how they were produced, so an error in a scan cannot be traced to its cause. This paper examines whether an open alternative, one whose every stage can be inspected, is feasible on the device. Mobile-LIO is a depth-inertial odometry pipeline that uses the phone's depth and inertial data and no ARKit poses. On seven ScanNet++ iPhone recordings it completed every scene with 0.2-2.0 m deviation from the ARKit-derived reference, where six open-source LiDAR-inertial estimators run as configured for dedicated scanners had at least 4.46 m in 41 of 42 runs (two of the six also failed a noise-free adapter check, and Mobile-LIO has a speed cap they lack; the comparison is not controlled and does not rone 15 Pro Max, a buildwith corrected phone code kept up with the sensor in 14 of 15 replay runs of three 7-13 s recordings; e estimator before thosecorrections. Laser-scanned meshes give the accuracy. Within 3 m, recorded depth differed from the m on three held-out scenes,maps fused with ARKit poses that the dataset scales and aligns to the mesh la a median 1.8-2.3 cm from 17 cm. Because thepipeline is open, the gap could be examined: in the scene with the largest error, noise-free renderefrom 1.97 m to 0.04 m, sorecorded depth, whose error reached 20-54 cm at 5-7 m, contributed alongside the estimator. An open de tracked on phone depth and kept up with the sensor in short phone replays, but it is not yet as accurate as ARKit-pose maps, whicheach only the coarsestUSIBD accuracy level (LOA10); its accuracy on the device was not measured.

Robotics.title: From Predictive Geometry to Action: Learning Complementary Predictive Representations for Embodied Manipulation
Robotics.summary: Effective manipulation requires a policy to capture not only about the current scene geometry, but also about how that geometry will evolve under interaction. Existing approaches either augment policies with geometric information from current observations or introduce future prediction as auxiliary supervision, leaving open how predictive geometry should be represented for action generation. Therefore, we propose a two-stage framework, which learns complementary predictive representations from multi-view video clips. During pretraining, a frozen 3D foundation model provides dense geometric features that are compressed into predictive geometric representations and optimized to preserve scene structure and its temporal evolution. Action supervision is then applied to geometric transitions to extract a complementary motor representation that emphasizes action-relevant transitions. During downstream post-training, predictive geometry is transferred through geometry queries, while the motor representation guides intermediate features along the action-generation pathway. Future observations are used only as privileged supervision during training and are not required at inference time. Across LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, SimplerEnv, and real-world bimanual and single-arm tasks, our approach consistently improves downstream policies, including an absolute gain of 10.4 percentage points on the WidowX evaluation. We further demonstrate transfer across multiple VLA architectures and WAMs, with improvements in both future-world and action prediction. The code will be available at https://github.com/xuxiaoxxxx/CPR.

Robotics.title: RoboColiseum: Co-evolution of Simulation, Evaluation, and Models
Robotics.summary: Simulation-based evaluation of embodied models requires calibrated interactions, diverse tasks, and explicit execution constraints. We present RoboColiseum, a platform combining system identification, composable physics and rendering, and multidimensional benchmarking. Recorded-command replay characterizes robot dynamics and object interactions, while a shared interface connects rigid and deformable simulation to rendering. Across 22 paired real--simulation robot--task configurations, task scores have a reported Pearson correlation of 0.9686. Eight evaluation tracks span instruction following, spatial reasoning, general manipulation, robustness, dexterous manipulation, precision manipulation, whole-body coordination, and execution across robot embodiments. Budget-aware scoring combines task progress, resource use, and completion rewards. We report 12 selected Season~I policies and all 11 systems on the public Season~II leaderboard, comprising eight Agent systems and three VLA policies. Agent2Act connects language models to robot-control execution; the VLA study uses mixed-task supervised fine-tuning. The results reveal substantial variation across tracks within each evaluation category. RoboColiseum connects simulation development with capability-oriented evaluation and provides a foundation for extending robot interactions and model assessment.
Robotics.comment: 11 pages, 8 figures. The first eight authors contributed equally. Maoqing Yao and Qian Wang are the corresponding authors

Robotics.title: LeadVLA: Learning Follower-Aware Route Execution for Robot Leading
Robotics.summary: Robot leading requires executing a route while continuously adapting to a designated follower. Existing robot-leading systems often mediate follower understanding and physical route execution through explicit states, planners, or modular interfaces; directly learning this coupling through end-to-end trajectory prediction can instead entangle route execution with follower response. We introduce LeadVLA, a structured multimodal policy that preserves the route as an explicit Path reference while learning a Pace for route progress and a Residual for local follower- and scene-conditioned adaptation. To make this problem trainable and measurable, we develop LeadInfra, a configurable Unreal Engine-based closed-loop data-generation infrastructure from which we instantiate an approximately 4M-sample training corpus, and LeadBench, a standardized benchmark with 108 fully held-out closed-loop episodes. LeadVLA achieves the highest task success (39.6%) among evaluated robot policies on LeadBench while maintaining strong route fidelity and follower responsiveness, and transfers to unseen real-world environments without real-world policy fine-tuning. Project Page: https://louiszengCN.github.io/LeadVLA_PAGE/

Robotics.title: RMR-VLA: Recurrent Memory Reasoning for Vision-Language-Action Models
Robotics.summary: Long-horizon, history-dependent robotic manipulation often requires acting on visual cues that have disappeared, such as an object indicated earlier or a target hidden under a moving cup. The key challenge is to maintain what past evidence means for the next action as the scene changes. We introduce Recurrent Memory Reasoning (RMR), an explicit reasoning step that connects memory to action inside a vision-language-action model (VLA), with no external reasoning model. At each update, the VLA first infers an event from visual evidence, then revises the task state and grounds a subgoal in the current scene to guide action generation. Carrying the state and subgoal across updates lets remembered identities and task progress determine the current target, doubling RoboMME success over an otherwise identical model without recurrence. Joint training lets one VLA both reason and act; because its memory decisions are text tokens with exact likelihoods, GRPO refines them from rollout rewards without making action generation stochastic. Among the compared methods, RMR-VLA achieves the best results on RoboMME (66.46% overall, 79.83% on the Reference category) and LIBERO-Mem (90.08%).

Robotics.title: Tripwire: Robot Agents that Program Their Own Interrupts under Human Disturbance
Robotics.summary: Agent harnesses are turn-based: the agent acts, waits for the result, then reasons. When the action invokes a pretrained robot policy, such as a vision-language-action (VLA) or world action model (WAM), the policy may react continuously to observations, but the agent cannot revisit its decision until the call returns. Meanwhile, a person may step into the robot's path or move the object it is about to grasp. Invoking the agent more often narrows this blind interval, but a reasoning model takes seconds per decision and most control steps need no new one. We propose TRIP, a training-free, event-driven harness in which the agent programs its own interrupts. With each call, the agent writes a tripwire: a lightweight, stateful Python program that runs alongside the policy, can query a compact VLM (for example, to locate a person and measure their distance), and decides whether the call continues or control returns to the agent. When it fires, the harness halts the policy and returns control with the reason; the agent then reassesses, adapts, and continues under a rewritten tripwire. We evaluate TRIP with three VLAs and one WAM on RoboHD, a benchmark of 168 RoboCasa365 scenes in which a simulated person disturbs the robot and any human-robot contact counts as failure. Compared with a turn-based harness using the same agent and tools, TRIP halves the rate of human contact with the strongest policy, raising safety from 61.3% to 81.3%, without sacrificing task success (38.7% vs. 31.0%). Real-robot experiments show that TRIP completes two manipulation tasks under human interference where the turn-based harness and the policy alone largely fail.

Robotics.title: Value function based Reward shaping for safety in quadrupeds
Robotics.summary: Reinforcement Learning (RL) has progressed from simple control tasks to complex real-world challenges with large state spaces. While RL excels in these tasks, training time remains a limitation. Reward shaping is a popular solution, but existing methods often rely on value functions, which face scalability issues. This paper presents a novel safety-oriented reward-shaping framework inspired by barrier functions, offering simplicity and ease of implementation across various environments and tasks. To evaluate the effectiveness of the proposed reward formulations, we conduct simulation experiments on the Unitree Go1 quadruped robot in Isaacgym. The policy was better than the existing baselines and reduced safety violations from 27% to 0.1% without almost any compromise on the performance.

Robotics.title: Prescribed Time Higher Order Control Lyapunov-Barrier Functions
Robotics.summary: We propose a framework based on Repeated-Root Prescribed Time Higher-Order Control Lyapunov- Barrier Functions (RR-Pxt-HOCL-BF) that guarantees convergence to a safe set/ goal set within user-specified time. Unlike conventional Higher-Order Control Barrier Functions, which does not provide any guarantee on reaching the safe set if the system is initially not in safe set, the proposed method enforces convergence within a prescribed time horizon. This is achieved through a structured differential constraint derived from repeated roots of the characteristic polynomial, leading to closed-form polynomial solutions that ensure convergence at the desired time. Analytical conditions for forward invariance and prescribed-time reachability are derived, with explicit formulations for second-order systems. The approach is validated on an acceleration-controlled unicycle and an inverted pendulum and compared with existing HOCBF methods. Simulation results demonstrate reliable convergence within the desired time horizon, even in scenarios where conventional approaches fail.

Robotics.title: Let It Be Simple: One-Step Action Generation for Vision-Language-Action Models
Robotics.summary: One-step generation from standard diffusion or Flow-Matching training is rarely effective for text-to-image or video generation without distillation or specialized one-step objectives. We find that VLA action generation behaves strikingly differently. Biasing only the training timestep distribution toward the noise endpoint yields strong one-step policies across LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, LIBERO-Pro, and real-world robot tasks. Moreover, for open-source VLA models with different architectures, simply replacing iterative decoding with a single forward pass often performs comparably to the original multi-step decoding on benchmarks such as LIBERO, CALVIN, and SimplerEnv. We attribute this difference to the condition-target structure of VLA generation, which is closer to image-to-text than text-to-image: rich observations strongly constrain a comparatively compact target. We formalize this intuition through the irreducible velocity loss $R_v(t,c)$ of standard Flow Matching, which becomes much smaller toward the noise endpoint for VLA, whereas image-generation models usually exhibit a U-shaped profile. The geometry induced by the learned generative map shows the same contrast: the Jacobian of this map with respect to the initial noise has a substantially smaller largest singular value for action generation than for image generation. Together, these results suggest that VLA's condition-target structure makes one-step generation unusually accessible to standard Flow Matching. Code and training configurations for this paper are available at https://github.com/bondtesty/let-it-be-simple.

Robotics.title: RoboThink: Let the Agent Think, Let the Policy Act
Robotics.summary: Robot policies act in real time but fail without knowing why, whereas a reasoning agent that watches the robot can often tell what went wrong. Existing systems either hand the agent control, which takes minutes per episode, or let it send instructions. Yet a policy follows a new instruction only from a fresh start, since a half-finished task leaves it in states outside its training data. Nor can an instruction fix how the robot moves. If a drift keeps pulling the hand to the left, "push right, slightly" is not a task the policy has learned. We propose RoboThink, in which the agent thinks and the policy learns to act on the agent's guidance. An instruction channel tells the policy what to do. When the user says "the milk, not the butter" after the robot has started, the agent rewrites the instruction and the robot undoes its own motion, with no training. A feedback channel tells it how to move. It is taught from the agent alone with agent-labelled DAgger, role tokens and counterfactual feedback, and is read only by the policy's action module. On LIBERO, RoboThink with Claude Opus 5.5 raises success from 0.09 to 0.87 under an unknown constant drift and from 0.42 to 0.84 under a random one. It also completes misheard and changed requests in 0.91 to 1.00 of the episodes. Acting alone, GPT-6 Astra needs 2.1 min per success and over a million tokens per episode, whereas RoboThink needs 55 s and 8k tokens. The same recipe works across policies, for both vision-language-action models and world action models, and across robots, from one arm to two arms and a mobile manipulator. On all 50 RoboTwin 2.0 tasks with two arms, success rises from 0.12 to 0.74 under the constant drift and from 0.31 to 0.56 under the random one. Finally, the agent is a plug-in. A policy taught by one agent works with other agents, including open-weight ones, and grows stronger with a stronger agent, without retraining.

Robotics.title: Agent on Guard: Self-Improving Runtime Intervention for Robust Robotic Manipulation
Robotics.summary: Robot foundation policies provide learned execution capabilities, while programming agents can reason about failures and construct recovery behaviors. Combining them effectively requires learning when intervention helps and when the policy can reliably resume. This challenge is inherently temporal: the physical world continues to evolve during reasoning, and a useful recovery may become infeasible before a decision takes effect. We introduce Agent on Guard (AoG), a hierarchical framework that improves collaboration between a frozen base policy and a programming agent through physical experience. An evolving outer planner allocates control as the physical state evolves, aligning decisions with the physical clock with attention to observation freshness, remaining recovery windows, and the time required for reasoning, recovery, and subsequent execution. Coupled inner loops jointly refine intervention timing, recovery skills, and handoff conditions. Rather than judging recovery by local correction alone, AoG uses downstream task progress, failure recurrence, final outcomes, and resource consumption to improve both recovery behaviors and scheduling. This turns temporary agent solutions into reusable collaboration capabilities that complement the frozen policy. On RoboDojo-Sim, AoG achieves a success rate of 50.57% and a task score of 57.26, exceeding the strongest evaluated baseline by 11.22 percentage points and 10.68 points, respectively. It also reduces end-to-end episode latency by 80.4% and online token consumption by 85.1% relative to the GPT-6 Astra agent.

Robotics.title: Policy-intrinsic Demonstration Curation
Robotics.summary: Fine-tuning a robot policy for a new target task requires target demonstrations, but only a few are available. Demonstrations of other tasks can fill this gap, and demonstration curation selects the useful ones among these candidates. Retrieval-based curation selects the candidates that are most similar to the target demonstrations. Since it does not use the policy, any candidate that looks similar receives a high score. Performance-aware curation therefore estimates the effect of each candidate on the policy. However, this requires training on the candidates and takes a long time. We propose a third branch, policy-intrinsic curation, which uses the policy and still takes little time. It estimates this effect with forward passes of the pretrained policy and needs no training. We instantiate this branch with PICKER (Policy-Intrinsic Curation from Known Errors). It selects the candidates on which the policy makes errors that agree with those on the target demonstrations. PICKER reaches success rates comparable to those of performance-aware curation and takes about as long as retrieval-based curation. Its selection is also stable across seeds.
Robotics.comment: 15 pages (including 1 page of references and 6 pages of appendices), 5 figures, 7 tables

Robotics.title: MotionServe: Efficient Multi-Robot Serving by Exploiting Robot Execution Slack
Robotics.summary: As robotic arms undertake diverse manipulation tasks, a deployment may need to serve many task-specific vision-language-action (VLA) policies concurrently. Dedicating a GPU to each robot is costly, motivating shared-GPU inference. Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) allows compatible policies to share a frozen backbone with lightweight policy-specific adapters, reducing model-weight memory and enabling cross-policy batching. However, robot inference must keep pace with physical execution. With action chunking, robots continue executing buffered actions while awaiting new predictions, and the remaining buffered time provides each robot's execution slack for serving its next request. Once this slack is exhausted, the robot stalls until new actions arrive, interrupting task progress. Observing earlier preserves more slack but can lead to disruptive replanning and lower task success, whereas delaying dispatch to form larger batches can improve GPU efficiency but consumes slack and risks stalls. To balance these competing demands, we present MotionServe, a shared-GPU serving system that coordinates robot observation timing with server-side batch formation. MotionExec selects observation triggers based on motion structure in predicted action chunks, allowing inference to overlap with remaining buffered execution. SlackBatch combines the resulting per-robot execution budgets with estimated outstanding GPU work to determine when to wait, which requests to batch, and when to dispatch them. We evaluate X-VLA on LIBERO and SimplerEnv's WidowX tasks and OpenVLA-OFT on LIBERO, with up to 96 simulated robots sharing one NVIDIA H200 GPU. At 96 robots, MotionServe reduces mean stall per episode by 43.4% and 32.6% and improves task success by 8.98 and 2.30 percentage points, respectively, over each model's lowest-stall baseline. Backbone sharing also reduces weight memory for 96 policies by 97.6% and 91.1%.

Robotics.title: RadarOSV: Unified 3D Scene and Motion Perception from mmWave Radars
Robotics.summary: Millimeter-wave radar offers weather-resilient sensing for 3D occupancy prediction. Existing radar occupancy methods mainly model geometry, with limited joint modeling of semantics and motion. Cascaded imaging radar provides fine spatial detail but has a limited unambiguous velocity range, whereas single-chip radar offers a wider range but coarser spatial resolution. We propose RadarOSV, to our knowledge the first radar-only framework that jointly predicts occupancy, dynamic object semantics, and ground-relative velocity from raw radar data in unified voxels, by exploiting complementary measurements from both radars. Its Polar-to-Cartesian Geometry (PCG) backbone maps polar imaging-radar features into Cartesian voxels through fixed and deformable sampling, guiding cross-radar fusion for geometry and attribute prediction. Single-chip detection outputs provide class evidence, while raw Doppler spectra supply motion features and radial-velocity candidates. The velocity readout selects from these candidates using fused features to resolve aliasing, then combines the selected radial estimate with learned motion. Ego-motion compensation uses radar-estimated velocity, so inference requires no external odometry or other sensors. On K-Radar, single-frame PCG achieves 40.7% mIoU within 12.8 m, compared with RadarOcc's reported 34.3%. On the BRIDGE-Liv dataset, compared with a cascaded-radar baseline predicting the same outputs with external ego velocity, RadarOSV improves macro-averaged accuracy across four dynamic object classes within annotated object regions from 63.1% to 75.5% and reduces object radial-velocity MAE against manual Doppler annotations from 1.03 to 0.51 m/s, while maintaining geometric occupancy mIoU.

Robotics.title: PushMimic: Learning Adaptive Humanoid Box Pushing via Dynamic Motion Augmentation and Reference Distillation
Robotics.summary: Humanoid box pushing is challenging when the physical properties of the task, such as the box mass and the ramp inclination, are unknown before the push begins. This paper presents PushMimic, a framework that learns adaptive humanoid box pushing from a single level-ground kinematic reference motion. The learned policy adapts its pushing posture to these properties without observing them. PushMimic augments the reference motion into a dynamically feasible motion dataset over these properties with sampling-based trajectory optimization, and distills the dataset into one motion tracking policy in one stage of training. Simulation results over box masses from 5 to 15 kg and ramp inclinations up to 15 degrees show that PushMimic raises the success rate from 57.8% to 88.8% compared with a baseline that tracks the original reference motion. It also reduces the cost of push of the arms by 22%. Hardware experiments on a Unitree G1 humanoid show that the policy adapts its torso pitch during continuous pushing on an inclined treadmill, with box masses up to 19 kg and ramp inclinations up to 12.6 degrees. PushMimic therefore needs only one reference motion, instead of one for every box mass and ramp inclination.
Robotics.comment: 9 pages, 10 figures, 3 tables. Website at https://silvery107.github.io/pushmimic/

Robotics.title: HERO: Hierarchical Region-Aware Reinforcement Learning for Autonomous Exploration
Robotics.summary: Autonomous exploration is widely used to map unknown environments, yet maintaining both path efficiency and low online computation remains difficult as environment scale increases. Hierarchical planners reduce global search through coarse regional representations but often rely on handcrafted local viewpoint-selection rules. Graph-based reinforcement learning can improve local decisions, but its inference cost grows with the exploration graph and global direction is usually represented only implicitly. To address these limitations, we present HERO, a hierarchical framework that assigns distinct responsibilities to global planning and learned local decision-making, enabling each level to focus on the function it is best suited to perform. To reduce the growing inference cost of graph-based policies, HERO restricts learned target selection to reachable candidates within the current region while using region-level planning to provide long-horizon guidance. To avoid informative targets causing excessive deviation from this global direction, the proposed Dual-Branch Graph Policy balances Frontier Utility with guidance toward the next region, improving both local exploration and global progress. Experiments on unseen 2D maps show the lowest overall mean path length and target-decision cost among the evaluated methods. MARSIM simulations and deployments at three real-world sites further demonstrate the framework's applicability with LiDAR-based mapping and chassis dynamics.

Robotics.title: How Latent Transition Geometry Matters for Planning in World Models
Robotics.summary: World models support planning by predicting how the environment evolves under candidate actions. However, one-step predictive accuracy alone does not characterize multi-step planning utility, which depends on distinguishing candidate futures. This raises a natural question: How does latent transition geometry shape planning? We investigate this through an action-conditioned transition-field view, using curvature regularization as a controlled intervention. Across four continuous-control tasks, appropriately tuned regularization improves planning, while excessive regularization can be detrimental. By decomposing the transition field into affine and non-affine components, we find that regularization reduces action sensitivity mainly through the non-affine component. To assess its role in planning, we directly manipulate the non-affine action response in frozen models and show that it affects candidate selection and closed-loop success. Further analysis shows that curvature generally brings predicted futures closer together, while preserving more of the differences along the goal direction. This helps explain why the planning effects vary across tasks. We observe broadly consistent planning trends across five sampling- and gradient-based solvers on LeWM and similar rollout-geometry trends on DINO-WM. Qualitative attention visualizations reveal accompanying shifts toward task-relevant visual structure. Together, these findings clarify how latent transition geometry influences multi-step planning.

Robotics.title: Mem-X: A Memory-Dependent Cross-Episode Benchmark for Vision-and-Language Navigation
Robotics.summary: Long-term memory enables embodied agents to reuse past observations across tasks. However, existing cross-episode vision-and-language navigation (VLN) benchmarks often leave it unclear whether successful navigation relies on historical memory or current exploration. We introduce Mem-X, a benchmark designed to evaluate memory-dependent cross-episode VLN. Mem-X organizes episodes into sessions in which subsequent instructions refer to objects or routes encountered in earlier episodes. Its three levels evaluate historical-object recall, in-memory localization and episodic indexing, and off-memory relocalization and historical-route reproduction. For the latter two levels, agents receive episode-local poses but no transformations between episode frames, requiring them to establish spatial correspondence with historical memory. Mem-X comprises 2,071 episodes across 710 sessions in 34 scenes, including 1,204 memory-dependent episodes. We also provide MemBridge, a modular baseline that combines semantic scene memory, cross-episode localization, and coarse-to-fine retrieval to support existing VLN agents. Experiments with state-of-the-art VLN methods demonstrate the benefits of MemBridge while revealing substantial room for improvement on memory-dependent navigation. The benchmark and baseline code are available at https://github.com/NJU-R-L-Group-Embodied-Lab/Mem-X.
Robotics.comment: 9 pages, 3 figures. Submitted to IEEE International Conference on Robotics and Automation (ICRA 2027)

Robotics.title: RoboLiveMem: Is Robot Memory Solved When the World Does Not Wait?
Robotics.summary: Robot agents built on frontier vision-language models now solve most robot memory benchmarks. Does this mean they can remember what they need in a home, where people and machines keep moving things? Existing memory benchmarks cannot answer this question, because they pause the simulator while the model thinks: nothing can change during a decision, so whatever the robot remembers is still true when it acts. We introduce RoboLiveMem, a benchmark that runs the same memory tasks twice, once with the world paused while the model thinks and once with the world running. It contains 29 task families in three tiers, from 16 realistic BEHAVIOR-1K scenes of homes, workshops and a restaurant to controlled ManiSkill tasks. Every task mixes real changes with harmless look-alikes and runs without any change, so that no fixed strategy succeeds, and most tasks have a twin that keeps the change in view, which separates forgetting from acting too late. Testing 16 models on 34,176 episodes, we find three surprises. (1) Paused results hide the problem: when a remembered object changes in a realistic scene, the 8 Claude and GPT models succeed in 97% of episodes on average with the world paused, but in only 50% with the world running, and their ranking changes: Claude Opus 5.5, which never fails when paused, succeeds in 44%. (2) Speed is not the fix: slower models do no worse, and models given only 2 s per decision still fall at least 36 points below their paused success. (3) Models see the change but act on camera frames from before it ended. Looking again just before acting closes most of the realistic gap, yet when identical objects are swapped several times, all nine models we test still lose points to memory.

Robotics.title: Orientation Learning and Adaptation towards Simultaneous Incorporation of Multiple Local Constraints
Robotics.summary: Orientation learning plays a pivotal role in many tasks. However, the rotation group SO(3) is a Riemannian manifold. As a result, the distortion caused by non-Euclidean geometric nature introduces difficulties to the incorporation of local constraints, especially for the simultaneous incorporation of multiple local constraints. To address this issue, we propose the Angle-Axis Space-based orientation representation method to solve several orientation learning problems, including orientation adaptation and minimization of angular acceleration. Specifically, we propose a weighted average mechanism in SO(3) based on the angle-axis representation method. Our main idea is to generate multiple trajectories by considering different local constraints at different basepoints. Then these multiple trajectories are fused to generate a smooth trajectory by our proposed weighted average mechanism, achieving the goal to incorporate multiple local constraints simultaneously. Compared with existing solution, ours can address the distortion issue and make the off-theshelf Euclidean learning algorithm be re-applicable in non-Euclidean space. Simulation and Experimental evaluations validate that our solution can not only adapt orientations towards arbitrary desired via-points and cope with angular acceleration constraints, but also incorporate multiple local constraints simultaneously to achieve extra benefits, e.g., achieving smaller acceleration costs.

Robotics.title: Spiking World-Action Models for Robotic Manipulation
Robotics.summary: World action models (WAMs) predict how the world responds to actions and offer a promising path toward general embodied intelligence, but they are large and run the network many times per plan, so they are hard to deploy on robots. Spiking neural networks (SNNs) compute with sparse binary spikes and use additions instead of multiplications, which saves power. However, existing WAMs use dense videos as the world state, so a spiking version would spend most of its computation on the background. We therefore introduce SpikingWAM, the first spiking WAM, which uses a sparse task skeleton as the world state. Inspired by biological motor control, which attends only to the key positions of a task, the Task Skeleton State (TSS) keeps the keypoints of the arm and the task objects, and a small spiking front end estimates the object keypoints from images. Body Frame Spike Coding (BFSC) and Grid Coincidence Attention (GCA) keep millimetre precision, and the Persistent Single Step Readout (PSR) runs the network once per plan. On the simulated benchmarks LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus and RoboTwin 2.0, SpikingWAM achieves competitive success rates with far less energy than ANN methods and surpasses all compared methods on LIBERO-Plus. Real robot experiments further confirm its effectiveness. These results show that a task skeleton lets spiking networks implement WAMs at very low energy, offering a new solution for low power embodied intelligence. Project page: https://wxqnl.github.io/spikingwam/

Robotics.title: Design of a Compact Cable-driven 4-DoF Salamander Robotic Limb with Large Range of Motion and High Load Capacity
Robotics.summary: A compact yet agile and powerful limb is essential for amphibious legged robots that transition between spine-based swimming and leg-based terrestrial walking, as salamanders do. Salamander limbs combine large ranges of motion (ROM), multiple degrees of freedom (DoFs), and high load capacity. These features enable swinging and body-weight support during walking, as well as folding alongside the body during swimming. Their proximal kinematics can be represented by three rotational DoFs at the hip and one at the knee. Replicating these capabilities within a compact robotic limb is challenging with direct-drive architectures, because multiple joint-mounted actuators must be sufficiently spaced or placed distally to avoid self-collision, increasing limb size and rotational inertia. Here we present a cable-driven 4-DoF salamander robotic limb with a spatial cable-routing architecture that relocates actuators proximally while preserving large ROM and load capacity. Transmission-induced coupling is mitigated by mechanically compensating multi-segment cable paths, model-based feedforward decoupling, and output-side joint angle feedback. Compared with a direct-drive limb, the proposed design reduces mass by 20.4%, projected envelope area by 20.5%, and estimated effective yaw-axis inertia by 31.9%. Experiments verify independent, decoupled control over joint-angle ranges of 45 deg, 118 deg, 118 deg, and 135 deg for hip pitch, yaw, roll, and knee flexion/extension, respectively. During lifting tests, the limb supported an equivalent vertical load of at least 5.4 times its own weight. The proposed limb provides a compact, biologically representative platform for future studies of salamander locomotion and neural control.

Robotics.title: FlexWAM: Learning Flexible Visual Routing for World Action Models
Robotics.summary: Humans dynamically adjust their reliance on sensory modalities across manipulation stages. Although existing World Action Models (WAMs) fuse multi-camera observations, they struggle to adapt their reliance on individual views based on the current observations. This raises a central question: how can the action expert integrate complementary visual evidence while prioritizing the views most relevant to the current action? FlexWAM addresses this challenge through three modules. First, we alternate within-view and cross-view attention to capture view-specific dynamics and complementary cues. For action prediction, View-Routed Action Attention uses an observation-conditioned router to prioritize relevant views. To calibrate routing, we train a critic using counterfactual view credit, estimated from action loss sensitivity upon suppressing each view's contribution to action attention. We evaluate FlexWAM with two video backbones on five challenging real-world manipulation tasks across two robot platforms. The two variants improve mean task success by 16.4 and 23.0 percentage points over the strongest baseline. Project website: https://flexwam.github.io/.

Robotics.title: MOVER: Planning Beyond Motion
Robotics.summary: Residual world models forecast a driving scene through its temporal change, so feature components that stay constant over time vanish from the residual pathway. We ask whether evidence with weak temporal change, such as a waiting pedestrian or a stopped vehicle, can be used more effectively for planning, and introduce MOVER, a complementary event-routing mechanism. A training-time teacher measures how each spatially grounded event query responds when a past frame is removed from shared history and contrasts that sensitivity with the event's pooled temporal residual, prioritizing events that depend on history but receive weak residual evidence. A student predicts the resulting priorities from unperturbed history, so the teacher adds no inference cost. Under fixed total routing mass, one distribution scales a low-rank future bird's-eye-view update and biases trajectory-conditioned event reading. On nuScenes, MOVER reduces ResWorld's UniAD-style average L2 from 0.65 to 0.55 m and its collision rate from 0.23% to 0.12% without direct planner ego status (0.50 m and 0.09% with it), adding 4.1 ms per frame. Matched controls show that the complementary teacher outperforms either signal alone and that the allocation acts mainly during training. Adapted to BridgeDrive-LEAD, MOVER reaches a 96.52 +/- 0.65 driving score over three seeds on the 220-route Bench2Drive closed-loop benchmark, exceeding matched controls in each paired seed by a margin within seed variation.

Robotics.title: One Latent World for Heterogeneous LiDARs: A Scan Pattern Agnostic 4D World Model via Direct Ray Decoding
Robotics.summary: LiDAR world models generate and predict metric 3D observations in the form of LiDAR scans. They typically synthesize scans following the scan pattern of their training sensor or render them from an intermediate 3D surface or field. However, following one scan pattern limits transfer to LiDARs with other patterns, and rendering from intermediate geometry can cause incorrect depths and false returns. In this paper, we propose a scan pattern agnostic 4D LiDAR world model that decouples the scene from sensor observation, so one spatial latent can be observed by heterogeneous LiDARs at the same mounting position without regeneration. Our decoder predicts the hit probability and depth of each ray directly from the latent, combining global scene context with local features retrieved at a preliminary depth. Without an intermediate surface or field, it reduces incorrect depths and false returns, and as each ray is decoded independently from one latent, LiDARs that share a ray receive the same return and observe one consistent scene. Finally, a diffusion transformer generates scenes in this latent and predicts 4D sequences from observed latents warped by the given ego and object motion. On KITTI-360 and nuScenes, our model generates realistic scenes and reduces the registration error between predicted frames by about 70% relative to the best compared world model. Its decoder yields 19 to 28% lower depth error than the rendering used by other world models, and generated scans benefit several downstream tasks. Our code will be open-sourced. More details are available at https://minwoo0611.github.io/OneLatentWorld.

Robotics.title: EnvTrap: Revealing the Environment-Only Attack Surface in Embodied AI via Consequence-Blind Action Execution
Robotics.summary: As AI models evolve from text and vision to physical agents, embodied AI faces a fundamentally different attack surface. Prior attacks on embodied systems have used crafted instructions, adversarial visual inputs, and training-time policy modifications; we study environment-only object rearrangements with unchanged models and instructions. We reveal an attack surface in safety-critical spatial relations among existing objects. An adversary who rearranges objects, without modifying instructions or accessing models, can cause hazardous consequences. In this work, we propose EnvTrap, a diagnostic pipeline that constructs paired safe, trap, and null-trap (benign but misleading) embodied scenarios. We demonstrate that environment-only perturbations raise hazardous-action rates to an average of 83.4% across the five evaluated action policies, with similar vulnerability patterns confirmed in world models. On a consequence-prediction task, model accuracy remains near chance, while human evaluators achieve high accuracy. We further propose a consequence-aware defense that reduces trap trigger rates by an average of 76.3 percentage points across action policies in simulation and by 62.9 percentage points pooled across physical backends. Together, these findings link environment-only attacks to a broader deficit in physical reasoning: embodied models recognize task-relevant objects yet fail to anticipate how spatial relations change the consequences of acting on them. EnvTrap makes this gap directly testable and turns hazardous layouts into training scenarios for safer embodied action. Our code and data are available at https://github.com/INKSIR/Envtrap.

Robotics.title: RoboARCade: Benchmarking Agentic Robot Control
Robotics.summary: Improvements in multi-modal capabilities have enabled agents to act directly as robot policies, a setting we refer to as agentic robot control (ARC). We introduce RoboARCade, a benchmark of long-horizon manipulation tasks across three embodiments designed to test in-context adaptation, memory, and reasoning for precise control. The tasks build on existing open-source benchmarks, which we make harder by widening the range of initial conditions. RoboARCade is easy to use and extend: all tasks run on a single simulation backend, MuJoCo, each task is a self-contained data pack, and agents connect through interchangeable interfaces, so new tasks, agents, and interfaces can be added independently. The benchmark separates leading agents: GPT-6 Astra achieves 49.8% compared with 43.6% for Claude Fable 5.1, leaving substantial room for improvement. Comparing two interfaces, we find that a richer visual interface adds only 1.5 to 6.8 points at 1.7 to 2.3 times the cost. Failures stem mostly from choosing a poor manipulation strategy or executing a good one imprecisely, rarely from misunderstanding the scene, and agents incorrectly claim success on 24% to 39% of attempted subtasks. Agents can also improve without human input: one successful demonstration in context raises Astra's score from 53.5% to 73.0% on a five-task subset, and a prompt the agent writes and revises itself reaches 72.0%. Code, videos and full traces are available at roboarcade.org.

Robotics.title: Vector-Quantized World Model: Latent Feedback Motion Planning for Robot Manipulation
Robotics.summary: Visual world models have shown strong potential for robot planning, yet long-horizon manipulation remains challenging due to compounding prediction errors, large search complexity, and latent plans that the low-level controller cannot reliably reach. In this work, we introduce Vector-Quantized World Model (VQ-WM), a latent feedback motion planning framework that integrates discrete long-horizon search with continuous visual feedback control: a discrete latent predictor models transitions between vector-quantized latent states, allowing the planner to look far ahead and find a shortest path to the goal through discrete search and a continuous learned controller sequentially reaches the planned states through visual feedback, correcting deviations to mitigate compounding errors. Whereas most vector quantization uses Euclidean distance, we use a novel estimator of the first-passage-time as a quasi-metric, which aligns the planning abstraction with the controller's capabilities. We evaluate on the physical robot manipulation of the Tower of Hanoi puzzle: whereas existing state-of-the-art foundation models (VLAs, WAMs) only succeed when the solution trace in their training dataset, our method achieves 100\% success rate with only short-play data, demonstrate its ability to compose long-horizon solutions beyond the short demonstrated trajectories and execute them reliably. Our solution also outperforms strongest world-models by 13.3--85.3 percentage points on simulation benchmarks spanning manipulation and locomotion, demonstrating consistent progress and new capabilities.

Robotics.title: TeleMultiStream: An Integrated Robot Teleoperation System with Low-Latency Multi-Stream Video Feedback
Robotics.summary: Training embodied-intelligence models requires large-scale, high-quality demonstration data. Robot teleoperation provides an important means of collecting these data. Low-latency teleoperation also helps human operators take control promptly and provide corrective demonstrations in DAgger-based interactive learning. This paper presents TeleMultiStream, a robot teleoperation system that combines multi-stream WebRTC video feedback with UDP pose downlink. The system supports heterogeneous video sources and uses buffer reuse, bounded queues, and native XR rendering to reduce processing and waiting. In wired-LAN ZED Mini tests, TeleMultiStream's software and high-performance hardware encoding modes achieved dominant-interval Glass-to-Glass latency medians of 60 and 66~ms, respectively. These medians were 26.8\% and 19.5\% lower than the 82-ms RobotVision-PC reference, respectively. At the lower tested resolutions, the two TeleMultiStream encoding modes provided comparable visual latency. Their respective medians in three-stream Configuration~1 were 72 and 66~ms. In the higher-resolution Configuration~2, high-performance hardware encoding outperformed software encoding in latency and CPU utilization. It reduced mean encoding time from 11.85 to 8.80~ms and the dominant-interval Glass-to-Glass median from 94 to 88~ms. Its CPU utilization was approximately 67\%, compared with 265\% for software encoding. During three-stream reception with high-performance hardware encoding, the mean corrected one-way UDP latencies at 100~Hz were 1.576 and 1.800~ms in Configurations~1 and~2, respectively. Mean estimated packet loss was 0.0033\% in both configurations. These results support responsive teleoperation for robot demonstration collection.

Robotics.title: BeyondEgo: Learning to Act Beyond Egocentric Perception via Humanoid Ego-Exo Foresight
Robotics.summary: Humanoid loco-manipulation requires coordinating whole-body motion to perform manipulation tasks in complex environments. Yet egocentric vision-language-action (VLA) policies can miss critical body--scene relationships, and action imitation alone provides no explicit supervision for future scene evolution. We propose BeyondEgo to extend VLA perception in space and time. Spatially, we encode a synchronized exocentric view with frozen DINOv3 and concatenate the resulting tokens with egocentric VLM tokens to condition the action expert. Temporally, we use future observations from both views as privileged supervision for a residual adapter on task-conditioned VLM features. A foresight expert regresses DINOv3 representations of both views 0.6s ahead. At deployment, the foresight expert is discarded and the 4.2M-parameter adapter is retained. We also introduce HELM, to our knowledge, the first closed-loop humanoid loco-manipulation benchmark with synchronized egocentric and exocentric views across five whole-body tasks. On HELM, BeyondEgo improves success from 48.0% to 92.0% in distribution and from 23.5% to 65.0% on 200 held-out scenes with layout, asset, material, and lighting shifts. Ablations show that dual-view DINOv3 foresight yields the best transfer results.

Robotics.title: Embodied-Harness: Towards Recursive Self-Improvement for Robotic Manipulation
Robotics.summary: Vision-language model (VLM)-based agents offer a promising approach to robotic manipulation, yet remain limited by inadequate memory organization, uncertain failure attribution, and limited reuse of execution experience. We propose Embodied-Harness, a dual-agent framework that improves manipulation by refining the execution harness without updating model parameters. The Actor interacts with the environment through a robot-control interface, while the Reflector converts execution evidence into reusable operational guidance. Hierarchical Memory Architecture maintains short-term execution context and long-term experiential knowledge to support execution and reflection. Evidence-based Experience Reflection grounds failure diagnosis in observed interactions, while Recursive Harness Self-Improvement refines operational guidance across successive attempts. Experiments on RoboTwin 2.0, RoboSPA, and RMBench demonstrate the effectiveness of Embodied-Harness in generalization under environmental variations, spatial reasoning, long-horizon planning, and memory-dependent manipulation. Our method achieves success rates of 82.4%, 76.7%, and 94.4% on the three benchmarks, respectively. Real-world evaluation further yields an average success rate of 96.7% across three manipulation tasks. These results highlight the potential of Embodied-Harness to improve robotic manipulation through experience-driven harness self-improvement.

Robotics.title: CaPS: A causal world model for out-of-distribution physical parameter shifts
Robotics.summary: A world model that serves as a robot's digital twin has to keep working when the robot changes, for example when its links become heavier than anything seen in training. We study this case on the TriFinger robot in CausalWorld, assuming that the link masses and the low-level control law are known. Our model, CaPS (a causal world model for physical parameter shifts), gives each finger a learned energy in which every movable link contributes a term scaled by its measured mass, plus one term that does not depend on mass. Inertia and bias forces both come from this energy, actions pass through the known proportional-derivative controller, and a residual network that never sees the masses accounts for contact. Trained with light links, CaPS forecasts 100 steps open loop on three disjoint test ranges whose mean masses are 1.86, 2.75, and 3.75 times the training mean, with median joint R2 of 0.773, 0.779, and 0.750; an ensemble-residual variant, CaPS-Ens, reaches 0.801, 0.784, and 0.753. Compared with separately trained controls that see only the training-mean mass, the true masses improve both models in all ten runs at every shift. A rigid-body calculation traces the mass-independent term to the fingertips, whose mass is not intervened on, and adding the same term to ModLaNet improves it at every shift.

Robotics.title: VLRLA: Deployment-Time Adaptation of Vision-Language-Action Models through In-Context Reinforcement Learning
Robotics.summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) models connect visual perception and language understanding with robot control, providing a foundation for instruction-conditioned manipulation. However, conventional pretrained VLA policies lack a mechanism for gradual adaptation through accumulated interaction experience during deployment. We therefore propose VLRLA, a general framework that equips existing VLA models with \textit{in-context reinforcement learning} capabilities for deployment-time adaptation. Our approach augments a VLA model with a reinforcement learning module that learns from historical observations, actions, rewards, and termination signals. During deployment, the policy gradually refines its action generation and progressively improves task success while keeping model parameters fixed. Our approach is also designed for general applicability and compatibility with diverse learning history construction strategies and model training pipelines. Finally, through extensive experiments, we systematically investigate the learning properties of VLRLA in simulation and demonstrate its ability to adapt to unseen scenarios during real-world deployment.

Robotics.title: SAGE-Drive: Benefit-Aware Adaptive Reasoning for Autonomous Driving Planning
Robotics.summary: Explicit reasoning enables autonomous vehicles (AVs) to interpret complex traffic interactions and support trajectory planning, but introduces additional computational demands. Determining when explicit reasoning can improve planning accuracy remains a key challenge, as its benefits vary across driving scenarios. To address this challenge, this study proposes Scene-Adaptive Gating of Explicit Reasoning for Driving (SAGE-Drive), a benefit-aware adaptive reasoning framework for autonomous driving planning.
