To eliminate the second reading, we design ShellPlan, which compiles a strict Bash subset once into a typed execution plan, validates utility arguments against positive capability specifications, and dispatches approved plans directly via execve without a shell. Over a formal operational model, we prove single-interpretation dispatch and bound touched programs and files under audited assumptions. ShellPlan admitted 0/4,174 active attacks across six static suites and 0/90 hits in a ten-model agent benchmark (62/90 unguarded) at 1.28 ms median gate latency, preserving 36/36 (100%) frontier standard-dev completion (74/100 overall) and 0/348 external over-allows outside modeled exceptions.
Cryptography and Security.comment: 20 pages, 3 figures. Preprint with coordinated-disclosure redactions (all affected vendors notified on November 22, 2026 under a 90-day disclosure window)

Cryptography and Security.title: Adaptation or Poisoning? Security Risks of Conversational Test-Time Learning in Large Language Models
Cryptography and Security.summary: Test-time learning (TTL) enables large language models to adapt to unlabeled inputs during deployment. The model updates a lightweight adapter by minimizing the next-token prediction loss on the input it receives. When these updates persist across conversation turns, every user query serves both as the request answered in the current turn and as adaptation data for later turns. By choosing the queries used for adaptation, an attacker can influence parameter updates and weaken safety alignment through ordinary interactions with a TTL chat service. To demonstrate this risk, we introduce Progressive Test-Time Adaptation Poisoning (P-TAP), a query-only multi-turn attack that jailbreaks the model by poisoning its session adapter through the service's own updates. A sequence of escalating adversarial queries shapes the adapter turn by turn; the final harmful request is then answered under the accumulated state without itself being used for adaptation. Across four open-weight instruction-tuned models, enabling updates raises attack success rates on average by 13.00 percentage points under greedy decoding and by 22.25 points under best-of-10 sampling, relative to matched sessions receiving the same queries without updates. Answering adversarial queries but adapting on unrelated text or on benign text about the same topic removes most of this increase. Among existing safeguards, screening incoming queries flags every attack stream before the final request, while a perplexity-based detector of unsafe adaptation flags none of the successful attacks.

Cryptography and Security.title: Products of Distinguisher Hulls
Cryptography and Security.summary: The distinguisher hull of two distributions is the convex hull of the pairs of acceptance probabilities of tests in a specified class. We study its behavior under independent products for size-bounded Boolean circuits. We derive a geometric consequence of Dwork and Tankala's supersimulator theorem (FOCS 2026), giving a substantially different proof of approximate product containment for distinguisher hulls. In particular, our construction uses nonadaptive sampling in place of adaptive score corrections.

Cryptography and Security.title: RSWP: Robust SO(3)-Equivariant Watermarking for Panoramic Images
Cryptography and Security.summary: Robust watermarking for panoramic imagery is impeded by the topological mismatch between spherical signals and planar representations. Conventional methods fail under $SO(3)$ viewing rotations due to non-linear geometric warping and struggle with viewport extraction, which typically necessitates computationally expensive inverse remapping. To address these challenges, we propose RSWP, a watermarking framework grounded in icosahedral group theory. Leveraging the property that the icosahedral group ($\mathcal{I}_{60}$) serves as the largest discrete subgroup of $SO(3)$, we decompose spherical rotations into tractable local planar rotations and combinatorial facet permutations. Accordingly, we introduce a decoupling architecture that embeds watermarks into discrete facets and a theoretically guaranteed Equivariance-to-Invariance decoding paradigm. By employing an equivariant feature extractor followed by a permutation-invariant sorting module, this paradigm rigorously synchronizes rotation-distorted features. Moreover, the dual-extractor design inherently supports direct, blind watermark retrieval from partial 2D renderings without geometric calibration. Extensive experiments demonstrate that RSWP achieves state-of-the-art robustness against continuous $SO(3)$ rotations and viewport transformations while preserving high visual fidelity.

Cryptography and Security.title: MARGIN: Margin-Aware Regularized Geometry for Imbalanced Vulnerability Detection
Cryptography and Security.summary: Software vulnerability detection is critical for ensuring software security and reliability. Despite recent advances in deep learning, real-world vulnerability datasets suffer from two severe challenges: frequency imbalance and difficulty imbalance. We reinterpret these challenges from an embedding geometry perspective, observing that such imbalances induce geometric distortions in hyperspherical representation space. To address this issue, we propose MARGIN, a metric-based framework that learns discriminative vulnerability representations through adaptive margin metric learning and hyperspherical prototype modeling. MARGIN dynamically adjusts geometric regularization according to the distribution structure estimated by the von Mises-Fisher concentration, aligning the probability mass of embedding distributions with their corresponding Voronoi cells, thereby reducing geometric distortion and yielding more stable decision boundaries. Extensive experiments on public vulnerability datasets show that MARGIN consistently outperforms strong baselines, achieving notable improvements in classification and detection, especially on challenging, imbalanced datasets. Further analysis demonstrates that MARGIN produces more structured embedding geometries, improving robustness, interpretability, and generalization.

Cryptography and Security.title: NRSnooper: Enabling Real-Time Bidirectional Traffic Decoding in Commercial 5G NR Networks
Cryptography and Security.summary:
Decoding both uplink and downlink cellular traffic reveals lower-layer protocol behavior, unprotected signaling, and encrypted higher-layer packets beyond what scheduling metadata exposes. In commercial 5G NR networks, however, passive decoding must overcome UE-dedicated configurations hidden in encrypted signaling, unknown identifiers of ongoing connections, and the computational demands of wideband traffic.
  We present NRSnooper, a passive sniffer that decodes downlink control and bidirectional data traffic in real time, including traffic from already-connected UEs and traffic after encrypted configuration updates. NRSnooper learns reusable physical-layer configurations through an instrumented open-source UE that reproduces commercial UE capabilities. It recovers connection-specific identifiers from ongoing transmissions and selects matching configurations through CRC-validated data decoding. A hybrid CPU-GPU pipeline sustains continuous wideband processing.
  Evaluations on a controlled testbed and two commercial networks show that, compared with using only configurations from unencrypted signaling, NRSnooper decodes 1.3x and 6.3x as many control messages and 9.0x and 17.7x as many downlink data blocks, respectively. NRSnooper also decodes traffic from an already-connected UE during an ongoing phone call and achieves real-time bidirectional decoding on 100 MHz commercial NR channels.

Cryptography and Security.title: NPUFHE: An Efficient CKKS Execution System for Ascend NPUs
Cryptography and Security.summary:
Fully homomorphic encryption (FHE) enables computation directly on encrypted data, but its substantial computational cost hinders adoption in privacy-preserving artificial intelligence (AI) applications. Neural processing units (NPUs) already deployed in AI infrastructure provide a practical platform for FHE acceleration. However, after mapping the number theoretic transform (NTT) to matrix multiplications on Ascend NPUs, modular arithmetic and representation conversion on the Vector backend still incur substantial overhead at stage boundaries. Evaluation-key material of key switching also increases storage and data-transfer costs, and whole-limb task assignment causes tail load imbalance.
  We present NPUFHE, an end-to-end CKKS execution system optimized for Ascend NPUs. To reduce modular recovery and twiddle costs in NTT, we propose Boundary-Optimized NTT, which eliminates intra-axis modular recovery, compiles intra-axis twiddle factors into matrix constants, and introduces two-level folded modular recovery at axis endpoints. To alleviate evaluation-key storage and transfer pressure, we design Compact Shoup encoding, which halves the key representation through local coefficient recovery. Finally, we propose Cost-Aware Parallel Tiling to mitigate tail load imbalance caused by whole-limb task assignment. It uses a cost model to adaptively partition tail tasks and smooth stepwise latency increases.
  We integrate the above designs into OpenFHE. On one Ascend 910B4, full-packing CKKS bootstrapping with real evaluation keys takes 0.95 s, encrypted CIFAR-10 ResNet-20 inference with bootstrapping requires 9.87 s per image, and encrypted MNIST inference achieves an amortized latency of 19.81 ms per image. The peak NTT throughput of NPUFHE reaches up to $184.22\times$, $2.04\times$, and $4.46\times$ that of OpenFHE on CPU, TensorFHE, and CROSS, respectively.

Cryptography and Security.title: DuetFHE: Compiling Dual-Lane Nonlinear Circuits for Complex-Packed CKKS Inference
Cryptography and Security.summary: Complex packing in CKKS stores two real streams in the real and imaginary lanes of each slot. Direct squaring couples the lanes, while squaring them separately requires two ciphertext-ciphertext multiplications (HMults). DuetFHE is a GPU compiler that uses a phase transformation to square both lanes independently with one HMult. It reuses dual-lane squares in polynomial activations and the modular-reduction stage of CKKS bootstrapping. The compiler further plans ciphertext scales and reuses conjugates to sustain the complex-packed representation across stages. On a single RTX 5090, DuetFHE accelerates four polynomial activations by $1.60$--$1.79\times$ over direct evaluation on two real ciphertexts. For two-image AESPA ResNet-20 inference, it maintains packed execution across convolutions, square activations, and bootstrapping, achieving a $1.97\times$ end-to-end speedup over the fastest tested EasyFHE batched baseline on both the RTX 5090 and RTX PRO 6000.

Cryptography and Security.title: Looking Is Not Picking: An Attention-Segment Account of Tool-Selection Failures in LLM Agents
Cryptography and Security.summary: LLM agents mis-call tools, and the natural guess is that the model failed to see the right tool in a crowded harness. We show the opposite through a lens concurrent work sets aside -- the model's attention to labeled tool-definition segments. On real BFCL failures, by per-candidate attention argmax the model attends most to the correct tool 80% of the time (vs. 21% chance), and the gold is the under-attended segment on only 10%: it looks at the right tool and still picks wrong. This directly refutes the intuitive "crowded-harness / lost-in-the-middle" explanation: the failure is at the decision readout, not the harness, and we pin it there three ways. (1) Input vs. readout: repairing the prompt (reordering or duplicating the gold tool) recovers <=23% of failures, while readout-side interventions recover 59-91%. (2) Representation-invariance: two gold-pointed interventions in different representations -- an additive attention-logit bias and a residual-stream steering vector -- recover largely the same failures (per-task Jaccard 0.865 pooled, 0.79-0.91 per model), so the bottleneck is localized to the readout independent of which representation is poked. (3) A training-free, gold-free selector: per-segment attention closes most of the gold-free-vs-oracle gap on BFCL (+11.9 pts pooled function-name selection vs. +17.9-pt oracle headroom) and adds +14.9 pts on Seal-Tools; every model positive (exact McNemar p<=8e-4 each). Scopes differ: the causal attention-bias dose-response is bidirectional and monotonic on 10 mask-honoring models (3-32B), the full 0.5-32B span carrying only the correlational diagnostic; the deployable selector is evaluated on 5 single-turn models and does not yet transfer to a multi-turn loop.
Cryptography and Security.comment: This submission is withdrawn by the author. Upon re-evaluation, I find the experimental design and validation in this version lack sufficient rigor, and the overall work does not meet the expected standard. I will conduct more careful experiments, strengthen the analysis, and submit a thoroughly revised manuscript when ready

Cryptography and Security.title: SWIFT: A Handcrafted, Arithmetic-Minimal FPGA Engine for Real-Time Audio Deepfake Detection
Cryptography and Security.summary: Generative voice cloning threatens voice-based authentication, yet current deepfake detectors rely on power-hungry, high-precision models unsuited to edge hardware. We present SWIFT (Streaming Whiten-Integer Forensic Trust-Engine), a handcrafted detector that works in the high-frequency noise domain where synthesis artifacts concentrate. A first-order integer high-pass residual drives nine families of fixed-point descriptors, among them integer lifting-wavelet cepstral quantiles, Mahalanobis anomaly distances, Poincaré phase-space geometry, and phase jitter, fused by calibrated gradient-boosted trees and a sparse L1-regularised meta-learner. Under leakage-controlled nested cross-validation, with one shared preprocessing chain for real and fake audio, this reference model reaches accuracy of up to 99.86% and an Equal Error Rate (EER) as low as 0.03% across eight benchmarks. Its integer front-end and a fixed-point linear classifier run on the programmable logic of a PYNQ-Z2 (Zynq-7020) board, with a 7.85 microseconds per-frame datapath latency (127.4k frames/s) at 1.734 W and 11.2% LUT utilisation. Integer-only audio deepfake feature extraction is thus feasible at the edge without pretrained neural models or floating-point units.
Cryptography and Security.comment: 13 pages, 2 figures, 8 tables, 1 algorithm. Accepted at ICISS 2026. Chirantan Banerjee and Soumita Chatterjee are joint first authors

Cryptography and Security.title: AscendFHE: Efficient Fully Homomorphic Encryption on Ascend NPUs
Cryptography and Security.summary: Fully homomorphic encryption enables cloud servers to run neural networks on encrypted inputs. In CKKS, inference requires costly arithmetic on high-degree polynomials. On Ascend neural processing units, preparing operands and reconstructing intermediate results add to this cost, while limited local memory constrains parallel execution. We present AscendFHE, a CKKS backend that coordinates Ascend's matrix engines and vector cores for bootstrapping and encrypted inference. It uses balanced-byte encoding and exact modular reconstruction to reduce vector work and packs intermediate results in the next operator's input format to avoid redundant transfers. Its two-task pipeline reuses shared buffers after their last read to overlap matrix and vector execution within the local memory budget. On Ascend 910B3, AscendFHE achieves a 4.61$\times$ bootstrapping speedup and 1.59$\times$--2.00$\times$ encrypted-inference speedups across ResNet-20, BERT-base, and Llama 3 8B over our Vector-based Ascend port of Cheddar.

Cryptography and Security.title: Near-Field Physical-Layer Authentication Under Noisy Enrollment
Cryptography and Security.summary: In near-field physical-layer authentication (PLA), the receiver estimates a spatial reference from noisy enrollment pilots. With a fixed residual-energy threshold, even a small reference error can cause the false rejection (FR) probability to approach one as the received energy increases. We derive the distribution of the overlap between the true and enrolled spatial directions and use it to calibrate a test based on the aligned energy and the residual-to-aligned energy ratio. The calibration bounds FR for arbitrary regional gains and all legitimate received energies above a prescribed minimum. For a fixed enrolled reference, we reduce the problem of finding the maximum acceptance probability of a multi-antenna attacker to a one-dimensional search. We also derive a pre-enrollment upper bound that holds when the attacker chooses its precoder after observing the enrolled reference. For a single region and a fixed angular threshold, the enrollment energy sufficient to preserve angular separation grows inversely with the square of the available angular margin. In the numerical study with 128 receive elements at 28 GHz, the FR upper bound was 0.9984, including the enrollment outage allowance. At a regional phase perturbation of 20, four regions provided the best trade-off among the tested partitions: its simulated FR was 0.1442, while its false acceptance (FA) at 9 m was 1.084 under the fixed transmit-energy setting.

Cryptography and Security.title: Holding Agents Accountable with Verifiable Agent Insurance
Cryptography and Security.summary: While AI agents are useful for many tasks, they regularly misbehave in destructive ways, such as deleting important data. While prior work has focused on preventing such misbehavior, we consider how to recover after an agent misbehaves. We propose verifiable agent insurance (VAI), a framework for agent providers to commit financially to promises, a list of programmatically-specified policies that an agent is meant to follow. These promises are embedded in a smart contract on an immutable ledger (e.g., a blockchain) to prevent tampering, along with a monetary escrow. A user who detects a violation of committed promises can prompt a verifier to review agent execution traces, which are logged through the agent harness's shared tool-execution path, without instrumenting each tool separately. Upon verification of the violation, the agent provider's escrow funds are paid to the reporting user. We instantiate VAI as an end-to-end implementation on an Ethereum layer-2 network, and evaluate its coverage on three prominent agent benchmarks, two of which we re-annotated to obtain task-level policy-compliance labels. Currently, many agents do not emit user authorizations and security-relevant information as explicit, structured data objects -- rather, they embed the data needed to verify policy violations in natural language exchanges. Even so, VAI manages to detect violations in 63.6% of runs containing violations across three benchmarks. By augmenting agents to explicitly emit such objects, violation detection rises to 79.8% of runs containing violations. Our findings suggest that for improved auditability, agents should be co-designed with their security policies to emit explicit, structured records of user authorization and security-relevant actions.
Cryptography and Security.comment: 22 pages, 1 figure, 9 tables; v2: measured results on updated harnesses replace the projected coverage, adds a human baseline for the labels, signed checkpoints, and claims funded in filing order

Cryptography and Security.title: Benchmarking Web Agent Defenses Against Adaptive Visual Prompt Injection
Cryptography and Security.summary: Multimodal web agents automate website interactions but remain vulnerable to visual prompt injection (VPI), where malicious webpage content manipulates their visual processing and induces unintended actions. Although several defenses focus on detecting injected instructions in screenshots, malicious destinations such as phishing URLs embedded in HTML can remain hidden yet accessible through agent interactions. Existing evaluations have also not sufficiently examined adaptive attackers who know the defense mechanisms. To address these limitations, we introduce AdaptiveVPI, the first benchmark for systematically evaluating adaptive VPI threats in web agents. Specifically, we present a dataset of 360 webpage instances spanning 6 distinct hijack strategies across 10 real-world websites, with malicious destinations not visible in screenshots. We design an adaptive attack framework that iteratively refines malicious instructions based on feedback from the defense mechanism being evaluated. We also introduce three metrics to measure the extent of agent hijacking at three different levels. Across 10 defense configurations for computer-use agents and 11 defense configurations for browser-use agents, our adaptive attacks achieve average success rates of 91.87% and 91.99%, respectively. These results reveal a gap between current VPI defenses and realistic threats and highlight the need for defenses designed with adaptive attackers in mind.

Cryptography and Security.title: Revealing Semantic Gaps in Zero-Knowledge Virtual Machines via Obligation-Targeted Semantic Fuzzing
Cryptography and Security.summary: Zero-knowledge virtual machines (zkVMs) prove correct execution of programs and underpin systems securing billions of dollars in digital assets. Their security depends on alignment between the instruction set architecture (ISA) that programs target, such as RISC-V, and the constraint system, polynomial equations that check the prover's record of every intermediate value (the witness). Mismatches, or semantic gaps, come in two kinds: underconstraint bugs let a malicious prover forge a proof of an execution the ISA forbids (a soundness violation), and divergence bugs make the zkVM itself deviate from the ISA or crash, so an honest prover cannot prove a legitimate execution (a completeness violation). Both cluster at corner cases such as division by zero that conventional fuzzing almost never reaches, and underconstraint bugs leave program output unchanged. Our key insight is that these corner cases correspond to constraint obligations derived from the ISA specification and the proof system's algebraic structure. We build Beak, a reinforcement-learning fuzzer in which obligations replace three random decisions: they supply inputs that trigger each obligation, reward executions that trigger new combinations of obligations, and direct witness tampering to the step where an obligation is triggered. Beak flags divergence bugs by comparing registers against a reference RISC-V emulator, and underconstraint bugs by checking whether the constraints accept a tampered witness. On six leading production RISC-V zkVMs, Beak detects 25 of 37 known bugs (67.6%) versus 5 (13.5%) for the prior state of the art, and discovers 14 previously unknown bugs, all responsibly disclosed and patched.
Cryptography and Security.comment: 18 pages. Accepted at the Network and Distributed System Security (NDSS) Symposium 2027

Cryptography and Security.title: TurboFHE: An Efficient and Scalable Multi-GPU Framework for Homomorphic LLM Inference
Cryptography and Security.summary: Fully homomorphic encryption (FHE) enables privacy-preserving large language model inference but remains computationally intensive. Existing multi-GPU FHE inference systems rely on expert-crafted parallelization plans that generalize poorly across hardware platforms and applications. We present \fwName, a framework that automatically compiles CKKS inference programs into efficient multi-GPU executables. Its compiler can split different nodes of the same computation graph at the ciphertext and polynomial level. Guided by a measurement-based performance model, its hardware-aware planner jointly optimizes task partitioning, placement, operand residency, and transfer scheduling. %Critical-path-guided rewrites extract shared computation and restructure homomorphic sums. Its backend then generates optimized GPU kernels and executes plans using CUDA graphs and selective point-to-point transfers. \fwName adapts its plans to diverse hardware configurations and FHE inference algorithms for large-scale models. On a single A100 GPU, \fwName achieves a $24.5\times$ speedup over THOR's reported BERT-Base inference latency. For Cerium's Llama-3-8B workload, \fwName outperforms Cerium's expert-crafted plans by $1.14\times$, $1.16\times$, and $1.24\times$ on 2, 4, and 8 RTX PRO~6000 GPUs, respectively. On A100 GPUs, \fwName achieves $98.0\%$, $91.8\%$, and $79.3\%$ parallel efficiency for the same workload on 2, 4, and 8 GPUs, respectively.

Cryptography and Security.title: FlowSteer: Prompt-Only Workflow Steering Exposes Planning-Time Vulnerabilities in Multi-Agent LLM Systems
Cryptography and Security.summary: Multi-agent systems (MAS) powered by large language models (LLMs) increasingly adopt planner--executor architectures, where planners convert prompts into subtasks, roles, dependencies, and routing paths. This flexibility enables adaptive coordination, but exposes an attack surface in workflow formation: prompts can shape agent organization without modifying MAS infrastructure. We study this risk through social influence probing workflows to identify high-impact subtasks and malicious-signal propagation. The analysis reveals two vulnerabilities: workflow position can amplify or suppress a malicious signal, and sycophantic framing makes downstream agents more likely to relay it. We translate these findings into FlowSteer, a prompt-only workflow steering attack that converts vulnerability priors into one crafted prompt. FlowSteer aligns a malicious signal with influential task components and guides replanning toward dependencies that preserve propagation. Experiments show that FlowSteer increases malicious success by up to 55% over naive prompting, transfers across MAS setups, and remains effective with black-box topology inference. As FlowSteer biases the planning signals that generate the workflow, MAS defenses that inspect only the generated workflow provide limited protection. As such, we introduce FlowGuard, an input-side defense that reduces malicious success by up to 34% while preserving prompt utility. Our results position workflow formation as a new safety frontier for multi-agent LLM systems, opening a planning-time security perspective on how agent coordination itself can be attacked and defended.

Cryptography and Security.title: Persistent Jailbreak Backdoor Attack
Cryptography and Security.summary: Safety alignment is widely used to align large language models (LLMs) to produce helpful and harmless responses. However, an attacker can plant a jailbreak backdoor in an LLM such that adding a universal trigger word or phrase to a harmful prompt elicits attacker-desired responses. Existing jailbreak backdoor attacks induce distinct behaviors on backdoored inputs and safety samples (harmful prompts paired with refusal responses), making the backdoors susceptible to subsequent safety alignment and advanced defenses. In this paper, we propose a persistent jailbreak backdoor attack that reduces the divergence between clean and trigger-conditioned continuations during LLM decoding, making backdoored samples difficult to distinguish from safety samples. We also introduce a deferred-response mechanism that postpones harmful generations, further disguising the backdoor behavior. We evaluate our attack, PJBack, on eight LLMs from five model families, ranging from 7B to 70B parameters. PJBack achieves an average attack success rate of 93.9% and bypasses all seven evaluated defenses while preserving benign utility. In contrast, five existing backdoor attacks either achieve limited attack success or fail to withstand the evaluated defenses.

Cryptography and Security.title: Ziv Meets Sumcheck: Zero-Knowledge Proofs of Floating-Point LLM Inference
Cryptography and Security.summary: Zero-knowledge proofs can show that a neural network produced a given output without revealing the network, but current systems for language models prove integer approximations of the model rather than the floating-point arithmetic that is actually deployed. Proving floating-point matrix multiplication has been regarded as hard, because rounding after every addition makes the result depend on the order of the additions. We avoid this obstacle by proving the correctly rounded product, in which every dot product is computed exactly and rounded once. This result is independent of the hardware and at least as accurate as standard kernels. We give an interactive proof for this relation whose cost is close to that of integer matrix multiplication, with roughly a thousand times fewer committed values than per-operation floating-point circuits need constraints, extend it to every layer of a transformer, and give a privacy construction for the complete argument whose zero knowledge we prove under explicit hypotheses. We implement the system and prove the full forward pass of GPT-2 small, including all twelve blocks and the output over the whole vocabulary, in 19 minutes on two processor cores; verification takes 21 seconds. The verifier rejects all 236 attacks we tested, and the model's outputs agree with high-precision inference at least as closely as standard 16-bit inference does.

Cryptography and Security.title: Rateless Lattice Codes over Fading Wiretap Channels: Finite-Length Secrecy and the Secret-Key Capacity of Degraded Sessions
Cryptography and Security.summary: In rateless transmission the transmitter keeps sending until the legitimate receiver (Bob) can decode. Over a wiretap channel this has a useful side effect: the eavesdropper (Eve) sees only as many symbols as Bob needs, although the transmitter knows neither channel. We study the secrecy of rateless lattice codes in this setting. First, using a public dither and privacy amplification, we prove a finite-length secrecy bound, in total variation distance, for every channel realization, even if Eve knows all codes and seeds and combines all packets. Second, stopping when Bob acknowledges successful decoding, as in hybrid ARQ, costs at most the logarithm of the number of possible feedback outcomes in secret bits. Third, for degraded sessions with state-based stopping and without a pre-shared key or other public discussion, the secret-key rate of a session cannot exceed its accumulated Gaussian secrecy capacity, and adaptive key generation with shaped rateless lattice codes comes within any $ε>0$ of this limit when Eve's channel states are revealed after the session. If only their statistics are known, choosing the key length after the session guarantees a prescribed secrecy-outage probability. Finally, over block Rayleigh fading with a CRC-based acknowledgement and joint belief-propagation decoding, and with Eve $20$~dB weaker on average, the scheme reaches $59$--$69\%$ of the outage-weighted throughput of an ideal infinite-length secure hybrid-ARQ benchmark for Bob SNRs of $8$--$20$~dB.

Computation and Language.title: How Do Large Language Models Learn Concepts During Continual Pre-Training?
Computation and Language.summary: Human beings primarily understand the world through concepts (e.g., dog), abstract mental representations that structure perception, reasoning, and learning. However, how large language models (LLMs) acquire, retain, and forget such concepts during continual pretraining remains poorly understood. In this work, we study how individual concepts are acquired and forgotten, as well as how multiple concepts interact through interference and synergy. We link these behavioral dynamics to LLMs' internal concept circuits, computational subgraphs associated with specific concepts, and incorporate graph metrics to characterize circuit topology. Our analysis reveals: (1) LLMs' concept circuits provide a non-trivial, consistent signal of concept learning and forgetting; (2) concept circuit topology evolves stage-wise, rising during concept acquisition, and transiently rising before declining during concept forgetting; (3) semantically similar concepts induce stronger interference than weakly related ones; (4) conceptual knowledge differs in their transferability, with some significantly facilitating the learning of others. Together, our findings provide a circuit-level view of concept learning dynamics and motivate concept-aware training strategies, such as Circuit-aware Experience Replay, which uses circuit topology to prioritize concepts vulnerable to forgetting.

Computation and Language.title: Wired for Overconfidence: A Mechanistic Perspective on Inflated Verbalized Confidence in LLMs
Computation and Language.summary: Large language models are often not just wrong, but \emph{confidently wrong}: when they produce factually incorrect answers, they tend to verbalize overly high confidence rather than signal uncertainty. Such verbalized overconfidence can mislead users and weaken confidence scores as a reliable uncertainty signal, yet its internal mechanisms remain poorly understood. We present a circuit-level mechanistic analysis of this inflated verbalized confidence in LLMs, organized around three axes: capturing verbalized confidence as a differentiable internal signal, identifying the circuits that causally inflate it, and leveraging these insights for targeted inference-time recalibration. Across two instruction-tuned LLMs on three datasets, we find that a compact set of MLP blocks and attention heads, concentrated in middle-to-late layers, consistently writes the confidence-inflation signal at the final token position. We further show that targeted inference-time interventions on these circuits substantially improve calibration. Together, our results suggest that verbalized overconfidence in LLMs is driven by identifiable internal circuits and can be mitigated through targeted intervention.

Computation and Language.title: ComplexIF: A Challenging Multi-Turn, Multi-Constraint Instruction-Following Benchmark
Computation and Language.summary: As frontier LLMs saturate existing instruction-following benchmarks, measuring further progress requires harder tests that remain faithful to real use. In practice, users often combine several constraints, add them at different turns of a conversation, and expect all of them to hold in the assistant's response. We introduce ComplexIF, a challenging benchmark for this setting, together with the automatic pipeline that generates it. The pipeline expands seed requests into multi-turn conversations, weaves constraints into their turns, and keeps only tasks that a strong model can solve, so difficulty can be raised by adding constraints or turns while every task stays solvable. ComplexIF's two splits test complementary sides of instruction following: a verifiable split of format constraints, checked by programs, and a rubric split of semantic instructions, such as a tone or an audience, checked with an LLM judge. Across 14 proprietary and open-weight models, even the strongest satisfies every constraint on fewer than half of the verifiable tasks, and no model leads on both splits.

Computation and Language.title: The Token Tax: Systematic Bias in Multilingual Tokenization
Computation and Language.summary: Tokenization inefficiency is associated with structural disadvantages for morphologically complex, low-resource languages, inflating compute resources and reducing accuracy. We evaluate 11 large language models (LLMs) on AfriMMLU (5 subjects; 16 African languages); for the 10 models whose fertility we could compute, higher token fertility is associated with lower accuracy: all 50 model--subject slopes are negative, 24 are significant at p<0.05, and 12 remain significant after false-discovery-rate correction. We further find that reasoning models (e.g., DeepSeek R1, o1) have the highest average accuracy and the smallest English-African gaps among the models evaluated. In terms of economics, a doubling in tokens results in quadrupled training cost and time, underscoring the "token tax" faced by many languages. These results motivate morphologically aware tokenization, fair pricing, and multilingual benchmarks for equitable natural language processing (NLP).

Computation and Language.title: Sánchez, Feijóo, or Abascal? Speaker Attribution and Ideological Congruence in LLM Personas Reading Posts on X of the Leaders of the Three Main Parties of the 29N General Election in Spain
Computation and Language.summary: Source cues are central to political communication, yet reception studies with large language model (LLM) personas as synthetic audiences have not tested whether personas respond to who speaks and not only to what is said. With Spain's general election of 29 November 2026 in mind, we run a speaker-attribution experiment using 1,075 anonymised X posts by the leaders of PSOE, PP and VOX on four topics (the economy and employment, household costs, immigration and corruption) and 791 distinct value-grounded, LLM-generated personas. Each post was assigned to 300 topic-selected persona profiles, 150 grounded in the Inglehart-Welzel cultural map and 150 in Moral Foundations Theory, under four conditions: no author, Sánchez, Feijóo or Abascal, yielding 322,470 complete persona-post quartets. Naming any leader lowered support for identical text, with the penalty for Abascal nearly twice as large as those for Sánchez and Feijóo. The penalty follows the persona's elicited left-right self-placement (ideological congruence): left personas spare Sánchez and right personas spare Feijóo, although ideology was never in the message-evaluation prompt. Corruption posts were penalised under every name, whereas on other topics the ideologically closest leader generally produced little or no penalty. The leader order matches public opinion in 48 CIS barometers (2022-2026) in all three groups and the sign of all twelve differences, but fits barometers before the model's 2024 knowledge cutoff better than recent ones. Our findings demonstrate that LLM personas evaluate political speakers through systematic, value-congruent priors: however, while they replicate human candidate rank-orders across survey barometers, this alignment is ordinal rather than quantitative, highlighting their utility for controlled source-effect experiments though not as substitutes for empirical public opinion surveys.
Computation and Language.comment: 24 pages, 7 figures, 31 tables. Code and configuration: https://github.com/VictorMYeste/spanish-political-communication

Computation and Language.title: Unsolvability Ceiling in Multi-LLM Routing: An Empirical Study of Evaluation Artifacts
Computation and Language.summary: Efficient routing across multiple LLMs enables cost-quality tradeoffs by directing queries to the cheapest capable model. Prior work attributes routing headroom to an "unsolvability ceiling", queries no model in the pool can solve. We present a large-scale study of multi-tier LLM routing with 206,000 query-model pairs across six benchmarks (MMLU, MedQA, HumanEval, MBPP, Alpaca, ShareGPT) using the Gemma 4 and Llama 3.1 families. Evaluating with both LLM-as-a-judge and exact-match metrics, we show that a substantial portion of reported unsolvability stems from evaluation artifacts: (i) systematic judge biases favoring verbosity over correctness, (ii) truncation under fixed generation budgets, and (iii) output format mismatches. Through dual-judge validation and exact-match grounding, we reduce measured unsolvability across tasks. We introduce a decomposition framework attributing failures to these artifacts, revealing consistent patterns across domains and model families. These artifacts also distort router training signals: standard routers collapse to majority-class prediction (~79% smallest-tier optimal), confirmed via random-feature and shuffled-label controls, incurring a 13-17 percentage point opportunity cost. We provide actionable recommendations including dual-judge validation, exact-match anchoring, and cost-sensitive objectives. Our findings suggest existing routing headroom estimates are substantially inflated, underscoring the need for reliable evaluation protocols in multi-LLM systems.

Computation and Language.title: Refine, Don't Reinvent: RASA-Bench for Source-Grounded Hindi Prose Refinement
Computation and Language.summary: For a producer of Hindi creative prose, drafting is cheap and editing is not: a machine-written episode, story, or essay reads as under-written and flat, laced with translationese, and it sometimes quietly alters what the source says. RASA-Bench targets that editing task across three Hindi prose forms, measuring how well a model refines an under-written AI draft, a task distinct from writing from scratch. Across 2,050 drafts and eight refiners (16,400 rewrites), a four-layer protocol credits a rewrite only after it passes a faithfulness check against its own source, then ranks the survivors by holistic editorial preference through per-form Bradley-Terry fits whose centered coefficients are standardized before equal-weight averaging. Staying faithful proves to be a decisive test that behaves differently by form: gate-failure rates range from 9.1% on short stories to 29.5% on audio fiction, and the drift that disqualifies a rewrite shifts from events and identity in narrative to claims and evidence in essays. A 600-case human audit puts gate agreement at 0.925 (0.91 to 0.94 across forms), whereas subjective preference is form-sensitive and least settled for essays, among human readers no less than the model judge. The benchmark, evaluation protocol, and Hindi prose diagnostics are available at https://abdur75648.github.io/rasa-bench.
Computation and Language.comment: Accepted to EACL 2027. 22 pages, 8 figures. Project page: https://abdur75648.github.io/rasa-bench

Computation and Language.title: A Tutorial on Diffusion Theory: From Differential Equations to Diffusion Models
Computation and Language.summary: Diffusion models have emerged as a leading framework for generative modeling, yet their mathematical foundations are often presented in separate treatments. This tutorial offers a unified, self-contained introduction organized into three parts. First, we construct a forward generative stochastic differential equation (SDE) that transports noise to data, marginalize over the clean data endpoint, and derive training objectives directly from the forward dynamics. Second, we begin with a conditional path from data to noise, marginalize it to obtain the forward process, and derive the corresponding reverse-time SDE and training objectives. Within this forward-reverse framework, we also establish the connection between denoising diffusion probabilistic models (DDPMs) and variance-preserving (VP) SDEs. Third, we review numerical methods for solving SDEs and discuss two approaches to guided generation: classifier guidance and classifier-free guidance.
Computation and Language.comment: A detailed tutorial on Stochastic Differential Equations and Diffusion Models

Computation and Language.title: LLM Persuasion Is in the Eye of the Evaluation
Computation and Language.summary: Large language models (LLMs) have already been shown to match or exceed human experts in persuasion. While their persuasive capabilities hold promise for beneficial uses such as education and health communication, they can also be used to manipulate and misinform, making their evaluation a growing priority for developers and regulators. That evaluation, however, remains fragmented: studies differ in what they treat as persuasion, and broad claims often rest on narrow, situation-specific assessments. Automated methods, often modelled on human studies, offer a way to compare such assessments directly, as they can be run on the same models at scale and can include high-risk forms of persuasion that would be difficult or unethical to test on people. In this study, we adapt nine published automated methods to a shared setup, run them on the same fifteen LLMs, and ask whether their rankings agree and why. We find that the methods agree only weakly (mean Spearman $ρ= 0.25$). Our analyses point to two contributing factors. Models that refuse some tasks but not others, directly or indirectly, lower agreement by about a quarter, and these refusals fall mostly on manipulation tasks. General capability also plays a part: most rational persuasion (non-manipulative) methods track it, whereas most manipulation methods do not. Together, these findings suggest that agreement depends more on the task a method sets than on how it scores persuasion, although this pattern is only indicative given the eight methods available for analysis. More broadly, our results suggest that persuasion scores combine a model's ability to persuade with its willingness to do so. A single score is therefore informative about its own setting, but says little about a model's persuasiveness across tasks.

Computation and Language.title: More Is Not More: What Matters for Opinion Diversity in LLM Simulations?
Computation and Language.summary: Large language models are increasingly used to simulate diverse human opinions in open-ended tasks such as synthetic surveys, focus group modeling, and public opinion prediction. However, LLM outputs exhibit systematic opinion homogenization, and a simulation cannot reproduce a population's opinion distribution without first covering its range of viewpoints. Interventions to increase diversity are evaluated in isolation with incomparable metrics and are typically deployed and upgraded simultaneously, making it difficult to attribute gains to specific components. We design a factorial experiment that separates two primary intervention dimensions: input conditioning (operationalized through persona depth) and interaction architecture. We evaluate all conditions on 100 real-user open-ended questions across 7 models, measuring diversity with multiple complementary metrics. Our findings challenge several common assumptions. First, more persona detail does not monotonically increase diversity. The initial step of persona conditioning already captures the majority of the gain, while further elaboration with demographic detail does not consistently improve and can reduce diversity on some models; a blinded human evaluation of matched Role and Basic responses points in the same direction. Second, rather than seeking a single best interaction architecture, we find that different architectures explore largely non-overlapping opinion regions. Combining multiple architectures yields broader coverage than optimizing any one. Third, commonly attempted low-cost alternatives such as raising sampling temperature and adding diversity instructions produce negligible effects compared to structured interventions. Overall, our results indicate that, within the tested settings, diversity does not scale along any single dimension but is sensitive to the structural form and combination of interventions.
Computation and Language.comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026 (Evaluations and Datasets Track). Code and data: https://github.com/MeYQY/more-is-not-more-neurips2026

Computation and Language.title: ReqSeek: Transformer-Based Automatic Requirements Identification for Building Large Requirements Datasets
Computation and Language.summary: Large, diverse, and high-quality datasets are significant for advancing AI in requirements engineering, yet automated identification of requirements from Software Requirement Specifications (SRS) remains a challenge. Automatic Requirements Identification (ARI) methods demonstrate limited generalization to unseen documents across heterogeneous SRSs. This work presents ReqSeek, a transformer-based, domain-agnostic ARI model for recognizing ISO 29148-style requirements in SRS documents, supporting dataset construction. We curated the Automatic Requirements Identification Dataset (ARID), comprising 2,396 training instances from 23 heterogeneous SRSs, and fine-tuned four transformer architectures. RoBERTa was selected as the base model for ReqSeek and achieved 95% precision, recall, F1, and F0.89 on the held-out evaluation set. Exploratory human-model benchmarking showed performance comparable to humans while requiring substantially less prediction time than manual annotation. Post-hoc evaluation on out-of-domain (OoD) SRSs provided evidence of requirement identification beyond ARID. Robustness analysis demonstrated ReqSeek's insensitivity to minor linguistic variations while maintaining sensitivity to major ISO 29148-style violations. We applied ReqSeek to construct the Software Requirements Dataset (SwaRD), identifying 10,201 ISO 29148-style requirements from 231 industrial SRSs. SwaRD aligns with textual and semantic properties of human-curated datasets while exceeding them in scale and domain diversity. Our results suggest that transformer-based ARI can provide precise and generalizable requirements identification.
Computation and Language.comment: Accepted for publication in ACM Transactions on Software Engineering and Methodology (TOSEM), 2026

Computation and Language.title: Loop-Count Schedules in Looped Transformers: An Empirical Study
Computation and Language.summary: Looped transformers apply one block of layers several times with shared weights, trading parameters for repeated computation. We study how the schedule of the loop iteration count R during training determines whether each extra pass acts as a full layer or as a small correction, using a controlled ladder of 46M-110M-parameter models trained on 2B tokens with learned residual gates on every loop pass and three schedules: R fixed to 2, R sampled uniformly from {1,...,6}, and R sampled from {2,3,4}. We find that the lower bound of the sampling range is the decisive choice. If the sampled range includes R=1, so that some training steps run the block only once and compute the loss on that single pass, the gates collapse to 0.1-0.5 and each additional pass becomes a small correction to the first; if the range starts at R=2, so that every training step runs the block at least twice, the gates stay at 0.6-0.9 and each pass keeps the strength of a full layer, while the model can still be run at any R from 2 up to twice the largest trained value with validation loss within a few hundredths of a nat of its best. The {2, 3, 4} schedule gives the best looped model, 2.909 nats against 2.951 for the parameter-matched plain model, and degrades by only 0.038 nats when run at twice its trained depth. We further show that under a fixed R the direction of the residual stream converges geometrically beyond the trained depth while the loss diverges, which refines a recent finding that static-depth training does not converge, and that reusing the first pass's keys and values on later passes costs 0.01-0.03 nats in every regime while making the per-token iteration uniformly contractive and halving the inference cache. The loop recovers about a third of what real depth provides at equal parameters. The code, trained weights, and per-token traces are released.
Computation and Language.comment: 16 pages, 4 figures, 11 tables. Code: https://github.com/kvoyager/gatedloop-transformer. Trained weights and per-token traces: https://huggingface.co/konstank/gatedloop-transformer

Software Engineering.title: Can Vibe Coding Produce Accessible Websites: An Empirical Study on LLM Coding Agents and Skills
Software Engineering.summary: Large language model (LLM) coding agents increasingly allow developers and non-professionals to create websites through natural-language instructions, with limited inspection of the generated source code. Although this ``vibe coding'' workflow lowers barriers to software creation, it may also propagate accessibility defects at scale. We investigate the accessibility of websites generated end-to-end by contemporary coding agents and whether agent-level accessibility interventions improve their output. We generated 90 websites for three projects using combinations of three coding agents, four language models, and multiple reasoning-effort levels. We evaluated complete interaction journeys using axe-core, IBM Equal Access Accessibility Checker, and QualWeb, and converged reports to observe violation prevalence and violated WCAG Success Criterion (SC). None of the 90 baseline websites was fully accessible, with an average of 80.43 violated interface elements. 13 WCAG SCs were violated at least once across the runs. Color contrast was the most prevalent issue, followed by labeling, semantic-structure, keyboard, and visualization failures. We reran 24 matched configurations with a general accessibility Skill and a contrast-specific Skill. Both significantly improved accessibility scores, but neither eliminated violations. User testing with blind individuals corroborated the experiential effects of the detected inaccessibilities. Moreover, functional correctness decreased with the inclusion of Skills. Our findings show that accessibility does not reliably emerge from vibe coding, and agentic interventions can both improve some accessibility issues and introduce new functional ones.

Software Engineering.title: Blind to What They Can Fix: A Detection Gap in Self-Improving Agents
Software Engineering.summary: AI agents can write programs that carry out a task without calling a model at every step, so the task runs fast and its logic stays open to inspection. Agents improve these programs by running them, studying their failures, and revising the code, a form of recursive self-improvement (RSI). We ask whether this process also yields runtime checks that can be trusted. In five task domains, with up to seven author models, agents bring their programs to high scores. Yet when the environment changes, the checks they were told to write stay silent on half or more of the resulting failures in four domains. These failures can be detected and repaired: a monitor built from records of normal runs catches most of them in three domains, and the same agents usually repair them once called. The checks do not examine the recorded relations that reveal the failures, and the strongest agent writes checks that catch most of them once told that its checks are the only thing that calls it back. An unreported failure stays unrepaired, which limits what self-improvement is worth in autonomous operation. Evaluations of self-improvement should measure not only scores but also whether a system notices its own failures.
Software Engineering.comment: 31 pages, 7 figures, 15 tables

Software Engineering.title: Generating Safety-Critical Driving Scenarios from Role-Typed Signal Temporal Logic Specifications Drafted by Large Language Models
Software Engineering.summary: Safety-critical scenarios are rare in recorded driving and must be generated to test and train motion planners of automated vehicles. In guided diffusion models, each scenario type needs its own weighted objective, separate from the validity check. Optimized together with the attacker, the vehicle under test can cancel the attack or draw it toward itself. We state each scenario as a signal temporal logic specification with clauses typed by role. Every clause names the agent it may change and the agents it may read, and the vehicle under test reads the attacker only from the attack onset. A large language model drafts the specification from a description, and a type checker accepts it. A compiler derives the optimization: it edits a diffusion model's samples by the smallest change that satisfies the specification, each clause moves only its owner, the attacker is solved against the unreacted vehicle under test before its response, and the monitor of the same specification decides acceptance. On nuScenes and CommonRoad, judged independently of the specification, one parameter set produced valid scenarios at a rate 0.14 above a weighted objective tuned per scenario type, and descriptions yielded at least one valid scenario for 11 of the 16 pre-crash types expressible in the public data. Learned planners fail more often on the generated scenarios than on their seeds. Fine-tuning on them lowers a planner's failure rate on critical scenarios, and the time headway one clause of the label requires, not the generator, sets the size of the gain.
Software Engineering.comment: Manuscript submitted to IEEE OJ-ITS and is currently under review

Software Engineering.title: Agentic Root Cause Reasoning and Localization of Unsoundness in Static Call Graph Analysis
Software Engineering.summary: Static call graph tools cannot soundly model every dynamic language feature, yet rarely reveal when, where, or why their results are unsound. We present CGRizz, an agentic framework that diagnoses unsoundness for developers and warns users about it. During training, CGRizz compares static and dynamic call graphs to identify boundary edges: calls observed at runtime but missing from the static graph. For each edge, an LLM agent proposes a root cause, including the unmodeled program pattern and responsible tool location. CGRizz validates each proposal using three independent forms of evidence: runtime instrumentation detecting the pattern, a test case reproducing the missing edge, and a warning inserted at the implicated tool location. Validated reports help developers diagnose limitations, while the warnings form an instrumented build that flags potential unsoundness in new programs without dynamic analysis. We evaluate CGRizz on three benchmark suites using WALA, OPAL, and Soot. Of 1,459 boundary edges, CGRizz reasons about 10.3% directly, all confirmed by manual audit, and resolves another 84.1% by grouping edges with validated root causes. Tool maintainers confirmed several limitations, some of which have been fixed. The warnings flag 74%-92% of unsoundness in held-out programs. Guided by CGRizz reports, a coding agent refactored programs to remove 64% of targeted root-cause patterns while preserving functionality.
Software Engineering.comment: 11 pages, 1 figure, 8 listings, 1 table

Software Engineering.title: Admitted Is Not Effective: Lessons from a Notary-Gated Retrospective Loop in an Agentic Pipeline
Software Engineering.summary:
Agentic software development pipelines with frozen prompts can repeat the same mistakes across pull requests (PRs), yet ungoverned additions to instruction files grow without bound and do not generally improve task success. We present a retrospective loop for a four-stage large language model (LLM) pipeline in which a Retrospective agent proposes edits to learned rules every ten PRs and a Notary admits, merges, or rejects them while recording each decision in a provenance ledger. In a pre-registered study of 880 PRs on two Python repositories, the loop ran end to end and the Notary admitted 55 of 89 proposals, rejecting 8 that cited nonexistent evidence.
  However, held-out review comments and hidden-test resolution did not improve after ten retrospectives. Tracing each step of the loop, we found that sparse review signal (0.45 comments/PR) left little to learn from and that rules admitted on their stated evidence did not show measurable held-out effects. We derive six lessons and argue that governed loops should admit and retire every learned rule as a testable hypothesis.
Software Engineering.comment: 5 pages, 2 figures

Software Engineering.title: ReqSeek: Transformer-Based Automatic Requirements Identification for Building Large Requirements Datasets
Software Engineering.summary: Large, diverse, and high-quality datasets are significant for advancing AI in requirements engineering, yet automated identification of requirements from Software Requirement Specifications (SRS) remains a challenge. This work presents ReqSeek, a transformer-based, domain-agnostic ARI model for recognizing ISO 29148-style requirements in SRS documents, supporting dataset construction. We curated the Automatic Requirements Identification Dataset (ARID), comprising 2,396 training instances from 23 heterogeneous SRSs, and fine-tuned four transformer architectures. RoBERTa was selected as the base model for ReqSeek and achieved 95% precision, recall, F1, and F0.89 on the held-out evaluation set. Exploratory human-model benchmarking showed performance comparable to humans while requiring substantially less prediction time than manual annotation. Post-hoc evaluation on out-of-domain (OoD) SRSs provided evidence of requirement identification beyond ARID. Robustness analysis demonstrated ReqSeek's insensitivity to minor linguistic variations while maintaining sensitivity to major ISO 29148-style violations.
