Software Engineering.comment: Accepted for publication in ACM Transactions on Software Engineering and Methodology (TOSEM), 2026

Software Engineering.title: AutoRPG: Harnessing Systematic AI for Non-Intrusive Low-Latency Mobile RPG Combat
Software Engineering.summary: Automated combat in mobile RPGs plays a critical role in game quality assurance, requiring real-time behavior control that closely resembles human gameplay. However, existing approaches fail to satisfy these requirements, either because they lack fine-grained behavioral control or because they incur high inference latency. To address these challenges, we incorporate user gameplay experience to design AutoRPG, a systematic AI framework for automating mobile RPG combat. At a high level, AutoRPG decomposes the combat process into two stages: a high-level strategic planning phase that formulates the overall combat strategy, followed by a systematic execution phase powered by a suite of carefully designed lightweight modules encompassing target tracking, character movement, dodge maneuvering, and abnormal-state handling. Experiments on three popular mobile RPGs, i.e., Genshin Impact, Wuthering Waves, and Arknights: Endfield, demonstrate that AutoRPG consistently outperforms four competitive baselines across both combat quality and generalization capability, while behaving the most similarly to human players among all evaluated agents.

Software Engineering.title: fx(hash): Salvaging The Source Code of 28k Generative Artworks
Software Engineering.summary: fx(hash), the most radically inclusive generative art NFT platform, went bankrupt and shut down on August 17, 2026. The ownership of its 2,705,350 artworks is immutable on the Tezos and Ethereum blockchains, but the source code that generates them is off-chain and in peril. We salvaged all 28,193 generative programs contributed by 5,532 international artists and archived them in Software Heritage. Here we explain why NFT generative art is fragile and the steps we took to salvage these software cultural landmarks.

Software Engineering.title: KernelShift: Benchmarking Kernel Optimization Across Evolving Hardware
Software Engineering.summary: Efficient AI computation depends on hardware that evolves over time, shifting the strategies needed to implement performant code. For CPU kernels, a key evolving factor is the set of available architectural extensions, which expose specialized hardware instructions that change the techniques used to optimize kernels. We study how effectively coding agents use these new, potentially unfamiliar extensions to write fast code. We introduce KernelShift, a benchmarking pipeline and a set of environments for evaluating coding agents in kernel optimization across evolving CPU architectures. Its agent-assisted, human-verified pipeline turns code repositories into benchmark instances, and its environments let agents optimize code with feedback from the target hardware. Using this pipeline, we construct 99 kernels from real-world, actively developed repositories (ncnn, llama.cpp, Arm SIMD Loops, and KleidiAI), including inference workloads derived from real model executions. KernelShift supports incorporating new kernels and hardware configurations as libraries and processors evolve. We evaluate agents with proprietary and open-weight models across progressively newer architectural extensions (Arm Neon, SVE, SVE2, and SME2), examining how performance changes as hardware evolves. On established extensions, agents beat the auto-vectorized compiler everywhere (2.4-19.8x) and exceed general-purpose libraries such as ncnn (getting up to 2.74x over its Neon kernels), but fall behind Arm's hand-tuned KleidiAI kernels (0.70x). In end-to-end inference of two LLMs, agent-written kernels achieve a 1.3-1.6x prefill speedup over llama.cpp's fast path. However, current agents do not yet reliably adapt to new extensions that require unfamiliar programming models, such as SME2's matrix tiles.
Software Engineering.comment: 26 pages, 9 figures, 22 tables. Project page: https://cmu-l3.github.io/kernel-shift/

Software Engineering.title: Agentic Harness Engineering: Observability-Driven Automatic Evolution of Coding-Agent Harnesses
Software Engineering.summary: Harnesses are now central to coding-agent performance, mediating how models interact with tools and execution environments. Yet harness engineering remains a manual craft, because automating it faces a heterogeneous action space across editable components, voluminous trajectories that bury actionable signal, and edits whose effect is hard to attribute. We introduce Agentic Harness Engineering (AHE), a closed loop that addresses these challenges through three matched observability pillars: (1) component observability gives every editable harness component a file-level representation so the action space is explicit and revertible; (2) experience observability distills millions of raw trajectory tokens into a layered, drill-down evidence corpus that an evolving agent can actually consume; and (3) decision observability pairs every edit with a self-declared prediction, later verified against the next round's task-level outcomes. Together, these pillars turn every edit into a falsifiable contract, so harness evolution proceeds autonomously without collapsing into trial-and-error. Empirically, ten AHE iterations lift pass@1 on Terminal-Bench 2 from 69.7% to 77.0%, surpassing the human-designed harness Codex-CLI (71.9%) and the self-evolving baselines ACE and TF-GRPO. The frozen harness transfers without re-evolution: on SWE-bench-verified it tops aggregate success at 12% fewer tokens than the seed, and on Terminal-Bench 2 it yields +5.1 to +10.1pp cross-family gains across three alternate model families, indicating the evolved components encode general engineering experience rather than benchmark-specific tuning. Ablations localize the gain to tools, middleware, and long-term memory rather than the system prompt, suggesting factual harness structure transfers while prose-level strategy does not.

Software Engineering.title: MARGIN: Margin-Aware Regularized Geometry for Imbalanced Vulnerability Detection
Software Engineering.summary: Software vulnerability detection is critical for ensuring software security and reliability. Despite recent advances in deep learning, real-world vulnerability datasets suffer from two severe challenges: frequency imbalance and difficulty imbalance. We reinterpret these challenges from an embedding geometry perspective, observing that such imbalances induce geometric distortions in hyperspherical representation space. To address this issue, we propose MARGIN, a metric-based framework that learns discriminative vulnerability representations through adaptive margin metric learning and hyperspherical prototype modeling. MARGIN dynamically adjusts geometric regularization according to the distribution structure estimated by the von Mises-Fisher concentration, aligning the probability mass of embedding distributions with their corresponding Voronoi cells, thereby reducing geometric distortion and yielding more stable decision boundaries. Extensive experiments on public vulnerability datasets show that MARGIN consistently outperforms strong baselines, achieving notable improvements in classification and detection, especially on challenging, imbalanced datasets. Further analysis demonstrates that MARGIN produces more structured embedding geometries, improving robustness, interpretability, and generalization.
Software Engineering.comment: 29 pages.10 figures, 6 tables

Software Engineering.title: Endpoint-Conditioned Process Value: What an Endpoint-Blind Process Score Adds Once Terminal Status and Cost Are Known
Software Engineering.summary: Trajectory metrics promise information beyond final-answer accuracy, but no one has measured what a process score adds once an evaluation knows the outcome and the cost. We build that comparison: a sealed consequence needing an artifact neither agent nor judge ever sees, an operational baseline of terminal status and cost, and judge scale and evidence access as experimental factors. On 1,255 trajectories over 158 test-generation tasks in 7 Python repositories, the answer is gated on the judge. Four judges from 4B to 14B, one reasoning before scoring, add nothing an interval separates from zero; a Qwen3 32B judge on identical trajectories adds +0.050 AUC (95% CI [+0.020, +0.081]) and survives a refitting bootstrap ([+0.013, +0.095]). Most of what it adds is recoverable from eight behavioural counters, so a harness should log them (the judge adds +0.020 beyond them). What the judge is shown moves it further: disclosing the terminal verdict inflates its standalone discrimination by +0.103, while reference disclosure and tool-output redaction move it by nothing an interval separates from zero. A process metric reported without the judge's scale and evidence access does not identify a quantity. We release the protocol, the sealed-endpoint harness, and all trajectories.
Software Engineering.comment: Accepted by EACL

Software Engineering.title: Looking Is Not Picking: An Attention-Segment Account of Tool-Selection Failures in LLM Agents
Software Engineering.summary: LLM agents mis-call tools, and the natural guess is that the model failed to see the right tool in a crowded harness. We show the opposite through a lens concurrent work sets aside -- the model's attention to labeled tool-definition segments. On real BFCL failures, by per-candidate attention argmax the model attends most to the correct tool 80% of the time (vs. 21% chance), and the gold is the under-attended segment on only 10%: it looks at the right tool and still picks wrong. This directly refutes the intuitive "crowded-harness / lost-in-the-middle" explanation: the failure is at the decision readout, not the harness, and we pin it there three ways. (1) Input vs. readout: repairing the prompt (reordering or duplicating the gold tool) recovers <=23% of failures, while readout-side interventions recover 59-91%. (2) Representation-invariance: two gold-pointed interventions in different representations -- an additive attention-logit bias and a residual-stream steering vector -- recover largely the same failures (per-task Jaccard 0.865 pooled, 0.79-0.91 per model), so the bottleneck is localized to the readout independent of which representation is poked. (3) A training-free, gold-free selector: per-segment attention closes most of the gold-free-vs-oracle gap on BFCL (+11.9 pts pooled function-name selection vs. +17.9-pt oracle headroom) and adds +14.9 pts on Seal-Tools; every model positive (exact McNemar p<=8e-4 each). Scopes differ: the causal attention-bias dose-response is bidirectional and monotonic on 10 mask-honoring models (3-32B), the full 0.5-32B span carrying only the correlational diagnostic; the deployable selector is evaluated on 5 single-turn models and does not yet transfer to a multi-turn loop.
Software Engineering.comment: This submission is withdrawn by the author. Upon re-evaluation, I find the experimental design and validation in this version lack sufficient rigor, and the overall work does not meet the expected standard. I will conduct more careful experiments, strengthen the analysis, and submit a thoroughly revised manuscript when ready

Software Engineering.title: DynaFix: Iterative Automated Program Repair Driven by Execution-Level Dynamic Information
Software Engineering.summary: Automated Program Repair (APR) seeks to generate correct patches for buggy programs, but recent Large Language Model (LLM)-based repair systems remain sensitive to superficial code changes and often rely on coarse test outcomes during iterative repair. We propose DynaFix, an LLM-based APR framework that integrates execution-level dynamic information into a closed-loop repair workflow. The distinguishing feature of DynaFix lies not in using execution-level information per se, but in repeatedly updating and exploiting such information throughout the iterative repair process. In each repair round, DynaFix uses ByteTrace to collect variable states, branch paths, and call stacks, incorporates these runtime signals into structured prompts, validates generated patches through re-execution, and feeds the resulting updated traces into subsequent repair iterations. This process grounds patch generation in concrete execution behavior rather than static code alone. We evaluate DynaFix on Defects4J v2.0, the Real-World Benchmark, and a code perturbation benchmark, Defects4J-Trans. DynaFix repairs 236 single-function Defects4J bugs with GPT-4 and 186 with GPT-4o, including 23 bugs not fixed by existing baselines. On Defects4J-Trans, DynaFix achieves 15.6%-32.1% higher aggregate repair counts than ReinFix and shows higher repair retention under semantics-preserving transformations. It also reduces token consumption by 60%-70% compared with state-of-the-art LLM-based APR methods. These results show that repeatedly updating and exploiting execution-level information throughout iterative repair can substantially improve the effectiveness, robustness, and cost efficiency of LLM-based program repair.
Software Engineering.comment: 34 pages, 12 figures. Accepted for publication in Journal of Systems and Software

Software Engineering.title: Multi-Agent Coordinated Method-Level Refactoring of Rust Code
Software Engineering.summary: As Rust codebases evolve, developers refactor code to reduce duplication, simplify complex methods, and keep related functionality together. Developers can make these changes manually or use IDE assists for supported operations, then check the resulting code with compiler diagnostics and tests. Method-level refactoring in Rust must preserve observable behavior while accounting for ownership, borrowing, and lifetimes. We present a large language model (LLM)-based workflow for extracting, inlining, and moving methods in Rust. The workflow combines candidate generation, configurable specialist review,and container-based validation. On six tasks from three open-source Rust projects, three end-to-end configurations passed all task checks on their first attempt, using 6, 13, and 31 model calls. To isolate the effect of review, we then gave four configurations the same six reference patches and six deliberately behavior-changing variants. A designated specialist rejected all six behavior-changing patches before container validation and let all six reference patches proceed, reducing Docker invocations from 24 to 12 relative to direct validation. The fixed specialist panel also caught all six faults early and rejected two reference patches over unmeasured performance concerns. On this workload, specialist review reduced execution work, while its effect on total time depended on review overhead and which patches reached validation.

Software Engineering.title: MetaSkill: Reusable Problem-Solving Methods for Adaptive Skill Orchestration in LLM Agents
Software Engineering.summary: Reusable skills provide specialized procedures, but large language model (LLM) agents must still determine how to organize and adapt their use. We introduce MetaSkill, a two-layer framework for reusing problem-solving methods across tasks and domains. The method layer selects from 26 curated methods and binds abstract roles to task objects. The execution layer uses the instantiated method to identify intermediate objectives, coordinate native skills, and guide repair or method reselection. On 89 SkillsBench tasks and 995 ToolHop examples, MetaSkill outperforms the evaluated baselines in all six configurations, with accuracy gains of 3.51-13.48% over the strongest baseline. Ablations support explicit method-guided orchestration beyond direct method injection and further gains from method reselection.
Software Engineering.comment: 16 pages, including appendices. The MetaSkill library is provided as ancillary material

Software Engineering.title: Validating Concurrent Correctness Witnesses with Ghosts by Thread-Modular Abstract Interpretation (Extended Version)
Software Engineering.summary: Concurrent programs are notoriously difficult to write and to reason about, and even tools based on sound theoretical foundations can produce incorrect results due to implementation bugs. Correctness witnesses have been proposed as a way to increase the confidence in the verdicts of software verifiers by enabling independent validation. Recently, correctness witnesses have been extended to the concurrent setting, by introducing ghost variables to allow encoding more expressive invariants. While different approaches to producing witnesses with ghosts exist, validation techniques are still lacking; instead of leveraging the information encoded in the ghosts to guide the validation process, validators merely treat ghost instrumentation and invariants over ghost variables as additional proof obligations. We propose a novel framework for the validation of concurrent correctness witnesses that exploits the semantic information encoded in ghost variables. It combines a checking phase, which establishes the semantic content of the ghost instrumentation, with an exploitation phase making use of this information. Both phases are formulated as thread-modular abstract interpretation. In particular, we consider two different classes of ghost variables and techniques for exploiting them, one based on resource invariants and one based on phases. Phase ghosts guide the degree to which the abstract interpretation considers interleavings instead of always abstracting them coarsely. In this way, the abstract interpreter can validate witnesses containing invariants beyond the reach of unguided thread-modular analysis, while still retaining its scalability benefits. We have implemented our framework in a static analyzer and evaluate it on witnesses encoding resource invariants obtained from a state-of-the-art software verifier, as well as on hand-crafted witnesses encoding phase information.
Software Engineering.comment: Accepted to POPL '27; Extended version with appendices

Software Engineering.title: Edit-Induced Dependency Mismatch: Propagation Omissions, Recovery, and Evaluation Blind Spots in Coding Agents
Software Engineering.summary: During iterative code modification, coding agents may continue to rely in subsequent reasoning on outdated dependency judgments whose text remains fixed in the context, leading to errors in subsequent reasoning and leaving consumer defects undetected by the original task evaluations, thereby exposing blind spots in the tested benchmarks. We study actual agent execution trajectories collected on benchmark tasks: deepseek-v4-flash runs on DeepSWE and SWE-bench Verified, supplemented by Qwen3.8-Flash cases on FeatureBench. Focusing on edit-induced consumer obligations, a full-corpus blinded human audit of the DeepSWE runs identifies terminal mismatches, including diagnoses whose task scope remains disputed. Following supplementary execution checks, all retained DeepSWE terminal events have execution support. The audit also shows that recovery within a trajectory can coexist with terminal omissions in the same run. The process analysis links the presentation of relevant consumer code to explicit dependency judgments and subsequent synchronization actions recorded in the trajectories. An explicit dependency-review prompt reduces terminal omissions under the tested conditions, supporting re-derivation of consumer obligations after edits. Local replays of selected DeepSWE cases show that synchronizing the diagnosed consumers restores the target behavior while the listed controls continue to pass. Cross-benchmark execution counterexamples show that the original task evaluations do not fully detect edit-induced dependency mismatches: patches pass those evaluations, yet additional execution checks confirm unintended defects along existing consumer paths. These findings support measuring task scores, terminal propagation states, and recovery separately.

Software Engineering.title: SatMend: LLM Agents for Automated Software Repair in Satellite Constellations with Intermittent Ground Contact
Software Engineering.summary: Satellite constellations rely on onboard software to sustain services across cooperating spacecraft. Maintaining this software requires handling related component versions and different failure causes while delivering repairs through intermittent ground contact. Automated software repair in satellite constellations remains underexplored, particularly the coordination of repairs across related versions with verified onboard recovery under intermittent ground contact. To address this gap, we propose SatMend, a software repair method driven by ground-based large language model (LLM) agents. SatMend organizes related versions into persistent sessions to retain diagnostic context and combines source and runtime evidence to select code repair or state recovery actions. It validates each version separately and submits ready candidates during continued repair, allowing ground preparation to overlap with onboard delivery and verification. Experimental results show that across configurations with 16 to 64 satellites, SatMend restores 192 of 224 faulty applications within 600 s, compared with 40 for SWE-agent, 77 for Agentless, 124 for RepairAgent, and 115 for SWE-Search. These results demonstrate SatMend's effectiveness in restoring applications and supporting service continuity in satellite constellations with intermittent ground contact.

Software Engineering.title: Fixed or Deleted? External Feedback Lets Cheaper AI Coding Agents Repair Rule Violations
Software Engineering.summary: Many defects violate project rules that the code itself does not reveal, such as layering constraints or required tests. We study whether LLM coding agents repair such violations better when an external checker reports them, with their location and a repair goal. Three models, a small, medium and large model, driven by an AI agent, worked on 25 pull requests with 31 planted defects in ten open-source projects, plus 5 correct controls, five times alone and five times with findings from CodeAssure (CA), a commercial checker. We also compare with GitHub Copilot code review, and compare CodeAssure's detection with nine free static-analysis tools run out of the box, including Semgrep and SonarQube Community. Counting a run as repaired only when the repaired code also compiles and keeps its feature, CA findings raised the repair rate from 26% to 69% for the smallest model, from 46% to 90% for the medium model and from 45% to 93% for the largest model (pull-request-level p < 0.001), and from 39% to 84% over all runs. Every Java, TypeScript and Python repair compiled. We found that agents often cleared a defect by deleting a newly added file. Metrics based on whether the defect is gone count feature deletion as a success. The largest model alone did so in 44 of 125 runs. CA includes a check for deleted files that largely prevents this. In an ablation with the check turned off, removals rose from 9 to 65 out of 375 runs and the repair rate fell to 54% (small), 70% (medium) and 85% (large model). The CA workflow also outperformed Copilot code review (p < 0.001). Together, the free tools detected 8 of the 31 defects, and CA detected all 31. With CA, the medium model repaired 90% of runs, against 45% for the largest model alone, at about one fifth of the mean cost per run ($0.17 against $0.91).
Software Engineering.comment: 14 pages, 9 tables. Data and analysis code: https://github.com/CodeAssureLabs/external-feedback-coding-agents v2: adds a build and feature check of all scored repairs (Section 4.6); corrects the scoring of one pull request

Software Engineering.title: Implementation and Software-in-the-Loop Evaluation of a Trans-Domain Digital Twin Architecture for Autonomous Guidance of the Phoenix VTOL UAV Without Online GNSS
Software Engineering.summary: Autonomous UAV guidance in emergency response, infrastructure monitoring, and cargo transportation requires reliable navigation. However, satellite-based positioning may become unavailable or unreliable in enclosed spaces, blind spots caused by natural obstacles and structures, and environments affected by radio interference and signal spoofing during electronic warfare. This study designs, implements, and evaluates a system based on a Trans-Domain Digital Twin (TDDT) for autonomous guidance of the Phoenix VTOL UAV. Independent navigation, flight dynamics, and meteorological models are coordinated within a cycle of state estimation, prediction, decision-making, command execution, and feedback. Data from inertial, magnetic, pressure, and airspeed sensors, together with environmental information, form the basis for estimation and prediction. Furthermore, a shared state, temporal synchronization, preservation of information provenance, and command traceability establish continuity between models and decisions. The system was tested with a simulated physical twin in a software-in-the-loop environment. Vertical takeoff, movement toward the destination, landing, and autonomous stopping were recorded, and the dynamic model was adjusted to a limited extent based on sensor-derived feedback. Separating the evaluation reference from navigation inputs enabled independent assessment of positioning error and computational performance. The results confirm operational coordination, decision traceability, and closed-loop guidance under the tested conditions, providing a reproducible platform for the development and evaluation of navigation without satellite-based positioning.
Software Engineering.comment: 34 pages, 17 figures, 4 tables. Software-in-the-loop evaluation of GNSS-independent Phoenix VTOL guidance using a trans-domain digital twin architecture. Source code and reproducibility materials: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24419538

Programming Languages.title: The Vienna Architecture Description Language
Programming Languages.summary: The Vienna Architecture Description Language (VADL) is a powerful processor description language (PDL) that enables the concise specification of processor architectures. From a single VADL processor specification, the VADL compiler can automatically generate a wide range of artifacts required for rapid design space exploration. These include assemblers, compilers, linkers, functional and cycle-accurate instruction set simulators, synthesizable hardware description language (HDL) specifications, as well as test cases and documentation. A distinctive feature of VADL is the separation of the instruction set architecture (ISA) specification from the microarchitecture (MiA) specification. This decoupling gives users the flexibility to combine various ISAs with different MiAs, offering a versatile approach to processor design. In contrast to existing PDLs, VADL's MiA specification operates at a higher level of abstraction, enhancing the clarity and simplicity of the design process. Notably, using a single ISA specification, VADL streamlines compiler generation and maintenance by eliminating the need for intricate compiler-specific knowledge. Because the original VADL implementation is subject to restrictive licensing, the open-source implementation OpenVADL was initiated. This article introduces VADL, compares the original implementation with the ongoing OpenVADL development, describes the generator techniques in detail, and demonstrates both the expressiveness of the language and the performance of the generators in an empirical evaluation. The evaluation highlights the conciseness of VADL and the efficiency of the generated artifacts. Finally, the viability of OpenVADL for design space exploration is demonstrated in a case study on CRC32 checksum computation for the RISC-V ISA.

Programming Languages.title: Cache the Knowledge, Not Just the Prompt: Dynamic Datalog as the Action Language for LLM Agents
Programming Languages.summary: An LLM agent that answers questions about a knowledge graph writes a program per question, and its tools evaluate each from scratch. We give the agent a Datalog REPL, a session over a dynamic Datalog engine, in which rules are inserted and retracted like facts while derived facts stay current. Prompt caching reuses the model's processing of what a session shares, and the Datalog REPL reuses the evaluation of it. On chains of questions over three knowledge graphs, agents reuse a relation that the REPL keeps in 179 of 180 cases, with two models, and write fewer output tokens: SQL and Python agents write 23 to 82% more. With SQL tables or a Python namespace, Claude Haiku 5.5 stores almost nothing for later questions, and a chain of seven questions at 13 million facts takes it a median of 48 and 56 s, against 31 s with the REPL. Claude Opus 5.5 matches the REPL by storing tables in SQL, and when the data changes it stores views, which are evaluated again at every read. A relation that the REPL keeps is read like a table and stays current like a view. Datalog is a niche language beside SQL and Python, and with thinking enabled the models answer as accurately with it.
authors: Bruno Rucy Carneiro Alves de Lima
Programming Languages.comment: Accepted for publication at AICCC 26

Programming Languages.title: Hashing Theorems Modulo Rewrites and Binder Permutation Enables Equivalence Search over 200k Mathlib Theorems
Programming Languages.summary: Like all code, Lean libraries accumulate technical debt and structural deficiencies over the course of their development. A particular concern is duplicate theorems: different parts of a big library can unwittingly contain and prove the same theorem, duplicating maintenance efforts. Tools can help detect redundancy and clean up. For instance, Mathlib's duplicate-declarations linter compares theorem types syntactically after sorting top-level binders and erasing binder information and universe levels. If detecting an equivalence requires unfolding, reorientation, or logical transformations, it escapes this comparison. In this work, we present a method to detect theorems which are equivalent with regard to argument order and currying/uncurrying of dependent types. We implement our method for Lean. By applying it to Mathlib, a library of more than 200k theorems, we demonstrate that it is computationally cheap and scalable. We discuss how our work may enhance efforts to tackle the maintenance burden of Lean libraries.

Programming Languages.title: Certified Split Windows for Parallel Lexing: Recovering Boundaries Where No Byte Certifies
Programming Languages.summary: A certified split point lets a parallel lexer cut unlexed input at one byte with the serial token stream provably preserved, but several conventional token sets in the predecessor's study certify no byte once string, comment, or whitespace-run forms are included (arXiv:2608.03473v2). We generalize from a byte to a bounded window, a byte string such that, whatever the context, the token covering its final byte begins at a known origin. Since the certificate is conditional on occurrence and may be vacuous, every applicability figure counts only windows carrying an asserted completely tokenizable occurrence witness. We give a conservative model of a maximal-munch scanner's possible histories across a window, prove it sound, and decide reachability in it exactly by exhausting a finite quotient of its reachable configurations. Within the flat, completely tokenizable scope, model-positive answers are semantic certificates; negatives are relative to the model, which refuses some windows a greedy scanner would allow. For both model and semantic certificates, existence is PSPACE-complete with or without a witness requirement, and a shortest window has $2^{Θ(n)}$ bytes in the worst case over at most $n$ live states. Two smaller searches decide plain model existence, the second shipped in release 2.2.0 of munch. Of 400 random token sets, 322 of the 337 certifying no byte gain witnessed windows and four more gain model certificates with occurrence unresolved. No model search reaches its threshold. The predecessor's exact-empty rows all gain witnessed windows of two to four bytes. A boundary profile marks each gap of an occurring window forced, crossed or open, and a window-local cut is sound exactly at forced gaps. Whether a given gap is ever a boundary and whether it is open are PSPACE-complete, while occurrence, the forced verdict and a given origin's certificate are NL-complete.
Programming Languages.comment: 53 pages, 4 tables. v4: existence of a certified window, for the model or the definition, with or without a witness, is PSPACE-complete and a shortest one has $2^{Θ(n)}$ bytes in the worst case; whether a gap is ever a boundary is PSPACE-complete, and a given origin's certificate NL-complete. Artifact: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21842344 . Companion to arXiv:2608.03473

Programming Languages.title: Certified Split Points for Parallel Lexing: Exact and Modulo Discarded Tokens
Programming Languages.summary: Table-driven DFA lexing is sequential, since each transition depends on the previous byte's state. Scanning one input in parallel needs each chunk's entry state, which existing methods recover by simulation, speculation, prescanning, or overlap. We give two conditions under which none is needed. For a longest-match scanner restarting from q0 at every token boundary, a byte b is a certified split symbol when no reachable state other than q0 has a b-transition whose target can reach acceptance, and q0 is not re-entrant if it has one. Every occurrence of such a byte in completely tokenizable input begins a token, so chunks starting there reproduce the serial sequence of kinds and lengths. The condition is necessary and sufficient, but one string, comment, or whitespace run can remove every useful certificate. Comments and whitespace are usually discarded, so we weaken the guarantee to equality after deleting a declared discarded set and give a second condition, a precomputed constant-time one-bit test. It is sound but incomplete and more permissive, strictly so on suitable token and discarded sets. It recovers newline for a conventional C-like tokenization and tab, newline and carriage return for JSON, and refuses newline where block comments are unrestricted. Safety modulo the discarded set is PSPACE-complete for general token automata and decidable in polynomial time for literal vocabularies, and every unsafe byte has a replayable counterexample. On the fifteen token sets studied the second condition is already exact. Splitting at exact certificates in munch reaches 92.6-95.3% parallel efficiency at eight threads on a restricted CPU set and a 512 MiB corpus, and a 3.46-3.94x end-to-end speedup at four threads, on one machine. It turns delimiter-based parallel lexing from a language-specific assumption into a property a compiler checks.
Programming Languages.comment: 52 pages, 2 figures, 4 tables. v5: proves safety modulo discarded tokens PSPACE-complete, already over three symbols, and that automata for the completely tokenizable inputs can need exponentially many states. Artifact: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24220471 . Certificate tables, composition figures and the validation sweep are generated from the compiled automata and asserted in CI

Programming Languages.title: Fuss-free cumulative universes: theory and practice
Programming Languages.summary: Universes are central to dependent type theory, and they are notoriously difficult to handle in a way that is both correct and usable. We propose a new "fuss-free" generalised algebraic presentation for polymorphic cumulative universes that dispenses with the intricate theory of coherent universe coercions in favour of a simpler formulation, which we prove equivalent by means of a normalisation theorem for the former. We study the fuss-free formulation by means of (1) an abstract specification of its bidirectional elaboration algorithm, and (2) a concrete implementation in Haskell. We also describe and implement an extension of the fuss-free universe hierarchy with a judgemental notion of datatype description from which prior notions of cumulative inductive type may be derived.
Programming Languages.comment: Extended version of a paper to appear in POPL 2027

Programming Languages.title: Constrained Code Generation with Diffusion Language Models
Programming Languages.summary: Diffusion language models (DLMs) are a powerful, emerging paradigm for code generation. They construct programs through iterative refinement of partially corrupted token sequences and enable parallel token refinement. Importantly, this paradigm exposes a global program state at each denoising step, which provides a natural intervention point for enforcing program-level functionality and security constraints, guiding the generation before the final code is committed. Building on this observation, the paper introduces Constrained Diffusion for Code (CDC), an inference-time neurosymbolic framework that integrates constraint satisfaction directly into the reverse denoising process without retraining the base diffusion model. CDC augments the base diffusion sampler with constraint-aware denoising operators that combine mathematical optimization with program analysis to identify constraint-relevant regions of the intermediate program state and locally adjust the denoising trajectory, steering generation toward feasible programs while remaining close to the base model. Across code generation benchmarks, CDC consistently improves constraint satisfaction in functional correctness, security, and even syntax, outperforming diffusion and autoregressive baselines with less corrective computation and more localized edits.

Formal Languages and Automata Theory.title: Attractors Is All You Need: Parity Games In Polynomial Time
Formal Languages and Automata Theory.summary: This paper provides a polynomial-time algorithm for solving parity games that runs in $\mathcal{O}(n^{2}\cdot(n + m))$ time-ending a search that has taken decades. Unlike previous attractor-based algorithms, the presented algorithm only removes regions with a determined winner. The paper introduces a new type of attractor that can guarantee finding the minimal dominion of a parity game. The attractor runs in polynomial time and can peel the graph empty.
Formal Languages and Automata Theory.comment: I withdraw this preprint because the algorithm is incorrect. Tom van Dijk provided a four-vertex counterexample, Odd owns all four vertices, labelled by priority. The moves $0\to1\to2\to4$ are forced; from 4, Odd chooses 0 or 2. Even wins every play, yet for d=4 the first pruning step discards the entire Even dominion, contradicting Lemma 3. The claimed polynomial-time result does not follow

Formal Languages and Automata Theory.title: A detailed verification of Neary's PCP(5) construction
Formal Languages and Automata Theory.summary: Neary proved that the Post correspondence problem remains undecidable for instances with five pairs of words. We give a detailed verification of his construction. We first verify the undecidability of the restricted binary tag-system halting problem used in the reduction. We then prove both directions of the reduction to the five-pair problem, using the longer closing pair proposed by Rote. In particular, we show that every solution of the constructed PCP instance yields a halting computation of the simulated tag system.

Formal Languages and Automata Theory.title: Cycle Counting and Character Expectations Using Alternating Structures
Formal Languages and Automata Theory.summary:
Recently, three related papers [arXiv:2412.13941, arXiv:2009.00897, arXiv:2409.03626] found a connection between two subjects: the w-cycle theorem, which is a theorem about counting appearances of cycles reading out a word w in certain graphs, and character expectations on word measures.
  The w-cycle theorem was proven independently by [arXiv:1410.2540] using stackings and by [arXiv:1410.2579] using bislim structures. In the current work, we generalize stackings and bislim structures to alternating stackings and alternating bislim structures. We show how this significantly strengthens the w-cycle theorem for words admitting such alternating structures, and as a result, also strengthens the recent results of [arXiv:2412.13941] and [arXiv:2409.03626]. We show that generic words admit alternating bislim structures, and therefore, the strengthened results hold for generic words.
  Using our new machinery, we address conjectures of Wilton, of Hanany--Puder and of Puder--Shomroni. We prove that all three conjectures hold for generic words, but we also find counterexamples for the first two.
Formal Languages and Automata Theory.comment: 56 pages, 22 figures

Formal Languages and Automata Theory.title: Certified Split Windows for Parallel Lexing: Recovering Boundaries Where No Byte Certifies
Formal Languages and Automata Theory.summary: A certified split point lets a parallel lexer cut unlexed input at one byte with the serial token stream provably preserved, but several conventional token sets in the predecessor's study certify no byte once string, comment, or whitespace-run forms are included (arXiv:2608.03473v2). We generalize from a byte to a bounded window, a byte string such that, whatever the context, the token covering its final byte begins at a known origin. Since the certificate is conditional on occurrence and may be vacuous, every applicability figure counts only windows carrying an asserted completely tokenizable occurrence witness. We give a conservative model of a maximal-munch scanner's possible histories across a window, prove it sound, and decide reachability in it exactly by exhausting a finite quotient of its reachable configurations. Within the flat, completely tokenizable scope, model-positive answers are semantic certificates; negatives are relative to the model, which refuses some windows a greedy scanner would allow. For both model and semantic certificates, existence is PSPACE-complete with or without a witness requirement, and a shortest window has $2^{Θ(n)}$ bytes in the worst case over at most $n$ live states. Two smaller searches decide plain model existence, the second shipped in release 2.2.0 of munch. Of 400 random token sets, 322 of the 337 certifying no byte gain witnessed windows and four more gain model certificates with occurrence unresolved. No model search reaches its threshold. The predecessor's exact-empty rows all gain witnessed windows of two to four bytes. A boundary profile marks each gap of an occurring window forced, crossed or open, and a window-local cut is sound exactly at forced gaps. Whether a given gap is ever a boundary and whether it is open are PSPACE-complete, while occurrence, the forced verdict and a given origin's certificate are NL-complete.
Formal Languages and Automata Theory.comment: 53 pages, 4 tables. v4: existence of a certified window, for the model or the definition, with or without a witness, is PSPACE-complete and a shortest one has $2^{Θ(n)}$ bytes in the worst case; whether a gap is ever a boundary is PSPACE-complete, and a given origin's certificate NL-complete. Artifact: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21842344 . Companion to arXiv:2608.03473

Formal Languages and Automata Theory.title: Certified Split Points for Parallel Lexing: Exact and Modulo Discarded Tokens
Formal Languages and Automata Theory.summary: Table-driven DFA lexing is sequential, since each transition depends on the previous byte's state. Scanning one input in parallel needs each chunk's entry state, which existing methods recover by simulation, speculation, prescanning, or overlap. We give two conditions under which none is needed. For a longest-match scanner restarting from q0 at every token boundary, a byte b is a certified split symbol when no reachable state other than q0 has a b-transition whose target can reach acceptance, and q0 is not re-entrant if it has one. Every occurrence of such a byte in completely tokenizable input begins a token, so chunks starting there reproduce the serial sequence of kinds and lengths. The condition is necessary and sufficient, but one string, comment, or whitespace run can remove every useful certificate. Comments and whitespace are usually discarded, so we weaken the guarantee to equality after deleting a declared discarded set and give a second condition, a precomputed constant-time one-bit test. It is sound but incomplete and more permissive, strictly so on suitable token and discarded sets. It recovers newline for a conventional C-like tokenization and tab, newline and carriage return for JSON, and refuses newline where block comments are unrestricted. Safety modulo the discarded set is PSPACE-complete for general token automata and decidable in polynomial time for literal vocabularies, and every unsafe byte has a replayable counterexample. On the fifteen token sets studied the second condition is already exact. Splitting at exact certificates in munch reaches 92.6-95.3% parallel efficiency at eight threads on a restricted CPU set and a 512 MiB corpus, and a 3.46-3.94x end-to-end speedup at four threads, on one machine. It turns delimiter-based parallel lexing from a language-specific assumption into a property a compiler checks.
Formal Languages and Automata Theory.comment: 52 pages, 2 figures, 4 tables. v5: proves safety modulo discarded tokens PSPACE-complete, already over three symbols, and that automata for the completely tokenizable inputs can need exponentially many states. Artifact: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24220471 . Certificate tables, composition figures and the validation sweep are generated from the compiled automata and asserted in CI

Symbolic Computation.title: IteraSong: LLM-Guided Iterative Symbolic Music Creation in a Web DAW
Symbolic Computation.summary: Music creation is inherently iterative, yet many symbolic generation systems still center on producing or regenerating isolated outputs. We present IteraSong, an interactive web-based Digital Audio Workstation (DAW) for LLM-guided iterative symbolic music creation. Unlike one-shot generation systems, IteraSong supports a generate-audition-edit-refine loop over a persistent multi-track project. Users initialize a fully labeled pop draft, then progressively refine it through natural-language instructions. The LLM maps requests to a hierarchical action space of editing primitives exposed via Model Context Protocol (MCP) tools, spanning global, track, section, and bar/note scopes. The demo enables attendees to edit multi-track compositions in natural language, apply deterministic and generative edits, and undo/redo changes in real time.
Symbolic Computation.comment: AAAI 2027 Demonstration Program (accepted). Extended version with appendix

Information Retrieval.title: Straight to the Product: What Online Retailers Miss When Shoppers Ask AI First
Information Retrieval.summary:
When people ask an AI assistant what to buy, what happens next at the store? We link the same people's assistant conversations to their later browsing at twenty large online retailers. People go to the product the assistant named: among shoppers who had not visited the store in the past week, visits to the named product within a day rise from 0.02 to 2.07 per 100 answers (+2.0 points [1.7, 2.4]), and on days with a product-page visit at the store, 44% show a product from their own answer, against 1.5% for a matched answer given to someone else. The result replicates in a separate five-month period. Few arrive through the assistant's link: after recommending answers, 89% of visits carry no sign of it, and 54% follow a web search, the same share as their usual visits. When a search comes just before the first visit, it names the answer's product 28% of the time (1% in earlier weeks), as if the search box were an address bar. The chat names the product; the store logs a search. Once there, shoppers keep browsing.
  We propose product follow-through, the share of answers followed by a visit to the product they named, as a way to evaluate shopping assistants and agents by what people do next: it needs no referral data or provider logs and can be computed for each assistant.

Information Retrieval.title: MusicRec: Audio, Lyrics, and Engagement Feature Enrichment for Music Recommendation
Information Retrieval.summary: Music recommendation systems typically treat songs as opaque tokens, relying on interaction histories that overlook semantic or acoustic content. Prior LLM-augmented, multimodal, and text-enhanced sequential recommenders partially combine semantic, acoustic, or engagement signals, and none jointly model all three within a unified LLM-based framework grounded in song content. In this work, we propose a multimodal framework for session-based music recommendation that enriches the LastFM-1K dataset with three complementary signals: (1) audio and lyric embeddings from pretrained music and text models, (2) LLM-generated semantic metadata using the MGPHot schema, and (3) listening completion ratios. We validate the generated metadata against human MGPHot annotations across all 58 attributes. We extend the E4SRec framework with multimodal features, ItemID encoder backbones including SASRec, BERT4Rec, and GRU4Rec, and LLM backbones including LLaMA-2-13B, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, and LLaMA-3-70B across zero-shot and fine-tuned settings. In addition, we evaluate four multimodal fusion strategies, benchmark five audio and five lyric encoders, and compare Spotify audio attributes with LLM-generated MGPHot metadata. Our experiments show that content-based features improve over ID-only baselines by up to 95% in Recall and 79% in NDCG, with the largest gains when the ItemID baseline is weakest. Fine-tuning substantially improves over zero-shot, after which the best audio or lyric setup outperforms the ID-only baseline for every backbone. Naive multimodal fusion does not always yield additive improvements, highlighting challenges in cross-modal integration, while structured LLM-generated metadata proves more useful than Spotify audio attributes. We release a large-scale multimodal benchmark for music recommendation research.
Information Retrieval.comment: Accepted at IEEE BigData 2026. Extended version: 18 pages, 5 figures, 14 tables

Information Retrieval.title: Where Do Fact-Checking Errors Arise? Separating Retrieval, Search Control and Judgement in Evidence-Grounded Verification
Information Retrieval.summary: An evidence-grounded fact-checker can fail because it does not find the evidence or because it does not use it; end-to-end accuracy does not tell the two apart. We present a protocol that follows the reference evidence from the store to the verdict and separates retrieval, search control, judgement and verdict validation. We assess 293 claims from FEVER, FEVER 2.0 and AVeriTeC with one open-weights 9B model under two evidence conditions: small stores of annotated evidence, where discovery is easy, and the full source collections. In the control condition a single hybrid retrieval pass delivers complete reference evidence for 226 of 228 evidence-bearing claims, and adaptive controllers and a tool agent spend two to nine times as many model calls without a consistent gain. Of 34 decisive claims labelled as lacking evidence, 33 have the complete evidence in the packet: in 15 the judge abstains, and in 18 validation rules overturn a decisive verdict. On AVeriTeC these rules lower single-pass accuracy by six points, to 65.0% (balanced accuracy 57.6%). Ten judges from eight model families also show abstentions and validation conversions on fixed packets. Against the full stores hybrid single-pass accuracy falls by 17 to 29 points. Wikipedia evidence recovery declines; AVeriTeC recovery changes from annotated answers to cited pages and is measured separately. No controller recovers the accuracy loss. The agent also shows no resolved gain on 714 further Wikipedia claims. Evidence recovery, judgement and validation should be measured separately before an error is attributed to search.

Information Retrieval.title: Multi Interests for Joint Search-Recommendation Modeling
Information Retrieval.summary: Search and recommendation are crucial for understanding user preferences. More and more studies are attempting to jointly model search behavior and recommendation behavior, by integrating user active search and passive recommendation behavior data to better mine user preferences. However, although existing cross-domain unified modeling frameworks can effectively compensate for the differences in behavior between domains, they overlook the expression of interests in different scenarios under mixed sequences. In this study, we propose a multi-interest-based mixed sequential modeling framework MIJSR, which performs multi-interest mining and adaptive integration on search recommendation mixed sequences from both structural and semantic perspectives. Specifically, our model can be roughly divided into three modules: cross-domain behavior fusion, multi-interest mining, and multi-task prediction. Firstly, we align the representations of query and item through contrastive learning training. Then, we extract the multi interests of the mixed behavior sequence from both structural and semantic perspectives. Structurally, we extract search interests, recommendation interests, and cross interests through subsequence partitioning and mask settings; In terms of semantics, we use the semantic information of queries for clustering and perform semantic segmentation on mixed sequences to construct semantic multi interests. Finally, the adaptive fusion of multiple interests is combined with other side information to use a progressive layered extraction model for multi-task prediction. Extensive experiments on two open-source datasets have shown that our model can further enhance its accuracy in search and recommendation by extracting users' multi interests at a fine-grained level. Codes are available at https://github.com/pxcstart/MIJSR.

Information Retrieval.title: MUSES: Retrieving the Literature That Shapes a Researcher's Next Paper
Information Retrieval.summary: Some of the work that shapes a researcher's next paper is not something they went looking for: it may arrive before the project has a question anyone could search for. How much can be anticipated from past publications alone? We introduce MUSES, a benchmark of 1.04 million cases built from the Semantic Scholar Open Research Corpus (S2ORC), with 140,278 held-out test cases. Given a researcher's papers before a cutoff, a system ranks 2.33 million earlier candidates for their next paper, scored primarily on works they had not cited before. Because citations alone do not show what shaped a paper, we also asked authors which works shaped or inspired their papers, yielding 1,633 evaluable cases, a distinct construct from citation-based targets. A classifier grounded in human coding adds citation contexts where the next paper describes building on a work. Across lexical, dense and citation-graph retrievers and supervised models, past publications provide a useful guide to the next paper's literature, but retrieval is harder for previously uncited works. In the main comparison, history-based retrievers place a newly cited work in their top 100 for 30--37% of cases, versus 5% for popularity. Among author-collected cases, one retriever finds an author-named work in 52% of cases (30% when targets exclude previously cited works). The researcher's own history also outperforms histories from topically similar researchers. For previously uncited works, even pooling the evaluated rankings leaves 36--58% of cases without a target in any top-100 list, across citation-based and author-reported targets. Project information helps narrow this gap: in hindsight, adding the next paper's title improves retrieval, and adding its abstract improves it further. MUSES provides a benchmark for developing systems that help researchers discover literature relevant to their next project.

Information Retrieval.title: Weight Coding: Evolving Web-Scale Recommenders through Direct Weight Edits with LLM Agents
Information Retrieval.summary: Web-scale recommender models evolve primarily through retraining or fine-tuning. We propose \emph{weight coding}, a methodology for model evolution through direct, executable weight edits. A large language model (LLM) agent inspects model structure and parameters, formulates hypotheses, and implements edits using evaluation feedback. The loop progresses from localized changes to targeted searches and composition, allowing edited components to adapt to one another. A cached engine enables rapid forward evaluation without backpropagation. On Pinterest's 147M-parameter Image Search two-tower retriever, weight coding improves held-out recall@10 of production model by up to 15.0 percentage points (+24\% relative) with few edits in about 1/4 GPU hours of a full post-training finetune, while a common launch only improves around 1\%. After reinitializing the entire 13.6M-parameter interaction module randomly while retaining the surrounding trained model, searching 2,448 mixing and normalization parameters yields 9.8 points above production. Offline gains span the full funnel including dense retrieval, generative retrieval and ranking, with up to 1.37B learnable parameters and different edits for each architecture. Steering edits provide explicit control of model performance over segments like freshness and product. Weight coding requires no serving change and online A/B tests increase saves per user from the edited retrieval source by 8.4\% to 10.7\%, aligned with the target business objectives. Our results establish weight coding as a practical and useful tool for model development and and behavioral control in a real web-scale production system, with potential to extend to both pre-training and post-training stages across the funnel.

Information Retrieval.title: Invisible to humans, visible to machines: a preregistered audit of Unicode fidelity across four biomedical bibliographic APIs
Information Retrieval.summary: To develop a reusable, preregistered method for auditing the character-level fidelity of bibliographic application programming interfaces (APIs), and to apply it to four public APIs used to build biomedical text corpora. Preregistered audit (OSF osf.io/zjevr). From the 2024 PubMed Central (PMC) Open Access subset, a simple random sample of 4,000 English-language research articles was drawn. Abstracts returned by the PubMed E-utilities, Crossref, OpenAlex and Semantic Scholar were compared with the PMC Journal Article Tag Suite (JATS) XML abstract for 51 registered code points, 34 of them in four primary classes: typographic punctuation, mathematical/scientific symbols, Greek letters and special whitespace. A cell (API x class) was classified as systematic loss when the upper 95% Wilson bound of conditional preservation was below 5%, and as faithful when the lower bound exceeded 90%. The mechanism of each loss was examined in the aligned text and the raw API responses. Two of 16 cells met the loss criterion. PubMed preserved typographic punctuation in 0.6% of eligible abstracts (12/2,113; 95% CI 0.3-1.0%), replacing it with ASCII equivalents. OpenAlex preserved special whitespace in 0.0% (0/1,085; 95% CI 0.0-0.4%), which its inverted-index format cannot store. Mathematical symbols and Greek letters were preserved by all four APIs (95.2-99.7%). Crossref returned an abstract for 75.4% of papers (95% CI 74.1-76.7%) and for none published by Elsevier (0/360) or the American Chemical Society (0/105). The same published abstract reaches text-mining pipelines with different characters depending on the API that serves it. Studies that analyze characters, including character-level markers of writing assisted by large language models, should take text from a source shown to preserve those characters, or normalize all sources identically, and report the API and retrieval date.

Data: doi:10.5281/zenodo.20556349; code: https://github.com/P-Czum/pmc-unicode-audit

Information Retrieval.title: MoR4Rec: Mixture-of-Recursion for Sequential Recommendation
Information Retrieval.summary: Sequential recommender systems aim to predict a user's next interaction by modeling temporal dependencies in historical behavior sequences. To capture such dependencies, recent approaches increasingly rely on attention-based architectures, particularly transformers. While effective at modeling long-range sequential patterns, these models apply a fixed computation depth to all interaction items, treating them as equally complex. However, user behavior is inherently heterogeneous, with many interactions following simple repetitive patterns, whereas others require modeling higher-order dependencies. This mismatch leads to inefficient utilization of model capacity and unnecessary computational overhead, particularly in deep transformer-based architectures. To address this issue, we propose MoR4Rec, a sequential recommendation framework based on a Mixture-of-Recursion paradigm, which enables item-wise adaptive computation through a shared transformer backbone. A learned routing mechanism dynamically assigns each item to an appropriate recursion depth, allocating deeper computation to complex interactions while processing simpler patterns more efficiently. To improve computational efficiency, we develop a cascade-based strategy with key-value sharing across recursion steps. We further introduce a gated attention mechanism that adaptively regulates contextual information during recursive sequence modeling. Extensive experiments on three benchmark datasets show that MoR4Rec consistently outperforms strong transformer-based baselines, achieving average gains of 2.28% in Recall@5, 2.50% in NDCG@5, and 2.0% in MRR@5 over the strongest baseline. The improvements remain consistent across top-10 and top-20 recommendation cutoffs, while comparisons with vanilla transformers demonstrate the computational efficiency of adaptive recursive processing.

Information Retrieval.title: CACO: Coverage-Aware Coordinated Optimization for Continuous Generative Retrieval
Information Retrieval.summary: Continuous generative retrievers powered by flow matching and diffusion sample multiple queries in item embedding space for approximate nearest-neighbor (ANN) search under fixed budgets. However, existing generative retrievers can suffer from retrieval overlap under uncoordinated sampling, whereas explicit diversity guidance to broaden the candidate set may induce relevance drift as it lacks direct feedback on the value of additional items. We introduce CACO (Coverage-Aware Coordinated Optimization), a self-supervised post-training framework coordinating queries from frozen flow-matching and diffusion retrievers toward complementary item coverage with negligible latency overhead. Using empirical retrieval frequencies across sampled reference queries as a relevance proxy, CACO formulates a label-free coverage objective that improves recall across all 30 backbone-dataset settings in offline experiments. To avoid the overhead of sampling reference queries at inference, CACO employs a coordinated query adjustment network combining inter-query bidirectional attention with gated relative directions, updating queries via bounded tangent-space projection and spherical retraction. During training, CACO applies tangential antithetic perturbations and counterfactual single-query replacement to measure each query's marginal gain, yielding an unbiased gradient estimator of smoothed set coverage across non-differentiable ANN search. On eight public benchmarks and an in-house 24-partition streaming industrial dataset, CACO improves Recall@100 and Recall@400 by up to 23.7% and 23.9% over the strongest baseline, cuts inter-query overlap by 53.3%-64.9%, and adds only 0.5%-3.0% inference latency.

Information Retrieval.title: VistaTree: Question Answering over Long Multimodal Documents with Image-Derived Summary Trees
Information Retrieval.summary: Answering questions over long multimodal documents requires locating relevant evidence across pages containing text, tables, and figures. When the document exceeds the model's context window, selective retrieval becomes necessary. We introduce VistaTree, a document question-answering agent that builds a summary tree directly from rendered page images. VistaTree segments documents into contiguous page spans, recursively groups them into a topic hierarchy, and refines sibling summaries to distinguish neighboring sections. At query time, the agent uses node summaries to select relevant nodes and reads the corresponding pages, using hierarchical navigation when the full outline exceeds the context budget. Experiments on MMLongBench-Doc and LongDocURL evaluate answer quality and retrieval cost using a locally hosted vision-language model, and quantify the performance gap between global and hierarchical access to the index.

Information Retrieval.title: Evaluating Small Open LLMs for Medical Question Answering: A Practical Framework
Information Retrieval.summary: Incorporating large language models (LLMs) in medical question answering demands more than high average accuracy: a model that returns substantively different answers each time it is queried is not a reliable medical tool. Online health communities such as Reddit have become a primary source of medical information for millions of users, yet they remain highly susceptible to misinformation; deploying LLMs as assistants in these settings amplifies the need for output consistency alongside correctness. We present a practical, open-source evaluation framework for assessing small, locally-deployable open-weight LLMs on medical question answering, treating reproducibility as a first-class metric alongside lexical and semantic accuracy. Our pipeline computes eight quality metrics, including BERTScore, ROUGE-L, and an LLM-as-judge rubric, together with two within-model reproducibility metrics derived from repeated inference (N=10 runs per question). Evaluating three models (Llama 3.1 8B, Gemma 3 12B, MedGemma 1.5 4B) on 50 MedQuAD questions (N=1,500 total responses) reveals that despite low-temperature generation (T=0.2), self-agreement across runs reaches at most 0.20, while 87-97% of all outputs per model are unique -- a safety gap that single-pass benchmarks entirely miss. The clinically fine-tuned MedGemma 1.5 4B underperforms the larger general-purpose models on both quality and reproducibility; however, because MedGemma is also the smallest model, this comparison confounds domain fine-tuning with model scale. We describe the methodology in sufficient detail for practitioners to replicate or extend the evaluation for their own model-selection workflows. All code and data pipelines are available at https://github.com/aviad-buskila/llm_medical_reproducibility.

Information Retrieval.title: LLM-Based Assistant for Dog Care Guidance
Information Retrieval.summary: This study investigates whether domain grounding through Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) and parameter-efficient fine-tuning using Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) can enhance the accuracy and reliability of pet care advice generated by large language models (LLMs). We curated a dataset of breed-specific dog care information and used it to develop two systems: a RAG pipeline based on TinyLlama-1.1B-Chat-v1.0, and a fine-tuned LLaMA-3.2-1B model adapted using LoRA. Both systems were evaluated on 15 dog care questions. The RAG model achieved a perfect average score of 2.0, outperforming the fine-tuned model (mean = 1.47). Statistical analyses, including Welch's t-test, Mann-Whitney U, and Wilcoxon signed-rank tests (all p < 0.05), confirmed the significance of the performance gap. Our findings suggest that retrieval-based domain grounding leads to more accurate, consistent, and trustworthy responses than standalone fine-tuning in specialized LLM applications.

Information Retrieval.title: Bayesian Rational Search Engine User
Information Retrieval.summary: A user faces a list ordered by a noisy proxy for relevance and decides whether to pay to inspect another item or stop with the best she has found. Because she does not know the page's quality, each inspection both produces a candidate and updates her beliefs about the remaining items. We show that the optimal policy is a standout rule: the user stops when her best find is sufficiently good relative to what she expects from the page, with the required margin changing with depth. The browsing dynamics collapse to a one-dimensional Markov chain, yielding the full distribution of inspection depth through a closed-form recursion. The model uncovers three reasons for stopping: trust, commit, and cut-losses, and yields testable implications. It also turns inspection depth into a learning-to-rank likelihood. Observed depth restricts the latent relevance path to a polyhedron of survival inequalities, while conversion identifies the terminal winner. Simulations show that the estimator recovers relevance under correct specification and improves ranking using only the incumbent ranker's features. Applied to public Baidu search logs, the inspection depth likelihood produces rankings that align more closely with expert relevance judgments than click-trained alternatives.

Information Retrieval.title: NoeVera: Can Knowledge Guide Experiments and Experiments Refine Knowledge?
Information Retrieval.summary: With the growing demand for large language model (LLM) services, optimizing LLM serving systems is becoming increasingly complex, and the bottleneck is no longer predicting how a given configuration will perform. The harder problem is deciding what to investigate: which mechanisms matter for a workload, which configurations are worth testing, and what evidence a decision still needs. In this work, we present NoeVera, an agentic Second Brain that goes beyond just one-shot retrieval by turning papers, code, benchmarks, and experimental results into a persistent, provenance-preserving knowledge base with three planes: source evidence, reusable synthesis, and agent memory. Decision-aware retrieval assembles compact evidence packs, role-specific agents reason over them and invoke a simulator (Vidur or GAUSS) whenever quantitative support is needed, and every finding is written back as a scoped evidence record, so knowledge guides experiments and experiments refine knowledge. In configuration search over four serving scenarios, NoeVera comes within 5% of the optimum in a median of 6-7 simulator calls, versus 9 for Bayesian optimization and 15 for a knowledge-free agent with the same tools; on A100 GPUs, its representative configurations deliver ~1.30x vLLM-default throughput and meet every scenario's latency objective. When reused, provenance-preserving evidence records over-generalize on only 8% of applicability traps, versus 28% for a general-purpose agent memory. On the held-out 48-task split of a 72-task benchmark, NoeVera scores 29% higher than an equally equipped agent and 36% higher than its single-call retrieval counterpart (0.80 vs. 0.62 and 0.59), and even when baselines receive NoeVera's own prompts, a statistically significant part of its evidence-evolution advantage remains.

Information Retrieval.title: Zarc: Exact Nearest Neighbors over a Billion Vectors in Seconds
Information Retrieval.summary: Exact k-nearest-neighbor vector search lies on the critical path of machine learning systems, from sparse attention in the latest large language models (LLMs) to long-context memories and training-data deduplication. Exhaustive GPU search scans the whole dataset for every query, while approximate indexes return inexact neighbors. Recent methods skip almost every vector with a cheap half-precision proof that it lies too far away, but only on one GPU that holds the whole dataset. Our insight is to keep only the short rows of these proofs in GPU memory and to fetch the few remaining full vectors from host memory. Our system, Zarc, answers Euclidean, cosine, inner-product, and filtered queries exactly under updates. On four H100 GPUs, it answers 10,000 exact queries over one billion vectors in 1.1 seconds instead of five minutes. On eleven open LLMs, it retrieves the exact top-10 attention keys 2.2x to 13.1x faster than exhaustive search. In sparse attention over one million tokens, it runs 3.1x faster than bf16 selection with FlashInfer, which misses the exact top-64 for most queries.

Information Retrieval.title: DataRecycle: Trustworthy Distillation of Structured Data from Scattered Web Evidence
Information Retrieval.summary: The web contains vast amounts of scattered quantitative evidence that is difficult to organize into comparable and verifiable structures. Yet its unstructured, sparse, and sometimes conflicting nature makes a systematic distillation costly and error-prone. Existing approaches force users to make a trade-off: search engines return document lists that require labor-intensive extraction and reconciliation, while generative AI systems produce fluent summaries that obscure data provenance, introduce reporting bias, and hide inconsistencies. We present DataRecycle, an interactive system that helps transform scattered web evidence into structured tables of comparable numerical facts. Given a user's query or statement, DataRecycle decomposes it into entities and attributes, retrieves candidate evidence, and organizes scattered, potentially conflicting records in a table-based evidence view. To address key challenges in automated data distillation (i.e., incomplete retrieval, untraceable generation, sparse data distribution, and multi-source inconsistency), DataRecycle adopts an ontology-guided, top-down data acquisition strategy, visualizes the recorded lineage from retrieved snippets to extracted values, and aligns heterogeneous data across dimensions such as time, definition, and scale. We evaluate DataRecycle through module-level experiments, a usage scenario, and a user study, showing that the system helps users organize numerical web evidence into provenance-linked tables and inspect uncertainty and conflicting sources.

Information Retrieval.title: Access Paths for Efficient Ordering with Large Language Models
Information Retrieval.summary: In this work, we present the \texttt{LLM ORDER BY} semantic operator as a logical abstraction and conduct a systematic study of its physical implementations. First, we propose several improvements to existing semantic sorting algorithms and introduce a semantic-aware external merge sort algorithm. Our extensive evaluation reveals that no single implementation offers universal optimality on all datasets. From our evaluations, we observe a general scaling relationship between sorting cost and the ordering quality for comparison-based algorithms. Building on these insights, we design a budget-aware optimizer that utilizes heuristic rules, LLM-as-Judge evaluation, and consensus aggregation to dynamically select the near-optimal access path for LLM ORDER BY. In our extensive evaluations, our optimizer consistently achieves ranking accuracy on par with or superior to the best static methods across all benchmarks. We believe that this work provides foundational insights into the principled optimization of semantic operators essential for building robust, large-scale LLM-powered analytic systems.

Information Retrieval.title: Bridging Blind Spots With Words: Decentralized Multi-View Spatial Reasoning via Language-Constrained Communication
Information Retrieval.summary: As multimodal LLMs (MLLMs) get increasingly used as collaborative partners across embodied robotics, AR/VR, and multi-user systems, spatial reasoning is now often distributed across agents with partial environment visibility, necessitating spatial reasoning integration. Prior work in language-mediated spatial integration is however strictly limited to simplified two-agent scenarios. To address this gap, we first formalize the general problem of decentralized multi-view spatial reasoning, where N agents observe distinct viewpoints, exchange budget-constrained natural language messages, and collaborate to enable a listener to answer spatial queries. We then introduce a novel multi-view spatial benchmark to isolate queries that demand non-trivial multi-view integration. Through an extensive empirical study, we discover that the penalty of restricting decentralized spatial reasoning to natural language with limited budget is far smaller than suggested by prior two-agent literature. Nevertheless, we observe that substantial headroom still remains for multi-agent spatial reasoning in this setting, as evidenced by a significant gap between current centralized performance and an oracle best-of-K ceiling. Moreover, we show that reinforcement learning with credit assignment substantially bolsters the decentralized model, effectively closing the gap with the centralized baseline.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Approximating TSP walks in subcubic graphs
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: We prove that every simple 2-connected subcubic graph on $n$ vertices with $n_2$ vertices of degree 2 has a TSP walk of length at most $\frac{5n+n_2}{4}-1$, confirming a conjecture of Dvořák, Král', and Mohar. This bound is best possible; there are infinitely many subcubic and cubic graphs whose minimum TSP walks have lengths $\frac{5n+n_2}{4}-1$ and $\frac{5n}{4} - 2$ respectively. We characterize the extremal subcubic examples meeting this bound. We also give a quadratic-time combinatorial algorithm for finding such a TSP walk. In particular, we obtain a $\frac{5}{4}$-approximation algorithm for the graphic TSP on simple cubic graphs, improving on the previously best known approximation ratio of $\frac{9}{7}$.
Data Structures and Algorithms.comment: 33 pages. This version corrects an error in the statement of Theorem 2.4 and fixes various minor issues

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Packed-Ring Queues: Lock-Free and Wait-Free Concurrent Queues on GPU
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: Concurrent queues are a foundational building block of parallel programming. On CPUs, decades of research have produced queue designs with well-understood correctness and progress guarantees -- from lock-free rings to wait-free constructions. On GPUs, where queues increasingly sit on the critical path of device-side task graphs and GPU-initiated I/O, no comparable foundation exists: SIMT execution serializes divergent retries across a warp; tens of thousands of threads contend on the same counter words; the double-width atomics that several CPU designs assume are absent; and GPU memory models are weakly ordered, so the classical algorithms do not transfer unchanged. We present the packed-ring queues (PRQs) -- two linearizable, bounded GPU queues that represent each compound atomic state in one native word of at most 64 bits: (1) PRQ-LF, a lock-free ring whose warp-batched fast path issues one atomic per warp on each of the queue's contended words, and (2) PRQ-WF, a wait-free ring in which peer threads cooperatively complete any operation that falls behind. To the best of our knowledge, PRQ-WF is the first GPU concurrent queue whose wait-freedom is proved as a theorem, with no assumption about how the GPU schedules threads. Across four GPUs from two vendors (NVIDIA A100 and GH200, AMD MI210 and MI300A), PRQ-LF outperforms the blocking Broker Queue by 5.0-20.4x at 32K threads, and PRQ-WF sustains throughput under producer/consumer imbalance where a prior design completes fewer than 0.1% of its attempts.
