A quadratic arithmetic program makes our hidden matrix low rank, so where their ciphertext encodes a basis of a matrix space, ours holds factors of width two, which a pairing multiplies. Weights and identities from an extension field tie copies of this matrix, so an adversary telling encryptions apart yields a witness or a Module-SIS solution. For the same Groth16 statement and $100$-bit security level, Praxis reduces the ciphertext size and the cost of encryption of either of their constructions by over ten orders of magnitude, and that of decryption by over six.

Cryptography and Security.title: On the Complexity of Symmetric Boolean Functions in Multiparty Private Simultaneous Messages
Cryptography and Security.summary:
Multiparty Private Simultaneous Messages (PSM), also known as Decomposable Randomized Encoding (DRE) or information-theoretic garbling, is a model for non-interactive secure computation. Each party encodes its input using shared randomness and sends a message to an evaluator who must recover the function output without learning anything else about the inputs. Perfect privacy requires identical transcript distributions on inputs with the same output. We also study the weaker notion of support privacy, which requires only that these distributions have the same support.
  We study the communication complexity of symmetric Boolean functions when each of the n parties holds one input bit.
  Lower bounds. We prove a $(1-o(1))n\log n$ lower bound for support-private PSM protocols computing $OR_n$, which is known to be tight. As a consequence, we obtain the same lower bounds for $MAJ_n$ and $EMAJ_n$. We also prove an $Ω(n\log q)$ lower bound for $MOD_q$. An alternative proof technique recovers most of these bounds as well as the previously known approach based on Nechiporuk's method.
  Upper bounds. We construct perfectly private and support private PSM protocols of total communication $\widetilde{O}(n^{3/2})$ and $\widetilde{O}(n)$ respectively for every symmetric Boolean function, improving on the known quadratic bound. For $MAJ_n$, known branching-program constructions yield an upper bound of $O(n\log^3 n\log\log n)$. For $EMAJ_n$ and $MOD_q$ with prime $q$, the lower bounds are tight up to constant factors.
  Earlier lower-bound techniques of Ball et al. (ITCS 2020) yield only trivial linear bounds for symmetric Boolean functions. Concurrent and independent work by Holmgren and Wu proves a $ω(n)$ lower bound for $OR_n$ using the same approach as our alternative technique. Both works used substantial AI assistance.
Cryptography and Security.comment: In this version we added a proof of a tight lower bound for the OR function

Cryptography and Security.title: Taint Analysis via Heap-Aware Propagation
Cryptography and Security.summary:
Taint analysis for C depends on how precisely the analysis tracks tainted values as they flow through memory objects. Without field sensitivity, a tainted object field can spuriously taint an entire object, producing significant false alarms. In this paper, we present a field-sensitive taint analysis that combines Data Structure Analysis (DSA) for field-sensitive points-to information with a data-flow analysis for tracking explicit dependencies. We identify that existing DSA-style analyses lose precision on a common object pattern: a C struct object that mixes scalar fields with a flexible array member. When such an array is accessed with symbolic indices, DSA loses points-to field sensitivity for the entire object, inflating false alarms in the data-flow analysis.
  To address this, we propose I-DSA, which extends DSA by representing field positions as intervals, so that a pointer with symbolic bounds merges only the fields within those bounds. We further develop a sound data-flow analysis based on abstract interpretation. We implement I-DSA on top of SeaDSA and the data-flow analysis inside Crab. Our tool targets LLVM IR and supports configurable taint policies by instrumenting the IR with taint intrinsics. Our experiments show that I-DSA reduces the false alarms caused by this pattern at little cost in the pointer analysis, that SVF, an inclusion-based pointer analysis, shows a similar field-sensitivity loss, and that our taint analysis scales better than PhASAR on real-world programs.
Cryptography and Security.comment: This is an extended version of the VMCAI 2027 paper. The artifact is available at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.19826762

Cryptography and Security.title: Weight-Space Backdoors in Open-Weight LLMs: Cross-Architecture Attacks and Blind Model Forensics
Cryptography and Security.summary:
Open-weight language models are vulnerable to trigger-conditioned behaviors introduced through sparse post-training weight modifications, creating supply-chain risks beyond conventional provenance checks. We present Neural Sentinel, a cross-architecture study of gradient-guided backdoor insertion and model forensics spanning 18 checkpoints across 14 architecture families (124M-31.3B parameters), including state-space and recurrent models.
  On Phi-2, modifying approximately 0.0002% of parameters induced an exact short-marker output after 300 steps (332 seconds), with mean next-token KL divergence of $1.5 \times 10^{-5}$ and 100% top-1 agreement over evaluated positions of eight fixed reference prompts. Separate experiments produced structured tool-call-formatted outputs without establishing downstream execution. We identify three procedure-dependent response regimes -- Gradient-Permeable, Scale-Threshold, and Gradient-Fragmented -- and evaluate PPO-based weight-space exploration, which showed no statistically significant advantage over random search.
  For defense, Neural Sentinel combines weight-difference analysis, trigger discovery, activation probing, and contextual output inspection. In a 22-artifact development cohort, its reference-optional scanner classified 4/5 backdoored artifacts as BACKDOORED; the remaining positive and all 17 clean artifacts were SUSPICIOUS. These findings establish the feasibility of sparse conditional-output insertion and evidence-producing forensic triage, while identifying limitations in behavioral-drift assessment and clean-model admission.

Cryptography and Security.title: SkillScreen: High-Recall Screening of Malicious Agent Skills with Decision Models
Cryptography and Security.summary: Agent skills turn natural-language instructions into actions, creating a security challenge: legitimate automation and malicious behaviour can look deceptively similar. A practical screen must catch nearly every attack while keeping the review load manageable. We present SkillScreen, a compact decision model trained to score skill maliciousness directly from SKILL$.$md in a single forward pass. On MaliciousSkillBench, SkillScreen flags 20-25% of benign skills at 99% recall on unseen attack families, substantially fewer than the word-level classifier and prompted LLM judges tested. Under the same training protocol, it also generalizes better than a fully fine-tuned encoder to unseen sources. Yet unfamiliar benign sources sharply increase false positives, showing that recognizing new attacks does not ensure reliable screening of new skill collections. Our results demonstrate the value of task-trained decision models for high-recall skill screening. Project page: https://jerroldh.github.io/SkillScreen-webpage/

Cryptography and Security.title: SoK: Splitting the Trigger or Adding Attackers? Disentangling Distributed Backdoor Attacks in Federated Learning
Cryptography and Security.summary: Distributed backdoor attacks split a trigger among several federated learning clients, so that the backdoor appears only in the aggregated model. Since DBA, a line of work has reported that such attacks are stronger, more persistent, and stealthier than a single attacker with the full trigger. We systematize this literature and test this belief. We code nineteen primary studies and fifteen papers that evaluate against DBA. The reported advantage is rarely measured against a complete trigger delivered by the same attackers, and none of the fifteen evaluations tests whether individual pieces remain effective. We then run 875 paired federated runs that separate adding attackers from splitting the trigger. In our image experiments, adding attackers raised attack success in every seed of all 30 cells where we measured it, by 7.5 to 83.4 percentage points on average. Splitting the trigger among the same attackers had a smaller effect, and its sign depended on the piece layout, the allocation, and the attackers' local training. With DBA's compact layout, splitting lowered attack success on CIFAR-10. A larger penalty on small CNNs vanished once the attackers trained longer, and an FCBA-style allocation gained a few points. Widely separated pieces helped on CIFAR-10, its grayscale version, and GTSRB. No model required all pieces. Neural Cleanse suppressed single pieces together with the full trigger, but split backdoors with separated pieces survived it better than complete ones. We derive reporting requirements for attack and defense evaluations.
Cryptography and Security.comment: 28 pages, 10 figures, 22 tables. Systematization of knowledge with original controlled experiments (875 paired federated learning runs). Under submission. Code and data: https://anonymous.4open.science/r/fl-pieces-artifact-BFF3/

Cryptography and Security.title: Optimal User-Level Private Stochastic Convex Optimization and Mean Estimation with Heavy Tails
Cryptography and Security.summary: We study stochastic convex optimization with heavy-tailed stochastic gradients under $(\varepsilon, δ)$-user-level differential privacy, which protects each user's entire collection of samples. Instead of assuming a uniformly bounded Lipschitz constant, we only assume bounds on the second- and $k$-th moments of the random sample Lipschitz parameters. This allows for unbounded, heavy-tailed stochastic gradient distributions and can lead to sharper excess risk bounds. We characterize the minimax optimal excess population risk up to logarithmic factors. Our algorithm achieves the optimal rate with only $\widetilde{O}(1/\varepsilon)$ users. As a byproduct of our algorithmic developments, we obtain tight bounds for user-level private mean estimation under norm-moment assumptions, improving over the guarantees of Esfandiari et al. (2022) and Zhao et al. (2024). Finally, for mean estimation under the directional-moment assumption of Agarwal et al. (2025), we close their remaining approximate-DP gap by removing the additional $d/\varepsilon$ user requirement and attaining the optimal sample complexity up to logarithmic factors.

Software Engineering.title: Operational Runbooks as Living Documents: A Longitudinal Study of Document Evolution under Assisted Post-Incident Revision
Software Engineering.summary: Operational runbooks increasingly function as living documents within operational workflows: they are maintained by people, used in incident support, and continuously revised as organizational knowledge changes. Yet little is known about how such document collections evolve over time in production settings, or which interpretable signals are useful for monitoring document change. We analyze 17 weeks of version-controlled runbook snapshots produced during post-incident revision with machine-assisted review and human oversight. We quantify document evolution using lightweight linguistic and structural signals grounded in prior work on procedural language, technical communication, and document organization. Correlation analysis shows mixed patterns of association, including both positive and negative relationships, with effect sizes ranging from negligible to moderate and varying across corpora. Temporal summaries further distinguish comparatively stable signals from revision-sensitive ones, supporting monitoring of document maintenance workflows rather than one-shot quality judgments. An illustrative analysis on public GitHub product documentation shows that signal behavior differs across corpora, reinforcing the need for context-aware interpretation. These results identify which metric classes provide stable anchors and which provide edit-sensitive indicators for managing operational documentation as an engineered document resource.
Software Engineering.comment: 11 pages, 1 figure. Accepted at the 2026 ACM Symposium on Document Engineering (DocEng 2026). Includes appendices

Software Engineering.title: SWE-Pruner Pro: The Coder LLM Already Knows What to Prune
Software Engineering.summary: Pruning long context for coding agents has been a vital technology for efficient context management. While existing context pruning methods such as SWE-Pruner realize this by attaching a separate code classifier, we find the agent itself encodes internal representations indicating the relevance of code context when reading tool output. Based on this finding, we propose SWE-Pruner Pro, which prunes tool outputs directly inside the agent. Concretely, a small head turns the agent's own internal representations into a keep-or-prune label for each line, with a length-aware embedding keyed to each tool output's line count. Across two open-weight backbones and four multi-turn benchmarks, SWE-Pruner Pro saves up to 39% of prompt and completion tokens while preserving task quality, with bounded inference overhead. Notably, on MiMo-V2-Flash SWE-Pruner Pro additionally raises the SWE-Bench Verified resolve rate by +3.8% and the long-context Oolong accuracy by +2.2 points.
Software Engineering.comment: Accepted by EACL 2027

Software Engineering.title: LITMUS - Literature Informed Testbed for Mapping Usecases and Synthesizing Risk-Cards
Software Engineering.summary: The proliferation of large language models (LLMs) and Artificial Intelligence (AI) in real-world applications has heightened the need for systematic, safety-oriented deployment frameworks. Existing approaches typically prioritize the construction of datasets and risk cards around the LLM and AI architecture itself, yet they provide scant consideration for the specific use-case that drives model selection. This omission is problematic because any practical AI deployment begins with a detailed use-case description that informs the assessment of contextual hazards. In this paper, we introduce a structured pipeline that, given a use-case, automatically produces a tailored dataset and an accompanying risk card. The process ensures that identified risks are tightly coupled to the use-case, and it offers traceable evidence from peer-reviewed literature to substantiate each risk to use-case relationship. Prior claim-verification methods (FActScore, FactReasoner) have been validated for factual claims. Risk-relevance is a hypothetical claim about possible harm, and whether evidence retrieval can meaningfully assess such claims remains untested. Literature-Informed Testbed for Mapping Use-cases and Synthesizing (LITMUS) risk cards are the first systematic attempt to characterize this adaptation. We evaluated the pipeline using the MIT Risk Taxonomy and achieved a 0.91 F1-score with a list of 320 samples from the benchmark risk dataset that was considered. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in generating robust, evidence-based risk assessments for LLM deployments.

Software Engineering.title: Watermark Claims Under Test: Lessons from Auditing a Production LLM
Software Engineering.summary: Can we tell whether an LLM is watermarked without knowing its secret key? Published black-box tests suggest that carefully designed prompts can reveal the statistical footprint of a watermark. This paper examines what happens when those tests move from controlled reference implementations to a deployed model whose watermarking parameters are undisclosed. We present an audit of the Red-Green watermark presence test on Claude. Across ten initial configurations, the published test never rejects on a model the provider states is watermarked, despite detecting a local reference at comparable sample sizes. Controlled experiments expose a failure mode: including the prompt in the watermark's repeated-context history suppresses marking exactly where the test measures it. The watermark remains active, but the probe becomes blind. Attempts to repair the probe reveal further confounds. Constructed contexts can trigger native digit-to-word preferences, while comparisons within a single response can measure how the model plans its answer. Tokenization changes which contexts the probe actually controls. These findings show why validation on a surrogate model does not establish validity on the model under investigation. A redesigned probe finds a substantial context-dependent shift on Claude Fable that is absent on two sibling controls. However, the pre-registered decision remains inconclusive because selective refusals violate the protocol, and the effect's watermark origin is unresolved. We show how to design controls, distinguish statistical rejection from evidence of watermarking and interpret a null without treating it as proof of absence. We provide researchers and practitioners working on LLM evaluation, watermarking, and provenance with an audit checklist grounded in concrete successes and failures. Code, prompts, and parsed responses are available for reproducing the analyses.

Software Engineering.title: GameEngineBench: Full-Session Verification of Coding Agents in a Networked Game Engine
Software Engineering.summary: Coding agents face new challenges in game development, where they must produce code that is not only syntactically correct but also consistent with engine-managed lifecycle, state, and networking behavior. Existing game-development benchmarks, however, do not combine assertions over engine-based runtime states with cross-client consistency, failing to evaluate how well generated code adheres to the desired behavioral specifications. To address these limitations, we present GameEngineBench, a benchmark of 110 C++ implementation tasks derived from 9 existing Unreal Engine 5 projects. Each task requires an agent to implement missing behavior within an established gameplay architecture. We also introduce Full-Session Verification, a testing framework that injects hidden tests after the agent finishes and evaluates the resulting implementation inside Play-in-Editor (PIE) sessions, with networked client worlds in 71 tasks. The tests evaluate Unreal's game loop, actor lifecycle, subsystems, and replication stack while directly inspecting runtime state. In 53 tasks, 119 tests additionally inspect a distinct client world to determine whether the authoritative server state is correctly replicated. To our knowledge, this is the first coding benchmark to evaluate cross-client replication. Across 11 model-harness configurations, the best-scoring configuration achieves 46.4% pass@1, while 43 tasks remain unsolved by every evaluated configuration. These results demonstrate that compilation and shallow verification overestimate agents' ability to implement behavior that remains correct during full engine execution.

Software Engineering.title: Consumer-Time Validity in Stateful AI Runtimes: Verifying Recovered State and Deferred Authority
Software Engineering.summary: Stateful LLM serving engines and agent runtimes reuse execution state and deferred permissions across components and sessions. A cancellation, rollback, or approval is recorded by one component and relied on by another, and recording it does not make the later use valid: a downstream consumer may read state or dispatch an action whose identity, production status, allocation, or target revision has since changed. We call the missing check consumer-time validity and separate two forms. State validity governs what a consumer reads. On vLLM with LMCache, an interrupted KV load leaves unwritten blocks indexed, and a host-only counter rewind desynchronizes the GPU position, so a second tenant generates a schema-valid tool call naming the wrong tenant in 10/10 native-fault runs; the call is recorded and not executed. Authority freshness governs what a consumer executes: on a multi-session approval runtime, an unrevoked deferred grant overwrote a newer revision in one admitted live execution. Output equality cannot test state validity: a fault-free run diverges at token 30 through BF16 batching alone while attended-KV digests match. We therefore specify consumer-bound recovery contracts that, for state recovery, jointly require exclusion, retention, and task completion, and an admissible-witness standard realized as a GPU-free offline trace verifier over scheduler metadata and persisted tool artifacts. On recorded traces the verifier agrees with the reference verdicts in 42/42 frozen GPU-matrix scenarios. An allocation-aware repair satisfies 7/7 triggered vLLM fault predicates on a pinned scheduler-case matrix, where upstream PR 61769 satisfies 2/7, and revision-bound dispatch blocks all 160 deterministic conflicting overwrites in a separate dispatcher cohort. Recovery must be checked where state and authority are consumed, with evidence bound to the consuming request.
Software Engineering.comment: 32 pages, 5 figures, 18 tables

Software Engineering.title: "What Should I Do?" Guidelines for Responsibly Integrating AI in Software Engineering
Software Engineering.summary: Speculations abound about the "right" ways for developers to integrate AI into their software engineering (SE) work, but the evidence that exists is sparse and contradictory. Yet, developers are held responsible for the products they ship with (or without) AI's help, so they need to integrate AI in responsible ways. To address this gap, we conducted a two-phase, large-scale investigation with 1,118 developers at Microsoft, GitHub, and Pfizer. In Phase 1, we surveyed 860 developers at Microsoft on where they sought and resisted AI support in their daily work, and from their accounts, synthesized 35 developer-facing guidelines: 29 across five categories of SE work and 6 cross-cutting ones. A year later, as AI capabilities and developers' experiences co-evolved, we validated them in Phase 2 with 258 developers in technology (Microsoft, GitHub) and biopharmaceutical (Pfizer) domains. Developers in our study found the guidelines clearly worded (92%) and relevant to their work (91%), and most wanted to adopt them in their own work (89%). We also report how developers described operationalizing these guidelines in practice: using AI to refine their craft and delegate verifiable work, while keeping judgment and accountability for themselves. For relationship-centric work, endorsement varied with developers' domain and their SE and AI experience. Overall, we offer concrete advice from in-the-trenches developers to other in-the-trenches developers, and a shared vocabulary that engineering teams can adopt to integrate AI well in their work.

Software Engineering.title: SaltBench: A Referee-Gated Protocol for Measuring Method Effects in Machine-Checked Software Work
Software Engineering.summary: SaltBench asks how a machine referee changes how a coding agent works. Outcomes are decided outside the agent's toolchain; on the Claude lane a wall probed before any scored run isolates the agent from the network, reference solutions and harness, and 5 Gemini-lane cells served web search results are declared and leave every comparison; a dated freeze of predictions authorizes each run; a budget stop is a halt, never a failure. Five Rust systems components on a pinned Verus toolchain are each refereed by a withheld test suite. The arms: plain; salt-diet, also instructed to specify and verify its code (a registered reduced rendering of the method); and two arms handed the specification a priori, where the registered sign test at k=4 reached no verdict (3 of 4, p = 0.3125). salt-diet cost more on all five components, by a practical margin: no premium exceeded 2.8879x under either reading of the declared set and the three cheapest sat below 1.4x, a bound of this population and not a promise about larger ones: the premium is near 1 on the smallest components and rises with size. Versions 2 and 3 add the complete pilot matrix: 200 conditions over four models, 181 with a result of record, 16 inexpressible and 3 declared unreached at the cost cap, with no verdict on the arms. Version 3 adds a correctness reading, declared post hoc and registered after every verdict it reads existed and many had been read by its author: 447 cells pass the withheld suite, 40 fail, 10 are censored at a registered budget, 4 are unscorable and 42 are read by condition. salt-diet's pass-rate interval lies wholly below plain's on 8 greenfield and 5 brownfield rows and wholly above it on 2 greenfield rows. It is descriptive, over three cells of record per condition, with no test, and says nothing about whether the method makes code more or less correct. The full record is public.
Software Engineering.comment: v5: corrects the abstract's network-isolation clause, which held for the Claude lane only; adds two temp-directory limits; adds three dated sections: a second model run on the same matrix beside a same-day control, and two first-stage reads of an explanation arm. No table of record changes. 56 pages

Software Engineering.title: Micro Operational Robustness of LLMs on Code Generation
Software Engineering.summary: It is now common practice in software development for large language models (LLMs) to be used to generate program code. It is desirable to evaluate the robustness of LLMs for this usage. This paper is concerned in particular with how sensitive LLMs are to variations in descriptions of the coding tasks. However, existing techniques for evaluating this robustness are unsuitable for code generation because the input data space of natural language (NL) descriptions is discrete and sparse. To address this problem, we propose a robustness evaluation method called scenario domain analysis, which aims to find the expected minimal change in the NL descriptions of coding tasks that would cause the LLMs to produce incorrect outputs. We have formally proved the theoretical properties of the method and also conducted extensive experiments to evaluate the robustness of four state-of-the-art LLMs: Gemini-pro, Codex, Llamma2 and Falcon 7B, and have found that we are able to rank these with confidence from best to worst. Moreover, we have also studied how robustness varies in different scenarios, including the variations with the topic of the coding task and with the complexity of its sample solution, and found that robustness is lower for more complex tasks and also lower for more advanced topics, such as multi-threading and data structures.

Software Engineering.title: Formally-Verifiable and Human-Interpretable RTL Generation with LLM-Guided Stepwise Refinement
Software Engineering.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are accelerating register-transfer level (RTL) development, but ensuring the correctness of generated designs remains a major challenge. Existing LLM-driven workflows rely heavily on simulation-based verification, which provides limited correctness guarantees, and often offer little insight into the design decisions behind the generated RTL. We present a framework for LLM-guided, correct-by-construction RTL generation that combines the generative capabilities of LLMs with the mathematical rigor of stepwise refinement. The framework translates natural-language requirements into a formal hardware contract and progressively refines the contract into an implementation. At each refinement step, the LLM proposes a design decision, while the refinement engine applies the corresponding transformation only after formally verifying its correctness. The resulting program is formally verified against the contract and then translated into synthesizable RTL. The recorded derivation allows every line of generated RTL to be traced back to the design decisions and requirements that motivated it. Beyond generating verified implementations, the framework provides reliable verification feedback and reusable design experience, laying the foundation for self-improving hardware generation.

Software Engineering.title: Refined, Reliable and Reproducible: Algorithmic Analysis and Reimplementation of the Popcorn Void Finder
Software Engineering.summary: Cosmic voids are vast underdense regions of the Universe that encode valuable information about its large-scale structure and evolution. By extending spherical voids into overlapping sphere structures, the Popcorn Void Finder demonstrated an improved statistical characterization of cosmic void populations. However, its origin as a research prototype progressively hindered its maintainability and extensibility. Moreover, post-publication algorithmic modifications have not been systematically evaluated, leaving their statistical and computational consequences insufficiently characterized. In this work, we present a comprehensive reimplementation of the Popcorn Void Finder, prioritizing algorithmic transparency, maintainability, and reproducibility. We document the complete identification procedure, revisit the original algorithmic choices, and evaluate their statistical and computational consequences. Comparisons between implementations revealed a significant change in the behavior of the Void Size Function, which is now characterized by a power-law regime transitioning to a Schechter-like distribution. These changes not only provide a better characterization of void sizes, but enable a new and more robust method to the determination of the shot-noise dominated regime, without implicit dependencies on internal finder parameters present in previous works. Performance benchmarks demonstrate a 1.62x speedup in spherical void identification and a substantial improvement in overlap-removal throughput. We determined the Popcorn algorithm to be negatively affected by load imbalance, and found a speedup of 63x in a tested configuration with a newly introduced early growth termination criterion. These results establish a more maintainable and reproducible foundation for popcorn void identification, while clarifying the statistical and computational trade-offs that govern its performance.

Software Engineering.title: CivilCADBench: Benchmarking Multimodal LLMs for Understanding, Reconstructing, and Designing Civil Engineering Drawing Sets
Software Engineering.summary: Civil infrastructure is designed, built, and maintained through engineering drawing sets, yet preparing and revising them remains labour-intensive and calls for automation. Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) are promising candidates, but assessing them requires a benchmark grounded in real engineering practice. We introduce CivilCADBench, a benchmark for understanding, reconstructing, and designing civil engineering drawing sets, built from real infrastructure drawings and source CAD files containing over 250,000 CAD entities. Unlike parametric 3D CAD models, these drawings are dense, layered, and multi-sheet; and since prints are lossy projections with no pixel trace of layers, a file can print correctly yet remain wrongly organised. CivilCADBench comprises three task families of increasing difficulty: understanding tasks are evaluated with 2,183 expert-reviewed questions ranging from single sheets to whole sets, while reconstruction and design tasks are agentic, requiring models to rebuild printed pages as editable CAD files, either as single pages or entire drawing sets, and to produce new designs. These tasks are performed across 232 pages, 28 sets, and 19 design tasks, and evaluated by a deterministic scorer that compares model outputs with the designers' source files on geometry, layers, text, and dimensions. We evaluate seven frontier MLLMs on CivilCADBench, and find that they read and redraw printed content accurately but recover the file structure poorly: the best model scores above 90% in understanding and single-page reconstruction, yet only 60% on layer assignment and 48% on design. Grounded in real engineering practice, CivilCADBench exposes both the capabilities and the limitations of frontier models in professional civil engineering, laying a foundation for next-generation models and agentic systems for intelligent civil engineering.
Software Engineering.comment: Project page: https://agenticivil.com/civilcadbench/

Software Engineering.title: Dhaani: A Data-Flow-Driven Tool for Greenfield Construction and Brownfield Modernisation
Software Engineering.summary: Large language models can generate plausible code quickly, but an end-to-end prompt leaves developers with little control over decomposition, interfaces, or the assumptions that must survive later revisions. We present Dhaani, a free desktop application for greenfield program construction and brownfield repository modernisation. It makes an annotated data-flow diagram (ADFD) the inspectable contract between intent and implementation. In the greenfield workflow, Build, a user turns natural-language requirements into a typed graph, reviews process specifications and pre/post-conditions, ratifies generated modules, and proceeds in dependency order for Python or .NET (C#). In the brownfield workflow, Migrate uses source inference to recover an ADFD from a Fortran repository, performs target generation in bounded dependency groups, and exposes source-target alignment, generated code, errors, time, token use, and cost. The tool keeps code and artifacts on the user's machine and supports cloud or locally hosted models. Two scientific synthesis case studies produced executable systems where matched low/no-code baselines failed or were substantially less accurate. On 50 open-source Fortran repositories, the migration workflow made all 382 fixed source-oracle probes runnable and passed 327 (85.6%); two direct translation baselines each passed 83 (21.7% of planned probes). Pre-built installers and usage instructions are freely available. Tool and usage guide: https://shraddhasurana.github.io/dhaani/. Video: https://youtu.be/SShWwOMgJ9c.
Software Engineering.comment: 4 pages, 4 figures

Software Engineering.title: When the Next Step Is Not One Step: Distribution-Aware Execution Modeling for Concurrent Go Programs
Software Engineering.summary: Predicting the next scheduler event of a concurrent program is ill-posed as single-label classification: repeated runs from the same trace prefix produce different, equally valid next events. We formulate next-event prediction for concurrent Go programs as estimating an empirical next-event distribution obtained from repeated executions, and release a benchmark with 945 training examples from hand-written and generated programs and 798 held-out predictions on 54 real-world GoKer bug kernels from systems such as CockroachDB, Kubernetes, gRPC and etcd. We fine-tune Qwen2.5-Coder-7B with low-rank adapters under a cross-entropy objective and a KL-to-empirical-distribution objective and compare them with zero-shot models and trivial baselines. The outcome is a neutral-to-negative result. The fine-tuned adapters (re-evaluated: 36.3% cross-entropy, 33.6% KL; originally reported 36.2% and 35.8%) are statistically indistinguishable from always predicting the majority event (35.5%), and an event n-gram model reaches 33-34%. Because each held-out prompt carries labels from about five runs, no deterministic predictor can exceed 58.9% top-1 accuracy, so we report macro-F1, balanced accuracy, per-class recall, program-clustered confidence intervals and binned calibration measured directly on both adapters. A sensitivity study with 100 runs per program shows that five-run targets are noisy (mean total-variation distance 0.24 from a 100-run reference), which plausibly limits what the KL objective can learn. Rare event types are essentially never predicted. A select-block goroutine-leak signature follows from scheduler semantics rather than learning. We release the data, adapters and tooling.
Software Engineering.comment: 15 pages, 5 figures. Accepted for poster presentation at ICTer 2026. Substantially revised evaluation with trivial baselines, adapter re-evaluation, corrected calibration analysis, and run-count sensitivity analysis; conclusions revised accordingly

Software Engineering.title: Rule-Guided and Trajectory-Aware Repair for LLM-Based HLS Generation
Software Engineering.summary: Large language models (LLMs) offer a promising path for directly generating functionally correct and synthesizable HLS-C from natural-language specifications. However, existing approaches often struggle to turn multi-round tool feedback and reusable HLS knowledge into effective revisions, limiting end-to-end generation success. We propose MementoHLS, an agentic HLS generation framework built around executable and falsifiable dual-memory-guided repair. MementoHLS combines an Executable Repair Contract Library (ERCL), which converts cross-task HLS knowledge into evidence-gated repair actions, with a Reviewer-Grounded Falsification Ledger (RFL), which converts task-local repair history into trajectory evidence to suppress ineffective routes and preserve validated progress. To ensure reliable outcome attribution, a Same-Candidate Reviewer binds Parse, Compile, Testbench (TB), and Synthesis (Synth) outcomes to the corresponding candidate, while a Single-Commit Arbiter commits at most one candidate per round. Across Llama-3-8B and Qwen2.5-Coder-7B/32B, MementoHLS improves same-candidate TB$\wedge$Synth pass@1/pass@5 over Zero-shot by an average of 16.1/12.1 percentage points on HLS-Eval (94 tasks) and 15.1/10.4 on Bench4HLS (170 tasks). The corresponding Bench4HLS gains average 11.0/8.5 percentage points across four strong proprietary LLMs.
Software Engineering.comment: 10 pages, 6 figures, 8 tables. Revised version with an updated author list

Software Engineering.title: Verifying Autoware Controller Node by Combining Model Verification and Runtime Monitoring
Software Engineering.summary: Formal modeling and verification of autonomous driving systems remain challenging due to the vast operational space and the complexity of the control logic. We propose a hybrid verification approach that combines formal model verification and runtime monitoring for the trajectory-following control node of Autoware, an open-source autonomous driving platform. We formalize the controller as a hybrid system in differential dynamic logic (dL), and introduce an abstract model that captures the essential control dynamics. We then prove safety and liveness properties of the model using the KeYmaera X proof assistant. Complementarily, we monitor the constraints that assure the compatibility between the model and the Autoware implementation across numerical simulation runs using the Autoware toolchain, quantifying to what extent the implementation's behavior is subsumed by the verified model. The experimental results confirmed that (i) monitoring provides a sound evaluation of target following with accuracy bounds, and (ii) the Autoware implementation reaches the target with an accuracy of approximately 0.2-0.4 (m) in position and 0.8 (m/s) in velocity.
Software Engineering.comment: 23 pages, 6 figures, 2 tables. Extended version of a paper accepted at SEFM 2026. Corrects the AWSIM monitoring results

Software Engineering.title: Zero-Trust Formal Methods: AI Agents Build Verified Checkers for Untrusted Solvers
Software Engineering.summary: AI coding agents now generate code faster than humans can review it. Security analyses rely on solver answers such as "unsatisfiable" (for example, no attack path exists) or "optimal." Unlike satisfying models, they cannot be checked by looking at them. Formal verification moves trust from code to specifications, but verifiers still place large SAT, SMT, and answer-set solvers, and the translation into solver queries, in their trusted computing base, and these have had soundness bugs. Unlike agent-based pipelines that trust their verifier and solver, our farm trusts no component by default: neither the AI agents, which might make mistakes or game their objectives, nor the solvers. A solver answer counts only if a verified checker accepts its certificate. Every theory, proof, and line of code is generated by AI. For each component, agents first create an Isabelle/HOL theory with a specification, a soundness proof, and a reference checker made by code generation, then a fast Rust implementation, verified with Verus against a specification that mirrors the Isabelle definitions line by line. Specifications are frozen after independent review and cannot be changed by the implementing agents. A trust manifest lists what is still trusted. We built trust chains for SAT (verified LRAT checking); SMT, with certificates from an extended z3 and verified bit-blasting for bit-vectors and floating point; answer-set programming, with native certificates from clingo, including weight rules and optimality; and, closing the loop, Verus's final verification-condition step, by translation validation. All 3,726 SMT queries from 20 crates are certified and validated, and 15,662 answer-set proofs are accepted by both the Isabelle and the Verus checker. We found soundness defects in three proof checkers, including drat-trim, and in five solvers, including clasp and z3, which report wrong unsatisfiability.
Software Engineering.comment: 17 pages, 2 figures, 7 tables. This work has been submitted to the IEEE for possible publication. Copyright may be transferred without notice, after which this version may no longer be accessible

Software Engineering.title: When to Test, Repair, or Regenerate: Decision-Guided Efficient RTL Generation
Software Engineering.summary: Large language models (LLMs) can generate register-transfer-level (RTL) designs from natural-language specifications. To improve functional correctness, many RTL agents use simulation feedback to guide refinement. However, without a reference testbench, generating one for every initial implementation incurs inference cost even when the RTL is correct. We therefore introduce an adaptive harness that uses a specialized decision model to orchestrate testing, refinement, and candidate selection. It accepts high-scoring initial implementations and generates testbenches for the rest. When further search is needed, the initial score guides repair--regeneration allocation, while defect rankings and simulation feedback guide repair. For final selection, the harness prioritizes test-passing candidates and ranks them using decision-model scores. Across three benchmarks, the harness with DeepSeek improves mean Pass@1 by 5.4--7.1 percentage points over initial implementations and reduces aggregate estimated inference cost by 11.0--14.3% relative to a testbench-guided repair baseline with the same candidate cap.

Software Engineering.title: VeriLadder: A Multi-Agent Specification Refinement System for Tool-Verified Verilog Datasets
Software Engineering.summary: Training data is a bottleneck in AI, especially for large language models (LLMs) that write Verilog, because register-transfer-level (RTL) code is rarely published and existing datasets mostly check code for syntax, not instruction correctness. This paper presents VeriLadder, a five-level Verilog dataset, and the multi-agent framework that builds it, in which LLM agents write and revise specifications, and EDA tools (a synthesizer and a formal equivalence checker) decide what is accepted. Its levels follow an engineer's checks. Level 1 labels designs from two large Verilog corpora, namely RTLCoder and PyraNet, with synthesis results, failure causes, critical warnings and post-synthesis metrics. 28% of RTLCoder designs fail synthesis and are kept as negatives. Level 2 grades each instruction on four specification qualities, and low grades predict failed rebuilds. Level 3 rewrites each instruction into a refined specification and accepts it only if an LLM from another model family, reading only that specification, writes a circuit formally equivalent to the original. This raises the share of rebuildable designs from 26.1% to 78.2%, keeping every failed specification with its counterexample. Levels 4 and 5 add verified paraphrases and one-fact variants, hard negatives that differ only in one behavior from the verified design. VeriLadder labels the synthesizability of 716,627 designs and, from RTLCoder, provides 11,247 refined specifications, 32,393 paraphrases and 8,397 one-fact variants. Fine-tuning Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct on VeriLadder raises functional pass@1 from 31.7% to 50.0% on VerilogEval v2 and from 35.0% to 45.2% on RTLLM v2. The dataset and fine-tuned models are publicly available.
Software Engineering.comment: 35 pages, 28 figures, 4 tables

Software Engineering.title: Right Verdict, Right Reason? An Execution-Grounded Study of Whether LLM Vulnerability Detectors Understand Vulnerabilities
Software Engineering.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to detect vulnerabilities, and their benchmark scores are often read as evidence that they understand the vulnerabilities they report. We test this reading against program execution. For 515 C and C++ functions from BigVul and PrimeVul whose vulnerability we reproduce with a proof of concept, we identify the line at which the fault occurs and the statements on which the faulting run depended. These facts ground a ladder of five tests, from telling a vulnerable function from its fixed version, through locating the fault and reacting to its removal, to judging execution-confirmed edits and predicting the outcome of a concrete run. Each test is paired with a baseline that needs no understanding, such as a rule that picks lines with risky calls, and we repeat the study on 195 vulnerabilities published after the training cutoffs of the models. Four findings emerge. First, telling a vulnerable function from its fixed version is hard. The open-weight models separate no more pairs than chance, although five of them show a weak sensitivity to the fix, and the commercial models still label many screened fixed versions vulnerable. Second, the commercial models locate the fault beyond a keyword rule, while removing that evidence changes the verdicts of the strongest model only on the newer vulnerabilities. Third, given the program input, the commercial models predict whether a run faults better than a rule that looks for added checks, and the prediction follows the input. Fourth, on the newer vulnerabilities this advantage disappears and the lead of the strongest model narrows, while localization persists. We release the framework, the per-function evidence, and an execution-confirmed counterfactual benchmark.
Software Engineering.comment: 25 pages

Software Engineering.title: Automated Safety Analysis for Agentic Workflows
Software Engineering.summary: LLM applications are increasingly built as agentic workflows: programs that combine model calls, external tools, and control logic to act autonomously on a user's behalf. Because these workflows execute real-world actions, logical flaws in how a workflow is wired can cause severe harm in deployed systems. Unlike prompt injections or malformed API calls, these workflow bugs stem from defects in the workflow's design, yet no existing tool can statically validate workflow logic across frameworks prior to deployment. We present Apsis, a static safety analyzer that detects workflow bugs before deployment. To operate across frameworks, Apsis lifts framework-specific code into a common intermediate representation (IR). This IR models a workflow as a semantic graph of steps, data dependencies, and shared state, while annotating each component with behavioral properties such as whether an input is mandatory or how a shared channel merges concurrent writes. Building on this representation, we introduce a bug description language that formalizes recurring classes of agentic failures as declarative patterns over the IR. By matching these patterns against the IR, Apsis detects structural and behavioral flaws and pinpoints the exact step responsible for each bug. To evaluate Apsis, we construct, to our knowledge, the first corpus of workflow bugs, distilled from real-world reports across 13 widely used frameworks. On a reproducible benchmark suite drawn from this corpus, Apsis detects workflow bugs with 91% precision and 84% recall, and uncovers 36 previously unknown bugs in real-world workflows.
Software Engineering.comment: Extended version of the paper accepted at ICSE 2027, with appendices

Software Engineering.title: PyMETA: Evaluating Student Code Diagnosis on and Beyond the First Execution Error
Software Engineering.summary: Code-diagnosis evaluation depends on how error supervision is constructed and what that supervision treats as a correct diagnosis. We introduce PyMETA, a dataset of 48,646 Python submissions with execution-derived single-error labels, and a targeted subset of 97 submissions annotated by experts through repair and re-execution. Under the first-outcome protocol, four recent prompted models obtain 87.5-93.8% macro F1, all above the strongest finetuned baseline at 80.6%. This reverses the comparison obtained with the earlier set of prompted models. The expert subset gives a less favorable account of complete diagnosis: exact-set match ranges from 43.3% to 48.5%, although sample F1 is approximately 79-81%. The evaluation setup also changes which behavior is visible. On the same 45 audited submissions without an expert-annotated Logic Error, none of the four recent models predicts that label when restricted to one output, whereas 46.7-57.8% include it under multi-error prompting, usually after an explicit-error label. These findings show that model comparisons and error-bias claims depend on what the gold label represents, which outputs the model is allowed to return, and how those outputs are scored.
Software Engineering.comment: Accepted at TAE (Trust-AI-Eval): Can We Trust AI Evaluation?, NeurIPS 2026

Software Engineering.title: Human-in-the-Loop Runbook Improvement with Agentic Support Automation
Software Engineering.summary: Operational support is an important component of production software services. Support requests are often emergent and can come in many forms such as customer escalations or unplanned service interruption. Engineers across organizations have been successful in implementing automation to help streamline support processes but many solutions remain in the hands of human operators. A successful strategy to improve operator response times is to maintain up-to-date runbooks which are documents enumerating triage steps and remediation procedures in the face of identified incidents. This paper is an investigation into an operational system which incorporates Agentic AI into a runbook based incident resolution pattern. The bot uses information in the runbook corpus along with some system-specific tooling to guide the manual operator through the mitigation process then evaluate the outcome and suggest edits to the runbook where it found gaps and in its ability to triage the situation. By using the runbook as a medium to bridge humans and automation, the process maintains explainability and can be decoupled from the agent system. This paper demonstrates a collaboration between human operators and Agentic AI with results from an 17 week study involving 232 production incidents. We conclude with lessons on integrating LLMs into DevOps workflows, related work in AI-assisted operations, and guidance for reproducibility.
Software Engineering.comment: 11 pages, 5 figures, 4 tables. Accepted manuscript of the paper published in the proceedings of the 2025 IEEE 7th International Conference on Cognitive Machine Intelligence (CogMI)

Software Engineering.title: Lean Census: A Distributional Analysis of AI-Generated Lean Code
Software Engineering.summary: We compare two human-written and four AI-generated Lean libraries with Mathlib through the distributions of simple statistics of their code. For each library we measure inline claims in proofs, proof length, how often each declaration is used, and design choices such as instances and private declarations, and we read each against the variation among Mathlib's own areas. The AI-generated libraries have more inline claims per theorem, longer proofs, fewer instances, and more private declarations than the human-written ones. We release the code for the analysis as a package, lean-census, at https://github.com/project-numina/lean-census.
Software Engineering.comment: 16 pages, 17 figures. Code at https://github.com/project-numina/lean-census

Software Engineering.title: The Defect Is in the Arithmetic Between the Files: Static Detection of Exactly-Once Violations in Payment Pipelines
Software Engineering.summary: Whether a streaming payment pipeline charges a customer twice after a restart turns on a comparison nobody performs: how long the provider remembers an idempotency key, against how stale a record can be when the pipeline processes it for the second time. The first number is in the provider's documentation. The second is not written anywhere. It is assembled from a checkpoint interval in one file, a recovery assumption in a runbook, a restart delay in a third and a source's lateness bound in a fourth. Each file is defensible alone; the fault is in the relation between them. We give a checker that gathers those facts and states the relations, and a synthesiser that turns 335 of the 515 findings into a runnable scenario: these records, kill the job here, bring it back after this long, and this is the observable. 245 of them produce two charges. The central measurement is how far apart the evidence lies. Across a corpus of 630 pipelines we generated, 210 of them cannot be derived from fewer than three artifacts, and no single artifact yields more than 35 of the 305 duration findings. Executing the witnesses corrected our own rules: two were demoted after their scenarios produced a repeated call the provider's idempotency absorbed rather than a second charge. All 16 selected live witnesses reproduced their predicted observable against a real Kafka broker with a real process kill, and a matched control in which the provider never forgets the key did not, attributing the second charge to the key lifetime, not the replay. Fault injection finds the same defects only if the tester already assumed a long enough outage: one willing to simulate five minutes finds 15% of them, and 12 hours is needed for all. A sweep also locates a configuration with no application-level fix, where above a 14-minute recovery assumption the transaction timeout required to survive it exceeds the broker's own cap.
Software Engineering.comment: 8 pages, 4 figures, 7 tables. Checker, corpus generator, Docker configuration and every raw results file are at https://github.com/abhisheksharma2411/streamcheck (release v1.0.2); make reproduce rebuilds every figure, table and number in the paper from the raw results. Archived at Zenodo concept DOI 10.5281/zenodo.24412123

Programming Languages.title: VERITAS: Verifier-Guided Proof Search for Zero-Shot Formal Theorem Proving
Programming Languages.summary: LLM-based formal provers often collapse the verifier's output into a pass/fail bit. We present VERITAS, a zero-shot framework that feeds what Lean reports (error messages with their position, verified partial proofs, and remaining goals) back into proof search. Phase 1 samples N whole proofs; Phase 2 searches a tree of verified partial proofs with a Tactician, automated step repair, a Critic that ranks states and allocates the budget, and a Retriever. On miniF2F test, VERITAS solves 86.9% with Claude Haiku 5.5 and 82.8% with GPT-6 Luna, against 71.7% and 61.1% for Best-of-5 sampling, and solves more theorems than three re-implemented feedback baselines at a third to a half of their search cost. We also evaluate on 55 combinatorics problems of CombiBench and release code and run logs at https://github.com/CoderDoge1108/VERITAS.

Programming Languages.title: An End-to-End Theory for Compositional Symbolic Execution: From Expressive Specifications to SMT (Extended Version)
Programming Languages.summary: Compositional symbolic execution (CSE) is a powerful technique for program verification and bug-finding, yet existing formal theories of CSE do not sufficiently bridge the gap between idealised models and real-world tools. We present progress towards a foundational, realistic, end-to-end theory of CSE in the Rocq proof assistant. Our theory advances realism at both ends of the CSE pipeline: it supports an expressive frontend with algebraic data types, logical functions, and lemmas; it also provides a verified connection to SMT-LIB compliant SMT solvers. Our contributions include: (1) a CSE theory that captures practical verification patterns; (2) a standalone, reusable Rocq mechanisation of the SMT-LIB standard; (3) a proven-correct encoding from CSE backend queries to SMT-LIB queries that accounts for semantic discrepancies and optimises using type information; and (4) empirical evidence for the backend by extracting our verified SMT-LIB encoding and running it alongside the CSE tool Gillian's own encoding on a majority of its solver queries.

The fine-tuned adapters (re-evaluated: 36.3% cross-entropy, 33.6% KL; originally reported 36.2% and 35.8%) are statistically indistinguishable from always predicting the majority event (35.5%), and an event n-gram model reaches 33-34%. Because each held-out prompt carries labels from about five runs, no deterministic predictor can exceed 58.9% top-1 accuracy, so we report macro-F1, balanced accuracy, per-class recall, program-clustered confidence intervals and binned calibration measured directly on both adapters. A sensitivity study with 100 runs per program shows that five-run targets are noisy (mean total-variation distance 0.24 from a 100-run reference), which plausibly limits what the KL objective can learn. Rare event types are essentially never predicted. A select-block goroutine-leak signature follows from scheduler semantics rather than learning. We release the data, adapters and tooling.
Programming Languages.comment: 15 pages, 5 figures. Accepted for poster presentation at ICTer 2026. Substantially revised evaluation with trivial baselines, adapter re-evaluation, corrected calibration analysis, and run-count sensitivity analysis; conclusions revised accordingly

Programming Languages.title: Right Verdict, Right Reason? An Execution-Grounded Study of Whether LLM Vulnerability Detectors Understand Vulnerabilities
Programming Languages.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to detect vulnerabilities, and their benchmark scores are often read as evidence that they understand the vulnerabilities they report. We test this reading against program execution. For 515 C and C++ functions from BigVul and PrimeVul whose vulnerability we reproduce with a proof of concept, we identify the line at which the fault occurs and the statements on which the faulting run depended. These facts ground a ladder of five tests, from telling a vulnerable function from its fixed version, through locating the fault and reacting to its removal, to judging execution-confirmed edits and predicting the outcome of a concrete run. Each test is paired with a baseline that needs no understanding, such as a rule that picks lines with risky calls, and we repeat the study on 195 vulnerabilities published after the training cutoffs of the models. Four findings emerge. First, telling a vulnerable function from its fixed version is hard. The open-weight models separate no more pairs than chance, although five of them show a weak sensitivity to the fix, and the commercial models still label many screened fixed versions vulnerable. Second, the commercial models locate the fault beyond a keyword rule, while removing that evidence changes the verdicts of the strongest model only on the newer vulnerabilities. Third, given the program input, the commercial models predict whether a run faults better than a rule that looks for added checks, and the prediction follows the input. Fourth, on the newer vulnerabilities this advantage disappears and the lead of the strongest model narrows, while localization persists. We release the framework, the per-function evidence, and an execution-confirmed counterfactual benchmark.
Programming Languages.comment: 25 pages

Programming Languages.title: VAPY: Circuit Optimization with Backpropagation
Programming Languages.summary: Parameter sensitivities of analog circuits enable the use of gradient-based design optimization methods and unlock a range of sensitivity analyses. However, it remains a challenge to compute exact design parameter sensitivities for circuits that use PDKs, which use Verilog-A device models comprised of thousands of lines of code. Finite difference methods, which estimate gradients through simulation, require N + 1 to 2N simulations for each gradient depending on the method, which can become prohibitively expensive when many parameters are optimized. We present VAPY, a Verilog-A to JAX transpiler that compiles Verilog-A device models into autodifferentiable JAX code, enabling optimization with Circulax, a JAX-based circuit simulator. VAPY employs taint analysis to ensure only the necessary control-flow is rewritten with JAX-compatible calls, reducing control-flow overheads. We use VAPY and Circulax to optimize three analog circuits implemented in the SkyWater SKY130 PDK, which is built on the BSIM4 device model. VAPY-generated model gradients closely match finite-difference gradients, achieving comparable design quality in over 40X fewer circuit solves and up to 40% lower loss than Bayesian optimization.
Programming Languages.comment: 7 pages, 2 figures

Programming Languages.title: Taint Analysis via Heap-Aware Propagation
Programming Languages.summary:
Taint analysis for C depends on how precisely the analysis tracks tainted values as they flow through memory objects. Without field sensitivity, a tainted object field can spuriously taint an entire object, producing significant false alarms. In this paper, we present a field-sensitive taint analysis that combines Data Structure Analysis (DSA) for field-sensitive points-to information with a data-flow analysis for tracking explicit dependencies. We identify that existing DSA-style analyses lose precision on a common object pattern: a C struct object that mixes scalar fields with a flexible array member. When such an array is accessed with symbolic indices, DSA loses points-to field sensitivity for the entire object, inflating false alarms in the data-flow analysis.
  To address this, we propose I-DSA, which extends DSA by representing field positions as intervals, so that a pointer with symbolic bounds merges only the fields within those bounds. We further develop a sound data-flow analysis based on abstract interpretation. We implement I-DSA on top of SeaDSA and the data-flow analysis inside Crab. Our tool targets LLVM IR and supports configurable taint policies by instrumenting the IR with taint intrinsics. Our experiments show that I-DSA reduces the false alarms caused by this pattern at little cost in the pointer analysis, that SVF, an inclusion-based pointer analysis, shows a similar field-sensitivity loss, and that our taint analysis scales better than PhASAR on real-world programs.
Programming Languages.comment: This is an extended version of the VMCAI 2027 paper. The artifact is available at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.19826762

Programming Languages.title: SafeJIT: A Speculating JIT Engine Verified Down to the Machine Code
Programming Languages.summary: JIT compilers are among the most attacked components of modern software. They compile attacker-chosen programs, speculate on attacker-influenced type feedback, and run the result at full native privilege. A single wrongly eliminated guard or a missing deoptimization becomes memory corruption. We present SafeJIT, a small JavaScript engine with a speculating baseline JIT, together with a machine-checked proof in Lean 4 that its statically linked RISC-V and x86-64 executables never crash, on any input, in a model of a Linux user process. The theorem is about the shipped binaries, executed instruction by instruction on Sail ISA models (for RISC-V, the official one), and it covers everything in them: the parser and bytecode compiler, the interpreter and its type-feedback recording, the JIT compiler, all machine code the JIT can generate for any program and any feedback (type guards, guard elimination, loop type facts, register allocation with deoptimization metadata, inline caches, deoptimization and on-stack replacement), a mark-sweep garbage collector, the runtime, and a freestanding libc. The C compiler, assembler and linker are not trusted, and neither is floating-point arithmetic. The proof uses separation logic (iris-lean) over a model of a Linux user process whose stuck states are exactly the ways a process can crash, including fetching code that has not been made executable or whose instruction cache has not been flushed.

Formal Languages and Automata Theory.title: Ensemble Logic
Formal Languages and Automata Theory.summary: Ensemble Logic (EL) is a family of modal logics whose modal parameters are terms with quantified variables. We interpret formulas over metric monoids, that is, commutative monoids equipped with translation-invariant metrics. Displacement evaluates a formula at a translated point, while bounded existence and bounded universality evaluate it at some or every point of a window of prescribed length. Quantification over points and lengths allows the same variable to occur in the parameters of several operators. This provides a common framework for temporal and spatial reasoning in discrete, dense and multi-dimensional settings. Our main result establishes a sharp undecidability boundary for satisfiability over the natural numbers: satisfiability is undecidable already for formulas $\exists N\,\exists n\,Ψ$ in which $Ψ$ is built from the letters of a fixed alphabet by conjunction, disjunction, displacement and bounded universality. We prove this by a reduction from Post's Correspondence Problem. We also present results, in part from companion work, that place this theorem in the general theory of EL. These include an atomic-displacement normal form for covariant windows and composition laws for discrete and dense time. The discrete logic admits an embedding of linear temporal logic, defines the accepting runs of every Büchi automaton, and has a sound equational calculus. For the rational logic, we show that every fixed formula can be evaluated in polynomial time on interval models in which atomic propositions are interpreted by finite unions of intervals. Finally, we represent timed words over positions and real time and compare two window geometries; with rectangular windows, two shared lengths yield undecidability on finite timed words.

Formal Languages and Automata Theory.title: Rate--burst safety languages: the Farey structure of the burst boundary and discrimination under erasures
Formal Languages and Automata Theory.summary: A leaky-bucket constraint with rate \(ρ\) and burst \(B\) allows at most \(ρn+B\) costly steps in every window of \(n\) consecutive steps. The infinite 0/1 words that satisfy it form a safety language. For a finite graph with edge costs 0 and 1, we study the least burst at which the cost word of some infinite path lies in this language, as a function of the real rate. This function is the exact tolerance of a monitor that distinguishes two finite-state systems observed through an erasure channel with a leaky-bucket bound. The language is \(ω\)-regular at every rational rate but not at irrational rates once the burst reaches 1, so ultimately periodic witnesses do not come from automata theory. We prove directly that simple lassos suffice at all real rates and that all breakpoints of the boundary lie in the Farey sequence of order N for a graph with N vertices. One lasso has a tight bound of order N to the power 2/3 on its affine pieces, whereas the choice among paths creates downward jumps and boundaries that are neither convex nor concave. One evaluation at the mediant of each Farey interval recovers the affine piece and an optimal lasso, and a greatest-fixed-point computation over decreasing integer bursts yields the whole function in polynomial time and linear working space. We also compute discrimination horizons and extend the Farey structure to turn-based safety games.

Symbolic Computation.title: Exact Algebraic Computation of Learning Coefficients for Two-Dimensional Singular Models
Symbolic Computation.summary: Classical information criteria such as the Bayesian Information Criterion (BIC) rely on regularity assumptions that break down for singular models, leading to incorrect model selection in settings such as deep learning. The Widely Applicable Bayesian Information Criterion (WBIC) relies on local learning coefficients $λ$, which in the analytic case coincides with local Real Log Canonical Thresholds (RLCT) of the Kullback-Leibler divergence of the model, to capture correct marginal likelihood asymptotics. Exact computation of the learning coefficients has been limited to special cases, and only sampling-based estimation methods are generally applicable. We present the first deterministic algorithm that computes local RLCTs exactly for any two-dimensional model whose Kullback-Leibler distance is contact equivalent to a polynomial, derive a bound on its complexity, and demonstrate its effectiveness for a broad class of models, with applications including polynomial neural networks. Beyond providing ground truth to calibrate sampling-based estimators, exact computation reveals algebraic structure in learning coefficients that sampling cannot and out-speeds it in the shallow regime.

Symbolic Computation.title: PopMelodyGen: A Copyright-Aware Platform for Controllable Pop-Melody Generation
Symbolic Computation.summary: Large-scale redistributable symbolic pop-melody data remain scarce due to copyright restrictions, creating a bottleneck for both practical deployment and reproducible research in music generation. We present PopMelodyGen, a copyright-aware platform for controllable pop-melody generation that combines rule-based synthesis with neural generation. Our approach first uses an expert synthesizer to produce large-scale labeled synthetic melodies from explicit musical knowledge and templates, providing scalable pretraining data with auditable provenance. A neural model is then pretrained on this corpus and adapted with a small licensed real-pop corpus to improve melodic naturalness while preserving controllability. The platform supports interactive melody creation with accompaniment playback and export for creators, as well as batch construction of annotated symbolic datasets for researchers. PopMelodyGen demonstrates a practical training and deployment paradigm for creative AI when large-scale reusable real-world data are limited.
Symbolic Computation.comment: AAAI 2027 Demonstration Program (accepted); extended version with appendix

Information Retrieval.title: HME-PFD: Heterogeneous Mixture-of-Experts Privileged Feature Distillation
Information Retrieval.summary: Knowledge distillation (KD) is widely used to transfer knowledge from large teacher models to smaller student models, facilitating efficient serving of machine learning systems. In the context of ads recommendation, privileged features distillation (PFD) extends KD by allowing the teacher model to leverage privileged features, i.e., features available only during training, to enhance distillation performance. However, in real-world scenarios, privileged features often have limited coverage and exhibit heterogeneous distributions, resulting in training examples of varying importance for distillation and model learning. We propose Heterogeneous Mixture-of-Experts Privileged Feature Distillation (HME-PFD), a novel approach that incorporates privileged features into the routing module of a Mixture-of-Experts-based student model. Our method introduces both hard-coded and learnable routing modules, enabling the student to dynamically determine expert assignment based on the availability and values of privileged features. This design allows the student model to better handle the heterogeneous data scenario, where privileged features are partially observed, by differentiating between high- and low-signal samples. Extensive experiments on two post-click conversion prediction tasks demonstrate that HME-PFD consistently outperforms baseline methods. Our results show that leveraging privileged features for expert routing in the student model leads to improved model performance, even when privileged features are incomplete or sparse.

Information Retrieval.title: Who Gets Re-ranked When a Clinical Model Gains New Data?
Information Retrieval.summary: Hospitals often update a deployed risk model by adding a data source, such as laboratory results, that only some patients have. Work on safe model updates assumes fixed inputs and so ignores patients who lack the new data. The update has no new measurements for them, yet their rank can change, and a sick patient not yet tested can drop off an alert list. We split rank-based compatibility by data availability and pair it with error correction and alert-list effects. We compared each update with ordinary retraining on the old inputs, predicting ICU admission or death and hospital admission, on 78,475 emergency department visits from MC-MED and, in a pre-registered replication, 100,000 stays from MIMIC-IV-ED at a second hospital. Radiograph report text gave no detectable gain and almost no extra re-ranking. Laboratory results improved prediction but, at both hospitals and with linear or tree models, pushed patients without labs down alert lists; linear updates also reshuffled them more than retraining did, without ranking them better. A top-20% admission list caught 4.2% of admitted patients without labs after the update, against 18.8% after retraining (second hospital: 4.9% against 22.6%), while catching more patients overall. This held for list sizes from 5% to 50% and in every patient group we checked, despite better measured calibration. Separate alert thresholds for patients with and without labs restored most or all of their catch rate at both hospitals at almost no cost. Teams should check these patients before deploying such an update.
Information Retrieval.comment: Accepted at the 6th International Workshop on Multi-Modal Medical Data Analysis (MMMDA), IEEE BigData 2026

Information Retrieval.title: ChatGPT Can't Sell (And That's Probably a Good Thing): Buyer-Aligned AI Advice, the Sales-Representative Gap, and Evidence from Commercial Conversations
Information Retrieval.summary: AI assistants and merchant sales agents have different objectives: assistants should help buyers compare options and preserve the choice not to purchase, while sales agents also guide qualified buyers toward an authorized next step. We study this sales-representative gap with three evidence streams. In 12,178 historical English GPT-family conversations screened for commercial or transactional intent, a 279-request sample contained recommendation language in 63 first replies (22.6%) and no narrow transactional action wording. In a 56-conversation explicit-buying sample, 24 replies (42.9%) contained recommendation markers, 32 (57.1%) qualification phrases, and none transaction-specific phrases. These lexical measures do not estimate successful selling. A 2026 brand-monitoring cohort of 1,050 GPT-5.4--Gemini answer pairs over 383 purchase-related prompts showed transaction-specific phrases in 0.0% of recommendation-worded prompts, 0.21% of price/comparison prompts, and 9.52% of explicitly transaction-worded prompts. The prompts are selected, not organic shopping sessions. In a prospective pilot across five matched hypothetical product scenarios, sales instructions produced more next-step language than general-assistant instructions (5/5 vs. 2/5), but no increase in clean product choice (3/5 in both); unsupported offers and fit errors also occurred. This pilot cannot establish a population effect. A separate company-affiliated randomized field study reports higher engaged-visitor conversion for Javo, a commercially trained sales agent, than for a frontier-model agent in shared tooling, but does not identify the mechanism. We argue that apparent reluctance to sell can be appropriate for buyer-aligned assistants. Merchant agents should optimize qualified decision progress through catalog grounding, truthful authorization, and safeguards against unsuitable sales.

Information Retrieval.title: A Study of Prior Case Retrieval Using Lexical, Semantic, and Rhetorical Role Information in Indian Legal Documents
Information Retrieval.summary: For retrieving prior cases in Indian legal judgments, the problem involves distinguishing relevant legal facts from mere lexical similarities because a prior case that shares a statute with the query judgment is not necessarily relevant. In this paper, we describe an empirical evaluation of three consecutive designs of retrieval systems for the IL PCR(Indian Legal Prior Case Retrieval) task. We demonstrate that the combination of the rhetorical roles (Fact, Ratio Of The Decision, Precedent, Argument, Statute) is better than either using individual roles or performing full text retrieval, that statute similarity is not discriminative, and that a legal entailment reranker with training data produced by an LLM is much worse in terms of official evaluation than its internal validation score. Two rankers, with excellent internal MRR up to 0.97, performed poorly in terms of official evaluation (MRR as low as 0.14). Thus, we propose a new design with query disjoint splitting and frozen validation fusion. The result is a four stage pipeline with Micro F1 0.2549, MRR 0.6081, and nDCG@10 0.4187.

Information Retrieval.title: The Price of Scale in Proactive Memory Recall
Information Retrieval.summary: An assistant that brings up memories unasked must decide at every turn whether anything in its store is worth an interruption. This decision is a multiple-testing problem whose difficulty grows with store size N. On replays of LongMemEval, a similarity threshold tuned to 5% false alarms at N=8 reaches 84-100% at N=2048 across embedding models and cue types; LoCoMo and LLM judges show it too. We prove that a gate which thresholds the best of N independent irrelevant scores at false-alarm rate alpha works at a per-item false-positive rate of about -ln(1-alpha)/N, which pins its hit rate to the far left of the ROC and makes it regularly varying in N under regular variation. If the relevant memory is equally likely to be any of the N, whatever a gate reads and however it decides, at false-alarm rate alpha it hits at most alpha+sqrt(alpha(1-alpha)chi^2/N), with chi^2 the divergence between a relevant and an irrelevant memory, and with equal-variance binormal scores the best-score gate is optimal. At matched false alarms the deployed score recalls 14-26 points more than raw cosine. A cue-swap conformal gate, which ranks the current cue among other cues on the store, has a finite-sample false-alarm guarantee under exchangeability.
