We develop a placement-aware framework for anisotropy-induced detection (AID), showing that orientation sensitivity is governed by harmonic modes shared by the locally visible target-direction distribution and the sensor trajectory-incidence response. The resulting AID measure admits an exact RMS interpretation for the retained-harmonic orientation response. We then introduce a sensor-induced directional discrepancy, derive a conditional bound on future orientation regret, and obtain sufficient certificates for robust orientation selection whenever the future sensor-relevant shift lies within a prescribed discrepancy radius. Using 2025 AIS ship-traffic data near Terrebonne Bay, Louisiana, historical AID is strongly correlated with held-out orientation sensitivity ($r=0.908$). Across four angular-response widths, AID explains orientation-sensitivity variation with $R^2=0.920$, compared with $R^2=0.239$ for target-only anisotropy. At the nominal threshold, 316 of 350 locations are empirically classified as orientation-useful, and all retain gain above the threshold across five held-out windows.
Systems and Control.comment: Submitted to L-CSS

Systems and Control.title: PIRA: Pan-CDN Intra-video Resource Adaptation for Short Video Streaming
Systems and Control.summary: In large scale short video platforms, CDN resource selection plays a critical role in maintaining Quality of Experience (QoE) while controlling escalating traffic costs. To better understand this phenomenon, we conduct in the wild network measurements during video playback in a production short video system. The results reveal that CDNs delivering higher average QoE often come at greater financial cost, yet their connection quality fluctuates even within a single video underscoring a fundamental and dynamic trade off between QoE and cost. However, the problem of sustaining high QoE under cost constraints remains insufficiently investigated in the context of CDN selection for short video streaming. To address this, we propose PIRA, a dynamic resource selection algorithm that optimizes QoE and cost in real time during video playback. PIRA formally integrating QoE and cost by a mathematical model, and introduce a intra video control theoretic CDN resource selection approach which can balance QoE and cost under network dynamics. To reduce the computation overheads, PIRA employs state space pruning and adaptive parameter adjustment to efficiently solve the high dimensional optimization problem. In large scale production experiments involving 450,000 users over two weeks, PIRA outperforms the production baseline, achieving a 2.1% reduction in start up delay, 15.2% shorter rebuffering time, and 10% lower average unit traffic cost, demonstrating its effectiveness in balancing user experience and financial cost at scale.

Systems and Control.title: A general-purpose safe manipulator planning framework for diverse environments without retraining
Systems and Control.summary: Nowadays, robots need to be retrained whenever their operating environment changes, and this prohibitive training cost keeps them far from daily use. The community is calling for innovations that bestow on a robot the ability to safely grasp different objects under different conditions without excessive training data and computing power. In response to this call, we present a general-purpose manipulator mission-planning framework, allowing a robot to safely perform manipulation tasks, such as grasping objects that fit in its gripper, across different operating environments without retraining its controllers. The framework rests on two innovations: a finite-state abstracted model, bisimilar to the original system dynamics, that describes accessibility of the space in front of the robot under its given arm and gripper, and a block-conservative specification generation method that turns each manipulation task under any specific operational environment into specifications about state accessibility of the abstracted model. A task proven feasible and safe on the abstracted model is guaranteed to be safe and achievable by the robot. Real-world case studies conducted on a Unitree G1 U1 humanoid show that manipulation tasks commonly encountered in daily life, such as grasping an object, pressing an elevator button or picking up a berry, can be handled within this framework, where an abstracted model of the G1 U1 robot is built only once to avoid costly model reconstructions, and different tasks are simply captured by specific block-conservative specifications, achievable by a generic mission planner with vision-based feedback control.
Systems and Control.comment: 46 pages, 7 figures; main text and supplementary materials

Systems and Control.title: Systematic study of the performance of small robots on controlled laboratory substrates
Systems and Control.summary: The design of robots able to locomote effectively over a diversity of terrain requires detailed ground interaction models; unfortunately such models are lacking due to the complicated response of real world substrates which can yield and flow in response to loading. To advance our understanding of the relevant modeling and design issues, we conduct a comparative study of the performance of DASH and RoACH, two small, biologically inspired, six legged, lightweight (10 cm, 20 g) robots fabricated using the smart composite microstructure (SCM) process. We systematically examine performance of both robots on rigid and flowing substrates. Varying both ground properties and limb stride frequency, we investigate average speed, mean mechanical power and cost of transport, and stability. We find that robot performance and stability is sensitive to the physics of ground interaction: on hard ground kinetic energy must be managed to prevent yaw, pitch, and roll instability to maintain high performance, while on sand the fluidizing interaction leads to increased cost of transport and lower running speeds. We also observe that the characteristic limb morphology and kinematics of each robot result in distinct differences in their abilities to traverse different terrains. Our systematic studies are the first step toward developing models of interaction of limbs with complex terrain as well as developing improved limb morphologies and control strategies.

Systems and Control.title: DynaSeek: Large Language Model-Driven Hybrid Dynamic Model Discovery for Grid-Tied Inverters from Limited Measurements
Systems and Control.summary: Discovering the unknown governing equations of grid-tied inverters from limited measurements is essential for the stability analysis of modern inverter-dominated power systems. However, existing identification methods struggle to jointly resolve unmeasured internal control memory and saturation-induced mode transitions from accessible terminal waveforms. To address this challenge, this paper proposes DynaSeek, a large language model (LLM)-driven framework for discovering explicit hybrid differential-algebraic equations (DAEs) of current-limited inverters. The framework integrates physics-constrained symbolic skeleton synthesis with the joint numerical estimation of shared model parameters and record-specific latent initial states across multi-island experience archives. Furthermore, two complementary structural diagnostics evaluating cross-record state closure and cross-window consistency are established to detect structural deficiencies across distinct input histories and transient stages. Guided by diagnostic feedback, DynaSeek directs variable-dimensional latent-state expansion and current-limiting and anti-windup refinement to yield self-contained hybrid DAEs unifying unsaturated regulation, current limiting, and post-fault recovery. Controller-hardware-in-the-loop (CHIL) experiments and closed-loop system-level simulations demonstrate that DynaSeek reduces transient trajectory reconstruction errors by one to two orders of magnitude compared with symbolic and neural baselines while accurately preserving reference critical clearing times, enabling reliable large-signal stability assessment of inverters with inaccessible internal controls.

Systems and Control.title: Online Identification Can Replace a Floor-Plan Prior on Unseen Buildings
Systems and Control.summary: The Smart Buildings Challenge asks for one HVAC control policy that runs office buildings and weather it has never seen, from the building's metadata and sensor streams alone. Our controller sees no data from the target building before it runs and is not tuned per building; its few global constants were set on development scenarios. Each zone has a first-order grey-box model that starts from coefficients computed from the floor plan and is updated online by recursive least squares, and a planner and a closed-form mapping turn the models into plant commands. On two sets of buildings and weather that we generated, a validation set and a stress set with real-year weather, it scores 0.145 and 0.159 times the starter kit's PID baseline, and 0.095 times on a holdout built after all versions were fixed and scored once. It improves on every building, also against our two implementations of ASHRAE Guideline 36: per set it scores 0.60 to 0.71 times a basic version and 0.83 to 0.96 times one partly tuned on the public leaderboard, which wins one of 54 scenarios; with a 5 °C frost target for empty zones on both, the margin over the tuned version shrinks to 1.4% on the stress set, where one of six buildings is 0.2% worse. In an ablation on a reduced-order model, removing both the floor-plan prior and online identification costs 28%, 20% and 42% on the validation, stress and holdout sets, far more than the two effects combined: either source of building-specific information recovers most of what is lost without both. On one office floor in a second simulator, BOPTEST, this does not carry over: with identification on, the two priors give similar results, but the floor-plan prior alone, with constants fitted on the competition's simulator, is the least stable arm. These simulation results motivate testing floor-plan-initialised adaptive control in buildings that have drawings but no operating data.
Systems and Control.comment: Smart Buildings Competition Track, NeurIPS 2026. First place, Round One paper prize. 8 pages main text, 21 pages in total, 8 figures, 5 tables

Systems and Control.title: Physics-Informed Learning for Multiplayer Differential Games
Systems and Control.summary: Computing per-player feedback strategies in $N$-player adversarial differential games is challenging as the associated coupled Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman system is high-dimensional and generally lacks classical solutions. We address this by approximating viscosity solutions using physics-informed neural networks within a policy iteration scheme with a vanishing-viscosity annealing schedule. Theoretically, we establish an explicit $\varepsilon$-Nash guarantee by bounding per-player regret via computable residuals and prove our method reaches this stopping criterion in finite time. For two-player zero-sum games, we further establish a computable bound on the approximation error of the value function. Numerical experiments on pursuit-evasion scenarios illustrate the tightness of these computed bounds and the framework's scalability to high-dimensional environments.
Systems and Control.comment: Accepted to IEEE Control Systems Letters (L-CSS) with presentation at CDC 2026

Systems and Control.title: Impact of the Performance of Autonomy and Communication Subsystems on the Level-of-Safety of Partially Autonomous Machine Systems
Systems and Control.summary: The level-of-safety of a partially autonomous machine system depends on two subsystems: the autonomy subsystem that manages the system between human interventions; and the communication subsystem that enables those interventions. These subsystems are typically evaluated independently. We model the level-of-safety analytically as a function of their joint performance. Three parameters characterize the autonomy subsystem: the Mean Time Between Interventions (MTBI); the urgency $\mathcal{U}$ or mean time within which an intervention must be completed to avoid failure; and the complexity $\mathcal{C}$ or mean time to understand, decide on and execute it. Two characterize the communication subsystem: its availability $P_A$ and its latency $\varepsilon$. A dimensionless criticality ratio $ρ=(\mathcal{C}+\varepsilon)/\mathcal{U}$ prescribes the shape of the Pareto tradeoff between the MTBI and $P_A$ at a constant level-of-safety. At $ρ=0.01$, a perfect link lowers the required MTBI by two orders of magnitude. At $ρ=1$, it only halves it. Under exponential timing assumptions the model is in closed form, and compliance with a safety budget can be stated at a chosen assurance level. We illustrate it for remotely piloted aircraft with assumed parameter values and propose a simulation procedure to estimate them.

Systems and Control.title: Neural Fidelity Calibration for Informative Sim-to-Real Adaptation
Systems and Control.summary: Deep reinforcement learning can seamlessly transfer agile locomotion and navigation skills from the simulator to real world. However, bridging the sim-to-real gap with domain randomization or adversarial methods often demands expert physics knowledge to ensure policy robustness. Even so, cutting-edge simulators may fall short of capturing every real-world detail, and the reconstructed environment may introduce errors due to various perception uncertainties. To address these challenges, we propose Neural Fidelity Calibration (NFC), a novel framework that employs conditional score-based diffusion models to calibrate simulator physical coefficients and residual fidelity domains online during robot execution. Specifically, the residual fidelity reflects the simulation model shift relative to the real-world dynamics and captures the uncertainty of the perceived environment, enabling us to sample realistic environments under the inferred distribution for policy fine-tuning. Our framework is informative and adaptive in three key ways: (a) we fine-tune the pretrained policy only under anomalous scenarios, (b) we build sequential NFC online with the pretrained NFC's proposal prior, reducing the diffusion model's training burden, and (c) when NFC uncertainty is high and may degrade policy improvement, we leverage optimistic exploration to enable hallucinated policy optimization. Our framework achieves superior simulator calibration precision compared to state-of-the-art methods across diverse robots with high-dimensional parametric spaces. We study the critical contribution of residual fidelity to policy improvement in simulation and real-world experiments. Notably, our approach demonstrates robust robot navigation under challenging real-world conditions, such as a broken wheel axle on snowy surfaces.
Systems and Control.comment: The code and demonstration videos are available at https://www.youwei-yu.com/nfc

Systems and Control.title: Public Battery Field Data
Systems and Control.summary: Battery systems and algorithms are developed and evaluated primarily on laboratory cycling data, but fielded battery systems are subjected to duty cycles, temperatures, and measurement conditions that cannot be reproduced in a lab. Field data from batteries in service has begun to appear in public releases attached to individual papers, but each release has its own format, units, labels, and other gaps that make it difficult to compare against others. We present a curated collection of 37 public field-data releases from 28 research groups, covering applications that span passenger EVs, buses, light electric mobility, grid-scale storage, distributed storage, consumer electronics, industrial robotics and satellites. Where the releases are complete enough to measure, this heterogeneous collection contains 256 GB of data from at least 150,626 lithium-ion cells, 3,287 batteries, 115.6 MWh of energy storage capacity, and 3,040 unit-years of service. Critically, it also contains 957 labeled or reported faults, which provide greater visibility into what real battery performance and safety issues look like outside the lab. We release a public repository of metadata and code for each of the field datasets. For each dataset it provides a registry entry with sources, license and access links, checksums to confirm a download is complete, a metadata table, and code for how to load it. We also report where released datasets differ from their papers. We hope the collection can help serve researchers (human or otherwise) as a useful platform for improving battery field diagnostics, fault detection and health estimation. Better field evidence can also feed back to improve manufacturing quality, inform second-life screening and residual-value estimates, and broadly accelerate electrification.
Systems and Control.comment: v3: 35 releases, matching v1.2.0 of the collection

Systems and Control.title: Optimization of a Hybrid Solar-Biogas-Battery Energy Storage Microgrid: A Case Study
Systems and Control.summary: Low-income regions like eastern Uganda often lack reliable grid power. This paper presents the techno-economic optimization of the Soroti Integrated Renewable Energy Microgrid (SIREM), a hybrid renewable system for grid-access expansion where Soroti District household grid access stands at 16.7\%. The microgrid integrates concentrating solar power (CSP) with thermal storage, biogas combined cycle generation, and lithium iron phosphate battery storage. Using Xendee optimization software with six years of NASA POWER data, the optimal configuration comprises a 37 MW CSP field, 70 MWh molten-salt storage, a 5 MW CSP turbine, a 6 MW biogas CCGT, and a 10 MWh battery system. The design delivers 61.3 GWh annually with a 42.91% IRR, 2-year payback, and levelized cost of electricity of 0.1991 USD/kWh generation (0.3752 USD/kWh load-served), achieving 32.2% total savings versus grid-only supply while exporting 28.8 GWh annually, demonstrating the viability of hybrid renewable microgrids for grid expansion in sub-Saharan Africa.
Systems and Control.comment: 6 pages, 6 figures, presented at IEEE PES/IAS PowerAfrica Conference 2026

Systems and Control.title: The Phases of Hierarchy
Systems and Control.summary: We develop a dynamical phase theory of hierarchy, in which depth decides whether a population of size $N$ that revises its own environment can correct it without overcorrecting. The statistics that let a large majority detect a small bias - the basis of the Condorcet jury theorem - also make its response grow as $\sqrt{N}$. Fed back into the environment it is judging, this sharpening destabilises the matched state through a flip bifurcation at a critical loop gain, which we obtain analytically for a class of models we term adaptive normal forms. We show that this instability can be attenuated by hierarchical layering, requiring a depth scaling logarithmically with $N$. This recovers known logarithmic bounds in organisational economics directly from dynamic stability conditions. Hierarchical depth carries its own costs however, and by analysing the signal chain transmission up the hierarchy we show that beyond a finite depth no correction reaches the top before its deadline, and that below it the cost of arrival grows exponentially with depth. A hierarchy that is too flat therefore oscillates and one that is too deep cannot be steered in time, leaving a bounded window of depth between an unstable flat phase and a frozen inertial phase. We further show that these results can be generalised by treating each layer as a real-space renormalisation step, classifying aggregation rules by how they transmit bias. This establishes a connection between these dynamic results to attention in Transformers, where a residual update is diffusion on the token graph and depth plays the role of scale. Finally we show these phase boundaries are observable in finite sampling, and propose measurements which may characterise the proposed phases in real adaptive systems.
Systems and Control.comment: 29 pages, 12 figures, ade with generative AI assistance. No clue what the right archive listing for it should be

Multiagent Systems.title: VoroPlex: A Python Framework for Multi-Threaded and Differentiable Voronoi Tessellation
Multiagent Systems.summary: Voronoi tessellations are widely used in computational physics, for example to measure local structure in particle systems and to generate meshes. We present VoroPlex, an open-source Python package for computing Voronoi tessellations in two and three dimensions. VoroPlex is built on the multi-threaded version of the C++ library Voro++, so that large tessellations can be computed in parallel. The package also makes the tessellation differentiable. Each Voronoi vertex is labeled by the generators that define it, and VoroPlex uses these labels to compute the derivative of the vertex with respect to the positions of these generators. PyTorch can therefore compute gradients of quantities such as cell areas, volumes, and interface areas with respect to the generator positions, so that these quantities can be optimized using standard gradient-based methods. The package also includes tools for extracting interfaces between groups of cells and for exporting meshes. For one million points using 28 threads, VoroPlex is 46 times faster than SciPy in 2D and 39 times faster in 3D. We demonstrate the package with three applications: centroidal Voronoi tessellations with a variable density, meshing of 2D shapes defined by signed distance functions, and the design of foams with a preferred cell orientation.

Multiagent Systems.title: CAMPS: Composable Adapters for Mixed-Precision Solvers
Multiagent Systems.summary: Mixed-precision solvers usually assign a fixed precision to each algorithmic component. This makes it hard to reuse a lower-precision solver at different depths inside a higher-precision solver. We introduce CAMPS (Composable Adapters for Mixed-Precision Solvers), a framework that uses iterative refinement to connect solvers across precisions. An adapter computes residuals and updates in the precision of its parent and passes each correction solve to a child solver in a lower precision. The child can be a direct solver, an iterative solver, or another adapter. The adapter checks every correction and keeps it if the residual does not increase. We prove three results. Adapters can be placed at any compatible set of precision boundaries in a solver tree without breaking the solver interface. Every output that the root solver reports as successful satisfies a backward-error bound set by the stopping tolerance and the root precision. Convergence follows from one sufficient condition per boundary, computed from the leaves of the tree to its root. We test five configurations on dense and sparse systems in 64-bit, 32-bit, and 16-bit floating-point arithmetic (FP64, FP32, and FP16). On dense well-conditioned systems, CAMPS is up to 9.6x faster than an FP64 direct solver for a single solve that includes the factorization. On sparse nonsymmetric systems, a three-precision hierarchy is the fastest method we tested. Compared with our implementation of the nested solver F3R, CAMPS is as fast and uses about 3.4x less peak memory. CAMPS does not always win. Plain conjugate gradient is faster on sparse symmetric positive definite systems. On very ill-conditioned systems, FP32 corrections fail, and the adapter detects the failure and switches to an FP64 fallback.

Databases.title: One Ocean, Many Tasks: A Data-Grounded Simulation Suite and Benchmark for Marine Robotics
Databases.summary: Simulation is essential for marine robotics, yet existing platforms often trade off between visually realistic worlds, high-throughput experimentation, and ocean-condition realism grounded in real data. We present OneOcean, a data-grounded simulation suite and benchmark built around a unified spatiotemporal ocean-environment product that harmonizes bathymetry with data-driven currents and tides, with optional pollution fields for cleanup-related evaluation. On top of this environment representation, OneOcean defines a task ladder spanning navigation and station-keeping under currents, waypoint and route following, depth-profile tracking, area scanning, pipeline inspection, and multi-agent coordination, including formation transit, fish protection and patrol (herding), and surface pollution localization, containment, and cleanup. The suite supports multi-agent settings with 2-10 vehicles. Our simulator supports three to six Degrees of Freedom (DoF) and produces standardized metrics and reproducible run manifests, enabling consistent aggregation across tasks, difficulties, and scaling settings. Experiments across dataset variants and scenes systematically stress planning and control under data-grounded disturbances and reveal trade-offs among heuristic baselines, Behavior Cloning (BC), and a Large Language Model (LLM)-based planner.
Databases.comment: 17 pages, 9 figures, 21 tables, including appendices

Databases.title: Shape-Aware Three-Way Merge for RDF Knowledge Graphs: The schema defines the conflict: an implementation and evaluation
Databases.summary: Merging RDF serializations creates ordering conflicts and misses semantic ones. We describe and evaluate a three-way merge in which the schema defines a conflict: set algebra combines canonical triples, and a slot is contended only where a SHACL shape bounds its cardinality and both sides' changes cannot stand within that bound. Unbounded predicates union; contended slots go to a person. The same shapes graph validates the result. We do not claim the first three-way merge for RDF. Our contribution is an implementation in a production multi-agent store and an evaluation against a reimplementation of Quit Store's Context Merge overlap rule, which it extends rather than replaces, and six other strategies. Across five synthetic seeds, the shape-aware operator raised 33 conflicts, all true positives as judged by the same shapes that define them, with no triples lost or fabricated and no SHACL violations admitted. The context-overlap baseline, counted per slot, detected the same 33 conflicts but asked 845 questions. A replay built from recorded production incidents covers 105 human alias repairs (93 after excluding 12 chained pairs) and 939 duplicate-value incidents. It reproduces a triple-level limit: different names for one entity remain invisible (0 of 93 alias repairs detected, matching 0 of 21 synthetic cases). In a study of evolving shape contracts, merging shape declarations first handles the tested cardinality changes, while datatype evolution exposes a detector blind spot caught by post-merge validation. An oracle that reads no shapes agrees with the shipped operator on the facts and history of all 23 reachable single-slot cases. Under wrong shapes, a missing bound loses data silently and a spurious one only adds questions. The supported claim is fewer human decisions with nothing silently lost, for cardinality conflicts in one deployment, not general merge correctness.
Databases.comment: 19 pages. Artifact, benchmark and replay corpus at https://github.com/intigraph/quipu ; every table names the command that regenerates it

Databases.title: Atunda: Building an Afrogenic Dance Movement Dataset for AI-Driven Classification
Databases.summary: This paper introduces Atunda, the first systematically collected video dataset of Afrogenic dance moves, designed for training and evaluating deep learning models for movement classification. The first phase of the dataset includes nearly 400 videos covering 13 distinct dance moves from African and African Diaspora performative culture, making it the first AI-ready resource of its kind. Using this dataset, we train and evaluate various configurations of temporal convolutional neural networks, achieving a classification accuracy exceeding 95%. The baseline results provide a benchmark for future studies in movement classification, especially in the understudied area of Afrogenic performative culture and tradition. This work lays the foundation for developing in the future digital metrics of similarity, automated attribution systems, and tools that preserve and promote the cultural heritage of Afrogenic dances.

Databases.title: DecisionReplay: A Corpus and Offline Simulator for Ensembling Decision Models
Databases.summary: Comparing ensembles, routers and cascades requires the output of every model on every item, and its cost. Stored collections built for routing keep no per-option probabilities. We provide a dataset on which ensemble methods, routers and cascades are simulated quickly, without new model calls. DecisionReplay holds the probability vectors of 17 commercial decision models, endpoints that return a probability for every answer option, on 35 benchmarks, with the token counts, billed cost and measured latency of every call, all released. A deterministic simulator replays any policy that selects, combines or cascades them. One well-chosen model per benchmark is hard to beat: pooling all models loses 2.7 accuracy points to it, and stacking gains 1.0 points at 3.4 times its cost. The models are wrong together: two that are both wrong choose the same wrong option in 72% of cases. The best router matches that model at 64% of its cost, and certified early exit cuts the cost of a stacked ensemble by 43% without changing an answer. DecisionReplay makes it cheap and fast to test whether a new method changes these results.

Databases.title: VulCPE: Context-Aware Cybersecurity Vulnerability Retrieval and Management
Databases.summary: The dynamic landscape of cybersecurity demands precise and scalable solutions for vulnerability management in heterogeneous systems, where configuration-specific vulnerabilities are often misidentified due to inconsistent data in databases like the National Vulnerability Database (NVD). Inaccurate Common Platform Enumeration (CPE) data in NVD further leads to false positives and incomplete vulnerability retrieval. Informed by our systematic analysis of CPE and CVEdeails data, revealing more than 50% vendor name inconsistencies, we propose VulCPE, a framework that standardizes data and models configuration dependencies using a unified CPE schema (uCPE), entity recognition, relation extraction, and graph-based modeling. VulCPE achieves superior retrieval precision (0.766) and coverage (0.926) over existing tools. VulCPE ensures precise, context-aware vulnerability management, enhancing cyber resilience.

Databases.title: Single-Database Rewards Are Hackable: Counterfactual Execution for Trustworthy Text-to-SQL RL
Databases.summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) for text-to-SQL agents pays a query when its result matches the reference on one database. However, a wrong query can match by luck when the data lack the rows that expose its bug. We study a counterfactual-database (CF) reward that also runs the final query on a few hidden, code-generated copies of the database and pays only if all results match (strict form) or by the share matched (mean form). On 1,302 synthetic audit questions, the strict form lowers the share of buggy queries paid in full from 29.5% to 16.8% and of reward hacks from 54.1% to 1.9%, rejecting 0 of 2,847 correct queries; copies from a family-blind generator do about as well. In a controlled GRPO comparison on a 3.35B model with three seeds per arm, training on the mean form did not improve in-domain accuracy (8.4% vs 11.7%), because the two rewards disagreed on only 5-7% of rollouts; on Spider it gained 1.6 points. One seed reverses both signs, so single-seed reward comparisons mislead. Code: https://github.com/RishiiGamer2201/counterfactual-sql-rewards ; data, models, demo: https://huggingface.co/counterfactual-sql
Databases.comment: 4 pages + references and appendix (12 pages total). Code: https://github.com/RishiiGamer2201/counterfactual-sql-rewards

Databases.title: Cache Replacement in Direct-Access Cloud OLAP-An Experimental Comparison and Practical Guidance
Databases.summary:
Direct-access cloud OLAP engines rely on local caches to hide remote object-store latency, yet the replacement design space remains poorly understood. Existing systems largely inherit recency- or Clock-oriented policies from DBMS buffer management, even though cloud misses combine a size-independent request overhead with a size-dependent transfer cost and cache objects vary widely in size. We present a broad experimental comparison of 22 cache-replacement algorithms and one semantic-caching baseline across seven analytical workloads and ten cache sizes. To compare them on a common basis, we formulate Unified Hit Ratio (UHR), a latency-weighted hit ratio that decomposes into a workload-specific weighted combination of object and byte hit ratios, and equivalently, the normalized fraction of aggregate remote-download latency saved by caching.
  Our results yield practitioner-oriented guidance. Classical size-aware policies developed outside the DBMS literature remain surprisingly strong, dominating object hit ratio on most workloads and staying near the UHR frontier. Byte efficiency depends primarily on aggressive filtering of zero-reuse objects, while under multi-tenant drift lightweight per-request adaptation is often more robust than retraining-heavy learned methods. We instantiate these lessons in LARA, a compact reference policy that validates the guidance through competitive UHR performance.
Databases.comment: 27 pages, 13 figures, 4 tables. Published in Proceedings of the ACM on Management of Data (PACMMOD), Vol. 4, No. 6 (SIGMOD 2027)

Databases.title: EMMA: Efficient and Effective Cooperative Multi-Modal Analytics over Embodied AI Data
Databases.summary: Embodied AI has seen growing real-world deployment, particularly in autonomous vehicles and robots. These vehicles and robots continuously capture large collections of multi-modal data, such as video, LiDAR point clouds, and GPS trajectories. Historical collections of these data support model improvement and safety assessment through scene retrieval, object trajectory extraction, and corresponding analysis. Processing such analytical queries is challenging because answering them may require combining information from different modalities and observations captured by different moving vehicles or robots, while extracting that information with deep models at every scene incurs prohibitive cost. We present EMMA, an operator-oriented query-processing framework for embodied AI data. EMMA compiles analytical queries into composable operators and executes them on demand. To support accurate query evaluation, EMMA performs modality-aware staged predicate evaluation and selectively combines overlapping observations. To reduce query cost, EMMA uses a temporal co-location index to identify joint-analysis candidates, adaptive scene skipping to reduce model calls, and a shared world store to reuse extracted information across operators and queries. EMMA trains execution policies offline and deploys them as plug-ins. Based on lightweight observations, these policies determine whether the current scene is analyzed independently or jointly and how many subsequent scenes can be safely skipped, balancing analytical accuracy and execution cost. Experiments show that EMMA substantially reduces query execution cost while preserving query accuracy.

Databases.title: Data Agents Need a Map: Evolving, Demand-Driven Knowledge of Large Collections
Databases.summary:
Most data that could power rich analysis sits unintegrated and uncataloged in open data portals, data lakes, and collections of independently published tables. Data agents now answer analytical questions over such collections with a full workflow per question, including dataset retrieval, join discovery and evaluation, and tailored program synthesis, most of which are discarded when a new task arrives. The knowledge these workflows depend on, such as what each column means, which context a dataset leaves implicit, and how datasets combine, is therefore perpetually rederived and never persisted.
  We argue for persisting this knowledge in an evolving semantic atlas that users and agents can navigate and extend. The atlas describes every dataset offline, through topics, semantic types, and profiles, so that agents can find the datasets that a task requires. Relationships between datasets and integrated views, which require comparing datasets, are instead built on demand for the areas of analysis that users declare. Every item is stored with its provenance and the confidence of the methods that produced it, so that agents can decide how far to trust it or whether to abstain. As datasets change, inconsistencies are detected and corrected automatically, while human users settle what the data leaves inconclusive. We present this vision and its challenges, namely building the atlas over large, multi-domain collections, keeping it correct and up to date, serving it to users and agents, and evaluating whether it improves their answers. A proof of concept on DAB, a benchmark for data agents, shows that with only part of the atlas a coding agent can already read a fifth to a third fewer tokens while achieving the same accuracy as without it.

Emerging Technologies.title: StochEP: Stochastic Equilibrium Propagation for Spiking Convergent Recurrent Neural Networks
Emerging Technologies.summary: Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) promise energy-efficient, sparse, biologically inspired computation. Training them with Backpropagation Through Time (BPTT) and surrogate gradients achieves strong performance but remains biologically implausible. Equilibrium Propagation (EP) provides a more local and biologically grounded alternative. However, existing EP frameworks for SNNs largely rely on deterministic neurons, which require complex mechanisms to handle spiking discontinuities and do not scale beyond simple benchmarks such as MNIST and Fashion-MNIST. Inspired by the stochastic nature of biological spiking mechanism and recent hardware trends, we propose a stochastic EP framework that integrates probabilistic spiking neurons into the EP paradigm. This formulation smoothens the optimization landscape, stabilizes training, and enables efficient and scalable learning in SNNs. We provide theoretical guarantees showing that the proposed stochastic EP dynamics approximate deterministic EP under mean-field theory, thereby inheriting its underlying theoretical guarantees. The proposed framework narrows the performance gap with both BPTT-trained SNNs and EP-trained non-spiking convergent recurrent neural networks (CRNNs) on CIFAR-10, DVS Gesture, and IMDB datasets, while preserving temporal and spatial locality. Our results highlight stochastic EP as a promising approach for neuromorphic and on-chip learning.

Emerging Technologies.title: Intelligence as a Founding Principle: The O-RAN Architecture for Artificial Intelligence and Its Reference Implementations
Emerging Technologies.summary: Since its inception, O-RAN has established openness and intelligence as founding principles of the RAN, transforming closed base stations into disaggregated, multi-vendor systems with a hierarchical RIC. This article traces AI/ML in O-RAN through open specifications and reference implementations to 6G design. We examine how open fronthaul, RIC interfaces, cloud orchestration, and AAL profiles support control loops across multiple timescales, model management, and hardware acceleration. Commercial deployments and OTIC testing demonstrate multi-vendor interoperability. Open-source stacks and testbeds support pre-standardization studies of in-node dApps. Within this architecture, GPU-based AI-RAN platforms realize the inline High-PHY split on shared RAN and AI compute, providing one reference implementation path for the O-RAN AAL alongside other implementations on heterogeneous hardware. Vector instruction sets and analog in-memory computing offer longer-term options for improving energy efficiency. For 6G, extending intelligence to time-critical radio processing and mobile agent services calls for deadline-bounded third-party inference, energy-efficient RAN/Edge-AI silicon co-design, and agent session continuity across handovers. We propose a RAC that coordinates agents across tiers through local shells and a shared exposure gateway, with in-node operating bounds delivered asynchronously. We also propose Recursive Standardization, in which results from federated open labs inform candidate 6G requirements and standards review guides the next round of implementation and testing.
Emerging Technologies.comment: 17 pages, 9 figures, 4 tables. Updated author list

Emerging Technologies.title: Sufficient quantum provenance: retained fields and certified recording precision
Emerging Technologies.summary: Quantum executions that share a provenance record can still produce different output distributions. We determine which execution details a record must retain, and at what precision, to guarantee agreement within a declared Hellinger tolerance. Under a specified channel model, a certificate combining independent stochastic mechanisms and coherent rotation differences fixes the recording precision without output simulation or explicit dependence on register dimension. For four-qubit quantum approximate optimization at depth one, a 13-bit comparison record suffices at tolerance 0.05 over a declared continuous noise range, uniformly in programmed angles for each fixed task, against 19 bits for a gate-by-gate sum over the same bin family. Pairwise separation constraints characterize sufficient field sets on finite context classes and expose omissions that pass individually but fail jointly. Separately, six-qubit measurements on an IBM Heron processor show, over six tested contexts, that raw outputs need a two-label record, supplied by qubit layout, whereas outputs after a fixed application decoder need no additional context bits, at tolerance 0.15 with 97% simultaneous confidence under stationary, independent shots. Execution records can thereby be designed to carry checkable agreement guarantees.
Emerging Technologies.comment: v4: Clarified hardware interpretation; added an IQM Garnet scout pointer and citation. Revised abstract and presentation. Scientific results unchanged

Emerging Technologies.title: Hardware-Aware Model Inversion in Memristive Spiking Neural Networks
Emerging Technologies.summary:
Hardware-accelerated spiking neural networks (SNNs) implemented on memristive crossbar arrays offer significant gains in energy efficiency, while device variability and analog noise are sometimes assumed to hinder information extraction. However, whether these hardware effects improve, preserve, or degrade privacy after deployment remains largely unexplored. Therefore, we ask whether model-inversion leakage characterized on an SNN remains representative after the same model is mapped to a non-ideal memristive substrate, and how hardware non-idealities and reliability faults affecting synapses, neuron thresholds, and spike processing reshape that leakage. To study this problem, we introduce Spiking Domain Model Inversion (SDMI), an inversion method that combines Expectation over Transformation (EOT) with surrogate gradients to optimize inputs through stochastic analog behavior and non-differentiable spiking dynamics. We use SDMI consistently across the SNN model, its memristive SNN, and the same memristive SNN under additional hardware perturbations.
  Across four datasets, reconstruction leakage does not vary monotonically with model accuracy or hardware variability. At comparable accuracy levels, neuron-threshold perturbations increase reconstruction fidelity, measured by SSIM, by up to 51.8%, whereas spike-level perturbations primarily degrade utility without consistently improving reconstruction. Weight noise, in contrast, reduces leakage under the same inversion procedure. These results show that hardware variability is not inherently privacy-preserving: model inversion leakage in memristive SNNs depends on the hardware state and cannot be inferred from model accuracy alone.
Emerging Technologies.comment: 15 pages, 8 figures

Emerging Technologies.title: Full-chip constrained quantum annealing via self-calibrating spin-susceptibility control
Emerging Technologies.summary: Discrete optimization in finance, power grids, and logistics requires minimizing Ising Hamiltonians under coupled linear constraints. However, quadratic-penalty formulations superimpose dense cliques that exhaust the minor-embedding capacity of sparse superconducting processors at 128-176 spins, and first-order dual subgradient schemes diverge or stall under constraint coupling. Accordingly, this study proposes a hardware-native quantum-classical closed-loop primal-dual workflow, designated as Self-Calibrating Quantum Susceptibility Quasi-Newton (SelfCal-QSQN), in which linear constraints are encoded in longitudinal fields with zero auxiliary quadratic penalty couplings and dual curvature is reconstructed from single-shot spin-fluctuation covariances. This workflow requires no slack qubits or perturbation queries. Evaluated over 891 runs on D-Wave Advantage (5,612 qubits) and Advantage2 (4,560 qubits), SelfCal-QSQN drives the pre-polish trajectory-minimum raw QPU sample violation to $0.108 \pm 0.017$ at 4,560 qubits (83.3% exact feasibility after a deterministic 1-bit polish with best-incumbent tracking, reaching 47.3% of the continuous linear-programming relaxation bound), reduces high-constraint error by 6.1- to 20.1-fold over K-scaled first-order updates, attains 5.35-fold deeper feasible energies than linear programming with the identical 1-bit polish within a 4.10-s compute-only budget at 256 spins, and achieves 95.0%-96.7% feasibility on non-native and inequality benchmarks. Moreover, the workflow is robust toward shot noise and freeze-out drift.
Emerging Technologies.comment: 14 pages, 5 figures, 3 tables. v2: expanded classical baseline comparisons, runtime breakdowns, and full-chip LP lower-bound verification

Emerging Technologies.title: Designing DNA-Based Molecular Communication Networks Using Experimentally Validated Components
Emerging Technologies.summary: Molecular communication is a novel paradigm for the design of nanonetworks. It uses molecules as information carriers and enables communication between nanodevices. DNA-based molecular communication is a promising approach for medical applications, such as in-body networks for diagnostics and drug delivery. However, the transition from theoretical models to practical experiments is still in its early stages. This survey reviews experimentally validated DNA-tiles, nanocarriers, and biosensors relevant to implementing DNA-tile-based nanonetworks in vitro. We evaluate these components based on their stability, compatibility, cost-effectiveness, and overall suitability for wet-lab implementation. Based on this analysis, we identify promising component combinations and derive a blueprint for a minimal proof-of-concept experiment. The resulting framework provides researchers with both a structured overview of experimentally relevant design choices and a concrete starting point for implementing and validating DNA-based nanonetworks in the wet lab.
Emerging Technologies.comment: 31 pages, 7 Tables, 8 Figures, under submission for Nano Communication Networks

Emerging Technologies.title: Coefficient-Range Mitigation on an 8-Bit Coherent Ising Machine
Emerging Technologies.summary: Mapping optimization problems to the restricted coefficient range of an 8-bit CIM can distort their encoded energy landscapes. We investigate whether three coefficient-range mitigation techniques previously studied for quantum annealing---interaction extension, bounded-coefficient encoding, and augmented Lagrangian penalties---improve end-to-end optimization outcomes. Experiments on weighted Max-Cut, multidimensional knapsack, and quadratic assignment show that the benefits are selective. At a fixed number of CIM calls, intermediate interaction extension yields higher mean best Max-Cut objectives, whereas aggressive extension degrades performance. Bounded-coefficient encoding improves the mean best feasible profit on one knapsack instance but not the other. Augmented Lagrangian perturbations increase feasibility when unshifted constraint penalties are too weak, but do not outperform the best unshifted penalty setting. Overall, coefficient-range mitigation is most effective when its strength is tuned to the problem and encoding, with aggressive mitigation potentially offsetting its benefits.
Emerging Technologies.comment: 42 pages, 12 figures, 2 tables

Emerging Technologies.title: From Entropy Source to Stochastic Bit-Stream: Low-Cost Converters for True-Random Stochastic Computing
Emerging Technologies.summary: Stochastic computing (SC) encodes values as the probability of ones in random bit-streams, which allows arithmetic circuits with very low area and power and a natural tolerance to faults. The accuracy and security of an SC system depend on the quality of those bit-streams. Conventional generators build them from pseudo-random or quasi-random sequences, which are predictable, periodic, and correlated across streams drawn from the same generator. This work proposes three methods for converting the unbiased outputs of a true random number generator (TRNG) into stochastic bit-streams (SBS) with arbitrary target probabilities: a block extraction and comparison circuit, a counter-logic circuit, and a cascaded majority-logic pipeline. All three accept bits from any true- random source and are built from standard CMOS logic. They reach the accuracy of a software random generator for both independent and correlated stream generation, and they support the common SC arithmetic operations with error that falls with stream length at the same rate. Hardware synthesis results show that the converters offer favorable area, energy, and area-delay trade-offs relative to pseudo- and quasi-random baselines. Under injected soft errors, block extraction degrades no faster than the best deterministic baseline. By bridging raw entropy sources and application-ready bit-streams, this work makes true-random SC practical on standard CMOS.

Emerging Technologies.title: STAR: Astrocyte-Inspired State-Augmented Repair for Supervised Memristive AI Hardware Systems
Emerging Technologies.summary: Memristive crossbar arrays have emerged as a promising platform for efficient on-chip learning, enabling local learning rules such as Equilibrium Propagation (EP) to be realized without the memory and data-movement overhead of conventional backpropagation. However, as these devices age, permanent stuck-at (SA) faults accumulate at individual synaptic elements, irreversibly corrupting the stored weights and degrading model performance in ways that in-situ retraining alone cannot address. Existing mitigation strategies either rely on hardware redundancy at significant area and power cost, or require explicit fault localization that is impractical to perform continuously on-chip. This paper adopts a brain-inspired fault recovery route motivated by self-repair functionalities enabled by astrocytes -- a type of glial cell. We couple a computational neuroscience study of astrocytic neuromodulation under permanent synaptic faults with an algorithmic recovery mechanism for faulted crossbar-mapped networks. Our computational neuroscience study characterizes how astrocytes modulate surviving synapses in a bidirectional EP-specific network setting under both SA-0 and high-conductance stuck-at fault conditions, revealing that recovery operates at the neural population level. Motivated by this observation, we propose a retraining-based repair mechanism that augments EP with an additional repair nudge anchored to pre-fault activation targets of the healthy network, encouraging surviving weights to collectively reconstruct pre-fault internal representations without any information of which weights are faulty. To our knowledge, STAR is the first astrocyte-inspired repair mechanism to operate under a supervised local learning rule and to scale to convolutional networks.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: A Perturbation-Driven Framework for Sensitivity Analysis of Dimensionality Reduction
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Low-dimensional representations produced by dimensionality reduction (DR) are commonly evaluated using distortion measures such as trustworthiness and continuity. In this paper, we study the sensitivity of DR methods to plausible input variations by quantifying changes in structural preservation and visually diagnosing how these changes manifest in the resulting representations. This perspective reflects the fact that real-world datasets are finite, noisy samples of an underlying distribution, and DR should not produce substantially different structures under small data changes. We introduce a model-agnostic, perturbation-driven sensitivity evaluation framework that treats perturbations as controlled probes of plausible data variation. Across multiple perturbation families and strength levels, we repeatedly perturb the input, apply a DR method, and evaluate the resulting low-dimensional representations using a set of distortion measures to derive sensitivity profiles for each DR method. We demonstrate the utility of our framework through case studies on DR method comparison, behavior analysis, and robustness improvement. We find that methods performing well according to conventional distortion measures (e.g., t-SNE) can still exhibit substantial sensitivity, leading to instability in visually salient structures such as trajectories and clusters, while certain methods (e.g., multidimensional scaling) may exhibit improved structural preservation under specific perturbations. These results highlight the importance of sensitivity analysis for comparing DR methods, diagnosing perturbation-sensitive visual patterns, and guiding the development of more robust DR methods toward trustworthy visual analytics.
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: This manuscript is currently under review

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Supporting Researcher Control in AI-Assisted Social Media Analysis: A Mixed-Methods Study of AI4OSN
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: High-quality annotated datasets are critical for advancing computational social science (CSS) research, yet collecting, curating, and analyzing large-scale data from dynamic sources, such as online social networks (OSNs), remain persistent bottlenecks. Researchers must also translate substantive questions into queries, relevance criteria, and defensible interpretations. Large language models (LLMs) can assist but can also obscure judgments, potentially reducing researcher oversight and critical evaluation. We present AI4OSN, a mixed-initiative platform that keeps researchers in control of data collection, relevance labeling, and sensemaking while making AI assistance available as an inspectable advisory resource. In a systematic user study (N=18) using X/Twitter data, participants reported above-benchmark perceived usability (mean SUS score of 79.7), increased self-reported confidence in data collection, labeling, and analysis. Notably, novice participants showed descriptively greater alignment and higher reported agreement with AI output than experienced participants, underscoring the need to support differentiated verification practices across expertise levels. These group comparisons are exploratory and motivate controlled follow-up studies of how AI assistance shapes confidence and annotation quality. Overall, this work contributes both a human-centered system for social data analysis and empirical insights into how AI-assisted interfaces shape researcher behavior, trust, and decision-making. Our findings highlight design opportunities and tensions in building accessible, transparent, and agentic AI systems for social media and web research.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: DevEx is for Humans, AX is for Agents: Measuring Context Health in Agentic Software Work
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Coding agents succeed or fail in the context humans give them, yet most evaluations measure only output. Drawing on developer experience research, we introduce Agent Experience (AX), an instrument that scores session transcripts on four dimensions of the CAFE(S) framework: Clarity, Actionability, Fidelity, and Efficiency; Security, a gate rather than a friction dimension, is out of scope. A rubric-guided language model rates each dimension from 1 to 5 and explains what the human could have provided. We report on three studies that tested this model. In the Stack Overflow Developer Survey, respondents reporting context problems were less likely to rate AI as very useful in all seven activities examined (12-28%). Across 882 rated agentic sessions from a pilot sample of 1,000, Actionability received the lowest ratings (59.6% of ratings at or below 3, versus 26.6% for Fidelity), and ratings were lower in longer sessions. One researcher's unblinded review of 15 randomly sampled sessions found all scores reasonable and explanations supported. In a controlled scenario, we injected context defects into one data-analysis task and ran it twelve times. Every defect condition used more tokens than the clean baseline (mean +91%), and five evaluator models flagged 50-85% of targeted dimensions and 14-36% of non-targeted dimensions. Fidelity defects were detected most consistently and Actionability defects least. Because interventions were imperfectly isolated, these results are exploratory. AX gives teams structured, actionable evidence about context-related friction that complements output and outcome measures.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: BLADE: Better Language Answers through Dialogue and Explanations
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Large language model (LLM)-based educational assistants often provide direct answers offering little incentive for students to explore or engage with course materials. We present BLADE (Better Language Answers through Dialogue and Explanations), a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) based conversational assistant grounded in course-specific content that guides students toward relevant materials through citation-grounded dialogue rather than delivering unsourced solutions. We evaluate BLADE in an advanced undergraduate NLP course with extensive instructional resources, in which locating and synthesizing relevant material is a central challenge. During quizzes, students are assigned to one of three conditions: BLADE only, direct course materials only, or both; we measure performance and resource usage. Results show that students consistently select BLADE over direct materials when both are available, and that quiz performance is highest when students use BLADE alone. In contrast, simultaneous use of both resources is associated with significantly lower performance. No statistically significant difference in quiz performance occurred between assigned resource conditions. These findings show the potential of RAG-based assistants as a citation-grounded interface for applying course content under open-book exam-like conditions, while suggesting that adding direct-material access does not necessarily improve in-task performance.
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: To appear, European Chapter of the Association for Computational Linguistics (EACL), Athens, Greece, March, 2027

Human-Computer Interaction.title: BuildOcc: A Large Language Model Occupant Agent Platform for Building Energy Research
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Occupants are a primary source of uncertainty in building energy consumption and management, yet existing occupant behavior models cannot capture adaptive and reasoning responses considering the occupant's personal history, current context, and the type of energy signal being delivered. This study presents BuildOcc, an open-source Python platform that grounds large language model agents in the American Time Use Survey (ATUS), a nationally representative diary dataset covering 16,684 respondents. Through BuildOcc, each simulated occupant agent can be instantiated with a demographic persona drawn from ATUS population statistics, a memory stream that accumulates and reflects on timestep-level observations, and an activity scheduler that samples empirically from ATUS time-at-activity distributions. The platform exposes a three-layer interface - Python library, REST API, and Model Context Protocol server - so that any building energy tool (EnergyPlus, Home Assistant) can integrate behavioral intelligence without bespoke coupling code. A plugin registry lets the community add new occupant strata, custom schedulers, and alternative memory backends as separate installable packages. Two validation tiers show that ATUS-grounded sampling reproduces empirically calibrated activity distributions and that demographic priors propagate into persona-consistent agent reasoning across timesteps, establishing internal consistency across strata. BuildOcc provides the building energy community with a reusable, openly available implementation of the occupant behavioral layer. BuildOcc is openly released at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21192895 under the Apache License 2.0 and installable via pip install buildocc.
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: Accepted manuscript. Published in SoftwareX. 19 pages, 4 figures, 11 tables, 3 appendices. Software: https://github.com/humanbuildingsynergy/BuildOcc. Re-set in the HUBS Lab paper layout (HUBS Lab Paper No. 2026-004); content unchanged

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Who Attributes a Mind to Whom? Mutual Theory of Mind in Simulated User-Assistant Conversation
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: When users assume that an AI chatbot has mental states, they are more likely to develop over-reliance, emotional dependence, and in extreme cases, psychological harm or self-harm. However, how these mind attributions arise in conversations and how human or AI factors influence this is still unknown. We study how users attribute minds using a minimal framework: a simulated user with different characteristics chats with assistants that differ in social style and memory. We also introduce a message-level measure of who attributes a mind to whom in four directions, checked with trained coders and applied by a fine-tuned encoder that reproduces an LLM judge. Our results show that, on average, nine out of thirteen characteristics raised simulated users' attribution to the assistant. We found that relational needs such as attachment anxiety raised it as theory predicts, some general personality traits raised it as well, and AI-specific characteristics the least. By contrast, the assistant's social style barely changed simulated users' mind attribution. Instead, sycophantic instructions raised the assistant's attribution to itself. Memory raised users' attribution only with some user models. The model playing the user changed overall attribution and the effects of characteristics, style, and memory. Our framework measures how persona descriptions affect mind attribution in simulation. It gives concrete hypotheses for human studies and shows the need for more consistent user simulators.
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: 32 pages, 11 figures

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Temporal Conditioning for Human Behavioral Cloning in Chess
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Behavioral cloning models in chess typically predict human moves from board states while ignoring temporal inputs such as the remaining clock. However, time pressure is a major determinant of human decision-making quality, and temporal state is a missing dimension of human behavioral modeling. This paper introduces a time-aware transformer that extends a Chessformer-style architecture with learned temporal conditioning tokens encoding player clock state, time control, and recent tempo, together with behavioral heads for thinking time and resignation. The model is trained on large-scale online chess data and evaluated against time-agnostic baselines and the state of the art. Results show that temporal conditioning yields modest overall accuracy improvements but substantially stronger gains under time pressure. Beyond move choice, it also produces more accurate thinking-time and resignation predictions. More importantly, the model better matches human move-quality degradation in critical time regimes, reducing the systematic over-strength observed in time-agnostic behavioral cloning models. These results suggest that temporal state is a previously underutilized but important signal for human behavioral cloning in chess.
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: 6 pages, 2 figures, 3 tables. Accepted manuscript of the paper published at the 2026 IEEE Gaming, Entertainment, and Media Conference (GEM). Code: https://github.com/Prof-it/temporal-chess-model; weights: https://huggingface.co/holymolyyy/temporal-chess-model

Human-Computer Interaction.title: The Radar-based Activities of Daily Living (R-ADL) Dataset
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Monitoring Activities of Daily Living (ADLs) supports safety and well-being for people living at home, especially older adults, and radar sensing is gaining increasing attention in the field of activity recognition for its ability to ensure privacy in the home while also surpassing technical limitations of other sensing modalities. However, radar-based activity recognition remains constrained by the limited availability of large-scale datasets. We introduce the Radar-based Activities of Daily Living (R-ADL) dataset to addresses the gaps identified in existing work: 1) it expands the scale of available data by providing over eight hours of annotated recordings in which a person performs eight distinct activities; 2) it overcomes room configuration limitations by recording from five different locations in a two-bedroom, two-bathroom apartment; and 3) it extends beyond primitive actions to focus on high-level ADLs. In addition to the dataset, this paper introduces practical guidance for future ADL dataset construction. We conducted a detailed analysis of how ADLs are prioritized across academic research, health survey tools, and clinical trials to identify clinically significant ADLs. Furthermore, we provide our experimental design, data collection and annotation strategies, post-processing pipeline for forming the R-ADL dataset from raw data, and baseline results on standard machine learning architectures. The R-ADL dataset serves as a valuable resource for advancing ADL recognition systems as we continue building larger and more diverse datasets.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: One Style Fits All? Cultural Values Embedded in Conversational AI via a People-Pleasing Lens
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Conversational AI systems trained on large-scale web corpora inevitably encode the cultural values and interactional norms embedded in their training data, yet our understanding of how deployed LLMs reflect or reinforce culture-specific social expectations remains limited. This study examined how supportive versus challenging chatbot interaction styles shape user experience and continuance intention, and whether people-pleasing tendency (PPT) moderates these effects across cultures. Taiwanese (N = 49) and Korean (N = 52) participants completed a collaborative tourism-planning task. Results showed that: (1) supportive chatbots consistently led to higher continuance intention, satisfaction, and trust; (2) PPT did not moderate these effects; and (3) cultural variation emerged only in perceived threat, where higher PPT was associated with greater baseline threat in the Taiwanese but not the Korean sample. These findings reveal how a general-purpose LLM style may differentially activate culturally situated social scripts, raising implications for culturally inclusive conversational AI design.
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: Accepted to the 4th Workshop on Cross-Cultural Considerations in NLP (C3NLP) at ACL 2026

Human-Computer Interaction.title: AI, Bias, and Inclusion: A Two-Phase Mixed-Methods Study of Gender Bias, Awareness, and Trust in Artificial Intelligence
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Artificial Intelligence (AI) systems are widespread across fields such as healthcare, finance, employment, and criminal justice, with a substantial impact on the lives of individuals and society. However, it has been established that AI systems perpetuate existing social inequalities, particularly through biases that are not easily discernible. Such biases are embedded in the technical and social structures of artificial intelligence systems, making them difficult to detect. These biases challenge the concept of Equity, Diversity, and Inclusion (EDI), which recognizes diversity as the acknowledgment of individual differences, equity as fairness and equal access, and inclusion as the value placed on all participants. This study argues that fairness in artificial intelligence systems cannot be achieved by focusing solely on their technical aspects, necessitating a holistic approach. This study employs a two-phase mixed-methods design. Phase 1 applies computational content analysis to 360 occupational narratives generated by ChatGPT across four countries (Canada, Germany, India, and Bangladesh) using gender-neutral prompts to examine whether professions are predominantly associated with one gender and whether these patterns remain consistent across regions. Phase 2 examines the extent to which students recognize potential bias in AI, their trust in AI for consequential decision-making, and how these perceptions relate to themes in EDI and AI ethics scholarship. By combining output-level bias analysis with user perception data, this study identifies the empirical foundations necessary for future EDI-AI co-design frameworks, outlining the sociotechnical dimensions that such frameworks must address to be effective.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Social sycophancy differs across access modes of large language models
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Large language models (LLMs) can display sycophancy, a tendency to excessively praise, agree with, or validate a user. Existing studies have tested LLMs for sycophancy primarily through application programming interfaces (APIs) rather than the consumer user interfaces (UIs) through which the public commonly interacts with LLMs. Access mode (API vs. UI) may affect observed sycophancy rates. However, it remains unknown to what extent prominent models show API-UI differences in social sycophancy, which includes behaviors potentially more likely in UIs (e.g., softening warranted criticism). We tested ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, and DeepSeek through both APIs and UIs on four dimensions of social sycophancy. Across models, UI access was generally associated with greater social sycophancy, with odds ratios up to 7.56 (95% CI [6.22, 9.20]). However, UI-API differences varied significantly across models for all sycophancy dimensions, including a pronounced reversal for DeepSeek moral sycophancy (43% UI vs. 82.3% API). Overall, our results suggest that API-based LLM evaluations may underestimate the prevalence of sycophancy in corresponding consumer-facing systems, making access conditions consequential for the external validity of LLM evaluation. To facilitate research on access-mode effects, we release 57,000 model responses and SycoUI, a browser-automation pipeline for standardized cross-interface LLM evaluation.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Found in Translation: Five Entry Points to Translate AI Literacy Frameworks in the Design of Educational Materials
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: While there is a plethora of AI literacy and informatics frameworks, in practice it is difficult for designers of educational materials and educators to decide where to start and how to use these in learning activities. At the same time, recent reviews show that despite the fact that most frameworks emphasize the socio-technical nature of AI, in practice interventions tend to center on preparing learners to use AI. To address these issues, we ask: How can multiple stakeholders negotiate and translate AI literacy framework ideas into common language that can be used to design introductory learning materials for primary school children, teachers and parents? We introduce five entry points into AI literacy that were developed from a computational empowerment perspective through a participatory design process involving primary teacher educators, curricular designers, media producers, and researchers. We present three vignettes that illustrate how the entry points were generative in the design of learning activities, learning tools and media content for school and home. This paper contributes an account of the participatory development of five entry points that serve as generative and negotiable resources for designing educational materials.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Protective-Design Pre-Emption in Child-Facing Generative AI
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Generative AI is adopted rapidly by children, yet unrestricted general-audience models dominate their usage. This paper presents the open problem of \emph{protective-design pre-emption}: Delayed market introduction, low access thresholds, utility gaps, habituation, and peer adoption foster unrestricted AI model lock-in, leading children to bypass child-centric platforms. With first signs of lower adoption of child-centric platforms, we argue that this shift may reinforce existing AI risks such as exposing children to deepened parasocial dependencies, skill erosion, and misinformation. To address this problem, we propose interdisciplinary research directions to quantify pre-emption, understand its socio-technical drivers, and develop interventions ensuring child-centric AI is actively adopted, not just available.
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: Accepted for NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on Child Safety in AI

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Blaming the Machine, Billing the Victim? How Mock Jurors Reassign Fault from Generative AI Systems and Respond to Liability Cliffs in Tort
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Generative AI complicates tort liability attribution when people blame a generative AI system that cannot itself bear legally relevant fault. We investigate where this blame goes when fault must be allocated among legal persons, and whether American discontinuous apportionment doctrines influence mock jurors' factual findings of fault. Such doctrines include Contributory negligence, Joint and several liability, and their 50% or 51% variations, all of which have a fault-percentage threshold or a "cliff" where the victim-entitled compensation (or a defendant's liability) jumps to zero (or to all compensatory damages). Our pre-registered human subjects experiment (N=199 Prolific participants) shows that as many U.S. mock jurors (36%) blame the AI system itself, the AI blame often "leaks" to the victim or to the AI user (in 27% to 73% of our AI-blaming records, depending on how leakage is calculated). Although mock jurors rarely change their blame assignment from one side of the liability cliff to the other, these participants do not acknowledge the legal doctrine or its monetary consequence when explaining their changes. Our empirical results illustrate how a narrow doctrinal exception in tort, carving out "joint and several liability" for those deploying or using Generative AI without reasonable care, might mitigate the impact of blame leakage on victims' deserved compensation without introducing significant jury nullification risks.
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: Under review at an AI Governance conference

Human-Computer Interaction.title: MyMuse: A Personal Museum for Post-Visit Inquiry and Reflection
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Artwork photographs may preserve what visitors saw without preserving why it mattered. Revisiting them can involve recalling earlier responses and developing new questions and interpretations as knowledge and personal experiences change. Yet recurring interests may remain difficult to recognize across individual exchanges. Informed by a formative study with ten visitors, we present MyMuse, a post-visit system that connects inquiry about individual artworks with reflection across visitors' accumulated records. In its Personal Museum, visitors revisit artworks, ask questions, and record interpretations that inform subsequent system responses. Its interactive Narrative Report reorganizes the same records across artworks through four interpretive lenses. In two within-subject studies with 16 participants, direct comparisons favored MyMuse for vivid revisitation. The report received higher ratings for recurring-interest awareness, cross-artwork connections, and unexpected discovery than a per-artwork presentation of the same records. These findings suggest that examining accumulated records can support reflection on recurring interests and relationships among visitors' responses across artworks.
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: 27 pages (18 pages of main text and references, 9 pages of appendices), 8 figures

Human-Computer Interaction.title: CHORAL: A Multi-Agent Scaffold for Longitudinal Prognostic Reasoning from Patient-Generated Health Data
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Longitudinal patient-generated health data can inform prognostic reasoning about how patients' conditions may evolve between follow-up visits. Existing approaches summarize trajectories or predict symptom states, but provide limited support for examining how heterogeneous evidence informs prognosis. We present CHORAL, a multi-agent scaffold that forms domain-specific appraisals before cross-domain synthesis and review, preserving evidence and revisions. Informed by a formative study with 12 psychiatrists, we evaluated CHORAL quantitatively and with 22 clinicians. CHORAL achieved balanced accuracy comparable to persistence (0.673 vs. 0.672), while detecting 40% of LOW-to-HIGH deterioration cases missed by persistence. Versus a single-agent baseline, it improved balanced accuracy from 0.639 to 0.673 and evidence coverage from 70.1% to 89.2%. Clinicians rated CHORAL significantly higher for evidence appraisal, alternative interpretations, grounds for challenge, and distinguishing what to rely on from what required verification. These findings show how multi-agent deliberation can support review by exposing alternative interpretations and grounds for verification.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Calm Agent: Reframing Agent Interaction around Intermittent Human Attention
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: AI agents can carry out auxiliary tasks while users focus on other work. Yet users still need to understand task state, make changes, and respond when help is required. We argue that agents for ongoing auxiliary tasks should be designed around intermittent human attention: tasks should continue between interactions, and users should be able to return with little effort to understand and control them. We develop this position as Calm Agent. It connects three on-demand interaction modes: Delegate, Adjust, and Check, through a persistent task representation. Generative interaction provides controls and feedback suited to open-ended goals, while existing controls support routine actions. We illustrate these principles with Orvlet, a desktop prototype for background execution and compact task interfaces.
