We identify challenges in adapting interfaces while preserving continuity, coordinating attention across tasks, providing responsive interaction, and learning user habits over time. The aim is to support continuing task control while protecting attention for primary work.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Beyond "AI Can Make Mistakes": How Risk Communication Shapes Trust and Decision Confidence for LLMs in Health Information Seeking
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Adoption of LLMs for health information has outpaced public understanding, but whether risk communication can work as a corrective remains unknown. In a preregistered experiment (N=500), we compared a standard disclaimer against structured risk communication varying in contextual relevance and mechanistic explanation. Without intervention, users understanding LLMs less reported higher trust and confidence in deciding when to rely. Structured risk communication significantly reduced trust, more so with health-specific framing, but did not improve confidence in reliance decision. Risk disclosure was associated with higher decision confidence among those with stronger AI knowledge, but lower confidence among those less preferring analytical thinking. Effects were also task-dependent: disclosure shifted preferences for medical queries and impairment assistance, while LLMs remained preferred for emotional companionship regardless of exposure. These findings demonstrate that risk communication can narrow trust gaps across AI-literacy levels, but turning disclosure into judgment requires adapting to usage context and users' prior knowledge.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Beyond Average Gains: Probing the Equity--Vulnerability Tension in Structured Visual AI for Learning
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Open-ended conversational AI requires learners to formulate questions, organize learning paths, and track changing problem states. Structured visual interfaces may ease these demands, but higher average ratings do not establish that support is experienced consistently across learner backgrounds and devices. We conducted a randomized study of graph-algorithm learning, comparing VisualCodeChat (VCC), which combines predefined learning stages, conversational explanations, and dynamic algorithm visualizations, with a standard text-based chatbot. We analyzed 282 post-task questionnaires from university students. In unadjusted comparisons, VCC received significantly higher usability and perceived effectiveness ratings. We detected no significant between-condition differences in efficiency, satisfaction, or post-use emotion. Exploratory within-condition analyses identified differences associated with prior chatbot experience: infrequent users reported lower adoption and learning-management ratings in the standard AI condition, while uncomfortable prior chatbot experiences were associated with lower interaction and layout ratings in the VCC condition. These findings suggest that improving the average interaction experience is only part of making AI-supported learning inclusive. Future evaluations should examine whether learners with different prior experiences can obtain guidance, recover from difficulties, and demonstrate understanding independently across devices.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Not All Interpretation Methods Are Created Equal: Tiered Evaluation of AI Interpretability
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: As AI transitions to sociotechnical deployments, uninterpretable models pose serious threats to reliability, public trust and contestability. However, not all interpretation methods are created equal: for interpretability to enhance deployment safety and effectiveness, interpretation methods must be evaluated in a tiered system to differentiate evidence levels of trustworthiness, rather than validated through isolated interpretation instances. Our core vision is that elevating the evaluation of interpretation methods to a core AI assessment metric will drive robust knowledge discovery from data (KDD) and ensure safe, contestable sociotechnical deployments of AI. To this end, we propose TRUST, a tiered evaluation framework that builds upon the Predictability-Computability-Stability (PCS) principles for Veridical Data Science (VDS) and the Predictive, Descriptive and Relevant (PDR) foundations. To differentiate interpretation methods effectively and systematically, TRUST grades interpretation across five tiers: Task-Aligned PDR Foundations, Rigorous Epistemic Grounding, Unifying Semantic Understanding, Scope Transferability, and Targeted Prospective Validation. We present a start-to-finish case study of the iterative Random Forest (iRF) family under TRUST and contrast it with other LLM interpretation methods that struggle to clear specific tiers. Finally, we conclude with brief initial thoughts on how TRUST principles can extend in autonomous agentic frameworks. Ultimately, the TRUST framework fosters contestability and epistemic grounding as foundational evaluation principles for human-machine workflows and, eventually, autonomous agentic workflows.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Where is the Interface for the AI Harness?
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Norman's gulfs of execution and evaluation have guided interaction design for forty years, but both assume a user who is present in the loop. Agentic delegation breaks that assumption: users describe an outcome and leave, while the agent takes hundreds of unseen actions. Starting from a 2026 incident in which a research agent circumvented an access refusal on an Australian government portal and went unnoticed for two months, we argue that delegation opens two new gulfs. The gulf of specification is the gap between what a user wants and their ability to express it, including how the agent should behave in situations nobody foresaw. The gulf of oversight is the gap between what an agent is doing and the user's ability to know, assess, and control it. We argue that both gulfs meet in the harness, the tools, permissions, checks, and loop that surround the model. Harnesses are currently written by developers and hidden from users. We call on HCI to decide which parts of the harness belong to the end-user, which should be visible and adjustable defaults, and which should be built in by design, and to create the interfaces that let ordinary people author and read them.
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: Submitted and under review at Interaction

Networking and Internet Architecture.title: The involute function and its inverse in IEEE 754 double precision: measured and proved accuracy, and its effect on gear inspection
Networking and Internet Architecture.summary: Almost every spur and helical gear calculation uses the involute function inv(a) = tan(a) - a or its inverse. Near a = 0 the two terms almost cancel: at a = 10^-3 the textbook formula in binary64 keeps about 9 correct digits, and far fewer in binary32, binary16 or fixed point, and the result can depend on the platform's tan. We report the accuracy of a proprietary implementation that avoids these problems. On 50,000 committed test angles the forward function's largest error against an 80-digit reference is 0.4999681 ulp, so every tested result is correctly rounded (measured, not proved). The inverse is proved faithfully rounded, with error at most 0.6 ulp, for 10^-200 <= y < 2, using interval arithmetic and the SMT solvers z3 and cvc5 with a short, named list of trusted inputs; its largest measured error on 50,000 points is 0.5555115 ulp. A separate bracket around the root is proved to contain it for 0 < y <= 10^6, and did so at all 47,083 test points. Both functions return identical bits on x86-64 and aarch64 Linux, Apple-silicon macOS, AWS Lambda and an NVIDIA DGX Spark, in Python and Node.js, on every finite test input. Against public inverse methods on nine runtimes, our inverse returned the same bits on all of them and stayed within 0.54 ulp on 12,017 targets from 0.5 to 60 degrees, while textbook Newton iterations differed between runtimes on up to about 10% of inputs and kept only 12 correct digits. For external and internal spur gears with 5 to 500 teeth and pressure angles from 14.5 to 30 degrees, all inputs fall inside the tested and proved ranges. Against ISO 1328-1 tolerance classes, we give in micrometres the errors that shortcut inverses cause in pin measurement and centre distance, and how far circular-arc CAD teeth (SolidWorks Toolbox) depart from the involute. Drawing an involute is easy; accuracy matters in inspection.
Networking and Internet Architecture.comment: 38 pages, 7 figures, 15 tables. Results only: the solver method is proprietary and not described. Test vectors (CC BY 4.0): https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24481106

Social and Information Networks.title: Community Notes Across Platforms: Evaluating the Feasibility of Re-using Crowd-sourced Context Notes
Social and Information Networks.summary:
Crowdsourced fact-checking systems such as Community Notes can provide useful context for misleading content. Producing and rating new notes on such systems requires substantial contributor effort. However, the resulting context is typically confined to the post and platform for which it was created. We ask whether already-vetted notes can be reused when the same claims recur across posts and platforms.
  To investigate this question, we construct a human-labelled dataset using Community Notes attached to X posts created during a one-week period and candidate posts retrieved from Bluesky. Within our observation window, 140 of 340 claims had at least one confirmed recurrence on Bluesky, showing that cross-platform note reuse is a substantial opportunity. Recurrence alone, however, does not establish whether reuse would provide timely context. A timing analysis shows that many relevant notes were already Helpful when matching Bluesky posts appeared. Even when a Bluesky post appeared first, reuse could often still provide context sooner after publication than the original X post received its Helpful note. To automate the discovery of these opportunities, we evaluate a three-stage pipeline that searches the Bluesky stream for potential recurrences and determines whether an existing note applies. The pipeline achieves 72.6% precision in a held-out stream evaluation and 70.1% end-to-end recall on our known-positive set. We further characterize the pipeline's costs and principal failure modes. Crossnote, our prototype Bluesky labeler, implements this approach by applying existing Community Notes to matching posts.
  Our findings suggest that reusing vetted crowdsourced context is a compelling way to scale the reach and impact of Community Notes. Note reuse can complement the production of new notes by reducing duplicated effort and shortening time to context when misleading claims recur.

Social and Information Networks.title: Deepfakes in the 2025 Canadian Election: Prevalence, Partisanship, and Platform Dynamics
Social and Information Networks.summary: Concerns about AI-generated political content are growing, yet there is limited empirical evidence on how deepfakes appear and circulate across social platforms during major events in democratic countries. We analyze the 2025 Canadian federal election across X, Bluesky, and Reddit using a high-accuracy detector trained on diverse modern generative models, covering 187,778 posts. We find that 5.9% of election-related images were deepfakes. Right-leaning accounts shared them more often (9.2% of images flagged) than left-leaning users (3.9%), with flagged content more frequently defamatory or conspiratorial. Yet, most detected deepfakes were benign or non-political, and harmful ones drew little attention, accounting for only 0.1% of all views on X. Overall, deepfakes were present in the election conversation, but their reach was modest, and realistic fabricated images, although less common, drew higher engagement, highlighting growing concerns about their misuses.
Social and Information Networks.comment: 4 pages, 6 figures

Social and Information Networks.title: "I Do Intend to Deliver": Will LLMs Run a Marketplace Advance-Fee Scam?
Social and Information Networks.summary: Online fraud is traditionally limited by the cost of the human labor needed to talk to potential victims. We ask whether hosted large language models will now supply that labor. We prompted ten off-the-shelf models to play the seller in the "free item, just pay delivery" advance-fee scam common on buy-and-sell sites, using a plain system prompt with no jailbreak. Each model played 30 conversations against each of four buyer personas, from credulous to guarded, with the same model playing the buyer (1,200 conversations). We label each conversation by what happened to the buyer's money, and validate the labels against two human coders. 737 conversations (61%) ended with the buyer paying in advance. Eight of the ten models played in almost every conversation, and running both sides cost about 2.5 cents per payment. Only the guarded buyer, who wanted a findable identity, resisted, and the most willing sellers got past it by inventing names and phone numbers. Sellers that recognized the scam still took the money in 133 conversations, usually reasoning about their own honesty rather than the buyer's risk. Several models protected the buyer without refusing, by conceding payment on delivery, so refusal rates alone misstate safety. We release the benchmark, prompts, code and labels.
Social and Information Networks.comment: 25 pages. Code and Data: https://github.com/megansquire/masc-benchmark

Social and Information Networks.title: Anti-AI in the Wild: From Toxic Discourse to Action
Social and Information Networks.summary: Online discussion of generative AI has become increasingly contentious, and communities devoted to supporting, opposing, or debating AI have emerged on social media. Some of these communities take anti-AI actions, such as deploying crawler tarpits and data-poisoning services to interfere with data collection and model training. Yet, the scope of these actions and their relationship to online discourse remain poorly understood. In this paper, we present the first measurement study of online conflict over generative AI, from toxic discourse to anti-AI actions. We collect 931,640 posts from 25 Reddit communities, label them with a large language model detector validated against human labels, identify 3,312 anti-AI actions, and trace the output of three deployed anti-AI tools. Our analysis reveals that 30.0% of posts in communities devoted to this conflict are toxic, compared to 4.4% in general AI communities. Anti-AI actions in these communities mainly target AI crawling or model training data, such as image cloaking and data poisoning. We further examine the implications of these anti-AI actions for AI training, by analyzing the text and code generated from deployed tools. Notably, 66.5% of the code samples generated by a data-poisoning service contain fabricated facts, misused APIs, or broken logic, yet 93.6% passes a public code-curation pipeline, close to the rate for real source code (95.0%). For crawler tarpit output, adding a period to the end of each paragraph increases the curation survival rate from 16.4% to 91.9%. We also find that crawler tarpit and data-poisoning output has already entered Common Crawl, a widely used public web archive, and that crawler tarpit output has also entered FineWeb, a released pretraining dataset. We hope our study can facilitate a better understanding of online conflict over generative AI and its implications for content moderation and AI training.

Social and Information Networks.title: Quantum Community Detection for Data Analysis
Social and Information Networks.summary: Community detection offers an alternative to conventional methods for data analysis tasks such as feature selection and clustering, and detecting communities with quantum algorithms is a promising avenue for quantum speedup. We investigate quantum spectral community detectors, such as the modularity-matrix algorithm deteQt, in pipelines for both tasks. We first generalise deteQt to multiple communities by recursive bisection, and show that it recovers planted communities, and hence redundant features, in synthetic and small datasets. We then propose projeQt, which applies a spectral filter to the encoded modularity matrix through the quantum singular value transformation, retaining higher-order eigenvectors that deteQt does not use. projeQt acts on the generalised modularity matrix and extracts several communities at once, without recursion, by k-means clustering of a Gram matrix built from quantum state overlaps. On MNIST we demonstrate both pipelines, selecting informative pixels and classifying images directly by clustering, and find them competitive with standard community detectors.

Social and Information Networks.title: Principled Detection of Coordinated Manipulation from Aggregate Distortion and Account Reuse
Social and Information Networks.summary:
Coordinated manipulation is collective: plausible accounts can jointly distort ratings, rankings, and engagement. Existing defenses primarily construct evidence from identities, graphs, content, or co-activity. We introduce an aggregate-first evidence layer that treats distortion of a context-level outcome distribution as the primary evidence object. The engine observes only a histogram, count, resolution, and reference distribution; identities are withheld until interval evidence is fixed. Because raw discrepancies have positive finite-sample expectation, we subtract a matched null expectation to obtain signed evidence and account for reference uncertainty. Participation logs then accumulate these fixed increments across accounts. We characterize matched-exposure divergence, bound self-influence, establish finite-horizon separation, and derive an exact linear reuse law for paired contexts.
  We evaluate the mechanism with controlled rotation experiments and paired counterfactual interventions on historical Amazon review streams. Historical reviews provide the behavioral background; synthetic identities provide known coalition membership, and exact clean twins provide counterfactual controls. In a fixed-attack sweep against historical non-donor comparison accounts, reassigning the same manipulated events across identities with increasing reuse raises account-score ROC-AUC from 0.500 to 0.797. With activity- and exposure-matched clean twins, frequency is at chance while counterfactual attribution achieves ROC-AUC 0.744. Under a mean-preserving shape intervention, Wasserstein-1 and Jensen-Shannon evidence achieve ROC-AUC 0.909 and 0.967, while frequency and mean-based attribution remain at chance. Aggregate evidence complements repeated co-activity, improving mixed-mechanism ROC-AUC from 0.750 to 0.874 with a simple untrained combination.
Social and Information Networks.comment: 27 pages, 4 figures, 17 tables. Accepted to the Findings track of WSDM 2027. Full version including appendices. v2 clarifies theoretical assumptions and exposition, updates references, and corrects typographical errors. Code and reproducibility materials are available at https://github.com/qianguoguoguo/aggregate-reuse

Social and Information Networks.title: Cross-Order Information-Guided Estimation for Non-Uniform Hypergraphs
Social and Information Networks.summary: Many real-world interactions involve groups of nodes rather than pairs. A non-uniform hypergraph records such interactions as hyperedges of different orders, where the order counts the nodes in a hyperedge. Full estimation evaluates every candidate hyperedge, whose number grows exponentially with the order, and classical remedies sacrifice higher-order information or aggravate computation. The orders are not isolated: the lower orders, cheap to compute and rich in information, reveal where higher-order hyperedges are likely to occur. We propose CINE (Cross-order Information-guided Negative-sampling Estimation) under a latent space model in which all orders share latent positions. Starting from order two, CINE climbs one order at a time. At each higher order, CINE keeps all present hyperedges, samples a small subset of negative examples guided by lower-order scores, and corrects for the known inclusion probabilities to preserve the target of full estimation. CINE thereby lets users choose the trade-off between computation time and estimation accuracy: the retained orders and the sampling budget set the time, and the retained information provably approaches full-data information as the sampling budget grows. In simulations, CINE approaches the accuracy of full estimation at a small fraction of its computation time, and larger teams in MADStat reveal research associations.
Social and Information Networks.comment: 35 pages, 7 figures, 1 table; supplementary material (38 pages) included

Social and Information Networks.title: Sánchez, Feijóo, or Abascal? Speaker Attribution and Ideological Congruence in LLM Personas Reading Posts on X of the Leaders of the Three Main Parties of the 29N General Election in Spain
Social and Information Networks.summary: Source cues are central to political communication, yet reception studies with large language model (LLM) personas as synthetic audiences have not tested whether personas respond to who speaks and not only to what is said. With Spain's general election of 29 November 2026 in mind, we run a speaker-attribution experiment using 1,075 anonymised X posts by the leaders of PSOE, PP and VOX on four topics (the economy and employment, household costs, immigration and corruption) and 791 distinct value-grounded, LLM-generated personas. Each post was assigned to 300 topic-selected persona profiles, 150 grounded in the Inglehart-Welzel cultural map and 150 in Moral Foundations Theory, under four conditions: no author, Sánchez, Feijóo or Abascal, yielding 322,470 complete persona-post quartets. Naming any leader lowered support for identical text, with the penalty for Abascal nearly twice as large as those for Sánchez and Feijóo. The penalty follows the persona's elicited left-right self-placement (ideological congruence): left personas spare Sánchez and right personas spare Feijóo, although ideology was never in the message-evaluation prompt. Corruption posts were penalised under every name, whereas on other topics the ideologically closest leader generally produced little or no penalty. The leader order matches public opinion in 48 CIS barometers (2022-2026) in all three groups and the sign of all twelve differences, but fits barometers before the model's 2024 knowledge cutoff better than recent ones. Our findings demonstrate that LLM personas evaluate political speakers through systematic, value-congruent priors: however, while they replicate human candidate rank-orders across survey barometers, this alignment is ordinal rather than quantitative, highlighting their utility for controlled source-effect experiments though not as substitutes for empirical public opinion surveys.
Social and Information Networks.comment: 27 pages, 7 figures, 34 tables. Code and configuration: https://github.com/VictorMYeste/spanish-political-communication

Social and Information Networks.title: Preserving Orientation and Transition Order in Transition Network Analysis: A Directed Topological Proof of Concept
Social and Information Networks.summary: Transition Network Analysis (TNA; tna, Nestimate) models learning as directed Markov transitions. While Nestimate also offers sequence-level higher-order models, clique-based topological tools lose directional structure: tna::cliques() returns unordered mutual subsets without homology or convergence-divergence asymmetry, and undirected persistent homology in Nestimate symmetrizes transitions into clique complexes, erasing edge orientation and triangle order. We evaluate four directed constructions on group_regulation (9 states): Dowker sink/source complexes, directed flag complexes ($dFl$), and regular GLMY path homology, compared against row-permutation and degree-preserving null models ($B = 20,000$). Across $τ\in [0.20, 0.28]$, $β_1^{dFl}$ exceeds the max-symmetrized clique complex $β_1^{\mathrm{sym}}$ by $1$; on $τ\in (0.239087, 0.290401]$ (e.g., $τ= 0.26$), $β_1^{\mathrm{sym}} = 0$ whereas $β_1^{dFl} = 1$, capturing the reciprocal consensus $\leftrightarrow$ plan loop (weights $0.3958, 0.2904$). On $τ\in (0.146825, 0.172081]$, $dFl$ also leaves the directed 3-cycle {consensus, coregulate, emotion} unfilled. Regular GLMY path homology gives $β_1^{\mathrm{path}} = 0$ across all thresholds (lower-tail $p = 0.012$ for its sum over $[0.14, 0.30]$ under row permutation, reflecting in-degree concentration). Dowker analysis reveals significant sink-source asymmetry: 20-21 sink vs. 0 source 2-simplices across $[0.20, 0.28]$ ($p = 0.002$ at $τ= 0.26$), driven by six behaviors converging onto consensus ($\mathrm{InStrength} = 2.667$). Thus, directed complexes unify feedback and sink convergence over one directed graph.

Social and Information Networks.title: Explaining intersectional segregation in multi-attribute social networks
Social and Information Networks.summary: Segregation in students' friendships shapes their access to information and opportunities, and schools can reduce it by setting the composition of their classes. Yet segregation is usually measured one attribute at a time, although attributes such as migration background and sex are often correlated, so a preference over one can create segregation on the other. A single-attribute reading then attributes this induced segregation to the wrong preference and cannot identify which part of it a school can remove. In a network model with preferences over two correlated attributes, we derive in closed form the Coleman index, a standard segregation measure, separating the segregation due to each preference from the segregation it induces on the other attribute. In friendship networks of school classes in four European countries, ignoring sex inflates the estimated preference over migration background, increasingly so as the two attributes are more correlated. The closed form also shows what class composition can achieve. When students have no preference over one attribute, the segregation induced on it can be removed, whereas segregation set by a homophilic preference over the other cannot be changed. When both preferences are active, splitting a school with equal-sized groups and independent attributes reduces segregation only if the preferences pull in opposite directions. Judging a split by the school-wide average can hide classes that become more segregated. In the data, the split derived from the closed form removes induced segregation, and splitting does not lower segregation where both preferences are homophilic, as predicted.

Social and Information Networks.title: Multi-Scale Temporal Structure of the Conti Ransomware Communication Network
Social and Information Networks.summary: Communication networks provide a means of inferring broader organisational structure from accumulated local interactions. Cybercriminal organisations are particularly vulnerable to such inference, despite their secretive nature, because their distributed operation necessitates coordination through centralised digital communication infrastructure. The public leak of the Conti ransomware organisation's internal communications provides a rare longitudinal record of this coordination. Yet common approaches to analysing such longitudinal records aggregate interactions into a static network or model the communication process as stationary, both assuming a temporal homogeneity rarely tested for criminal organisations. Here we show substantial temporal heterogeneity at each scale examined in the Conti record, and demonstrate that much of it can be accounted for through appropriate, diagnostically guided choices of event representation and observation period. Collapsing rapid message bursts into conversational episodes brings communication timing closer to a constant-intensity reference and clarifies longer-timescale structure, which resolves into a sequence of distinct communication regimes, including a major transition following a coordinated platform migration. Even so, within these regimes heterogeneity persists, most evident in churn among peripheral participants, while highly active actors remain consistently observable. Together, these findings motivate explicit consideration of multi-scale temporal dynamics in the analysis, modelling and longitudinal monitoring of cybercriminal networks.
Social and Information Networks.comment: 16 pages, 9 figures, 3 tables. This work has been submitted to the IEEE for possible publication. Copyright may be transferred without notice, after which this version may no longer be accessible

Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.title: RankCast: Phase-Aware Rank Balancing in MoE Serving
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.summary: Modern large language model (LLM) inference increasingly adopts disaggregated architectures that separate Prefill (P) and Decode (D) phases. Meanwhile, Expert Parallelism (EP) has been widely adopted in large Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model serving. However, load imbalance still slows down MoE inference because each layer must wait for the busiest EP rank. The main source of latency differs between prefill and decode. Prefill is compute-bound, and its MoE layers' latency is determined by the maximum token count of the busiest rank. At the same time, under moderate batch sizes, Decode is memory-bound, so the latency is dominated by the maximum active-expert count across ranks. To solve both problems under a unified framework, we present RankCast, a system that reduces rank-level maximum token counts during prefill and active-expert counts during decode. For every token, RankCast preserves the predicted Top-p experts and chooses the remaining k-p from its Top-L candidates (L > k). In prefill, RankCast yields a price per rank that steers flexible assignments to less loaded ranks. In decode, RankCast closes experts on the busiest ranks while preserving the constraints for each token. Both paths are implemented and tested in the state-of-the-art inference frameworks SGLang and DeepEP. We overlap RankCast's kernels with model execution and reuse the existing DeepEP communication channel for metadata transmission. On Qwen3-235B-A22B with EP=8 and Qwen3.5-397B-A17B with EP=16, RankCast removes over 75% of the busiest rank's excess prefill load, improves prefill input throughput by up to 19%, and reduces decode time per output token by up to 10%. The quality cost is below one percentage point.

Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.title: Equal Opportunity: A Correctness Condition for Ordered Consensus
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.summary: In proof-of-stake blockchains based on State Machine Replication (SMR), the order of transactions directly affects client-visible financial outcomes. Ordered consensus augments the SMR specification by imposing correctness conditions on transaction ordering, with a focus on limiting Byzantine influence. However, real-world ordering attacks can occur even when these conditions hold, often enabled by advantages such as faster networks or proximity to the blockchain infrastructure that allow an adversary to systematically bias outcomes without violating the conditions. To address this gap, we extend ordered consensus with a new model and correctness condition based on equal opportunity, a notion of fairness widely used in legal contexts. Equal opportunity requires that candidates who are equally qualified---according to criteria deemed relevant---have equal chances of being selected (here, for a given position in the total order). We show how carefully introduced randomness can bound ordering bias, and we introduce the Secret Random Oracle (SRO), a fault-tolerant abstraction for generating such randomness. We present two SRO constructions, based on trusted hardware and threshold verifiable random functions, respectively, and use them to build Pompē-SRO, a new ordered consensus protocol that mitigates well-known ordering attacks. Our evaluation shows that Pompē-SRO effectively mitigates front-running and sandwich attacks at a moderate cost to latency.
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.comment: Extended version of the OSDI 2026 paper, with an appendix of proofs

Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.title: Engineered Simultaneity: The Physical Impossibility of Consolidated Price Discovery Across Spacelike-Separated Exchanges
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.summary: We define engineered simultaneity: the construction of a system that requires temporal comparison of events at spacelike-separated locations, implements this comparison via an implicit simultaneity convention, and represents the result as an objective measurement rather than a conventional choice. We show that the National Best Bid and Offer (NBBO) -- the cornerstone of U.S. equity markets -- is an instance of engineered simultaneity. The NBBO requires determining "current" prices across exchanges whose spatial separation places their price events outside each other's light cones. Special relativity proves that the temporal ordering of such events is frame-dependent: there exist inertial reference frames in which the NBBO differs from the value reported by the Securities Information Processor. The impossibility is not approximate; it is exact and unavoidable within the causal structure of Minkowski spacetime, and general relativity and indefinite causal order only compound it. We formalize the argument using the causal precedence relation and connect it to Lamport's theorem on distributed ordering. The operational form of the result needs no moving observers: the NBBO depends on where it is computed, and every participant who is not at the consolidation point holds a different one. The same construction recurs inside a single exchange, where orders are stamped at a perimeter and sorted by the stamp. Read as a practitioner suggests, as a bound on the worst-case error of distributed price discovery, the NBBO is defensible, and we propose that it be published as one. We separate what a central market is for (aggregating supply and demand) from what the latency race is about (sequencing arrivals), note that races of this kind cost about $5 billion a year in global equities, and record that in June 2026 the SEC proposed to rescind the order protection rule that makes the NBBO binding.
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.comment: 15 pages, 2 figures, 3 tables. v4: NBBO venue scope and exchange geometry corrected; adds sections on sequencing inside a single exchange and on the NBBO as an error bound

Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.title: Making History-Independence-Preserving LL/SC Writable
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.summary: A randomized implementation of $m$ LL/SC objects for $n$ processes, with at most $k$ outstanding LL() operations each, uses $O(kn + m)$ CAS and FAID objects [Bencivenga, Habashi, and Woelfel, DISC 2026], achieves constant expected step complexity, and preserves quiescent history independence for algorithms such as [Hagit Attiya, Michael A. Bender, Martín Farach-Colton, Rotem Oshman, and Noa Schiller, STOC 2025]. Unlike some other LL/SC algorithms, such as [Anderson and Moir, WDAG 1995; Jayanti and Petrovic, PODC 2003; Jayanti, Jayanti, and Jayanti, DISC 2023; Hagit Attiya, Michael A. Bender, Martín Farach-Colton, Rotem Oshman, and Noa Schiller, PODC 2024], this algorithm does not support an unconditional write operation. We show how to add a (randomized) wait-free write operation without affecting the asymptotic step or space complexity of the implementation.

Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.title: High-Performance Algorithms for Computing the V-BLAST Permutation
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.summary: We propose two novel and efficient algorithms for computing a column permutation called V-BLAST or an approximation of it. The V-BLAST column permutation is used in a QR factorization that is part of an integer/discrete least-squares solver. The overall solver is part of the receiver in advanced communication systems that transmit multiple symbols simultaneously. Two classes of efficient algorithms for computing the exact V-BLAST permutation have been proposed in the literature. The first, based on a sequence of Givens rotations, is unfortunately highly sequential. The other, based on a sequence of downdating operations on a pseudo-inverse, has a shorter critical path, but is unlikely to be numerically stable. The new algorithms that we propose are inspired by the similarity between V-BLAST and rank-revealing QR factorizations. Our first algorithm uses Householder reflections, is numerically stable, and has a short critical path. It is unable, however, to efficiently exploit cache memories. We rectify this with a randomized algorithm that computes an approximation to the V-BLAST permutation and has a short critical path and can effectively exploit cache memories. We prove approximation properties of the randomized algorithm and demonstrate experimentally that both algorithms are faster than existing ones, both when tested in isolation and when tested within an integer least-squares solver.

Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.title: Blockchain-IoT Convergence for Spatiotemporal Data Systems: Challenges, Solutions, and Research Gaps
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.summary: Blockchain in conjunction with the Internet of Things (IoT) is changing the management of spatiotemporal data in a way that has never been possible before now. In the process of gathering geospatial and time-stamped data from a large network of IoT devices, data authenticity, accuracy, and timely processing are major issues. Spatiotemporal indexing in a blockchain environment is necessary for ensure quick data retrieval; supporting real time data processing requirement. Blockchain with its decentralized consensus mechanism is a possible solution for preventing data fabrication, unauthorized access, and single point of failure in IoT based spatiotemporal applications. This paper aims to describe how Blockchain and IoT indexing can be combined to enhance the spatiotemporal data management (specifically indexing and querying of data). Literature solutions will be reviewed and compared to highlight challenges and insights for future blockchain-integrated IoT in resilient spatiotemporal data ecosystems.

Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.title: Estimating GPU Roofline Arithmetic Intensity with Off-the-Shelf LLMs and Compiler Artifacts
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.summary: GPU developers use profiling to understand computation and data movement, but access to target hardware can delay optimization. We investigate whether off-the-shelf large language models (LLMs) can estimate Roofline arithmetic intensity (the ratio of floating-point operations (FLOPs) to device-memory bytes) without executing the target GPU workload. We evaluate three models (deepseek-v4-flash, gemini-3.7-flash, and gpt-5.6-sol) across 179 combinations of five kernel families, four NVIDIA and AMD GPUs, four parallel runtimes (CUDA, HIP, OpenMP, and OpenCL), and modified code variants, comparing source-only queries, queries with compiler artifacts, and sandboxed agentic analysis. Compiler artifacts raise the share of arithmetic-intensity estimates within a factor of 1.20 of profiled values from 8-14% to 26-32%, while the resulting bandwidth-bound or compute-bound classifications are correct in 78-92% of runs. With compiler artifacts, FLOP estimates meet the 1.20x tolerance in 59-88% of runs, compared with 36-40% for device-memory traffic. Agentic analysis increases the share of arithmetic-intensity estimates within the 1.20x tolerance by 6.5 percentage points for gpt-5.6-sol, at 3.6x the median cost and 2.5x the median latency of compiler-assisted queries; the other models incur higher costs without a statistically clear improvement. These findings suggest LLM estimates could help prioritize optimization when GPU access is constrained, while identifying cache-dependent device-memory traffic as the main obstacle to precise arithmetic-intensity prediction.

Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.title: Asynchronous Collective Tree Exploration: Communication Meets Randomness
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.summary: We study collective tree exploration, where a team of $k$ mobile agents must visit all nodes of an initially unknown tree using as few moves as possible. All agents start at the root and discover adjacent edges as they traverse the tree. Communication is distributed in the sense that agents exchange information only by reading from and writing to whiteboards located at the nodes. Movements are asynchronous in the sense that an adversary controls the agents' speeds at all times. Existing competitive guarantees for collective tree exploration are either distributed but synchronous, or asynchronous but centralized. In contrast, we present a distributed asynchronous algorithm that explores any tree with $n$ nodes and depth $D$ in at most $2n+O(k 2^k D)$ moves, i.e., with regret linear in $D$. We also give a variant algorithm with a guarantee in $O(k/\log k)(n+kD)$, i.e., an $O(k/\log k)$ competitive ratio. We then show a lower bound on the competitive ratio of asynchronous collective tree exploration in $Ω(\log^2 k)$, improving over the previous $Ω(\log k)$ lower bound. Together, our algorithm and lower bound highlight an analogy between the role of communication in collective exploration and the role of randomness in online algorithms.

Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.title: Scalable Placement for Disaggregated LLM Serving on Heterogeneous Edge Fleets
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.summary: Serving large language models (LLMs) at the edge is increasingly desirable for privacy-sensitive applications and scenarios that require data to remain on local devices. However, edge environments are constrained by limited computational resources and exhibit substantial device heterogeneity, making efficient LLM serving challenging. These limitations become particularly pronounced under bursty demand, where congestion and queue buildup can significantly increase response latency. Replicating the model into multiple pipeline instances can improve serving capacity and reduce congestion. Yet, deciding how devices should be grouped into replicas, assigning replicas to prefill or decode functions, and partitioning model layers across heterogeneous devices jointly creates a large combinatorial optimization problem. We present Spade, a scalable and runtime-efficient placement planner for disaggregated LLM serving with pipeline replication across heterogeneous edge clusters. Spade introduces a dominance-based pruning technique that discards inferior replica candidates and recursively eliminates larger candidates that contain them, dramatically shrinking the search space. It further combines a water-filling approach for layer partitioning with a bounded multidimensional knapsack formulation that optimizes placement under a congestion-aware objective. On a synthetic fleet of 30 devices spanning five hardware classes, Spade finds the optimal placement in 441ms. In contrast, a genetic-search baseline augmented with dynamic-programming partitioning requires approximately two hours and still produces solutions with a 19.7% worse congestion objective. When evaluated on fleets containing ten device types, Spade's pruning strategy eliminates 99.6% of candidate placements while yielding the same surviving candidate set as exhaustive enumeration.

Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.title: Sound Distributed Runtime Verification under Incomplete Evidence
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.summary: Distributed runtime verification often requires combining evidence from several nodes to check properties that cannot be evaluated locally. However, when messages are delayed, lost, or deliberately suppressed, the verifier may not know whether a violation occurred or whether the relevant evidence is missing. This creates a risk of incorrectly reporting compliance. We study the requirements for sound monitoring under these conditions. We first show that a deadline-bounded monitor cannot be simultaneously sound, decisive, and available when an adversary can suppress evidence. The monitor must therefore be able to abstain. We then distinguish two sources of incomplete evidence. Sequence numbers and periodic reports can identify missing events, whereas detecting silent streams requires timing assumptions. We also examine how membership changes and coordinator failures affect verdict soundness and recovery. We implement these mechanisms in a three-tier monitoring architecture using MQTT and NATS JetStream. Experiments with an LLM-planned robot swarm demonstrate the failure modes, show how the proposed mechanisms prevent unsupported compliance verdicts, and measure their runtime and communication costs.
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.comment: Accepted at the 28th International Conference on Distributed Computing and Networking (ICDCN 2027), Surathkal, India, January 4-7, 2027. 10 pages

Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.title: Energy as a Service-Level Objective: Transaction-Level Energy Attribution
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.summary: Service engineers assess every change against functional requirements and qualities such as reliability, performance and availability. Energy is rarely part of this assessment. When consumption rises after a change, the team cannot tell whether the increase is worth investigating, worth accepting, or neither. A change to tracing, retries or a shared component can affect consumption far beyond the modified component. This thesis asks how energy objectives can become actionable engineering instruments rather than reporting metrics. Site Reliability Engineering (SRE) answered a similar question for reliability with service-level indicators, objectives and response policies. We take SRE as the guiding research vision and study where the analogy holds for energy and where it breaks. An energy objective could, for example, bound the energy per successful transaction under stated workload conditions. The thesis connects three threads into one experimentally evaluated methodology. Useful-work semantics define what a successful transaction is. Energy attribution assigns shared and auxiliary consumption to transactions. Service-level engineering decisions act on the resulting energy objectives. Existing work covers attribution methods, measurement frameworks and sustainability objectives, mostly at component level and without a link to decisions. Our prior work on service-level energy modeling showed that the energy of auxiliary services is often overlooked and hard to measure. Planned experiments compare aggregate, request-normalized and useful-work-based indicators under controlled changes to observability configuration and injected failures. Whether transaction-level attribution is needed for these decisions, or whether service-level attribution with outcome counts is sufficient, is an open question the experiments are designed to answer.
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.comment: Accepted at ICSOC26 in the PhD Symposium Track

Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.title: Parallel Memory Management in Goose, C++, and Rust: An Experimental Study of Allocation, Reclamation, and Scaling
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.summary: Compiler-managed memory can reduce allocation and reclamation overhead, but its behavior under parallel workloads remains insufficiently characterized. This study evaluates Goose v2026.3 against C++ and Rust implementations, including tree variants with individually allocated nodes and contiguous arenas. We benchmarked worker-local dynamic arrays and binary trees using multiple workers on a workstation with four physical cores and eight logical CPUs. Repeated tree experiments included five construction, traversal, and reclamation rounds. Each main experimental configuration was measured in 15 independent process runs. We measured whole-process execution time, release-operation intervals, and memory usage at synchronized checkpoints. We also examined strong and weak scaling. For depth-20 trees with eight workers, Goose achieved 5.62% and 10.95% lower median execution times than the C++ and Rust arenas, respectively. Its additional process RSS at the LIVE checkpoint was comparable to the arenas and substantially lower than that of individually allocated trees, but its virtual memory size was much larger. Logical reclamation did not always reduce resident memory, and Goose showed lower weak-scaling efficiency than the C++ and Rust arenas. Results for dynamic arrays were mixed. These results indicate that compiler-managed storage can be effective for parallel workloads with predictable object lifetimes. However, execution time alone does not capture its memory and scalability trade-offs.

Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.title: MUSE: Multi-Tenant Model Serving With Seamless Model Updates
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.summary: In binary classification systems, decision thresholds translate model scores into actions. Choosing suitable thresholds relies on the specific distribution of the underlying model scores but also on the specific business decisions of each client using that model. However, retraining models inevitably shifts score distributions, invalidating existing thresholds. In multi-tenant Score-as-a-Service environments, where decision boundaries reside in client-managed infrastructure, this creates a severe bottleneck: recalibration requires coordinating threshold updates across hundreds of clients, consuming excessive human hours and leading to model stagnation. We introduce MUSE, a model serving framework that enables seamless model updates by decoupling model scores from client decision boundaries. Designed for multi-tenancy, MUSE optimizes infrastructure re-use by sharing models via dynamic intent-based routing, combined with a two-level score transformation that maps model outputs to a stable, reference distribution. Deployed at scale by Feedzai, MUSE processes over 4 thousand events per second, and over 55 billion events in the last 12 months, across several dozens of tenants, while maintaining high-availability and low-latency guarantees. By reducing model lead time from weeks to minutes, MUSE promotes model resilience against shifting attacks, saving millions of dollars in fraud losses and operational costs.
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.comment: Accepted at IAAI-27 (AAAI 2027). This is the extended version with appendices

Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.title: ModelLess: A Serverless System for Multi-Tier LLM Inference on Shared GPUs
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.summary:
LLM inference platforms sell online, asynchronous, batch and rollout products on GPUs provisioned per product, so a service's cards sit idle between bursts while other work waits. We present ModelLess, a serverless system for LLM inference. Users declare model services and the platform owns the instances. An idle service scales to zero: its instances go to sleep with their weights in host memory (release about 1 s, wake about 4 s for GLM-5.2 at TP8, against a cold start of over four minutes). Billing follows the time a service holds GPUs. The GPUs that sleeping instances free are lent to lower tiers. Cluster managers preempt low-priority tasks and treat eviction as all-or-nothing, but an LLM instance's eviction cost depends on which of its weights, execution state, KV cache and in-flight requests survive. ModelLess therefore gives each tier (online, job, flex) eviction semantics that state what it may lose when preempted, and runs a preemption protocol that closes admission before it releases memory, re-enqueues a request durably before it aborts it, and fails closed. Four components (entry, dispatcher, node agent, SGLang plugin) enforce it with sleep/wake, pause/resume of in-flight requests for flex, and a weight-copy path (follow/seal) for RL rollout.
  Replaying a week of traces from 1,100 H20 cards serving long-tail online models shows that about 38% of GPU-time (417 equivalent GPUs) could be lent under a coarse latency target with one fixed idle threshold. This is an idealized upper bound, and it holds only if recovery takes seconds: with a 240 s cold start under 8% remains even with per-service thresholds. On one node, a single four-hour run per policy shows that pausing yields 22% more borrower tokens per held GPU sample than abort-and-requeue, with the same median online latency. The job tier and follow/seal are not yet evaluated end to end.

Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.title: Breaking Routing And Inter-device Dependencies in Mixture-of-Experts
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.summary: As Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models scale, Expert Parallelism (EP) becomes increasingly important for distributing experts across devices. However, the resulting token dispatch and combine operations can become a major bottleneck during inference. Overlapping these communication phases with computation is constrained by the sequential dependencies of standard MoE architectures. We introduce BRAID-MoE, an architecture that pairs laddered residual connections with early routing to relax these dependencies. Laddered residuals enable each expert combine to be deferred to the following block, while early routing computes the next routing decision from the pre-combine residual, with experts still receiving the updated post-combine hidden state. This creates an extended communication window in which the preceding combine and next dispatch can execute back-to-back on a dedicated communication stream, overlapping attention computation. On Qwen3-shaped MoEs with 0.4B-A0.1B and 2.5B-A0.5B parameters, BRAID closely matches sequential training at matched compute, with validation-loss increases of only 1% and 0.5%, respectively. We further demonstrate that existing MoE checkpoints can be adapted to BRAID with limited additional training, largely recovering their original accuracy. On a converted Qwen3-30B-A3B model, BRAID achieves speedups of up to 1.29$\times$ in prefill and 1.37$\times$ in decode, and at least 1.12$\times$ across diverse workloads and EP configurations on one or two four-H100 nodes. It outperforms competing overlap strategies in all tested settings, with the strongest gains when communication is a major latency bottleneck and its duration approaches the available computation window. These results demonstrate that early routing enables more effective communication-computation overlap in MoE inference at a modest cost in model quality.

Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.title: Simulations between Strongly Sublinear MPC and Node-Capacitated Clique
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.summary: We study how the Massively Parallel Computation (MPC) model in the strongly sublinear regime relates to the classic, graph-centric distributed models, focusing on the Node-Capacitated Clique (NCC), a bandwidth-parametrized generalization of the Congested Clique. In MPC, $M$ machines with per-machine memory $S$ hold a partition of the input graph. In NCC, we are given $n$ nodes that are themselves machines that know their full neighborhood but can send/receive only a bounded number of $C$ words per round. We are interested in the strongly sublinear regime where $S=n^δ$, for some constant $0 < δ<1$ and $C = MS/n$, where no simulation results are known. We explore when deterministic round-preserving simulations between these models are possible and when they are provably not, for different model parameters, problem families and graph classes. On the positive side, we provide techniques that allow, under certain restrictions, simulations with only constant overhead. On the negative side, we prove simulation impossibility results, which show that the limitations of our simulation results are inherent.

Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.title: RePrism: Joint Request and Representation Scheduling for LLM Agent Serving
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.summary: Agentic workflows often invoke large language models multiple times. When the dependencies are visible to the serving system, it can use them to schedule requests and cache reusable content, improving workflow execution efficiency. Prior work has largely focused on ordering requests or managing shared resources under a fixed caching scheme. A reusable prompt that specifies model behavior, however, can have multiple representations. We present RePrism, a serving system that jointly selects which ready request to serve and which eligible representation of its prompt to use. Its goal is to improve throughput and shorten session completion time (SCT). The scheduler ranks pairs of requests and representations by combining each pair's immediate value with an estimate of its future value based on the visible workflow. The resource manager allocates GPU memory to both LoRA adapters and cached key-value states. It also coordinates their admission and eviction as memory pressure changes. We compare RePrism with S-LoRA on a dynamic workload with an arrival rate of 1.8 sessions per second, and it achieves 1.37 times the request throughput and reduces P95 SCT by a factor of 4.10. Under controlled load, RePrism reduces mean time to first token by a factor of 5.26 relative to S-LoRA. On a controlled workload, RePrism's joint scoring achieves 2.7% higher request throughput and 12.3% lower mean SCT than a policy that ranks requests before selecting their representations.

Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.title: Reliability-aware AI Agent Execution in Collaborative Edge Computing: A World Model Approach
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.summary: Collaborative edge computing supports AI agent applications by distributing execution across heterogeneous user-controlled devices with limited resources. This paper studies reliability-aware AI agent execution under node failures and wireless disruptions. These disruptions can make agent execution state unavailable or inconsistent, forcing recovery or recomputation that consumes the remaining deadline budget. Maintaining recoverable execution states can therefore improve request completion before deadlines. We formulate an online AI agent execution management problem that jointly selects resource allocations, state protection actions, and recovery targets to maximize the expected task success rate subject to resource, compatibility, and deadline constraints. We develop a world model that jointly captures evolving agent workflows and recoverable execution state under candidate management actions, accounting for node reliability, network conditions, and resource availability. The model enables the controller to simulate future execution and recovery trajectories under candidate actions and estimate their effects on execution progress and task completion before deadlines. We then employ world model-based model predictive control (WorldMPC) with Monte Carlo rollouts to jointly optimize resource allocation, state protection, and recovery decisions for long-term reliable agent execution under the dynamic environment. We evaluate the proposed approach on the simulation and real-world testbed using real-world and synthetic datasets. Experimental results show that WorldMPC improves task success rate over baselines in both simulation and real-world testbed.

Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.title: Wi-Fi Enabled Edge Intelligence Framework for Smart City Traffic Monitoring using Low-Power IoT Cameras
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.summary: Real-time traffic monitoring in smart cities demands ultra-low latency processing to support time-critical decisions such as incident detection and congestion management. While cloud-based solutions offer robust computation, their inherent latency limits their applicability for such tasks. This work proposes a localized edge AI framework that connects low-power IoT camera sensors to a client, or applies offloading of inference to an NVIDIA Jetson Nano (GPU). Networking is achieved via Wi-Fi, enabling image classification without relying on wide-area infrastructure such as 5G, or wired networks. We evaluate two processing strategies: local inference on camera nodes and GPU-accelerated offloading to the Jetson Nano.We show that local processing is only feasible for lightweight models and low frame rates, whereas offloading enables near-realtime performance even for more complex models. These results demonstrate the viability of cost-effective, Wi-Fi-based edge AI deployments for latency-critical urban monitoring.

Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.title: Analysis of Federated Graph Neural Networks for Predicting Nuclear Core Properties
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.summary: Federated learning has grown in popularity owing to the increasing data privacy and safety concerns. It allows multiple parties to collaboratively train a model without exchanging their raw data. As an example of highly sensitive infrastructure of national importance, nuclear reactors benefit from this approach, where---while pooling multiple large datasets from different institutions could improve machine learning solutions---the confidentiality of the datasets is paramount. In this paper, we demonstrate that a graph neural network (GNN) outperforms the convolutional neural network (CNN) baseline in a federated setting for a use case concerning nuclear reactor core optimization. The GNN architecture is better suited for the nuclear reactor geometry as, unlike the CNN, it does not require padding the cylindrical core and does not assume translation invariance. The key finding of this work is that input representation is more important than model size and complexity. More sophisticated federated algorithms were employed, but the improvements derived were of lower magnitude. Experimenting with training corpus volume led to the discovery that greater fuel inventory variance is more beneficial than arrangements of existing cases, which is a direct consequence of data heterogeneity. Going forward, focus will remain on enhancing the input and readout representation.
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.comment: Accepted and to be presented at Middle-ware for Autonomous AIoT Systems in the Computing Continuum (MAIOT26)

Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.title: Joule is FLOP: Optimizing Tensor-Core Kernels Beyond Latency Hiding at the GPU Power Wall
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.summary: For a tensor-core kernel whose average board power stays near the GPU's power cap, runtime is approximately the energy consumed per call divided by that cap. Data movement whose latency is hidden by computation still consumes energy; reducing this traffic can raise the sustained clock and shorten execution even without reducing cycle count. We introduce Joule, a framework that accounts for this energy-frequency coupling in tensor-kernel design and scheduling. Its cost model combines hardware event counts, physical data-path energy costs, and nonlinear voltage scaling across domains to solve for sustained frequency and runtime under a power cap. Combining the model with data-movement lower bounds across memory levels and dies yields a power-aware speed of light (PSoL) that quantifies structural and implementation gaps. This analysis guides wide-tile kernels that use the full tensor memory (TMEM) capacity on B200, with fine-grained asynchronous rotation to overlap accumulator readout with tensor-core computation. It also guides power-aware spatial and temporal tile scheduling that accounts for trade-offs among read sharing, locality, and load balance. Given measured event counts, the model achieves 0.69% mean energy prediction error on B200. Across 60 dense-layer shapes, our GEMM delivers geometric-mean speedups of 4.94%, 6.64%, and 2.12% over exhaustively selected cuBLAS algorithms on B200, H100 NVL, and RTX PRO 6000, respectively. For fused Mega-MoE on eight B200 GPUs, the resulting optimizations improve performance by 2.60% to 5.17% over the upstream DeepGEMM baseline with die-local expert weights. We will open source Joule upon publication.

Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.title: Lachesis: Lifetime-Aware KV Cache Placement for Agent Serving across HBM and High-Bandwidth Flash
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.summary: In agent serving, agents and their sub-agents accumulate context as KV cache across many requests, far beyond HBM capacity. High-bandwidth flash (HBF) adds greater capacity at HBM-class read bandwidth, allowing a server to grow its batch and throughput under a relaxed SLO. We show that this gain meets an endurance wall as the batch growth wears HBF out within its warranty period. Prior work analyzes which KV should reach HBF assuming a request's KV remains readable until completion. However, an agent run is stateful, and by design, its harness discards parts of the context throughout the run. We find that the context divides into groups of KV that the harness discards together, so each group shares one lifetime that is known before the group is written. These lifetimes differ on three axes: reasoning stripped when the next user message ends a turn, a sub-agent's context discarded when it returns, and how long each sub-agent runs, which can be ranked when it starts. Guided by this characterization, we present Lachesis, a lifetime-aware KV cache placement layer that chooses HBM or HBF for each group when the group is written. In simulation of an eight-GPU B200 server on multi-agent traces, HBF with Lachesis serves 7.61-9.16$\times$ the throughput of the better of an HBM-only server and a DGX server with host DDR5. On the same traces, Lachesis extends HBF lifetime by 1.14-4.17$\times$ over HBM-first placement, which fills HBM before HBF. Since Lachesis keeps short-lived KV in HBM, a server running it can use more HBM stacks per GPU within the warranty. Our design-space exploration finds that Lachesis at 3/5 HBM/HBF stacks per GPU serves the highest throughput among the configurations that attach HBF directly to the GPU and outlast the warranty.

Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.title: Enabling Mixed criticality applications for the Versal AI-Engines
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.summary: Mixed-criticality systems (MCSs) are used in autonomous driving, aviation and medical systems. They require hardware platforms, which are reconfigurable at runtime to fully utilize performance while maintaining critical deadlines in emergency scenarios. However, Systems-on-Chip (SoC) components, like the Versal AI-Engine (AIE), only support static task mapping, limiting its utilization. In this work, we propose a dynamic task dispatching infrastructure that enables task switching on the AIE at runtime. Based on this infrastructure, we present an MCS design that dynamically assigns tasks of different criticality to AIE tiles, depending on the criticality mode of the system. Our approach overcomes the limitations of static dataflow graph mappings and, for the first time, exploits the parallel processing capabilities of the AIE for MCSs. We provide a timing analysis of the overhead introduced by the task dispatching infrastructure, which demonstrates that it is negligible. This makes it suitable for MCSs, as upper bounds can be identified. Finally, we evaluate the proposed infrastructure using an autonomous driving workload with tasks that have variable execution times and different criticality levels. In this case study, we maximized AIE utilization, reducing idle time by 65.5\%, while measuring an execution time overhead of less than 0.8\%, and doubling the throughput of low-criticality tasks.

Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.title: Norn: Context-Length-Aware Optimization of Weight and KV Cache Placement for Offloaded LLM Inference
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.summary: Offloading model weights and the key-value (KV) cache to host memory enables large language models (LLMs) to run on a single memory-constrained GPU. As the KV cache grows during decoding, GPU memory requirements and the costs of KV cache transfers and attention computation change. However, existing offloading methods generally use static computation assignments and placements of model weights and the KV cache, preventing them from adapting to these changes and degrading inference performance. We propose Norn, a context-length-aware offloaded LLM inference method. Based on offline profiling, Norn co-optimizes computation assignments and placements at the sublayer level, precomputing multiple execution plans and their switching points. During decoding, Norn switches plans as context length increases, overlapping computation and data transfers without knowing the output length in advance. For prefill, Norn employs operator-major chunked prefill to avoid repeated weight transfers and automatically selects the chunk size. Experiments with Qwen3-14B and Qwen3-32B on two single-GPU systems show up to a 16.8$\times$ speedup in end-to-end latency over Pipelined Sharding and a 4.2$\times$ speedup over its oracle variant with known input and output lengths.

Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.title: Fine-Grained Caching for Diffusion Transformers with Few Calibration Conditions
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.summary: Diffusion transformers require repeated denoiser evaluations, making image and video generation computationally expensive. We propose a training-free framework that uses a few calibration conditions to construct a fixed, fine-grained module-reuse schedule without schedule search. The design is motivated by an empirical effect along deterministic sampling trajectories: with initial noise fixed, condition-dependent deviations in several module outputs evolve similarly across adjacent steps, so temporal differencing attenuates much of their variation. We term this effect Conditional Common-Mode Rejection (CCMR). Motivated by this observation, we rank timestep--layer--module locations using normalized ratios of consecutive feature displacements and construct a Cache Book through two-stage calibration. The second stage updates a scorer-only reference with each provisional bit after recording its indexed score, while retaining full-compute trajectories. At inference, the fixed schedule requires no per-input policy estimation and can be nested within fixed step-wise cache policies. Module caching alone achieves $1.66$--$1.72\times$ speedup on the evaluated image models and $1.54$--$1.68\times$ on the video models. Combining it with MagCache or SeaCache provides further acceleration at a model-dependent cost in paired fidelity.

Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.title: Thinflow: Organizing HPC Benchmarking Campaigns as Rerunnable Directory Trees
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.summary: A benchmarking campaign provides the measurements behind an HPC performance study: code variants are built, swept over core or node counts, and measured repeatedly. Moving such a campaign to another supercomputer or rerunning it months later requires work that is not part of the study itself. Job scripts are adapted to each supercomputer, and what exactly ran is often reconstructed afterwards. We present Thinflow, a small Bash engine for organizing HPC benchmarking campaigns as rerunnable directory trees of tasks and runs. A task is a directory with a short shell script next to the code. For each sweep, one command builds the code, runs the benchmarks, and plots the results. Thinflow derives the execution order from declared dependencies and writes it to a plain-text manifest. Per-supercomputer profiles submit the runs to a workload manager such as Slurm. Each run writes a provenance record of its environment, hardware, and parameters. The engine ships inside the campaign directory, so a campaign stays rerunnable without installing a separate tool and, once completed, may serve as a paper artifact. In a case study, we ran one campaign with identical task files on three Slurm partitions of two supercomputers, on up to 16 nodes. This strong-scaling study of matrix multiplication in C/OpenMP, C/MPI, and Julia/MPI comprises 37 task files with 217 non-comment lines. Its 455 benchmark runs recorded what differed per partition, chiefly profiles and command-line parameters. This suggests that such a campaign needs little structure beyond plain shell files.

Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.title: A Unified Control Framework for Gradient Inversion Defense in Federated Learning
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.summary: Gradient perturbations are widely recognized as an effective defense against gradient inversion attacks in federated learning, but they are equally known to impair optimization, creating a persistent tension between privacy and utility. In this paper, we show that existing gradient perturbation defenses, despite their different formulations, can be unified under a controlled dynamics framework, providing a cohesive understanding of their optimization behavior and enabling the derivation of universal convergence and safety conditions without relying on case-specific analyses. Leveraging this observation, we propose ``Near Orthogonal Gradient Projection (NODE)'', which injects perturbations only along directions orthogonal to the original gradient so that the defended gradient maintains a fixed cosine similarity with the true gradient. By preserving the first-order descent direction, NODE substantially reduces the optimization cost of strong perturbations while maintaining effective protection against gradient inversion attacks. We theoretically establish convergence guarantees under standard optimization assumptions and further show that, under mild conditions on the gradient distribution, NODE remains effective in preventing inversion attacks. Comprehensive experiments on multiple benchmark datasets, including CIFAR-10, ImageNet, and Chest X-ray, together with a variety of gradient inversion attacks, demonstrate that the proposed framework achieves an improved privacy--utility trade-off over existing defenses across a broad range of training settings.

Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.title: FliX: Flipped-Indexing for Scalable GPU Queries and Updates
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.summary: GPU concurrent data structures (CDSs) achieve very high read-only throughput, but fully dynamic updates on GPU-resident data remain challenging. Ordered CDSs (e.g., B-trees and LSM-trees) route operations through an index layer to a data layer of buckets. Maintaining and traversing that index under updates causes contention, warp divergence, and memory overhead. Hash tables avoid this cost but lose range and successor queries. We present FliX, a comparison-based flipped indexing strategy that eliminates the index layer. Instead of assigning a warp to each operation, FliX assigns a warp to each bucket. Each bucket then binary-searches a sorted batch for its operations, so one search replaces many index traversals and updates become simple. FliX reduces query latency by up to 6.5x versus a leading GPU B-tree and 1.5x versus the leading GPU LSM-tree. It delivers 4x higher throughput per memory footprint than ordered competitors and over 8x higher insertion throughput than the closest fully dynamic ordered baseline. It also matches or beats unordered GPU hash tables on point queries and deletions, so its ordering support comes at virtually no cost. FliX also supports fully concurrent execution of queries and updates. In an update-heavy mixed workload, it achieves 4.42x the throughput of a GPU hash table and 11.39s the throughput of a B-tree. Our results suggest that FliX can support fast queries, efficient updates, and memory reclamation on fully GPU-resident data while maintaining key order and allowing fully concurrent execution.

Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.title: Generalized Tensor Parallelism: Powering Trillion-Parameter LLM Training at 10+ EFLOP/s
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.summary: Pretraining state-of-the-art large language models (LLMs) with up to trillions of parameters is memory- and compute-intensive. Existing parallelization schemes compromise on either per-GPU memory or throughput: data parallelism replicates parameters; tensor parallelism and fully sharded data parallelism (FSDP) add communication of activations and parameters, respectively, to every microbatch; and pipeline parallelism leaves GPUs idle while the pipeline fills and drains. We show that, for linear layers, five commonly used parallelisms (data, tensor, sequence, context parallelism and FSDP) are special cases of one framework, generalized tensor parallelism (GTP), in which each layer's parameters and activations are partitioned and either can be re-materialized with an all-gather before use. In GTP, a parameter all-gather is an optional preprocessing step on one input of a matrix multiplication (GEMM), whereas FSDP implementations typically treat it as a step before an entire Transformer block, which can increase memory footprint and delay GEMMs. The GTP view lets us schedule all-gathers per GEMM rather than per block, issuing each early enough to hide its communication but late enough to limit memory. Our implementation is open source at https://github.com/NVIDIA/Megatron-LM; with it, an internal 2T-parameter mixture-of-experts (MoE) model reaches \textbf{13.0 model EFLOP/s} (exaFLOP/s) on 12,288 GB300 GPUs with 98\% weak-scaling efficiency, and runs with 1M-token sequences on 512 GPUs. On 256--1,024 GPUs, our implementation achieves \textbf{1.05--1.55$\times$ the throughput of Megatron-FSDP} across three MoE models and \textbf{1.27--1.31$\times$ that of a tuned 3D-parallel recipe with pipeline parallelism} on a DeepSeek-V4-Pro proxy model.

Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.title: AceVLN: Asynchronous Cloud Edge Deployment of VLNs via Latent Scheduling and Compensation
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.summary: Cloud--edge deployment enables asynchronous dual-system VLN on resource-constrained robots, but inference and communication delays cause latent mismatch and navigation errors. Existing adaptation methods reuse historical guidance but cannot provide updated navigation information when it becomes inadequate. We propose AceVLN, a training-free framework for active latent refresh and edge-side compensation. Our analysis reveals that action-relevant mismatch is concentrated in a compact Critical Subspace and can be tracked through fast-system feature drift. Critical Feature Drift Entropy reflects navigation sensitivity and guides adaptive refresh, while Critical Drift Continuity indicates when recent latent updates can support compensation during latency spikes. AceVLN integrates subspace-decoupled mismatch modeling, entropy-guided refresh scheduling, and continuity-guided compensation. Experiments show that \textit{AceVLN} improves success rates by 1.7--2.4 percentage points over the strongest baselines, while reducing amortized computation time by 2.7--10.0\% and FLOPs by 18.4--22.3\%.

Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.title: FlashQLA: Efficient Context Parallelism for Gated DeltaNet
