We further identify a dimension-permutation attack specific to HDC, which reorders hypervector coordinates to evade verification without altering predictions, and counter it through encoder realignment. Finally, an AMD ZCU104 FPGA implementation confirms that HDMark adds no hardware overhead, remains bit-exact under aggressive undervolting, and stays verifiable under timing faults until the classifier itself fails.

Cryptography and Security.title: BODYBENCH: Evaluating Adversarial Image Defenses Against AI Nudification Inpainting
Cryptography and Security.summary: Adversarial perturbation defenses protect images from unauthorized edits by adding imperceptible noise. Yet none of these methods have been evaluated against nudification, despite AI-generated non-consensual intimate imagery (AIG-NCII) being among the most documented harms of generative AI. Moreover, nudification edits are readily carried out through inpainting, the primary setting these protection methods are designed to defend against. We argue this is a problem-formulation failure since prior threat models do not correspond to nudification edits (also called attacks). The misalignment of existing approaches is structural, spanning mask shape, training and testing prompt distributions, and success criterion which causes existing evaluations to systematically overestimate protection effectiveness. We reformulate image protection against unauthorized editing around this documented harm. We introduce BODYBENCH, a benchmark of 648 fully synthetic clothed adult subjects, each paired with 11 mask variants spanning body, face, and context regions. We propose three harm-aligned metrics: sexualization, naturalness, and recognizability that jointly determine whether an inpainted output constitutes a successful nudification attack. Auditing four recent protection methods (PhotoGuard, DiffusionGuard, AdvPaint, DiffVax) on BODYBENCH, we find that protection succeeds in only one configuration of one method, and only under exact mask alignment between defender and attacker---a condition no real defender can guarantee and one that we show is easily always bypassed. We also show that standard evaluation metrics such as peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) are essentially uncorrelated with nudification protection. BODYBENCH makes this misalignment measurable and provides a foundation for defenses grounded in documented harm.
Cryptography and Security.comment: Li Qiwei and Salma Abdel Magid contributed equally to this work and share first authorship

Cryptography and Security.title: TACT-Bench: Testing Adaptive Conversational Threats against Tool-Use Agents
Cryptography and Security.summary: The growing autonomy of AI agents in using external tools and making decisions has created an urgent need for comprehensive safety benchmarks. Existing benchmarks test compromised tool channels or adaptive multi-turn attacks, though they may not capture the unique capabilities of policy-governed tool-use agents, which must resist unauthorized requests without abandoning the legitimate work embedded in the same interaction. To fill this gap, we introduce TACT-Bench, a stateful benchmark built around scenario-specific stories, personas, manipulation tactics, and response-adaptive escalation. Each adversarial task targets an action explicitly prohibited by the policy provided to the assistant, while the policy remains hidden from the attacking user. TACT pairs each adversarial task with at least one benign counterpart, and its adversarial tasks retain authorized ground-truth actions when a compliant resolution remains available. We define these base tasks as TACT-Base. We additionally introduce TACT-TrustPrime, which places an independent benign task before an unrelated attack in the same conversation. We also propose Paired Selective Trustworthiness (PST), which combines explicit safe refusal with demonstrated capability on matched benign tasks, to analyze an agent's overcautiousness and practicality. Averaged across 6 different models as assistants, TACT-Base raises Attack-Induced Failure Rate (AFR) by 17.53% over four compatible attack baselines, and TACT-TrustPrime raises it by a further 17.01%. The two evaluated defense methods reduce AFR by only 8.35%--9.41% on average and do not consistently improve PST, underscoring the need for stronger policy-enforcement methods.
Cryptography and Security.comment: Code and data are available at https://github.com/IliaHashemiRad/TACTBench

Cryptography and Security.title: Separating Measurement Failures from Defence Failures in Split Language-Model Privacy
Cryptography and Security.summary: Split-training privacy evaluations fail through distinct mechanisms. Evaluators can overlook an exposed gradient channel, align reconstructions against shifted labels, or deploy uncalibrated probes before testing a candidate defence, while calibrated attacks can also refute real defences. Separating these failure modes alters which claims survive. We conduct a retrospective evidentiary reanalysis across four split-LLM campaigns and two cross-cutting scope checks covering host key custody and variational mutual-information bounds, mapping every recorded claim to one of five admissibility states (breach, non-detection, undetermined coverage, invalid measurement, or out-of-scope inference). Across a 19-configuration exploration, only four of 24 required probes qualified, yet those four calibrated probes still established qualified privacy breaches in 13 configurations, while utility or learning-gain failures eliminated the remaining 6. In a seven-cell defence-redesign pilot, 2 quantised configurations failed utility gates, calibrated next-byte structure probes breached the 0.02 gate on all 7 cells (0.097 to 0.112), and qualified punctuation-property probes reached 0.79 to 0.89, yielding 4 failed and 3 undetermined composite privacy assessments (the latter from marginal null-band excursions on punctuation bindings). Negative evidence against both defence families remains intact. Scope checks further show that shared-key orthogonal wrappers protect passive network captures without hiding activations from a compromised restoring host, and why near-zero variational lower bounds leave worst-case leakage unconstrained. Rerunnable scripts verify 1,522 checks across 122 SHA-256-pinned artifacts while preserving each campaign's native seed intervals and retrospective boundaries.

Cryptography and Security.title: Mixed-Initiative Mining of Root-Cause Analyses into Audit Priors for C/C++ Vulnerability Hunting
Cryptography and Security.summary:
Vulnerability auditing of large C/C++ codebases is constrained by limited review attention. Human auditors and LLM-based agents need operational priors that indicate where to look first and what to suspect, but such priors are rarely available in directly usable form. Rather than proposing a new vulnerability detector, we derive audit-steering artifacts from evidence-backed root-cause analysis (RCA) reports.
  We introduce two complementary representations: Occurrence Context (OC), a location prior based on file role, function role, and data-structure class; and Vulnerability-Inducing Structural Patterns (VISP), reusable failure-mechanism priors. OC guides where to inspect, while VISP guides what to suspect.
  On 108 CVEs from Vul4C, OC's parser-based priority ranking, without LLM inference, outperforms generic prioritization baselines with moderate-to-large effect sizes. Packaged as executable SKILLs, OC and VISP form a dual-SKILL workflow that improves audit-relevant broad coverage, defined as match-or-partial findings within ground-truth functions that share the patch's failure mechanism, as assessed by three LLM judges. Across the 108-CVE cohort, dual-SKILL improves function-level broad matches by 5.3 percentage points; gains reach 7.2 points on mid-size projects and 15.0 points on large (1500-4999-line) vulnerable files. These results suggest that RCA-derived priors help direct limited audit attention toward vulnerable code. The agent-coverage evaluation is a single-run operational probe, with one run per commit, characterizing the direction and scale of the effect rather than its precise magnitude.

Cryptography and Security.title: SigK: rPPG-based key agreement scheme for mHealth
Cryptography and Security.summary: As mobile health advances, the use of biomedical sensors for disease monitoring, diagnosis, and treatment is increasing. These sensors often need to be connected through wireless communication technologies to process physiological information from various body parts effectively. Since the data transmitted in these devices usually contain sensitive personal medical information, it is crucial to establish secure communication between devices. In recent studies, the inter-pulse intervals between heartbeats are often used as the key source. They can be extracted from physiological signals such as photoplethysmogram (PPG) or electrocardiogram (ECG), allowing key agreement schemes without pre-key distribution. However, traditional solutions are based on contact measurement devices (e.g., wristbands, chest straps), which limit their applicability in contactless healthcare scenarios. In this paper, we propose a remote PPG-based key agreement scheme to facilitate secure communication between contactless medical devices. We leverage medical devices equipped with cameras to capture remote PPG signals from human faces, and then utilize the signal's power spectral density and peak-peak interval to establish a key agreement with signals synchronously acquired in the Body Area Network (BAN). We have carried out performance evaluations on three publicly available datasets to demonstrate the feasibility of our proposed scheme. In addition, we have also presented a comprehensive proof of the security of our proposed scheme.

Computation and Language.title: Representation Redistribution in Sparse Autoencoders
Computation and Language.summary:
Presenting the same request with different context or formatting can change which sparse autoencoder (SAE) features respond inside a language model. Understanding these changes raises two questions. Which feature responses recur across related inputs, and which of them contribute to downstream computation?
  We study this phenomenon as representation redistribution and introduce the redistribution sensitivity score (RSS) to identify large feature changes that recur in a consistent direction. We select features on one set of prompt variants and evaluate them on separate variants. Across 27 pretrained SAEs spanning eight language models, RSS reveals a consistent pattern of redistribution. Context and wrapper transformations produce stronger recurring responses than local edits.
  We then use two frozen safety readouts to measure how these changes contribute to downstream computation. RSS identifies features with approximately twice the mean held out contribution of features selected by the largest readout coefficients, using activation responses alone. An exact decomposition explains how feature changes and readout coefficients determine their effects on the decision margin. Combining RSS contributions with the clean margin improves recurrent failure AUROC from 0.863 to 0.935 and from 0.901 to 0.958, approaching the full readout results of 0.965 and 0.964.
  These findings show that recurring changes in sparse representations provide a way to identify features with meaningful downstream contributions. Code is available at https://github.com/OpenSAE/Redistribution-Sensitivity-Score.

Computation and Language.title: Behavioral Compositionality of Sparse Autoencoder Representations
Computation and Language.summary: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) provide features that can be combined to explain and steer language model behavior. Understanding these combinations requires knowing how reliably individual feature effects predict their joint impact on the model. We study this relationship by retaining or removing subsets of SAE feature contributions and measuring the resulting behavioral responses. We introduce SAE Additivity Residuals (SAR) to quantify how much behavioral variation is explained by feature interactions beyond a chosen order. We prove that, under independent feature subset sampling, SAR measures the normalized energy of these interactions and bounds errors in ranking feature combinations. Across 18 model and behavior settings, learned SAE coordinates have lower first order residuals than matched rotations of the same activation subspace. This shows that SAE coordinates support comparatively simple descriptions of joint feature effects. Pairwise modeling further improves the ranking of held out feature combinations in all 18 settings. We also demonstrate the practical value of modeling these interactions. Across five challenging benchmarks, pairwise models select feature combinations that give higher probability to the correct answer and preserve the original behavioral response more closely than first order models. In MMLU-Pro steering, pairwise modeling improves rank fidelity from 0.5874 to 0.7790 and reduces ordering error from 0.1444 to 0.0606. These results establish behavioral compositionality as a measurable property of SAE representations and show how modeling feature interactions improves the analysis and selection of feature combinations.

Computation and Language.title: Large-scale factor analysis shows machine intelligence is only partially interpretable
Computation and Language.summary: A common assumption in language model development is that cognitive abilities are organized around a general, domain-free intelligence factor, like fluid intelligence in humans. This assumption is rarely tested directly, and prior attempts have done so only at a much smaller scale. We take a latent variable approach to intelligence in language models, similar to how psychometricians study psychological constructs. Using factor analysis, we analyzed 13,230 published evaluation scores covering 1,618 language models across 456 text-only benchmarks. Because the data are sparse, we triangulate our analysis across different data densifiers and imputation methods. Across the imputations that pass our quality filter, the general factor's share of variance in the summed score ($ω_h$) ranges from 0.04 to 0.76, and its share of the common variance (ECV) from 0.11 to 0.52. A robust pattern across different modes of bias is that 1. same-subject benchmarks are not guaranteed to place closely in vector space, with weak median label cohesion, 2. benchmarks loading highest on $G$ tend to be miscellaneous rather than thematically coherent, and 3. standard "intelligence" benchmarks do not dominate the share of ability variance the general factor explains, and there is a lack of evidence that $G$ is well-proxied by them. We hypothesize that targeting a single conceptual ability has little support, since the first-order abilities it would have to reach are often partially idiosyncratic and not identifiable in practice. This would mean that, from public benchmark scores alone, general intelligence is hard to define, identify, and target as a single construct in language model development. Future experiments should run training regimes that target both theoretically abstract general ability and tasks with semantic similarity and examine how abilities transfer across test sets of diverse formats.

Computation and Language.title: LogToPersona: New Benchmark and Efficient Persona Prediction through Semantic Log Filtering
Computation and Language.summary: Detailed knowledge of a user's persona is valuable for personalizing generative AI models and agents, yet such details are difficult to obtain and change over time. We address the task of inferring persona attributes from a single day of mobile activity logs. No suitable publicly available benchmark exists for this task, so we introduce a synthetic benchmark of 1,600 persona-log pairs. We target on-device inference so that raw logs never leave the phone, which makes memory rather than speed the limiting constraint: a day of activity yields roughly 30K tokens, whose key-value cache alone exceeds the INT4 weights of a 4B-parameter model. We therefore propose a log filtering method that retains only behaviorally distinct entries. Filtering reduces the memory footprint by up to 39% across nine models from four families and more than halves prefill time, while maintaining or improving prediction quality. For Qwen3-4B it removes 2.5GB, bringing the model from well beyond a realistic per-process budget to a manageable one. Within our benchmark, these results indicate that preserving diverse behavioral events matters more for persona prediction than retaining every semantically similar log entry.

Computation and Language.title: Using AI to Simulate the Behaviour of European Populations
Computation and Language.summary: Language models can stand in for survey respondents, but leading approaches build their simulated people from interviews or individual records. We show that a model can learn how European population groups respond from published statistics, without interviews and without training on individual records. We fine-tune an open-weight language model on more than 12 million published group-level answer distributions from about 40 European countries, setting it up to predict each group's departure from a reference distribution. On opinion surveys from its training families it calls the direction of group differences right 84% of the time, ahead of a demographic statistical model (77%, paired test) and level with Claude Opus 5 and 5.5, which it also ties on accuracy; the frontier models are more accurate on new questions. On 278 held-out questions, almost all from the survey families seen in training, its error is 12% lower than that statistical model. It runs on a single 32 GB GPU or a high-memory laptop, and in a test with an earlier model, an evidence gate calibrated on half of a survey's questions fell back to the reference where the model's adjustments did not help. Coupled to a transport simulation of a planned metro closure, with a conventional elasticity as the reference, it adds a testable age gradient to the response, which we freeze for later scoring.

Computation and Language.title: Evaluating Large Language Models on conversational African American English: Feature classification and next-turn generation
Computation and Language.summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) are known to misinterpret and misrepresent regional and social varieties of English other than Mainstream American English (MAE), such as African American English (AAE), yet most evaluations of these biases have relied on synthetic, stylized or decontextualized data. This paper instead evaluates LLMs on authentic, conversational AAE to more closely reflect how such models may encounter AAE when deployed as chatbots. Concretely, we perform two complementary evaluation tasks on 100 six-turn segments randomly sampled from the Corpus of Regional African American Language (CORAAL; Kendall and Farrington, 2024), comparing three closed-weight LLM configurations: Gemini 2.5 Flash with and without reasoning, and GPT-4.1 mini. The first task compares the models against gold-standard manual annotations for five AAE morphosyntactic features, while the second assesses their ability to generate contextually appropriate next turns, evaluating outputs for AAE feature frequency, diversity (Self-BLEU), and pragmatic quality. Reasoning-enabled Gemini is the strongest feature detector by a clear margin (macro F1 of 0.91), outperforming both other LLMs as well as a finetuned BERT-based baseline (Masis et al., 2022). In generation, however, all LLMs underproduce AAE relative to the human speakers and produce relatively uniform continuations, with reasoning-enabled Gemini producing the least AAE and the least diverse output. We conclude that a model's ability to detect AAE does not straightforwardly translate into its spontaneous use of AAE in generation, and argue that addressing this gap requires changes upstream, in how pretraining and alignment data represent dialectal variation.

Computation and Language.title: CA-RAG: Constraint-Aligned Retrieval for Structurally Faithful Long-Form Generation
Computation and Language.summary: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) typically optimises evidence selection for semantic relevance, whereas compliance-sensitive long-form generation also requires evidence supporting explicit structural obligations. Semantically relevant retrieval may therefore omit information needed for mandatory downstream clauses. We propose Constraint-Aligned RAG (CA-RAG), a retrieval-conditioning framework that augments section-specific queries with ontology-derived structural constraints and policy-grounded knowledge-graph relations before evidence selection. Retrieval-only evaluation with manually annotated evidence shows consistent improvements across retrieval budgets. At $k=6$, CA-RAG increases Precision@$k$ from $0.5268$ to $0.5692$, pooled Recall@$k$ from $0.5402$ to $0.5950$, and F1@$k$ from $0.5389$ to $0.5672$ over standard RAG. Generation experiments further show improvements in compliance and reliability in several model--domain settings, while generation-only constraints achieve higher clause coverage but lower overall compliance and reliability. These results indicate that structurally aligned retrieval can improve evidence sufficiency in compliance-sensitive long-form generation.

Computation and Language.title: Large Language Model Agents for Evidence Based Genetic Disease Severity Classification
Computation and Language.summary: Disease severity classification for genetic conditions is subjective and labor-intensive, creating bottlenecks in genomic screening, where commercial panels vary widely in size and overlap. We developed an autonomous AI agent integrating Reasoning and Acting (ReAct) with Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) to classify 10,211 Human Phenotype Ontology terms. It uses American College of Medical Genetics (ACMG)-endorsed severity guidelines and American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG) quality-of-life criteria to retrieve PubMed literature, generate interpretable reasoning chains, and independently verify claims. At the phenotype level, using expert-curated cohorts, the agent achieved 93.55% accuracy (MCC 0.9237) with 82.6% to 91.4% of claims supported by direct evidence or valid inferences. Gene-level severity was aggregated across 8,738 pairs, identifying 3,283 autosomal recessive pairs with severe or profound presentations. External validation showed 95.2% concordance with Mackenzie's Mission gene list. This system enables standardized panel design by providing reliable, automated classification supported by direct evidence.

Computation and Language.title: Attention Routing Stabilizes Early: Working-Set Inference for Recurrent Language Models
Computation and Language.summary: Recurrent-depth language models, such as looped Transformers, repeatedly apply shared network blocks to refine latent representations, enabling additional test-time computation without generating explicit intermediate reasoning tokens. However, recurrent inference repeatedly accesses long contexts: full attention incurs quadratic computation during prefill, while autoregressive decoding repeatedly reads large key-value (KV) caches, introducing substantial memory traffic and capacity pressure. We study how attention routing evolves across recurrent depth and uncover a consistent separation in convergence timescales: routing-related quantities, including the attention support and the attention distribution, stabilize substantially earlier than representation-related quantities such as hidden states and attention outputs. This suggests a two-stage structure in which the model discovers a sparse working set and then refines representations over largely the same routing support. Motivated by this structure, we introduce WISE (Working-set Inference with Support Exploitation), a training-free method that uses unrestricted global attention during early recurrent steps to discover a block-structured working set, and then reuses it as the routing support in later steps while keeping recurrent refinement and within-support attention computation dynamic. By combining sparse recurrent attention with compact KV-cache management, WISE reduces both redundant attention computation and memory movement during inference. Across reasoning and long-context benchmarks, WISE closely approaches full-attention accuracy on key evaluated workloads while outperforming early-static support baselines. At 64K context, our implementation achieves up to a 6.46x decode throughput improvement under GPU memory pressure. Our code is available at https://github.com/tbn5pj/WISE_code.

Computation and Language.title: BLADE: Better Language Answers through Dialogue and Explanations
Computation and Language.summary: Large language model (LLM)-based educational assistants often provide direct answers offering little incentive for students to explore or engage with course materials. We present BLADE (Better Language Answers through Dialogue and Explanations), a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) based conversational assistant grounded in course-specific content that guides students toward relevant materials through citation-grounded dialogue rather than delivering unsourced solutions. We evaluate BLADE in an advanced undergraduate NLP course with extensive instructional resources, in which locating and synthesizing relevant material is a central challenge. During quizzes, students are assigned to one of three conditions: BLADE only, direct course materials only, or both; we measure performance and resource usage. Results show that students consistently select BLADE over direct materials when both are available, and that quiz performance is highest when students use BLADE alone. In contrast, simultaneous use of both resources is associated with significantly lower performance. No statistically significant difference in quiz performance occurred between assigned resource conditions. These findings show the potential of RAG-based assistants as a citation-grounded interface for applying course content under open-book exam-like conditions, while suggesting that adding direct-material access does not necessarily improve in-task performance.
Computation and Language.comment: To appear, European Chapter of the Association for Computational Linguistics (EACL), Athens, Greece, March, 2027

Computation and Language.title: Learning from Recurrence: Internalizing Depth-Induced Preferences in Looped Language Models
Computation and Language.summary: A looped language model repeatedly applies the same block to its hidden state before predicting each token. The number of passes is its recurrent depth. Increasing this depth gives the model more computation per token with the same parameters. Can the shared block learn from the predictions it makes at greater depth? Following prior work, we retrofit pretrained OLMo-2-1B with a shared recurrent block and continue mid-training over varying recurrent depths. In the four-pass model, additional passes mainly redistribute probability among tokens that already rank highly after one pass. We use the continuations generated at greater depth to train only the shared block through a single pass, without reference answers or correctness filtering. We call this transfer preference write-back. Write-back further improves one-pass and multi-pass accuracy on most tasks. At their target depths, the updated models outperform a non-recurrent control matched for mid-training data and token budget on all six mathematical reasoning benchmarks, with a mean relative gain in accuracy of up to 46.2% across tasks. At four-pass inference, one-pass training outperforms full-depth training on the same targets in the model with input injection. This advantage disappears in the matched model without injection. On GSM8K, using the updated block only on passes two through four recovers nearly the entire four-pass gain, showing that an update learned in one pass can improve later applications of the same block.

Computation and Language.title: PAC Learning to Sample: On Computational Aspects of Language Generation
Computation and Language.summary:
The success of language models has motivated theoretical work on learning to sample from distributions on discrete domains. A prominent abstraction is the model of language generation in the limit, introduced by Kleinberg and Mullainathan (NeurIPS 2024), in which the algorithm must generate from the target language after some finite but unspecified number of positive examples. While its positive results are surprisingly general, most guarantees are qualitative. In this work, we seek quantitative guarantees on sample and time complexity, inspired by statistical and computational learning theory.
  To this end, we study a PAC model of language generation, proposed (in a different context) by De, Diakonikolas, and Servedio (SODA 2015), in which a Boolean concept class $C$ over $\{-1,1\}^n$ defines the target languages: given uniformly random positive examples of an unknown concept $f \in C$, the learner must output a sampler whose output distribution (conditioned on the training data) is close in total variation to the uniform distribution over $f^{-1}(1)$. Their work implicitly gives an efficient algorithm for PAC learning to sample $C$, given three primitives for $C$: an online learner, approximate sampling and counting oracles, and an SQ learner.
  We ask whether these ingredients, in particular online learnability, are necessary. First, we construct a Boolean concept class $C$ for which online learning is cryptographically hard, yet PAC learning to sample is computationally efficient. Then, we develop new algorithms that use offline ERM oracles instead of online learners, together with approximate sampling/counting oracles for intersections of concepts in $C$ and an SQ learner for $C$. We view our results, together with the work of De, Diakonikolas, and Servedio, as a first step towards understanding the computational complexity of language generation.

Computation and Language.title: AI-human hybrid conversations: Can AI Agents Improve Discourse Quality?
Computation and Language.summary: Conversations are central to how people exchange information, share experiences, and develop collective understanding. Yet, across conversational settings, discussions often suffer from uneven participation, unanswered contributions, and a narrow range of perspectives. As generative AI agents increasingly participate alongside humans, hybrid human-AI conversations present a new opportunity to address these challenges. We investigate whether AI agents can serve as catalysts for human interaction, improving conversational engagement and broadening collective discourse. We develop a framework for introducing generic and persona-conditioned AI agents into evolving discussions and evaluate it through two complementary studies. First, using agent-based simulations grounded in Reddit discussions across four domains, we find that AI-generated conversations are more positive and less toxic than human conversations, but substantially less semantically diverse. Persona conditioning produces more human-like contributions and narrows this diversity gap, while increasing the representation of underrepresented personas can shift which perspectives emerge without necessarily increasing overall diversity. Second, we conduct a pre-registered experiment with 221 participants across nine discussion threads, comparing human-only conversations with those involving generic or persona-conditioned AI agents. We find that AI participation increases responsiveness, reduces unanswered contributions, and broadens the range of ideas expressed by human participants, even though the AI agents themselves do not fully reproduce human conversational diversity. These findings suggest that the value of hybrid human-AI conversations lies not simply in the content AI agents generate, but also in their potential to stimulate more responsive and diverse interactions among humans.
Computation and Language.comment: Ishita Chakraborty and Xingjian You contributed equally

Computation and Language.title: NOLLI: A Difficulty-Calibrated English-Korean Puzzle Benchmark
Computation and Language.summary: We introduce NOLLI, a procedurally generated, difficulty-calibrated English-Korean puzzle benchmark with 15 puzzle types (25 tasks; 7,500 items). Each instance is seed-regenerable, has a verified unique solution, and is scored deterministically. We calibrate difficulty behaviorally by tuning generator parameters to target accuracy bands on a reference model. NOLLI has three task families: matched direct translations, script adaptations over Hangul jamo (sub-syllabic letters), and Korean-only cultural or orthographic tasks. We evaluate 15 frontier, open-weight, and Korean-developed models; gap analyses use the 12 above a 3% overall-accuracy floor. On matched direct translations, English and Korean accuracy is equivalent within a prespecified $\pm 10$ percentage-point margin. Script adaptations behave differently: Korean Cipher trails English by up to 68.7 percentage points, while Cryptarithmetic over the same jamo shows no systematic Korean penalty, and Jamo Composition strongly correlates with Korean Cipher performance. Korean-only tasks are also heterogeneous: rule-application performance varies across models, while Kinship remains below each non-floor model's Korean direct-task baseline. Finally, structural size does not increase from Easy to Hard in 7 of 15 types, showing that size alone is an unreliable proxy for empirical difficulty.

Computation and Language.title: HumblePRM: Improving VLM Abstention in Ambiguous Situations through Process Reward Modeling
Computation and Language.summary: Reliable deployment of Vision Language Models (VLMs) requires that a model's expressed confidence remain grounded in what it can actually see, and that it recognize when the visual evidence is too ambiguous to commit to a confident response. Standard post-training uses outcome reward models (ORMs) that supervise only the final decision, rewarding a confident answer regardless of whether the image supports one, while existing methods either tend to detect uncertainty post-hoc or assume an objective verdict always exists. We instead split multimodal reasoning into two stages: perception, where the model must factually describe the scene, and calibration, where it must judge whether that evidence is sufficient to commit to a conclusion. We introduce HumblePRM, a lightweight process reward model (PRM) that scores each stage independently, rewarding agreement between evidence and expressed confidence rather than outcome correctness alone. Training with HumblePRM increases abstention due to uncertainty on ambiguous inputs considerably while leaving accuracy on clear images roughly unchanged. We also find that the improvement transfers to Gemma 4 E4B, a larger, popular edge model. Our findings show that process reward supervision is a promising route to VLMs with better calibrated abstention, ensuring more reliability rather than unpredictable behavior.

Computation and Language.title: Do Language Models Need a Trainable Input Embedding Table? Fixed Minimal Token Codes at 1.7B-Class Scale
Computation and Language.summary: A token must be identifiable before a language model can learn how to use it. Must its input coordinates also be learned? We replace the trainable input table of a decoder-only Transformer with a predetermined 16-bit identifier for each of 49,152 tokens. Repetition lifts the code to width 2048 without a learned projection. We train five models from scratch to 100B prediction targets each: a learned-input control and four fixed-input variants using canonical codes, an invertible recoding, an extra Transformer block, or row-normalized codes. At the endpoint, the four fixed-input models attain 51.44-53.34% HellaSwag normalized accuracy, 70.46-71.49% PIQA accuracy, and 42.29-44.52% LAMBADA accuracy. The normalized model attains the upper endpoint on all three; the learned control scores 57.79%, 72.69%, and 47.72%, respectively. At unchanged depth and parameter count, the normalized model's LAMBADA advantage over canonical codes is 1.80 percentage points at 48.44B targets and 1.77 points at 100B. A complementary smaller-scale study observes successful fixed-code learning across three training seeds per interface. At matched backbone depth, the compact input buffer stores 128 times fewer scalar values than the untied learned input table. The construction separates symbol identification from learned lexical coordinates and provides a working model family in which to study how shared computation builds representations from immutable inputs.

Computation and Language.title: Open-Source FUTO Keyboard Layouts and Predictive Text for a Few Endangered Languages
Computation and Language.summary: We present open-source FUTO Keyboard layouts and predictive text dictionaries for five endangered Uralic languages: Erzya, Moksha, Komi-Zyrian, Livonian, and Skolt Sami. Existing Divvun Android keyboard layouts are converted automatically into the YAML format used by FUTO Keyboard. For predictive text, we construct weighted AOSP dictionaries using translated Finnish lemma frequencies together with morphological frequencies extracted from small target-language corpora using finite-state transducers. This combination provides a practical way to rank inflected word forms when large monolingual corpora are unavailable. The resulting resources offer reusable mobile keyboard support for endangered Uralic languages.

Software Engineering.title: Cross-Layer Characterization and AI-Assisted Diagnosis of C-to-Rust Performance
Software Engineering.summary: Migrating C code to Rust can significantly improve software security, but understanding the performance implications of such migrations remains challenging. While Rust is often claimed to match C's performance, runtime safety checks, compiler optimizations, and hardware microarchitecture interact in ways that complicate performance diagnosis. We first conduct a systematic cross-layer characterization of 12 benchmarks comprising C implementations and their Rust counterparts. Our study reveals that runtime safety checks do not necessarily dominate performance overhead, as compiler and microarchitectural optimizations often mitigate their costs. Across 8 of the 12 benchmarks, at least one Rust implementation performs within 10% of its C counterpart or outperforms it. Motivated by these findings, we introduce FerroScope, an AI-assisted performance debugger that integrates source-level analysis, compiler optimization remarks, dynamic instruction traces, and hardware performance counters to diagnose performance differences between C and Rust. FerroScope reproduces our manual findings while providing more precise explanations in several cases, including identifying compiler optimizations inhibited by redundant bounds checks. Guided by these diagnoses, we develop an LLVM compiler pass that hoists redundant bounds checks through guarded loop versioning while preserving Rust's panic behavior. The pass enables downstream compiler optimizations, including loop unrolling and conditional-move conversion, reducing Selection Sort's overhead from 2.95x to 1.00x and improving Merge Sort from 1.43x to 0.91x relative to C. Together, our results demonstrate how cross-layer performance characterization and AI-assisted diagnosis can guide safety-preserving compiler optimizations for efficient C-to-Rust migration.

Software Engineering.title: DevEx is for Humans, AX is for Agents: Measuring Context Health in Agentic Software Work
Software Engineering.summary: Coding agents succeed or fail in the context humans give them, yet most evaluations measure only output. Drawing on developer experience research, we introduce Agent Experience (AX), an instrument that scores session transcripts on four dimensions of the CAFE(S) framework: Clarity, Actionability, Fidelity, and Efficiency; Security, a gate rather than a friction dimension, is out of scope. A rubric-guided language model rates each dimension from 1 to 5 and explains what the human could have provided. We report on three studies that tested this model. In the Stack Overflow Developer Survey, respondents reporting context problems were less likely to rate AI as very useful in all seven activities examined (12-28%). Across 882 rated agentic sessions from a pilot sample of 1,000, Actionability received the lowest ratings (59.6% of ratings at or below 3, versus 26.6% for Fidelity), and ratings were lower in longer sessions. One researcher's unblinded review of 15 randomly sampled sessions found all scores reasonable and explanations supported. In a controlled scenario, we injected context defects into one data-analysis task and ran it twelve times. Every defect condition used more tokens than the clean baseline (mean +91%), and five evaluator models flagged 50-85% of targeted dimensions and 14-36% of non-targeted dimensions. Fidelity defects were detected most consistently and Actionability defects least. Because interventions were imperfectly isolated, these results are exploratory. AX gives teams structured, actionable evidence about context-related friction that complements output and outcome measures.

Software Engineering.title: Designing an Integrated Learning Ecosystem for Introductory Python Programming: Scaffolded Problem Solving, Tablet-Inspired Navigation, and AI-Enhanced Instruction
Software Engineering.summary: Introductory programming requires students to represent problems, develop and test programs, debug errors, and apply computational ideas in new contexts. In this paper, we present an artifact-centered design analysis of an integrated learning ecosystem developed for a 16-lab introductory Python course. The analyzed corpus comprises 18 instructional artifacts: the course syllabus, a tablet-inspired homepage, and Labs 1-16. We examined course navigation, problem representation, scaffolding, independent transfer, application development, debugging, AI integration, and assessment. All 15 scaffolded labs shared seven elements: input-processing-output (IPO) reasoning, instructor-guided programming, an independent task, a Google Colab/Gradio extension, debugging support, a task checklist, and submission requirements. Lab 16 departed from this structure as an integrative Pygame-based Hallmark Assignment. The analysis identifies four connected design features: a navigation layer that coordinates multiple tools; two forms of transfer, from guided to independent problems and from console programs to interactive interfaces; distinct roles for instructor-side AI-enhanced communication and student-side AI assistance; and a transition from repeated scaffolds to integrative problem solving. The case also identifies unresolved tensions involving tool fragmentation, accessibility, interface distraction, student authorship, and overreliance on AI. Because student learning outcomes were not examined, we make no claims about instructional effectiveness. Instead, the paper offers a transparent design precedent and identifies priorities for future empirical evaluation. Demo - https://xinxingwu-uk.github.io/COS107_Demo/Homepage/index.html Source codes - https://github.com/xinxingwu-uk/Course_Integrated_Learning_Ecosystem
Software Engineering.comment: 13 pages, 3 figures, 2 tables

Software Engineering.title: The Illusion of Safety: Multi-Tier Verification of AI vs. Human C++ Code
Software Engineering.summary: As large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed for systems programming, their ability to generate secure C++ code remains a critical concern. Yet most security evaluations of AI-generated code rely on static analysis alone, which flags warnings without confirming runtime violations or reasoning about untested paths. This study investigates whether C++ code generated by open-weight LLMs is measurably less safe than human-written code, and whether common verification tools agree on the risk. We introduce VULBENCH-CPP, a benchmark of 8,918 C++ programs from three open-weight LLMs (Gemma 3 27B IT, LLaMA 3.3 70B Instruct, Qwen 2.5 Coder 32B Instruct) and human authors across 851 competitive-programming tasks. Each program is annotated by four verification tiers: functional testing, static analysis (cppcheck, clang-tidy), dynamic analysis (ASan/UBSan), and bounded model checking (ESBMC). Under static analysis the two look equally safe, but this is misleading. Accounting for the correlation among solutions to a shared task, we find that code from these models is roughly twice as likely as human code to trigger a confirmed runtime violation, even after controlling for code length and test pass-rate. Furthermore, bounded model checking disagrees with the sanitizers in direc- tion, flagging human code more often among the programs it can decide. The overall results suggest that different verification tiers flag different programs, and no single tier is sufficient. We release the benchmark, harness, and annotated results

Software Engineering.title: GhostAPI-V: Evaluating Audited Diagnostics for Internal API Migration Repair
Software Engineering.summary: API migrations require callers to adopt target-version usages while removing incompatible legacy usages. GhostAPI-V represents these obligations as human-audited temporal contracts and supplies candidate-specific repair diagnostics, with correctness assessed by independent behavioral tests. We evaluate 48 internal migrations from eight Python repositories using Claude Code and Codex, with two initial runs per agent and task. Five revision arms branch from the same 192 initial candidates, controlling generation budget, version evidence, and development-test feedback. Hidden-test success is 120/192 (62.5%) for raw version-difference feedback, 130/192 (67.7%) for required-only contracts, and 148/192 (77.1%) for full bidirectional contracts. Full feedback improves over raw version-difference feedback and required-only feedback by 14.6 and 9.4 percentage points, respectively. The package-level effect is positive in all eight repositories and survives the reported repository sensitivity analyses; the forbidden increment is analysis-sensitive. Postfreeze challenges expose symbolic-behavioral disagreement. The results support the complete audited package beyond the same raw evidence and test failures, while leaving human interpretation, obligation wording, and checking entangled.

Software Engineering.title: Building a Unified Inline Code Editing Model for GitHub Copilot
Software Engineering.summary: AI-assisted coding ranges from fully agentic coding to inline code suggestions in the editor. Inline suggestions require predicting a developer's most likely next edit from an editing session. The next edit may lie at the cursor, in nearby lines, or farther away, and one editing intent can span several of these. The preceding system queries separate completion, nearby edit, and long-distance edit models, each with its own output format, in a fixed sequence; it thus cannot express intents spanning distant locations in one response, can require several sequential model calls per suggestion, and prioritizes completion even when a correction would serve better. We present a unified model that predicts all three edit types in one output space: a sequence of anchored diff patches specifying locations, deleted lines, and added lines. This representation permits multiple edits per response, so the client can serve later edits from a cache without further model calls. We train this model in two phases, first unifying next edit and long-distance edit prediction, then adding code completion. We synthesize multi-edit supervision from single-edit data via model pseudolabeling and edit history playback. We use a binary LLM-graded reward, a patch validity taxonomy shared by data filtering, reward, and evaluation, and grader boosting for targeted failure modes. Phase 2 also adapts how the client processes and presents model outputs. In controlled online A/B experiments in GitHub Copilot, Phase 1 significantly reduces time to display by 6.77% and output tokens by 58.93% relative to the three-model baseline. In Phase 2, the 3-in-1 model and client adaptations reduce dismissed suggestions per user by 10.06% relative to the 2-in-1 model paired with the completion model. Throughout this report, we also share our methodology and learnings in evaluation, training, and end-to-end model and system design.
Software Engineering.comment: 67 pages, 31 figures, 21 tables

Software Engineering.title: PORTA: Systematic Discovery of Vulnerabilities in Identity Brokers
Software Engineering.summary: Identity brokers such as Keycloak, Vault, and Dex translate authentication proofs from an upstream identity provider into sessions for downstream services. Due to their central role in authentication and trust mediation, a single vulnerability in a broker compromises every downstream service behind it. In fact, recent incidents have demonstrated that even widely adopted platforms are not immune to such issues, highlighting the critical need for systematic analysis. To build such an analysis, this work first defines invariants for broker operation. These invariants are not completely covered by existing authentication specifications, primarily because brokers are unique in their duality, i.e., acting simultaneously as a relying party and an identity provider. The invariants capture the properties that identity brokers must uphold throughout their workflows, as all 60 previous CVEs we consider violate at least one invariant. Within these workflows, we further define high-level action categories. Equipped with this information, our automated tool PORTA leverages a large language model (LLM) to generate API invocation sequences corresponding to the high-level action categories, and oracle assertions aligned with the specified invariants. PORTA identifies 33 previously unreported security vulnerabilities in seven popular open-source brokers. We study these novel vulnerabilities and trace them to eight recurring patterns. We responsibly disclosed all discovered vulnerabilities: 29 have been confirmed, 14 patched, and 19 assigned CVE numbers, with 10 CVEs rated as critical.
Software Engineering.comment: In Proceedings of the 2026 ACM SIGSAC Conference on Computer and Communications Security CCS26

Software Engineering.title: SpecEngineeringBench: Evaluating Coding Agents as Autonomous Specification Engineers
Software Engineering.summary: Autonomous specification engineering requires coding agents to translate functional requirements into executable tests and use the results to discover and validate defects. However, existing benchmarks evaluate coding agents on explicitly specified test generation tasks, commonly providing an issue description, a designated test entry point, or files to inspect, leaving the ability to determine what to test and where to investigate insufficiently evaluated. Relying on such clues bypasses the challenge of mapping requirements to implementations and proactively uncovering unknown defects. We propose SpecEngineeringBench, comprising 100 instances from 78 open-source Python repositories across 16 application categories, with multiple recorded defects in each instance. Two independent tasks evaluate complementary capabilities: generating test suites and discovering defects through execution analysis. The evaluation combines test validity, defect detection, and coverage with localization precision and recall. Across seven frontier coding agents, results reveal that test validity and coverage decouple from defect exposure: agents achieve a 91.47% Head Pass Rate and 80.48% Change-focused Coverage alongside a 26.36% Fail-to-Pass Rate, while localization recall drops from 78.11% at the file level to 51.29% at the function level. Autonomous test generation improves file, function, and hunk localization recall by 4.99, 2.77, and 2.69 percentage points over relying solely on existing repository test suites.
Software Engineering.comment: 31 pages, 3figures

Software Engineering.title: ShellBench: What Matters More for AI Agents, Models, or Harness for Everyday Tasks
Software Engineering.summary: The use of AI agents among the general public has been increasing exponentially throughout 2026, though it is often hard for users to determine which configuration is most effective for their personal use. To help provide clarity here we introduce ShellBench, 100 day-to-day tasks based on more than 10 million user requests, each set in a realistic workspace with messy files and competing data sources, and graded for both correctness and safety. We evaluate 12 models across 5 agent harnesses at 3 reasoning levels for a total of 53,100 rollouts, 20% of which are on tasks designated for public release. We find that model choice impacts performance more than harness choice, but the three leading models differ by only 1.1 percentage points. GPT-6.1 Sol passed 61.4% of attempts at about one-sixth of GPT-6 Astra's estimated token cost per attempt, while GPT-6 Astra led at 62.5%. We also found that harness choice had little effect on either performance or safety with all harnesses scoring between 42.9 (Claude Code) and 45.2 (OpenClaw) for pass@1.
Software Engineering.comment: 17 pages, 9 figures, 10 tables

Software Engineering.title: How Use Case Tables Enable the Elicitation of Explanation Needs
Software Engineering.summary: [Context and motivation] While software systems get more integrated into people's daily lives - like driver-assistance systems or smart-home applications - they are also becoming increasingly complex. When complex software is used, needs for explanations may arise. At present, explanation needs are usually elicited through the testing of prototypes or existing software. However, detailed documentation of software interactions, such as use case tables, might be a suitable alternative. Since use cases provide early insights into the key interactions within the system, they are appealing to employ as resources for explanation needs. [Question/problem] As of now, it remains unclear whether use cases allow the elicitation of explanation needs. Or, from a different perspective, whether their utilization for this purpose is desirable. [Principal ideas/results] We conducted a study in which users perused the description sections of use cases extracted from existing software. While reading through these use cases, they reported any explanation needs they encountered. Our findings indicate that use case steps are sufficient to induce explanation needs in the participants as they read the steps. [Contribution] This paper explores the novel idea of utilizing use cases for the elicitation of explanation needs and reports on a study that provides insights into the applicability of this concept with stakeholders.
Software Engineering.comment: Submitted to the REFSQ'27 conference. Awaiting reviews

Software Engineering.title: PRAXIS: Graph-Grounded Tacit Knowledge for Domain Coding Agent
Software Engineering.summary: LLM agents have achieved strong performance on general software engineering tasks, yet struggle with domain-specific code generation. We identify the root cause as the agent's lack of tacit knowledge, including domain-specific business rules, interface contracts, and operational conventions that developers internalize through practice but never document. This knowledge is deeply buried beneath the domain code, dispersed across code entities and their dependency relations, and invisible to the agent that lacks it. These properties make tacit knowledge inherently difficult to retrieve or learn. In this work, we propose PRAXIS, a framework that enables agents to systematically extract, represent, and reuse tacit knowledge for domain code generation. PRAXIS acquires tacit knowledge by simulating human development workflows within the target codebase, distills it into structured units organized on the code dependency graph, and proactively surfaces it to the agent at the point of code interaction. Extensive experiments demonstrate that PRAXIS outperforms state-of-the-art agents equipped with powerful agentic search capabilities, as well as experience-based and skill-based methods. The approach integrates seamlessly into various agent frameworks and LLMs with consistent performance improvements, and supports continual evolution with performance steadily scaling as practice accumulates.
Software Engineering.comment: Accepted by ICSE 2027

Software Engineering.title: Energy as a Service-Level Objective: Transaction-Level Energy Attribution
Software Engineering.summary: Service engineers assess every change against functional requirements and qualities such as reliability, performance and availability. Energy is rarely part of this assessment. When consumption rises after a change, the team cannot tell whether the increase is worth investigating, worth accepting, or neither. A change to tracing, retries or a shared component can affect consumption far beyond the modified component. This thesis asks how energy objectives can become actionable engineering instruments rather than reporting metrics. Site Reliability Engineering (SRE) answered a similar question for reliability with service-level indicators, objectives and response policies. We take SRE as the guiding research vision and study where the analogy holds for energy and where it breaks. An energy objective could, for example, bound the energy per successful transaction under stated workload conditions. The thesis connects three threads into one experimentally evaluated methodology. Useful-work semantics define what a successful transaction is. Energy attribution assigns shared and auxiliary consumption to transactions. Service-level engineering decisions act on the resulting energy objectives. Existing work covers attribution methods, measurement frameworks and sustainability objectives, mostly at component level and without a link to decisions. Our prior work on service-level energy modeling showed that the energy of auxiliary services is often overlooked and hard to measure. Planned experiments compare aggregate, request-normalized and useful-work-based indicators under controlled changes to observability configuration and injected failures. Whether transaction-level attribution is needed for these decisions, or whether service-level attribution with outcome counts is sufficient, is an open question the experiments are designed to answer.
Software Engineering.comment: Accepted at ICSOC26 in the PhD Symposium Track

Software Engineering.title: AI-Generated Code Issues: A Taxonomy from Repository Histories, AI Conversations, and Developer Interviews
Software Engineering.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to generate source code, yet the quality issues in such code remain only partially understood. Understanding these issues can help developers adapt quality assurance practices, such as code review and testing, to better detect problems that may be more common in AI-generated than in human-written code. We study how quality issues in AI-generated code manifest in real software development activities through a mixed-method empirical study that draws on evidence from three complementary sources. First, we mine GitHub commits whose messages explicitly attribute a fix to a problem in AI-generated code, and we manually inspect the 914 matched commits to remove false positives and classify the quality issue being corrected. Second, we collect developers' shared conversations with AI tools, identify conversations including source code and textual signals of model mistakes, and manually analyze 299 of them to classify the underlying quality issue. Third, we interview 20 practitioners and researchers who use AI coding tools to enrich and validate the obtained catalog of quality issues. From these analyses, we derive a taxonomy of 87 types of developer-attributed quality issues in AI-generated code, going beyond functional bugs. Our findings contribute an empirically grounded taxonomy and implications for the design and evaluation of AI coding assistants and agents.
Software Engineering.comment: Accepted for publication at ICSE 2027

Software Engineering.title: The Elephant-Goldfish Model for software design review: what a fresh reviewer can see
Software Engineering.summary: A design can be easy to understand and still specify the wrong system. Google's Elephant-Goldfish Model asks fresh agents to review a design without the conversation that produced it. We examined how this choice affects detection of omissions, agreement violations and internal defects. We seeded nine defects in each of 47 public software design documents and supplied each with a scripted drafting conversation. A fresh reviewer given the conversation as its own earlier exchange detected 94.8% of omitted-decision instances, compared with 62.4% for the same model given the document alone. It detected 98.3% of violations of conversation-only requirements. On document-visible defects, recall was 87.5% with the conversation and 88.4% without it, equivalent within a prespecified 15-percentage-point margin. Three model judges scored detection and were calibrated on constructed controls. In document-only runs, the plugin's five-stage review took a geometric mean of 9.03 minutes against 1.81 for one reviewer. Its estimated recall was lower under both judging procedures, with a difference distinguishable from zero under one. A later generic-prompt comparison gave a similar result. The experiment separates two objectives for automated design review: testing whether a new reader can reconstruct the design and checking whether the design preserves the decisions that govern implementation.
Software Engineering.comment: 12 pages, 1 figure. Review protocols, data and reproduction scripts are included as ancillary files

Software Engineering.title: Generating Property-Based Regression Tests from Source Code Semantics
Software Engineering.summary: Conventional unit tests (CUTs) check a method under test at fixed concrete inputs. A test can therefore miss a regression if its input produces the expected output despite a fault. Property-based testing (PBT) checks universally quantified specifications across many randomly generated inputs, but writing properties and input generators by hand is difficult. Existing approaches automate PBT creation by generalizing an existing or generated unit test suite. They either over-approximate concrete inputs across repetitive tests or apply single-path symbolic analysis along concrete test runs. This paper presents an approach that derives property-based regression tests directly from source code semantics via multipath symbolic execution (SE). For each explored path through a target method, the approach records a path semantics comprising the path condition, the symbolic return value, and the state change map. Each path semantics induces a Hoare triple that compiles into an executable property. Because SE leaves parts of a class unspecified, the approach complements the generated properties with search-based CUTs for the whole class. We evaluate our Java implementation against EvoSuite and the test generalization tool Teralizer on EqBench and on 11 projects from TOGBench. On EqBench, our approach keeps validated properties for 82.0% of all methods. Its mean mutation score of 63.8% exceeds the 55.2% of EvoSuite and the 60.3% of Teralizer. On TOGBench, target selection, SE limitations, and property validation restrict validated properties to 2.8% of all methods. The resulting mean mutation score of 48.6% falls below the 50.9% of EvoSuite and the 51.1% of Teralizer. Failures during test generation leave a few classes without effective tests and lead to this gap.
Software Engineering.comment: 12 pages

Software Engineering.title: VISE: Verifier-Independent Skill Self-Evolution with Feedback from Tool Implementations
Software Engineering.summary: Agent skills provide reusable workflows that guide LLM agents in using tools. Refining these workflows requires feedback on missing or incorrect instructions, but task-specific verifiers are not always available. We propose VISE (Verifier-Independent Skill Evolution), a scripts-first approach that uses tool implementations to guide skill revision. It extracts tool capabilities, input requirements, usage conditions, and output formats from source code. Using the task request and execution trace, it compares this information with current workflow instructions to identify missing or conflicting steps. It then recommends specific edits to SKILL.md, linking each change to the relevant implementation and usage conditions. We evaluate VISE as an additional revision stage for four evolution methods on SkillsBench and SkillLearnBench. Compared with the corresponding No-verifier conditions, it improves overall average task success by 9.14-13.35 percentage points. The proportion of tasks solved in all three runs increases by 12.36-18.29 points. A case study shows how revised instructions connect tool outputs to later steps. These results support tool implementations as a practical feedback source for skill self-evolution.
Software Engineering.comment: 23 pages, including appendices

Software Engineering.title: Does Research-Paper Context Improve LLM-Generated Quadruped Navigation? An Exploratory Simulation Study
Software Engineering.summary: Large language models can write competent robot navigation code, but not only does the research on the topic advance, a model may also, due to the volume of findings, fail to recall relevant findings and apply them to the task at hand. In this work, we test whether providing particular research papers as context improves the LLM-written navigation code for the Go2 quadruped, with the LLM (Claude Opus 5) and locomotion policy frozen. Specifically, we compare the navigation controllers the LLM writes when provided with and without particular papers across three settings: behavior trees, navigators edited from a shared base, and controllers written from scratch. When a maze's shortest route is blocked mid-episode, 2 of 8 controllers written with the context of an incremental-replanning paper complete all four trips under Isaac Sim physics, against 7 of 8 without it (two-sided Fisher's exact test, p = 0.041). This difference appears only under physics: in an idealized kinematic simulator, the controllers written with and without the paper are indistinguishable. We hypothesize that an LLM provided research papers as context tends to overweight both their content and their goals -- in this case, the efficiency of incremental replanning -- negatively affecting the fulfillment of the main task and leading to less robust code.
Software Engineering.comment: 10 pages, 4 figures, 6 tables

Software Engineering.title: Validating Multi-Model AI-Generated Acceptance Criteria in Requirements Engineering
Software Engineering.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in software engineering to generate artifacts such as requirements, user stories, acceptance criteria, documentation, and code. Their use in requirements engineering raises important questions about correctness, traceability, and hallucination, especially because flawed specifications can affect later design, implementation, and verification activities. While much recent work on AI-assisted software engineering has focused on code generation and code-level validation, the validation of AI-generated specifications has received less attention. This paper addresses this gap by presenting a validation-oriented approach for AI-generated acceptance criteria. The approach combines retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), multi-model generation, and an explicitly structured human-in-the-loop workflow. We describe a working prototype that allows users to prepare or enter user stories, generate acceptance criteria using several LLMs, optionally augment generation with retrieved requirements-related examples, compare outputs side by side, inspect retrieved context, and select, edit, or regenerate candidate criteria before explicitly submitting a reviewer-finalized version. The system also records model outputs, user interventions, retrieval settings, and final criteria as part of a logged decision process. Rather than claiming that generation accuracy is already improved, the contribution of this work is to operationalize validation as an explicit, inspectable, and accountable process for AI-generated requirements artifacts.
Software Engineering.comment: Accepted for publication in the proceedings of VeriFAI 2026, Springer Lecture Notes in Computer Science (LNCS). Official publication forthcoming

Software Engineering.title: LITMUS - Literature Informed Testbed for Mapping Usecases and Synthesizing Risk-Cards
Software Engineering.summary: The proliferation of large language models (LLMs) and Artificial Intelligence (AI) in real-world applications has heightened the need for systematic, safety-oriented deployment frameworks. Existing approaches typically prioritize the construction of datasets and risk cards around the LLM and AI architecture itself, yet they provide scant consideration for the specific use-case that drives model selection. This omission is problematic because any practical AI deployment begins with a detailed use-case description that informs the assessment of contextual hazards. In this paper, we introduce a structured pipeline that, given a use-case, automatically produces a tailored dataset and an accompanying risk card. The process ensures that identified risks are tightly coupled to the use-case, and it offers traceable evidence from peer-reviewed literature to substantiate each risk to use-case relationship. Prior claim-verification methods (FActScore, FactReasoner) have been validated for factual claims. Risk-relevance is a hypothetical claim about possible harm, and whether evidence retrieval can meaningfully assess such claims remains untested. Literature-Informed Testbed for Mapping Use-cases and Synthesizing (LITMUS) risk cards are the first systematic attempt to characterize this adaptation. We evaluated the pipeline using the MIT Risk Taxonomy and achieved a 0.91 F1-score with a list of 320 samples from the benchmark risk dataset that was considered. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in generating robust, evidence-based risk assessments for LLM deployments.

Software Engineering.title: Web Fuzzing Commons, Dataset, Guidelines and Evaluations to Support Experimentation in REST API Fuzzing
Software Engineering.summary:
Fuzzing REST APIs is an important research problem, with practical applications and impact in industry. As such, lot of research work has been carried out on this topic in the last few years. However, there are three major issues that hinder further progress: (1) how to deal with API authentication; (2) how to catalog and compare different fault types found by different fuzzers; (3) what to use as case study to facilitate fair comparisons among fuzzers.
  In this paper, to address these important challenges, we present Web Fuzzing Commons (WFC), Web Fuzzing Dataset (WFD) and Web Fuzzing Evaluations (WFE). WFC is a set of open-source libraries and schema definitions to declaratively specify authentication info and catalog different types of faults that fuzzers can automatically detect. WFD is a collection of 56 open-source APIs, configured to run with Docker-Compose, supported by WFC. WFE provides scaffolding scripts to automatically run experiments and collecting/analysing their results, employing different REST API fuzzers configured via Docker, using WFD as case study.
  This is a community driven work, currently stewarded by the authors of the most popular open-source REST API fuzzers, including CATS, EvoMaster, Schemathesis and WuppieFuzz. To show the usefulness of WFC/WFD/WFE, a set of experiments is carried out with these fuzzers on WFD, using WFE. In our empirical analyses, we also include other state-of-the-art fuzzers such as ARAT-RL, EmRest, LLamaRestTest, and RESTler.
  We also discuss common pitfalls in tool comparisons, as well as providing guidelines with support of WFC/WFD to avoid them.

Software Engineering.title: Real Package, Wrong Controller: Static Auditing of Vendor--Protocol Mismatches in LLM-Generated PLC Code
Software Engineering.summary: Language models can generate Python that drives industrial protocols on programmable logic controllers, yet existing code-grounding checks ask whether an imported package or symbol exists rather than whether it suits the declared industrial target. We define \emph{metadata-conditioned, import-level vendor--protocol incompatibility} and build \textsc{Proteus-OT}, a label-free static verifier over a version-pinned graph of documented bindings. Across 883 generated scripts, 180 carry an import-level mismatch against the declared target (20.4\%); restricting to single-vendor targets gives 16.3\%, and additionally requiring the offending library to reach a protocol communication call gives 14.2\%, which we read as conditional on the corpus metadata rather than on verified intent. None of the 28 adjudicable human control files carries one, a sample too small to estimate a prevalence. Within the balanced subset, 96.6\% of mismatching scripts import packages and call methods that exist, so an existence baseline does not represent them, and every positive ships with an inspectable witness. We also audit machine-versus-human classification on the same corpus, where character $n$-grams reach macro-F1 1.000 under task, model and vendor-disjoint partitions and survive comment removal, an AST round trip and identifier anonymisation. The trailing newline present in 95.2\% of human files and in none of the generated ones separates the classes on its own. Vendor--protocol consistency is a useful static audit target, whereas provenance classification on repository-labelled corpora is not authorship detection.

Software Engineering.title: SCOPE: Evaluating and Enhancing Permission Explanation Transparency in Mobile Apps
Software Engineering.summary: Permission explanations, explanatory text accompanying mobile app permission requests, are crucial for user privacy transparency and informed consent. Despite their importance, current practices often fall short of regulatory expectations due to the lack of systematic evaluation mechanisms. Through an empirical study of 600 mainstream mobile apps, we reveal widespread deficiencies: 15\% of permission requests provide no explanation, others use vague language or technical jargon, and critically, many fail to disclose third-party SDK data access despite these components actively using granted permissions. To address these transparency gaps, we present SCOPE, an automated multi-agent framework that systematically evaluates permission explanation compliance and generates targeted optimization recommendations. SCOPE employs four specialized agents working collaboratively: multimodal LLM-based explanation extraction, few-shot learning-based linguistic analysis, dynamic API-based purpose inference, and adaptive report generation. Comprehensive evaluation demonstrates SCOPE's effectiveness, achieving 98\% accuracy in explanation extraction, 93.5\% consistency in compliance analysis, and 92\% accuracy in purpose inference. A user study with 30 participants shows 84.6\% preference for SCOPE-optimized explanations, confirming practical utility. Our work provides the first systematic analysis of permission explanation practices and establishes a scalable solution for enhancing mobile app privacy transparency.

Software Engineering.title: DeepAVR: Deep Analysis via Multi-Agent Collaboration for Automated Vulnerability Repair
Software Engineering.summary: Automated Vulnerability Repair (AVR) has emerged as a promising approach to identifying and fixing software vulnerabilities autonomously. Early LLM-based approaches focused on patch generation under the assumption of perfect fault localization, while recent end-to-end methods attempt to repair vulnerabilities directly from sanitizer logs. However, these methods often fail when the root cause is deeply hidden, either physically distant from the crash site or logically masked by interdependent errors, making the initial report insufficient. We propose DeepAVR, a multi-agent framework that transforms intermediate repair outcomes into structured diagnostic feedback. It coordinates specialized agents for fault localization, patch generation, compilation, security and functionality validation, and patch review to iteratively refine localization and patch hypotheses. Specifically, DeepAVR introduces patch-conditioned re-localization, using execution results from intermediate patches to uncover hidden root causes, and root-cause-oriented patch review to identify symptom-level fixes and incomplete repairs that escape execution-based validation. Evaluation on VulnLoc, a real-world C/C++ vulnerability repair dataset, shows that DeepAVR outperforms prior methods, generating correct patches for 92.3% of vulnerabilities. Evaluation on SAN2VULN demonstrates its ability to repair vulnerabilities unseen during training. On SEC-bench, DeepAVR outperforms the evaluated baselines on cases whose fixes lie outside the crash-site function.
Software Engineering.comment: 29 pages, 12 figures, 7 tables. Code is available at https://github.com/rimwoohan/DeepAVR

Software Engineering.title: Automated Smoke Testing for Multi-ending Game Quests via Large Language Models
Software Engineering.summary: Modern game quests are increasingly trending toward high freedom and multiple endings, making their design and testing more complex. Smoke testing in games aims to rapidly validate quest functionality, but existing automated testing approaches face critical limitations when handling quests with branching narratives, and multiple possible endings. These challenges result in insufficient exploration of endings, redundant action sequences, and prohibitively high interaction costs. To address these challenges, we propose EndWeaver, an automated smoke testing framework specifically designed for multi-ending game tasks. EndWeaver leverages LLMs to interpret quest descriptions and game environments, generating high-level methods to guide global exploration, complemented by the generated primitive task sequences for fine-grained planning. By combining this multi-level planning structure with the dynamic construction of state-transition graphs, EndWeaver ensures comprehensive coverage of all possible endings and enables efficient testing. We evaluated EndWeaver on four game environments---Mini RPG, Overcooked Plus, Minecraft, and PySC2 against baseline methods. In all environments, EndWeaver achieved stable quest completion with high reliability, significantly outperforming the baselines. In terms of testing cost, EndWeaver required only a few thousand steps, while baseline methods required millions of steps, all while ensuring comprehensive coverage of all possible quest endings. Ablation studies further demonstrated the critical contributions of each framework component, validating the effectiveness and robustness of our approach.
